11726-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for 5 July 1890 opens with Week by Week on the House of Commons. Careful observers note disturbance there over three weeks. One politician hints darkly at cave-men, or troglodytes, dwelling in barrows.

Weather notes follow in mock science, dividing hat nap by costermonger buttons. Aspirates picked up in the Old Kent Road on a Saturday afternoon are added to the sum. A later scene brings Druriolanus Operaticus at the wings, with a nervous stage manager's assistant nearby. The curtain rises a little way, falls again, and rises suddenly. The issue turns Parliament, weather, and theatre into elaborate jokes.
11907-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's July 12, 1890 issue, volume 99, opens its Voces Populi column at the Military Exhibition, in the avenue facing the arena, with an unreasonable visitor as its comic target. The weekly's illustrated jokes and verses follow the familiar Punch pattern: overheard speech, social satire, and topical cartoons.

Set in the high Victorian summer, the number looks back to an age of exhibitions, military display. Confident empire, before the wars and crises of the next decades. Its humor depends on voices: the things people actually say at shows and in streets, sharpened just enough to make a reader recognize himself and laugh.
11919-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's July 19, 1890 issue opens its Booking-Office column with a parallel: Joe, the Fat Boy in Pickwick, startles an older reader, a joke that assumes a public steeped in Dickens. Verses, cartoons, and comic prose follow in the weekly's high Victorian manner.

A love lyric plays on changed perceptions, where penguins are weasels, cheap things dear. Jumps but measles when the beloved is near, while a dialect sketch describes a collection of smiling beauties and a bridesmaid whose look went right through a young man's heart. The number shows Punch at its most literary and most playful, trusting readers to catch allusions and enjoy nonsense in equal measure.
12262-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for September 27, 1890, volume ninety-nine, opens with Modern Types, a series by Mr. Punch own type writer. Number nineteen profiles the Servant of Society, a man who has abdicated independent thought to live as an appendage in great houses.

The sketch mocks the professional tuft-hunter, who attaches himself to the skirts and coat-tails of the great and mistakes proximity for rank. Other items in the number follow the usual Punch mix of verse, cartoons, and short jokes on London life. The issue captures late Victorian satire at its most social: less concerned with party politics than with the manners and climbers of fashionable society.
12292-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for July 26, 1890, volume ninety-nine, continues the Modern Types series by Mr. Punch own type writer. Number sixteen profiles the Hurlingham Girl, whose spirits run higher than her aspirations.

The sketch says her aspirations, if they ever existed, have been recklessly puffed into space, leaving a young woman of fashion, sport, and small talk. Other items in the number cover parish charity, with notes on poor rates and self-sacrificing women relieving parishes of an incubus of four hundred. The issue shows Punch social satire at full stretch: amused by new women, sharp on institutions, and confident that types can explain a whole age.
12305-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for August 16, 1890, volume ninety-nine, continues Modern Types with number seventeen, The Spurious Sportsman. The sketch describes men who aspire perpetually toward something higher than their actual selves, in sport as in society.

The point is that society admits by birth or wealth without effort, while sport, properly understood, demands achievement before admission. Other items include Mrs. Jeune appeal for pecuniary help to continue excellent holiday work for poor children. The number balances satire with sentiment: mocking pretenders while praising charity. It captures Punch in holiday time, when London empties for the country and the paper turns to types.
12306-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for October 4, 1890, volume ninety-nine, announces Mr. Punch Prize Novels, a new series of parodies. The announcement calls the age an age of prizes, noting acrostic solvers, hard-case expounders, doll-dressers, and epigram makers who have all had their turn.

The number then offers prize-novel burlesques, mocking the fashions of popular fiction with verse on calomel, castor oil, and infusions that have taken wings. Punch parody works by exaggeration: it takes a famous style and pushes it until it collapses. The issue shows the weekly at its most literary, trusting readers to know the novels it teases. For modern readers, the jokes double as a guide to what Victorians actually read.
12323-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for August 2, 1890, volume ninety-nine, opens with a Highland scene. An ill-used husband under a bed defies his wife, saying she may crack and thrash him but cannot break his manly spirit. The cartoon sets the tone for a number of domestic satire.

Punch to the Second Battalion asks who will guard the Guards, as the battalion sails for Bermuda amid talk of rebellion. The verse quotes Juvenal on guarding the guards themselves. Other items mock French opera heroes blubbering on matronly bosoms. The issue shows Punch mixing barrack humor, marital farce, and literary parody. It is a typical summer number, light in subject but sharp in execution.
12378-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's 30 August 1890 number opens with a mock letter asking why not live out of London. The writer proves, in comic figures, that it is cheaper for wife and family to live in the country while he keeps a club room in town. One theatre ticket, he notes, costs less than four. The joke turns on the breadwinner's self-interest dressed as household economy.

Other cartoons, verses and squibs follow the weekly pattern, lampooning London life, politics and fashion. The issue shows Punch at its most domestic, finding satire in marriage, money and the daily train. For readers now, its charm lies in that small-scale comedy, a Victorian city laughing at its own habits.
12392-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for August 23, 1890, volume ninety-nine, offers Novelty Up to Date. It is a mock Scotch drama called Telmah, written to test whether the plot of The English Rose at the Adelphi had been done before. The editors note that treatment is everything, and plagiarism is the feeblest charge.

The number also follows Mr. J and his bottle-nosed, flounder-eared friends, with Talleyrand quoted on duties absorbing time. Punch parody here is self-aware: it steals openly to prove that originality lies in handling, not in plot. The issue shows the weekly literary games, trusting readers to catch theatrical references. For modern readers, it is a window onto West End tastes of 1890.
12393-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's 6 September 1890 number carries a Modern Types sketch of the undomestic daughter, written by Mr. Punch's own typewriter. Mothers expect a comfort, fathers expect cheapness, and brothers expect a slave to their triumph, the sketch jokes. The public, meanwhile, sees daughters as mild, colourless beings without desires of their own.

Daughters themselves, before marriage absorbs them, seem content with that picture, the writer adds, with a satirist's wink. Cartoons and shorter pieces around the sketch keep the weekly mix of London comment. The piece survives as a comic witness to Victorian ideas of girlhood, duty and the family home, laughed at from inside its own conventions.
12394-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for September 13, 1890, volume ninety-nine, sends its impartial and not-to-be-biased critic out for a holiday to St. Margaret Bay, between Deal and Dover. The critic had heard the bay called magnificent from the Channel, and noted Alma-Tadema made it headquarters for part of the summer.

The piece follows a ticket to Martin Mill, a desolate walk, and the discovery that fame and beauty do not always match. Verse elsewhere in the number scolds butter-churning friends and trumpet-blowing self-praise. The issue is a holiday number in tone: light, travel-minded, and gently mocking of art-world pilgrimage. It shows Punch at leisure, laughing at its own critics as well as its subjects.
12395-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's 18 October 1890 number prints a How It's Done sketch, A Handbook to Honesty, on the straight tip. In a wholesale house sanctum, a pompous principal with an imposing watch-chain scolds a sleek, nervous head of department named Scroop, who washes his hands with invisible soap in imperceptible water.

The comedy lies in business euphemism: a tip, a favour and a quiet understanding, all denied in polite language. Punch uses the dialogue form to expose how respectable firms talked around bribery. With cartoons and squibs beside it, the sketch shows the weekly at its sharpest, turning office manners into moral satire.
12466-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's 20 September 1890 number sends its impartial, not-to-be-biassed critic on holiday to Ostend, called a town of palaces. Leaving delicious Dover, the critic crosses a calm sea to the Belgian coast. Steamers, he jokes, perpetrate practical jokes: one mail-carrier started early, smashed a gangway and dropped a portmanteau into the ocean.

Holiday sketches, cartoons and squibs follow, mocking tourists, hotels and seaside manners. Punch's critic affects high impartiality while enjoying every absurdity. The issue is a light Victorian travel satire, funny on cross-Channel boats, Belgian resorts and the English abroad, and it shows the weekly's holiday mood at full stretch.
12467-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This 11 October 1890 Punch carries a Modern Types sketch of the divorcée, written by Mr. Punch's own typewriter. It opens in the divorce court of Sir James Hannen, set up to purify morals by separating ill-matched couples. With irony it notes that the new procedure still favoured the husband: a wife's infidelity counted more heavily than a husband's.

Satire, not law, is the point, as Punch turns court procedure into social comedy and tests Victorian double standards. Cartoons and shorter pieces around it keep the weekly mix. The sketch survives as a sharp, funny witness to how divorce was talked about in 1890, when the law had opened a door but left old morals standing in the frame.
12468-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's 25 October 1890 number parodies Mrs. Humphry Ward in Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, with Bob Sillimere, by Mrs. Humphry John Ward Preacher, author of Master Sisterson. A note on the manuscript claims a highly religious story. It asserts that George Eliot could not write properly about religion, and demands a thousand-pound prize for an institute to encourage new religions in St. Pancras alleys.

Chapter one opens in Oxford, where evenings, the parody insists, hold more true, inward, mystic spirit than evenings anywhere else, Cambridge offering only weak imitations. Punch thus mocks high seriousness and Oxford mystique in one stroke. The piece is literary satire at its most pointed, a weekly magazine laughing at a famous novelist's manner.
12469-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's 8 November 1890 number offers a parody novel, Mignon's Mess-Room, in its Mr. Punch's Prize Novels series. The mock author, Tom Rum Summer, claims a real, true story of soldiers and children, praises soldiers as grand, noble fellows who smoke a great deal, and charges extra for pathos. The joke targets sentimental military fiction of the day.

Soldiers of the Purple Dragoons gather in their ante-room, and the parody rolls on through nursery rhyme tags and barrack-room bluster. Around it the issue keeps Punch's usual cartoons and squibs. The piece is best enjoyed as literary satire, a weekly magazine puncturing a popular genre by doing it, lovingly, a little too well.
12517-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's 15 November 1890 number parodies Barrie in Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, with Thrums on the Auld String, by J. Muir Kirrie, author of A Door on Thumbs and Eight Bald Fiddlers. A glossary of Scotch expressions came with the story, Punch says, and was consulted as they went, though no room remains to print it.

Chapter one seats the company on a pig-sty at T'Nowhead's Farm, a seat not strictly eligible, but chosen for special reasons. The wrapper promised Arcadia Mixture, strength and aroma combined, sold in six-shilling cases. Punch mocks sentimental Scots idyll and its dialect apparatus in one affectionate stroke. The parody remains funny even for readers who never met Thrums.
12737-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This November 22, 1890 issue of Punch offers the weekly's usual blend of jokes, cartoons, and satire on London life. A cartoon mocks retired actor S. B. Bancroft for offering a thousand pounds to General Booth's relief scheme if ninety-nine others follow. A storm item jokes that a squall which broke men's ribs still showed a kind of mercy.

Other pages carry a ghostly serial tale, with men gathered in a parlour inn on a frost-bound moorland night. The mix of topical jest and story shows Punch at its late Victorian height. Readers get a lively snapshot of what amused middle-class London in 1890.
12738-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's 29 November 1890 number parodies Frenchified English fiction in Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, with Jonnie, by Dick Dody, author of Le Nabab Boffin-Newcome and other mock-French titles. Part one, Le Higlife Scolastique, opens in French, as a rector eyes with a roguish air the crumpled muzzle of pretty Madame Copperfield.

Madame wishes to place her little boy in the most distinguished school in Paris. Each child brings three vermeil covers and six dozen fine batiste shirts, and extras, port wine, beef-tea and sandwiches often exceed the fees. Punch mocks pretentious bilingual snobbery in its own French. The parody is a clever, if now obscure, joke on literary fashion.
12739-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This December 6, 1890 Punch leads with a satirical type study, The Manly Maiden, mocking a woman who apes men's bluff, sporting manners to earn the title of good fellow. The piece argues, in Punch's teasing voice, that such imitation wins neither admiration nor courtesy. Theatre notes follow, praising actors in a popular burlesque.

Arthur Williams as Zuniga and Lonnen as the spoony soldier earn special praise, with Lonnen's Bogie Man song and dance called the hit of the evening. Costumes, scenery, and graceful staging add to the fun. The issue captures Punch's double habit: social satire beside cheerful stage gossip.
12825-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This August 9, 1890 Punch opens with a comic letter from a former Yeomanry man visiting the Military Exhibition. Lame and leaning on a friend, he seeks battle pictures to study his country's glories, and his bumbling tour sets the comic tone. Later pages turn to a mock war dispatch, complete with a clock tower carried off by a land torpedo.

A president who flees to the provinces with a toothache, after raising a band of gaol desperadoes, adds to the farce. The issue shows Punch's taste for gentle military satire in peacetime. Readers get jokes, pictures, and invented news in the magazine's familiar weekly mix.
12905-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This December 13, 1890 Punch carries a prize-novel parody, The Curse of Cognac, by Water Decant. He recommends it to lower Christmas cheer and to punish mothers-in-law locked in bare rooms with a guttering candle. George Ginsling, alone in his Cambridge college rooms after his friends leave, opens the mock-gothic tale.

A later scene finds Angelina teasing Edwin about faces he made before the footlights and a dose of cod-liver oil he mistook for Scotch whiskey. The issue mixes literary parody with stage jokes. Readers get Punch's Christmas-season wit at its most mischievous.
12917-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This December 20, 1890 Punch opens with Voces Populi, a riding-class scene in a bare, bleak school on a raw afternoon. Mrs. Bilbow-Kay explains that her son Robert, out of practice, takes lessons on a doctor's order, while a friend wonders if riding is itself sedentary. The riding master, cane in hand, promises real riding this time.

Later pages turn to fairground shows, where a visitor weighs spending sixpence on performing fleas or a shilling on a mesmerist, and finds a mystic named Muriel barred by a half-crown fee. The issue blends social comedy with holiday-show gossip. It captures Punch's eye for everyday London absurdity.
12934-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This November 1, 1890 Punch leads with a Modern Types study, The Average Undergraduate, scolding young men for lost courtesy. Middle-aged censors complain that youths are selfish, arrogant, slangy, and wanting in reverence, unlike the modest, chivalrous young men of their own day. Punch lets the complaint run in full, teasing both generations.

A later piece in broad dialect tells of a guest who answers a riddle about how many Gests stand while one drinks. Three, he says: one to hold the cover, one to bow and drink, one to guard the drinker from a stab. The issue blends social satire with comic dialect. It captures Punch's November humour.
12944-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This December 27, 1890 Punch opens its booking-office with notes on books and magazines of the season. The origin of Le Coup de Jarnac, well told by MacDowall in Macmillan's Magazine, earns a joke about the Two Macs. Two seasonable ghost stories in the Argosy, by Charles W. Wood, and Harry Fludyer at Cambridge, with letters from a modern Cantab, earn praise.

A tall tale follows about a man who buys a doomed horse from a knacker's yard. The price is four shillings and elevenpence three farthings a pound, he pays a hundred pounds in notes, and the driver vanishes. Punch's year-end issue mixes book talk with comic invention. It shows the weekly in holiday form.
13244-punch-or-the-london-charivari-the-:
Punch's Christmas Number for 1890 opens with Father Time on his observatory tower, taking a last look at the old year. Mr. Punch enters with his dog Tobias, quotes that he is not for an age but for all time, and lights a cigar at Time's lantern. Together they set out in search of a brighter, better, and truer world.

Their tour visits Jupiter, where men in red coats play earnest games with odd sticks on dry grass by the sea. Later they reach crystal halls, opal walks, and birds of paradise, with alabaster steps to a vast hall on columns. The number is Punch at its most fanciful, a Christmas fantasy of time, satire, and hope.
13688-mr-murray-s-list-of-new-and-recent:
John Murray of Albemarle Street issued this list of new and recent books in July 1890. It advertises the firm's current titles with prices, formats, and short press notices. History, travel, biography, and speeches fill most pages. A few novels and illustrated works appear beside serious nonfiction.

Speeches delivered in India by the Marquis of Dufferin lead the list, praised for wit and good sense. Other entries cover railways, science, and foreign affairs. Reading it now shows what a leading London house pushed in a single season. It also records Victorian prices and reviewing taste. Book historians will find it a handy snapshot of the trade.
14631-the-american-missionary-volume-44-:
The American Missionary for October 1890, published by the American Missionary Association at Bible House in New York, reports mission work at fifty cents a year. The contents list an annual meeting and notes from the West and South.

Items cover the Federal Election Bill, the Mississippi convention, Straight University, temperance in Tennessee, the Chinese, and woman's work in North Carolina and the Southern mountains. Church reports from Nashville tell of baptisms, conversions, and envelope collections. The issue shows a missionary magazine at work in the post-Reconstruction South. The association founded schools and churches across the South.
15231-the-american-missionary-volume-44-:
This February 1890 number of The American Missionary, organ of the American Missionary Association, reports missions at home and abroad. Editorial notes, southern notes, and a revival at Straight University fill the opening pages. A letter from Miss Collins at Grand View, Tennessee, adds a field voice.

Bureau of Woman's Work notes tell how one mission band raised its money, and state organizations list receipts. The issue, priced at fifty cents a year, shows a missionary network at work in the post-Reconstruction South. Historians of missions and race will find it a useful, if partisan, source.
15362-the-american-missionary-volume-44-:
This March 1890 issue of The American Missionary, the monthly paper of the American Missionary Association in New York, reports the work of a Protestant mission body across the United States. Editorials open the number, followed by notes from New England, the South, Indian schools, and Chinese missions. A list of receipts closes the issue.

Inside, readers find accounts of revival meetings and watch-night services, plus a report on the Ramona school for Indian pupils. An address on the future of Black Americans in the country, by C. H. Richards, follows. A section on women's work adds short notes on Christian life in humble homes. The issue gives a clear window on mission aims of its day: schools, churches, and aid, funded by small gifts from many donors.
15609-the-american-missionary-volume-44-:
The American Missionary for April 1890, volume 44, number 4, came from the American Missionary Association at Bible House, New York, at fifty cents a year in advance. Rev. William M. Taylor presided, with vice-presidents from New York, Massachusetts, Illinois, and Missouri. The number reports missionary work among Southern Black communities, Native peoples, and Chinese immigrants.

Editorials cover a removal, Indian civilization, emigration of colored people, and the stereopticon in New England. Southern pages dedicate Chandler Normal Institute and report Congregationalism around Paris, Texas, with the White Cross League and Berea and temperance. Indian pages offer streaks of light and an exemplary mother. Chinese anniversaries and an address by a colored man speaking for his race follow. The issue shows the association's schools, churches, and relief work in 1890.
15647-the-american-missionary-volume-44-:
The American Missionary for May 1890, volume 44, number 5, came from the American Missionary Association at Bible House, New York, at fifty cents a year in advance. Rev. William M. Taylor presided, with vice-presidents from New York, Illinois, and Massachusetts. The number centers on Ballard Normal School at Macon, Georgia, with pictures of its teachers' home, girls' dormitory, and industrial building.

Editorials cover removal, finance, the Alaska mission, Southern notes, and facts about Ballard School. Christian Negro leaders, a conference of educators, and a prize poem follow. Southern pages offer notes in the saddle, then and now, the Central South Association, and Tougaloo University, with the death of Eli Tapley. Indian pages report a January trip, Chinese pages report Chinese work, and the Bureau of Woman's Work closes with a letter from a Southern lady.
15909-the-american-missionary-volume-44-:
The January 1890 number of The American Missionary, volume forty-four, number one, organ of the American Missionary Association. Editorials greet the new year and discuss the collection in the Corinthian church. Africa, its shadow and sunshine, and conventions of coloured people fill the front pages. The magazine served friends of missions at home and abroad.

Field notes from the South report revivals at Washington, Straight University in New Orleans, and Tillotson Institute. Missionary life among the Dakota Indians and a new church at Fort Yates follow. China for Christ closes the foreign news. The issue gives a clear view of mission work in 1890: schools, churches, and hope amid hardship.
16036-the-american-missionary-volume-44-:
June 1890 brings volume forty-four, number six of The American Missionary, the monthly of the American Missionary Association in New York. Editorials discuss the removal of an office, Dr. Storrs on the Negro problem, missionaries to Alaska, higher schooling for Black Americans, and spring conferences. Southern reports cover school work, church work, a revival at Wilmington, and schools at Macon and in the mountains.

Further pages report a mission to the Skokomish Indians, jottings on Chinese work, women's state unions, letters from young teachers, and the receipts that paid for it all. The number shows a church network stretching from Alaska to Georgia. It serves as a detailed record of mission schooling, race, and charity in 1890 America.
20012-the-hawarden-visitors-hand-book-re:
The Hawarden Visitors' Hand Book, in its revised 1890 edition, guides guests through a Welsh village. Hawarden was W. E. Gladstone's home, and visitors came in numbers. Two crosses once stood in the churchyard, the Upper and the Lower. Both were destroyed in 1641, during the civil wars. A lime tree planted in 1742 marks the Lower Cross's site. The parish stocks stood near that eastern end too.

Gladstone's retirement made Hawarden a place of pilgrimage. The handbook serves sightseers touring his church and castle grounds. Local history fills it more than politics does. Crosses, stocks, and trees carry a thousand years of parish life. Such handbooks were the apps of the excursion age. This one preserves Gladstone's village as visitors saw it.
21590-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, the London comic paper, opens its January 18, 1890 number among amateur actors. The Thespian Perambulators stage Heads or Tails? at the Theatre Royal, Blankbury. Lady Surbiton and Mrs Gagmore take their stalls seats as the house fills.

A sketch mocks a manager who insists a parrot belongs in a drawing-room scene. Lady Surbiton lends hers, since it scarcely ever talks. Jokes at critics, proud amateurs, and fond relations fill the piece. The whole number, volume ninety-eight, gives a week's worth of Victorian wit, sketches, verses, and drawings at the height of Punch's fame.
21596-the-american-architect-and-buildin:
Volume twenty-seven of the American Architect and Building News covers January to March 1890. Ticknor and Company issued the weekly from Tremont Street, Boston. Its index alone runs to hundreds of entries, from abbeys to accidents.

Reports treat the fall of a hotel in Sydney and of a St Louis music hall roof. Other items cover aluminium from bauxite, American bricks, and faulty gutters on the Albany Capitol. A design contest for a new White House, under a travelling scholarship, draws note. Architects of the day kept such volumes as a working record of their fast-changing craft.
22051-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, the London comic weekly, had mocked British life since 1841. This single issue, volume 98 for February 1, 1890, shows the paper at its Victorian height. Verse, jokes, dialogues, and cartoons fill its pages. One poem teases a hostess about a guest whose lyric theories threaten everything she cares for.

Politicians, fashions, and drawing-room manners all take their turn under the lash. Punch's writers assumed readers who followed Parliament and the season alike. A lone issue like this one freezes a week of London talk. It also shows the house style that made "Mr. Punch" a national institution for a hundred years.
25685-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume ninety-eight for 4 January 1890, published at the office on Fleet Street, opens with a preface in verse. On a midsummer night, Mr. Punch in his sanctum dreams a dream, adapting the Laureate's lay after reading Camoens' Lusiads.

Gama's glories glow in the Portuguese epic, but Stanley's wondrous tale turned the sage's thoughts to Africa and exploration. The issue that follows mixes jokes, verses, and pictures in Punch's weekly style, catching London humour at the start of a new decade, with empire, literature, and daily life as targets.
25828-history-of-australia-and-new-zeala:
Alexander Sutherland and George Sutherland trace Australia and New Zealand from first Dutch sightings in 1606 to 1890. Captain Cook takes the lead early on, naming Botany Bay for the plants Banks and Solander gathered there, and claiming New South Wales with cannon and musket fire. The book then follows governors, explorers, and settlers as Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, Perth, and Brisbane take shape.

Printed in 1894 with maps and portraits, the history covers inland treks, the Blue Mountains crossing, sheep runs, gold finds led by Edward Hargraves, and the growth of towns, ports, and parliaments. Flinders, Sturt, Collins, Macquarie, and Latrobe each get their turn. The result is a broad school history of two young lands finding their feet.
25832-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
The January 11, 1890 number of Punch packs the week's jokes, verse, and cartoons into one comic number. Its long verse piece, Untiled, or the Modern Asmodeus, sends a demon guide and his guest floating over night London. They pass shuttered shops, tavern doors, and tired streets where law's beat echoes and a waif's moan goes unheard. The pair muse on toil, slumber, and the unrest beneath the city's calm.

The rest of the number is pure Punch variety. A boxing bout in verse pits Dares against Entellus before a loud ringside crowd. Answers to readers, holiday work jokes, and sharp quips on justice and goodwill fill the remaining pages. Drawings and captions carry much of the fun. The issue gives a lively snap of London humor at the start of a new decade.
29930-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume ninety-eight, is dated February 15, 1890. Its verse piece Untiled, or The Modern Asmodeus, part twenty, quotes Le Diable Boiteux: the demon gladly shows changing pictures. Sweet odours, radiant colours, and glittering light open a scene changed swift from London's dusk, sodden midwinter night. There Titania could make merry, while fair forms drift as softly as Paphian foam and as brightly as a splinter of iceberg.

Dianas doubtless, yet their frost holds fire, and the snowiest bosom covers soft desire. Waltz measures ripple merrily, yet a strange dearth of glee haunts the graces. The Shadow smiles that good form demands men look half dead and women semi-frozen. Somewhere, sometimes, an energy that strains against caste's rigid rule keeps nature alive beneath modish masks. Pygmalion's prayer breathed life into stone, but here marble seems to invade flesh.
29992-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume ninety-eight, is dated March 1, 1890. Its verse piece Untiled, or The Modern Asmodeus, part twenty-one, quotes Le Diable Boiteux: the demon gladly shows changing pictures. The speaker tells his shade London is not Rome, though the coxcomb is cold, the boor coarse, dulness haunts the rich, and pain haunts the poor in this colossal city. No later Juvenal should find her dead to purity and pity.

 Zoilus's tale still carries a moral: such critics are mere blowflies, devoting their small skill wholly to carrion. Not all Romans of Domitian's days lived in Juvenal's savage lays, and not all Latian ladies were Hippias or Collatias. For the sound, the scalpel holds no terrors, the cynic sees sharply but not far, and the star too great for scorn's detection may escape the eye hunting the mote.
30018-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume ninety-eight, is dated February 22, 1890. Its front picture is The Scientific Volunteer, with a quotation from Professor Tyndall's reply to Sir W. V. Harcourt in The Times of February 13, 1890. Tyndall says that if he ever must choose, he will without hesitation shoulder his rifle with the Orangeman. The issue that follows is Punch at its most topical and quarrelsome.

A verse letter, 'Arry on Equality, opens with a man down with influenza, sneezing his head off and likening himself to a cup-and-ball toy. Mending, he reads his dear old Daily Telegraph and finds Robert Buchanan slating Huxley. Buchanan says men are born free and equal, Huxley says no, and 'Arry backs Huxley without a doubt. The verse keeps 'Arry's Cockney voice throughout, brisk, comic, and partisan.
30033-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch for February 8, 1890, gives a week of London jokes, verse, and drawings in the magazine's sharp satiric voice. The lead poem watches a late-night debate from above. It mocks party zeal, grand talk, and the fine room where members argue for hours over who shall hold power. Cartoons and short squibs around it take the same aim at proud peers, brisk commoners, and the wire-pullers behind them.

As one number of volume 98, the issue shows Punch at its late Victorian best. It turns the news of Parliament and town life into rhymes and pictures that bite without long essays. Readers who know the period will catch the party labels and the London types, while others can still enjoy the verse craft and the scorn for pomp on every page.
30056-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume ninety-eight, is dated March 8, 1890. Its front picture jokes on the County Council's Licensing Bill for places of entertainment. The London County Council does not count theatres as places of entertainment, which is rather hard on the theatres. The leading piece treats the London County Council and the Lyceum Theatre, with Henry Irving's appeal and its result.

The piece poses as a not impossible extract from next year's morning papers. Irving, actor and manager, appears in person before the theatres committee and speaks at length on the pieces he has mounted, with their care and expense. Mr. Hecklebury asks about Hamlet, Irving's favorite part. The play drives his fiancee to madness and suicide, slays her father and brother and his own stepfather, and procures the death of two schoolfellows. Irving admits it is so, to a sensation.
30182-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch for March 15, 1890, opens with a moral music-hall drama, Jack Parker, or the Bull Who Knew His Business, the eighth in Mr. Punch's series. Jack Parker, a cruel boy whose sole employ is mischief, faces Lydia Banks, who will never do what is rude or wrong. Farmer Banks vents his irritation on his bull with a cudgel. The bull, shown with forelegs folded in calm defiance, accepts an apology and fastens his own stall door.

As one number of volume 98, the issue pairs such stage jokes with the magazine's usual verse, pictures, and satire on London life. Miss Jane Taylor's rhymes supply the moral frame, and the Griffiths brothers play farmer, bull, and chorus of farm hands. The result is a light, sharp weekly number, best enjoyed as a sample of Victorian comic theater in print.
30414-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume ninety-eight, dated 22 March 1890, offers the magazine's usual mix of jokes, cartoons, and satire. An early illustration gives maxims for the bar, advising readers always to laugh at the judge's jokes, since his lordship will not have the court turned into a theatre.

A dialect piece called Justiss for the Pore tells of old Christian patriots who left money for the poor of a large city parish. Their gifts were meant for charitable objects, such as rewarding respectable female servants who kept their places for at least four years despite rampageous masters. Punch pairs high satire with low comedy in a lively Victorian weekly.
30492-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume ninety-eight, dated 5 April 1890, opens with Mr. Punch's Dictionary of Phrases, journalistic edition. It translates press clichés into plain, comic truth, turning genteel court reporting into satire.

A prisoner fashionably attired and of genteel appearance becomes, in Punch's gloss, an ill-got-up swell mobsman, while a powerful-looking fellow becomes an awful ruffian. A rumor reaching the paper means the journalists hide in impenetrable recesses, and nothing fresh transpiring means the local reporter's invention is exhausted. Punch skewers journalistic cant with sharp, brief jokes.
30534-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume ninety-eight, dated 12 April 1890, opens with a suggestion from Pump-Handle Court. A writer claiming to suggest the law, rather than to represent justice in person, appeals to Punch for redress for hundreds, even thousands, of a noble and learned profession.

He notes that the law courts are congested, and that the daily list, once term recommences, will show Chancery doing fairly well while Common Law scarcely moves. The reason, he says, is obvious, and his letter sets up a comic legal grievance. Punch frames the plea in its usual mix of letters, jokes, and satire on Victorian public life.
30569-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume ninety-eight, dated 19 April 1890, opens its lane column on Monday with Carmen, exceptionally excellent. Miss Zelie de Lussan sang admirably with a light, pleasant voice, and Punch jokes that one cannot have too much Zelie.

Mr. Barton McGuckin, as Don Jim-along-Jose, did all that can be done with a weak-minded soldier, and no holes could be picked in his performance. One portion of his costume, Punch adds, would have gained from the Spanish tailor Signor Soanso. A horse entering the scene, like the old woman who lived on victuals and drink, would not be quiet and nearly gave Carmen fits.
30625-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume ninety-eight, dated 3 May 1890, presents Mr. Punch's Moral Music-Hall Dramas, number ten, Tommy and His Sister Jane. Punch draws again on its favorite source, poems by the Misses Taylor, and its dramatist trusts the soon-to-be-appointed county council play censor will approve the piece.

The play aims to teach useful lessons, starting with the poem's moral that fruit in lanes is seldom good. It also warns that taking a hint is not always prudent, and that constructive murder is distinctly reprehensible, especially for persons who cannot control their countenances. Punch turns children's verse into comic, moral theater.
30739-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
A March 1890 Punch number, volume ninety-eight, dated 29 March, presents Mr. Punch's Moral Music-Hall Dramas, number nine, Under the Harrow, a conventional comedy melodrama in two acts. Characters include Sir Poshbury Puddock, a haughty baronet, his daughter Verbena, her lover Lord Bleshugh, and Spiker, a needy adventurer.

Blethers, an ancient and attached domestic, opens act one in the morning room at Natterjack Hall, Toadley-le-Hole, with a large window open at back. Blethers notes it is Sir Poshbury's birthday and gentry are giving presents, then hints he could tell much, and must tell before long, but not yet. Punch turns melodrama into comic, moral theater.
30818-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Held here is one weekly issue of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 98, dated January 25, 1890. Punch was London's leading comic and satirical paper, mixing verse, jokes, cartoons, and comment on the town's social life. This issue opens with a long verse piece called Untiled, or the Modern Asmodeus, in which a shadowy guide shows the humours of the town.

The poem moves through gilt rooms, crowded parties, councils, and talk, noting how men throng to meet for reasons strong and vague alike. Its lines recall Beau Brummell and dandy days, then turn to the bright, noisy London of 1890. For modern readers the issue offers both humor and a sharp sketch of late Victorian city life, in the paper's own witty voice.
30937-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Held here is one weekly issue of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 98, dated May 17, 1890. It opens with a letter called All in Play, from a writer who sat in the stalls of the St. James's Theatre while the editor feasted at Burlington House among pictures and Royal Academicians. The writer watched a minority of the gallery shout themselves hoarse before the show, then howl at the overture, jeer at the scene, and yell at the actors.

The Tiger, the letter notes, had already played well on two occasions the year before, so no verdict was needed from the howlers. Charles Colnaghi then made his bow as a professional, as did J. G. Taylor, despite the riotous unfriendlies. Then came Esther Sandraz, with Mrs. Langtry lovely and powerful in an unpleasant part. The issue gives a lively, gossipy view of London theatre manners in 1890.
31039-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Dated May 24, 1890, this issue of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 98, opens with one of Mr. Punch's Moral Music-Hall Dramas, The Rival Dolls, a nursery piece in which two girls' soldier and sailor dolls seem to come alive and flirt. The jokes play on music-hall manners, childhood make-believe, and the vanity of grown-up performers.

Beyond that set piece, the issue carries the magazine's usual mix of short satire, verse, and cartoons aimed at Victorian London life. For modern readers it is a light, funny window on 1890, showing how Punch turned everyday fashions, stage acts, and social types into a week's worth of laughter.
33281-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, for May 31, 1890, volume ninety-eight, edited by Sir Francis Burnand, offers a week of Victorian satire. Its opening piece, Voices of the People, watches carriages bound for Buckingham Palace on drawing-room day, as crowds peer for a glimpse of satin trains and bouquets. The number mixes cartoons, jokes, and verse in the paper's familiar, sharp style.

The issue captures London at the height of the season, when society, politics, and street life all fed the comic press. Its humor is topical and knowing, aimed at readers who followed the news. For students of Victorian life, this number of Punch is a lively snapshot, full of wit that still bites more than a century on.
33292-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, for June 7, 1890, volume ninety-eight, edited by Sir Francis Burnand, offers a week of Victorian satire. Its opening piece, Voices of the People, moves to the Royal Academy, where visitors climb stairs full of zeal not to miss a picture, while others descend in exhaustion. Two shy friends meet at the turnstiles, each wishing he had avoided the other.

The number mixes cartoons, jokes, and verse in Punch's familiar, sharp style, skewering art, society, and politics alike. Its humor is topical and knowing, aimed at readers who followed the London season. For students of Victorian life, this issue is a lively snapshot of art-going, talk, and laughter in 1890.
33366-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, for June 14, 1890, volume ninety-eight, edited by Sir Francis Burnand, offers a week of Victorian satire. Its pages include maxims for the bar, urging a lawyer never to miss a chance to win the jury, even at the judge's expense, and a doggerel on Dr. Grace, who forgot his lameness and played with great vigor and dash. The number mixes cartoons, jokes, and verse.

The issue captures London in high summer, when cricket, law, and society all fed the comic press. Its humor is topical and knowing, aimed at readers who followed the news. For students of Victorian life, this number of Punch is a lively snapshot, full of wit that still amuses more than a century on.
33488-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
An issue of Punch, or the London Charivari, for June 21, 1890, edited by Sir Francis Burnand. The number opens by saluting two women scholars: Miss Fawcett at Cambridge and a Romanian lady, Mlle. Belcesco, newly a Doctor of Law in Paris. A verse tribute hails both women for taking top places in examinations where men had long led.

The rest of the issue offers the magazine's usual mix of satirical verse, cartoons, and weekly commentary on London life. A week-by-week column notes wet weather emptying the streets of summer dresses and pokes fun at fashionable calculation. The issue gives a vivid snapshot of late Victorian humor, politics, and attitudes toward women's education.
33526-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, for June 28, 1890, volume ninety-eight, edited by Sir Francis Burnand, offers a week of Victorian satire. Its Modern Types series presents the Lady from Cloudland, a new planet in London's firmament of fashion, whose arrival stirs society's torpor. The number mixes cartoons, jokes, and verse in Punch's familiar, sharp style.

The issue captures London in high summer, when fashion, gossip, and politics all fed the comic press. Its humor is topical and knowing, aimed at readers who followed the season. For students of Victorian life, this number of Punch is a lively snapshot, full of wit that still amuses more than a century on.
33685-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
An issue of Punch, or the London Charivari, for April 26, 1890, edited by Sir Francis Burnand, continues Mr. Punch's Moral Music-Hall Dramas with a conventional comedy-melodrama called Under the Harrow. Its second act opens in the morning room at Natterjack Hall.

Verbena, torn between betraying her father and lying to her suitor, tells Lord Bleshugh she never loved him, in a scene of mock-melodramatic agony. The issue otherwise offers Punch's usual satire and illustration. It captures the magazine's talent for parodying popular theatre while commenting, through laughter, on courtship, class, and sentimental convention.
aphorismi-urbigerani-or-certain-rules-cl:
Aphorismi Urbigerani, printed in 1690, sets out one hundred and one aphorisms by Baro Urbigerus. The rules claim clearly to demonstrate the three infallible ways of preparing the grand elixir, the circulatum majus of the philosophers. Along the way they promise to discover the secret of secrets and to detect the errors of vulgar chymists in their operations.

An engraved allegorical frontispiece by William Faithorne opens the book. Bound within it, with its own title page, stands the Circulatum Minus Urbigeranum, the philosophical elixir of vegetables, extending the system from minerals to plants. The aphorism form packs Urbigerus's whole doctrine into short numbered rules, a portable summa of the elixir art for English readers.
arxiv-2412-00790:
Hedieh Abdollahi and a team of co-authors hunted for long period variable stars in a small galaxy. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, covers And Two, a dwarf companion of the Andromeda galaxy. The wider project watched fifty-five dwarf galaxies and four star clusters near our own galaxy. They used a large telescope camera in two light bands across nine runs.

The team sought old giant stars whose light swells and fades by a set amount. Such stars help trace how these small galaxies formed and changed. Their catalog gives fresh facts on size, key star brightness, and distance. Readers who study small galaxies get a firm list of these marker stars for And Two.
arxiv-2412-00990:
Eric Wagner, Roman Matzutt, and Martin Henze present a 2024 paper on Seldom, an anonymity network designed with a lawful back door that cannot be quietly abused. Networks like Tor protect privacy, a real social good, but also shelter crime, which scares ordinary users away. Seldom tries to keep the protection while deterring the abuse.

Under strict rules, investigators may unmask only misbehaving users. Every access needs approval from a consortium of impartial parties and is disclosed to the public once investigations allow. The design's technical guarantees aim to make misuse itself impossible, not merely forbidden. The authors argue such translucency could make anonymity respectable enough for mainstream use.
arxiv-2412-01590:
Sandesh Pokhrel and co-authors present NCDD, a score that flags gastrointestinal images falling outside what a model was trained on. Deep learning tools for gut images often predict with high confidence even for diseases they have never seen. That overconfidence undermines trust in the tools. NCDD works in feature space. An image from a known class should sit close to the centroid of its class. An unfamiliar image sits at a similar distance from all centroids. The gap between the nearest centroid and the rest gives the score.

Gut images overlap more than ordinary photos, so methods built for natural images often miss here. Across two benchmarks and several network types, the score beat leading methods. The code is publicly available. Reliable flags for new diseases could make gut imaging tools safer to trust in clinics, the authors argue.
arxiv-2412-01990:
Francesco Monticone, Dimitrios Sounas, and Matteo Ciabattoni survey time-periodic systems in classical wave physics. Materials whose traits pulse in time can steer light and sound in fresh ways. Interest is surging, with echoes in Floquet quantum materials and time crystals. The opinion piece first recaps the standout effects that pulsing enables.

Two themes then get deep treatment. Time variation can break reciprocity, so waves pass one way but not back. It can also beat classic bounds on bandwidth, gain, and other device limits. The authors weigh where each theme stands today. Open snags and the juiciest chances ahead close the survey.
arxiv-2412-02290:
Every December, programmers worldwide spend 25 days solving the Advent of Code puzzles and swapping solutions online. Francesco Cauteruccio, Enrico Corradini, and Luca Virgili study what that sharing reveals about the developer community. They build a data set from the challenge's Reddit forum for the 2019 to 2021 editions.

A time-aware graph model links participants, comments, and programming languages. The top languages barely changed across the three years. Most solvers stuck with one language through a whole edition, but those returning the next year usually switched. Languages rated popular or loved in a big developer survey kept users engaged longest. Users of those languages were also most likely to finish all 25 days. The study shows how a yearly contest can mirror wider technology habits.
arxiv-2412-02690:
Kefan Chen and five co-authors teach a diffusion model to draw hands on demand. Their 2024 paper presents FoundHand for single and paired hand images. Hands defeat image generators with their joints, angles, and overlaps. A hand-only model can learn that anatomy deeply.

Training drew on FoundHand-10M, a dataset of ten million hand images. Each carries keypoints and mask labels. Keypoints serve as the shared code for pose and camera view. The model can repose hands, swap their look, and invent new views. It can even repair malformed hands in old images. Video sequences of hands come within reach as well.
arxiv-2412-03790:
Chayce Hughes and co-authors study young galaxies crowded in a dense early cluster, in work from 2024. The cluster sits so far away that its light dates from when the universe was young. The team watched twenty-five dusty, star-forming galaxies in its core with a radio array in Chile.

They gauged two glow lines from carbon atoms in the galaxies' gas. The line balance in cluster galaxies ran much higher than in lone galaxies of like brightness. That points to hotter, denser gas in the cluster set. The authors read this as a sign that close encounters in the crowd push gas into galaxy cores. Local crowding thus seems to shape how these early galaxies grow.
arxiv-2412-04190:
Zeki Doruk Erden and Boi Faltings propose, in a 2024 preprint, networks that grow their own structure instead of starting oversized and fixed. Fixed, overgrown networks hit statistical conflicts in their data: one structure cannot fit clashing patterns. The authors' DIRAD method complexifies a network in a directed way, adding structure only where the data demands it. It escapes the conflicts that cap fixed designs. Grown networks reach high performance while staying orders of magnitude simpler.

On top sits PREVAL, a framework for learning task after task without forgetting. It spots when new data does not match what it knows. The data is then routed to a model fitted for it, with no task labels needed anywhere. Tests show the system adapting to fresh tasks while still recognizing old ones. The authors offer proof of concept for learning by structure, not by size.
arxiv-2412-04590:
Soumit Kanti Saha, Fazle Rabbi, Song Wang, and Jinqiu Yang ask how well large language models translate code when a plain English spec sits in the middle, in a 2024 study. Models handle plain language well, so a spec in words seems a natural bridge between two coding languages. Whether that bridge helps in general, or only in some settings, was not clear.

The team tested the idea on three data sets, five coding languages, and 29 pairings of source and target. Specs alone gave no gains, they report. Specs plus source code helped for some pairs, notably with Python and C++ as sources, but not across the board. They also grade the quality of the code that came out.
arxiv-2412-05090:
Henry Thompson, writing solo in 2024, argues that generative AI will reshape the law unevenly across its branches. He treats the technology as a labor-augmenting tool that cuts the cost of both writing fuller contracts and fighting cases in court. Those two effects pull in opposite directions: fuller contracts need courts less, while cheaper litigation draws more disputes in.

Where contracts are common, as in property and contract law, the net change in litigation is unclear because the effects offset. Where contracts are rare, as in tort law, litigation should rise. Following classic work from the 1970s, Thompson argues that this pressure will speed tort law's drift toward efficiency.
arxiv-2412-07390:
Malin Sjodahl wrote this physics letter, published in two thousand twenty-four, on a bookkeeping problem in particle physics. Particles that carry the strong force's color charge come in patterns, and sorting those patterns into clean bases makes hard calculations tractable.

For the common patterns found in quarks and gluons, orthogonal bases, whose parts do not overlap, are well known. Exotic patterns beyond those basics were worked out only lately, and only in bases that overlap. Sjodahl shows how to build orthogonal multiplet bases for processes that include the exotic patterns too. The letter extends a standard tool to a wider class of particles. That should ease future calculations that involve exotic states of the strong force.
arxiv-2412-07590:
Jiahua Xu and co-authors clean motion artifacts from MRI scans with a diffusion model guided by frequency data, in work from twenty twenty-four. Motion blur in scans can block diagnosis. Most cleaning tools need paired clean and dirty scans, which clinics rarely have, and they ignore frequency space damage.

Their unsupervised method needs no paired data. Low frequency parts of the noisy scan guide the model to keep true tissue texture. Alternating masks in pixel and frequency space break artifact structure while saving shape and detail cues. Tests across tissue types beat rivals on standard scores. Radiologists also rated the cleaned scans better for clinical use. Code was shared in public.
arxiv-2412-07690:
Qiangang Fu and Liviu Nicolaescu present a 2024 probability paper on where random waves peak and dip. They study a random function on a flat torus built from white noise smoothed by a spectral filter, and count its critical points, weighted by any continuous test function. The first result pins the variance of that count: inside a small geodesic ball, it grows in proportion to a constant times the radius parameter to the dimension's power.

From the variance law, they prove a law of large numbers for dimension two and up. The rescaled counting measures settle, almost surely, onto an explicit multiple of the volume measure. In plain terms, critical points spread evenly over the torus in the long run. The result adds rigor to the statistics of random fields.
arxiv-2412-08490:
Chris Broekema and Rob van Nieuwpoort lay out SuperCode, a project vision for AI-aided co-design of efficient scientific code. Their paper from twenty twenty-four starts from a climate bind. Data-heavy science eats vast compute, and unchecked energy use no longer flies. New hardware sips power, but dull software wastes the gain. Their plan pairs specialized language models with hardware design in one loop.

The method aims to draft code tuned for fresh chips, with sustainability as the headline score. Two radio astronomy codes will test the loop. The text is a recast of the funded project proposal, shared for openness. The authors invite feedback, partners, and new use cases to join. It is a vision paper, not a results report, and says so in plain terms.
arxiv-2412-08590:
Tanguy Bosser and Souhaib Ben Taieb fix a training clash in models of labeled event streams, in work from 2024. Such models forecast both when the next event comes and what kind it will be. The two jobs share one set of settings, and their learning signals can point in opposed directions.

When signals clash, following their average can harm both jobs and drag overall quality down. The authors recast the model so each job gets its own form and training path, which removes the clash by design. Tests on several real event data sets beat the original model forms. The work frames a common glitch in two-task learning and offers a clean structural cure.
arxiv-2412-08890:
Junhyuck Kim and co-workers compressed the memory cache of text models to a fraction of its size in a 2024 paper. During making, models store key and value vectors for every past token, and that cache dominates memory for long conversations. Their Lexico method watches that cache entries can be rebuilt as sparse combinations of a few atoms from one small. Universal dictionary of a few thousand entries, shared across prompts, tasks, and models.

A matching pursuit method picks the atoms, and sparsity straight sets the squeezing rate. Across several model groups on math and long-context tests, Lexico kept nearly all first accuracy while using a small slice of the cache memory. Beating quantization and token dropping, above all where two-bit methods collapse.
arxiv-2412-09190:
Smith, Steenkamp, and Tame prove path links in lone light bits from a gem flaw in this twenty twenty-four paper. Path links are a key stock for light-based quantum work of all kinds. Their bits come from a nitrogen flaw in a tiny cut gem stone.

Inside, a run of tests grades the bits the flaw sheds under a plain laser wash. A time-gate trick then builds the linked path state from those lone bits. The tests that check the link do not lean on a pulsed laser at all. That sets this proof route apart from past work in the same field. The team casts the route as a base for more link checks.
arxiv-2412-11590:
Han Liu, Tian Liu, and Kai Huang build a real-time system to plan and run drone deliveries in cities. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-four, rests on a hub-and-stop model.

City logistics grow fast, and drones can cut jams and cost. But the fleet must be planned and run as one. The system sits in the middle: it turns high plans into exact orders the craft can run. That lets the plan layer work in the real world, not just in tests. The team adds three joint schemes that mix ground robot cars, drones, and staff. Wide tests show the system is sound and can be built.
arxiv-2412-11890:
Fu, Lou, and Yu present SegMAN in 2024, a segmentation model that reads scenes at every scale at once. Labeling each pixel of an image needs global context, fine local detail, and features at many sizes. Earlier models rarely deliver all three together.

Their encoder mixes sliding local attention with state space models, which scan efficiently in linear time. The decoder adds a module that extracts context at multiple scales and grows with input size. The base encoder reached 85.1 percent accuracy on ImageNet. The full model scored 52.6 percent mean overlap on ADE20K and 83.8 on Cityscapes, beating strong rivals with fewer operations. Code is publicly available.
arxiv-2412-13090:
K El Bourakadi and G Otalora review star and galaxy birth during the cosmic dark ages in this 2024 paper. After the early universe cooled, neutral gas filled space and no stars shone. Gravity slowly pulled gas into the first collapsing clouds. Molecular hydrogen cooling let those clouds shrink further.

Emission lines serve as tracers of that hidden era. Lyman alpha light and a carbon line at 158 micrometers reveal star formation and gas conditions. Simulations of the scattering profiles show what telescopes should look for. Metal content of the gas also leaves marks in those lines. The framework helps observers read high redshift data as the first galaxies switch on. Darkness to light is the universe coming of age story.
arxiv-2412-13190:
Maham Tanveer and co-authors wrote a paper in 2024 on MotionBridge, a system that generates the frames between two images to create smooth video transitions. Video inbetweening is an essential tool for editing and for synthesizing long videos. Traditional methods struggle with large, complex motion, while recent video generation models often give users little control over the intermediate frames.

MotionBridge accepts many kinds of control: trajectory strokes drawn by the user, keyframes, masks, guide pixels, and text. Two generator components extract the control signals faithfully and encode them through dual-branch embedders to resolve ambiguities. A curriculum training strategy teaches the system the various controls in stages. Experiments, both quantitative and qualitative, show transitions that are more dynamic, customizable, and true to what the creator intended.
arxiv-2412-13390:
Luke Woolcock and Robert Schmid extend phase-based stability tests, in a 2024 preprint, to systems with structured uncertainty. Control engineers have long used gain-based tests, through the small gain theorem and mu-analysis, to certify that a system stays stable under perturbations. A newer small phase theorem mirrors that logic with phases instead of gains. Until now it handled only unstructured perturbations, a worst case. Systems have perturbations with known structure. The authors define a phase robustness metric for that structured, multivariable setting.

They tie the metric to a family of multiplier functions used in integral quadratic constraints. An upper bound on it falls out of a linear matrix inequality problem, which computers solve. Mixed with gain-based measures, the new metric certifies stability in cases where mu-analysis alone is too cautious. The paper aims at control designs that waste less margin on imaginary worst cases.
arxiv-2412-13890:
Andrei Gaidash, Alexei Kiselev, Anton Kozubov, and George Miroshnichenko develop algebra for tracking open quantum systems with many light modes, in a 2024 paper. Such systems leak energy to a warm surroundings, and their motion is written with a large operator called the Liouvillian. The team builds the algebra of square combinations of left and right versions of that operator. With it, they strip the jump terms away and lay the operator bare.

A simpler effective Hamiltonian, blind to temperature, then governs the system's spectrum. Special points where behavior turns sharp, called exceptional points, appear exactly where that Hamiltonian's matrix cannot be diagonalized. The team derives a cold-temperature shortcut for the system's propagator. They work out the two-mode case of light polarization in detail, mapping its exceptional points and timing its evolution.
arxiv-2412-14790:
Rasheed and Zarkoosh tune the YOLOv11 object detector to use fewer resources. YOLO models spot objects in images in one pass, and the eleventh version is widely used. Their plan trims layers and reshapes the design by target size. Small, mid, and large object versions each drop parts they do not need.

A helper program reads a data set and picks the right trimmed version. Tests across data sets set the trims against the full model and its prior version. Accuracy held at the full model's level while size shrank. Speed of inference rose, and some trims even beat the full model on detection. Weights and the picker tool are posted in a public repository.
arxiv-2412-15090:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports how well its rebuilt inner tracker should find particle paths at the upgraded Large Hadron Collider. The report appeared in twenty twenty-four. The high-luminosity phase will pack up to two hundred proton collisions into each crossing, far above today's load.

That crowding would swamp the current inner detector. A new all-silicon tracker will replace it before the new phase starts. The team has adapted the tracking software to the new device and to the harsher conditions. Drawing on the latest design work, the paper sets out the expected accuracy and speed of path reconstruction. Good tracking is vital, since nearly every ATLAS physics result depends on it.
arxiv-2412-15190:
Sagar Soni and co-authors published a 2024 paper on a conversational assistant for satellite Earth observation. Satellites pour down images and sensor readings faster than analysts can read them. Generic vision-language models handle ordinary photos well but stumble on remote sensing data. Specialized geo models, meanwhile, accept only fixed resolutions and a few sensor types. EarthDial was built to close both gaps.

The system turns multi-sensory Earth observations into interactive dialogue: a user can ask questions about a scene and get answers grounded in the data. It accepts varied sensors and resolutions, matching how Earth data actually arrives. The promised uses are environmental monitoring, disaster response, and resource management, fields where a question answered in minutes can redirect real crews. The authors frame dialogue as the interface that makes the satellite archive usable by non-specialists, not just remote-sensing experts with code.
arxiv-2412-15390:
Svetlana Makarova and Junyu Meng wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2024. It builds a complete exceptional sequence, a kind of ordered basis, for the derived category of a space that parametrizes representations of a small arrow diagram.

The space in question encodes the ways to represent the 3-Kronecker quiver with dimension vector two and three, and it relates to the space of three points in a plane. The paper first sketches the space's geometry and its ring of cycle classes. The authors then view the space as a line bundle over a simpler base and apply a quantization method to lift objects into an exceptional sequence. A covering argument and computations with mutations prove the sequence spans everything. Such sequences are basic tools for studying the homological shape of geometric spaces.
arxiv-2412-15490:
Trung Hieu Giang, Nguyen Minh Tri, and Dang Anh Tuan work on the function-space foundations behind a class of equations whose difficulty is uneven across directions. The motivating problem is a semilinear elliptic equation on a smooth bounded region in three dimensions. Where one term carries a weight that grows away from an axis and the solution must vanish at the boundary. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the authors aim to prove embedding theorems for weighted Sobolev spaces, the toolkits that say which derivatives of a solution can be controlled by which others.

The key step is a new inequality of Polya-Szego type for the weighted setting, won by solving an isoperimetric problem for the matching weighted area. With it, the embedding results extend earlier two-dimensional work into three dimensions. The paper is a technical stepping stone toward well-posedness results for the degenerate equation class.
arxiv-2412-15690:
Hongbo Li and Lingjie Duan bring mixture-of-experts theory to mobile edge computing. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, treats each edge server as an expert. Phones offload learning tasks to the nearest server for speed. That habit stops servers from specializing, and old skills get forgotten as new tasks stream in.

Their model adds a gating network that routes each new task. Routing weighs data transfer time and compute time, plus which servers are free. Over time each server settles into a task specialty. The authors derive the least expert count needed to cover arriving tasks. The theory aims to cut the error growth that plagues continual learning at the edge.
arxiv-2412-16490:
Jiayi Chen, Yubin Ke, and He Wang build a fast grasp maker for robot hands in a 2024 computing paper. Dexterous hands with many fingers need huge sets of sample grasps to train on. Older methods made those samples slowly and tested them on few objects. Their system, called BODex, frames grasp building as a two-level math problem and runs it on graphics chips.

The lower level solves hand posture as a tidy quadratic problem, while the upper level adjusts by gradient steps. Thousands of grasps are synthesized side by side, reaching over forty-nine finished grasps per second on one card. A shared bench test in a physics simulator lets rivals be compared fairly. Fast sample factories can unstick data-hungry robot learning.
arxiv-2412-16890:
Lu Chen, Qiaoqiao Hua, Guozhen Lu, Shuangjie Peng, and Chunhua Wang study a nonlinear equation on a hyperbolic model space in this two thousand twenty-four math paper. The Moser-Trudinger equation, with exponential nonlinearity, is studied in the Poincaré disk, the model of hyperbolic geometry. The team sets firm traits of its positive solutions under a bounded Dirichlet energy claim, tracking how solution energy acts as the equation's parameter shifts.

Far-limit study shows the least energy solution's energy blows up as the parameter nears its critical value, one quarter. From this they prove a thing that can not hold in the flat Euclidean disk. The Moser-Trudinger functional has a critical point under an energy constraint, up to Möbius transformation. A local Pohozaev identity near the origin backs the case, as do uniqueness results for a problem. The clash shows how negative curvature changes exponential nonlinear problems.
arxiv-2412-17390:
Mattias Paul Heinrich presents PointVoxelFormer, a method for three-dimensional medical scans, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The method works with point clouds, which mark only the spots that matter in a scan. That saves space, since empty parts of a scan need no data at all.

Point clouds also hide who the patient is, which helps when data is shared. But they have been used far less than grid-based scans. Heinrich mixes point steps with a step that lays points back on a grid for local work. Tests on three data sets, for both outlining organs and lining up scans, show small models that run fast and score well.
arxiv-2412-17590:
The CMS Collaboration builds a multivariate classifier to spot low momentum muons in the CMS detector, in proton proton collisions at high energy. Such soft muons show up in heavy flavor decays and rare tau decays, so catching them well matters. The work came out in twenty twenty-four.

Old selection rules leave yield on the table, and multivariate tools have beaten them. The new classifier uses a gradient boosted decision tree tuned for the current run of the collider. It splits signal from background far better than the like tool from the past run. Its skill was gauged on two years of CMS data, a large sample by particle physics norms.
arxiv-2412-17690:
Chatting with a knowledge graph usually means translating questions into a stiff query language, and that translation breaks on tangled or vague asks. Rishiraj Saha Roy led a team that built RAGONITE, a system that answers in conversation without leaning on that language alone. It fuses two searches: database queries over a table form of the graph, and text search over plain-word versions of the graph's facts.

When either search comes back thin, the system loops for another round on its own. A language model then writes the reply from everything gathered. On a knowledge graph of BMW cars, the system beat several rival setups. The team argues the mix fits how people really ask follow-ups.
arxiv-2412-18390:
Xiaoping Wu, Jie Hu, and Xiaoming Wei published a 2024 paper on making image generation work more like language generation. Diffusion models, the engines behind modern image synthesis, operate on continuous pixel latents, unlike language models that predict discrete tokens one by one. The authors bridge the two styles. Their model adds noise to an image's latent form step by step, encoding it into quantized tokens in a recurrent fashion.

Generation then becomes token prediction across timesteps: starting from pure noise, the model forecasts each next token code until the image resolves. This recurrent diffusion runs on a discrete domain, a first for the diffusion family, the authors claim. The design borrows the machinery and intuitions of sequence models for pictures. If images can be handled as sentences of tokens, tools built for text, from scaling laws to interfaces, may transfer. The paper opens that door with a working framework.
arxiv-2412-20190:
Daniel Smolyak, Courtney Paulson, and Margrét Bjarnadóttir present FAIR, a modeling framework that lifts prediction quality for small groups without dumbing down the rest. Their paper appeared in 2024. In health care, fairness cannot mean making a model worse for one group to match another. Small subgroups give models little data, so their predictions lag. FAIR starts from the linear models clinics already trust.

It lets every factor interact with group membership, weights patients by group size, and tunes a separate penalty per group. This balances borrowing strength from big groups with tailoring to the small one. Number tests and a real case show the gains. The model stays readable, which the authors stress matters for clinical use.
arxiv-2501-00390:
Roy Steinberg and Kiril Solovey, two researchers in robotics, wrote this study of how simple robots can gather at one point. The work appeared in 2024 and takes up a basic task called aggregation. The robots in question have almost no hardware. They cannot compute, cannot store past states, and cannot talk to each other. Each one only senses whether another robot sits right in front of it.

Earlier work had shown a control rule that gathers two such robots from any start. The same rule often works for larger groups but not always, and whether any rule always works stayed open. Steinberg and Solovey show that no such rule exists for groups of any size. They also find a flaw in the old two-robot proof and give a new rule with a clean proof.
arxiv-2501-00790:
Muhammet Anil Yagiz and Polat Goktas build a light, explainable guard against network intrusions. Industrial internet systems face threats that heavy detectors handle too slowly. Their LENS-XAI framework blends knowledge distillation with an autoencoder that learns normal traffic shape. Attribution tools then show why each alert fired.

Training used only a tenth of the data to keep costs low. Four benchmark sets tested the system across attack styles. Detection scores ran from about ninety-five to nearly one hundred percent. False alarms stayed low, and the system bent to fresh attack patterns. The light design suits sites with scarce computing power. Plain reasons for each call build the trust that field use demands.
arxiv-2501-01290:
Vaskar Nath and co-authors introduce ToolComp, a 2025 benchmark for judging how well AI systems handle jobs that need several tools in sequence. Real tool work is a chain of steps, and grading only the final answer hides where chains break. Existing benchmarks, the authors argue, miss that real-world tangle. ToolComp grades both the outcome and the intermediate steps.

The data set was built by models and human editors together, with checked prompts, final answers, and labels on each step. Six model families were tested, and most scored under fifty percent. The team also trained reward models on synthetic traces: those that grade each step beat those that grade only outcomes, ranking good traces far more reliably. The authors conclude that watching the process, not just the product, is key to building agents that can be trusted with real tool chains.
arxiv-2501-01390:
Massimiliano Berti and co-authors extend a result on the instability of large water waves, in a 2025 paper. Stokes waves are steady wave trains on water. At high frequency some of them turn unstable when stretched along their length, and the unstable modes form bands called isolas.

An earlier proof showed the key test value never vanishes as depth shrinks. The new work computes how that value behaves as depth grows without bound. For the first three cases it fades to zero at an exponential rate. The paper is a survey style note that records this deep water limit. It serves specialists in wave stability.
arxiv-2501-02190:
Kazuki Tokuda and co-authors wrote this astronomy paper in 2025. Star-forming clouds in our galaxy often stretch into filaments, long threads of gas. The team asked whether that holds in a poor-metal setting, the Small Magellanic Cloud, a small neighbor galaxy. They used ALMA data at fine scale on clouds tied to seventeen young, massive stars.

About sixty percent of the clouds showed the steep fall-off that marks a filament. The rest spread more smoothly and glowed cooler. Filament clouds tied to outflows ran hotter, a sign of youth. The authors read this as filaments fading as clouds age in this galaxy, a path not seen in rich-metal regions. That shift, they say, helps explain how star birth differs across cosmic time.
arxiv-2501-02590:
The Stokes equations describe slow, smooth fluid flow, and solving them on meshes built from many-sided cells is a challenge. Chunmei Wang and Shangyou Zhang present a weak Galerkin finite element method that needs no added stabilizer terms, the extra parts many methods use to keep answers steady. Their version builds the steadiness in by itself, so they call it auto-stabilized, and it works on meshes whose cells may be convex or non-convex.

The key tool is a set of bubble functions, simple shapes that live inside each cell. With them, the authors show the method is symmetric and positive definite, traits that make the equations easier to solve. They also prove error bounds of the best possible order, in both a slope-based norm and a plain size norm. The result is a cleaner method for flow problems on the flexible meshes that real shapes demand.
arxiv-2501-03190:
Andrew Chang, David Poeppel, Dustin Freeman, and co-workers taught a model to predict when video calls feel awkward in a 2025 paper. Videoconferencing is routine, yet calls often lack the ease of face-to-face talk, and the bad moments are rare and hard to catch. The team sampled thousands of short clips from the RoomReader corpus of recorded calls, extracting audio embeddings, facial action. Body motion traits, then trained models to flag low conversational fluidity, low enjoyment, and set events like backchanneling, interruptions, and gaps.
