The best models scored strongly on held-out calls, and general audio traits mattered most. Beyond videoconference design, the work shows multimodal signals can predict high-level subjective outcomes. Pointing to tools that catch a call going sour in time to fix it.
arxiv-2501-05190:
Yuxuan Li, Cheng Zhang, Wen Wang, and Yongming Huang build a model, in a 2025 preprint, that predicts how radio signals fade across a map. Such pathloss maps guide the planning and running of wireless networks. Older physics-based methods are slow and often off the mark. Deep learning models can learn the patterns from terrain maps instead. Most leading models rely on convolutional networks alone. The authors blend in transformer blocks, which read context at many scales.

Their model, RMTransformer, pairs a multi-scale transformer encoder with a convolutional decoder. The encoder pulls features from the map, and the decoder rebuilds the signal map pixel by pixel. In simulations, the hybrid cut the root mean square error by over thirty percent. That gain came against typical leading methods. The authors say sharper radio maps mean cheaper and more reliable network design.
arxiv-2501-05390:
Sahala, Muhsin, and Sahoo study, in 2025, a tiny self-propelled particle that also spins, moving on a flat surface. Such active particles model swimmers and driven grains. The team blends theory with simulation to track the particle's position, velocity, and stored energy over time, both during the early transient and at steady state.

Unlike a non-spinning active particle, this one moves ballistically at first, then stalls in a sub-diffusive or nearly frozen phase, and only later diffuses normally. The stall comes from spin-induced temporary confinement. Spinning harder cools the effective temperature. Both long-run spread and speed depend on spin strength and activity persistence, so each can be tuned.
arxiv-2501-06090:
Marco De Paoli and four colleagues simulate how carbon dioxide mixes convectively in underground porous rock, a process central to geological carbon storage. They run large three-dimensional simulations at Rayleigh-Darcy numbers up to eighty thousand. The setup holds concentration fixed at the top of a semi-infinite domain with no flux at the bottom.

Mixing starts with a diffusion-dominated phase, then solute fingers grow, and finally the process shuts down as fingers reach the bottom. At higher flow strengths a constant-flux regime appears, with dissolution about thirteen percent above two-dimensional estimates. The team also gives a simple physical model for total solute uptake across the whole process.
arxiv-2501-07990: Alfred Dabson introduces a stronger kind of repeating module in algebra and ties it to a symmetry question in this 2025 paper. A module is strongly periodic when a certain construction returns it to itself in a tight way. Dabson proves that such modules exist over special stripped-down algebras exactly when the original algebra admits a two-step self-perverse equivalence, a structured self-symmetry of its module world. The survey closes with what the link buys for the symmetric groups, whose algebra drives much of representation theory.
arxiv-2501-08090:
Archit Patke and co-authors present an autoscaler for serving large language models in a 2025 paper. The head title names the system Chiron. Cloud hosts must size their fleets as demand shifts. Requests split into live chats that need answers in seconds and batch jobs that can wait minutes or hours, and mixing the two can break both sets of promises.

Older scalers ignore those time promises, so they scale too much and waste hardware. Chiron uses a layered backpressure signal built from queue size, hardware use, and the promises themselves. It adjusts both the number of serving copies and their batch sizes. In tests, it met promises far more often than rival tools, with gains up to ninety percent in attainment. It also used graphics hardware up to seventy percent more efficiently.
arxiv-2501-08490:
Isaac Corley and six co-authors present FLAVARS, a pretraining method that teaches models to read satellite images with words and place. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Labeled orbit images are scarce, so models learn first from raw image and caption pairs.

Word-based training alone weakens pure vision skill. FLAVARS blends three signals: matching images to captions, masking and rebuilding parts of images, and matching images to their location on Earth. On vision-only tests like nearest-neighbor sorting and pixel labeling, it beat a leading caption-based rival. One benchmark gained six points. Unlike masked-only methods, it keeps the power to classify new images from text alone. The authors pitch it as a foundation for Earth observation tools.
arxiv-2501-10190:
Maksim Gladyshev and co-workers gave causal models a sense of time in a 2025 logic paper. Structural equation models are the standard way to state causal dependence, where each variable is worked out from its causes. The authors reinterpret the math rules as mechanisms that transform streams of outside inputs into streams of outcomes over time. Lets counterfactual questions, what would have happened, merge with time-based logic about when things occur.

Their new logic reasons about such time-based causal forms and admits a fast model-checking procedure. Cycles in the dependence graph, feedback loops long banned by the standard recursive restriction, are allowed and meaningful here. New equivalence notions for time-based causal models round out the setup.
arxiv-2501-10890:
Yonatan Messica, Alex Levchenko, and Dmitri Gutman study electron flow in an exotic metal in a 2025 paper. Weyl semimetals break time symmetry, and their electrons can flow like a fluid with odd viscosity, a sideways form of friction. Sideways Hall currents in such materials run through two channels at once: the deep Fermi sea and the Fermi surface.

The team model disorder as a sparse set of hard round impurities in the fluid's path. Electron collisions reshape the surface channel, while the sea channel stays untouched. They compute how current flows in both directions for each regime. With normal conduction present, the Hall angle shrinks sharply in the fluid regime. When normal conduction vanishes, the ratio of sideways to forward resistance simply matches the ratio of odd to even viscosity.
arxiv-2501-11490:
Ronald Orozco López presents a family of figurate numbers built on generalized Fibonacci polynomials, in a 2025 paper. The new simplicial d-polytopic numbers extend classic triangular-style counts into higher dimensions with a Fibonacci flavor. Working with algebra, the author proves basic identities for them and recovers known q-identities as special cases.

Generating functions are derived both for the new numbers and for the squares of the generalized triangular numbers. The paper closes by summing reciprocals of these polynomials and of the triangular numbers, and it defines a zeta function on the polynomials as a tool for that analysis.
arxiv-2501-11990:
Bruno Högl and Guy Moore estimate, in a 2025 paper, how a heavy quark shifts a key quantity in the hot early universe. The quantity, the QCD topological susceptibility, gauges how the strong force's topological structure responds to heat. Axion cosmology needs it between 400 and 1100 MeV. In that range the bottom quark is awkward: too light to ignore, yet heavy enough to complicate lattice simulations.

The pair work in a caloron gas approximation, a picture of rare topological events. They compute the relevant determinant from both the small-mass and large-mass ends. A Padé approximant then joins the two expansions into one smooth curve. The ratio of the susceptibility with and without the heavy quark falls out of that curve. The result feeds axion mass estimates for the young universe. It also spares lattice teams a costly extra quark.
arxiv-2501-12490:
Tobias Heß and Aaron Molt present a 2025 paper on a faster way to find feature groups in product line models. In such models, some features must always be picked together for a valid product. Groups like that can be merged into one feature, which speeds many later checks.

Old methods often leaned on counting valid products, which is slow on hard real world systems. The new method uses only a solver that tests whether a set of choices can hold at once. Tests show it handles tough systems with ease. It even succeeded on a recent version of the Linux kernel model, a known hard case.
arxiv-2501-12990:
Konstantin Haubner and co-authors used X-ray data in 2025 to study Westerlund 1, a dense star cluster in our galaxy. The cluster sits near a source that may speed tiny space particles to very high energy. Past gamma-ray data could not tell whether those particles are light ones or heavy ones, and the two cases point to distinct physics.

The team mapped the soft X-ray glow spread across the cluster with a space telescope survey. They asked whether the glow comes from hot gas or from fast particles, and they hunted for a bright X-ray shine that fast light particles would leave. Their checks set new limits on the field strength in the source and on how many light particles it holds.
arxiv-2501-13390:
An agent facing a stream of new tasks should reuse what earlier tasks taught it, without assuming those tasks nicely cover the shared structure. Thang Duong, Zhi Wang, and Chicheng Zhang tackle that gap in a 2025 paper on sequential multi-task bandits.

Each task's reward rule lives in a low-dimensional subspace shared by all tasks. Older work assumed the tasks span that space evenly, so it could be learned up front. Their algorithm instead learns and transfers the shared representation as tasks arrive, with a proved regret bound. When tasks are many and the shared space is small, the bound beats learning each task alone by a wide margin. Simulations confirm the edge over diversity-based rivals.
arxiv-2501-14090:
Bolian Li and Ruqi Zhang tackle, in a 2025 paper, classification where a few classes dominate and mistakes are not priced equally. In long-tailed problems, calling a sick patient healthy is far worse than the reverse, yet most methods chase plain accuracy.

Their framework, RF-DLC, folds the cost of each error type directly into learning through Bayesian decision theory, using an integrated gain that respects both the skewed data and the decision rule. A variational method makes the training efficient, and any cost table can be plugged in. A new metric, the false head rate, measures tail risk. Tests covered large image tasks and uncertainty checks.
arxiv-2501-14590:
Guchhait and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on two magnetic compounds built on a triangular lattice. Each holds ytterbium ions in a three plus state. Such lattices are a hot test bed for odd quantum magnetism. The team gauges heat and magnetization at low temperatures and works out the crystal field that splits the ion's levels.

Both compounds settle into a ground pair of levels that acts like a spin of one half. Links between those spins are very weak, as a small Weiss score and curve scaling show. Sums from the field levels match the gauge data in full. A wide gap to the next level pair keeps the spin one half picture clean at low heat.
arxiv-2501-14790:
Ji-Ha Park and three co-authors work toward a speech prosthesis that reads the brain in a 2025 paper. People who cannot speak might one day communicate through devices that decode their brain signals. Past systems mostly decode short intentions or broken fragments, not flowing speech.

The team trained people on grouped speech sounds, called visemes, each tied to a shape of the lips. A diffusion model then read non-invasive brain signals and rebuilt the matching lip movements, for single trials and for whole sentences. The rebuilt faces carried coherent visual speech. The authors present viseme decoding as a step toward live neural communication and speech aids for patients.
arxiv-2501-17390:
La Van Thinh, Hoang The Tuan, Dongling Wang, and Yin Yang set out a broad fractional Halanay-type inequality for coupled systems. Halanay inequalities are workhorse tools to prove stability of delay equations. The fractional form serves time-fractional functional differential equations. It fits those that show Mittag-Leffler type stability. There, solutions decay like the special functions of fractional calculus, not like exponentials.

The main tool is a sub-additive trait of the Mittag-Leffler function. With it goes a best gauge of its asymptotic decay rate. The results improve several past results. Two uses show the reach of the inequality. With the positive representation method, it gives a stability test for linear fractional coupled systems with bounded delays. Through energy gauges, it also sets up contractility and dissipativity for a class of fractional neutral equations.
arxiv-2501-17590:
Antonio Baeza, Pep Mulet, and David Zorío improve how a class of flow solvers handles the edges of a wing profile, in this 2025 paper. The solvers, called WENO schemes, are good at tracking sharp features in fluids governed by conservation laws. Near a solid boundary, though, a solver must invent values outside the body, and doing that sloppily wastes accuracy.

The authors pair the scheme with a high order method for filling those outside, or ghost, cells by extrapolation. Their test problem is flow around standard NACA airfoil shapes, a classic benchmark in aerodynamics. The results match what others get with far more complex meshes that wrap around the wing. The paper argues that careful boundary treatment lets a simple grid rival body fitted ones.
arxiv-2501-17790:
Chan-Jan Hsu and co-authors present BreezyVoice in a 2025 paper on text to speech for Taiwanese Mandarin. Many characters in the language can be read in several ways, so choosing the right sound is a central challenge. The system builds on an existing speech model and adds phonetic control.

Components include a speech tokenizer, a large language model, a flow matching model, and a grapheme to phoneme predictor. Tests showed strong performance in general and code switching contexts, with realistic, high fidelity speech. The team also discuss hard cases, such as rare speakers and polyphone choices, and what they reveal about neural speech systems.
arxiv-2501-18290:
Sachleen Singh, Isaac Nape, and Andrew Forbes improve structured light in a 2025 arXiv paper. Structured light tailors the shape of beams for uses from communication to microscopy. Moving the shaping into nonlinear crystals is recent, and the output can lose fidelity.

Their fix aligns light with light. One beam's structure acts as a virtual aperture for the other, guiding the overlap in space and depth. They demonstrate the idea with orbital angular momentum modes and difference frequency generation. Control of the overlap proved precise. The trick should transfer to other nonlinear processes such as harmonic generation.
arxiv-2502-00290:
Huan Ma and co-authors tackle in 2025 a known weakness of large language models: they sometimes state falsehoods with confidence. To flag risky answers, users need a measure of the model's own uncertainty. Common methods read token probabilities, but the authors show those scores lose a key signal.

Their method, LogTokU, rebuilds uncertainty from the evidence strength the model stored during training, token by token. It works in real time, with no need to sample many answers. Tests show it spots unreliable tokens better than probability-based scores. The measure can then steer later steps, such as checking or re-asking, toward the shaky parts of an answer.
arxiv-2502-00490:
Jonathan Wenshøj, Bob Pepin, and Raghavendra Selvan rethink a training quirk in a 2025 paper on shrinking neural networks. To run on small devices, networks are quantized, their numbers rounded to coarse steps. During training for that rounding, weights wobble around the steps, a side effect long treated as a nuisance.

In a simple model the team shows the wobble is built into the method's math, not an accident. They then craft a training aid that deliberately induces the wobble. Networks trained with it, then rounded afterward, matched the performance of full quantization-aware training in most tests. Image benchmarks at several rounding levels back the claim. The authors recast wobble as a feature that simpler pipelines can exploit.
arxiv-2502-00590:
Prashant Mehta and Sean Meyn survey work on why large linked systems fall into sync, and how that sync can be steered, in a paper from 2025. Such systems span physics, brains, markets, power grids, and neural networks. Group behavior can surprise, and methods to forecast and guide it are in demand.

The survey uses the lens of mean field games, a framework for many-player choices pioneered by Peter Caines. Coupled oscillators serve as the test case throughout. The authors lay out how the framework frames prediction of group patterns and the design of spread-out controls. Learning questions raised by that program are also mapped.
arxiv-2502-01390:
He, Demartini, and Gadiraju test trust and team ends when chat aides plan then act. Chat tools have spread to day life since ChatGPT's rise in fame. With out tools for set jobs, aides can aid hands in day work. Those jobs span flight books and clock tools in the day set. Aides show hope as day aids, yet trust facts stay dim. Plan and step acts by such aides ground that dim zone.

Past work backs man-in-loop plan forms for hard plan tasks. Their test took 248 hosts in a sim world for day tasks. Six stock tasks, with split risk tiers, formed the test frame. Flight books and card pays sit in that risk set in the work. Aides plan step by step, then act step by step there. Host say at each stage forms the trust read base.
arxiv-2502-02190:
Maxence Faldor, Robert Tjarko Lange, and Antoine Cully use meta-learning to discover new Quality-Diversity algorithms, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quality-Diversity methods evolve a varied crowd of strong solutions instead of a single best one, using local competition much like nature. Their contest rules, though, rest on hand-made shortcuts such as grids or nearest-neighbor checks.

The authors let a learning system search for the rules itself, encoding them in attention-based neural networks. The discovered algorithms matched or beat the standard ones on test problems. They also carried over to bigger problems, larger populations, and new domains like robot control. Even when trained only for raw performance, the new methods kept their populations diverse, as if the search had rediscovered why diversity helps.
arxiv-2502-02490:
Hannes Vogt and co-authors port a core lattice physics calculation to graphics processors, aiming to speed up simulations of the strong force, in a 2025 paper. Such simulations are the only non-perturbative tool for testing the Standard Model, and they crawl because each chain update is serial. The heavy step is inverting a huge sparse operator, which graphics hardware can accelerate.

The team linked their simulation code to a specialist library for the inversion step. Early results on state-of-the-art problem sizes show a large potential speedup. Only small extensions to the library were needed, and the interface keeps the host code's reliability while gaining portable performance.
arxiv-2502-03190:
Muhammad Yarahmadi wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It fits a coupled gravity model to the newest DESI data, to see if it can ease the two big strains in cosmology at once.

The model joins Hu-Sawicki f(R) gravity with a dark-sector link to neutrinos. The team runs a full Bayesian chain over Planck sky data, lensing, DESI distance marks, cosmic clocks, and supernova sets. The linked model beats both the standard tale and the plain f(R) one. Its Hubble value climbs toward the local gauge while its clustering gauge falls toward the weak-lensing one, so both strains shrink to near one sigma. Neutrino mass bounds stay in line.
arxiv-2502-03290:
Henry H Mattingly and Yuhai Tu give a new account of how bacterial flagellar motors switch with such sharp sense. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The motor turns a tail that lets the cell swim, and it flips direction in response to cues. Past work tied its sharp response to a spread of shapes between near parts, as in a magnet model.

Fresh measures show the switch is driven out of balance, which that old picture cannot explain. They propose that local twists on motor parts shape their states, and parts pull against each other at a distance. That tug-of-war gives sharp joint responses with no need for near-neighbour links. Their model also makes a fresh claim: sharpness grows with the count of drive units.
arxiv-2502-03490:
David Johnston and co-authors ask how well transformer models handle two-step reasoning in this 2025 paper. A two-step question links two facts, such as naming the boss of someone's mother. Earlier work found that models learn such questions in an uneven way. The team tests how this skill grows as models get bigger.

Their tests suggest that silent two-step answers force a model to learn each fact twice. When the model spells out its steps, that double cost goes away. The team also shows that very small models can get stuck just memorizing answers. The work offers a new way to probe how these models store and link facts.
arxiv-2502-04790:
Yuting Zeng and co-authors cut the cost of debates between large language models, in work from twenty twenty-five. In such debates, several models argue in rounds and reach better answers on hard math and logic tasks. More rounds help, but the word count and cost climb fast.

Their method trims weak or empty exchanges from the debate, so agents share less waste. Tests across data sets and models kept the loss in score under two parts in a hundred. At the same time, word cost fell by up to about ninety-four parts in a hundred. The plan makes model debates cheaper to run at scale. It keeps most of the gain that debate brings.
arxiv-2502-05390:
Baturay Saglam and co-authors study how large language models store the task hidden in a prompt. Such models learn new tasks from a few examples in the prompt, with no retraining. The team builds a task vector, a single summary of the task, from the model's attention heads. Weights for the heads are tuned step by step so the vector keeps the task intact.

Older ways to build such vectors fail once the task leaves plain text. The team adds a test bed based on fitting curves to data. Their method pulls task facts from examples and works for both text and curve tasks. The results suggest one vector can carry a task across kinds of data, a step toward reading how models adapt.
arxiv-2502-07690:
C. Aguiar and I. Camps test whether ring-shaped carbon molecules can trap greenhouse gases in a 2025 computational study. Carbon nanobelts are short loops of fused carbon rings, and a twisted Mobius version adds a half turn. Trapping gases on such structures could aid sensing or capture technology.

Semi-empirical tight-binding calculations cover many gases, from carbon dioxide and methane to nitrogen oxides and ammonia. Topological analysis tools examine how each gas binds. The Mobius belt binds several gases more strongly than the plain belt, with nitrogen oxide among the strongest cases. The comparison suggests twisted carbon loops deserve attention for environmental applications.
arxiv-2502-08990:
Jihua Zhang and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on a flat optical chip that pours out pairs of entangled photons. Such biphotons power quantum communication and sensing, but bright sources with broad color and angle spread have resisted both bulky crystals and newer flat metasurfaces. The design from the team stacks a nano-grating on a periodically poled lithium niobate film.

Three resonances, at the pump, signal, and idler colors, are engineered to overlap, and the poling pattern phase-matches all three across a wide band. Predictions promise over 100 million pairs per second per milliwatt, a color spread of 165 nanometers near telecom wavelengths, and rates a thousand times past the state of the art. The ultrathin source could shrink free-space quantum hardware toward chip scale.
arxiv-2502-09990:
Xiaoya Lu and co-authors present X-Boundary, a defense that shields large language models from multi-turn jailbreak attacks without making them refuse harmless requests, in a 2025 paper. Jailbreaks coax a model, over several turns, into answers it should withhold. Older defenses often buy safety at the cost of usability, over-refusing or dulling the model.

Looking inside the model, the team found the flaw: older methods blur the line between safe and harmful inner representations, so safe content near the line gets damaged. X-Boundary pushes harmful patterns away from safe ones until an exact boundary forms, then erases the harmful side cleanly. Tests showed top defense scores against multi-turn attacks, about a fifth fewer false refusals, and nearly full general skill. Training also converged faster under the method.
arxiv-2502-10190:
Huh and five co-authors present VideoDiff, an AI video editor built around comparing alternatives, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Engaging videos sequence strong moments and layer rolls and text effects. Generative models produce variations quickly, but creators struggle to compare many options. VideoDiff generates multiple recommendations for each editing step.

Aligned timelines, transcripts, and previews highlight differences between alternatives side by side. Creators can regenerate and refine suggestions while comparing them directly. Twelve study participants compare and customize alternatives with ease. Results satisfy creators more than single-suggestion workflows. The design treats abundance as a feature, not a burden, for creative tools.
arxiv-2502-11690:
Peter Davies-Peck, in a solo paper from 2025, gives a new analysis of algorithms based on the Lovasz Local Lemma. The lemma is a probability result. It shows that bad events can all be avoided when each one is rare and depends on few others.

Such algorithms resample the variables of any bad event that still occurs. The analysis shows that most final assignments are decided by a surprisingly small neighborhood. Events that may still need resampling can also be spotted from those neighborhoods. That locality improves running times in several parallel and distributed computing models. Query methods also probe far fewer variables per question.
arxiv-2502-11890:
Deqing Zou and nine co-authors revisit how grammatical errors should be classified for language learning systems, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. How errors are grouped shapes the feedback learners receive. Existing taxonomies often lack strict validation. The result is mixed, unreliable feedback for students.

The authors present a systematic, qualitative frame for judging a taxonomy. It examines exclusivity, coverage, balance, and usability. They built a high-quality dataset of grammatical errors labeled under multiple taxonomies. Each taxonomy is then scored against the frame. The tests expose clear drawbacks in the past schemes. The authors aim to make error analysis more precise. Better classification, they argue, gives learners feedback they can grasp and act on.
arxiv-2502-12290:
Ivano Basile and co-authors assess asymptotic safety in quantum gravity against swampland ideas in a 2025 paper. Asymptotic safety promises a simple, predictive quantum theory of gravity with few free parameters. The swampland program, by contrast, lists conditions any gravity theory must meet to fit with quantum gravity as a whole, argued to be universal from effective theory reasoning. The authors ask whether the two frames are compatible at their foundations.

They revisit arguments and loopholes linking field theory descriptions of gravity to swampland claims. Black hole thermodynamics, spacetime topology change, and holography form the core of the relation. Lessons follow on what a field theory of gravity must and must not do. Readers get a conceptual audit of two major research programs.
arxiv-2502-12690:
Emil Njor, Colby Banbury, and Xenofon Fafoutis argue that designing tiny AI systems means tuning the data, not just the model. Tiny machine learning runs on low-power chips in health monitors, field sensors, and factory gear. Automated search tools already hunt for the best model shape under hardware limits. The input settings, such as image size or sampling rate, are usually picked by hand.

Their method searches data settings and model shape together, using a supernet shortcut to test candidates quickly. On a new wake-word vision dataset built for tiny devices, the joint search consistently found better systems than shape-only search, across varied time and hardware budgets. The winning designs traded a little input detail for large savings in energy and memory.
arxiv-2502-13290:
Sachini Weerasekara, Sagar Kamarthi, and Jacqueline Isaacs explore neural point processes for predicting when clinical complications will strike. In critical care, anticipating events such as cardiac arrest, sepsis, or respiratory failure before they manifest is paramount for outcomes and resource management. Machine learning forecasts of adverse events have surged, but their interpretability often lags.

Most models predict whether a specific event will occur within a fixed interval. Point processes instead model the timing and patterning of events themselves, which can explain clinical pathways. The authors test six state-of-the-art neural temporal point processes across six critical care datasets, each focused on the onset of a distinct adverse event. They frame the study as a novel application class for neural point processes in event prediction. The work aims at forecasts clinicians can interrogate: not just that a crisis is likely, but how the patient's event history points toward it.
arxiv-2502-14090:
Romina Aalishah, Mozhgan Navardi, and Tinoosh Mohsenin present a 2025 paper on MambaLiteSR, a small model that sharpens low-resolution images for edge devices. Phones and cameras need super-resolution in real time, but strong models are too heavy for their chips and memory. The design builds on the Mamba architecture, a sequence model known for efficiency.

To shrink it further, the team compresses the model's internal blocks to low rank. They also use knowledge distillation: a larger teacher model's know-how is transferred into the small student through careful tuning. The aim is a sharpener that keeps most of the quality while fitting the tight budgets of edge hardware.
arxiv-2502-14690:
Felipe Garrido-Lucero and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on college-style matching when seats come with resources, like dorm rooms or rent subsidies, that are rationed by region. A student may take at most one resource, and may also be admitted with none, a freedom that breaks older models. Under such caps, perfectly stable matches may not exist.

The team studies three weakened fairness notions that restore existence: envy-freeness with efficiency, non-wastefulness, and a new direct-envy stability. They design mechanisms for each and race them on synthetic markets. The most sophisticated direct-envy mechanism delivered the most stable outcomes, and the authors recommend it as the default for capped matching markets.
arxiv-2502-16590:
Yuchao Wang constructs error-correcting codes over group algebras in twenty twenty-five. The setting is the dihedral group, the symmetries of a polygon, over a finite field. Conditions are set on the group size and the field's characteristic. The field is taken to be a splitting field for the group.

First, Wang gives the Wedderburn decomposition of the group algebra. Specific forms for the linear primitive idempotents follow from it. Those pieces are then used to build the codes. Two families of MDS codes result, with stated length and dimension parameters. MDS codes are optimal for their size, correcting the most errors possible. Readers in coding theory get explicit optimal codes from an algebraic construction, not a random search.
arxiv-2502-17290:
Søren Fournais, Yannick Bonthonneau, Léo Morin, and Nicolas Raymond calculate quantum tunnelling between magnetic wells. Their twenty twenty-five mathematics paper studies the magnetic Laplacian in two dimensions. The two lowest energy levels split by a tiny amount. That split reflects tunnelling between two symmetric wells.

The magnetic field never vanishes under their assumptions. Earlier tunnelling results relied on electric wells instead. Their proof uses microlocal analysis in depth. A purely magnetic distance between the wells governs the formula. Surprisingly, energy states need not decay in the usual way outside wells. Decay inside a special manifold carries the proof. The result opens magnetic tunnelling to rigorous study.
arxiv-2502-17690:
Zhixin Lu, Łukasz Kuśmierz, and Stefan Mihalas present a method to infer the rules of a noisy system from snapshots that have no time order, in a paper from 2025. Many fields collect such scattered data, often from only part of the space. Standard time-series tools cannot use it.

Their framework, called DyNoSeD, fits unknown parameters by shrinking the mismatch in a classic equation for how probability spreads. One route handles data from a limited region using local score estimates. A second route uses global samples and a kernel test that avoids estimating the density itself. For systems that depend in a straight-line way on the unknowns, they prove when a unique answer exists. Tests recover a chaotic system's parameters and a gene network's links.
arxiv-2502-18190:
Chao Wu and co-authors propose a way to get three ferroic orders at once in a flat material in a 2025 paper. Materials that combine magnetism, electric polarization, and valley polarization could shrink spin and valley devices. Such a mix is rare in a real material. The team studied a monolayer compound in two structural phases, one magnetic and one not.

Switching phases changes the valley behavior in distinct ways, they show. In stacked layers, sliding one layer over another can flip valley and electric polarization. Adding lithium ions or shining infrared light can drive the phase switch. Valley splits reached large values in the magnetic phase. Readers see a design route for nonvolatile devices with several switchable states.
arxiv-2502-18390:
Todor Antić and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on drawing graphs with right-angle edges. A recent trend shows one graph through several drawings instead of a single crowded picture. The authors ask whether every flat graph with at most four links per point can be drawn so that each edge is straight, with no bends, in at least one drawing.

They prove that three drawings always suffice, and that no smaller number works in general. They also give exact rules for when two drawings are enough. A second goal was cutting the total bends across all drawings. They show that task is NP-hard, yet they offer a method that stays within three times the best count. Special cases get exact answers too.
arxiv-2502-18990:
Jie He leads a nine-author team presenting GenTool, a training framework that teaches language models to use unfamiliar tools, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Tool use lets AI assistants reach information beyond their training. Models are usually fine-tuned on tool examples, yet their grip on new tools stays shaky.

GenTool trains for two kinds of generalization. Zero-to-one generalization covers queries where no suitable tool exists at first, then one appears. Weak-to-strong generalization covers upgraded tools replacing weaker versions. Simulated training scenarios exercise both situations. The goal is an assistant that adopts new tools gracefully instead of failing or ignoring them. That robustness matters as tool libraries keep growing and changing.
arxiv-2502-19590:
Sil Hamilton and co-authors (2025) release a dataset of social networks pulled from tens of thousands of books. The collection holds 70,509 networks drawn from fiction and nonfiction narratives. Metadata covers about 30,000 of the texts, written between 1800 and 1999 in 58 languages, mostly nonfiction. The networks name more than two and a half million individuals. They record nearly three million pairwise relationships, each labeled for closeness and type.

Earlier scholars extracted such networks by hand, one book at a time. The team automated the work by turning an existing annotation task into a language model prompt, with structured output to keep the huge run consistent. The result offers humanities and social science researchers a view of historical social worlds at a scale no manual project could reach. The authors frame the data as evidence about how people imagine social reality, not just records of real ties.
arxiv-2502-19890:
Minseok Kim, Yeongjong Kim, and Yeoneung Kim use a learning method to plan the fastest possible end to an epidemic. Their setting is the classic SIR model, where people move from susceptible to infectious to recovered, with steady infection and recovery rates. The goal is the earliest time the infectious count falls below a set line and stays there, under the best vaccination plan.

That time obeys a partial differential equation, and the team solves it with physics-informed neural networks, which bake the equation into the network's training loss and need no grid. A scaling trick keeps training stable, and the authors prove it works in this setting. Tests confirm the method finds both the shortest eradication time and the matching vaccination control, offering a flexible rival to classic numerical solvers.
arxiv-2502-20990:
Rose Connolly and three co-authors studied personal space in virtual reality in a 2025 paper. In social VR, how close people stand to digital characters shapes comfort, and crowding can cause stress. A common way to move in VR is teleportation, which jumps the user between spots and leans on their sense of distance.

Seventy people chatted with embodied virtual agents while either teleporting or walking naturally. With teleportation, people stood closer to the agents. Women kept more distance than men in both modes. Walking gave a stronger sense of agency and body ownership, while feeling present with the agents stayed the same. The authors link the closer stance to the mental load of judging jumps.
arxiv-2503-00190:
Matteo Boselli, Joel Grebel, Ambroise Peugeot, Rémy Dassonneville, Benjamin Huard, and Audrey Bienfait wrote a 2025 paper on a flaw in ultra-quiet microwave amplifiers. These superconducting devices boost signals for quantum machines with almost the least noise physics allows. When hit with strong pulses beyond their range, the devices give off echoes a few microseconds later.

The team traced the echoes to tiny defects in the amplifier's insulating layer, which soak up energy and release it slowly. By varying temperature they measured how much loss the defects cause and how they drag down the device's efficiency. They also offer a fix, called BLAST, to blunt the effect. Quantum hardware depends on such amplifiers, so hidden flaws matter.
arxiv-2503-00890:
Theodore Curran and co-authors test in 2025 whether a camera can read blood pressure from a face. Cuff devices are hard to get and easy to skip, yet high blood pressure harms many people. A phone camera can pick up the faint pulse signal in skin, with no touch at all.

The team recorded one hundred forty-three patients at a heart clinic, many with heart disease or uneven heart rhythm. A learning model used the face signal plus basic facts to estimate pressure. Results matched studies done on healthier people, and uneven rhythm did not hurt accuracy. The model flagged most patients whose top pressure passed a key limit. The authors see promise for home checks.
arxiv-2503-01290:
Andreas Sauter and co-authors present a method to predict what happens when a system is intervened on, in a 2025 paper. Such predictions usually need either experiments or a known causal map, and each new task often needs fresh fitting. Their system, called ACTIVA, learns from many training tasks at once using a transformer-based model.

Once trained, the system answers a new task in a single pass, without intervention data or a causal graph. The authors prove what the system aims at when data and capacity are ideal: a blend of the outcomes from all causal models that fit the observations. On synthetic and gene-based tests, it beat a correlation-based rival and matched strong baselines. It also cut false effects on unrelated variables.
arxiv-2503-02090:
Cameron Heather and co-authors test whether the brightest early black holes fit current galaxy models in this 2025 paper. Telescopes keep finding fiercely bright active galaxies in the young universe. Their feeding black holes shine in X-rays at extreme levels. The team applied extreme-value statistics to the problem. That math predicts how bright the brightest should be. Several standard brightness distributions fed the predictions.

Predictions were checked against a deep X-ray catalog field. Models and data agreed in general, with some strain for certain versions. The method extends to even earlier cosmic times. Future finds at those depths will test the models harder. The paper is observational cosmology with a statistics twist. It asks whether early giants are truly anomalous.
arxiv-2503-03390: Sonia Pérez-Díaz and three co-authors study the far-off behavior of algebraic curves in a 2025 paper. Their objects are curves in three-dimensional space defined by two polynomial equations. A known link ties each such curve to a flat curve that is easier to study at infinity. They use the flat partner's asymptotes to describe the space curve, and give a practical algorithm that computes its asymptotes once the flat ones are known.
arxiv-2503-03590:
Supat Roongpraiwan and colleagues used a digital twin to keep vehicle millimeter-wave links alive in a 2025 paper. Millimeter waves offer cars huge bandwidth and tiny delay, but buildings and trucks block them easily and their range is short, so messages must hop between vehicles without dropping. Their system mirrors traffic in a mobility digital twin that feeds the routing control plane a live, rich view of vehicles, infrastructure, and looming blockages.

A routing algorithm combines that environmental precision with trajectory forecasts to reroute before links break. Simulations built on a twin of a real Tokyo district showed the strategy holding connections where naive routing fails. Twins turn blockage from surprise into schedule.
arxiv-2503-05690:
Franco Vargas Pallete, Yilin Wang, and Catherine Wolfram connect the Schwarzian action to geometry through Epstein's construction of surfaces in the hyperbolic disk. Their work is inspired by the holographic duality between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity and Schwarzian field theory. They prove identities linking the Schwarzian action, the length of the corresponding Epstein curve, and the area it encloses.

The horocycle truncation in the construction defines a renormalized geodesic length matching a known observable of Schwarzian theory. The identities extend to higher coadjoint orbits. The team also shows the Schwarzian action is the derivative of the Loewner energy of a welded Jordan curve, yielding two quick proofs of its non-negativity.
arxiv-2503-05790:
Joshua Chen builds models of homotopical type theory inside the theory itself, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The frame loosens the standard family model into a wild, early-coherent form. Set coherence terms then restore the traits a model must show.

Both the syntax and the standard universe model fit the new frame. That fit yields a clean inner reflection: a map from syntax to the standard model. Low-dimension versions drop out by trimming the terms. A container model is guessed as a further case. Readers in type theory get self-hosting with its seams shown.
arxiv-2503-06290:
Bojan Lukic, Thorben Knust, and Andreas Rausch split recorded software signals into segments of steady behavior with a variance based method, in work from twenty twenty-five. Modern car software logs vast signal data as parts interact. Hidden scenarios drive stretches of like behavior in those logs.

The task splits into two hard sub problems: how many segments exist, and where they break. The authors expect the joint problem to be hard in the formal sense. They test segment finding methods on a real system trace from automotive partners. Quality metrics for a given split are also discussed. Segment classification into scenario classes is left out of scope. The goal is cleaner analysis of odd system behavior.
arxiv-2503-06890:
Xiaowei Li and colleagues built a drone swarm platform from cheap consumer drones in a 2025 paper called AirSwarm. Swarm research usually needs costly custom aircraft with motion-capture rooms or heavy onboard sensing, which keeps most labs and students out. AirSwarm instead coordinates off-the-shelf drones like Tello through a layered control design that tolerates the toy hardware's limits.

A visual SLAM system localizes the drones without any external positioning rig, and a ROS-based framework simplifies programming missions. Tests showed centimeter-level tracking, low-latency control, formation flight, and survival of communication dropouts. Full instructions and open code are promised, aiming to democratize multi-drone teaching and research.
arxiv-2503-07490:
Novotný and thirteen co-authors build and grade first-run carbide spark eyes in this twenty twenty-five paper. The stiff stuff bears harsh rays and wide heat swings with small fade. Its flaw is a weak blip from thin motes that cross its face.

Inside, a boost coat sunk a hair's depth down lifts that blip by design. One chip firm cast the eyes on its line in the past year's start. Lab grades since then check heat firmness and boost coat yield. Reads match the team's chip sims with good faith in the match. The eyes pitch the stuff as a top pick for next wave track gear.
arxiv-2503-08390:
Lukas Krelle and ten co-authors read the magnetic state of a layered crystal from the color of its glow, in a 2025 paper. The material, chromium sulfur bromide, is a semiconductor whose atomic layers each carry magnetism, stable even in air. Its light-emitting states couple to the magnetic order, so optics can report magnetism without touching the sample.

Inside a magnet that points in any direction, the team watched layers flip one by one as the field grew. Each flip shifted the energy and brightness of emission and absorption sharply. Comparing reflection and glow spectra showed ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic layer arrangements coexisting in one crystal. Lower-energy glow lines faded steadily with field while lines near the main bright exciton brightened near saturation. The contrasting trends let them cross-identify transitions reliably.
arxiv-2503-08890:
Zhiwen You and Yue Guo introduce, in a 2025 paper, a new score for checking whether plain-language summaries of medical studies stay true to the source. Models can invent facts, a real risk when lay readers make health choices. Standard checkers struggle with plain summaries because they add definitions and background not in the source.

Their score first sorts each sentence by type, then uses a question-based check backed by retrieved facts. They also built a hand-labeled data set for training and testing. Old scores failed most on the added explanation sentences, while the new score beat them in every setting. The team offers both the data set and the score as tools for safer summaries.
arxiv-2503-09190: Takahito Kashiwabara published this math paper in 2025. It sharpens error bounds for the finite element method on curved domains. Engineers mesh a shape with small elements to model physics; when the boundary curves, flat pieces leave gaps, so curved isoparametric pieces are used instead. Kashiwabara proves the best possible convergence rate for the worst-case error, for pieces of degree two or more solving the Poisson equation. The proof extends his earlier approach for the lowest degree and different boundary conditions.
arxiv-2503-09590:
Md Mohaiminul Islam and co-authors present BIMBA, a state-space model that answers questions about long videos without drowning in frames, in a 2025 paper. Attention over every frame token is too costly, and cheap shortcuts like sparse sampling miss brief but telling moments. Their model uses a selective scan to learn which information matters, compressing the video into a short token stream for a language model.

Across six long-video benchmarks, covering perception, daily activity, and egocentric footage, the system reached state-of-the-art accuracy. The authors release code and models, pitching selective compression as the practical route to long-form video understanding.
arxiv-2503-09890:
Juan Carlos D'Olivo and four co-authors present a 2025 study of using atmospheric neutrinos to probe both Earth's core and exotic physics. Neutrinos change flavor as they cross the planet, and matter steers that change, so their pattern carries news of the core's makeup. Unknown extra interactions, called non-standard interactions, could muddy that news. The authors focus on one kind, mediated by a scalar particle, and ask how strongly it could hide the hydrogen content of the outer core.

They simulate muon events from neutrinos in a 55-shell Earth model. Then they map where changes in core composition and changes in the exotic strength become hard to tell apart. The two effects blur below a one-sigma level in the mapped regions. The study warns that core tomography must reckon with this possible confusion.
arxiv-2503-10790:
Near-term quantum computers are too noisy for full error correction, but simple error detection may already help. Tom Ginsberg and Vyom Patel build a framework for compiling and simulating algorithms guarded by small detection codes. These codes use just two extra qubits to catch mistakes.

The key design choice is how often to run the detection checks: too often wastes effort, too rarely lets errors through. Simulations under realistic noise, including a run of Grover's search, show that tuning the schedule lifts success odds about 6.7 times on average. Post-selection still caps how far the trick scales. The authors add a data-driven way to predict good settings from circuit and noise features. They release their data and compiler for others to build on.
arxiv-2503-12090: Ron Shnapp offers a short 2025 arXiv paper on time asymmetry in turbulence. Particles carried by a turbulent flow drift apart faster when the motion is traced backward in time than when it runs forward. Shnapp shows that this one-way behavior has a plain kinematic root. Viewed backward, the relative velocities of particle pairs line up better than they do viewed forward, and that better alignment explains the faster backward spread.
arxiv-2503-12990:
Roba Al Majzoub and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper introducing HistoVL, an open benchmark for vision-language models that read pathology slides. Such foundation models promise general skill across diagnostic tasks, yet existing tests are narrow, unimodal, or locked away by privacy rules. HistoVL goes wide and public: images from up to eleven acquisition tools, captioned with class names plus varied pathology descriptions.

The set spans 26 organs and 31 cancer types from 14 patient cohorts, more than five million patches cut from over 41,000 whole-slide images at several magnifications. Grading the current crop of models on it exposed sharp sensitivities, including to the wording of captions. The authors offer the benchmark as shared ground truth for a field that has been grading itself in private.
arxiv-2503-13090:
Václav Truhlařík, Tomáš Pivoňka, Michal Kasarda, and Libor Přeučil present a teach-and-repeat navigation system that lets different robots retrace a taught route by sight, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The robot learns a route once, then follows it again by recognizing places in camera images, without building a full map. Changing light and seasons make that recognition hard.

Their system rests on a new place-recognition method built from deep-learned image features, plus a new way to compute sideways drift from the matched images. The design runs across several robot types. The team also released a public dataset for testing such systems. In real-world trials, indoors and out, day and night, their system beat leading rivals in several settings.
arxiv-2503-13290:
Raymond Carlberg uses the GD-1 star stream to probe starless dark halos in the Milky Way. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. The stream's stars spread in speed far past what a dissolved star cluster in a smooth galaxy would show. Something stirs it.

He runs the stream in a growing model galaxy stocked with subhalos drawn from cosmic runs, for both cold and warm dark matter. Cold dark subhalos heat the stream to the seen spread across the age of its stars. Warm ones, if the grain is light, heat it far less. Mid-mass halos below the dwarf galaxy range do most of the stir.
arxiv-2503-13590: Alexey Ermakov and Alessandro Principi published a research paper in 2025 on how spin and charge move through a material pairing electrons with the excitations of a Kitaev quantum spin liquid. Such liquids split spins into fractional particles, including Majorana modes. The pair analyze transport where electrons meet a spin liquid layer, as in a ruthenium chloride crystal beside graphene. They find temperature patterns reflecting the liquid's energy gap and Majorana spectrum, strongest when the two speeds match. Checking those patterns could expose them.
arxiv-2503-14090:
Jan Göpfert, Patrick Kuckertz, Jann M. Weinand, and Detlef Stolten published this data paper in 2025. It presents two large data sets built from Wikipedia and its sister project Wikidata. Both sets mark numbers in article text, such as lengths, masses, and energies, so computers can learn to find them.

The first set holds over 1.2 million marked quantities. The second, smaller set holds 38,738 quantities, each linked to what was measured and to any extra details. Hand checks of one hundred samples each found the first set fully correct and the second mostly correct. Such data helps train tools that pull facts out of papers in science and engineering. The authors also share the code, so others can rebuild the sets from newer copies of Wikipedia.
arxiv-2503-14490:
Bharath Sambasivam and colleagues present a quantum algorithm for preparing thermal states in this two thousand twenty-five paper. A Gibbs state describes a system settled at a fixed temperature. Preparing such states on a quantum computer is key for studying matter, above all at low temperatures. Their method, TEPID-ADAPT, grows a trial circuit step by step. It also recovers the system's lowest energy states along the way.

A mixed-state trial form lets them compute entropy with no extra cost. The method can run with a small number of extra qubits, or with none at all. It works from a trimmed list of the system's energy levels. The paper serves quantum computing researchers who simulate physics. Better state preparation widens what near-term machines can study.
arxiv-2503-14890:
Zhengze Xin wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It studies perverse-Hodge complexes for Lagrangian fibrations on holomorphic symplectic spaces.

The author proves a symplectic form of the Hard Lefschetz theorem, and the symmetry of the complexes, when the space has a symplectic resolution. That extends a smooth-case result by Schnell and settles a guess by Shen and Yin. Along the way the paper treats the perverse coherent traits of Hodge modules on such spaces. One payoff is a fresh proof of a known count claim. The tools also reach singular Higgs moduli spaces over reduced curves.
arxiv-2503-15290:
Wiebe and a large team reported lessons in twenty twenty-five from a robotics competition on athletic intelligence. The second AI Olympics with RealAIGym, held at a twenty twenty-four robotics conference, tested controllers on a real double pendulum. This swinging two-arm system is underpowered and chaotic, making it a hard control challenge.

Four teams submitted reinforcement learning methods, where the controller learns by trial and error. The paper describes each method and scores them on the swing-up task using several criteria. It focuses on two practical questions: does skill learned in simulation carry to real hardware, and does control hold up under outside disturbances? Comparing the entries side by side shows the strengths and weaknesses of current learning-based control.
arxiv-2503-15690:
Palastro and co-authors show how to build laser pulses whose bright peak travels at any chosen speed in this 2025 paper. Such shaped pulses keep a near-constant profile as they move. In plain media their colors blend freely, while in a guiding channel they lock to set modes.

The team formed and sent these pulses through a plasma waveguide, a channel of ionized gas. Plasma tolerates far stronger light than solid guides, so peak power can rise by orders of magnitude. Choosing the peak speed at will opens new setups for making radiation and for speeding particles, including schemes for terahertz light and wakefield acceleration.
arxiv-2503-16190:
Sergey Nemirovskii studies how the tangle of vortex lines inside a superfluid grows from thermal kicks toward its resting density. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A superfluid's rotation lives in thin vortex filaments, and their total length per volume tracks the turbulence. How that length evolves in time was the open piece.

At first, random thermal fluctuations stretch the filaments. A classic theorem ties that early growth to the statistics of the random force. As the tangle thickens, vortices start interacting and the simple picture breaks. Nemirovskii then joins the growth to the Feynman-Vinen decay theory. The combined view follows the tangle from birth to balance. Several applications with striking results are worked through. The theory serves both cryogenic engineering and basic turbulence science.
arxiv-2503-16390:
Junkai Dong, Ophelia Evelyn Sommer, Tomohiro Soejima, Daniel Parker, and Ashvin Vishwanath wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a low-energy theory of sound waves, or phonons, in electron crystals that carry Berry curvature.

The work covers the anomalous Hall crystal, which holds a nonzero Chern number. Its slow phonons act like those of a field-free Wigner crystal, not a magnetized one, since its shift generators commute. The authors show how stiffness and mass come out of small-scale models, and work two model families. Berry curvature swells the mass and slows the sound. In layered graphene a new cross term makes sound run at unlike speeds by direction.
arxiv-2503-16690:
Telescope optics must sense warped starlight and correct it thousands of times a second, and pyramid sensors are the tool of choice. Landman and a large team of co-authors report the first sky test of such a sensor run without its usual dithering motion. Dithering widens the sensor's range but costs sharpness and blinds it to some errors. A neural network instead untangles the raw sensor output.

Running on a telescope in Chile, the smart sensor held a stable correction loop at over two thousand cycles a second. On bright stars it nearly matched the classic dithered setup. On a fainter star in strong wind it did better. The team plans faster loops, easier calibration, and tests on fainter stars, where the gain should grow.
arxiv-2503-17390:
Rahman wrote this methods paper in twenty twenty-five on how experiments affect individuals, not just groups. Psychology studies usually compare group averages, which can hide what happens to each person. The proposed spotlight instead tracks how one person's whole pattern of responses shifts across conditions. Reaction time data serve as the test case.

Ten people did a visual search task while the study varied set size and target presence. The author measured shifts in each person's response-time distribution directly. Those raw shifts were compared with fits from two standard models. Direct measurement gave the clearest picture and split people into two subgroups. One subgroup showed neither effect, while the other showed only the target effect. The paper argues averages can mislead.
arxiv-2503-18590:
Luan Fiorio and six co-authors teach a neural beamformer to pick the right voice out of a crowd by using where a listener tends to look. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Beamforming microphones aim an ear at one speaker and mute the rest. In a group, the machine must first know which speaker is the target.

People usually glance toward the speaker they follow, landing a bit short of the exact spot. The team's training trick feeds that glance pattern into the network. It learns which direction to favor from the layout of listener and speakers. Once trained, the system needs only sound to work. In simulated rooms it beat a classic filter and its own untrained twin. Speech came through clearer, cleaner, and less distorted. The step brings machines closer to solving the cocktail party problem.
arxiv-2503-19290:
In a 2025 paper, Lakeisha M. Ramos Rosado and co-authors study the atmosphere of a warm Neptune-sized planet, HAT-P-26b. Using the Hubble Space Telescope under a program reanalyzing all its exoplanet data uniformly, the team built a transmission spectrum spanning ultraviolet to mid-infrared light.

New and reprocessed Hubble data joined older infrared points. The spectrum shows a scattering slope gentler than pure Rayleigh scattering, best matched by haze alone. Retrieval modeling put the air's metal content near fifteen times the Sun's share, with wide error bars. That richness hints the planet formed farther out, where hydrogen and helium dominated, then migrated inward. Upcoming Webb telescope spectra should sharpen the picture.
arxiv-2503-19890:
Victor Ayala, Thiago Matheus Cavalheiro, and Alexandre Santana wrote a mathematics paper in 2025 on the observability of linear systems on the Heisenberg group. Observability is a central property in control theory: it allows the complete internal state of a system to be deduced from its outputs over time, even when direct measurement is impossible.

The paper studies linear systems defined on the three-dimensional Heisenberg group, a curved space used in mathematics and physics. The authors use homomorphisms between the group and its simply connected subgroups to pass to a quotient space, which serves as the output space. On that quotient they derive sufficient conditions under which the system is observable. The results add to the basic rules for how dynamical systems on curved spaces can be monitored and controlled from limited information.
arxiv-2503-19990:
Kexian Tang and co-authors present a 2025 benchmark that tests how well vision-language models reason about space in steps. Real tasks, from robot control to assembly, need chains of spatial calls. The team built LEGO-Puzzles, a test drawn from brick building. One set holds 1,100 questions on basic spatial skills. The other asks for full build plans of up to eight steps.

Twenty-nine top models took the test. Even the best fell at least 20 percent behind human scores on the basic set. On plan tasks, accuracy fell to zero as step counts grew. Human players solved all plan tasks without error. A switch in input form, noted at the close, also shifted scores. The gap marks spatial chains as a weak spot for current models.
arxiv-2503-20690:
Sifis Lagouvardos and co-authors present a static analysis that finds data structures inside deployed Ethereum smart contracts, in this 2025 paper. Smart contracts are small programs stored on a blockchain, which serves as their memory. Analysts often have only the deployed code, yet they need to know what data the contract stores. The best prior tool missed nearly all complex structures and handled under half of contracts.

The new method reads the code without running it and reasons about how storage slots are computed. It names the exact types of maps and arrays with about ninety-nine percent precision. Recall passed ninety-two percent, far above the older tool. Often the result even beats the storage map the compiler itself emits. The work aids audits and tools that inspect contracts for flaws.
arxiv-2503-20790:
Hsiang-Ting Chen, Yuan Zhang, Gustavo Carneiro, and Rajvinder Singh report field work on AI help during colonoscopy in Australia. Software that flags possible cancers during the exam promises better screening, but the team finds a gap between lab success and clinic use. Developers, both in research and in industry, tend to chase model accuracy while giving little weight to screen design, fit with daily workflow, and the doctor's own experience.

The study rests on watching real exams and interviewing the specialists who perform them. The authors argue that the human-computer interaction community should push user-centered design, so these systems stay usable, back the endoscopist's skill rather than fight it, and truly improve patient outcomes. They frame the paper as a call to build for the clinic, not just the benchmark.
arxiv-2503-21490: Tsz Ho Chan asks how short an interval can be while still holding near-cube and near-fourth-power numbers in a paper from 2025. The targets are products of three nearly equal factors, or four nearly equal factors. Short interval problems are classic in analytic number theory. The novelty is importing a second moment method, usually reserved for almost-all results, into a statement about every interval. That transfer lets one argument cover all cases at once rather than most of them.
arxiv-2503-21590:
Zorar Ahmadi and Bashir Mojaveri compare quantum heat engines in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Their working substance is a two-qubit Heisenberg XXZ chain, a small quantum spin system. They introduce a generalized quantum Otto cycle with two distinct ways of coupling to heat reservoirs.

The generalized cycle shows potential for one hundred percent efficiency, beyond the standard quantum Otto cycle. The authors derive the conditions needed for positive work output and for reaching that peak efficiency. They also propose a lab realization using quantum electrodynamic circuits and a transmon qudit. The work highlights how non-equilibrium steps and uneven coupling can boost work extraction in quantum engines.
arxiv-2503-21690:
Micro-expressions are brief flashes of feeling that cross a face too fast to hide, and therapists read them for clues. Nikin Matharaarachchi, Muhammad Fermi Pasha, Sonya Coleman, and Kah Peng Wong note that research on these flashes covers adults only. Children's expressions differ, and no data set of child micro-expressions existed, partly because children are hard to record in a controlled way.

The team builds the first such data set, called CMED, from spontaneous videos captured during online video calls. With real child examples in hand, they compare child and adult micro-expressions and point out key differences. They also set a first benchmark for spotting and naming these expressions automatically, trying three approaches that mix hand-built features and learned models. The data set opens a new line of work for emotion-aware tools that support child therapy.
arxiv-2503-22090: Georgios Mavrogiannis proves fade scores for waves on spin black hole fields with a plus term for the world at large. He works on the Klein-Gordon law on Kerr-de Sitter fields not at the edge. His aim is a fade score built by sums that does not drop in the plain pain spots. The find takes a mode firm claim for the split spoke law. It holds with no terms for holes that spin quite slow and for fixes the same round an axis.
arxiv-2503-22890:
Labeling medical scans pixel by pixel is slow, so doctors often mark only rough scribbles as training labels. Ke Zhang and Vishal Patel present MedCL, a 2025 method that learns good scan outlines from such sparse marks.

MedCL leans on a simple fact: body parts have typical layouts that repeat across scans. The method mixes features within and across images, then groups them so the layout stays consistent at both small and large scales. Built on two known backbones, it was tested on heart, multi-organ, and heart-disease scan sets. Even with fewer scribbles than rivals need, it beat standard methods. It handled both regular organs and irregular disease regions, a long-standing weak spot.
arxiv-2503-23090:
Sungmin Sohn, Namwoo Kim, Mark Hansen, and Yoonjin Yoon built a data-driven framework in twenty twenty-five for choosing sites for urban air mobility ports. Flying taxis and cargo drones need ground sites, and poor placement can worsen unfairness or pollution. Their framework, USE-LFA, judges sites with latent factor analysis, a method that finds hidden drivers behind many measures.

Using twenty-five city measures for Seoul, the method found six hidden factors grouped into two scores: suitability and attractiveness. A tunable blend of the two lets planners match local goals. Maps showed clear clusters of strong sites and gaps between districts. Small shifts in the blend changed the winning sites a lot, a warning that weights need care. The authors offer the method as a portable tool for other cities.
arxiv-2503-23790:
Lorenzo Barban, Gianluca Occhetta, and Luis Solá Conde build geometric bridges that realize the jumps between a prized class of algebraic varieties. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Mori Dream Spaces are varieties whose geometry is unusually well controlled. Birational maps link them by blowing parts up and down, but the link is abstract.

The team constructs an actual projective space that embodies each such map. That realization is itself a Mori Dream Space. Better, the map factors through it as a chain of wall crossings, a standard set of moves. For toric cases they supply computer tools to build a key polytope by hand. Embedding into toric varieties then spreads the result to all dream spaces. Examples test when the bridge is a Fano variety.
arxiv-2503-24090:
Dario Melegari, Rabia Abdul Razaq, Giovanni Minuto, and Paolo Solinas compare two ways to run variational quantum methods, one that reads the detector in a way that spares the quantum state. Such methods hunt the lowest energy of a complex quantum system. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

In the standard way, direct reads pull out the slope of the energy. In the non demolition way, slope data is stored in a quantum detector that is read at the end. Both ways find the energy low point on lithium based molecules and on harder systems. The new way needs far fewer total resources, and its edge grows in a straight line with system size.
arxiv-2503-24190:
Xiaomeng Ma and Qihui Xu ask whether language models pick up patterns the way people do: quietly, without being told the rules. Humans learn language largely by implicit learning, soaking up structure without clear awareness. The team rebuilt three classic artificial language experiments, covering word parts, word-part grammar, and sentence structure, and ran them on two leading OpenAI models at the moment of use, not in training.

The match between model and human behavior depended on the domain. The smaller reasoning model, o3-mini, lined up better with humans on word parts, while both models lined up on sentence structure. The authors read this patchwork as evidence that in-context learning in models is not one uniform skill. Some corners of it resemble human implicit learning more than others.
arxiv-2504-00090:
Zsofi Igo and Andrea Merloni tally, in a 2025 paper, the energy that radio-bright black holes return to their host galaxies. Such output, called kinetic feedback, shapes how galaxies evolve. Past work lacked a full account tying feedback to galaxy mass, halo mass, and radio shape.

The team use a complete sample of 682 radio AGN from a sky survey, all at low redshift. They work out average jet power by galaxy mass and halo mass, and split sources by radio morphology. Compact sources dominate the energy count for most mass bands. Total jet output beats any plausible inventory of light-driven feedback for massive galaxies. The jets lack the force to tear a galaxy or halo apart. They can still offset gas cooling in small halos and help in large cluster cores, giving a yardstick for models of galaxy growth.
arxiv-2504-00290:
Julia Becker Tjus, Julien Dörner, Leander Schlegel, and Wolfgang Rhode wrote a 2025 review paper on how gamma-ray observations constrain the way cosmic rays travel through space. Cosmic rays are high-energy particles from space. Gamma rays, produced when cosmic rays interact with matter and light, reveal where the particles have been.

Measurements from gigaelectronvolt to petaelectronvolt energies now cover diffuse emission and individual sources in detail. The authors summarize how three-dimensional transport modeling, using the CRPropa simulation software, can be tested against these measurements. They cover environments from the Sun to the Milky Way to active galaxies. Better transport models matter for identifying the still-mysterious accelerators that produce the highest-energy cosmic rays.
arxiv-2504-00890:
Xiao Guo, Xuming He, Xiangyu Chang, and Shujie Ma propose, in twenty twenty-five, a privacy-safe way to find groups in network data. Networks can hold sensitive links, such as contacts, that cannot be shared raw. Their method, TransNet, learns from extra source networks that stay local and are privacy-shuffled before release. Each holder flips some links at random, so no trusted third party is needed. The target network then borrows strength from the sources.

Weights adapt to how useful and how private each source is. Theory shows the error depends only on the helpful sources. That makes the method robust when some sources are poor or heavily shuffled. Tests show strong gains across privacy levels.
arxiv-2504-01390:
Joan del Castillo and Pedro Puig offer ways to estimate very extreme probabilities without committing to a probability model. Guessing chances beyond anything ever observed usually forces a leap of faith in a chosen distribution, and a wrong choice poisons the answer. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their methods rest only on order statistics, the sorted values of the sample, plus one mild assumption: the average of the quantity must be finite. The same recipe works even for small samples, the authors note.

Because no model is fitted, there is no model risk to hide, which they pitch as clarity and security for the user. Finance is the showcase application, where estimating rare market moves matters most. The authors suggest comparing their model-free answers with the output of extreme value theory, the standard model-based approach, as a sanity check.
arxiv-2504-01790:
Sveinung Johan Ohrem, Bent Haugaløkken, and Eleni Kelasidi present a data set in twenty twenty-five. The data came from an underwater robot working at a real sea-based fish farm. It was gathered for SINTEF Ocean and named SOLAQUA. The robot moved through a net pen, at times steered by hand and at times on its own.

Sensors on board recorded sonar, cameras in single and stereo pairs, and motion and depth data. Other records cover power use, pressure, and temperature. The nets filmed were undamaged, with some fish and sea growth present. The authors expect both researchers and the fish farming industry to gain from the data. It gives robot teams real farm conditions to train and test against.
arxiv-2504-02190:
Benyamin Ghaseminia and Mohammad Salavatipour gave an approximation scheme in twenty twenty-five for a hard routing problem. In the classic traveling salesman problem, a tour must visit each client at the cheapest cost. In the version studied here, each client is a whole segment on the plane, and the tour need only touch each segment once. All segments run parallel, with lengths within a fixed range.

This case had resisted good approximations for over two decades, and the broader problem is known to be hard. Their algorithm finds tours within any chosen margin of the best possible, in time that grows in a controlled way. That settles how well this case can be approximated at all. The result closes a long gap in the theory of routing with neighborhoods.
arxiv-2504-02390: Michael Cowling and Ji Li work on flag Hardy spaces in analysis in twenty twenty-five. After an introduction to flag geometry on the Heisenberg group, they take up the problem of identifying flag atoms. That problem reduces to a question about partial differential equations. They establish a conjecture of Stein for the flag Hardy space on the Heisenberg group. Their argument hinges on a key result due to Baldi, Franchi, and Pansu.
arxiv-2504-02490:
Marco Caroccia and Nicolas Van Goethem wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five refining a zooming technique for irregular functions. Blow-up analysis magnifies a function around a point until its local shape becomes clear. For functions of bounded variation, that shape reveals how smooth and how wild parts divide.

The authors sharpen the iterated blow-up method and pair it with a rigidity result and a careful projection choice. They aim to fully linearize the blow-ups along at least one sequence. They apply the argument to two function classes tied to elasticity and image analysis, deriving flat limits at most points and naming the exceptional points where the method fails.
arxiv-2504-02990:
Matthew Fields and three co-authors wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on young stars and their disks. Planet-forming disks are usually assumed to line up with the spin of their star. Yet some disks look warped, so the team set out to measure how well the two really align.

Their paper lays out what must be measured, such as spin speed, star size, and spin period. It shows these values can often be pinned down within a small margin. A shared statistical model then corrects for bias across many systems at once. Tests on fake data recovered the true pattern well, even with a modest group of stars.
arxiv-2504-03790:
Goncalo Faria and Noah Smith wrote a machine learning paper in two thousand twenty-five on improving chatbot answers at reply time. Spending more compute while generating can lift quality when retraining is impossible or the model is private. But search methods guided by a reward model often overfit that imperfect guide as compute grows.

Their method, QAlign, samples replies instead of searching for a single best one. As compute scales, its output converges to the ideal aligned distribution for each prompt. It uses sampling methods borrowed from statistics and needs no access to the model's internals. Tests on math word problems show steady gains over common rivals.
arxiv-2504-04590:
Shreenanda Ghosh and co-authors use scattered light to probe a candidate exotic material in this 2025 paper. The compound, written V1/3NbS2, has been proposed as a Weyl semimetal, a material whose electrons behave as if they had no mass near special points. Proof needs evidence about both its electrons and its magnetism.
