Shining polarized light on the material, the team saw a smooth spread of electronic response that grows in a straight line with frequency. That shape is the expected sign of the special electron points in a flat, layered structure. Below fifty degrees above absolute zero, the light also showed paired magnetic waves near fifteen millielectronvolts. Calculations matched those waves and confirmed the magnetic order runs in opposing rows. Seeing both signs in the same spectra supports the claim that the material is a magnetic Weyl semimetal.
arxiv-2504-04890:
Nashed and Amare Abebe build a star model in a 2025 paper on an alternate form of Einstein's gravity theory. The theory is called the symmetric teleparallel equivalent of general relativity. The authors seek a model of a star that is the same in all directions, with no push toward any one axis.

They start from the theory's equations for a round sphere and face more unknowns than equations. To close the set, they fix one part of the metric by choice and set the uneven push to zero, which fixes the other part. They then test the model for stability with standard checks. The model also matches the known masses and sizes of several pulsars. The authors present it as a sound star model within this theory.
arxiv-2504-06490:
Xiang Chen, Xin Guan, and Bernhard Mistlberger push, in a 2025 paper, the precision frontier for the Higgs boson's commonest production channel. When a Higgs appears alongside a single jet of hadrons at a collider, predicting the rate exactly enough to test the Standard Model requires corrections order by order in the strong force. The team computed the third order, the three-loop corrections, for the scattering of a Higgs with three partons, working in a simplified limit that keeps the dominant color structure.

The results are written in a standard family of functions, multiple polylogarithms, ready to drop into prediction codes. They supply the missing ingredient for the production rate at proton colliders and for the Higgs decay rate into three jets at future lepton colliders. Papers like this are infrastructure: no plots of new particles, just the sharper arithmetic that lets experimentalists notice when nature disagrees with theory.
arxiv-2504-06690:
Sebastian Andres reviews recent progress on the Random Conductance Model, which describes a walker moving on a network whose links carry random strengths. The focus is homogenization: showing that, seen from far away, the messy random walk behaves like a clean, predictable diffusion.

The review stresses results that hold for almost every layout of the environment. These include central limit theorems describing the walk's spread, local versions that pin down probabilities at single points, and bounds on heat flow. The walk's link strengths may be unbounded, but they must meet certain average conditions. The piece surveys how far the theory has come for these degenerate environments, where some links can be arbitrarily weak.
arxiv-2504-07090:
Nicholas Kern presents a 2025 arXiv paper on a fully differentiable forward model for 21-centimeter cosmology. Radio telescopes hunting the faint hydrogen signal from the early cosmos must pick it out from blazing foregrounds and their own quirks. Kern's framework treats the signal, foregrounds, and instrument together, at field level, inside one Bayesian model.

With that design, samplers can climb its hundred-thousand-dimension landscape efficiently; a Hessian-tuned Monte Carlo does the search. A test on the HERA array's reionization hunt still found signals despite messy foregrounds. A new spherical harmonic basis for drift-scan surveys rounds out the toolkit.
arxiv-2504-07490:
Nanmanas Linphrachaya, Irving Gómez-Méndez, and Adil Siripatana try to locate geological resources from text alone, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Their test case is factory minerals, and the tool is natural language processing.

Word embeddings trained with the GloVe model capture meaning links between target keywords and a corpus of geological texts. Filtering keeps place-based words such as city names, ranked by cosine similarity to the target. Shrinking methods, from principal component analysis to variational autoencoders, sharpen the features. Checking the ten most related cities against known mine locations puts results in the right region, though accuracy still needs work.
arxiv-2504-07590:
Xingyuan Wei and co-authors published this computer security paper in 2025. It concerns harmful apps on Android phones, which attackers often disguise by scrambling their code, a trick called obfuscation. Detectors that read fixed features of an app can miss scrambled samples, while detectors that run the app are slow. The team set out to build a detector that stays accurate even when code is scrambled.

Their method scores each feature for importance and stability, keeps the ones that hold up under scrambling, and joins them with facts about the app's structure. A graph neural network then sorts the app into a malware family. The team tested 8,664 samples from eight families plus nearly 45,000 scrambled variants. Scores stayed high, with an F1-score above 92 percent on the scrambled set.
arxiv-2504-07790:
Bo Peng and Michele Pizzochero compute the electron behavior of ribbons made from fullerene cages, in work from 2025. Fullerenes are hollow carbon balls that can link into flat nets. Cutting those nets into thin strips yields ribbons whose traits may suit tiny devices.

Using first-principles math, the pair vary strip width and edge shape and track the results. Some ribbons let electrons cross a small energy gap head-on, while others force a slant path. Some bands are flat, which means heavy electrons, while others spread wide. The pair map this range in full, as a guide for later device design. Their work rests on known net forms, so builders can test the forecasts in the lab.
arxiv-2504-07990:
Mohammed Mallik, Laurent Clavier, and Davy Gaillot compare two neural network styles for mapping radio-frequency exposure across a city, in a 2025 paper. Knowing where electromagnetic fields are strong or weak guides health risk studies for people, wildlife, and plants. Seventy real sensors in Lille, France, supply sparse readings, far too few to draw the map directly. The authors test finite convolutional networks against their infinite-width counterparts for filling the gaps.

Both methods were judged on running time and on how well their maps match reality. The paper also looks at how to sharpen estimates at the high end, where accuracy matters most for safety. Sparse-sensor mapping of this kind could let cities chart exposure without blanketing every street in hardware.
arxiv-2504-08190:
Maldonado Naranjo and Annaswamy design adaptive control for a Dubins vehicle with loss of turning effectiveness, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Dubins vehicles move at fixed speed with bounded turn rate, modeling cars and aircraft. Actuator faults can sap turning authority mid-mission dangerously. A complex state-space model captures the vehicle dynamics compactly.

Adaptive control guarantees bounded closed-loop signals and path tracking despite the fault. Waypoint paths with minimum turn radius are specified via a reference model. Nominal design blends the complex model with a PID controller. Input constraints are handled by a modified design variant. Simulations complement the stability proofs throughout.
arxiv-2504-08490:
Robin Pesl's doctoral thesis from 2025 asks whether large language models can wire business software together on their own. Large firms run many services, each doing one job and described in a standard format. Linking them by hand is slow, while older automatic methods demand heavy formal modeling and saw little use in practice.

Pesl built an architecture that takes a plain-language request and returns a working composition as program code. Even when the output is not fully correct, it gives engineers a close draft that needs little fixing. The thesis also studies retrieval methods for finding the right services and proposes a benchmark for that search. Extending the tests to full compositions remains open work.
arxiv-2504-08590:
A large team led by Nicola Horst built Playpen, a place to test if word games can teach language models. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses dialogue games, which are rule-based games played mostly by talking. A learner plays the game, and the play gives feedback for training.

The team trained a small model, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, in three ways. Plain copying of good play helped on new rounds of known games but hurt other skills. A play-based method called GRPO gave gains with no such loss. The group shares the code and setups so others can build on this path.
arxiv-2504-12990:
Matteo Becchi and Giovanni Maria Pavan present a data-driven method for pulling the most information from data, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Trust in pulling information usually rests on prior knowledge or user experience. An objective criterion has been hard to define. Their approach uses Shannon entropy as a transferable yardstick.

Data are clustered into statistically relevant micro-domains, each carrying its own entropy. A first test uses molecular dynamics time series of water and ice coexisting at the melting transition. The method splits information in the distributions from extra gains in time correlations. Micro-domain entropies match experimentally known thermodynamic parameters. A second test on high-dimensional data carries a warning. Adding barely informative but noisy traits can harm information extraction.
arxiv-2504-13590:
Alexander Rusnak and Frédéric Kaplan bring open-vocabulary understanding, in a 2025 preprint, to city-sized clouds of 3D points. New methods let users query a 3D scene with any words, not just fixed labels. They work on room-sized scenes but choke on whole cities. The authors' method, HAEC, clusters a graph of superpoints, which are small same-looking patches of the cloud. A mixture-of-experts graph transformer does the heavy lifting. They run it on a city-scale dataset, a first for this task type.

Labels come from a pipeline that reads the raw point clouds alone. No hand annotation is used. The authors say this opens urban scans to queries. City digital twins could then answer questions about objects that no fixed label list foresaw. The approach is a path to working with the huge 3D maps cities now collect.
arxiv-2504-14390:
Steven Chaplick, Grzegorz Gutowski, and Tomasz Krawczyk settle the complexity of a graph problem in a twenty twenty-five note. In defensive domination, an attack is a small set of vertices, and a defense is a small set that can match each attacker to a nearby defender. The question is whether a fixed-size defense can counter every attack of a set size.

The problem was known to be hard, and it sits in a class above plain NP. The team proves it is complete for that class, the sharpest such result. A variant that lets the defense reuse vertices is just as hard, but on interval graphs it can be solved fast.
arxiv-2504-15490:
Harpreet Kaur and three co-authors compute weak long range forces between copper and silver atoms and a wide set of partner atoms, in this 2025 physics paper. These forces, called van der Waals dispersion forces, matter for work with ultracold atoms. The paper reports strength values for pairs of atoms and for triples, the latter capturing how a third atom shifts the pair force.

Partners span alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, zinc group metals, and several singly charged ions. To get the numbers, the team first worked out how each atom's charge cloud responds to an electric field over a range of frequencies, using relativistic methods. They check their values for copper and silver against known results, and compare the pair values with earlier reports in the field.
arxiv-2504-16890:
Lauren Conger and co-authors wrote a paper in 2025 on a game-like method for computing optimal transport plans. Optimal transport is a classic problem: how to move goods to where they are needed at the least total cost. The problem can be posed as a game between two players. One player picks the transport plan. The other prices each route.

At the point where neither player can gain by changing strategy, the plan is the optimal one. The team shows that paired gradient flows, run at separated timescales, converge to that optimal plan. Their implementation uses a particle method, in which a swarm of particles stands for the piles of goods. The constraints on the plan are enforced weakly, using a divergence score that tunes its own weight as the run proceeds. Tests compare the standard and reversed forms of that score, highlighting the advantages of each.
arxiv-2504-17790:
Kenta Kasai presents a construction for quantum error-correcting codes with girth sixteen, in a research paper from 2025. The codes build on non-binary low-density parity-check codes, whose graph structure sets error performance. Standard constructions with circulant matrices stop at girth twelve, since short cycles in the graph are hard to avoid.

Kasai uses affine permutation matrices with a randomized step-by-step selection that removes short cycles. The resulting codes hold far fewer low-weight codewords. Decoding tests over a depolarizing channel show a slight loss in one region but a large gain in the error floor. Distance bounds also beat standard constructions. The method suits fault-tolerant quantum hardware design.
arxiv-2504-18390: Ivan Hetman, Taras Banakh, and Alex Ravsky present a 2025 enumeration of special designs called unitals of order five. A unital of this order is a Steiner system with 126 points, where each block holds six points and each pair of points shares exactly one block. The authors count those whose symmetry group sweeps across all points at once, and those with a symmetry turning the rest around one fixed point. The census narrows where new unitals can hide and gives design theory a checked shelf of examples.
arxiv-2504-19090:
Hulya Atmacan and a large team of co-authors reported this detector paper in 2025. It describes the imaging Time-of-Propagation detector at Belle II, a particle experiment in Japan. The device tells apart pions, kaons, and protons by the Cherenkov light they shed while crossing polished quartz bars. The light bounces inside the bar to sensors at one end, while a mirror at the far end sends strays back.

Both the arrival times and hit spots of the light are logged. Together they fix the light's angle, which betrays the particle's kind for speeds up to a set range. The paper covers the build, the running, and the scores of the device. By its writing, the detector had logged nearly 600 inverse femtobarns of collision data. Such tagging is key to sorting the rare decays Belle II hunts.
arxiv-2504-19490:
Kiran Bajar, Ronen Shekel, Vikas Bhat, Rounak Chatterjee, Yaron Bromberg, and Sushil Mujumdar wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It speeds up the fix of warped wavefronts for photons that are entangled across space, a key stock for quantum tech.

Travel through tangled media bends the photons and spoils their links. The team notes that only the even part of the warp harms the pair signal. Their symmetrized genetic algorithm builds that fact in, which halves the search space. The fix then lands faster and lifts the signal more within a set count of rounds. They also map how the lift leans on the noise in the feedback signal.
arxiv-2504-21090:
Correia, Carvalho, and de Oliveira ask if a web-like link between parts of a quantum system is a must for a claim about heat and rest. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The claim, called typicality, says most single states of a big system look warm and settled. It swaps out the old mixed-set stance. In quantum work, the link, called entanglement, is often cast as a must-have.

The team tests pure states and tunes how much of this link each holds. When the link grows as the system grows, swings in measured things shrink at a fast, compounding pace. When the link stays fixed, swings shrink at the slow pace of the old, non-quantum case. So the link counts most for small quantum systems settling into heat. For big systems at rest, it is not a must, and that split is the point.
arxiv-2505-00190:
Hans Peter and Anders Sogaard test a cheaper way to build feature extractors from neural networks in a 2025 study. Sparse autoencoders pull readable features out of model activations, aiding interpretation and control. Training many sizes of them is expensive, yet users often need several sizes for different jobs.

The authors show that feature importance inside a standard autoencoder follows a power law, so a few features carry most weight. Progressive coding then prunes one large model into smaller nested ones. They compare that shortcut with training nested models jointly. The comparison tells practitioners when pruning alone gives good multi-size coverage for less compute.
arxiv-2505-00890:
Fabio van Dissel and Oriol Pujolàs describe a new kind of soliton wave in this 2025 paper. Solitons are self-held wave packets that keep their shape as they move. The new type, called soft oscillons, can grow to unlimited size, unlike the standard kind.

Their shaking rate is set by their size, and they carry a rich mix of tones that shapes a pulsing core. The waves appear in many field theories where the energy curve has a flat top. A large disturbance traps light modes inside itself, like a cavity, which holds the wave together. The authors study how fast the waves fade and how they handle uneven stretching.
arxiv-2505-01790:
Markos Stamatakis and co-authors test whether vision and language models can write good study questions for teaching videos, in a 2025 paper. Online videos teach flexibly, yet keeping viewers active is hard. Auto written questions could prompt thought and check grasp.

The team probed models as shipped, then after fine tuning on course content. They varied which video channels the model saw, from frames to speech, and judged the effect on question quality. Teachers rated sample questions for relevance, answerability, and difficulty. Raw models fell short on variety and fit, while tuning helped. The paper lists what future data sets need and where the work should head.
arxiv-2505-02090:
Lukas Nulens and co-authors demonstrate a memory cell that works at extreme cold, in this 2025 paper. Cold computing systems, both classical and quantum, need fast, low-power, reliable memory. Devices based on phase slips in superconductors promise those traits, but writing and reading them proved clumsy. The team stores each bit in the winding state of a superconducting loop.

The loop uses a material with high kinetic inductance and couples to a microwave resonator. The design borrows measurement tricks from quantum circuit work. A single-shot readout told the stored state correctly about 99.7 percent of the time. Each read took just twenty-five nanoseconds of active measurement. The authors present the simple design as a step toward practical cryogenic memory.
arxiv-2505-02190:
Reshetnyak wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on the theory of higher-spin fields. Such fields extend the idea of particles with spin to larger values, with mixed symmetry in some cases. Building action formulas that let these fields interact without contradiction is a long-standing hard problem.

The author works within a method that uses an incomplete BRST operator and added constraints applied off shell. The paper finds the exact conditions under which a consistent action can be built. The constraints must form a simple algebra with the operator and with the interaction terms. For the first interaction step, the term must solve a set of generating equations. Explicit forms are given using projectors onto the allowed modes.
arxiv-2505-04290:
Voronchikhin and Kirpichnikov hunt a scalar gate to dark stuff in beam dump tests in this twenty twenty-five paper. Dark stuff may come in two weights that swap by a light gate bit. Light dark stuff of that kind sits in a range lab beams can reach.

Inside, heat curves for the pair are drawn for a range of weight splits. Three beam tests are then graded on their reach for the gate's glow birth. The gate bit sheds to the dark pair in a hid step past its birth. Beam tests with both charge types split the hunt work by their own reach. The team maps which test rules which part of the dark range.
arxiv-2505-04490:
León-Torres and co-authors demonstrate a quantum microscope that images with mid-infrared light but detects only visible light in a 2025 paper. Mid-infrared light reveals chemical fingerprints of molecules, yet cameras for it are poor. A quantum trick uses paired photons: one probes the sample in the infrared while its twin is measured in visible light.

Earlier versions relied on spatial correlations between the twins, which are never perfect and blur the image. The new design scans point by point instead, sidestepping that limit. The result is a route to chemical imaging of lipids and other molecules with ordinary visible-light detectors, opening delicate samples to infrared inspection.
arxiv-2505-04590:
Alexandre Binninger and co-authors present TetWeave in 2025, a way to build the surface mesh of a 3D shape. Computer graphics often needs a clean mesh that wraps a shape's surface. A classic method cuts the shape with a grid of tetrahedra, small pyramid-like blocks, and reads the surface from the cuts.

TetWeave builds its grid fresh each time from the points at hand, rather than using a fixed grid. It also learns a signed distance at each point, which says how far the surface lies away. The meshes it makes are watertight and free of self-crossings. It can add points where the fit is poor, so detail lands where it counts. Memory use grows slowly with mesh size.
arxiv-2505-04790:
Gino Biondini and four co-authors build a spectral theory for a Dirac operator with a repeating potential. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The operator is not self-adjoint, which makes its spectrum harder to pin down. Their work is tied to a key wave equation, the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation, with repeating edge rules.

They frame the inverse task as a Riemann-Hilbert problem and prove that its solution is unique. That proof gives a fresh way to get the potential back from spectral data. The frame works for both finite- and infinite-genus potentials. As in the defocusing case, just one set of special values is enough to rebuild the potential.
arxiv-2505-05190:
Yixin Cheng, Hongcheng Guo, Yangming Li, and Leonid Sigal break text watermarks with SIRA, a cheap paraphrase attack that targets high-information tokens. Their paper from twenty twenty-five explains the flaw: watermark schemes hide their signals in high-entropy tokens to protect text quality. That design choice paints a target on exactly the tokens that carry the mark.

SIRA scores each token's self-information, flags the likely pattern carriers, and rewrites those spots. Seven recent watermarking methods fall at near-total success rates. The cost runs under a dollar per million tokens, and the attacker needs no access to the scheme or its model. Even phone-grade models can carry the attack. The authors call for watermark designs that survive targeted rewriting.
arxiv-2505-05390:
Jaeyeong Kim, Jeong-Eun Lee, Chul-Hwan Kim, Woong-Seob Jeong, and Yao-Lun Yang analyze ices around four protostars using spectra from the AKARI and Spitzer space telescopes, in a two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. Ice absorption features record the chemistry of material feeding young stars.

The team combined near- and mid-infrared spectra spanning 2.5 to 30 micrometers. After careful continuum and silicate subtraction, they fit laboratory ice data to separate each component. Water ice column densities come from two bands at once, and ammonia, methanol, carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide abundances are compared across evolutionary stages. Possible organic ices are also explored. The method transfers directly to James Webb Space Telescope spectra.
arxiv-2505-05890:
Dobrycheva and colleagues teach a neural network to spot polar ring galaxies, rare systems where a ring of stars and gas orbits over the host's poles. Such galaxies record ancient accretion and merger events, but catalogs hold only dozens. Training a finder on so few examples is the core difficulty. The team assembled eighty-seven strong and good candidates from existing catalogs as the seed sample.

Augmentation, segmentation, and ensembles all helped somewhat. Transfer learning with synthetic images rendered by a galaxy fitting code helped most, enlarging the training set convincingly. Run over a large survey's low-redshift galaxies, the system discovered three new polar ring galaxies. A visual sweep of about twenty-two hundred ring galaxies added four more by eye. One discovery's energy distribution was modeled in detail. Rare-object astronomy, the work shows, can bootstrap its own training data.
arxiv-2505-08890:
Beatrix Mühlmann, Vladimir Narovlansky, and Ioannis Tsiares derive three-point constants for a timelike Liouville theory. Conformal field theories are fixed by such constants, which set how fields combine. The theory here is a supersymmetric form with one unit of the N label. Its charge sits in the timelike regime, where signs flip against the spacelike case.

Bootstrap methods tie the constants to symmetry rules on the sphere. The results come out as inverses of the spacelike forms, a neat mirror. Shift rules in both spin sectors explain why the mirror holds. At special momenta, the constants match those of minimal models, as in the plain case. The authors eye a supersymmetric string model as a next use.
arxiv-2505-09690:
Robin Eappen and Pavel Kroupa ask whether modified gravity can grow supermassive black holes at galaxy centers as well as the standard picture does. Their framework is MOND, Milgromian dynamics, with no cold dark matter invoked. Monolithic collapse models of early-type galaxies, built earlier in this program, supply the test beds. Stellar masses span a good range of the observed population.

The young galaxies' gravitational wells deepen fast, and gas pours inward at high rates. Such conditions favor efficient central accumulation to feed a growing black hole. Assigning between ten and one hundred percent of the central stellar mass to the hole reproduces the observed mass-velocity dispersion relation, especially at high dispersions. Substantial inner collapse proves necessary. The authors conclude MOND's early gas dynamics naturally support the observed black hole scaling laws.
arxiv-2505-09890:
Daiki Miura and co-authors weigh the hidden partner in Cygnus X-3 with a new X-ray telescope. Their 2025 paper uses XRISM spectroscopy of iron emission lines. Cygnus X-3 pairs a compact object of unknown kind with a Wolf-Rayet star. Its orbit holds clues to mass transfer and binary evolution.

Iron lines were tracked across the orbit in a hypersoft state. Emission lines swing with the compact object's motion, at about four hundred thirty kilometers per second. Absorption lines instead trace the star's wind. Combining the swing with mass-loss clues bounds both partners' masses. The data narrow what the compact object could be. High-resolution spectra thus turn line wiggles into orbital evidence.
arxiv-2505-09990:
Cheng and fourteen co-authors present PointArena, a 2025 platform for testing how well AI models point at what language refers to. Pointing grounds words in the visual world, a skill robots and assistive tools need. Earlier benchmarks mostly checked simple object finding. PointArena adds a bench of about 1,000 pointing tasks across five reasoning types. It also adds a live arena where models duel blindly, already holding over 4,500 votes, and a robot arm setup for real-world trials.

Across open and proprietary models, Molmo-72B led, with commercial models closing in. Training aimed at pointing clearly boosted scores. Results across the three stages correlated strongly. The authors argue precise pointing is the hinge between abstract model reasoning and physical action.
arxiv-2505-11190:
Thaler and three co-authors release a software library that brings uncertainty-aware learning to the JAX computing platform. The library, JaxSGMC, implements sampling methods that estimate what a neural network does not know. These methods scale to large datasets and big models, suiting them to Bayesian deep learning.

The package ships several modern samplers and lets users snap together custom ones from standard parts. Lowering the switch from plain training to sampling, the authors argue, helps teams ship predictions with honest confidence ranges. They expect the modular design to speed research into new sampling schemes. The library is application-agnostic, fitting many domains.
arxiv-2505-11890:
Xue and eleven co-authors forecast power prices with language model help in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Electricity prices swing hard, and plain models miss the drivers. Their framework, FAEP, asks a large language model to craft better input features. Weather data and sudden price jumps join the raw series.

A retrieval system helps the model pull the right context for feature building. The enriched features then feed a hybrid of gradient boosting and a memory network. Tests ran on the New South Wales market in Australia, a famously volatile one. The framework topped rival predictors there. The authors credit the engineered features and hybrid design for the edge.
arxiv-2505-13090:
David Stap and Christof Monz wrote a 2025 paper on teaching large language models to translate. Past studies disagreed on whether training with many languages helps or not. Some found gains, others found none, and the split blocked clear advice.

The pair ran controlled tests across 132 translation directions. Adding languages helped both pairs with training data and pairs without any. More data in one pair did not beat a broader mix. Gains leveled off and then fell once diversity grew too large. They link the gains to internal codes that drift free of any one language. The results give trainers a clear rule for mixing languages.
arxiv-2505-13290:
Soon a new sky survey will watch exploding stars by the thousands, and those blasts can trace how fast space itself is growing. Bastien Carreres and the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration test that plan in a 2025 paper built on mock data. They fake ten years of survey records, add the drift of galaxies from a large computer run, and give each blast traits tied to its host galaxy.

For most ways of faking the spread in blast brightness, the growth rate came back clean and sharp. One dust-based model skewed it by about a fifth, since its errors lean to one side. Fixing that model did not blur the answer much. Most of the error stayed random, and the lead doubt sat with one term for how drifts fade with scale. The team urges new fixes for one-sided errors.
arxiv-2505-13390:
Soft-body animation, used for cloth, flesh, and rubbery objects, slows down when scenes get detailed and stiff. Chunlei Li and co-authors speed up a popular physics method, XPBD, whose solver stalls on slow, broad errors. Their solver, MGPBD, adds a multigrid method that fixes errors at several scales at once.

The design reuses costly setup work across steps, guided by the matrix structure, which trims the overhead that usually eats multigrid gains. A cheap routine builds the coarse problem's key components in a few sweeps. Tests show faster convergence and steadier results than the standard solver. High-resolution, high-stiffness scenes that once stalled now run efficiently. The authors present the method as a drop-in engine upgrade for interactive graphics and simulation.
arxiv-2505-13890:
Zhen Xiong and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on mapping the reasoning of large language models as a graph. New reasoning models think out loud in long chains, yet their behavior can be odd and unstable, dipping when given examples that help other models. The authors convert those chains into maps: first they cluster the wordy output into clean steps, then they draw arrows for the logical links between steps.

Across models and prompting styles, the maps' shapes tracked accuracy closely. How densely a model explored, how much it branched, and how often it converged all carried signal. Prompting choices visibly reshaped the graph, which in turn moved the score. That gives prompt designers a gauge beyond final answers. The team offers the framework as a tool for judging reasoning quality and for studying how these models think.
arxiv-2505-15490:
Isidora Jeknić, Alex Duchnowski, and Alexander Koller built a dialogue game in twenty twenty-five where two agents solve a traveling salesman problem together. Many tasks dialogue agents help with are hard optimization problems needing careful joint exploration, not one-shot answers. Their game makes partners negotiate a route through cities, turn by turn.

Their agent combines language model prompting with symbolic machinery that tracks the game state and grounds the conversation in the actual graph. In self-play it solved forty-five percent of games optimally. It also collaborated successfully with human partners and generalized to graphs it had never seen. The work offers a testbed for studying how conversational agents can genuinely co-reason about combinatorial problems instead of merely chatting about them.
arxiv-2505-16390:
Ken Chen and Zi-Gao Dai model what telescopes would see when a relativistic jet fires inside the disk of gas around a feeding black hole, in this 2025 paper. Some jets punch out of the disk and others choke inside it, and each path heats a cocoon of gas. The team follows the jet and cocoon together and computes the glow from each part.

Soft X-ray flares turn out to be the loudest signal, lasting from minutes to about a day and sometimes peaking twice. Ultraviolet and visible flares appear only for the strongest jets but can linger for days to weeks. Such thermal flashes could serve as light based partners for other signals from the same events. The authors stress quick multi wavelength follow up to tell these flares from the black hole's normal flicker.
arxiv-2505-16590:
Renyi Zhong and co-authors wrote this software engineering paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on writing log lines with small language models. Logs record what a program did and are vital for upkeep, but hand-written log lines are often sloppy or missing.

Big cloud models can write them, yet they raise privacy and cost worries for companies. The team ran the first large study of small open-source models on this task. Four models were tested with varied prompting styles and cheap fine-tuning tricks. A fine-tuned coder model beat existing tools and big-model baselines at picking where to log and what to write. It also held up across many unlike code bases. The authors say small local models are a private, cheap path to better logs.
arxiv-2505-18190:
Yuezhou Ma and five co-authors built a frame that places sensors and rebuilds fields as one job. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with physics sensing. Fields in science and machines must be read from sparse points, then filled in. Deep learning fills well, but past work takes sensor spots as given. That leaves a two way gain on the shelf: good spots ease the fill, and good fills show where spots pay.

Their frame, PhySense, runs in two stages that feed each other. A flow based model with cross focus fills the field from sparse reads. Spot picks are tuned to serve that fill. Readers in sensing get both halves of the task in one learn loop.
arxiv-2505-18590:
Zehao Wang and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on path planning for a truck with a trailer on curvy roads. The trailer's drift from the road's center line has no neat formula. That gap makes cost and edge rules hard to state in a solver. Fine time steps fix the truth of the motion model but swell the problem size.

They first state the drift in plain space terms by geometry. A coarse path then seeds the solver. Their frame starts with few sample points and adds more step by step, reseeding each round from the last. Tests in simulation and on real runs show good paths at less compute cost than rivals.
arxiv-2505-19090:
Si, Pei, Li, Pei, and Xie present a paper from twenty twenty-five on an ultra-light model for time series forecasting. Recent results hint forecasting tasks are simpler than assumed. Their model skips shape embeddings entirely. It instead maps how chunks of different series correlate in space. A mixing trick captures varied correlations with very few parameters. An optional rhythm injection speeds learning further. The model uses a tiny sliver of a known lightweight rival's size.

Tests still beat leading forecasters across many datasets. Learned weights read clearly, revealing time structure to users. Practitioners gain insight alongside accuracy. The authors rethink forecasting through chunk correlations.
arxiv-2505-20290:
Vincent Liu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on teaching robots from videos of people wearing smart glasses. Robots still trail humans at everyday manipulation, and robot-collected training data is scarce. Human hands, though, generate rich demonstrations all day. The EgoZero system learns from those alone, with zero robot data.

From egocentric video shot on Project Aria glasses, the system extracts complete actions a robot can execute. It compresses what the person sees into state descriptions that ignore body shape. Policies trained this way ran on a Franka Panda arm and transferred with no extra tuning. Across seven manipulation tasks they succeeded seventy percent of the time, from only twenty minutes of human video per task.
arxiv-2505-20590:
Xu-Jie Lin and co-authors study how people move through cities in linked trips, in a 2025 paper on tour behavior. A tour joins several stops into one chain, such as home to work to shops and back. Past models of city movement often skipped the length of such chains.

Using check-in data from the Foursquare app, the team found that tour length follows a cut-off power law. They then built a simple model in which each step either ends the tour or extends it. The model also matches known patterns for how people find new places and how far they range. City planners can use it to test travel choices.
arxiv-2505-21590:
Lorraine Saju and co-authors wrote a paper in 2025 on the computational reproducibility of R code supplements shared on a public repository platform. Being able to rerun published code is a foundation of sound science. Much shared code, however, lacks the documentation needed to recreate the environment it originally ran in.

The team assessed 296 R projects from a known data set. Of those, 264 could still be retrieved, and nearly all lacked a formal description of the software dependencies required to run them. The researchers built an automated pipeline that infers the dependencies directly from the source code, then executed each project inside a sealed container. Just over a quarter ran successfully to completion without error. Failures came from undeclared dependencies, invalid file paths, and system-level problems. The authors conclude that such pipelines can verify code at scale and make science more open.
arxiv-2505-21790:
Bandit algorithms learn by trial and error, choosing among options while seeing only the payoff of the choice they made. Hilal Asi, Vinod Raman, and Kunal Talwar ask how to run such learning while protecting the data behind the payoffs, under differential privacy. For adversarial settings, where payoffs can be arranged to mislead, they give a simple recipe that converts any ordinary bandit method into a private one.

The conversion beats the best regret bounds known before. It still learns well at privacy levels where local methods provably cannot, the first such separation for this problem. They also give the first private methods for learning from expert advice, with rates tuned to different mixes of actions and experts.
arxiv-2505-22190:
E Garrido and co-authors study how well a math method can describe three protons moving together, in a physics paper from 2025. Such three-particle data come from collider tests, where the pattern of motion, called a correlation function, reveals how the particles interact. Exact treatment must handle long-range electric force and the fact that the protons are identical.

An earlier study with the same method covered low energies near the peak of the pattern. New data reach higher energies, so the team checked how many states the method must include there. They show that states up to a high spin value are needed to match the tail of the pattern, while higher states can be treated as free. With those states in, the match to test data was excellent.
arxiv-2505-22590:
Paulo Luz and Filipe Mena prove that Einstein-Cartan gravity, Einstein's theory extended with torsion, has a well-set starting problem. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Torsion twists the connection of spacetime, making it lopsided, which complicates the classic proofs.

Following the path of a landmark theorem for Einstein's equations, the pair splits spacetime into space plus time. They derive the evolution and constraint equations for the twisted system, including the Gauss-Codazzi-Ricci relations with torsion. The constraints, they show, survive evolution. In a chosen gauge the system takes a form fit for a classic existence theory. Local well-posedness follows for smooth enough starting data. Zero torsion recovers Einstein.
arxiv-2505-23790:
Shaojie Wang, Sirui Ding, and Na Zou grade how well large language models hold the sense of a sentence, by a shared-news score. Past grades lean on set tasks, which mix sense with task craft. Their 2025 frame takes sense as the news kept from a sentence into its hidden form. Word-level shares sum to the sentence score, with bounds proved each way.

A floor for the word score comes from a known bound and turns on one test: can the source words be won back from the hidden form. Run that test and models can be ranked by kept news. Read-only models kept more news than write-on models, which shed news in late layers past a peak. Tuning to win words back raised task sense with no task training.
arxiv-2505-24190:
Nguyen and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about teaching image classifiers from very few labeled pictures. Adding made-up images can help, but fake images differ from real ones. That gap can drag a trained model down. The team built a theory frame that measures how the gap affects learning. From that frame they drew practical rules for making and using synthetic data.

Their algorithm mixes prototype learning with careful splitting of the data. Prototypes are average examples that stand for each class. Tests across several data sets beat leading past methods. The work matters because labeled data are often scarce and costly. A theory-backed way to use extra images could make small-sample learning more reliable.
arxiv-2505-24290:
Zhaopin Chen and co-authors published this attosecond physics paper in 2025. High-harmonic generation is the process where an intense laser drives a material to emit light at many times the laser's frequency. In gases, the driving pulse can exhaust the ground state, and the harmonics fade at the pulse's tail. The team reports the same kind of saturation in a solid: graphite, a gapless Dirac semimetal whose electrons behave as if massless.

Graphite generates harmonics at laser intensities far below what gases need, thanks to its vanishing bandgap. By adding a second laser color, the team watched the excitation of electron-hole pairs in real time. As hot carriers piled up near the Dirac points, one family of harmonics was suppressed and emission times shifted. Simulations based on semiconductor Bloch equations matched the picture. The authors present harmonic emission as a sensitive all-optical probe of ultrafast carrier dynamics.
arxiv-2506-00290:
Tianqi Chen, Shujian Zhang, and Mingyuan Zhou speed up diffusion language models in a 2025 study. Diffusion models build text by refining noisy drafts over many steps, which is slow. Their framework trains a student model to produce good text in a single step, guided by a trained teacher model.

Training aligns the student's output scores with the teacher's scores in the noisy space where diffusion operates. The method works across different model designs and two kinds of continuous representation spaces. Experiments report large speedups in steps and in clock time, with text quality staying competitive. The authors also study where one-step generation breaks down.
arxiv-2506-00790:
Joseph Strauss and four co-authors check how ready mobile apps are for quantum computing in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Quantum machines could break widely used codes such as RSA and ECC. New post-quantum standards exist, but phone apps may lag behind. The team scanned the code of more than four thousand Android apps. They looked for weak or soon-to-break crypto methods.

They found heavy use of dated tools like MD5, SHA-1, and RSA. No app in production used post-quantum methods. The team then tested whether large language models could fix the code on their own. The models handled simple swaps, such as moving from SHA-1 to SHA-256. None managed a full post-quantum upgrade, which spans many files. The study warns that app makers need better tools and plans for the shift.
arxiv-2506-01490:
Luo and five colleagues present a method to judge mood from mixed data when some data are missing in twenty twenty-five. Mood can be read from text, voice, and video at once. In real use, one or more of these streams often drops out. Older fixes rebuild the lost stream or force all streams into one shared form.

The new method scores how sure the model is about each mix of streams. A teacher form of the model then guides a student form to be less unsure. Tests on three standard data sets beat prior methods. The work aims to keep mood tools useful when inputs are patchy.
arxiv-2506-02490:
Yong Xiang and co-authors built a diagnostic assistant in 2025 for Kubernetes, the software that orchestrates most cloud applications. When a group misbehaves, builders must find the root cause inside a sprawling system of controllers forever reconciling desired and actual state, where failures, network hiccups, and timing races tangle. Language models could help, but incidents are diverse, fast-evolving, and context-heavy, which defeats naive prompting.

Their tool, SynergyRCA, grounds the model in two graphs built from the group itself: a StateGraph catching how resources relate across space and time. And a MetaGraph outlining the entities and their links. When an incident fires, the model first predicts the most related resource, then the system queries both graphs and hands the model context-certain evidence, supplemented by expert-written prompts. The authors test the tool on incident data sets from two sources.
arxiv-2506-02990:
Lorantos and Spector seek open ended growth in a digital life system called Lenia in twenty twenty-five. Lenia hosts smooth, cell based worlds where forms drift, split, and change. Keeping such worlds inventing new forms forever is a core hard problem in artificial life. Their method ranks each form by how it stacks up against its peers.

Forms gain rank for being unlike others, for living in sparse zones, and for keeping inner balance. That mix pushes the search toward fresh, varied forms without capping what can emerge. Tests showed the ranking kept exploration broad and lively. The authors argue this inner drive is a step toward truly open ended evolution.
arxiv-2506-03290:
Optical flow, the map of how each pixel moves between two frames, is usually refined by a fixed number of passes in today's neural networks, easy frames and hard frames alike. Leyla Mirvakhabova and co-authors replace that fixed count in a 2025 paper with a smooth model borrowed from differential equations. The network learns the rate of change of the flow, and a solver walks it to a settled state.

Because the walk can stop early or run long as the input demands, compute follows difficulty. With the right setup the smooth model can copy the exact updates of the step cells used in older networks, so nothing is lost. On standard flow benchmarks it beat the base models while taking a single refinement step, a rare mix of better and cheaper.
arxiv-2506-03590:
Minh Luu and co-authors present VCDiag, a tool that sorts failed chip tests by their likely cause, in a paper from 2025. Checking why a chip design failed is slow work done by hand. Engineers read specs, logs, and wave traces to find the fault. Machine learning has helped other test tasks, but not this sorting step for large designs.

The tool reads the wave data saved from a failed run. It picks the key signals and shrinks the data by more than a hundred fold, while keeping what matters. A classifier then ranks the parts of the design most likely at fault. In the largest test, the true fault sat in the top three ranked parts more than ninety-four times in a hundred. The tool fits many design styles and test setups.
arxiv-2506-03990:
Hongzhi Zhang and co-authors present DynTok, a method to shrink visual tokens for video understanding, in a research paper from 2025. Video models turn frames into long token lists, which cost much compute, above all for long videos. Cutting tokens before the main model runs can save that cost if key content survives.

DynTok groups visual tokens in an adaptive way and merges each group. Dense regions keep more detail, while sparse regions compress hard. The token count falls to under half with like task scores. Adding more frames helps further. Tests on two video benchmarks score well. The method shows how much slack video tokens hold.
arxiv-2506-04190:
Yuxuan Cao and six co-authors borrowed outside graph data to help spot odd nodes in a graph, in a paper published in 2025. Odd node hunts face thin labels, vague definitions of oddity, and mixed kinds of anomalies. Learners that use only their own data need a full map of the normal, which thin data cannot give. Their framework first builds a wide bank of graphs from many fields, all in one feature space.

Selection rules then choose bank graphs that fit the task, both close relatives and wide-spread examples. On six real datasets the framework beat the best rivals by clear steps on two scores. The authors say outside data, picked with care, fills the gap in knowledge of the normal. The bank and rules free others to reuse the method.
arxiv-2506-04390:
Sarthak Choudhary and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a quiet weakness in retrieval-augmented chatbots. These systems fetch passages to ground their answers, and attackers slip in poisoned text that bends the reply. The authors show current attacks are loud: a few planted passages shout over the honest ones, which makes them detectable.

They frame stealth as a formal game about telling poisoned from clean runs. Any attack strong enough to steer the answer must lean on the model harder than honest text does. That lean shows in the model's attention weights. Their score and filter use uneven attention to flag planted passages, lifting defense accuracy by up to about twenty percent. Attackers who adapt still fail most of the time.
arxiv-2506-04890:
Fredrik Cumlin and co-authors present a joint model of speech quality in this 2025 paper. The usual quality score is a single average opinion number. A low score alone does not say what went wrong. The NISQA dataset rates four extra traits, covering noisiness, coloration, discontinuity, and loudness.

Their model predicts all five scores together as a multivariate Gaussian distribution. A Cholesky decomposition lets the covariance stay flexible without hard assumptions. Affine transforms from earlier work are extended to the joint setting. Point predictions matched the best prior methods. The model also yields uncertainty and correlations between traits. Engineers can thus see which flaw drives a poor score and fix that flaw first.
arxiv-2506-05490:
Mohammed Almutairi explores, in a 2025 paper, adding sentiment analysis to online learning platforms. When classes moved online during the pandemic, teachers lost the facial cues that show how students feel, and written feedback alone can hide confusion or frustration.

The proposed system reads student comments for emotional tone at scale. A deep neural network using word embeddings, memory cells, and an attention step was trained for the task and compared with a simpler statistical baseline. The aim is to give teachers a live read on class mood, so they can adjust pace and support. The work frames emotion-aware feedback as one bridge across the online communication gap.
arxiv-2506-05790:
Minghan Wang and co-authors wrote this study in 2025 on whether language models sense time passing. The models ace tasks like ordering events, yet no one had asked if they feel duration itself. The team set three tests. First, a Token-Time Hypothesis: models may map counts of text tokens to real clock time. A dialogue-length judging task backed that link.

Second, when users signaled hurry, models trimmed their answers while keeping accuracy, as if aware of the clock. Third, a game called BombRush put models under rising time pressure in a maze, and they changed tactics as the fuse shrank. The sense of time proved real but uneven, growing with model size and reasoning skill. The authors lay ground for time-aware tools in urgent settings.
arxiv-2506-07090:
Fontoura and co-authors model, in a 2025 physics paper, how heavy-flavor hadrons are born when atomic nuclei smash together at near light speed. The crash creates a hot quark-gluon plasma, and as it cools, heavy quarks must gather into finished particles.

The team uses a coalescence model, in which nearby quarks merge into hadrons as the plasma freezes out. Particle wave functions come from one shared quark model, so normal mesons, baryons, and exotic four-quark states are all predicted in a single frame. They compute yields and momentum spreads for many species. The study also tracks how a partial return of a broken symmetry at the freezing temperature shifts the output.
arxiv-2506-07290:
James Alcala, Yat Tin Chow, and Mahesh Sunkula give moving-anchor algorithms a stochastic form in two thousand twenty-five. Anchor methods speed up extragradient schemes for saddle problems, the tug-of-war tasks behind much machine learning. Their proofs, though, assumed exact answers from the oracle, while real problems use noisy samples.

The team moves the anchor step by step rather than fixing it, and lets the oracle answer with random draws. They prove fast convergence still holds in that noisy world, and bench tests back the math. A trial Popov variant, a leaner cousin scheme, also shows promise, hinting at a wider theory still to be built. The work bridges tidy proofs and messy practice.
arxiv-2506-07690:
Alexander Bakhtin, Matteo Esposito, Valentina Lenarduzzi, and Davide Taibi published this paper in 2025. It looks for early warning signs that a microservice system is rotting. Such systems split software into many small services linked as a network, and their structure decays quietly over time.

The team rebuilt the architecture of an open-source project across seven releases, covering forty-two services. For each service they computed size, complexity, and network centrality scores, which grade how central a service sits. They also coined a new score for how prone each service's centrality is to change. Centrality tracked steadily with several size and complexity measures. The new score did not drive those measures, which makes it a fresh, independent signal. The authors offer it as an early indicator teams can watch.
arxiv-2506-08690:
Hugo Porta and co-authors present CanadaFireSat in 2025, a data set for forecasting wildfire across Canada at fine scale. Canada's severe 2023 fire season showed how much boreal communities need better warning tools. Earlier models used coarse data and predicted fire risk on grids near ten kilometers wide, too rough for local planning.

Their benchmark targets forecasts at one hundred meter resolution. It joins high-resolution satellite images, mid-resolution satellite products, and weather reanalysis data as inputs. Tests with two deep learning designs showed that mixing these input types beat using any one type alone across all measures, with peak performance near sixty percent on their main metric. The data set gives fire researchers a shared, sharper test bed.
arxiv-2506-10190:
Abhay Ashtekar and Badri Krishnan prove constraints on symmetry near growing black holes in this two thousand twenty-five general relativity paper. A dynamical horizon is a surface tracing a black hole as it gains mass, foliated by marginally trapped two-spheres. The authors ask what Killing fields, the spacetime symmetries, can exist in a neighborhood of such a horizon segment. Intuition might allow many, but the geometry is restrictive.

Generically, the only allowed Killing field is a rotational one, and it must leave every marginally trapped cross-section of the horizon invariant. If the field is also hypersurface orthogonal nearby, the conclusion sharpens dramatically: angular momentum and every spin multipole vanish on all cross-sections. Such horizons are then indistinguishable in their entire spin structure from spherically symmetric ones. The result limits how asymmetric a growing black hole's surroundings can be.
arxiv-2506-10290:
Tiankuo Zhang and co-authors study how small freight carriers could cooperate through shared hubs instead of hauling shipments end to end. Less-than-truckload shipping is fragmented: many carriers serve their regions, disconnected from one another, wasting capacity and keeping drivers on long hauls. Following Physical Internet ideas, the paper builds an optimization model consolidating relay loads, coordinating shipments, and synchronizing driver hand-offs across a hyperconnected network.

A simulation of the eastern United States compares three worlds: carriers alone with end-to-end trips, carriers using relays, and all carriers in the shared network. The comparison scores cost, trip duration, and greenhouse gas emissions. The authors present relay cooperation as the lever improving all three while letting drivers work short legs near home. The work is a blueprint for an industry built on rivals. Its promise depends on competitors trusting a shared schedule.
arxiv-2506-10990:
Roberto Vergallo and co-authors test a Follow-the-Sun plan for cutting the carbon cost of AI work in the cloud, in a research paper from 2025. The plan moves computing jobs around the globe to wherever clean power is most available at that hour. Whether it truly helps AI training had not been measured.

The team benchmarked four anomaly detection algorithms under four plans: no plan, Follow-the-Sun, and two known rivals. They used real carbon intensity records from 2021 for seven European cities. Follow-the-Sun cut emissions by up to 14.6 percent on average, with a peak cut of 16.3 percent. It also kept training time about the same, unlike plans that pause work and wait.
arxiv-2506-11090:
David Palzer and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a compact system that tells who speaks when, in a recording of mixed speech, a task called diarization. The task is hard: it needs clean representations for each voice, efficient work, and robustness under rough conditions. Their system joins three parts. A deep listening network reads the recording. Anchor points, called attractors, are refined by a transformer. A clustering technique then sorts the anchor points by type.

The clustering technique is extended here, with label vectors built for each anchor point. The embeddings are aligned by their direction, not just their position. Set rules keep active anchors apart and suppress inactive ones, so a silent voice is not falsely called active. A final loss function, blind to the order of speakers, trains the detection of who is speaking. The system achieves low error rates while staying small, the team says.
arxiv-2506-13090:
Chidera Biringa and Gökhan Kul use language models to find hard-coded secrets in software code stores. Their 2025 paper covers passwords, private keys, and tokens that developers leave in code by mistake. Such secrets open a path for attackers to slip into systems.

Older tools turned secrets into number codes and sorted them with classifiers, but they flagged too many false hits. This team feeds model-based codes into a deep learning classifier instead. Language models read the context around a string, which helps tell real secrets from look-alikes. Their model beat the best prior tool by a clear margin on a benchmark test. They also shared their code and data, so others can check and build on the result.
arxiv-2506-13590:
Ken Huang, Akram Sheriff, Vineeth Sai Narajala, and Idan Habler propose a protocol for cooperation among software agents in a 2025 study. Modern multi-agent systems mix agents with different skills and owners. Older communication rules assumed similar agents or fixed patterns, which breaks down in open and changing settings.

Their protocol covers discovery, negotiation, and binding of capabilities between agents. It works with a naming service that helps agents find and verify each other. A structured process with ten steps takes a pair from first contact to a confirmed working link. The design stresses security and verifiability, so agents can team up without prior trust.
arxiv-2506-14190:
Tuan Nguyen and Huy-Dat Tran improve speech recognition for speakers who switch languages mid-sentence, using Malay and English as the test case. Code-switched speech is scarce and expensive to collect, while earlier fixes synthesized audio from text at heavy computational cost. Their framework, AsyncSwitch, leans on plentiful text instead.

Training runs in three stages. First the decoder learns from code-switched text alone, then cross-attention aligns it with the encoder using limited paired speech, and finally the whole model fine-tunes. On Whisper, word error rate fell by about nine percent relative. Monolingual performance in Singlish, Malay, and other English variants improved at the same time.
arxiv-2506-14990:
Ten researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five introducing a benchmark for learning agents that must keep learning. Most tests of continual learning use only a handful of tasks in sequence, because the simulators run slowly on ordinary processors. Learning in teams of cooperating agents was barely explored at all.

Their benchmark, MEAL, uses GPU acceleration to run sequences of one hundred tasks in a few hours on a single graphics card. It targets cooperative multi-agent learning specifically. Long sequences expose failure modes that short ones hide, the authors find, which changes what researchers should measure.
arxiv-2506-15090:
Nikhel Gupta and eight co-authors present EMUSE, a search engine for radio sources in the vast data of the Evolutionary Map of the Universe survey. The same tool may serve other big data tasks in astronomy. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The engine fine tunes the OpenCLIP foundation model on a curated set of thousands of radio galaxies. Classes span the main shapes plus rare and odd forms. Adapter based tuning keeps compute low while catching what makes radio sources distinct. Users can then search the survey by image or by text. Results show strong recall of clear shapes, though rare forms stay hard to spot.
arxiv-2506-15190:
Jiyi Wang, Jingyang Ke, Bo Dai, and Anqi Wu published a 2025 paper on discovering the reusable building blocks of animal movement. Animals meet endless situations by recombining a small set of core motor motifs. Earlier analysis tools chopped behavior into discrete syllables, neat but forced: real movement flows continuously, blending one motif into the next. The authors' framework learns the motifs and the blending together.

Their method represents behavior as a continuously shifting mixture of latent basis patterns, found from the structure of transitions in recordings. It was validated on a gridworld task, a labyrinth navigation task, and freely moving animals. Across settings it recovered reusable components and generated realistic movement trajectories. The payoff is a cleaner language for neuroscience. Instead of asking which syllable an animal is in, researchers can ask how its motif mixture evolves, moment by moment, as it solves its world.
arxiv-2506-15790:
Chenyang Peng and co-authors present ETrace in this 2025 paper, a tool for finding flaws in smart contracts. Smart contracts run on blockchains, and bugs in them can cost users dearly. Older checkers mostly read the contract code, yet code is not always open to view.

ETrace works instead from event logs left by past transactions. It pulls fine-grained event sequences from those logs and uses a large language model to rebuild what happened, step by step. Pattern matching then links the behavior to known attack styles. Early tests suggest the approach can flag real flaws without ever seeing the source code.
arxiv-2506-15890:
Thomas Manzini and co-authors report a 2025 field account of drone aid after two hurricanes. Small drones flew over storm damage in Florida for Hurricanes Debby and Helene. A learning system read the images to grade damage. The authors say the review of past work suggests a first: a drone learning system used in real storm response, not just in tests.

Four main problems slowed or blocked the flow of results to response teams. The flights still gathered large stitched images over a few trips. The authors set out three research paths to fix the weak points. Response planners can see what breaks when lab tools meet real storms. Drone teams get plain lessons on data, timing, and trust. The paper values honest field limits over clean lab scores, which makes it useful for the next storm season.
arxiv-2506-16490:
Yifan Jin, Alexander Kiselev, and Sean Stoll present a 2025 paper that measures how well a new photon detector catches single photons. The device, a high-rate picosecond photon detector, is bound for ring-imaging Cherenkov cameras that need fine detail on place and timing. Its quantum efficiency had been reported, but the real rate folds in collection losses too.

Using a pulsed diode laser, the team counted photoelectron pulses at one pixel near the center of the device. The detection efficiency came out at about 17.1 percent at a wavelength of 398.6 nm. Quantum efficiency at the same spot was about 24.4 percent. Dividing the two gives a collection efficiency near 70 percent, in line with hopes. The check anchors performance claims for the coming collider detectors.
arxiv-2506-16590:
Deng and co-authors propose a safer way to transfer knowledge from a trained teacher agent to a new reinforcement learning task. A teacher can guide exploration, but bad guidance hurts when the new task differs too much. Their method uses energy scores to detect when the learner wanders outside the teacher's experience.

The teacher then steps in only for states it knows well. Theory links the energy scores to how often states get visited during training. Tests in single-task and multi-task settings show faster learning and better final performance. The authors aim the method at continual learning, where agents face a stream of related tasks.
arxiv-2506-17090:
Murtaza Nazir, Matthew Finlayson, John Morris, and a wider team wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It recovers the hidden prompts fed to a language model, including secret system messages, from nothing but the model's own output probabilities.

Prompt inversion matters because a leaked system message can expose private instructions. The key insight is geometric: a model's next-token probability vectors live in a low-dimensional subspace. So the full distribution across many generation steps can be compressed without loss by a linear map, preserving far more evidence for the detective work. The resulting method multiplied exact recovery rates two to three and a half times over prior art, in one case from seventeen to sixty percent. An inverter trained on short generations even improved when given longer ones at test time.
arxiv-2506-17190:
Mauricio Gutiérrez and three co-authors compare chip designs for quantum error correction in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their platform is spin qubits in silicon, held in dots of charge. They test two codes, the surface code and the Bacon-Shor code, on flat arrays of dots. Two qubit styles are compared: plain Zeeman qubits and a hybrid that mixes in singlet-triplet qubits.

They judge how well logical states can be prepared and how a full correction cycle performs. Real lab parameters feed the simulations. The hybrid style beat the plain one across both codes. The study names the error types that hurt most. Hardware teams get concrete targets for the next design round.
arxiv-2506-17290:
Yuqi Li and co-authors shrink large three-dimensional scene models by teaching a small model to copy a big one, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Point clouds are sets of dots in space, and labeling each dot is costly with big transformer models. Their student model holds under a seventh of the teacher's size.

Copying runs on three tracks: shape relations between points, stable structure across samples, and meaning distributions. A similarity grid carries the shape lessons from teacher to student. Ground truth labels add a final guide. The small model hit top scores with far less bulk, aiding real deployment.
arxiv-2506-17590:
Mihir Godbole, Xiangbo Gao, and Zhengzhong Tu build DRAMA-X, a fine-grained test for how driving models read the intent of people on foot and on bikes. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes a gap: no benchmark grades multi-class intent in risky scenes. Vision-language models give open-vocabulary sight, yet their intent skill was untested. The set grows from the DRAMA data by an automated labeling pipeline.

Thousands of accident-prone frames carry boxes, nine-way directional intent labels, and binary risk scores. Expert action advice for the ego car and motion summaries ride along. Four tasks are graded: detection, intent, risk, and action choice. A training-free baseline, SGG-Intent, reasons over scene graphs step by step. Recent vision-language models were scored across all tasks. Graph-based reasoning lifted intent and risk marks most when context was spelled out.
arxiv-2506-17690:
Julian Herreilers, Christiaan Jacobs, and Thomas Niesler introduce, in 2025, a method to spot keywords in radio speech for languages with almost no training data. Their model learns sound-based word embeddings, fingerprints of spoken words, trained by contrasting matched and unmatched pairs. Tests used broadcasts in Luganda and in Bambara, a severely under-resourced language.

The transformer-based model beat several rivals, including embeddings from large pre-trained speech models and a classic time-warping method. Gains held in both languages. Keyword spotting is a first step toward searchable audio archives in such languages, where transcribing everything is impossible. The work shows contrastive training squeezes much from little data.
arxiv-2506-17890:
Tobias Weinberg, Claire O'Connor, Ricardo Gonzalez Penuela, Stephanie Valencia, and Thijs Roumen study how users of communication aids give small signals during talk. Their paper from twenty twenty-five covers backchanneling: the nods, hums, and short sounds that keep a chat flowing. These signals show listening and shape turn-taking. For people with speech and motor limits, channels for such signals shrink.

A workshop with aid users probed how they signal while talking. Pairs of aid users were compared with mixed pairs. Speech-language pathologists added depth in interviews. Users build their own channels and norms, a micro-culture of signaling. Attention demands of the gear make partner cues hard to catch. The authors rethink body and mediation in this setting. They close with design advice for timely, multi-channel backchannel tools.
arxiv-2506-20290:
Berkay Kemal Balioglu and co-authors uncover an unfairness hidden in privacy tools in a 2025 paper. Local differential privacy lets people share data with noise added on their own device, so no raw values leave their hands. Many such protocols use hash functions, a scrambling step, to encode each value before the noise is added.

The authors show the choice of hash function changes how exposed a user is. People under the same protocol and privacy budget can face very distinct risks of inference or poisoning attacks, based only on which hash they drew. To fix this, they propose a variant of a known protocol that screens hash choices with an entropy-based fairness rule. Tests showed the fix cut the unfairness with only a modest time cost. The work warns that small design choices can quietly split users into safe and exposed groups.
arxiv-2506-20790:
Lucius Bushnaq, Dan Braun, and Lee Sharkey decompose neural network weights into sparse, studyable parts with Stochastic Parameter Decomposition. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works inside linear parameter decomposition, which writes a network's parameters as a sum of rarely used vectors. The prior method in that frame was too costly and touchy about hyperparameters to scale. SPD replaces its brittle core with a stochastic procedure.

Toy models show SPD recovering the true mechanisms without shrinking the learned parameters. It also decomposes models slightly larger and more complex than its predecessor managed. The authors bridge causal mediation analysis with decomposition technique and release their library openly. Mechanistic interpretability gains a sturdier wrench for taking networks apart.
arxiv-2506-20890:
Dmitry Ammosov, Mohammed Al Kobaisi, and Yalchin Efendiev build in 2025 a cheaper way to model flow in rock that also bends under pressure. Such poroelastic models matter for reservoirs and groundwater, but real rock mixes soft and stiff zones so sharply that standard averaging fails.

Their method defines several overlapping average states, one per material type, and derives the equations linking them with care. Small test problems in oversampled patches capture the local effects. The result is a model family ranging from fully general to simplified versions guided by experiments. Tests on varied rock patterns showed high accuracy against fine-scale solutions, at far lower cost.
arxiv-2506-20990:
Tuning a vision-language model usually needs gradients, which edge devices cannot spare. Yifan Yang and co-authors offer a tuning method that uses only forward passes. Their approach runs in two stages. First, a sharpness-aware search explores widely and smooths the loss surface, yielding a strong start. Then a sparse local search refines the prompt with small probes. No backpropagation appears anywhere in the pipeline.

Experiments on CLIP models show gains of up to seven percent over the best forward-only rivals. Convergence also came faster. Theory sections back the design choices. Prompt tuning that fits on memory-tight hardware could bring smart vision to cameras and phones. The method trades gradient access for clever searching.
arxiv-2506-21490:
Tin Dizdarević leads a ten-author team launching a benchmark challenge for human-AI teamwork, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Their testbed is Hanabi, a cooperative card game with hidden information. Players must communicate within strict limits and reason about each other's minds.

Testing AI agents with real humans is expensive and hard to reproduce. The challenge instead supplies human proxy agents trained on a large human dataset. These proxies act as cheap, repeatable, human-like partners. To encourage data-efficient methods, the team open-sources a deliberately limited dataset of 3,079 games. Competitors must build agents that coordinate well with the proxies. The setup aims to make human-AI coordination research measurable at last.
arxiv-2506-22290:
Bougas and co-authors propose a way to test the stiffness and flow of dipolar supersolids, a strange state of ultracold matter. Their paper appeared in 2025. A supersolid acts both like a crystal, with a fixed pattern, and like a superfluid, which flows without friction. The team modeled two fragments held apart in a double well, then let the barrier drop.

In the model, supersolid fragments swing back and forth, and the swing fades at a rate set by how well the superfluid links them. A sudden phase jump also stirs dark solitons, lone dips that travel through the fluid. These stir a second kind of sound, where the crystal pattern and the fluid drift against each other. The authors say the setup gives labs a real path to detect second sound and stiffness in supersolids.
arxiv-2506-22590:
Counting the whole-number grid points inside a shape is a classic problem in number theory. The hard part is pinning down the error size between the count and the shape's volume. Nilmoni Karak studies this error for bodies of revolution, shapes made by spinning a smooth curve around a coordinate axis in three dimensions. Their boundary curves gently and never flattens out. Work by Kühleitner and Nowak set a lower bound on how large the error must sometimes be.

Using a resonance method developed by Mahatab, Karak proves a stronger lower bound, called an omega estimate. The result says the counting error cannot stay as small as one might hope; for this family of shapes, it must reach the stated size at arbitrarily large scales. The paper is a short advance in analytic number theory, improving the record for this shape class.
arxiv-2506-23190:
Kamran Shafafi, Manuel Ricardo, and Rui Campos park flying base stations where their signals can actually see the users. Drones serving as aerial access points patch coverage gaps and traffic surges, but city buildings block line-of-sight links. Their algorithm, VTOPA, reads the environment with computer vision. Obstacles and user locations are extracted automatically, and the drone positions itself accordingly.

Line-of-sight connectivity is the priority, with real-time adaptation to shifting traffic demand. Network simulations in obstacle-rich scenes show aggregate throughput rising by up to half. Delay fell by up to half as well, without sacrificing fairness among users. Benchmark approaches trailed in the same cluttered settings. Vision, usually a payload for other missions, here becomes the radio planner's eyes.
arxiv-2507-00490:
Zijian Chen and a team of co-authors published a 2025 study of the smallest visual change that large AI models can notice. For humans, this threshold is called the just noticeable difference. The authors asked whether today’s multimodal models, which combine vision and language, share similar blind spots.

They built a dataset of 21,500 reference images and nearly half a million altered versions across twelve distortion types. Leading models, including GPT-4o, often failed simple comparison questions that humans find easy. The design of both the vision and language parts shaped how sharp the model’s eye was. The authors argue that measuring this threshold matters for safety and efficiency. Their benchmark gives the field a shared yardstick.
