arxiv-2507-00790:
Huaqiu Li and five co-authors restore damaged photos with no task-specific training. Their 2025 paper presents LD-RPS, a zero-shot image restoration method. Classic restorers are built per flaw or trained on paired examples. Both habits trap them in closed sets of damage types.

A pretrained latent diffusion model supplies the image sense. Sampling runs in rounds, steering each pass toward the clean picture. A vision-language model adds meaning cues without knowing the flaw. A light module aligns the damaged input with the model's taste. Across tests, the method beat leading rivals in quality and steadiness. One blind tool now handles many kinds of damage.
arxiv-2507-01190:
Shokhruz Kakharov and Abraham Loeb calculate how much of the dark matter near Earth comes from beyond our galaxy in this 2025 paper. Direct detection labs hunt dark matter particles passing through Earth. Most are assumed to belong to the Milky Way. The team used the galaxy's escape speed, by direction, as the sieve. Particles too fast for the galaxy's grip count as outsiders. About a quarter of local particles qualified as extragalactic.

Those outsiders carry an outsized share of the mass flow. Their share also varies strongly across the sky. Detectors could see that directional pattern in their rates. The predictions give experiments a new signature to hunt. Local Group surroundings supply the incoming particles. The paper is theoretical astrophysics.
arxiv-2507-02190:
Max Argus and six co-authors move robot action prediction into the camera's own frame to cut training cost. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works on vision-language-action models, which turn sight and text into robot motion. Past models emit low-level controls and train at great expense. Their cVLA instead predicts path waypoints as seen in the image.

A next-token design learns those waypoint paths from demonstrations. Robot shape drops out of the output, so one model serves many bodies. Depth images, decoding tricks, and demo-conditioned generation are probed for extra gains. Training runs on simulated data, yet the skill carries to real hardware. Tests mix simulated and real trials. The authors claim strong transfer for a light build, which suits labs without huge compute.
arxiv-2507-02990:
Annika Schoene and Cansu Canca show how crafted prompts can trick chatbots into giving self-harm instructions, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Safety filters are meant to block such content, yet creative multi-step prompting can slip past them. The authors built two test cases, one on suicide and one on self-harm.

Across six widely used models, the bypass worked reliably, and the systems produced detailed harmful content. User intent, the authors note, was effectively ignored once the framing took hold. They weigh the tangled ethics of publishing such tests and urge systematic adversarial testing for safety-critical systems. Some guardrails are a must, they argue, but total safety across all uses remains out of reach for today's general models.
arxiv-2507-04190:
Anqi Yang and co-authors propose, in a 2025 imaging paper, camera sensors whose gain and pixel grouping change from place to place within one shot. Shrinking pixels gather less light, so resolution gains usually cost noise and dynamic range.

Matching gain to local brightness can make read noise negligible and stretch dynamic range about tenfold, the authors show. A simple analysis then picks the pixel binning size that best trades sharpness against noise at each light level, again varying across the scene. Surprisingly, digital binning beats analog when larger gain is allowed. Demonstrations cover high dynamic range scenes, vignetting, and lens distortion.
arxiv-2507-04290:
Weilun Feng and co-authors present MPQ-DMv2 in a 2025 paper on shrinking diffusion models for edge devices. Such models generate strong images but cost much compute. Quantization, storing numbers in fewer bits, can speed them and save memory, yet very low bit settings break existing methods.

The team identify problems in quantizer design, starting values, and training strategy. Their framework adds a residual branch that handles outlier values with flexible steps. A temporal distillation idea guides training across time steps. Analysis of a common adapter module supports the design, aiming at two to four bit models that still perform.
arxiv-2507-04590:
Rui Meng and co-authors widen the reach of multimodal search in this 2025 paper. Embedding models turn pictures and text into numbers that can be matched, powering search and clustering. Most were raised on natural photos and stumble on videos and document pages, which real systems handle daily.

The team built a new version of their model to embed text, images, video, and visual documents in one space. They also built a benchmark adding five task families, from video retrieval and moment finding to document search and video questions. Trained on the mix, the model scored strongly on the new video and document tasks and improved on the older image tests as well. The authors use the results to draw lessons on what makes one embedding serve many media.
arxiv-2507-05090:
Dimitri Veras and Matija Ćuk set limits on how fast minor planets break up around white dwarfs. White dwarfs are the dense cores left by dead stars, and some host rubble from torn planets. Watchers have tracked this rubble for up to ten years as its signals fade and return. The authors focus on planets that skirt the zone where tides would shred them.

Such planets meet the terms for a known breakup path called the sesquinary catastrophe. In that path, debris thrown off a body returns and strikes it hard enough to erode it to bits. The danger zone spans about one to four times the shred radius. Breakup there takes a mere hundred to a hundred thousand years. Discs of rubble must then be fed fresh material on an ongoing basis.
arxiv-2507-06090:
Swapnil Bhattacharyya and co-authors present Nyay-Darpan in this 2025 paper, an AI assistant for consumer law in India. AI tools for courts have mostly served criminal and civil cases, leaving consumer disputes unstudied. Their framework does two jobs: it summarizes consumer case files, and it retrieves similar past judgments to guide decisions. The name means Mirror of Justice.

The system scored over seventy-five percent accuracy at predicting similar cases. Summary quality reached about seventy percent across their material measures. The team also built a fresh way to grade those summaries. They plan to release the framework and its data set openly. The goal is faster, more consistent handling of consumer complaints in a crowded legal system.
arxiv-2507-08990:
Arka Ghosh and Aliaume Lopez published this algebra paper in 2025. Gröbner bases are the workhorse tool for computing with polynomial ideals. The paper asks whether they can still be computed when the polynomial ring has infinitely many variables but a group of symmetries keeps things under control. An ideal that respects those symmetries is called equivariant.

The authors show that when every equivariant ideal is finitely generated, a property tied to Hilbert's basis theorem, Gröbner bases for such ideals are computable. It follows that testing whether a polynomial belongs to an equivariant ideal is decidable in that setting. They also give a condition under which membership becomes undecidable. That condition covers most of the common examples that lack the finite generation property. The paper thus draws a sharp line between the computable and uncomputable cases.
arxiv-2507-10190:
Zhao and co-authors linked two radio telescopes across 8,600 kilometres to sharpen high-frequency observing, in a 2025 paper. The telescopes, in Chile and Spain, observed the same source at two bands at once through a shared optical path. Air wobble scrambles the higher band's phase, but the lower band feels a matching wobble. That match allows a fix called frequency phase transfer.

Using the calm lower band to correct the higher one slowed phase drift a great deal. The coherence of the high-band signal rose clearly after the fix. The test used a newly installed receiver that opened the low band at the Chilean site. The authors say the method can lift sensitivity and image quality for future work above 250 gigahertz.
arxiv-2507-11690:
Amaya Dharmasiri, William Yang, Polina Kirichenko, and a wider team wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It asks a pointed question about shrinking training sets: when we keep only a small coreset of examples, what happens to the biases the model learns?

Coresets promise equal performance on far less data. But datasets carry spurious correlations, shortcuts that fail in the real world. The team ran the first broad study of the issue, across ten bias benchmarks, five ways of scoring example importance, and five selection policies at many sizes. Picking by embedding-based scores was safer than picking by learning behavior. Prioritizing hard examples could lower the bias in the kept set. Yet those low-bias coresets did not reliably yield tougher models. The authors map where data dieting helps fairness and where it quietly does not.
arxiv-2507-12090:
Panos Kakoulidis and co-authors present a 2025 paper on judging speech quality across recording rates. Human opinion scores rate speech in listening tests, and automatic predictors usually assume one sampling rate. Recordings at higher rates break that assumption. Their model, MambaRate, was built for a 2025 challenge track on high-rate speech.

It combines self-supervised speech embeddings with a selective state space model. Target scores are encoded smoothly through radial basis functions. In a few-shot setting with no pretraining, an early version beat the pretrained baseline by about fourteen percent and placed fourth of five systems, six percent behind the winner. Extra tests on a standard corpus and input ablations improved on that first version.
arxiv-2507-12890:
Chen and nine co-authors upgrade a diffusion-based system that generates full-length songs with vocals and accompaniment. The earlier version suffered from lopsided training data and weak control over style. Songs came out uneven, with repeated or dropped lyrics.

The new system trains on a larger, balanced dataset. Users can steer style through written descriptions or a reference clip. A preference-tuning step nudges the model toward outputs listeners rate higher. Tests showed gains in naturalness, arrangement richness, and listener satisfaction over the earlier system. The authors present the work as a step toward songs a creator can shape in detail.
arxiv-2507-12990:
Sparse autoencoders decode the inner features of large language models, but they go blind to domain traits that were rare in their training text. The six authors fix that blindness with residual learning rather than retraining. They train a second autoencoder on the reconstruction error the first one makes on domain texts, so the helper captures exactly the features the primary model missed.

At inference the two models' outputs are summed. Across several specialized domains the pair improved both the language model's cross-entropy and the explained variance, while general-task performance held up. The authors present the trick as a cheap way for researchers to sharpen autoencoder interpretability for a chosen domain of interest.
arxiv-2507-13290:
Aaron Councilman and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a system that formally checks code written by language models from plain English requests. Model-written code is handy but far too shaky for critical systems without proof. Their answer is a formal query language that reads almost like natural speech, so users can confirm it captures their intent before any checking starts.

The system, built for a widely used system-setup language, adds a formal model of program behavior, a symbolic runner, and a matching engine. A knowledge base stores machine-specific facts so queries stay simple. On twenty-one tasks, the checker confirmed correct code in most cases. The work aims to make AI coding help safe enough for critical use.
arxiv-2507-14490: Oleg Aristov studies two versions of the holomorphic quantum plane in a 2025 mathematics note. He gives power series descriptions for two completions. One is known as the Arens-Michael envelope. Another is tied to Banach algebras with polynomial identity, in the case of a non-unitary parameter. Explicit series forms make the two versions easier to compare and to use in later analytic work on noncommutative spaces.
arxiv-2507-14590:
Lukasz Radlinski, Mateusz Gusciora, and Jan Kocon compare in 2025 data augmentation methods for emotion classification in text. Many language tasks suffer from scarce data and uneven class balance. Large language models now offer new ways to expand training sets beyond older tricks.

They test four approaches, including backtranslation and paraphrasing powered by ChatGPT, against purely generative methods. Experiments run in several setups on an example data set. Quality of the added data and its effect on classification were both judged. Backtranslation and paraphrasing matched or beat pure generation, the authors find.
arxiv-2507-15290:
Emile Anand and Sarah Liaw wrote a machine learning paper in two thousand twenty-five on a decision strategy called Feel-Good Thompson Sampling. Bandit problems force a running choice between exploring options and exploiting the best known one. The classic Thompson method samples from its beliefs, but theory shows it explores too timidly in high dimensions.

The feel-good variant adds an optimism bonus that favors high-reward models. It shines when beliefs are exact, but large problems use rough approximations instead. The authors give the first systematic test across eleven benchmarks. Bigger bonuses helped when samples were accurate and hurt when sampling noise took over.
arxiv-2507-15590:
Jorge Junior Morgado Vega, Sachin Sharma, and Federico Simonetta present a study from twenty twenty-five on the tools of computational musicology. Computer tools have shaped the study of music since the last century, from score analysis to models of how music is made. The team surveyed working scholars on what they use and what they lack. Four domains frame the poll: scores, images, audio, and text.

They log use patterns, chief tasks, joy with the tools, and the shape of the data. Gaps stand out in all four domains between what tools do and what users need. The team hopes the map spurs builders to close those gaps and make the tools more open to all.
arxiv-2507-16490:
Du Toit and Dunaiski test in 2025 whether joining a language model with a topic model improves sorting text into a class tree. Sorting into layered classes is a core language task for large archives. Language models catch fine meaning, while topic models catch broad themes across a whole corpus.

Their method pulls features from both models and passes them through split layers. The joined output feeds label wise attention, which weighs the best features for each class. The study asks whether the paired features beat either source alone in general. Such a result would guide design of sorters for deep class trees.
arxiv-2507-16590:
A large collaboration reconstructs the present-day clumping of matter in the universe in a paper from 2025. The catalog names one author, but the text head lists the full DESI team, and the description follows the head. Galaxy maps record clumping as it was in the past. The team uses survey data from the DESI instrument plus microwave background observations to translate that record to today.

They model galaxy clustering with an effective field theory that handles small-scale effects. Two cosmic models are compared, the standard one and a variant with evolving dark energy. Comparing data across distances can expose flaws in the assumed expansion history. Past work found the standard model consistent, and this study extends the test with better data.
arxiv-2507-16990:
Zheyi Ding and a large team of co-authors report solar events seen by the Solar Orbiter craft in twenty twenty-five. Solar energetic particle events help show how particles gain speed and travel through the solar system. Most such events stream outward along open magnetic field lines. The events here were rarer, with particles flowing both toward and away from the Sun at once.

The team studied two of these two-way events in detail. Both showed two clear speed patterns with opposed flows at their start. Sunward protons had delayed features that the team traced further. Such events give clues about magnetic field shape and about more than one source speeding particles up. Readers get a close look at an uncommon solar pattern.
arxiv-2507-18190:
Keyu Wu and a large team of colleagues tackle root cause analysis for alarms in telecommunication networks, the detective work of finding which fault triggered a flood of alerts. The task demands reasoning over network graphs and lacked any realistic public test set. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team builds a benchmark of several hundred fault scenarios drawn from expert-checked knowledge graphs of real networks. They then grade leading language models on it and find even the best score well below a passing level, which marks the task as genuinely hard.

Their companion system improves its own code solution in rounds: run, study all failures together for shared patterns, then repair the systemic flaw rather than patching single cases. That loop raised the final score dramatically in their tests. The benchmark and the self-improving agent are offered as research starters.
arxiv-2507-18690:
Daisuke Fujii, Akihiro Iwanaka, and Mitsuru Tanaka show that a scale anomaly dominates the squeezing pressure inside pions in a holographic model of the strong force, in work from twenty twenty-five. Gravity dual models let physicists read a particle's inner stress from its gravity response factors. Whether anomaly pressure rules in pions as in protons was open.

Working on the light front, they derived the pion's energy density and stress spread. The anomaly share indeed dominates the confining pressure, echoing the proton result in another frame. In the large color limit, a scalar glueball carries that pressure across the pion. The authors read this as support for a universal stabilizing role of the anomaly in hadrons.
arxiv-2507-18790:
Wenbin Zhao, Volker Koch, and Feng Yuan study in 2025 how particles inside a high-energy jet move in step with each other. A jet is a narrow spray of particles made when quarks or gluons fly out of a crash. How the spray's energy spreads by angle holds clues to how the jet formed and what it passed through.

The team compares a measured energy-energy pattern in jets with a pattern built from two lone energy flows. True linked motion stands out more strong at mid and wide angles, which points to linked splitting inside the jet. At small angles the links grow with jet energy in an odd pattern. That pattern could help probe how jets lose energy in heavy ion crashes. The method offers a fresh tool to split apart unlike effects.
arxiv-2507-19290:
Noah Amsel and co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, how few probes it takes to learn a structured copy of an unknown matrix. The only access allowed is multiplying the matrix, or its transpose, by chosen vectors. Such learning underlies fast solvers, preconditioners, and operator learning.

Earlier work handled specific families like low-rank matrices one at a time. This study tackles general finite families at once. Classic sketching needs a number of probes growing with the log of the family size, and that is achievable for weaker probes too. Surprisingly, the stronger two-sided probes studied here cannot always do better, the authors show, reshaping expectations for matrix learning.
arxiv-2507-19390:
Altaf Abbassi and co-authors present ReCatcher in this 2025 paper, a framework for regression testing of code-generating language models. Models change fast through fine-tuning, merging, and new releases, and updates can quietly hurt old skills. ReCatcher compares a current model with a candidate across three axes: logical correctness, static code quality, and run speed. It uses Python generation tasks.

Trials covered three update kinds on four well-known models. Fine-tuning on mixed-language data raised syntax errors by up to twelve percent. Merging with a general model cut correctness by up to eighteen percent. A flagship model regressed sharply on missing-import handling against its predecessor. ReCatcher beat baseline checkers in consistency. The authors urge systematic regression checks before any model swap.
arxiv-2507-20890:
Zhecheng Li and colleagues improve the conversion of photographed math expressions into LaTeX code, a chore every scientist knows. Vision-language models handle broad visual tasks well, but they trip on fine print such as subscripts and superscripts, producing code that compiles into the wrong formula. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's framework makes the model reason visually in rounds. Attention maps show which symbols it is looking at, and an attention-guided refinement loop lets it re-check regions and correct itself step by step. More rounds kept helping in their tests.

To measure progress honestly, the authors built a hard test set of over a thousand curated examples designed to stress exactly these weak points. Gains appeared on both text-level and visual-level metrics across models. The work targets document digitization pipelines where one wrong exponent can silently change a formula's meaning.
arxiv-2507-22890:
Saadiq Rauf Khan, Vinit Chandak, and Sougata Mukherjea test how well popular large language models handle data visualization in both directions. They asked the models to write code that produces charts from simple prompts. They also quizzed the models about charts shown to them.

Simple outputs like bar and pie charts came out well, and basic questions about visualizations were answered correctly. Harder work exposed limits: some models failed at violin plots, and several misread relationships between close boundaries or judged shape lengths wrongly. The authors offer the findings as guidance for improving both the models and visualization tools. Careful users should verify generated charts rather than trusting them blindly.
arxiv-2507-23090:
Evgenii Kokin proves a link between two holonomy groups in a special class of spaces. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five and belongs to differential geometry. The space is a K-contact Riemannian manifold, which carries a Reeb field that sweeps out orbits. Kokin studies the adapted connection on such a space. Its holonomy group records how vectors twist under parallel transport.

He shows the group matches that of a simpler space built from the orbits. When the orbit space is itself a smooth manifold, the two groups are isomorphic. The second group comes from the standard Levi-Civita connection there. A quick proof of a de Rham-type result follows. If the first group splits, the orbit space splits locally into a product. The theorem turns hard questions on the big space into easier ones below.
arxiv-2507-23590:
Jack Collins and co-authors present a 2025 paper on spotting moments of hearing difficulty in conversation. People often miss words in everyday talk, and hearing aids could help most if they reacted at exactly those moments. The task is to flag, in a stream of audio, the utterances where a listener struggled.

The team compares several machine learning approaches to the detection problem. A simple speech-recognition hotword search sets a baseline. A fine-tuned audio-only model, built on a leading speech architecture, does better. Audio language models, which reason over sound and text together, win by a wide margin. The results point to richer models as the ears of future real-time hearing assistance.
arxiv-2508-00990:
Jordan Tweddale and co-authors present Hubble Space Telescope views of a rare magnetic binary star in this 2025 paper. The system, J0240, is only the second known case of a cataclysmic variable acting as a propeller, flinging gas away. Five telescope orbits covered one full 7.34-hour orbit of the pair. Ultraviolet spectra and light curves form the data.

A flicker every 24.939 seconds confirms the fastest-spinning white dwarf known in such a system. Gas line ratios hint at a past phase of fast mass transfer, though weaker than in the other propeller case. The system also shines fainter than its twin in both calm and bright states. A wind-like profile in one line matches gas sped up by the propeller. New temperature limits allow the dwarf's core to be crystallizing.
arxiv-2508-01290:
Yan and co-authors show in 2025 that partially relevant knowledge can awaken answers inside large language models for questions about unseen entities. Retrieval systems add outside knowledge, which splits into direct evidence, clues, and weak context. Weak context with partial relevance is usually treated as noise.

Their view flips that assumption, since models may already hold the missing link. Gold reasoning paths were trimmed to build partial knowledge, and theory plus tests on two graph question datasets back the effect. A new task mimics failed entity linking in incomplete graphs. Their approach beat embedding similarity methods in practical trials, which reframes partial retrieval as an asset.
arxiv-2508-01490:
Rushin Gindra and co-authors built a large benchmark in a 2025 paper for tools that join tissue images with gene data. Spatial transcriptomics reads which genes are on in each spot of a tissue slice, right beside its photo. Models that learn from both views could forecast gene reads from cheap photos alone.

Their benchmark, HESCAPE, pools a pan-organ set across six gene panels and 54 donors. They then graded the main cross-modal training methods in a shared way. Past grades used small, unlike sets, so winners were hard to trust. A common yardstick should speed fair gains in this fast field.
arxiv-2508-02690:
Benoit Cloitre turned a famous but impractical formula for prime numbers into a working method. The Golomb-Keller formula expresses each next prime through the primes before it, using the Riemann zeta function, but it needs a limit taken to infinity, so it cannot be computed directly. Cloitre proved that a finite parameter, no larger than the current prime, is enough when the result is rounded up.

The smallest workable parameter for each step forms a sequence with surprising structure. Its relative size dips toward zero infinitely often, and its peak value ties to the densest patterns primes can form, linking the method to the twin prime question and the Hardy-Littlewood conjectures. The approach also extends to Dirichlet L-functions.
arxiv-2508-03290:
Henry Davenport, Frank Schindler, and Johannes Knolle studied excitons in rhombohedral five-layer graphene in twenty twenty-five. Sandwiched between boron nitride layers and slightly twisted, this material hosts flat bands and rich physics. The authors built a lean two-band model that captures its band structure more faithfully than earlier ones.

Within that model, exciton wave packets — bound electron-hole pairs — sit not at the moiré cell's center but at special symmetric points on its boundary, displaced by a quantized amount. An applied electric field can swap the exciton's home between inequivalent corners, making the shift tunable. The excitons also inherit Berry curvature from the electron bands, enriching how they move. The findings suggest hunting for exotic corner and edge modes in this platform.
arxiv-2508-03690:
Youquan Liu and co-authors teach a computer to imagine what a laser scanner would see, given only an ordinary photograph. Robots and self-driving cars rely on LiDAR point clouds, but collecting real ones is expensive, and earlier generators offered little control over the output. A single camera image is a cheap control signal, yet it is a hard one: its depth and meaning cues vary across the scene, and its look differs from laser geometry.

Their system, Veila, answers with three parts: a conditioning step that weighs the image's cues by local trustworthiness. An alignment step stays robust while the generator is noisy, and a coherence step keeps the full panorama consistent. Tests on three driving datasets, including a new bad-weather benchmark, show top fidelity, and the synthetic clouds even improve real detection training.
arxiv-2508-04290:
Yonghui Zhou, Xiaowan Li, Shuguan Ji, and Zhijun Qiao analyze a two component Novikov system in two thousand twenty-five. The system is a generalized form with weak dissipation, or slow loss. They study its Cauchy problem, which sets a start state and asks how it evolves. Such wave systems can break in finite time.

First they prove that solutions exist and stay unique for a short span. The proof uses a classic theorem of Kato. Next they give a sharp rule for when wave breaking must occur. Last they check how strong solutions keep their traits in weighted spaces. The class of weights is broad.
arxiv-2508-04390: Herbert Ullrich and Jan Drchal describe in 2025 the fact-checking system that won the FEVER 8 task. Their pipeline has two steps: fetch evidence, then judge the claim against it. It improves on their entry from the year before. The notable point is where it runs: on the owner's own hardware. On a mid-range graphics card with 23 gigabytes of memory, and a 60-second limit per claim, it matched the best scores on the task's evidence-aware measure. Strong fact checking need not depend on cloud services.
arxiv-2508-04490:
Savin, Korznikova, and Dmitriev bend and twist carbon nanosprings in simulation to see how they break. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. These helical ribbons of graphene promise springs and sensors at molecular scale, but stretching was the only deformation well studied.

Molecular dynamics runs probed bending and twisting modes for springs built from coronene and kekulene units. Depending on the coil's proportions, two flaw types emerged: structural defects and places where the helix flips its handedness. The springs also expand with heat far more strongly than common metals and alloys. That outsized thermal response, awkward in some designs, is a gift for sensors working across wide temperature swings. The authors map where each failure begins.
arxiv-2508-04890:
Faruk Alpay, Hamdi Alakkad, and Taylan Alpay build a math framework for endlessly repeated transformations in this 2025 paper. Start with an operator on a Hilbert space, the setting for quantum math. Apply a chosen change again and again, past any finite count, into transfinite steps. The team asks where such a process settles.

Under mild rules, the sequence stops changing at some stage. The resting operator is unchanged by the transformation, a true fixed point. Its spectrum shrinks to what survives every pass of a spectral map. For simple changes like squaring, the limit projects onto the steady directions. The framework extends older results and lists open problems by stage.
arxiv-2508-05090:
Mojtaba Fayazbakhsh, Danial Ataee, and MohammadAmin Fazli warm up preference learning when no labeled examples exist yet, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Learning what people prefer by asking a few smart questions is efficient, but the method stumbles at the start, before any answers arrive. Fixes existed for image and text tasks, not for preference learning.

Borrowing from social and economic research practice, the method begins with a self-taught phase. A standard compression technique reads the data's own structure and invents rough labels, giving a warmed-up model. Questions to a noisy stand-in expert then refine it. On datasets covering creditworthiness, career success, and social status, the approach beat cold-start rivals throughout.
arxiv-2508-05490:
Zhuoran Geng and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a tiny heat gauge built from superconducting tunnel junctions. The gauge blocks phonons, the quanta of heat in solids, to keep its sensor well shut off. On-chip cooling of electrons adds to the sharpness. The aim is fast, fine reads of energy from single events.

They set out the full theory of the device and short forms for its key gauges. Those gauges cover cooling strength, response time, noise floor, and energy sharpness. Flaws like subgap leaks and heat backflow are weighed. The team maps how each dial steers the scores. They claim the design can match or beat the best sensors of today.
arxiv-2508-06090:
Javad Jafari and Mohammad Akbari Tootkaboni published a 2025 proof of a classic result about patterns in whole numbers. Van der Waerden’s theorem says that if you paint the whole numbers in a finite set of colours, one colour will hold long, evenly spaced runs. A stronger form swaps the even steps for steps set by a polynomial, such as squares.

That stronger form was first proved in 1996 with tools from the study of moving systems. Jafari and Tootkaboni give a fresh proof that stays inside algebra. Their route uses symbol-like polynomials and a compact space built from an endless discrete system. A purely algebraic proof can be easier to check, teach, and adapt to new problems.
arxiv-2508-06290:
Alexandre Landry, Yassine Sekhmani, and colleagues construct wormhole solutions in modified gravity in a 2025 theoretical physics study. A traversable wormhole needs a throat that stays open, no horizon blocking passage, and space that flattens far away. The authors work in a teleparallel gravity theory with an added massive graviton term.

Using the standard static, round wormhole shape, they derive the governing equations and split matter effects into torsion and mass parts. Exact solutions follow for three profiles of gravitational redshift, each in two versions of the massive sector. The authors check the flaring condition at the throat and whether standard energy rules hold.
arxiv-2508-06590:
Aritra Sanyal and colleagues study bouncing universe models in which gravity is modified, and ask whether each bounce cycle leaves the universe changed. In cyclic models the cosmos contracts, rebounds, and expands again, avoiding a first moment. The team works with a modified gravity theory built around the curvature of spacetime, reconstructing the exact theory behind two chosen bounce shapes, one exponential and one power-law. A simple matter field rides in the model, and its pressure is tracked through expansion and contraction.

Pressure did not retrace the same path in the two directions. Each full cycle therefore did net thermodynamic work, forming closed loops when plotted against a measure of the field state. The authors read that imbalance as a natural arrow of time arising inside cyclic gravity models, with net energy transfer per cycle.
arxiv-2508-06690:
Seth Taylor, Alex Bihlo, and Jean-Christophe Nave learn the flow of evolving systems through shape changes of their domains in this 2025 paper. Many dynamics can be seen as fields carried along by moving coordinates. Their method learns a lift into the group of smooth reshaping maps. Time steps then compose reshapes instead of updating fields directly. A relabeling symmetry of the dynamics holds exactly by design. Structure that physics demands is built in, not approximated.

Resolution behavior and links to image registration are studied. Tests forecast turbulent fluid motion. The method kept the conserved traits such flows should keep. Operator learning usually trades structure for speed; this keeps both. The paper is numerical analysis meets machine learning. Fluid forecasting is the showcase use.
arxiv-2508-07190:
Qi and co-authors study in 2025 the technical base of non fungible tokens, or NFTs, through the standards that define them. Past work looked at markets, user habits, and single security flaws. The rules that make NFTs work had not been mapped as a whole.

The team read 191 token linked proposals and over ten thousand forum posts up to July 2025. They parsed code interfaces, charted how standards inherit from each other, and profiled who writes them. Core standards split from new ones in their account. Poor fit across versions stood out, and growing feature load raised security risk, a warning for builders in this space.
arxiv-2508-07690:
Luyao Zhuang and Qinggang Zhang lead a team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five, whose text lists Juhua Liu and Qing Li while the catalog shows Yujing Zhang and Xiao Huang. It presents LoSemB, a tool finder for language models that can meet tools it never saw in training.

Tool stores grow daily, so a finder trained on a fixed set meets fresh tools cold. LoSemB mines the logic that links known tools and lays it over new ones, like a person who maps a new gadget to old skills. An alignment part curbs the shift between old and new, and a relation part backs up plain likeness scores. Tests lead in the fresh-tool case and hold up in the known one.
arxiv-2508-07890:
Ori Gabai and five co-authors report a link between light noise and atomic-style swings in a semiconductor amplifier in a 2025 paper. Squeezed light, whose noise dips below the vacuum level, is usually made with passive crystals. Amplifiers add their own noise, yet they can also calm photon fluctuations.

Working with quantum dot amplifiers at room temperature, the team fired short pulses that drove Rabi oscillations in the material. The noise pattern then cycled with pulse energy: at some energies the light was squeezed below vacuum, at others it stayed thermal. Under special settings a strange two-lobed pattern appeared, hinting at a cat-like quantum state blurred by losses.
arxiv-2508-08090:
Mingwen Fei, Xiang Fei, Daozhi Han, and Yadong Liu analyze a coupled flow model for two viscous fluids that mix at their interface. Realistic pairs like oil and water can differ in density, which breaks the usual divergence-free velocity assumption and pushes pressure into the chemistry side of the model. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors first prove global weak solutions exist in a three-dimensional periodic box. They use a stepwise time approximation with a fixed-point argument. They use a new regularity estimate earned from the damping that surface tension provides.

They then show the model settles into the classic incompressible two-phase model as the density gap closes. The delicate part is controlling pressure uniformly without pressure regularity, drawn from the momentum equations and the improved order-parameter estimate. The result certifies the quasi-incompressible model as a sound bridge to the classical theory.
arxiv-2508-09490:
Omar Abdul Halim, Daniyar Omarov, and Brendan Pass study semi-discrete variational problems where continuous agents match to finitely many one-dimensional outcomes. Their paper from twenty twenty-five grows from economic matching and game theory: Cournot-Nash equilibria and hedonic pricing both fit the frame. Cast as optimal transport between spaces of unequal dimension, the problems strain standard solvers. The authors prove solutions take a particularly simple form under stated conditions.

That structure pays numerically. Their purpose-built algorithms scale far better than generic transport solvers when outcomes are many, and convergence guarantees ride along. Worked examples show wide margins over alternatives. The continuum-strategy theory of earlier work gains a discrete twin that computers can actually run at scale.
arxiv-2508-10490:
Amir Mehrpanah, Matteo Gamba, Kevin Smith, and Hossein Azizpour measure the trade-off between simple and faithful AI explanations in a 2025 paper. Gradient-based explanations of image networks are noisy, because the networks can hinge on single pixels. Popular fixes smooth the explanation with a stand-in model, but smoothing can distort what the network really did.

The authors build a spectral framework that scores smoothness and faithfulness on common ground. With it, they quantify how much of the distortion comes from the network's own high-frequency behavior. They define an explanation gap and measure it across methods. Experiments over design choices, data sets, and ablations back the theory. The aim is principled control of explanation quality rather than eyeballing heat maps.
arxiv-2508-10990:
Wang and colleagues build in twenty twenty-five woven multi-part quantum states from microwave light pulses. Such cluster states underpin one-way quantum computing and fine measurement. Their gear uses a superconducting circuit with one artificial atom, a ring, and a filter. It emits photons one after another, each at its own pitch, so time and pitch together carry the pattern.

Coding each unit on two pitch rails lets them spot a lost photon as a flagged gap. Tests confirmed true shared entanglement across chains of several units. After dropping the flagged losses, quality stayed high for larger states. The authors say the scheme beats single-rail designs on loss and scales toward light-based quantum work.
arxiv-2508-11290:
Safety-tuned chatbots sometimes refuse harmless requests that merely sound dangerous, annoying users with false alarms. Utsav Maskey and co-authors traced how that happens inside the model. As text flows through the layers, its representation follows a path they call a constellation. Each task traces a consistent path. Refusals show up as predictable detours from the benign route.

Their fix, applied at inference time, nudges the representation back onto the task's non-refusal path. The steering applies only to task types prone to over-refusing, leaving other behavior alone. Tests showed fewer false refusals with little loss of usefulness. The authors offer the method as a principled, targeted alternative to retraining.
arxiv-2508-11490:
Subhajyoti Bid and Henning Schomerus present a mechanism that forces a whole class of materials into an extreme spectral state. In non-Hermitian systems, special points called exceptional points make the response to small changes huge, but reaching them usually takes fine-tuning. A stronger condition, exceptional deficiency, makes every energy level such a point. The authors realize this condition in topological square-root insulators, a family built from simpler lattice models.

Lattice sum rules in these materials enforce the deficiency directly, with no tuning. The paper identifies what the state does in practice: broad-band amplification of steady signals and a non-Abelian form of amplification as states change slowly. The authors separate effects that arise in the bulk from those at the boundary. They also outline how labs might build such systems on real platforms.
arxiv-2508-11990:
Evan Dogariu, Anand Brahmbhatt, and Elad Hazan wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies how to predict the next step of an unknown nonlinear system that sits at the edge of stability, from past readings alone.

The team gives a method built on spectral filtering, which learns a map from past readings to the next one through a spectral form of the system. With tools from online convex optimization, they prove the error fades to zero for a broad class of such systems. A fresh control-based gauge of learnability sets the rate. The core is a new spectral filter for linear systems that takes in past data and fixes noise, of use on its own.
arxiv-2508-12690:
Dongjae Jeon and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv technical report on adapting object detectors to shifting driving conditions. A challenge entry from a 2023 workshop, their method, TTA-DAME, adjusts models at test time as weather and light change. It augments source data toward target conditions and uses a domain detector to catch sharp shifts, such as day turning to night.

Several detectors are trained and their outputs merged by a standard suppression step. The team reports clear gains on the SHIFT benchmark for driving scenes. The report frames test-time adaptation as a practical answer to the domain swings that road systems face daily.
arxiv-2508-13690:
Wei Shao and co-authors present a way in 2025 to unlock devices by pulse, using a smartwatch. The watch reads the pulse at the wrist with light, a method called PPG. Unlike heart-tracing methods that need chest contact, this one runs all the time without bothering the user.

The team built the system on a real watch and tested it at a low sampling rate to save power. Short four-second pulse clips were enough to tell users apart in most cases, with an average accuracy near eighty-eight percent on their data set. Training on clips from active times, not just rest, made it work better on the move. The low rate cut sensor power use by about half versus high-rate setups.
arxiv-2508-15090:
Matt Pauk and Maria Leonor Pacheco study prompt-based structured prediction in a 2025 paper. Large language models can do many language tasks from prompts alone, but they can also invent facts and give uneven answers. Tasks with a fixed output structure, such as labeling each word in a sentence, expose those flaws.

The authors pair the models with combinatorial inference, a method that enforces valid output structure. They test many prompting styles to see which ones give confidence scores that the inference step can use well. In every style, adding inference gave more consistent and more accurate results than prompting alone. Extra gains came from calibration and from training with structured goals. The work argues structured learning still matters.
arxiv-2508-15390:
Woojin Chung and Jeonghoon Kim wrote this 2025 paper on why bigger vocabularies help language models, and what actually does the helping. Token streams are lopsided: a few words dominate while most appear rarely. In a controlled study the pair scaled vocabulary from 24,000 to 196,000 tokens while holding data, compute, and tuning fixed.

Larger vocabularies simplified the tokenized text, measured by Kolmogorov complexity. Past 24,000, every common word is already a single token, so growth only deepens the imbalance. Loss breakdowns show the gain lands almost entirely on the 2,500 most frequent words, even as rare-word loss rises. Those words cover about 75 percent of downstream test text, so the edge transfers. Growing the model instead produced the same frequent-word benefit, reframing tokenizer design as complexity control.
arxiv-2508-15490:
Eray Genc, Angus H. Wright, and Hendrik Hildebrandt weigh the dust hiding in galaxy halos by watching background galaxies dim. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Dust reddens light that passes near a galaxy, and the Kilo-Degree Survey gave them the sky to measure it.

Mock catalogs first proved the pipeline could recover halo and dust masses separately. Near-infrared bands confirmed the dimming carried no color there, as pure magnification predicts. Optical bands, analyzed jointly with lensing, pinned the halo mass tightly. Dust mass came out near seven times ten to the seventh solar masses. The match with quasar-based studies supports halos rich in gas and dust, spread by galactic feedback.
arxiv-2508-16190:
Sandro Paval, Ivan P. Yamshchikov, and Pascal Meißner build a scene dataset for comic analysis. Their 2025 paper introduces ComicScene154, drawn from public-domain comic books. Comics blend words and pictures in ways plain text or video do not. Scene-level story arcs, though, lacked a labeled resource.

Human annotators marked scenes across books of varied genres. The team treats comics as a stand-in for multimodal narrative data in general. A baseline pipeline for splitting scenes sets a first benchmark. Results suggest the dataset can drive better narrative tools. The authors invite language researchers to take comics seriously as data. Future methods now have a shared target to beat.
arxiv-2508-16290:
Rubi and eleven co-authors find superconductivity that a strong magnet field lifts, not kills, in this twenty twenty-five paper. Fields most oft crush such flow by spin and whirl caps on its pairs. Rare stuffs break that rule, yet their flow points sit cold and low.

Inside, flat nickel films hold a far higher flow point than those rare kin. Both a low-field and a high-field flow state show in the films' runs. A pay-back trick, where a hid field cancels the cast one, could drive both. The find hints that top flow caps in hot such stuffs can stretch far. That could widen their use in high-field gear down the line.
arxiv-2508-16690:
Vaastav Anand, Deepak Garg, and Antoine Kaufmann present a 2025 framework that tunes a running software system to its actual work. Tailoring a system to its hardware and load can speed it greatly. In practice the tailoring is hard: the best form is unclear, narrow forms lose range, and loads keep shifting. Their framework, Iridescent, searches for the best form while the system runs.

Developers mark the space of allowed variants up front. The framework then builds and trials variants live, using whole-system speed as the guide. Fast build tools make the swaps cheap enough to run in production. Tests show the approach works, helps, and is easy to use. Live tailoring could suit cloud services whose loads swing by hour.
arxiv-2508-16990:
Diana-Alexandra Onutu, Yue Zhao, Joaquin Vanschoren, and Vlado Menkovski wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a score-based generative model that fakes the clustering of galaxies, as a fast stand-in for heavy gravity simulations.

Such models must scale, stay true to physics, and honor the symmetries of space. The team's graph net respects those symmetries and treats the box as wrapped at its edges. A new noise plan tuned to large geometric graphs proves key. The model can mint full point clouds with galaxy counts in the hundreds of thousands. It beats past diffusion models at matching clustering stats, at far less cost.
arxiv-2508-17690:
Danny Wang, Ruihong Qiu, Guangdong Bai, and Zi Huang rethink how to spot odd data in text-rich networks, in a 2025 paper. In such networks, each node carries words as well as links: a user has a bio, a paper has an abstract. Strange cases can hide in the wording, the wiring, or both at once.

The team builds an evaluation frame covering four kinds of shift, from edited text to rewired links. Their detector fuses each node's local link pattern into its text features through an attention step. A second network then customizes the transform for each node. Across the scenarios, the paired reading of text and topology separates normal from out-of-place nodes better than methods that read either alone.
arxiv-2508-18490:
Thomas Coons, Aniket Jivani, and Xun Huan present a 2025 paper on knowing when a cheap rehearsal has taught you enough. Engineers quantify uncertainty by Monte Carlo sampling, but high-fidelity models make each sample pricey. Multi-fidelity methods blend cheap and dear models, and their best blend depends on a covariance matrix estimated from pilot samples.

Too few pilot runs poison the blend; too many starve the final estimate. The authors wrap the pilot stage in a Bayesian frame that tracks covariance uncertainty itself, using a flexible prior that stays computable as samples accumulate. A loss rule then splits the cost of stopping early into accuracy loss versus saved budget. Demonstrated on control variate estimators, the framework suits any scheme that must rehearse before performing.
arxiv-2508-19090:
Juneja and six co-authors present an invited paper from twenty twenty-five on an open ecosystem for reconfigurable chip arrays. Such coarse-grained arrays balance flexibility with energy efficiency. Modern AI and edge workloads demand tight hardware-software co-design. Closed toolchains slow that joint work. Their ecosystem spans open chip generators and software tools. One array design moves data in single-cycle hops across the fabric. A low-power chip embeds it beside a RISC-V core for edge use.

An open design framework supports exploration, compiling, and testing. The authors call for one shared abstraction layer across such accelerators. That layer would free software from hardware specifics. Portability and compiler progress are the promised payoffs.
arxiv-2508-19490:
Neilha Pinheiro computes the stability index of the cosmological horizon in a rotating, charged, expanding universe. The spacetime is Kerr-Newman-de Sitter: spin, charge, and a positive cosmological constant together. A spatial slice of its cosmological horizon forms a marginally outer trapped surface, whose index counts its unstable directions. Pinheiro works in the symmetrized sense suited to the geometry.

For small positive spin the index is at least one. Impose a lower mass bound and it equals exactly one. Impose instead an upper mass bound and it rises to at least two. The paper then proves an estimate tying area and charge for index-one trapped surfaces in initial data obeying the dominant energy condition. That bridge connects the abstract index to concrete general relativistic inequalities. Horizon stability, in this corner of theory, is a matter of mass windows.
arxiv-2508-19790:
Liding Zhang and seven co-authors present APT*, a sampling-based planner that finds near-best paths for robots. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that many planners fix batch sizes in advance and ignore obstacle data. That one-size stance wastes effort on easy tasks and starves hard ones. APT* adapts both its batch size and its neighbor search as it works.

Batch size follows the volume of the informed set. Points are also treated as charges that push and pull under a Coulomb-style rule. These forces shape a stretched neighbor search that favors the path's long axis. Charge sizes adjust in a nonlinear way to speed settling. Tests across spaces from four to sixteen dimensions beat rival planners. A real robot arm task confirmed the gains.
arxiv-2508-19990:
Xiaodong Cui, Saif, Brian Kingsbury, and Tianyi Chen pre-train speech models on mixed data without letting one source swamp the rest. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in self-supervised learning for speech recognition. Standard training pools all data and trims one pooled loss. Mixed-domain and multilingual sets then settle at a bland middle.

Their fix adds local constraints to the pooled goal. After a few gradient steps from the shared model, each source should sit near its own best point. The setup is cast as a two-level optimization and solved with a first-order shortcut. The team notes its kinship with model-agnostic meta learning. Tests on multi-domain and multilingual sets show clear gains. Fine-tuned downstream scores rose, which marks a more adaptable base model.
arxiv-2508-20390:
Andreas Kirchner and Steffen Bass propose a better starting model for heavy-ion collisions in a 2025 paper. When heavy nuclei collide, the pattern of the crash depends on how many partons, the quarks and gluons inside nucleons, take part. That number fluctuates from event to event, and those fluctuations leave signals in the debris.

Their extension of the TRENTo model samples the parton count using parton distribution functions, the measured maps of nucleon contents. That ties the sampling to the momentum scale of each collision in a natural way. They examine how the resulting distributions shift with momentum transfer. Better initial conditions sharpen every later inference about the hot matter the collision creates.
arxiv-2508-20990:
Hong-Yan Zhang, Haoting Liu, Rui-Jia Lin, and Yu Zhou publish a correction to a signal-processing method in a 2025 paper. The method, symplectic geometry mode decomposition, splits a time series into parts and has been used to diagnose compound faults in rotating machines. It grew out of an older method, singular spectrum analysis, whose averaging step it inherited.

The correction says the inherited step was never updated to match the new method's wider matrix form, which leaves the original flawed. The authors point out the limits that follow and repair the computation with a pulling-back theorem. That fix recovers a series part from its matrix part correctly, restoring the method's soundness for fault work.
arxiv-2508-21690:
Two people meeting on a narrow sidewalk sometimes mirror each other's dodges left, then right, in the awkward dance Dutch researchers call the sidewalk salsa. Olger Siebinga and David Abbink want delivery robots to avoid that dance. They start from a model of pedestrian behavior built on implicit communication, the glances and drifts people use to negotiate passage.

A reinforcement learning agent then practiced against that model. It learned to cooperate with the virtual pedestrian. A risk-aware version did better still: given access to the model's sense of risk, it learned to signal its intentions through motion. The modeled pedestrian's perceived risk and effort dropped sharply. The authors offer the approach as a design path for polite robots.
arxiv-2509-00090:
Yi Cao and Paulette Clancy build a benchmark in 2025 to test whether materials scientists should train specialist force fields or fine-tune broad ones. Machine-learned force fields mimic quantum accuracy at far lower cost for atom motion sims. Which route wins on data needs, accuracy, cost, and failure risk was unclear.

Defect migration paths, traced by an elastic band method that finds the route an atom takes to hop, serve as probes of both interpolation and extrapolation. Tests use chromium-doped antimony telluride within the MACE design, across balance, motion, and layer sliding tasks. Fine-tuned models beat from-scratch ones by a wide margin in the reported checks. The probe gives labs a sharp way to pick a training route.
arxiv-2509-00390:
Wenqing Wu and Hang Wang study K-theory for group algebras built on the rationals and the adeles in 2025, by way of winding numbers. K-theory is a branch of algebra that sorts structures by stable traits. The adeles package all completions of the rationals into one ring. Functions on that ring can be periodic, and sorting their deformation classes calls for a winding number that stays fixed under smooth change.

The authors first define pre-periodic functions and build their winding number. They then show periodic adelic functions match those pre-periodic ones in a firm way. The winding number turns out to sort the deformation classes in full. From that, they write out the K1 group of the rational group algebra in explicit form. A like strategy gives the structure for the adelic case as well.
arxiv-2509-00490:
Zhongmiao Qi leads seven authors in total, with Yan Jiang, Bolin Zhang, Chong Wang, Lijun Guo, Pengjiang Qian, and Jiangbo Qian, on fast video search for group activities. Hashing here means turning video into short codes so similar clips can be found quickly.

Qi and his co-authors propose STVH, a method that models single object motion and group interaction together, tracking how visual and position features change over time. Its enhanced version, M-STVH, adds layers that let search focus on the activity meaning or on object looks, as a query needs. Tests on public datasets give strong results, which matters as video collections grow in busy, complex scenes.
arxiv-2509-00690:
Xuecai Ma and one co-author, Yifei Zhu, work in spectral algebraic geometry, where spaces are built from ring spectra, objects that blend algebra with homotopy theory. With motivation from chromatic homotopy theory, they define relative effective Cartier divisors, a spectral version of a classic geometric notion, for stacks over a ring spectrum.

Ma and Zhu prove this notion is representable, meaning it is governed by a geometric object, as a functor from connective algebras to spaces. That result lets them solve moduli problems for level structures on spectral abelian varieties, even at primes dividing the level. Passing to infinite level, they obtain a Jacquet-Langlands dual to Morava E-theory, with dual spectral sequences that may help compute periodic homotopy types.
arxiv-2509-00890:
Avi Kadria and one co-author, Liam Roditty, present new approximate distance oracles and their applications. A distance oracle is a data structure that answers approximate distance queries in a graph, balancing low stretch, the error factor, efficient space, and fast query time.

Prior work focused on constant query time. Kadria and Roditty comprehensively study oracles with non-constant query time, exploring trade-offs among space, stretch, and query time for weighted and unweighted graphs in stretch regimes below and above two. They give a new three-way trade-off extending the classical Thorup-Zwick oracle to larger query times, with explicit space and query bounds. Applications follow to the n-pairs shortest paths problem and the all nodes shortest cycles problem.
arxiv-2509-00990:
Deepak Bastola and Woohyeok Choi introduce Topic-Graph Spherical Fusion for legal document clustering. Legal documents challenge unsupervised discovery in several ways. They use specialized domain terminology throughout. Their lengths vary across multiple scales. Expert annotations for training are scarce as well.

Their framework unifies two kinds of representation on a joint unit hypersphere. Dense topic discovery comes via Top2Vec. Relational graph embeddings come via Node2Vec, which learns from random walks. A connected multi-relational document-topic graph is built between them. It combines topic centroid bridges with semantic nearest-neighbor edges. Fused representations are then partitioned with KMeans clustering. Evaluations on ACORD, CUAD, and LEDGAR beat several baselines. Gains appear in normalized mutual information across datasets.
arxiv-2509-01090:
James Tian introduces a class of network models that blend random features with layered kernels, functions that measure how alike two inputs are. In these models, depth comes from stacking fixed kernel steps, while chance enters only in the last layer. The design extends older random feature models, which use one random layer to approximate complex functions.

Tian proves that the deeper form can match some functions using fewer random samples than any shallow form could. That gap is stated as a depth separation result about sample cost. The finding matters because it shows layering itself, not just more data or more units, can make learning more efficient. It gives theory support for building such models with depth in mind.
arxiv-2509-01390:
Neural audio codecs compress speech into sequences of discrete tokens, and those tokens may behave like a language of their own. Joonyong Park, with five co-authors, compares the statistical and linguistic traits of tokens from several codec models. They test whether the tokens obey laws seen in natural language, such as Zipf's law for word frequency and Heaps' law for vocabulary growth.

Entropy and redundancy measures add a view of how much information the tokens carry. The team then links these traits to how well speech is understood after resynthesis, using recognition error rates and a quality score. Tokens, especially groups of three, did show language-like patterns. Those patterns, with information measures, tracked better recognition and resynthesis results. The findings can guide the design of stronger generative speech models built on codec tokens.
arxiv-2509-01590:
Market theory holds that prices already reflect all public information, so grouping stocks by price history should be hard to beat. Bingyang Wang, Grant Johnson, Maria Hybinette, and Tucker Balch test that claim by comparing three ways to cluster stocks. One uses past return correlations, one uses the standard industry classification set by humans, and one uses language model embeddings of news headlines about each stock.

Each clustering is turned into a synthetic factor model under arbitrage pricing theory, giving a consistent way to judge predictive power. The test rolls forward out of sample over S and P 500 firms from 2022 through 2024. Wang and the team report how the price-based method, consistent with the efficient markets view, fares against the information-rich alternatives. The study asks, in direct form, whether all the information really is in the price.
arxiv-2509-01690:
Josephine F W Baggen, Frank C van den Bosch, and Kaustav Mitra study how normal matter skews mass estimates drawn from small companion galaxies. Watching how satellites move can reveal the mass of the dark halo around a galaxy. Past work often treated those halos as pure dark matter and left out stars and gas. The authors build a math model that adds stars, gas, and the pull back of dark matter.

Gas blown out of a halo lowers the speeds of its satellites by a few percent in mid sized halos. The drop is tiny for the largest halos but can reach higher in rare cases. The team gives a fix that can plug into a survey analysis tool. With the fix, central galaxies shift to higher halo masses at the same brightness.
arxiv-2509-01790:
Andong Hua leads five co-authors in asking whether large language models are truly fragile to prompt wording. Small rewordings of a prompt often shift model scores a lot, a flaw called prompt sensitivity. The team tests seven models on six benchmarks with twelve prompt styles. Tasks span choice questions and open ended answers.

Much of the swing traces to scoring rules, like rigid answer matching that marks right ideas wrong when phrased in new words. When a model judges the answers instead, score swings shrink a lot. Rankings of models also line up far better across prompt styles. The authors conclude that modern models are sturdier than past reports claimed, and the flaw sits largely in the tests.
arxiv-2509-01890:
K Perry leads five co-authors in a high pressure study of graphite mixed with water. Raman spectroscopy reads molecular vibrations from scattered light to track structure under pressure. Water serves as the pressure medium, the fluid that squeezes the sample evenly, up to near ten gigapascals, a unit of huge pressure. In graphite rich zones, three hallmark bands are tracked as pressure climbs.

The main band shifts strongly toward higher frequency, signaling tighter coupling between graphite layers. In water rich zones, shaking bands and three stretch bands of water appear. Past a set pressure, the shift slope drops versus an earlier report, likely due to the water medium itself. The authors call for more work at higher pressures to settle the cause.
arxiv-2509-01990:
Jeremy Chastenet leads fourteen co-authors in probing how the silicate to carbon dust ratio varies across the Andromeda galaxy. Dust glow in the infrared can reveal grain makeup, but the ratio of silicate rich to carbon rich grains is barely studied. The far infrared slope of dust emission serves as their proxy for that ratio. Modeling snags cloud that slope estimate.

Recovering the slope depends on the local radiation field estimate and on assumed grain abundances. PRIMA hyperspectral imaging should pin the radiation field down far better. Polarization data from the same mission add another handle on grain traits. Together they promise a clean map of the ratio across the galaxy disk. The study frames what the new data can and cannot settle.
arxiv-2509-02090:
Ao Sun leads four co-authors on how to pick and mix blood marks to spot disease with more truth. Blood marks are traits in blood or tissue that flag a health state. One mark on its own is too weak for most tasks. The Youden index weighs hits and false alarms as if both count the same. Real clinic needs often weigh them in an uneven way.

Their frame tweaks that index with weights and picks which marks to mix at once. A smooth score plus a pruning term drives the pick of marks. A fast method solves the hard, non-smooth goal in one pass of work. Sims back the speed and skill of the frame in tests. A skin rash scale built with the frame shows real world use.
arxiv-2509-02490:
Arian L. von Blanckenburg, Domenico Giulini, and Philip K. Schwartz wrote a 2025 general relativity paper on a no-go result for the trace-free Einstein tensor, a modified version of the quantity linking gravity with matter. A known theorem says it cannot come from varying a symmetry-respecting action with the metric as the variable.

The authors strengthen that result. They show the statement survives even for fully general local actions, with no assumption that the action respects coordinate symmetry. In other words, dropping the symmetry requirement does not open a loophole. The finding closes a possible route around a classic limitation in variational formulations of gravity.
arxiv-2509-02590:
Mohammad Dindoost and six co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on community detection in huge networks. Standard clustering often returns groups that are split or barely linked. Such groups hurt interpretation. Post-processing can fix them, but slowly.

Two repair methods are Well-Connected Clusters and Connectivity Modifier. Both fix weak outputs, yet both crawl on massive graphs. The team rewrote them in Chapel, a parallel language. They also built them into the Arkouda/Arachne analytics framework. The new versions use many cores at once. They handled a network with over two billion edges in minutes on 128 cores. That network is the OpenAlex scholarly graph. The task was out of reach before. The work makes connectivity-preserving clustering practical at web scale.
arxiv-2509-02690:
L. K. Hunt and eighteen co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper studying the interstellar medium of I Zw 18, a nearby dwarf galaxy with only a few percent of the Sun's metal content. Spectra come from the James Webb Space Telescope's mid-infrared instrument.

The team examines warm molecular hydrogen and warm dust in small apertures around eleven regions. Seven hydrogen rotation lines appear, some among the weakest ever measured. Population diagrams fit dense gas under a strong radiation field. Three regions show an ortho-to-para hydrogen ratio above the equilibrium ceiling, a first measurement of its kind in interstellar gas, likely shaped by self-shielding. Warm dust glows in all regions, with one unidentified feature near fourteen micrometres. No hydrocarbon emission appeared despite stacking.
arxiv-2509-02990:
Liang Xie and Wenke Huang proposed a 2025 method for building detailed simulated road networks without the usual cost. Traffic simulators need lane-level maps, yet making them has meant huge data collection and hand editing. Their pipeline starts from street view photos gathered on open platforms.

A deep learning model reads those photos and picks out lane lines, counting them and locating them in space. Coordinate conversion and map matching then merge those lane details with road layouts from open map services. The result is a high-precision, lane-level network made with far less manual work. Such maps can support city traffic studies, self-driving navigation, and planning for smarter transport systems.
arxiv-2509-03390:
Eric Gottlieb and 4 co-authors introduced a combinatorial game called Row Impartial Terminus in 2025. Impartial games give both players the same moves from any position; this one is played on integer partitions, ways of writing a number as an ordered sum of parts. The authors ask who wins under both normal play and misère play, where the last move loses.

Their first step splits any position uniquely into a core and a remnant. The central result says the position's Conway pair, a two-sided value that settles both play variants, equals that of a matching position in Nim, the classic take-away game. That identity hands players a complete winning strategy for both variants at once. The game lands in a known hierarchy as forced and miserable but not pet.
arxiv-2509-03490:
Zhihan Jin and three co-authors' 2025 mathematics paper links graph eigenvalues to cliques, cuts, and a long-standing cosine problem. A graph is a network of points joined by edges. Its smallest adjacency eigenvalue measures how its connections spread across frequencies.

They prove that any graph whose average degree is high, while that smallest eigenvalue stays small, must contain a large clique, a fully connected set of points. One consequence delivers a first polynomial bound addressing Chowla's cosine problem from 1965, which asks how low a sum of cosines can dip. Another advance concerns MaxCut in graphs without large cliques, a problem raised in the 1970s. There they guarantee a cut noticeably bigger than half the edges.
arxiv-2509-03690:
Kelvin Daniel Gonzalez Amador discusses VulcanV3, a low-cost robotic hand that signs the American Sign Language alphabet, in a 2025 research paper. Robotic signing could support accessible communication for deaf communities, yet existing systems are often expensive and limited. The hand is three-dimensionally printed, open-source, and ambidextrous, working in mirror image for either side.

Twenty-three direct-drive servo motors move the fingers and wrist with precision, run by an Arduino Mega board through two driver modules. The design reproduces all 52 handshapes of the alphabet, counting right-hand and left-hand configurations separately. Bench tests confirm accurate reproduction of every shape. In a study with 33 participants, viewers recognised the signs with high accuracy, which improved further after a video demonstration. The team shares all design files and code under permissive open-source licences so others can rebuild and extend the hand.
arxiv-2509-03890:
Yineng Yan and seven co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to FaMA, a conversational agent for consumer-to-consumer marketplaces, built for Facebook Marketplace. Platform tasks like listing, renewing, messaging, and searching sit behind complex graphical interfaces, taxing buyers and sellers. A language-model agent that plans, remembers, and uses tools offers an alternative front door: plain conversation.

Sellers can update and renew listings through commands, and send bulk messages without repetitive clicking. Buyers search conversationally, describing what they want instead of fighting filters. The paper lays out the architecture and argues this agentic model is lighter and more accessible than the traditional app interface. Reported experiments reach a task success rate near ninety-eight percent on complex marketplace tasks. Commerce, in this design, becomes something users direct in words while the agent handles the interface labour underneath. The authors frame it as a template for other complex platforms.
arxiv-2509-04090:
Egor Dogadin and one co-author, Alexey Peregudin, design controllers for systems whose behavior repeats over time in a 2025 research letter. Their systems face disturbances, meaning outside pushes, that stay within known bounds but are otherwise unknown. The authors track regions called inescapable ellipsoids: once the system state enters one, disturbances can keep it trapped there. Shrinking those regions is the goal.

New equations describe how the trapped regions change over each cycle, with a single size score to minimize. A related equation-based method then gives exact designs for several controller types, including ones that only see partial measurements. A worked numerical example confirms the approach behaves as predicted.
arxiv-2509-04390:
Hannes Rosseel and one co-author, Toon van Waterschoot, use graphics hardware to recreate echoing spaces interactively in a 2025 research paper. Auralization lets listeners explore the sound of concert halls or historic worship spaces that are lost, altered, or far away. The system must blend live input with long synthesis filters modeling each space's response, and heavy reverberation makes those filters very long. Ordinary processors then introduce delay that breaks the real-time feel.

Moving the convolution work, the heavy blending step, onto a GPU cut latency enough for true real-time performance. Acoustic feedback cancellation runs on the same chip, unifying the loudspeaker-based setup. Visitors could one day walk through vanished sacred spaces and hear them answer back.
arxiv-2509-04490:
Abel van Elburg and five co-authors test whether face-reading software can tell when self-driving car passengers feel unsafe in a 2025 research paper. Thirty-two participants rode a driving simulator under calm and dynamic automated styles, sometimes meeting a crossing pedestrian. Continuous comfort ratings, motion, webcam video, eye tracking, heart rate, and skin conductance were recorded. Discomfort spiked during cornering and braking, then eased; the dynamic style hurt more, and the pedestrian doubled its comfort drop.

Faces told a different story. Most participants showed no detectable reaction to the critical event, and several who reacted looked happy rather than afraid. Fear never dominated. A neural network using motion and skin conductance tracked reported risk well instead.
arxiv-2509-04790:
Symmetry rules can limit what heat-driven operations a quantum system can perform. Unnati Akhouri studies that limit in a solo 2025 quantum thermodynamics paper. The focus is how global energy conservation and coherence resources shape the local dynamics of small parts.

Akhouri proves a no-go result: dynamics with U(1) symmetry cannot create local coherence from plain thermal states. Breaking that limit needs coherence from the surroundings, with a specific charge property. A two-qubit build shows the minimal resources for changes beyond thermal operations. The paper also shows gains in work extraction and in telling states apart, both from coherence.
arxiv-2509-04890:
When do fixed point data and equivariant cohomology determine a space with a circle symmetry? Liat Kessler and one co-author address that rigidity question in a 2025 paper. They study six-dimensional semi-free Hamiltonian circle actions, a setting where earlier published conditions proved wrong as stated.

The authors had previously proved a corrected version that relied on a restrictive distribution of fixed points. Here they swap that assumption for a global condition on equivariant cohomology, one that any isomorphism requires. They also extend the result beyond the symplectic setting to the equivariant topological setting, aiming for a final statement.
arxiv-2509-04990:
A long-standing conjecture links algebras of infinite dominant dimension with self-injectivity, the trait of embedding tightly into oneself. Call that claim the Nakayama conjecture. Hongxing Chen and one co-author approach it through virtually Gorenstein algebras in a 2025 paper. They study self-orthogonal modules. The end rings of those modules have that virtually Gorenstein property.

Under one more condition on the Nakayama translation, they prove such a module must be projective, a well-behaved type. It follows that the claim holds for strongly Morita algebras of that type. That re-proves a recent result. They also show algebras of that type can be built from Frobenius extensions. That widens the supply of examples for testing the claim.
arxiv-2509-05590:
Networks shaped like stars, with one central site linked to all others, are shown to be exactly solvable by Angela Foerster and Jon Links in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. Their networks are bosonic, meaning the particles at the sites can share quantum states freely, as photons do.

The authors introduce this class of star networks and prove the systems are superintegrable, possessing more conserved quantities than needed for exact solution. They present the energy eigenvalues in two forms of Bethe Ansatz solution, a classic technique for exactly solvable quantum models. A brief discussion covers possible applications.
