Andrea Macrì, Sebastian Jaimungal, and Fabrizio Lillo study how a trader can act well when part of the market signal stays hidden. Their trading signal drifts back toward a long-run mean, but the rules behind it switch between regimes. The trader sees prices, not the hidden state, and must guess that state from past data.

The team pairs recurrent neural networks, which read time series, with reinforcement learning agents that learn trading rules. They test three ways to feed hidden-state guesses into the trader. Feeding in the odds for the long-run regime works best, giving higher rewards and clearer rules. Simulations and a pairs-trading test support the result.
arxiv-2511-00290:
Ashwin Gerard Colaco and seven co-authors introduce NOMAD, a system that enriches live data streams by choosing which machine learning models to run on each item. Running the best model on everything is costly, so NOMAD builds chains: cheap models filter first, and pricey ones run only when needed. A formal safety rule keeps quality close to a chosen reference model.

The design borrows predicate ordering ideas from database query processing. Beliefs update as predictions arrive and data patterns shift, and the system also handles linked models such as early-exit networks and stacked ensembles. Across several datasets, NOMAD saved large amounts of computing compared with fixed setups, while matching the accuracy of the most expensive single model.
arxiv-2511-00490:
Gero Junike and Marco Oesting ask how wrong a neural network's answer might be. Networks can approximate any continuous function, but the leftover error, the bias between the true function and the network, is hard to quantify. In practice the large errors matter most, so the authors reach for extreme value theory, the statistics of rare, large events.

Beyond a high threshold, the error's distribution follows a generalized Pareto form. The authors build a new estimator for that distribution's shape parameter, tailored to neural network errors. Numerical experiments demonstrate the estimator in action. For engineers who must certify a network's worst behavior rather than its average, the method offers a principled way to size the tail of the error.
arxiv-2511-00590:
A Cherchiglia, O L G Peres, and E S Souza study how the DUNE neutrino experiment could expose non-standard interactions of neutrinos. DUNE's high-energy beam will produce tau neutrinos, a channel rarely accessible, and the authors focus on charged-current non-standard effects that could alter pion decay, the primary source of the beam's neutrinos. Such effects, if real, would signal physics beyond the standard model.

Their analysis shows the near detector's expected sensitivity to these interactions could surpass present bounds drawn directly from pion decay by about an order of magnitude. In other words, watching how neutrinos are born may beat studying the parent decays themselves. The result adds a concrete target to DUNE's broad physics program and sharpens the case for precision at the near detector.
arxiv-2511-00690:
Shravan Pradeep, Emanuela Del Gado, Douglas Jerolmack, and Paulo Arratia coin a design philosophy: geomimicry, learning from Earth materials the way biomimicry learns from organisms. Soils and sediments are soft, messy materials that also feed industry, concrete included, and they evolve under stress, chemical gradients, and living activity over long times. The authors argue these materials follow design rules written by steady natural forces.

Two research routes follow. A top-down route reads natural geomaterials, maps their building blocks to mechanical roles, and studies how training by the environment tunes the interactions. A bottom-up route assembles Earth materials component by component under fluctuating stresses, testing the framework while building. The prize is matter with programmed functions, erosion resistance or self-healing, and fresh thinking for resilient soils and even terraforming.
arxiv-2511-00890:
Kanabar Jay studies the end state of a star in collapse, when the matter inside pushes back with unequal strength in each direction. The case treated is a highly magnetized, radiation dominated star with spherical symmetry, which also loses energy as it falls inward.

A single factor with no units, built from the angular pattern of radiative opacity, which depends on magnetic field, temperature, and density, steers the motion. From the field equations, Jay derives threshold rules, sensitive to direction, that decide whether collapse starts, halts, or reverses. These inequalities place black hole birth, bounce behavior, and delayed trapping of light paths inside one geometric picture. The analysis is meant to work with ready made opacity tables for real stellar profiles.
arxiv-2511-00990:
Iryna Dubovets'ka and Mykhailo Moklyachuk solve a filtering problem in probability theory. They estimate a quantity that depends on the unseen values of a periodically correlated random process, given noisy observations of that process. Such processes, whose statistics repeat on a cycle, appear in fields from communications to seasonal data analysis.

When the spectral densities are known exactly, they give formulas for the mean square error and for the spectral characteristic of the best linear estimate. When the densities are only known to lie in some allowed class, they find the least favorable densities in that class and the corresponding minimax, or robust, estimate. The results cover both the ideal and the uncertain case in one treatment.
arxiv-2511-01090:
Vlad Negoita, Mihai Masala, and Traian Rebedea study how to build better Romanian language data for pretraining large language models. Data quality is decisive for model quality, and for under represented languages like Romanian, good corpora are scarce, so filtering matters even more than for English.

They first compare the coverage and character of Romanian corpora with English data. Then they train a lightweight multitask model on Romanian texts annotated by language models, rating educational value, topic, and format, and use it to filter at several levels. The filtered data sets improved pretraining performance across multiple benchmarks. The study also reports notable differences in which topics the Romanian and English corpora actually contain.
arxiv-2511-01190:
Lijia Yu, Xiao-Shan Gao, and Lijun Zhang ask a pointed question about chain of thought prompting: does it expand what transformers can reason about, across all tasks? Chain of thought clearly helps on some mathematical problems, but the authors recast reasoning as memorization, so the question becomes what chain of thought transformers can memorize.

They give a complete description of the memorization capabilities of fixed precision transformers, with and without chain of thought. For each case they give necessary and sufficient conditions for memorizing a finite reasoning data set, and matching parameter count bounds. The two conditions turn out not to imply each other. So there exist reasoning tasks where chain of thought does not enhance a transformer's power. That is a negative answer to the opening question.
arxiv-2511-01290:
Kana Makino, Natsumi Makigusa, and Masahiro Kojima design seamless early phase cancer trials that reuse phase one data wisely. United States regulators now push dose optimization earlier in oncology development. Designs that flow straight from phase one to phase two are gaining ground, provided the earlier data are borrowed with care.

Their nonparametric method discounts phase one observations according to how similar the patient covariate distributions are between the phases. Similarity is measured with a kernel based maximum mean discrepancy and turned into a dose specific weight inside a power prior for judging efficacy in phase two. They derive a confidence interval for the weight analytically, avoiding resampling. Simulations show better detection of truly effective doses without false alarms at weak ones, and a pancreatic cancer trial illustrates the method.
arxiv-2511-01490:
Max Schaffelder and Albert Gatt ask what happens when a large language model is fine-tuned on text that other models generated. Their study tests whether drawing that synthetic training data from many different sources, rather than one, changes how the fine-tuned model behaves.

Three effects are measured: distribution collapse, robustness against attacks, and self-preference bias, meaning a model favoring its own outputs. Diverse sources eased collapse and kept the model's outputs broad. Both human and synthetic data could strip away safeguards, though synthetic data gave higher-quality outputs, which the authors note makes them more usable and more dangerous. Fine-tuning also cut self-preference bias, with human data working best.
arxiv-2511-01590:
Yongcun Hu and six colleagues train a neural video codec that can slide its bitrate up and down, a flexibility real streaming needs but neural codecs find hard to learn. Their system, EV-NVC, attacks the weakness at high bitrates, where variable-rate neural compression usually loses ground to conventional codecs.

Two pieces carry the design: a piecewise linear sampler that improves rate-distortion behavior in the high-bitrate range, and a long-short-term feature fusion module that strengthens context modeling across frames. Mixed-precision training and stage-specific strategies are worked through in detail. In tests, the codec cut BD-rate by about 30.6 percent compared with the HM-16.25 reference encoder in low-delay mode.
arxiv-2511-01690:
A. Dal Din and a large team report a new kind of spin polarization in the altermagnet manganese telluride. Altermagnetism is a recently found magnetic phase. It splits a material's electronic bands by spin, in a pattern that waves across momentum space. The team probed single-domain MnTe crystals with spin- and angle-resolved photoemission.

The spin pattern they found comes from spin-orbit coupling, so it is relativistic in origin. Yet its alternating sign runs across, not along, the magnetic ordering vector. It is collinear, even in parity, and odd under time reversal. That mix has no match among known forms of relativistic spin polarization. Symmetry analyses back the result. So do ab initio calculations of the ground state and of the photoemission process itself.
arxiv-2511-01790:
Thorben Prein and four colleagues add a reality check to computer-led materials discovery. Search programs propose thousands of crystal structures that look stable in density functional theory. But many can never be made in a lab. The math favors low-energy forms that real synthesis cannot reach.

The team built a score for how makeable a compound is, mixing makeup and structure cues. They scored entries not yet synthesized from the Materials Project, GNoME, and Alexandria. Several hundred candidates scored as highly makeable. For 16 targets, they predicted synthesis routes, ran the work, and checked the products. Seven of the 16 were made, all in three days of lab work. The runs also exposed holes in lists of supposedly known made structures. The claim: such a score belongs at the heart of discovery work.
arxiv-2511-02190:
Honggeun Kim and sixty-three co-authors test whether simple statistics of radio sky maps can reveal how the first stars reheated the universe. The Hydrogen Epoch of Reionization Array listens for the redshifted 21-centimetre signal of early hydrogen. Instead of the usual power spectrum, this study examines one-point statistics of the maps, the variance and a third-moment measure, which are sensitive to non-Gaussian features that spectra miss.

Working with 94 nights of Phase I observations plus simulations, the team tracked how the instrument itself and a foreground-removal filter distort these statistics. The variance measurement disfavoured a cold reionization scenario with weak X-ray heating, consistent with other results. The third moment proved too contaminated by instrumental effects to constrain models, and forecasts show filtering will remain the central challenge even for the full array.
arxiv-2511-02390:
Raphael Holzinger, Nico Bassler, Julian Lyne, Susanne Yelin, and Claudiu Genes solve a classic problem in quantum optics. The case is excited atoms that can emit light collectively through several channels at once. Dicke superradiance is the burst of emission from many emitters acting in sync; with two or more competing decay channels of adjustable rates, the dynamics had no general closed solution. Their symbolic quantum-trajectory construction supplies one.

Populations and observables come out as finite sums of exponential terms, for any number of emitters and any decay rates. With two channels, the final ground-state distribution behaves like a first-order phase transition exactly where the two rates balance. For many balanced channels, scaling laws give the time and height of the superradiant peak. The authors offer the formulas as a compact tool for cavity and waveguide experiments with multilevel emitters.
arxiv-2511-02490:
Rajan Das Gupta and five co-authors present a software system meant to help detect and monitor Alzheimer's disease where advanced diagnostics are scarce. BRAINS, short for Biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Intelligence for Neurodegeneration Screening, pairs two modules around a large language model. A diagnostic module, fine-tuned on cognitive test scores such as MMSE and CDR together with brain volume measurements, performs a structured assessment of Alzheimer's risk for a new patient.

A second module retrieves similar past cases from a curated knowledge base by comparing encoded patient profiles. A fusion layer merges those cases with the current profile before the final inference, which is guided by clinical prompts. Evaluations on real-world datasets showed the system classifying disease severity effectively and flagging early signs of cognitive decline. The authors position it as an assistive, explainable screening tool rather than a replacement for clinicians.
arxiv-2511-02590:
T. K. T. Nguyen, J. Rech, T. Martin, and M. N. Kiselev listen to the noise in a quantum circuit that mimics one of condensed matter's effects. Their system is a two-channel charge Kondo circuit. In it, an island's charge plays the role of a magnetic impurity, driven across a weak link by a voltage or a temperature difference. They study fluctuations of the electric and heat currents, and the correlations between the two.

Voltage-driven noise ratios oscillate with gate voltage, echoing the behaviour of the thermoelectric coefficient, while temperature-driven ratios follow the pattern of the thermal coefficient and the conductance instead. The mixed noise, correlating charge and heat flow, behaves in the opposite way. A logarithmic dependence on temperature betrays non-Fermi-liquid physics, and the oscillations reflect particle-hole and time-reversal symmetries. The links between noise and transport survive beyond the Fermi liquid picture.
arxiv-2511-02790:
Kate Thomas studies Niven numbers, whole numbers that divide evenly by the sum of their own digits. Her 2025 paper shows that in any base of three or more, these numbers form an asymptotic basis of order three. In plain terms, every large enough whole number is the sum of three Niven numbers written in that base.

Thomas also gives an asymptotic formula counting how many ways a large integer splits into three parts with fixed digit sums, chosen near the average. Digit sums link arithmetic to the look of a number's written form, and results like this show that link is rich. Any long number, however it is written, can be assembled from just three self-dividing pieces.
arxiv-2511-02890:
Maxence Lepers surveys his own research since his 2009 doctorate in this habilitation manuscript, a French qualification document for directing research. The work falls into two halves, both about atoms and small molecules at very low temperatures or inside solids. Lepers studies how their inner structure and long-range forces shape what they do.

The first half covers atomic-structure calculations for neutral and trivalent lanthanide atoms, in settings from ultracold gases to rare-earth doped solids. The second half treats long-range interactions among alkali atoms, diatomic molecules, and lanthanides in ultracold gases. Those force laws explain effects like photoassociation, where light joins atoms into molecules, and collisional shielding, which can protect molecules in a trap. The manuscript ties a career's threads into one account.
arxiv-2511-03190:
Mingtao Zhang, Guoli Yang, Zhanxing Zhu, Mengzhu Wang, and Xiaoying Bai make attention cheap for long time series. Attention spots patterns across a sequence, but its cost grows with the square of the length, choking long records. Their 2025 method rests on a theoretical observation about entropy: distributions whose probability rankings line up and whose entropy values match tend to share the same structure.

From that fact they build an algorithm that estimates the needed entropy in linear time, yielding a linear attention mechanism based on entropy equality. Their analysis suggests attention works in forecasting not mainly through its softmax curve, but by keeping weights moderate and balanced. On four spatio-temporal data sets, the method matched or beat rivals while using far less memory and time.
arxiv-2511-03690:
Xingyao Wang and colleagues present a software development kit for building production-grade coding agents on the OpenHands foundation. Agents now help write software widely, yet shipping one that is safe, flexible, and pleasant to use is hard. The kit is a full redesign of the agent parts of the popular OpenHands framework.

A simple interface lets a basic agent be written in a few lines, while richer agents add custom tools and memory as needed. Secure, reliable execution sits beside user-facing controls for steering and watching runs. The authors aim to move agent building from bespoke demos to repeatable engineering. Teams can experiment with new agent designs without rebuilding the safety and interface layers each time.
arxiv-2511-03790:
Samuel Awelewa and Maxim Dzero study how the order parameter of an unusual superconductor rings after a sudden disturbance. They focus on a d-wave superconductor, where pairing strength varies with direction, and track the lengthwise collective mode often called the Schmid-Higgs mode.

After a weak kick at time zero, the amplitude oscillates and its envelope fades slowly as a power law. Using a standard method, the pair find the oscillation frequency equals twice the pairing amplitude in the anti-nodal direction, with decay following one over time squared. Direct numerical solutions for the Anderson spin model confirm the same behavior, supporting the analytic result.
arxiv-2511-04190:
Josef Mayr, Anna Reithmeir, Maxime Di Folco, and Julia A Schnabel test covariance profiles built from general vision encoders for medical image classification. Such profiles capture second-order stats and work well in general vision, yet they remain little used in medical imaging, where a network built for positive definite matrices offers a natural classifier.

Profiles from two pretrained encoders, one general and one medical, were compared with handcrafted profiles across eleven test sets from a medical benchmark suite. Encoder-based profiles steadily beat handcrafted ones. The specialised network did best with general encoder features, beating leading methods. Pretrained features plus covariance structure look like a strong pairing for medical classification.
arxiv-2511-04290:
Amogh Sirnoorkar, Winter Allen, Syed Furqan Abbas Hashmi, and N Sanjay Rebello examine how introductory physics students use analogies, comparing self-made ones with AI generated ones. Analogies link abstract ideas such as circuits to familiar systems such as plumbing, and self-generated versions are thought to teach better than handed-down ones, though prompting them at scale is hard.

Around eight hundred student responses were analysed for spontaneous analogy use and for comparisons built in preferred everyday contexts. Students explaining a potential curve in simple language seldom used analogies on their own, unlike model responses. Themes of ease and difficulty in generating them round out the results for large courses.
arxiv-2511-04390:
Kristóf Bérczi and three colleagues study online selection when items arrive in any order. The setting extends the matroid secretary problem, a classic model of hiring under uncertainty. Their bipartite graph framework unifies matching, matroid intersection, and secretary problems in one model.

Agents and items form the two sides, and picks must obey independence rules on both. For the intersection of k matroids, the team designs an algorithm with a proven competitive ratio. They also define k-growth systems, a new class sitting between simpler systems and matroids. The framework shows how far free-order choice can go under layered constraints.
arxiv-2511-04490:
Yameng Zhu and two colleagues propose TAL-PINN, a neural method for conservation laws near the inviscid limit. Sharp shocks break the standard residuals used to train physics-informed networks. Tiny viscosity fixes the math but creates thin layers that networks struggle to resolve.

Their framework runs in two stages and adds a learned helper field to the coordinates. That geometry comes automatically from a cheap, high-viscosity first solution. It steers the network toward steep-gradient zones with no prior knowledge of the shocks. The fully autonomous design aims to make neural solvers usable for flows where shock position is the whole problem.
arxiv-2511-04890: Jiahe Wang, writing alone, bounds when very general hypersurfaces in weighted projective spaces are algebraically hyperbolic. Weighted projective spaces allow coordinates with unequal weights and can carry isolated singularities. The hypersurface is cut out by a section of a multiple of an ample line bundle. Wang gives a bound on that multiple which guarantees the property. Algebraic hyperbolicity restricts the curves lying inside the hypersurface, a guiding theme in the study of hypersurface geometry.
arxiv-2511-05290:
Tommy Mordo and co-authors study when cooperation can hold in distributed games where talk between agents is slowed by the network. Each player fields an agent at every site, and local play follows a prisoner's dilemma, where lone greed can wreck joint gains.

Building on a 1999 frame by Monderer and Tennenholtz, they derive a term that can secure a cooperative balance. That term rests on the network's diameter and the count of sites. Edge cases of instant, fixed-delay, and scaled-delay talk show how lag eats at cooperation, a lesson for online teams and swarms.
arxiv-2511-05490:
Sascha Gehrmann and a co-author build exact strong zero mode operators in integrable quantum circuits and in the spin-half XXZ chain, for open ends of a general kind. A strong zero mode sits at a boundary and never decays, which gives endless coherence at that edge.

Their boundary terms break the bulk symmetry of the time steps, yet the mode stays exact and local to one end. They also show the mode turns non-local under the map to an exclusion process, so it plays no big role there. The contrast is a sharp lesson in how a change of variables can hide a trait.
arxiv-2511-06090:
Jeffrey Jian Ma leads a team benchmarking whether AI agents can make real software faster without breaking it. Performance work on big codebases demands deep code reasoning, and most benchmarks ask what to fix rather than how. Their suite, SWE-fficiency, hands the agent a full repository and a slow workload.

The suite holds hundreds of tasks across nine widely used data-science and scientific repositories. Tasks were mined from GitHub pull requests where experts had already sped code up, verified by execution and linked to the right unit tests. Leading agents earned less than a quarter of the expert speedup on average. They stumbled at finding the bottlenecks, reasoning across functions, and keeping edits correct. The benchmark and its pipeline are released publicly.
arxiv-2511-06390:
Suqing Wang, Ziyang Ma, Li Xinyi, and Zuchao Li present GhostSpec, a way to check whether a language model was secretly derived from another one. Fine-tuning open models is cheap and common, and some developers falsely claim they trained their model from scratch. Verifying lineage matters for licenses and intellectual property, yet training data is usually unavailable.

GhostSpec fingerprints a model from the singular values of invariant products of its attention weight matrices. The fingerprint is compact, needs no training data, and never alters the model's behavior. Experiments showed it survives fine-tuning, pruning, expansion, and deliberate disguise attempts, tracing model lineage with little computing overhead.
arxiv-2511-06590:
Maria Capcelea and Titu Capcelea solve Fredholm integral equations whose data jump at known points along a smooth closed curve. Because the smooth integral part stays continuous, the solution keeps exactly the jumps of the data. Ordinary methods smear those jumps or invent new ones, wrecking accuracy near the breaks.

Their method pairs one global periodic spline with Heaviside step functions carrying precisely the prescribed jumps. The scheme turns triangular: jump sizes come first, then a modest collocation system yields the smooth remainder. Stability and convergence rates are proven for spline orders two through four, quadrature effects are bounded, and numerical tests match the predicted accuracy against established rivals built for jumps.
arxiv-2511-06690:
Jens Flemming and Bernd Hofmann propose a fresh classification of ill-posed operator equations in Banach spaces. Ill-posed problems, where tiny data errors can swamp the solution, were sorted into two types by Nashed in a seminal 1987 paper. Much has changed since, especially for operators that are not injective and whose null spaces lack complements.

The new scheme classifies bounded linear operators between infinite-dimensional Banach spaces by ill-posedness type, giving those awkward cases a proper place. Strictly singular operators whose range still contains a closed infinite-dimensional subspace form a prominent hybrid case. New theorems also extend the theory of l1 regularization and clarify a continuity condition's role for such operators.
arxiv-2511-07190:
A Parkosidis, S Toonen, E Laplace, and F Dosopoulou extend the theory of mass transfer in binary stars to eccentric orbits. Most studies assume circular binaries, but observations show mass transfer also happens on elliptical paths, especially in systems with compact objects. Part two of their series examines how nonconservative transfer, where some mass and angular momentum leave the system, reshapes such orbits under four angular momentum loss modes.

The modes behave distinctly: Jeans loss generally widens orbits and pumps eccentricity, loss through the outer Lagrange point shrinks and circularizes, and the other two sit between. Eccentric transfer can produce compact binaries that merge by gravitational waves within a Hubble time where circular modeling predicts merger during transfer instead. The system may also explain circumbinary disks seen around eccentric evolved binaries.
arxiv-2511-07390:
Long proteins can be hard to make, deliver, or join with other proteins in medicine. Ethan Baron and colleagues want shorter versions that still do the same job. Cutting sequences by trial and error in the lab is slow and costly, so they turn to learned models of natural sequences.

Their model, SCISOR, is a discrete diffusion system trained to delete letters from protein sequences. It learns to reverse a process that adds random insertions, so it can propose natural-looking shortened proteins. The approach searches the huge space of possible deletions more efficiently than standard models. Early results point toward faster design of compact, working proteins.
arxiv-2511-07490:
Barry Smyth and Pádraig Cunningham ask whether review papers are losing their crown. Reviews once earned prestige and heavy citations by summing up whole fields. Lately their numbers have surged across disciplines, both in count and in share of all papers.

The citation bonus that reviews enjoy is shrinking, and the authors weigh why. Since generative AI tools spread in 2022, signs point to widespread AI help in writing reviews, further swelling supply. Fields flooded with similar summaries gain less from each new one. The analysis cautions editors, authors, and evaluators who still treat reviews as automatic prestige.
arxiv-2511-07590:
Eric Van Clepper, Felipe Alarcón, and Edwin Bergin propose a recycling trick that enriches giant planet air. A planet forming beyond the carbon monoxide snowline should inherit plain disk gas, yet solids drifting inward can carry ice that later vaporizes. Their DRIVE mechanism follows that loop.

Three-dimensional fluid simulations with radiative transfer track dust grains through planet-driven spiral flows. Small dust rides looping currents toward the planet, warms, and sheds its ice as vapor. That vapor can feed the growing atmosphere. The result links grain traffic around a young giant to the chemistry telescopes will one day measure.
arxiv-2511-07890:
Soowon Kim, Byung-Kwan Ko, and Seo-Hyun Lee decode spoken words from brain waves, and let the system abstain when unsure. Non-invasive speech interfaces promise communication for people who cannot speak, but wrong guesses carry real cost. Confidence awareness separates a helpful tool from a reckless one.

Deep ensembles of compact speech-tuned convolutional networks produce the decodings. Predictive entropy, top-two margins, and mutual information quantify doubt, followed by calibration and selective classification with an abstain option. Evaluation uses leakage-safe blocked splits respecting time order. Trustworthy decoding, where silence beats error, suits clinical communication aids best.
arxiv-2511-08090:
Wassim Kabbani, Kiran Raja, Raghavendra Ramachandra, and Christoph Busch present StableMorph for creating realistic morphed face images. Face morphing attacks let two people share one identity document, threatening biometric systems. Testing defenses needs strong example morphs, but older methods leave blur and artifacts that make fakes easy to spot.

StableMorph uses diffusion based synthesis to make full head morphs with sharp detail and few visual flaws. Its images rival genuine photos in quality while still fooling face recognition systems at high rates. That strength makes it a harder benchmark for morph attack detection and a tool for building more robust defenses.
arxiv-2511-08290:
David Towers, Ismael Gutierrez, and Luis Fernandez introduce the solvable graph of a finite dimensional Lie algebra. Vertices are algebra elements outside the solvabilizer, and two vertices join when jointly they generate a solvable subalgebra. The construction mirrors graph methods used for groups, but the Lie setting behaves differently in ways the authors map carefully.

Basic theory covers solvabilizers, divisibility rules, coset decompositions, and degree limits for these graphs. Worked cases show solvable graphs can be disconnected, unlike the group case. Degree sequences are computed for two standard matrix algebras, where matrix spectral types drive the patterns, and a GAP and SageMath setup supports practical computation.
arxiv-2511-08390:
Vishal Bhatoy, Colin Ingalls, Felix LaRoche, and Ravali Nookala compute pieces of the moduli space of Koszul Artin Schelter regular algebras in dimension four. These algebras form a noncommutative family behaving like polynomial rings. For known families of these algebras, the authors compute Hochschild cohomology and the Kodaira Spencer map, which tracks how an algebra deforms as parameters move through its family.

When the Kodaira Spencer map at a point is surjective, the family image forms a whole component of the moduli stack. When the map is bijective, the family maps to the stack in a generically finite way. Those criteria let the authors spot several concrete components of the moduli stack for these algebras.
arxiv-2511-08690:
Vaibhav Sharma and Erich Mueller examine how entanglement organizes itself across many qubits in circuits that are watched as they run. Random measurements compete with entangling gates, and at a critical measurement rate the circuit crosses a measurement-induced phase transition between entangling and disentangling regimes.

Using one-dimensional Clifford circuits, the authors track entanglement depth, the size of the largest cluster of mutually entangled qubits. That size grows as a power law in system size on both sides of the transition. The exponent falls smoothly from one toward zero as measurements take over. The largest cluster also fills space like a fractal whose dimension the measurement rate tunes. The authors trace the pattern to clusters merging under gates and fragmenting under measurements.
arxiv-2511-08790:
Paula Moraga Baez and eight co-authors map the molecular hearts of six nearby planetary nebulae with the ALMA radio array. These nebulae, the shed envelopes of dying stars, share an extreme bipolar shape with pinched waists, and their dense equatorial tori hold the clues to how the lobes formed.

Maps of carbon monoxide and rarer molecules, several detected in these objects for the first time, trace where the molecular mass sits and how fast it moves. In every case most gas forms an expanding equatorial torus, moving at fifteen to fifty kilometers per second. Torus ages run from about five hundred years to about eleven thousand, which supports a model where the torus is ejected before the bipolar lobes. The progenitors were likely relatively massive stars in interacting binary systems.
arxiv-2511-08890:
Sensen Lin and four co-authors explain why lithium atoms move so strangely inside a liquid lithium-lead alloy proposed for fusion reactor blankets. The alloy, seventeen percent lithium in lead, works at high temperature, and its performance depends on atomic-scale motion that simulations can now watch directly.

Ab initio molecular dynamics shows lithium does not wander freely; lead atoms form cages around it, and diffusion proceeds by repeated cage breaking. Structural analyses confirm lithium sits preferentially among lead neighbors, while electronic analyses pin the cage on a polar covalent lithium-lead bond. Surface cages and bulk cages release their lithium on different timescales, giving a double-exponential relaxation. The authors name this the chemical cage effect and offer it as a new lens on transport in multi-component liquid alloys.
arxiv-2511-08990:
Xiaolan Huang and four co-authors design the antenna array that will feed the NEW-MUSIC camera, a six-band polarimeter for trans-millimeter astronomy on the Leighton Chajnantor Telescope. The instrument spans eighty to four hundred twenty gigahertz, two point four octaves, aimed at explosive transients, hot cluster plasma, and dusty galaxies near and far.

The design stacks superconducting slot-dipole antenna arrays in a phased hierarchy. Three groups of on-chip filter banks, mixing low-pass and band-pass elements, sum the broadband antennas step by step. They carve the incoming light into the six science bands before sending it down microstrip lines to the detectors. Hierarchical summing solves a wiring and bandwidth puzzle: thousands of antennas must merge into few readout lines without losing the spectrum. The paper presents the architecture the camera will be built around.
arxiv-2511-09190:
Alexander Chebykin, Tanja Alderliesten, and Peter A. N. Bosman improve Population Based Training, a method that tunes neural network settings while training runs. Such methods adjust hyperparameters every few steps, and the gap between updates strongly affects results. Until now there was no efficient way to choose that gap.

Their variant, Iterated Population Based Training, adjusts the gap automatically through restarts that reuse learned weights in a task-agnostic way. A time-varying Bayesian optimization step reinitializes the hyperparameters at each restart. On eight image classification and reinforcement learning tasks, it matches or beats five earlier Population Based Training variants and other tuners. It does so with no extra budget and no changes to its own settings.
arxiv-2511-09590:
Jake R. Patock, Rinki Ratnapriya, and Arko Barman find clusters of related genes in RNA sequencing data with a graph-based pipeline. Knowing which genes associate with a disease matters, but so do the clusters genes form together, which hint at shared regulation. Their method starts from a dataset of genes already tied to a disease.

They build a gene co-expression network, embed its genes with the Node2Vec+ algorithm, and cluster the embeddings spectrally. Every stage is jointly tuned with a tree-structured Parzen estimator for stability and optimality. Applied to age-related macular degeneration data, the pipeline gives consistent, statistically robust clusters despite the randomness inside its steps. The authors note it transfers directly to RNA sequencing data for other diseases.
arxiv-2511-09690:
The Omnilingual ASR team introduces an open-source speech recognition system covering more than 1,600 languages, the widest reach attempted so far. Most of the world's seven thousand languages have no speech recognition at all, and extending older systems was costly and architecturally awkward. Over five hundred of the covered languages had never been served by speech recognition before.

The system scales self-supervised pretraining to seven billion parameters and pairs it with an encoder-decoder design built for zero-shot generalization. Communities can add an unserved language with only a handful of samples. Training data mixes public resources with compensated community recordings. Models range from 300-million-parameter versions for low-power devices to the full seven-billion flagship, all released openly.
arxiv-2511-09790:
Eshika Pathak, Ahmed Aboudonia, Sandeep Banik, and Naira Hovakimyan tackle the gap between the motion a robot plans and the motion it actually makes. Learning from demonstration can generate smooth task-space plans, but unmodeled dynamics, steady disturbances, and delays pull the real robot off course. Their architecture, called L1-DS, wraps any demonstration-based planner with extra control layers.

One layer is a nominal stabilizing controller, and another is an L1 adaptive controller that explicitly compensates for the mismatch. A windowed dynamic time warping selector keeps the target phase-consistent when timing slips. Tests on the LASA and IROS handwriting datasets show the architecture tracking the intended motions effectively despite the disturbances it was built to absorb.
arxiv-2511-09890:
Masahiro Kojima, Keisuke Hanada, and Atsuya Sato propose a new way to group sub-studies inside basket trials, where one treatment is tested across several related conditions at once. Baskets can respond very differently, and grouping them by a single endpoint such as response rate may mislead the analysis. Their model-free framework clusters baskets by transition probabilities drawn from each patient's treatment response trajectory over time.

The number of clusters is chosen by the data rather than fixed in advance, and baskets in a cluster are then analyzed with a hierarchical Bayesian model. Simulations showed the method finding the true cluster structure in mixed settings. It also held the type I error rate at its nominal level while improving statistical power.
arxiv-2511-09990:
Duttatreya, Ipsika Mohanty, and Sanjib Dey examine whether non-Hermitian quantum dynamics can keep a qubit coherent longer. Decoherence from contact with the outside is the basic obstacle to quantum computing's promised speedups. The authors study a qubit evolving under parity-time symmetric non-Hermitian rules, both for the system alone and when its surroundings share that symmetry.

Coherence times came out greatly longer than in the standard Hermitian setup. The improvement was strongest when system and environment were both parity-time symmetric. Stranger still, greater non-Hermiticity outside the system correlated with longer coherence, against the usual expectation that a harsher outside world destroys information faster. The authors present the effect as a possible plan for managing decoherence in quantum information processing.
arxiv-2511-10190:
Eklavya Sarkar and Mathew Magimai-Doss argue that the order of sounds inside an animal call carries information that most bioacoustics pipelines throw away by averaging features over time. They convert self-supervised speech model embeddings of vocalizations into discrete token sequences using vector quantization, in both standard and Gumbel-softmax forms. Those sequences preserve the temporal structure of each call as a string of symbols.

Pairwise distance analysis showed the token strings can distinguish call types and individual callers across four bioacoustics datasets. Classifying with nearest neighbors under Levenshtein string distance gave reasonable call-type and caller accuracy. The authors present token sequences as a promising representation for exploiting sequential structure in animal communication studies.
arxiv-2511-10590:
Miles Wang-Henderson and eight co-authors address the bottleneck of drug discovery: testing candidate molecules is slow, so each batch chosen for synthesis should count. They build probabilistic surrogate models of binding affinity on top of large structure-informed foundation models, for use in batch Bayesian optimization.

Their approach uses epistemic neural networks to produce joint predictions across a whole batch of designs, which parallel acquisition strategies need in order to hedge sensibly. A central finding concerns the prior networks inside these models: pretraining them on synthetic data improves downstream performance. On benchmarks, the method rediscovered known potent EGFR inhibitors in up to five times fewer rounds, and found potent compounds in a real-world library in up to ten times fewer.
arxiv-2511-10690:
Juntu Zhao, Jialing Zhang, Chongxuan Li, and Dequan Wang peer into the hidden language of multimodal AI systems by playing telephone with them. When a system compresses an image into text and another expands the text back into an image, the systems' built-in preferences shift which concepts survive and co-occur, and those shifts are measurable.

Running multi-round telephone games, the team quantifies how strongly concepts are connected inside a system's understanding. They contribute Telescope, a dataset of more than ten thousand concept pairs, as the game's database. The method can map concept connections globally, expose training-inherited biases, and find stable pathways for fragile connections. Reasoning models then help surface unexpected relationships that go beyond textual and visual similarity.
arxiv-2511-10790:
Girish, Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar, Farhan Sheth, and Muskaan Singh tackle forensic tracing of manipulated speech: not just whether audio is synthetic, but which generator made it and how the emotion was altered. MiCuNet is presented as the first curvature-adaptive system built for this multitask tracing problem.

MiCuNet combines embeddings from speech foundation models, which carry semantic and prosodic cues, with fine-grained spectral features from auditory inputs. A mixed-curvature projection spreads the evidence across hyperbolic, Euclidean, and spherical spaces, guided by a learnable gating mechanism. Trained to predict the original emotion, the manipulated emotion, and the manipulation source at once, it was tested on the EmoFake dataset in both English and Chinese, steadily beating standard fusion strategies.
arxiv-2511-10890:
Tiantian He and six co-authors model how Alzheimer's disease spreads through the brain, arguing that the map it travels on has been drawn too simply. Standard models let pathology follow a single-modality connectivity network, which mispredicts long-term spread. Purely data-driven graph learning cannot pin the graph down without more constraints.

Their framework recruits large language models as expert guides on how regional variables interact. It uses the models' ability to synthesize multi-modal relationships and diverse disease mechanisms. It jointly builds long-term disease trajectories from irregularly sampled patient data and learns the biologically constrained interaction graph between brain regions. Tested on tau-PET imaging from an Alzheimer's cohort, the method predicted pathology propagation more accurately and interpretably than traditional approaches, and surfaced disease-driving factors beyond conventional connectivity.
arxiv-2511-11190:
Tianlang He, Zhongming Lin, and their colleagues present LoRaCompass, a learning system that guides a mobile sensor to find a lost long-range radio tag in the fewest moves. Such tags are worn by people at risk of going missing, and the sensor must follow a fluctuating signal strength in unknown places. Older learning methods can be thrown off by signal shifts, and one bad step can cascade into a poor search.

LoRaCompass learns a sturdy spatial reading of signal strength that favors moves toward the tag, aided by a distillation loss. A confidence-guided exploration rule, modeled on an upper bound idea, steers the hunt. Ground tests validate the design.
arxiv-2511-11290:
Jean-Christophe Aval and Sébastien Labbé give three counting interpretations for q-analogs of rational numbers, a deformed version of fractions introduced by Morier-Genoud and Ovsienko. In a q-analog, each integer is replaced by a polynomial in q that reduces to the integer when q is one. Earlier readings of these q-rationals covered only fractions above one, which left half the picture missing.

Their readings use a new Ostrowski numeration system, order ideals in fence posets, and perfect matchings of snake graphs, all working for every positive fraction from one shared object. Order-preserving bijections carry the proofs. A formula for a q-analog of Markoff numbers is recovered, plus a fourth reading via lattice points in a polytope.
arxiv-2511-11490:
Joan Font-Quer Roset, Devina Mohan, and Anna Scaife estimate the intrinsic dimension of the Radio Galaxy Zoo data set, the effective number of directions needed to describe its radio galaxy images. They use a score-based diffusion model for the estimate and study how it shifts with a Bayesian network's energy score, which gauges how alike a source is to a curated subset. Sources far from that subset showed higher dimension.

Overall dimension for the zoo exceeded values typical for natural image sets. Across the two classic Fanaroff-Riley shape classes no clear split appeared, while lower dimension weakly tracked higher signal-to-noise. The authors suggest the dimension-energy link could help study and improve self-supervised representations.
arxiv-2511-11590:
Robert Gigiu proposes a safety framework for artificial intelligence inside Britain's National Health Service, where AI tools increasingly support clinical work. Existing NHS safety standards, DCB0129 and DCB0160, were written for fixed, predictable software and say little about transparency, interpretability, or models that drift over time.

The Explainability-Enabled Clinical Safety Framework folds explainable AI outputs into the existing safety lifecycle, so clinical safety officers can use them as structured evidence in safety cases, hazard logs, and post-market monitoring. A cross-regulatory mapping links NHS clauses to wider machine learning practice. Compliance routes stay unchanged, which is the point: AI evidence is added without rebuilding the system.
arxiv-2511-11790:
Peter Kirgis probes the moral outlook of large language models using moral foundations theory, the psychological framework that sorts values into foundations such as care, fairness, loyalty, authority, and purity. Models now advise in politics, business, and education, yet the character of their ethical judgment stays opaque.

A synthetic experiment elicits value judgments from a wide range of models by major providers and compares them with the human baseline from the original survey work. Descriptive statistics document each model's bias and spread across foundations. Models lean on different foundations from one another, a finding with practical weight for anyone deploying them where values are contested.
arxiv-2511-12290:
Purnima Bindal, Vikas Kumar and Vasudha Bhatnagar propose AugAbEx, a pipeline that strengthens legal case summarization by adding a second kind of summary to an existing dataset. Summarizing judgments is hard for lawyers because the language is complex, jargon depends on context, and documents are long. Abstractive systems also carry known risks in this domain.

AugAbEx takes a dataset with human-written gold summaries and augments it with extractive silver summaries that select key passages and reflect expert opinion. The authors check the added summaries for structure, wording and meaning within a legal framework. Tests across seven English legal datasets support the value of having both summary types available.
arxiv-2511-12390:
Sanjar Atamuradov replaces the standard control pipeline for humanoid robot teleoperation with a learned neural policy. In virtual reality teleoperation, a human guides a robot through hard manipulation tasks. Classic systems solve inverse kinematics and use hand-tuned controllers, which cope poorly with outside forces, new users and dynamic motion.

The learned policy maps VR controller input straight to robot joint commands, trained first from demonstrations made with the classic system and then fine-tuned with force randomization and rewards for smooth motion. On a Unitree G1 humanoid, the authors report much lower tracking error, smoother trajectories and better force adaptation than the baseline, while staying real-time.
arxiv-2511-12490:
Mainak Singha documents an equity trading factor that he reports achieves very high out-of-sample performance by switching on only in certain market regimes. The strategy combines value and short-term reversal signals, but activates them only for stocks in a drift regime, defined by a trailing window in which the stock rose on most days.

Singha reports walk-forward tests over twenty years of S and P 500 data with frozen parameters, plus randomization trials and checks that exposure to standard risk factors is small. Those are the author's reported results, presented as evidence that regime conditioning uncovers cross-sectional predictability hidden in unconditional tests. Readers should weigh the extraordinary claimed returns with that framing in mind.
arxiv-2511-12590:
Guoqing Xu, Yiheng Li and Yang Yang present TopoFG, a framework for reasoning about lane topology in autonomous driving, where knowing how lanes connect guides navigation and control. Most methods represent each lane with a single query and infer connections from similarity between those queries. That coarse design struggles with complex lane structures and gives unreliable topology.

TopoFG breaks the path from bird's-eye-view features to topology into three phases with fine-grained queries. A prior extractor gathers global spatial cues and local keypoint sequences along lanes. A decoder builds and refines fine queries by sampling the lane mask region, and a final stage reasons about topology from robust boundary points.
arxiv-2511-12690:
Sina Rashidi and Hossein Sameti build a direct speech-to-speech translation system for Persian to English. Direct systems translate spoken words into spoken words in one joined model, which is simpler and faster than chaining separate tools. Their weakness is hunger for parallel speech data, which barely exists for Persian. The authors answer with a three-part model: an encoder for source speech, a decoder that predicts discrete speech units, and a vocoder that turns units into sound.

To feed the model, they also built a pipeline that makes synthetic parallel data. Persian transcripts were translated by a large language model, then spoken aloud by a zero-shot text-to-speech system. That grew the available speech pairs roughly sixfold. On a standard Persian-English test set, the model beat direct baselines by a clear margin in translation quality. The recipe may help other low-resource language pairs.
arxiv-2511-12890:
Arth Sojitra and Omer San remove the numerical solver from training neural operators. Neural operators learn maps between function spaces, such as from a forcing field to the solution of an equation, but training them normally needs huge datasets from expensive solvers or experiments. Their Method of Manufactured Learning borrows an old verification trick: invent smooth candidate answers first, then apply the governing equations to compute the forcing that would produce them. Training data is thus manufactured analytically, with physics built in by construction.

At inference, zero forcing restores the real equations, and the trained operator predicts genuine solutions. Using a Fourier neural operator, the method reached high accuracy and low residual errors on heat, advection, Burgers, and diffusion-reaction benchmarks, and generalized to unseen conditions. Because the method accepts any architecture, the authors offer it as a scalable, solver-free path to physics-grounded operator learning.
arxiv-2511-12990:
Sixtus Dakurah tests whether two groups of brain networks differ in shape, not just in wiring strength. Judging weighted networks by their raw edge weights lets small random noise masquerade as structural difference. Dakurah's framework first splits network signals with combinatorial Hodge decomposition, separating flow-like components, then compares groups using the two-Wasserstein distance between persistence diagrams, which summarize the shape. The test statistic is a variance ratio: how much dispersion shrinks within groups relative to between groups, measured in Wasserstein space.

Tests show the method suppresses small random perturbations while staying sensitive to genuine shape differences, working best on the Hodge-decomposed flows rather than raw weights. Dakurah applies it to functional brain networks from a multimodal ADHD treatment dataset, comparing cannabis users and non-users. Shape-aware statistics offer neuroscience a way to ask whether connectivity differs in kind, not only in degree.
arxiv-2511-13090:
Arun Kumar Pati, Vlatko Vedral, and Erik Sjoqvist prove a simple law about the phases a quantum system picks up as it evolves. A total phase splits into a dynamical part, from energy and time, and a geometric part, from the path the state traces. The split matters for robust quantum gates. The authors show the fraction that is geometric is fixed, at every instant, by one quantity alone: the Bargmann angle, a measure of distance between quantum states.

That gives an exact, universally applicable way to say how geometric any evolution is while it happens. The authors point to real-time design of high-fidelity geometric gates, quantum speed limits, and coherent control as immediate uses. The paper is short and theoretical, five pages with no figures. A long-standing partition problem turns out to be governed by a single angle.
arxiv-2511-13690:
Shyam Kamal and 3 co-authors introduce a Ramanujan inner product as a new yardstick for stability of discrete and hybrid systems. Classic checks rely on Euclidean distance, but number-based sums carry structure that standard tools ignore. Their framework builds a norm and conditions directly from Ramanujan summation and its arithmetic links.

New epsilon-delta style criteria state when a system stays stable under the Ramanujan measure, with stronger robustness guarantees claimed than the standard route. All main results are proven in full. Numerical simulations on sample systems back the theory, suggesting number traits of a system's dynamics can inform how engineers judge its stability.
arxiv-2511-13890:
Nick Waddoups, Jonah Boe, Arnd Hartmanns, and four co-authors verify the reliability of network-on-chip designs, the communication fabrics inside modern chips. Traffic swings cause power supply noise that can corrupt data transfers, and chip layouts vary widely in size and use. Their case study builds models in the Modest language that mirror how designers actually structure these systems.

Starting from one generic router model, they assemble networks of many sizes and check both function and quantitative behavior with the Modest Toolset. Functional correctness is proven for the router, its links, and whole networks. Statistical checks then cover power noise properties for grids up to eight by eight.
arxiv-2511-14090:
Luke Piszkin and Dervis Can Vural argue that evolution can recall the path it took. They study this memory effect, called hysteresis, with theory, computer models, and real data. In a two-gene model, links between genes make the fitness landscape bistable, so a population can sit in one of two states. They find two kinds of memory loops when selection cycles or jitters.

A gene-linked population even reached its best mean fitness at a mid level of noise in its habitat. The loops also show up in a larger messy model and in protein motion models. In twenty years of lake DNA data, about sixty-five percent of season-cycled gene variants showed clear hysteresis.
arxiv-2511-14590:
The JUNO collaboration presents initial performance results for its large neutrino sensor after physics running began in August 2025. The sensor pairs a twenty kiloton liquid scintillator core with a water Cherenkov veto and a top scintillator veto. It sits under a deep rock overburden. Commissioning covered water filling, scintillator filling, and first physics runs.

The scintillator reached a long attenuation length at blue wavelengths. Light yield at the center is high thanks to dense photomultiplier coverage. Energy resolution measured with calibration sources meets design needs. The paper documents that the full system works as built. It provides the baseline for all later JUNO oscillation and astrophysics results.
arxiv-2511-14690:
P. O. Mchedlov-Petrosyan and L. N. Davydov revisit a classic two-equation model for materials that change order and separate into phases at the same time. The Eguchi-Oki-Matsumura system tracks one quantity that is conserved and one that is not, driven by a free energy with gradient terms and a quartic coupling. It belongs to a broad class known as type C models.

The authors change the conserved dynamics to a convective, viscous version of the Cahn-Hilliard equation. Under that change, the full system gains an exact traveling wave solution, a rare closed-form result for such models. Exact waves give a firm test case for simulations of alloy cooling and phase change.
arxiv-2511-15090:
Wenhan Yu, Zhaoxi Zhang, and six co-authors build SciEGQA, a data set that tests whether AI systems can answer questions about scientific papers using the right evidence. Scientific documents mix text, figures, and tables, so finding the exact region that supports an answer is hard. Most benchmarks grade only the final answer, leaving the evidence unmarked and the reasoning unchecked.

SciEGQA marks the supporting evidence as coherent document regions with boxes around them. One part is a human-annotated benchmark of high-quality question-answer pairs; the other is a much larger training set built automatically. Systems can now be scored on grounding their answers, not just guessing them, which matters for trustworthy research assistants.
arxiv-2511-15190:
Yuxuan Gu, Weimin Bai, and three co-authors speed up a hybrid image generation model so it can finally be trained with reinforcement learning. Masked autoregressive diffusion models generate by unmasking pieces in a chosen order while a diffusion chain refines each piece. That double loop makes generation slow, and slow generation blocks the trial-and-error training that modern post-training depends on.

Their framework, MARVAL, distills the inner diffusion chain into a single autoregressive step while keeping the flexible unmasking order. The distilled model should retain the original's expressive power at a fraction of the inference cost. Fast sampling is the gatekeeper for reinforcement learning on generators, so the speedup is the real deliverable.
arxiv-2511-15390:
Haidong Kang, Lihong Lin, Enneng Yang, Hongning Dai, and Hao Wang address a practical problem with large language models: the models work well but are too big to run easily. Cutting away parts of a model, called pruning, usually needs expert hand design. Their method, AutoPrune, asks a language model itself to design a good pruning method.

A graph-based prompting method helps the model reason through the design and produce clear, strong pruning plans. A second part shares out the cuts unevenly, so rare but important large values do not cause a sharp drop in quality at high cut rates. Tests on common model benchmarks show AutoPrune beating leading rival methods.
arxiv-2511-15690:
Yushi Huang, Zining Wang, and six co-authors present MoDES, a method to speed up multimodal mixture-of-experts models by skipping experts that are not needed. Such models route each token to a subset of specialized sub-networks, which is powerful but costly at inference time. Skipping methods built for text-only models lose much accuracy on multimodal ones because experts differ across layers and token types.

MoDES estimates each token expert importance by blending global layer importance into local routing chances. Separate thresholds for each data modality then set the skipping schedule, found by a search that cut tuning from days to hours. Across three model series and thirteen benchmarks, MoDES far outperformed earlier approaches, even when most experts were skipped.
arxiv-2511-15990:
Osama Zafar and three co-authors present a digital agriculture sandbox where farmers and researchers analyze farm data collaboratively without exposing private information. Farm data could address global food challenges, yet farmers hesitate to share it. Privacy fears limit learning that would improve farming practice. Their secure online platform is built for users with limited technical resources.

Federated learning, differential privacy, and related methods protect data while preserving research utility. Farmers can find similar peers through a simplified process inside the system. Researchers gain aggregate insight without seeing raw records. The sandbox model tries to align incentives: farmers keep control, science still advances. Such trust infrastructure may matter as much as sensors for data driven agriculture.
arxiv-2511-16190:
Mengyu Cheng, Xianjin Cheng, and Zhenxin Liu ask whether McKean-Vlasov stochastic equations possess random attractors, the random sets that pull long-run behavior toward them. These equations depend on the distribution of the solution itself, which breaks the usual stochastic flow property and blocks standard attractor theory.

The authors lift the equation onto a product space pairing the state with its probability law, where cocycles can be defined for two coupled dynamical systems. On that space they build a general existence theory for pullback random attractors. They then apply it to stochastic ordinary, reaction-diffusion, and two-dimensional Navier-Stokes versions of the McKean-Vlasov equation. In one case the attractor is a single random point, which is exactly the stationary solution of the decoupled equation.
arxiv-2511-16690:
Saleh Almohaimeed and four co-authors expose a fairness problem in AI text detectors. Human writing that an AI merely polished gets flagged as machine-written, at least in Arabic, where the issue had not been studied. Such false accusations can damage authors and discredit the detectors themselves.

The team built two datasets, one of 800 Arabic articles split between human and machine authorship, and Ar-APT, with 400 human articles polished by ten language models under four settings each. Fourteen candidate detectors were screened, and the best eight faced the polished texts. Every detector misattributed a large share. The best commercial tool fell from ninety-two percent accuracy to twelve percent on lightly polished text, and the best language model judge dropped by about a quarter. That is a stark warning for Arabic academic integrity tools.
arxiv-2511-17290:
Marii Ojastu and five co-authors create an Estonian version of WinoGrande, a widely used commonsense reasoning benchmark for language models, and study what translation does to the test. Specialist translators adapted the test set to local culture rather than translating it literally. The authors then measured both proprietary and open-source models on the human-translated benchmark, and compared their scores with the original English version.

Performance on the human translation ran slightly below English, while performance on machine-translated data was notably worse. The team also tried to close that gap with a detailed prompt encoding lessons from the manual process, aimed at Estonian's linguistic features and the dataset's traps. Prompt engineering helped little. Their conclusion is practical: reliable evaluation in a smaller language needs language specialists in the loop, not just better machine translation.
arxiv-2511-17690: V V Kiselev examines heavy quark fragmentation at high energies, the process by which a heavy quark turns into a hadron that carries it. He puts forward a form for the fragmentation function that describes that transition. He argues it agrees with a reciprocity relation linking fragmentation to how the heavy quark is distributed inside the hadron as a virtual parton. He then analyses how well the relation fits empirical data.
arxiv-2511-17790:
O. P. Mykhailiv, Yu. A. Mishchenko, and A. M. Gavrilik derive a deformed version of Einstein's equations for gravity using a modified model of a Bose gas and an approach adapted from Verlinde. The deformation is controlled by a parameter that changes the effective value linked to the spread of the universe.

In their treatment, that parameter lets the effective cosmological constant vary, so choosing it well can bring the value down toward what observations suggest. The authors present this as a possible route to a long standing problem about why that constant is so small, and they note a link to dark matter.
arxiv-2511-18190:
Harshith Alagandala studies when a smooth surface placed in complex space stays well behaved near a special point. At most points the surface meets complex lines in a clean way, and a key good trait holds there. At rare points, called CR points, that clean meet fails, and the trait may break.

Such points split into two kinds, named elliptic and hyperbolic. Elliptic points are known to block the good trait. In two complex steps the trait is known to hold at hyperbolic points. Alagandala asks if the same holds in higher steps, where far less is known. The work sets up the terms and tests the claim case by case.
arxiv-2511-18290:
Jungho Lee, Minhyeok Lee, Sunghun Yang, Minseok Kang, and Sangyoun Lee speed up dense 3D rebuilds of large scenes. Rebuilding a street or hall from photos forces a trade: fast methods blur detail, while sharp methods run slow. Large scenes add drift, since small pose errors pile up across a long path.

Their method, SwiftVGGT, needs no training and cuts run time while it keeps detail high. It closes loops on its own, with no outside place matcher, which trims waste and holds shape over spans near a kilometer. A lean point match step lines up chunks in one pass. The design suits scans of big sites where both speed and scale matter.
arxiv-2511-18390:
Ajay Tak and Mayank Baranwal study a two level optimization task spread across a network of agents. Each agent can talk and compute only with its near peers, yet the group must cut a joint cost while it obeys shared limits. Such tasks model large sensor and control networks well.

The pair propose a scheme that pools gradient steps across agents. They prove it homes in at a linear rate, a fast pace, under a mild claim: the joint cost as a whole must curve up in a strong sense. Past proofs asked each local cost to curve that way, a far stricter ask. Tests on a sensor network task back the proof. The weaker claim widens where such methods can be trusted.
arxiv-2511-18590:
Kaley Brauer, Aditya Prasad Dash, Meet J Vyas, Ahmed Salim, and Stiven Briand Massala work on carrying galaxy knowledge from simulations to real surveys. Coming telescopes will image billions of galaxies, and fast automated tools must infer traits like shape, stellar mass, and star formation rate. Simulations supply images with known labels, but differences in blur, noise, backgrounds, and selection between simulated and real data degrade the transfer.

The team builds an early pipeline that trains on simulated galaxies from a major simulation suite and tests on real survey galaxies with shape labels. Three model backbones are compared, with class-balancing tricks and a feature-level loss that pulls the two domains together using several distance measures. A matching loss focuses effort on the worst-matched cases.
arxiv-2511-18890:
Yonggan Fu and 14 co-authors design Nemotron-Flash, a small language model tuned for low delay on real devices, not just few parameters. Small models serve apps with strict lag limits. Past design chased parameter counts, yet a lean parameter bill does not mean a fast reply on hardware.

Two design facts rule real lag: the depth to width ratio, key at small batch sizes, and operator choice, which shapes both lag and large batch throughput. The team map lag best ratios and build a hybrid model on those rules. Training follows the same lag first lens. The result targets quick replies where users wait. Principles, not one model, are the export.
arxiv-2511-18990:
G A Bobkov, I A Shvets, I V Bobkova, A M Bobkov, S V Eremeev, and E V Chulkov calculate the behaviour of a Josephson junction. Its middle layer is an ultra-thin film of a rare-earth compound, GdIr2Si2. In such junctions, two superconductors are separated by a magnetic film, and the ground state can settle at an unusual phase shift. That shift enables a superconducting diode effect with no applied field, whose strength and direction can be controlled, and it couples the superconducting phase to the film's magnetisation.

Using density functional theory, the team studies the material and computes the current-phase relation of the junction. Their results show both the anomalous phase shift and the diode effect in this specific interlayer. Such junctions are candidates for superconducting memory and logic circuits, where the magnetisation could store a state the phase can read.
arxiv-2511-19390:
Rudy Morel and twenty co-authors forecast systems where only part of the state can be seen, using the Sun as a leading case. Solar observers watch the surface and atmosphere, while the drivers of change sit hidden inside. Standard rollout forecasts lose long-range links because each step forgets too much of the past.

A multiscale inference scheme for diffusion models is built to carry past information across scales while generating future paths. The method targets long-memory behavior in physical processes such as evolving solar active regions. The result is a probabilistic forecast that keeps long-range structure instead of drifting into short-term guesses.
arxiv-2511-19690:
Niklas Haas, Sören Schmitt, and Rob van Stee study an online scheduling problem where processors conflict with each other. Jobs flow into buffers on processors over time, and running processors drain them, but conflicting pairs cannot run at once. Conflicts form a graph, and the goal is to keep the largest buffer load as small as possible.

Unlike the older model, work arrives continuously over intervals rather than in blocks at set times. The authors give tight bounds for every graph on four vertices except the path, which was already solved, and for complete and complete bipartite graphs. Almost tight bounds cover general graphs as well.
arxiv-2511-19790:
A. Sanny and eight co-authors build and test the beam combiner at the heart of NOTT, a visitor instrument for the Very Large Telescope Interferometer. NOTT will study hot dust near young stars and Jupiter-like planets at the water snowline by nulling interferometry, which cancels starlight. Four telescopes feed the instrument, so their beams must be merged precisely.

The combiner is a chip of mid-infrared glass, patterned by ultrafast laser writing, in a double-Bracewell design. In the lab, four fake telescope beams test its modal, color, and polarization behavior plus throughput. The couplers hold steady splitting ratios across the band, a step toward on-sky nulling.
arxiv-2511-19990:
Yaoli Liu, Ziheng Ouyang, Shengtao Lou, and Yiren Song present OmniRefiner, a framework for polishing a generated image against a reference. Reference-guided generation is improving fast, but fine detail is often lost in refinement. Latent compression in the model's autoencoder discards subtle texture, so identity and attribute cues vanish, and many edits clash with the original lighting or shape.

OmniRefiner corrects the draft in two stages. First, a single-image diffusion editor, fine-tuned to take both the draft and the reference, refines the whole image while keeping its structure. Reinforcement learning then strengthens local editing, rewarding detail accuracy and semantic consistency. On hard reference-guided restoration benchmarks, the method beats open and commercial rivals in alignment and detail.
arxiv-2511-20390:
Wen, Li, Luo, Li, and Wang make image-generating transformers finish faster. Their 2025 paper speeds up Diffusion Transformers, which create images by gradual denoising. That denoising runs step by step, so latency is high. Speculative methods draft ahead and verify in parallel. On these transformers, drafts are too inaccurate to help much.

The team studied how features evolve during denoising. The final layer's features stay consistent over time and carry rich meaning. Their framework, FREE, drafts in that feature space instead. A lightweight drafter proposes six speculative drafts per round. The big model verifies them in a single pass. Rejection triggers a reflection step discarding later drafts. Prediction uncertainty grows in later denoising steps, though. A relaxed variant lowers acceptance demands when uncertainty rises. On ImageNet at 512 by 512 resolution, FREE reached 1.86 times speedup. The relaxed version hit 2.25 times while keeping image quality.
arxiv-2511-20490:
Vasilev and colleagues test AI doctors on realistic cancer case conferences. Their 2025 paper introduces MTBBench, a benchmark in oncology. Real molecular tumor boards unite oncologists, radiologists, and geneticists. They weigh imaging, genomics, and history as cases evolve. Existing benchmarks ask isolated, single-modality questions instead. That gap hides how unreliable medical models can be.

MTBBench simulates board-style decisions with questions that evolve over time. Clinicians checked the ground truth through a co-developed app. Open and closed language models were all benchmarked. Even large models hallucinated and mishandled time-resolved data. Conflicting evidence across data types tripped them up repeatedly. The authors add an agent framework with foundation model tools. Tool access lifted task scores by up to nine percent. Time-based reasoning tasks gained up to 11.2 percent. The testbed pushes testing toward dynamic, decision-focused settings.
arxiv-2511-20590:
Muszynski and colleagues build a digital twin where microgrid parts negotiate like traders. Their 2025 paper introduces EnergyTwin, a multi-agent simulation platform. Microgrids juggle solar panels, batteries, and loads under shifting prices. Power simulators assume one central controller runs everything. Agent frameworks model negotiation but ignore real physics.

EnergyTwin couples grounded physical models with agent choices. Each asset, from panels to storage, acts as its own agent. A weather agent and forecast agent feed predictions in. A central aggregator allocates energy through contract-based deals. Planning rolls forward in short spans with fresh forecasts. A campus scenario tested several strategies side by side. Forecast-driven planning raised local energy self-sufficiency clearly. Battery reserves stayed higher under that strategy too. Exposure to fragile states dropped in those runs. The platform targets the slow supervisory layer of control.
arxiv-2511-20690:
Kaytki Chakankar, Xinhui Tang, and Yiguo Zhang bring quantum mechanics to a classic strategy puzzle in 2025: the centipede game. Two players take turns choosing to grab a growing reward or pass it along and let it grow. Reasoning backwards from the last move, pure logic says the first player should grab everything in round one. Yet real people cooperate far more often.

Following earlier quantum work on the prisoner's dilemma, they let players use quantum strategies, built on linked particles and operations impossible classically. They ran their algorithm in Qiskit, a standard quantum programming toolkit. The quantum version produced two new Nash equilibria, stable outcomes neither player can improve by switching alone, and both beat the classical result. Payoffs rose for both players, and outcomes matched real-life play more closely than backward induction does. The authors end with a general conjecture for similarly built quantum games.
arxiv-2511-20890:
Ilyas Djafer-Cherif and Bartlomiej Waclaw solve in 2025 a mundane but ruinous microscopy problem: over hours of time-lapse imaging, thermal drift and mechanical shifts slowly push a living sample out of focus. Commercial autofocus hardware fixes this but can cost a large share of the microscope's price. Their imPerfect Focus System needs a motorised focus drive and marks drawn on the far side of the coverslip, the glass the sample sits on, photographed to measure drift.

The marks sit opposite the sample, so focusing on them never disturbs the image, and each field of view is corrected independently, needing 10 to 20 seconds between measurements. The authors ship a Beanshell script and test the method across objectives. Benchmarked against hardware autofocus, it performed comparably. Nikon's hardware samples 200 times per second, accurate to a third of the focal depth, but costs accordingly. The method proved itself in live imaging of bacterial colonies.
arxiv-2511-21090:
Qin Wu and Ralph-C Bayer ask in 2025 whether fining the coach as well as the athlete actually deters cheating. In contests from sport to corporate research, prizes tempt contestants to cheat, but usually only the contestant is punished, while coaches or managers share the winnings and can encourage the act. That mismatch is an agency problem. The authors model joint liability, shifting part of the sanction onto the second agent, and test the prediction in laboratory experiments, with funding from the IOC's anti-doping research programme.

Theory gives a twist. When fines are harsh, joint liability reduces cheating, as hoped. When fines are lenient, spreading liability can perversely raise cheating, because the contestant's own expected penalty shrinks.
