Experiments confirmed the first effect: joint liability worked when fines were high. The predicted backfire at low fines, however, did not appear. Policy takeaway: shared sanctions help, provided the fines bite.
arxiv-2511-21190:
Astronomer T. Mishenina and five coauthors report new measurements of two rare elements in old stars in a 2025 paper on how the Galaxy built its heavier atoms. The elements, molybdenum and ruthenium, form inside stars and explosions through neutron-capture processes, where atomic nuclei absorb neutrons one by one. Where these elements came from is still debated, so fresh abundances for single stars help test the competing production routes.

The team measured spectra, meaning light split into fine detail, for 154 giant stars in the Galactic disk. They obtained molybdenum for all of them and ruthenium for 110 stars, most for the first time. Both elements grow scarcer relative to iron as a star's iron content rises, a trend shared with zirconium, while strontium stays nearly flat across the same range. That contrast helps separate which nuclear processes fed the disk over time.
arxiv-2511-21290:
Wanyun Chen, Haoqi Li, Chih-Ting Lu, and Qiulei Wang test whether a future muon collider could settle a galactic mystery in 2025. The mystery is the Galactic Center GeV Excess, an unexplained glow of gamma rays from the Milky Way's core. One suspect is muonphilic dark matter, invisible matter that talks only to muons through a new mediator particle, which would explain the glow while dodging earthbound detectors.

Chen and her coauthors simulate a 3 TeV muon collider and study three search strategies: visible mediator decays, invisible decays seen as a lone photon plus missing energy, and off-shell mediator production. Their cut-and-count analysis sets projected exclusion limits at 95 percent confidence for seven representative models across a wide span of mediator masses. The projected reach covers a significant share of the parameter space that fits the excess, making the collider a decisive test.
arxiv-2511-21490:
Taehoon Kim, Donghwan Jang, and Bohyung Han teach neural networks new classes by literally averaging their brains with their younger selves, in 2025. Class incremental learning adds categories in stages, and the standing curse is catastrophic forgetting: mastering stage two erases stage one. Their method, Merge-and-Bound, works directly on model weights instead of on data or loss functions.

Kim and his coauthors merge weights two ways. Inter-task merging averages the models from all finished stages into one consolidated network. Intra-task merging blends checkpoints within the current stage to speed learning. A bounded update rule keeps each stage's training on a short leash near its starting weights, so new knowledge lands close to old knowledge. The recipe plugs into existing incremental methods with no architecture or objective changes. On standard benchmarks it beat leading methods, with the clearest gains when the memory budget for old examples was tightest.
arxiv-2511-21590:
Muhammad Siddique and Sohaib Zafar design a control architecture for power grids that must think fast and locally, in 2025. Modern smart grids juggle stop-start renewable supply, shifting loads, and cyber threats like false data injection, while central control suffers latency and single-point failures. Their hybrid cyber-physical framework stacks three layers, physical, cyber, and control, around a central energy management system.

Adaptive dynamic programming and AI-based optimization drive the control layer, tuning dispatch as conditions change. The design runs in two modes: cloud-independent, for low-latency decisions made on site, and cloud-assisted, for central coordination with heavier computation. Simulated on the standard IEEE 33-bus test system, the framework maintained grid stability, optimized power dispatch, and responded effectively to changing operating conditions in both modes. The authors present it as a scalable template, though the evidence is simulation-based rather than from a field deployment.
arxiv-2511-21690:
Seungjae Lee and ten coauthors teach robots from videos of hands and other robots, in 2025. Robot demonstrations are scarce and costly, while videos of humans and different machines abound, differing in body, camera, and setting. Their answer is a shared representation: a compact 3D trace-space recording scene-level motion trajectories, abstracting away appearance while keeping the geometry manipulation needs.

TraceGen is a world model over trajectories: it predicts future motion in trace-space instead of pixels. Its training pipeline, TraceForge, converts mixed human and robot videos into uniform 3D traces, yielding 123,000 videos and 1.8 million observation-trace-language triplets. The pretrained motion prior adapts fast: with just five target robot videos, TraceGen reached 80 percent success across four tasks, running 50 to 600 times faster than video-based world models. From only five uncalibrated phone videos of a human, it still achieved 67.5 percent success on a real robot.
arxiv-2511-21890:
Bertsimas and colleagues improve classification using a blend of kernels, mathematical similarity measures, where few kernels keep models interpretable. Instead of the usual penalty that only approximates sparsity, they impose an exact limit on how many kernels may be used, plus a stabilizing penalty. The resulting hard non-convex optimization problem is attacked with an alternating best response algorithm that switches repeatedly between two easier subproblems. One solved with a standard SVM solver and one with a greedy selector method.

They also build convex relaxations whose solutions certify near-optimality and warm-start the algorithm. On ten standard UCI benchmark datasets, their method beat the best competing multiple-kernel approach by 3.34 percentage points of out-of-sample accuracy on average with random starts in the reported tests. With warm starting from the relaxation, the average gain rose to 4.05 percentage points, and in several cases certificates proved global optimality.
arxiv-2511-21990:
Ghosh and colleagues at NVIDIA present a safety and security framework for agentic AI systems that plan, call tools, and execute multi-step tasks. Safety, they claim, is an emergent property of the whole interacting system, so failures cascade in ways single-model tests miss.

The framework supplies an operational risk taxonomy unifying classic safety and security concerns with agent-specific risks such as tool misuse, cascading action chains. Unintended control amplification, where outputs become unchecked instructions. Its core is dynamic risk management with helper AI models and human oversight, plus sandboxed AI red teaming. They demonstrate it end-to-end on NVIDIA's flagship AI-Q Research Assistant. An enterprise-grade research agent with complex workflows, where the risk discovery phase surfaced novel agentic risks that were then contextually mitigated without breaking the assistant's usefulness. They also release over 10,000 attack and defense traces from the case study.
arxiv-2511-22190:
Menon, Prasad, Mallick, and Sahoo, nuclear physicists in India, sort simulated proton-proton collisions by shape to learn how charmonium production depends on event topology. They generate collisions at 13 TeV with the PYTHIA8 event generator and measure J/psi mesons, bound charm-anticharm states. They separate prompt ones made in the collision from nonprompt ones fed by beauty-hadron decays, as a function of transverse spherocity. Spherocity is an observable distinguishing jet-like events from soft, isotropic ones.

Spherocity correlates with the average number of multiple parton interactions in each collision, an experimentally measurable quantity rather than a simulation-only one. It offers a handle for selecting events to expose the underlying QCD processes driving production. The study maps how both prompt and nonprompt yields, reconstructed through dielectron and dimuon decays at mid- and forward rapidity, vary across event shapes. The predicted correlation now awaits experimental validation.
arxiv-2511-22390:
Van Ditmarsch, French, Galimullin, and Kuijer study logics quantifying over ways information can change in a group of agents. A refinement represents agents becoming better informed, while a simulation represents them being less informed, as at an earlier stage before learning, or after forgetting. Refinement quantification is well studied, but its simulation dual has received much less attention.

The team relates the two directions and adds modalities for mutual factual ignorance, where agents share no factual knowledge at all, capturing a system before any facts were learned. They build a stack of logics, each extending the previous one with simulation, refinement, or ignorance operators, and give reduction-based axiomatisations for several. Reduction axioms translate statements about information change into equivalent ones without change operators, so richer logics inherit the proof machinery of simpler ones.
arxiv-2511-22490:
Inadumi and colleagues build the missing dataset for automatic scientific poster design. Conference posters decide how research is communicated, yet nobody had a large collection pairing papers with their posters' layouts. The link between a paper's structure and its poster's design could not be studied. Their dataset, SciPostGen, contains 18,097 paper-poster pairs from four major machine learning and computer vision conferences, annotated for paper content and poster layout elements.

Analysing the dataset, they find a paper's structure is associated with how many layout elements its poster uses. Building on that link, their Retrieval-Augmented Poster Layout Generation framework searches for layouts matching a new paper and uses them as guidance for a generator. In experiments with and without creator-specified layout constraints, the retriever picked layouts aligned with paper structures, and the generator produced layouts respecting the given constraints, a step toward automatic poster drafting.
arxiv-2511-22690:
Borse and colleagues at Qualcomm AI Research split drawing groups of people into planning and painting. Text-to-image models routinely botch multi-human scenes, duplicating faces, merging identities, or miscounting heads. Their framework, Ar2Can, uses an Architect module predicting a layout, bounding boxes saying where each person should appear. An Artist, a diffusion model, renders the photorealistic image inside that plan, keeping faces at planned locations with planned identities.

Fidelity is enforced by a spatially grounded face matching reward combining Hungarian spatial alignment with ArcFace identity similarity. The system is optimised with Group Relative Policy Optimization using rewards for count accuracy, image quality, and identity matching. On the MultiHuman-Testbench, Ar2Can substantially improved count accuracy and identity preservation over proprietary and open-source baselines while keeping perceptual quality high. Remarkably, it trains on synthetic data, no real multi-human photographs required, sidestepping a data bottleneck.
arxiv-2511-22990:
Fay and colleagues address shortcut learning in medical image AI. A model may diagnose from a misleading clue, such as the scanner or a patient's sex, instead of the anatomy that actually causes a disease. Such models score well at home but fail in new hospitals, and real datasets usually contain several tangled shortcuts at once, not just one.

Their framework, MIMM-X, separates the features that carry the true signal from several spurious factors at once by minimizing mutual information between them. Mutual information is a measure of how much one signal reveals about another. Tested on brain MRI from UK Biobank and the German NAKO cohort and on chest X-rays from CheXpert, it held up where rivals collapsed. When the shortcut correlation was flipped, most comparison methods fell to near 50 percent accuracy, close to guessing. MIMM-X reached 70.4 percent, the best of the group.
arxiv-2512-00190:
Split graphs are networks whose vertices divide into a fully connected clique and an independent set with no internal edges. Daniel Jaume and co-authors study the nullspace of their adjacency matrices in a 2025 study. The nullspace collects the vectors that the matrix sends to zero.

The authors introduce the clique-kernel, a subspace that decides whether clique vertices appear in the support of a kernel eigenvector. They prove its dimension is at most one. Results like these help algebraists and network scientists predict when a graph's structure forces special spectral behavior. The clique-kernel keeps the analysis focused on the clique side of the split. Its tight dimension bound is the kind of clean answer graph theorists prize.
arxiv-2512-00290:
Language models show promise for education, yet putting them in classrooms without checks risks real harm. Guoqing Ma and co-authors introduce EduEval in 2025, a benchmark for evaluating large language models in Chinese education. It is organized as a hierarchy of cognitive skills.

EduEval targets kindergarten through grade twelve education and tests models across subjects and thinking levels. Rigorous evaluation is needed because fluent answers can still be wrong, biased, or badly pitched for a child's level. Such benchmarks give schools and developers evidence for deciding where these models help and where they should stay out. Chinese classrooms give the benchmark a concrete national curriculum to test against.
arxiv-2512-00390:
Language models are increasingly used to judge which search results are relevant, but their judgments can be primed. Nuo Chen, Hanpei Fang, and co-authors study this threshold priming effect in 2025. Earlier relevance judgments can sway later ones, biasing the labels.

Psychological theories link personality traits to such biases, yet it is unclear whether simulated personalities in models show similar effects. The authors test mitigating the bias by infusing personality into the judging model. Cleaner automated labels matter because search engines and AI training both depend on trustworthy relevance judgments. Relevance labels train the rankers that decide what searchers see first. Priming is a human bias, so finding it in models raises pointed questions.
arxiv-2512-00690:
Takuya Miyamoto proves a finiteness result in a 2025 algebra paper. His subject is derivations, which are rules for taking a kind of derivative inside abstract algebras. Integrable derivations can be lifted step by step, and the steps where new behavior appears are called leaps.

Miyamoto shows that the leaps of these modules are finite in number for algebras and schemes essentially of finite type. The setting is an algebraically closed field of positive characteristic, where familiar calculus rules change. His proof answers a question posed by L N Macarro. Finiteness results like this keep wild behavior in algebra within bounds.
arxiv-2512-01090:
Yannick Omar wrote a 2025 theory paper on how protein clumps drift in cell membranes. Many membrane proteins assemble into aggregates, groups that can change the protein's function. These assemblies affect key cell processes such as signal transduction, how signals cross the membrane, and endocytosis, how cells pull material inside.

Omar presents a theoretical description of the instantaneous translational diffusion coefficients of such aggregates. Diffusion coefficients measure how fast the clumps wander sideways in the membrane. The theory covers both free membranes and supported ones resting on a surface, using Kirkwood-Riseman theory. Knowing drift rates helps interpret microscope tracking of proteins.
arxiv-2512-01190:
Nagham Osman and four coauthors present LGDC in a 2025 paper on graph generation. Generating realistic graphs matters across science, from molecules to social networks. Existing methods come in two broad kinds. Autoregressive models grow a graph step by step, while one-shot models, such as diffusion, produce the whole graph at once.

LGDC performs latent graph diffusion with spectrum-preserving coarsening. Coarsening shrinks a graph while keeping its spectrum, a summary of its structure, intact. Working in a latent space and coarsening carefully could make diffusion faster without losing the traits that make a graph realistic.
arxiv-2512-01290:
Edhin Mamani studies flows along curved paths on closed shapes. The shapes have no conjugate points, a trait that keeps paths from crossing in a set way. Their cover space lets one see far in all directions. On such shapes, flows settle into balance states.

Mamani asks when that balance state is the only one of its kind. He looks at weight rules that stay flat on some sets formed by horospheres. A weak gap in pressure is part of the test. Proofs of single balance states help link the shape of a space to how paths move through it.
arxiv-2512-01490:
Marius Ottosen, Magnus Parlo, and Philippe Bonnet study how DuckDB uses local storage. DuckDB is a database built to run anywhere. It serves on laptops, cloud hosts, and smart devices. How it talks to disks shapes its speed a lot.

The team looks at that link through xNVMe, a lean storage path. They ask where time is lost and where gains can be made. In cloud or edge use, storage is often the slow step. Leaner storage calls could make queries much faster for the same hardware cost. Findings feed back into core DuckDB design, where storage calls can be shaped to suit fast local drives far better than before.
arxiv-2512-01590:
Nick Huggett and co-authors derive a direct way to compute Wigner functions for open systems. The Wigner function spreads a quantum state over position and momentum. It has wide use in quantum work. Open systems leak to their surroundings as they evolve.

Their case is one particle linked to a general environment. The partner may even be relativistic. They give a formula that builds the Wigner function from its start values. Direct forms save steps in studies of decoherence, where quantum traits fade through contact with the world. Direct forms help most in real-time control, where a state estimate must be rebuilt at each step without a costly detour.
arxiv-2512-01690:
Philip Garrett and co-authors give auto-generated API tests descriptive names. Auto tests guard software quality in API-based systems. Their names are often bare labels like test0. Bare names slow reading and upkeep a lot. A tester cannot tell what a test checks from its name.

The team generates names that state the test's intent. Clear names speed failure triage and code review. They also help new staff trust and keep auto tests. The work targets REST APIs, where test suites can grow to thousands of cases. Name quality is scored by human raters as well, since a name can be technically apt yet still confuse the staff who read it.
arxiv-2512-01790:
Bernard Bercu, Luis Fredes, and Emeric Gbaguidi build a hybrid stochastic Newton method for logistic regression. Large-scale binary classification needs second-order speed. Pure Newton steps are too costly on big data. Stochastic gradients are cheap but noisy.

Their Hessian estimate blends two weighted parts. One part is the natural Hessian estimate. The other comes from stochastic gradient data. Blending aims for Newton-like speed at stochastic cost. Fast logistic fits serve fraud, medical, and recommendation systems with huge row counts. Logistic models sit inside credit and health scoring, so a faster second-order fit shortens the loop for testing fairness across groups.
arxiv-2512-01890:
Knowledge graphs keep growing as new facts arrive, but the neural models trained on them tend to forget old facts when they learn new ones. Gaganpreet Jhajj and Fuhua Lin test a remedy in 2025: Elastic Weight Consolidation, a method that protects the weights a model relied on most for earlier tasks.

They apply the method to link prediction with TransE embeddings on the FB15k-237 benchmark, repeating the experiments across multiple random seeds. Their measurements show that the consolidation approach cuts the forgetting that plain sequential training suffers. The study gives practitioners a grounded sense of how far this regularization trick goes for ever-changing knowledge graphs.
arxiv-2512-02190:
In fast-growing African cities, a community cut off from motorable roads is cut off from jobs, care, and markets. Sebastian Hafner and a large team build in 2025 a new accessibility metric and road-quality measure to model road access deprivation across Sub-Saharan Africa.

Access to passable roads is a basic dimension of urban infrastructure, yet many communities, especially poorer ones, remain poorly served. A metric that joins road quality with real accessibility can show where deprivation concentrates and how severe it is. Such maps give planners and aid programs a defensible way to aim investment at the neighborhoods that need it most.
arxiv-2512-02290:
Oil spills at sea show up in radar satellite images, but models trained to spot them in one region often fail in another. Andre Juarez and three co-authors tackle in 2025 that transfer problem for the Peruvian coast, where labeled Sentinel-1 radar data are scarce.

Sea state, backscatter statistics, and slick shapes all shift between regions, defeating models that memorized one coastline. The authors perturb spill shapes morphologically and generate synthetic radar images from labels to train on. Cross-domain segmentation that works with little local labeling could extend spill monitoring to coasts that currently go unwatched.
arxiv-2512-02390:
Semi-Lagrangian schemes solve transport problems by tracing where fluid parcels came from, and they pair naturally with high-order interpolation. Haruki Takemura establishes in 2025 rigorous error estimates for such schemes applied to one-dimensional conservation laws that also carry a dispersive term, including the Korteweg-de Vries equation.

Dispersion, which spreads waves by speed, makes these equations harder than plain conservation laws, and the schemes' accuracy needed proof. Error estimates tell users how fine the grid must be for a trustworthy answer. Soliton-bearing equations like Korteweg-de Vries appear across physics, from water waves to plasmas, so dependable numerics travel far.
arxiv-2512-02590:
Kanoy Kumar Das, Rajiv Kumar, and Paramhans Kushwaha study ideals built from the edges of a graph. To each simple graph they attach a binomial edge ideal, an algebraic object in a polynomial ring. Numbers called Hilbert coefficients summarize how that ideal grows in size.

The team relates those coefficients to the regularity of the ideal, a measure of its complexity. Graph structure, such as shape and connections, leaves fingerprints in these algebraic values. Results of this kind let algebraists read graph properties from equations, and let graph theorists borrow algebraic tools. Two small counts can hide a lot of shape, and the pair finds what shape they hide in each case.
arxiv-2512-02790:
Keming Ye and nine co-authors build a large dataset and benchmark for AI image editing. Powerful multimodal models now edit images well, but closed systems outpace open ones. The gap, the authors argue, stems from scarce large scale, high quality training data and weak benchmarks.

UnicEdit-10M uses unified verification to raise data quality while growing to ten million examples. A matching benchmark diagnoses model weaknesses across many editing behaviors. Open data and honest tests could let open models catch up, and show exactly where each model still fails. Ten times the data, with checks at each gate, is the kind of base open teams have lacked for years on end.
arxiv-2512-02890:
Seunghyun Baek and three co-authors design a quantum computer that both moves ions and shares them across modules. Trapped ion systems offer high fidelity, deterministic operations through physical shuttling of qubits. Distributed quantum computing instead links separate modules, gaining parallelism and pipelining.

Their SDQC architecture combines both strengths in one hybrid design. Entangled ion qubits are distributed by deterministic shuttling to carry out nonlocal operations. Blending movement with distribution may scale ion machines further than either approach alone, a key step toward useful large quantum computers. Fleets of small rigs that share work beat one big rig. The catch is that share links must hold firm when the load grows past the first tests.
arxiv-2512-02990:
S. Korpar and nine co-authors characterize a large area photon detector built from microchannel plates. The LAPPD, in its second generation, senses light through a capacitively coupled readout electrode. Large, fast photon detectors serve particle physics, medicine, and neutrino observatories.

Two variants with different geometries and materials were tested with a picosecond pulsed laser system. The team measured single photon timing response and how charge spreads across segmented electrodes. Careful characterization tells experiment builders exactly what timing and position precision this detector can deliver in the field. Fast eyes with true aim are rare in one box. This round of tests tells crews which of the two builds comes close to that rare pair in real use.
arxiv-2512-03090:
Surfactants help detergents clean and stay stable on the shelf. Sayeedul Sheikh and four co-authors study how to design new ones in this 2025 work. The old way to make them is slow, hard, and based on trial and error.

New data-driven tools can suggest fresh surfactants and guess their traits. Yet most tools tune just one trait or learn from very few cases. The authors push for a broader digital approach to design. Faster design could cut lab time and cost. It could also lead to cleaners that work better and harm nature less. For detergent makers, a digital design path promises fewer failed trials in the lab.
arxiv-2512-03190:
Metal-organic frameworks are crystals built like tiny scaffolds. Sahar Andarzi Gargari, Emilio Méndez, and Rocio Semino simulate how one such crystal grows in this 2025 work. Making these materials still relies on trial and error, since their self-assembly is poorly understood.

Past simulations studied how the crystals start, but not how they grow. The team models growth at fixed chemical potential, which mimics a steady supply of building blocks. Detail at the molecular level could guide better recipes. These materials are used in gas storage, filters, and catalysts. Growth at steady supply mirrors real synthesis, where fresh building blocks arrive throughout.
arxiv-2512-03290:
Some partial differential equations are stiff and span many scales. Julian Evan Chrisnanto and Nurfauzi Fadillah present ASPEN, a network for such problems, in this 2025 work. They target the Ginzburg-Landau equations, used for superconductors and phase change.

Physics-informed networks solve equations without a mesh, but they struggle with high-frequency parts. Standard networks have a spectral bias toward smooth outputs. ASPEN adds spectral and physics-aware design to capture sharp features. Better solvers help in materials science and fluid work, where such equations appear often. Stiff equations model superconductors and alloys, so a solver that handles them has wide value.
arxiv-2512-03690:
Cooling tiny particles that float in laser light is a route toward studying quantum behaviour in objects large enough to see. Jialin Li, Guangyu Zhang, and Zhang-qi Yin examine that problem in a 2025 quantum physics preprint. Standard schemes use an optical cavity to remove energy. Losses inside the cavity and noise from the surroundings set a floor on how cold a particle can get.

Their proposal links two floating particles in a one-way, nonreciprocal fashion. One particle is cooled directly by the cavity. Energy then flows to the second particle through the uneven coupling. Calculations and simulations show that stronger nonreciprocity improves this transfer. The indirectly cooled particle ends up with fewer phonons, the units of vibrational energy, than cavity cooling alone would allow. The authors offer the scheme as guidance for controlling energy flow in sensing devices.
arxiv-2512-03790:
Process mining studies how work actually flows inside an organisation, but it needs structured logs, while much evidence sits in free text. Iris Beerepoot, Vinicius Stein Dani, and Xixi Lu present ExOAR in a 2025 preprint on databases and society. Their method targets object-centric process mining, where records must name the objects involved and the activities performed on them.

ExOAR pairs a large language model with a human checker in a staged workflow. The model proposes object types, activities, and individual instances, guided by context such as the user's profession. The user reviews and corrects each round before the next begins. After a demonstration, the tool was tested on real window-tracking data from five users. It turned messy text into structured logs with clear meaning, while keeping flexibility and human oversight throughout.
arxiv-2512-04290:
High entropy oxides mix many cations into one crystal lattice, and the disorder is supposed to stabilise exotic phases. Ksenia Khoroshun, Mario U. González-Rivas, and Alannah M. Hallas test that expectation in a 2025 materials science preprint. Their question: does adding configurational entropy actually deliver the targeted material?

They attempted the trick in four oxide families, perovskite, pyrochlore, Ruddlesden-Popper, and zirconium tungstate. In each, a site holding one tetravalent cation was offered an entropic mixture of four, benchmarked against a non-disordered reference compound. Ionic radius rules said all four should form. Only the high entropy perovskite did. The pyrochlore attempt yielded an entropy-stabilised defect fluorite instead. The Ruddlesden-Popper phase arrived mixed with competitors. The tungstate precursors melted at an unexpected eutectic before any high entropy phase formed. Stability, the authors conclude, cannot be read off radius and charge rules alone.
arxiv-2512-04590:
Kenan Begovic, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, and Qutaibah Malluhi turn a Linux tracing tool into a source of features for machine learning. The kernel's ftrace framework can record every function call a program makes, drawn as a graph over time. Such traces expose what software truly does, beyond what its files claim. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests whether those traces can teach a model to spot encryption at work.

The team built features from function graph traces across a large file set. Several learning algorithms then judged which files showed encryption activity. Accuracy reached well past ninety-nine percent in their runs. A second test asked models to name which program was running, from traces alone, across many labels. That check also scored well. Trace-based features could help security tools catch ransomware and hidden crypto miners by behavior, not signatures.
arxiv-2512-04790:
Maddalena Amendola, Chiara Pugliese, Raffaele Perego, and co-authors present WalkRAG, a conversational guide that plans walkable city routes with the help of retrieved local data. Language models make charming travel guides, yet they invent places and fumble spatial facts. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds them in real records; spatial retrieval adds maps and distances. Their 2025 arXiv paper applies that blend to walkability and urban discovery.

A visitor states wishes and limits, such as distance, shade, or step-free paths. WalkRAG fetches fitting streets, sights, and services, then reasons over them in dialogue. The chat format lets users refine the route step by step. Because answers rest on retrieved map data, invented shortcuts and phantom cafes fade. Such tools could help tourists, new residents, and walkers with limited mobility find routes that truly fit their feet.
arxiv-2512-04890:
Ramya Muthukrishnan, Borjan Gagoski, Aryn Lee, and co-authors present E(3)-Pose, a fast method for tracking a fetus's head position during MRI scans. Babies move, and each diagnostic slice must be prescribed against the head's current pose in six degrees of freedom. Quick low-resolution volumes before each slice provide the raw data. The catch is symmetry: a fetal head looks alike from several angles, so pose tools get confused, on top of noise and blur. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds the symmetries into the method itself.

E(3)-Pose models rotation equivariance and object symmetry explicitly, by construction. Ambiguities that break generic estimators are handled as features, not noise. Tests on public and clinical fetal MRI sets show robust pose estimates where older tools falter. Automatic, reliable pose tracking could shorten scans and cut repeat visits for expectant mothers.
arxiv-2512-05190:
Farshid Jafarpour introduces an exactly solvable model of growing cell populations. Cells grow exponentially, but with a twist: the random fluctuations in a cell's growth scale with the square root of its size, and cells divide under general size-control rules. Models that can be solved exactly, rather than merely simulated, are precious because they anchor the rest.

Three exact results follow. First, the population's growth rate equals the average single-cell growth rate exactly, whatever the noise strength or division scheme. Unlike models with size-independent noise, square-root noise costs the population nothing in fitness. Second, Jafarpour solves for the steady spread of cell sizes, which growth noise widens. Third, the rescaled population size settles into a fixed distribution depending only on the growth noise, untouched by division noise or lopsided splitting. The model becomes a benchmark with clear fingerprints for telling noise types apart.
arxiv-2512-05490:
Monchai Kooakachai, Tiwakorn Chapalee, Chairat Thitiyan, and Patsaya Jumnongwut check whether family DNA searching behaves the same across Southeast Asian populations. Forensic databases name offenders by exact matches; when none exists, investigators search for first-degree relatives using likelihood ratios. If several subpopulations are plausible, those ratios can be worked out per population and combined in ways such as taking the mean or the maximum or minimum. Which strategy is fairest may depend on the population structure. United States studies cannot settle that for Asia.

The authors test the strategies in Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore. As earlier research found, statistical power varies by strategy. Within Thai subpopulations, the minimum-ratio strategy is preferred: it keeps detection power high while shrinking differences between subpopulations. The study gives regional forensic practice an evidence base of its own rather than a borrowed one.
arxiv-2512-05790:
Lorenzo Livi builds a statistical theory of how far back in time a gated recurrent network can learn to look. Their gates decide what to remember. Learning long lag patterns is hard with finite samples. Livi defines a maximal horizon for each network size: the longest lag whose structure gradient training can still recover. The theory rests on an envelope describing how learning strength fades with lag, shaped jointly by the gates and the optimizer.

Under heavy tailed fluctuations, the envelope's decay law decides the regime. Horizons can grow logarithmically, polynomially, or exponentially with sample size. Slower envelope decay widens the window far more than extra data does; heavy tails squeeze it. A complex network with a slower decaying envelope can thus learn long range structure from fewer examples than a simpler one. The work helps designers match architecture to the memory a task demands.
arxiv-2512-05890:
Kassie Archer, Aaron Geary, and Robert Laudone count a family of Lie algebras that can be drawn as pictures. Seaweed algebras are picked out by two compositions, ways of cutting a number into parts. The pair is drawn as a planar graph called a meander. From the picture, the algebra's index can be read off mechanically. The paper asks a counting question: how many seaweed algebras have a fixed index, when the part sizes of their compositions are restricted?

The restriction studied in depth is to part sizes drawn from acyclic sets, special collections with no hidden cycles. The counting comes with a bridge: indecomposable seaweed algebras with restricted meanders correspond to permutations with restricted displacements. In some cases the index is a simple statistic on the permutation. Turning one into a permutation problem unlocks a whole family at once.
arxiv-2512-05990:
Xin Li's paper, published under a title joining Poincaré and Bellman, is about what a learning system should remember, and what remembering costs. Memory consolidation decides present competence and future flexibility. Li joins two traditions: state abstraction and optimal control. Poincaré stands for qualitative dynamics, the reusable structure of how actions and responses pattern; Bellman, for dynamic programming that prices acquiring, keeping, reusing, merging, and forgetting memories.

The analysis is careful about its claims. Merging states is distinguished from erasing history; exact repair is characterized exactly. A Bellman recursion runs over the joint law of the hidden state and the deployed memory, and a first return model yields an explicit rule for what to retain. The limits are stated plainly: no open ended learning, no tractable global planning. An exact benchmark for small models is a discipline the field needs.
arxiv-2512-06390:
Mehrab Hosain and seven co authors survey how the modern web is defended at its edge, where content delivery networks sit between users and the sites they visit. Web apps and the interfaces behind them now face AI aided attacks that shift shape without pause. Because edge networks see traffic first and can run code close to users, they are a natural place to post AI driven guards.

The survey covers four fronts. Smart firewalls learn normal behavior. Other defenses blunt floods of junk traffic, and bot control resists software mimicking humans. Further tools map hidden interfaces and flag odd patterns in encrypted streams. The authors add a shared method, a threat map, metrics, and deployment playbooks. They close with open problems, from clearer AI reasoning to self acting guards, and warn that edge AI brings risks of its own.
arxiv-2512-06490:
Agatsya Yadav and Renta Chintala Bhargavi show that a large language model can be shrunk enough to run on a plain Android phone. Big models are too large and hungry for such small hardware. The team applies post training quantization, a compression that rounds the model's numbers to far fewer bits after training is done, using common open tools on Meta's Llama model of modest size.

At four bit precision the model lost more than two thirds of its size. It was then converted into a mobile friendly file format with tools from the llama.cpp project. The shrunk model ran on an Android device inside a terminal app through a local serving tool, and it answered inference tasks well in hands on checks. The study makes the case that four bit compression plus phone ready formats is a practical path to capable on device language tools.
arxiv-2512-06590:
Tendai Mukande and four co authors build a recommender that thinks in webs and talks through a team of language models. Recommenders drive shopping and social apps, and a newer breed generates suggestions directly with large language models. That breed can hallucinate goods that do not fit, and it costs a lot to run. Their system, HGLMRec, attacks both problems at once.

A hypergraph encoder first maps the tangled, multi behavior links between users and items, where one edge can join many nodes at once. A team of language model agents then works from that map, fetching only the tokens that matter at answer time, which trims cost while enriching context. In tests the system beat leading baselines on recommendation quality while running cheaper. The work points toward generative recommenders that stay grounded in the real structure of user behavior.
arxiv-2512-06790:
Lingyun Fu and seven co authors give black hole superradiance a full quantum treatment. A spinning black hole can amplify waves that scatter off it, and light bosonic particles can pile into a dense cloud around it, draining its spin. That makes such black holes probes for ultralight particles that might fill the universe. Past work treated the field classically, leaving open how particles are produced and the cloud grows.

The authors quantize a massive scalar field around a Kerr black hole in the canonical way. They work within standard quantum field theory in curved spacetime. In it, the cloud's particle count, energy, and angular momentum all evolve consistently. The cloud's growth does not depend on the state the field starts in. They also treat Hawking radiation, back reaction on the spin, and self interaction shifts. The result is one coherent quantum picture.
arxiv-2512-06890:
Roger K Moore argues that comparing animal calls with human speech sounds simple but is easy to do badly. Both fields are mature: speech science has long studied how voices are made, and animal research has catalogued countless vocal displays. Moore says a fair comparison first needs a shared checklist of basic facts. Without it, researchers risk matching things that only look alike on the surface.

His list has seven items. It covers how many moving parts the vocal apparatus has, and whether each part can be controlled on its own. It adds the sound properties of the setting, how striking the sounds are to listeners, and whether sounds truly contrast with each other. The last items ask whether calls can be combined into larger meaningful units, and how much information the signals carry per second. Any cross-species claim should be measured against it.
arxiv-2512-07090:
Jungmin Lee and co-authors trim the cost of running large language models by discarding tokens that carry little new information. Pruning methods usually decide what to cut using offline calibration data, which may not match the text a model actually meets, making cuts unstable. Their method, Token Filtering, decides online, during inference itself. It measures how similar each token's key and value vectors are to its neighbors, and skips attention work for the redundant ones.

A variance-aware fusion rule weighs the key and value signals head by head, protecting informative tokens even when pruning is aggressive. The scheme adds no memory overhead. Across several open model families and sizes, it beat earlier structured pruning methods on commonsense reasoning tests. It also held up on the demanding MMLU benchmark even with half the tokens pruned.
arxiv-2512-07190:
Pengfei Gu and co-authors give medical image classifiers a sense of shape that pixel-based networks miss. A scan's meaning often lives in anatomy, in structures and holes that topology, the mathematics of shape, can summarize. Earlier attempts used only simple topological summaries from a single viewing rule. This framework computes persistence diagrams, maps of which shape features appear and vanish across scales, at several image resolutions and under several filtrations.

A vineyard algorithm then merges those diagrams into one stable picture spanning the whole organ down to small local irregularities that can signal early disease. A cross-attention network reads the merged diagram directly, and its embedding is fused with the features of an ordinary image backbone, convolutional or transformer. On three public data sets, the enriched models improved consistently and considerably over strong baselines, including recent state-of-the-art systems.
arxiv-2512-07590:
Kaili Qi, Zhongyi Huang, and Wenli Yang wrote this 2025 paper on splitting images into meaningful regions. Noise and blurred or broken edges make that task hard in many real images. Pure neural networks can learn the job, but their choices are hard to explain.

Their system, a robust form of VM_TUNet, blends older mathematics with deep learning. It builds physical prior knowledge into a modified Cahn-Hilliard equation. An edge detector plus a mean curvature term guides the boundaries toward smooth, sensible lines. Two modules share the work inside the network. One cleans the image in the frequency domain to avoid poor local traps. The other handles careful local computation, backed by a stability estimate. Across three benchmark datasets, the hybrid matches strong rivals at fair cost. Its results look cleaner than plain convolutional networks. The design shows math-based structure can still sharpen modern image tools.
arxiv-2512-07690:
Robert Gray and Alex Levine wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on equations in three-dimensional worlds. The fundamental group of a manifold encodes its loops and twists. Two open questions ask whether equations over such groups can always be solved by algorithm.

The questions come from Aschenbrenner, Friedl, and Wilton, and they resist easy answers. Gray and Levine encode Hilbert's tenth problem inside group equations. That encoding works for a wide family of Seifert fibered manifold groups. Any group there that is not nearly abelian carries the undecidable payload. Equation problems and first-order theories both turn undecidable as a result. The authors then classify which Seifert groups keep decidable theories. The answer is clean when the base orbifold has non-negative curvature-like charge. A single equation stays decidable for that class. Negative cases are partly settled through work on hyperbolic group extensions.
arxiv-2512-08390:
Daniele Loco, Kisa Barkemeyer, Andre Carvalho, and Jean Philip Piquemal, computational chemists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They test whether today noisy quantum computers can do a real drug discovery task: predicting where water molecules sit inside a protein pocket. Those hydration sites shape how a drug binds, so placing them well matters for lead design and docking setups.

They recast water placement as a binary optimization problem and solve it with a hybrid scheme. A classical liquid theory method supplies the physics, and a quantum optimizer runs on hardware with over a hundred qubits. The results matched classical precision on real protein ligand complexes, reproducing experimental predictions. A resource analysis shows accuracy should grow as qubit counts rise, putting full quantum utility within reach, with hints of advantage where classical optimization struggles.
arxiv-2512-08490:
M Castellano, L Napolitano, B Moreschini, and a large international team of astronomers posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their target is GHZ2, a bright, compact galaxy seen as it was when the universe was very young, at redshift twelve point three. Understanding such early galaxies matters, because the early universe holds surprisingly many bright ones.

Deep spectroscopy from the Webb telescope measured a rich set of emission lines. The nitrogen to oxygen ratio came out near twice the solar value. One oxygen line appeared in only the first observing epoch, flickering over weeks in the galaxy own time, strongly suggesting an active nucleus. Combining data from other telescopes, the team shows no single density model can reproduce the spectrum. Star formation must proceed in a layered interstellar medium, with dense and thin gas side by side, plus an extra hard ionizing source beyond stars alone.
arxiv-2512-08890:
Krzysztof Burnecki, Marek Teuerle, and Martyna Zdeb study how to price catastrophe bonds that cover risks in several regions at once. Catastrophe bonds are a major part of the insurance linked securities market, which offers an alternative way to transfer risk. That market has grown steadily, and many bonds are tied to losses in different areas.

The authors build pricing models under different assumptions about how catastrophe losses in separate regions depend on each other. They cover the independent case, a proportional case, and a general two dimensional distribution case. They also derive a normal approximation for the prices, which can simplify practical use. A standard transform is applied to include the market price of risk. Using property claim data, they illustrate how prices differ across dependence scenarios and how well the approximation performs. The work helps issuers and investors handle regional dependence more carefully.
arxiv-2512-09390:
Mathis Cohen leads a team demonstrating a compact device that converts single photons from a semiconductor source into telecom-wavelength photons. Quantum networks face a mismatch: good photon emitters work at one wavelength, while optical fibers carry light best at another, in the telecommunication C-band. Frequency converters bridge that gap.

Their setup combines a fiber-coupled nonlinear lithium niobate waveguide with a fiber-pigtailed single-photon source based on semiconductor quantum dots. Photons starting in the near infrared were converted to the C-band with an end-to-end efficiency close to half. Crucially, the converted photons kept their single-photon purity and their indistinguishability, the properties quantum applications depend on. Because both modules are fiber-based and reach top-level performance together, the authors present the work as an important step toward linking future quantum processors that operate at different wavelengths.
arxiv-2512-09590:
Emmanuel Gnabeyeu, Gilles Pagès, and Mathieu Rosenbaum study stationarity, the settling into a stable regime, for inhomogeneous affine Volterra processes, a class of processes with memory, used in finance. True Volterra equations are non-stationary, so over any finite horizon they cannot reach a steady state. That complicates their use in models like the Volterra Heston model for option pricing.

The authors introduce a fake stationary regime, where all one-time distributions share the same expectation and variance even though the process is not stationary. For their fake stationary Volterra Heston model they derive a closed-form characteristic function. They then examine the long-time limit and show limiting distributions exist. Those may depend on the starting state unless the memory kernel is the fractional integration kernel, in which case the dependence vanishes. The message: finite-time, fake-stationarity analysis gives a handle on systems that are non-stationary.
arxiv-2512-09890:
Anna Bison and Alessandro Sperduti compare two ways of measuring over-smoothing in graph neural networks. Over-smoothing is the failure mode where node features in a network all blur into sameness as messages pass between neighbors. Researchers track it with Dirichlet energy, a measure of how much features vary across edges. Two versions exist, built from the unnormalized or the normalized graph Laplacian. They look similar but behave differently, and the literature has used them loosely. The authors sort out which one deserves trust.

They show the normalized version fails the axiomatic definition of a node similarity measure proposed by Rusch and coauthors. By spelling out the basic spectral properties of both definitions, they clarify which distinctions matter. The practical payoff is guidance: pick the energy that is spectrally compatible with the network architecture being monitored. With that settled, over-smoothing measurements rest on firmer ground.
arxiv-2512-09990:
Sergio Guerra Arencibia and colleagues settle a dispute about the globular clusters of an ultra diffuse galaxy, MATLAS-2019. Estimates of its cluster population had varied widely. Using Hubble Space Telescope images in three bands plus deep imaging from the Gran Telescopio Canarias, the team built the cleanest sample yet of the galaxy's clusters. Better resolution and color coverage let them separate true clusters from contaminants. Their count comes to about thirty-three clusters, supporting the lower earlier estimates.

The clusters are strongly concentrated toward the galaxy's center, with most inside its effective radius. From the cluster count, a standard relation gives the galaxy's dark halo mass. The cluster brightness distribution favors a particular distance to the galaxy. One oddity stands out: the clusters are distributed asymmetrically, even though the galaxy's starlight is symmetric. The authors warn that counting methods which assume symmetry can mislead when numbers are this small.
arxiv-2512-10190:
Xizhi Liu, Sijie Ren, and Jian Wang strengthen a celebrated theorem of extremal graph theory. The Andrásfai-Erdős-Sós theorem says, roughly, that a graph with high minimum degree and no clique of a given size must split into a fixed number of parts with no edges inside them. The authors add the maximum degree to the picture. Their condition balances minimum degree, maximum degree, and the number of vertices. When the minimum degree exceeds an explicit bound involving the maximum degree, any clique free graph of that kind must be multipartite in the required way. The bound is tight for every feasible maximum degree.

A parallel tight result holds for graphs whose shortest odd cycle is large. Notably, the proof does not use the original theorem. It therefore doubles as a fresh, independent proof of the classical result, always welcome for a theorem this central.
arxiv-2512-10390:
Vijay Prakash S addresses a curve-fitting problem from magnetism. How a ferromagnetic material's magnetization grows as an applied magnetic field gets stronger. His paper explains the physics in plain terms, as tiny magnetic regions inside the material line up with the field while the regions pointing the other way shrink away.

Instead of a standard formula, he fits the curve with a continued fraction built from straight line pieces. That form still lets a researcher estimate the key parameters through nonlinear regression. He then uses the fit to make sense of how growing and shrinking magnetic domains behave as the field changes. The paper runs seventeen pages with twelve figures and four tables of supporting detail.
arxiv-2512-10590:
G Arunkumar and Puja Samanta study a graph property known as property (P) and its tie to perfect matchings in bipartite graphs, networks split into two camps with edges only between them. Recent work by Sharma and Panda showed every bipartite graph with a perfect matching has the property. And proved the converse for trees and for graphs with at most one independent cycle.

The present paper pushes the converse much further. First, every bipartite graph with property (P) must be balanced, with equal-sized camps. The converse then holds for all bipartite graphs whose cycle rank is at most three, and for several more families beyond that. Finally, the authors derive algebraic constraints that balanced bipartite graphs without perfect matchings must obey, and use them to exhibit a family of graphs that provably lack property (P).
arxiv-2512-11090:
Biraj Dahal and fellow authors introduce WeldNet, a method for building small stand in models of complex systems that evolve over time. Full model runs of such systems are high in extent and costly to run. WeldNet learns a compressed description of the motion from case data, then predicts how that compressed state evolves.

The time span is split into overlapping windows. Within each window, an autoencoder learns the compressed codes, a propagator network advances them, and a transcoder links codes between neighbouring windows. Breaking long horizons into short segments makes training much easier while keeping the pieces steady. The authors also prove, under a standard manifold assumption, that the architecture can represent such motion. Tests on several differential equations beat both standard projection methods and recent non-linear reduction techniques.
arxiv-2512-11390:
Mert Senkardesler, Irmak Karpuzcu, and Deborah Levin simulate a hypersonic boundary layer particle by particle to watch a dangerous instability grow on its own. At six times the speed of sound, the thin layer of air hugging a flat plate can develop second mode waves that help trigger turbulence, heating a vehicle severely. Their direct simulation Monte Carlo method tracks simulated gas particles rather than solving averaged flow equations.

Spectral analysis found the expected dominant frequencies, matching linear stability theory, and the disturbances stayed inside the predicted unstable region. The waves emerged spontaneously from the gas's own kinetic fluctuations, with no artificial seeding, and rose above the method's own noise floor, which the authors derived analytically. Forcing the surface to vibrate at an unstable frequency amplified waves downstream, while a stable frequency damped them. The work supports particle simulation as a tool for studying and eventually controlling hypersonic transition.
arxiv-2512-11590:
Jin Lei presents HPRMAT, a fast solver for R-matrix calculations in nuclear physics. These calculations model how particles scatter off atomic nuclei, a core task for reaction studies. Older codes invert big matrices, which is slow, and HPRMAT replaces that step with direct solving tuned for speed.

The package offers four backends: exact solving, mixed precision with cleanup steps, a shortcut that uses the matrix structure, and graphics chip solving. At size 25,600 the graphics chip ran about 15 times faster than the best chip free solver and 41 times faster than the old code. Mixed precision also lets cheap home graphics cards do work that once needed costly hardware.
arxiv-2512-11790:
Seiji Fujimoto and a large team report deep Webb telescope spectra of GLIMPSE-16043, an odd galaxy at redshift 6.20. It had been flagged from photos as a possible Pop III galaxy, a first generation system with no heavy elements, because its oxygen lines looked absent.

The spectra show clear oxygen emission, so the galaxy is not pristine after all. Yet its light holds a huge Balmer jump of minus 1.66 magnitudes and extreme hydrogen emission that no standard star or nebula model can fit. A hot blackbody inside a cool nebula comes closest, hinting at a tidal disruption event or a microquasar. The team tightens photo based Pop III rules and re-estimates how common true Pop III systems are.
arxiv-2512-12090:
Samar Fares, Nurbek Tastan, and Karthik Nandakumar present SPDMark, a watermarking scheme that hides its mark inside a video generator weights. As video models get better, proving where a clip came from grows urgent. Older marks are pasted on after generation or cost too much to embed well.

SPDMark shifts a chosen subset of model parameters. The shift is built from layer wise basis pieces picked by the secret key, using low rank adapters to stay light. Training jointly tunes the shifts and the mark reader against recovery, looks, and smoothness losses. A hash makes each frame carry its own message, and matching logic restores frame order after tampering. Marks stay invisible yet survive common edits.
arxiv-2512-12190:
Xiang-dong Shi and seven co-authors report 88 new Beta Cephei stars in a 2025 paper. These are hot, bright stars that pulse in brightness. The team combined light data from the TESS space telescope with position and temperature data from Gaia Data Release 3.

They found 85 new stars in short cadence data and 3 in full frame images. The stars span magnitudes 8.0 to 12.0 and temperatures of 18,000 to 30,000 K, matching known groups. Four sit near the cool edge of the pulsing zone, where modes are sparse and useful for testing models. Most lie in the disk of the Milky Way, within 20 degrees of its plane; two high ones may be runaway stars.
arxiv-2512-12290:
Krystian Ilkiewicz and Henryka Netzel search for X-ray emission from pulsing stars in a 2025 paper. RR Lyrae and Cepheid stars swell and shrink in a steady rhythm, and astronomers use them to measure distances. The team matched such stars against X-ray sources from the first eROSITA all-sky survey.

They found seven RR Lyrae and eight Cepheid matches by position. Most Cepheid matches look reliable, but most RR Lyrae matches seem spurious. One source, OGLE-BLG-RRLYR-00252, may be the first real X-ray detection of an RR Lyrae star. Its brightness suggests RR Lyrae stars are at least a hundred times fainter in X-rays than the brightest Cepheids.
arxiv-2512-12990:
Yuseon Choi and co-authors present SliceMoE, a way to run Mixture-of-Experts models on small devices. Such models are huge, and moving expert parts in and out of memory costs energy. Older tricks such as prefetching can waste power or narrow the choice of experts.

SliceMoE caches experts in thin slices and assigns precision as needed, which stretches the effective cache. A new quantization scheme keeps low-bit and high-bit slices compatible without storing copies twice. A warmup step reshapes the cache early to cut cold misses. On two named models, decode energy fell by up to 2.37 and 2.85 times, with faster decoding too.
arxiv-2512-13990:
Hiroshige Shiga studies the moduli spaces of generalized Cantor sets, a topic in analysis on fractals. For each sequence omega in the unit interval sequence space, a generalized Cantor set can be built inside the unit interval. The moduli space collects all sequences whose Cantor sets are quasiconformally equivalent to a given one.

Shiga shows each such moduli space is measurable in the sequence space. He gives a necessary condition for a sequence to belong to a given moduli space. Using that condition, he proves there are uncountably many distinct moduli spaces. He also shows that, except for at most one of them, each moduli space has volume zero under the standard product measure. The results map how rare each equivalence class is.
arxiv-2512-14090:
Taig Singh, Shreshth Rajan, and Nikhil Jain present Arithmetic-Intensity-Aware Quantization for neural network inference. Modern networks are often memory-bound: throughput is limited by DRAM bandwidth, not by raw compute. Quantization shrinks weights, and their method chooses per-layer bit-widths to raise arithmetic intensity while limiting accuracy loss.

AIQ is a post-training method that searches over per-layer schemes to minimize a weighted loss over intensity and accuracy. On ResNet-20 with CIFAR-10, it raised arithmetic intensity by about 50% over an FP32 baseline while keeping accuracy within about 1 point. On MobileNetV2, its configurations gave 1.66 times the throughput of FP32 within the same accuracy margin. Larger layers were naturally quantized more aggressively by the search.
arxiv-2512-14190:
Stefano Goria, Levent Menguturk, Murat Menguturk, and Berkan Sesen argue for random bridges in a 2025 paper on generative models. A random bridge is a random process forced to reach a chosen distribution at fixed times, so it can carry data from one distribution to another.

The authors show how to start from general probability statements and branch into concrete learning and simulation methods. Depending on the driving process, bridges can be Markovian or not, and smooth, jumping, or mixed. Tests with Gaussian bridges made high quality samples in far fewer steps than standard methods, with competitive Frechet inception distance scores. They conclude the approach is cheap to run and suited to fast generation.
arxiv-2512-14390:
Jakub Balabán studies b-colorings of graphs, where vertices are colored so that neighboring vertices differ and every color has at least one vertex touching all the other colors. Deciding whether such a coloring exists with a given number of colors is NP-complete in general, although trees are easy. Progress has been slow on measures of how tree-like a graph is.

Measuring closeness to a tree by the feedback edge number, the few edges whose removal leaves a tree, Balabán shows the problem becomes fixed-parameter tractable, meaning fast when that number is small. He also gives a fast algorithm for graphs close to complete multipartite graphs, and notes hardness for tree-depth.
arxiv-2512-14790:
C. Esteban and colleagues make the northern telescope case through nearby dwarf galaxies that are still forming stars. The ones poorest in heavy elements look much like the first galaxies, which lit up when the universe was young. Telescopes today cannot catch the faint light lines needed to measure the gas in these dwarfs well.

Deep spectra from a 30 to 40 meter telescope would reveal faint lines from heavy elements and rare hot gas lines such as He II and C IV. Those lines would show what heats the gas, and whether stars like the first stars ever made hide inside. The team says the results could reset the scale used to track how galaxies gained heavy elements over cosmic time.
arxiv-2512-14890:
Chase Wilson settles a counting question in graph theory about how many copies of a tree a graph must contain. Mubayi and Verstraete had conjectured a sharp lower bound. For a graph with n vertices and average degree d, the bound counts labeled copies of any tree on t+1 vertices. It should reach at least a product that starts at d and steps down by one, t times over, once d is large enough.

Wilson proves the conjecture in full. He also pins down exactly when the bound is met. If the tree's diameter is at least 3, equality holds only for a disjoint union of cliques of size d+1. If the diameter is 2, equality holds only for d regular graphs, where every vertex has the same degree. The result closes the problem and names the extremal graphs.
arxiv-2512-15090:
Tengfei Peng and seven coauthors characterize a cobalt magnet whose atoms sit on a slightly squashed triangular lattice. The compound, Na2SrCo(VO4)2, belongs to the glaserite family, a favored playground for quantum magnetism. X-ray and neutron diffraction at room temperature confirm its structure: monoclinic, with distorted triangular layers of cobalt ions.

Cooling brings a ferromagnetic transition near 3.4 kelvin, marked by a sharp lambda shaped spike in heat capacity. The magnetic entropy recovered by 55 kelvin reaches about 90 percent of R ln 2, supporting an effective spin one half state for the cobalt ions. Neutron data at 2.3 kelvin show long range order with moments tilted, or canted, lying in the ac plane at about 2.6 Bohr magnetons. Set beside sister compounds with different orders, the study shows how the tetrahedra around cobalt tune the magnetism.
arxiv-2512-15190:
Dao Thanh Hai and two coauthors propose a network design that computes with light while it carries it. Optical computing and all optical signal processing have advanced fast on heavy investment. Their paradigm, the optical computing-communication integrated network, would let one optical layer both transport data and process it along the way.

The key notion is optical layer intelligence: doing computing at the scale of a lightpath, where paths crossing the same node can interact. A case study on optical aggregation shows how this differs from today's optical bypass designs, which only route light through. The authors give a mathematical formulation for optimal aggregation enabled networks. On the realistic NSFNET topology, their design beats the bypass model, promising more capacity from less spectrum.
arxiv-2512-15490:
Valentin Haberl, Piotr Szewczak, and Lyubomyr Zdomskyy bound the size of universally meager sets in certain set theory models in a 2025 paper. Universally meager sets of reals are small in a strong sense that survives many mappings. The question is how large such sets can be forced to remain in specific models of set theory.

Working in the Miller model and in a model built by Goldstern, Judah, and Shelah, the authors prove all universally meager sets have size at most the first uncountable cardinal. The same limits follow for Rothberger and Hurewicz spaces with no copy of the Cantor set. In the Miller model, strong measure zero sets obey the same bound.
arxiv-2512-15590:
Cesar Venegas and Helbert Venegas survey the Zariski cancellation problem through locally nilpotent derivations in a 2025 paper. The cancellation problem asks whether adding a trivial factor to an algebra can hide a real difference between two algebras. Derivations that become zero after repeated application give a key invariant for attacking it.

The survey unifies cancellation results across commutative algebras, noncommutative algebras, and skew Ore type extensions. It stresses rigidity and the Makar Limanov invariant, which collect what these derivations see. The method detects cancellation well in rigid settings. Its limits also show clearly, above all in the skew case, where Makar Limanov stability fails.
arxiv-2512-15790:
Akhil Sharma and co authors present XAMT, a framework for covert memory tampering attacks on mixed multi agent systems, in a 2025 paper, dated December 15. Modern agent systems blend reinforcement learning agents, which share an experience replay buffer, with language model agents that draw on a shared knowledge base. That shared memory is a common weak point.

XAMT frames attack design as bilevel optimization: the upper level keeps changes tiny for stealth, while the lower level pushes system behavior toward an attacker chosen target. Tests use SMAC and SafeRAG benchmarks at poison rates at or below 1 percent for the learning agents and 0.1 percent for the retrieval agents. The work defines a threat class meant to guide intrinsic defenses.
arxiv-2512-15890:
Jiyuan Fang, Qicheng Tang, and Xueda Wen uncover universal maximal entanglement swapping in fermionic Gaussian states in a 2025 paper. Entanglement swapping transfers entanglement through a joint measurement, and how much survives non unitary steps is a basic question. Fermionic Gaussian states, common in free fermion physics, are the setting here.

Take two decoupled, half filled copies of a free fermion system and perform projective Bell measurements on half the matching sites. Remarkably, the post measurement state factors into a product of Bell pairs, giving maximal interlayer entanglement regardless of the starting Gaussian state. The authors derive the state exactly for particle number conserving cases, with simulations as checks.
arxiv-2512-15990:
Arpan Akash Ray and Boris Skoric wrote this quantum communications paper, uploaded to arXiv in 2025. Quantum key distribution lets two parties share secret keys whose safety rests on physics, not on hard math problems. The continuous-variable kind uses standard telecom gear, but over long distances the signal is weak and error correction becomes slow and heavy.

The authors propose a random codebook method for fixing errors in these weak signals. It scores blocks by likelihood ratios and rejects bad blocks by a threshold rule, and it can run in parallel for real-time use. Under cautious assumptions about computing power, they predict a key rate of at least 8 percent of the theoretical Devetak-Winter value. That beats existing correction schemes for long links.
arxiv-2512-16090:
Huali Zhang opens a new line of analysis in this 96-page 2025 paper on arXiv. The relativistic Euler equations describe fluids moving near light speed, as in astrophysical jets. The Cauchy problem asks whether starting data evolves into a unique solution, and the hard part is allowing rough, low-regularity starting data.

Zhang rewrites the two-dimensional system using good variables: a rescaled velocity, a logarithmic enthalpy, and a carefully defined vorticity. That turns the equations into a coupled wave-transport system open to modern tools like Strichartz estimates. Well-posedness is proved at lower regularity than before for general pressure laws. In the stiff special case, where the acoustic metric becomes flat, even weaker data works, and small irrotational flows are shown to exist globally. The work adapts famous methods from non-relativistic fluid theory.
arxiv-2512-16190:
Sahil Kalra and Niraj K Shukla revive a classic number tool in their arXiv paper from 2025, accepted by a harmonic analysis journal. Ramanujan sums, introduced by the famous mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan, extract periodic parts from a signal. Filter banks built on them split signals into channels for analysis and recovery.

The authors prove these filter banks can reconstruct signals perfectly and study how robust they are when some channels are erased. Non-uniform versions fix limits of the uniform design. Using the uniform banks, they prove an uncertainty principle for a tight frame built from shifted Ramanujan sums, with recovery conditions stated through Euler's totient function. Exploiting a signal's known periodicity improves recovery algorithms in practice, raising signal-to-noise ratios and sharpening reconstructions after data loss or noise.
arxiv-2512-16690:
Justus Teller and coauthors report how to best make stencil masks for Josephson junctions, devices at the heart of superconducting circuits. Stencil lithography builds the junctions in place, in vacuum, and is now used for junctions with many terminals.

The team made and checked 270 mask designs under a scanning electron microscope. They report yield, the smallest safe sizes, and how results shift as terminal count grows. The verdict is that the method is reliable for multi-terminal junctions, with side sizes down to about 40 nanometers on average. The data give builders concrete design rules for a method with few other guides.
arxiv-2512-16790:
Aaron Imani, Mohammad Moshirpour, and Iftekhar Ahmed probe how large language models use code comments when they do software tasks. Comments do not run, yet models lean on them for completion, translation, and code fixes, and no one knew where that lean lives inside the model.

Using concept activation vectors, the team shows models store comments as distinct inner concepts, split by type such as Javadocs, inline, and multiline notes. Turning those concepts up or down shifted task scores from minus 90 percent to plus 67 percent, by model and task. Across ten tasks, code summarization lit the comment concept most, and completion least, opening a path to tools that steer inner concepts.
arxiv-2512-16890:
Jason Aebischer, Luigi C. Bresciani, and Nudzeim Selimovic complete the one-loop anomalous dimensions for general effective gauge theories, covering the fermionic sector. Combined with their past bosonic results, the work closes the leading renormalization group equations for such theories.

On-shell methods drive the derivation, with renormalization effects kept at order one over the new physics scale squared, for both renormalizable and higher couplings. The template equations include mixing between operators of unlike dimension and hold for any gauge group, with scalar and fermion fields present. Such templates let model builders evolve couplings from high scales to lab scales without redoing loop math per model.
arxiv-2512-17590:
Malak Sadek, Loraine Clarke, Stefania Forlini, and Uta Hinrichs ask what gets lost when a rare book becomes a flat scan on a screen. Library closures during COVID pushed readers online, where digital collections are easy to search yet strangely lifeless: no weight, no paper feel, no browsing by hand. The team invited creative professionals and collection experts to imagine richer ways in.

Their answer is digital bricolage, a design stance borrowed from making do with materials at hand. Interfaces, they argue, should let readers handle digital objects playfully, shuffling, juxtaposing, and poking around, much as hands do in a reading room. Such handling invites the casual, curious wandering that keyword search tends to kill. The paper offers speculations and prompts for designers, not a finished product.
arxiv-2512-17790:
Jasmin Katz, Xiaopan Lian, Alexandru Malekshahian, and Andrey Shapiro work in Ramsey theory, which asks how big a structure must be before a pattern is forced to appear. They color the edges of a large complete graph with labels from a group. They ask when a given graph must show up with edge labels that add to zero.

The team proves the size needed grows only in a straight line with the graph's vertex count, as long as each vertex touches few edges. The bound holds for any finite abelian group whose size divides the graph's edge count. A linear bound is far stronger than the loose bounds known for many such problems.
arxiv-2512-17890:
Callum Deakin and Xi Chen study a new way to shape light signals for very fast fiber optic links. The usual method mixes signal parts with electronic parts that have speed limits. Their method passes light through a chain of phase shifters and spreaders, which in theory wastes no light and dodges those limits.

The pair maps out the trade offs: how many stages are needed, how much spread, and how much power. Fewer than six stages can still reach the clean signal quality that links above 200 gigabaud demand. They also measure how small errors in phase, strength, or spread would hurt the signal, which guides real builds.
arxiv-2512-18090:
Benjamin Xiao and Dong Ye settle a question about packing tight clusters into a network. A clique is a set of points all linked to each other. They ask how large a share of a graph can be covered by cliques that stay separate, for graphs that avoid a certain dense pattern called a K4 minor.

Their proof shows the best share is exactly one half, which closes two conjectures posed by Biró, Collado, and Zamora. The same one half value holds for graphs where each point has at most three links. Clean cut values like this give network designers a firm rule for dividing such graphs into dense blocks.
arxiv-2512-18390:
Vassilis Digalakis and three co-authors ask a management question with a statistical core. When a company gains a new data source, when should it replace its working prediction model? The replacement, a challenger, would be trained on the richer data. The catch is that the challenger can only train on new data, which piles up slowly, while retraining again and again costs money.

Their framework links learning curves, which chart how a model improves with more data, to the economics of switching. They show the best moment to test the challenger grows as a power of the total time horizon. They also give an evaluation algorithm that needs no knowledge of the curve in advance. A real credit-scoring study shows the method performs near the level of an all-knowing oracle. It beats both greedy checks, which quit too early, and one-shot tests.
arxiv-2512-18590: Tenglin Hu of the Chinese Academy of Sciences computes the mapping class group for a family of seven dimensional manifolds. Each space is the total space of the sphere bundle of a three dimensional real vector bundle over the complex projective plane, with first Pontryagin number 8n + 5. The family includes the Milnor hypersurface and its generalizations M_k for odd k. Knowing this group catalogs the essentially distinct symmetries of these spaces, a basic step in understanding their geometry.
arxiv-2512-18690:
Lijuan Liu and Hanzhao Yang report a possible warning sign before big solar flares in this 2025 study. Magnetic field changes at the Sun's surface during eruptions are well known, but changes just before them are rarely documented. Using fast vector field data from the HMI instrument on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, they analyze an X1.8 class flare and find the horizontal field weakening beforehand along the flaring polarity inversion line.

Over the 30 minutes before the flare, the horizontal field dropped by about 100 gauss in a coherent patch, with no matching flux emergence or cancellation. Images show the erupting filament rising slowly at the same time and place.
