Their system, MetaGen, evolves both the roles and the topology, the pattern of who talks to whom. The team shapes itself as it learns what the work demands. Self shaping teams could beat hand designed ones on jobs too varied for a single fixed org chart.
arxiv-2601-19390:
Javier Silva Lafaurie and six co-authors give a sampling method a speed limit. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo explores a probability landscape by gliding through it like a frictionless particle. The shape of the landscape and the choice of starting momenta together set the glide.

Their sampler, Almanac, bounds the velocity of that glide. A bounded speed can keep the sampler stable where wild leaps would waste steps or break the math. Samplers of this kind sit under modern Bayesian statistics, so a sturdier one helps every field that fits models that way.
arxiv-2601-19490:
Ricardo Campos and a large team build a data set of claims in Portuguese news for fact checkers. Fact checking is slow, skilled hand work that cannot keep pace with how fast falsehoods spread online. Debunking takes longer to reach readers than the false claim itself, so speed tools matter.

Their set, ClaimPT, annotates claims inside news articles in Portuguese. Most claim data sets serve English, leaving other languages under tooled. A solid Portuguese set lets automated help reach the large share of the world's news that English tools skip.
arxiv-2601-19890:
Kenan Qu and Nathaniel J. Fisch propose a way to detect swirling turbulence inside hot plasmas. Theory suggests solenoidal turbulence, made of rotational flows, can greatly raise fusion reaction rates. No standard diagnostic can measure these flows directly in high-energy-density plasmas. Nor can existing tools separate rotational turbulence from compressional kinds.

Their method uses cross-polarization scattering of a probe laser. The laser's polarisation rotates in a way that reveals the turbulence's energy and spatial structure. A working diagnostic would let fusion experiments check whether the helpful turbulence is present. It could guide efforts to exploit the effect deliberately. The proposal joins plasma theory with a concrete measurement plan.
arxiv-2601-19990:
Xuan Chen and five colleagues compute a key process for Higgs physics to unprecedented precision. Pairs of Higgs bosons reveal the shape of the Higgs potential, which governs how the field holds the universe together. At hadron colliders, Higgs pairs are produced mainly through gluon fusion mediated by a top-quark loop. The authors report the first fully differential predictions at third order in the strong coupling.

The calculation also includes the effects of the top quark's mass. Fully differential means experimentalists can apply realistic cuts to the predictions. Precision at this level is needed because Higgs pair production is rare and backgrounds are large. The result sharpens the coming tests of the Higgs potential at the LHC.
arxiv-2601-20090:
Amirmohammad Farzaneh, Salvatore D'Oro, and Osvaldo Simeone give users of AI agents a way to ask what if. Language model agents turn a user's stated intent into plans and actions. After seeing an outcome, a user may wonder whether different wording would have done better. The authors build a framework for that counterfactual reasoning.

The framework explores alternative phrasings of the original intent and estimates their outcomes. Crucially, it provides formal reliability guarantees on those estimates. Without guarantees, counterfactual answers are just more model guesses. Reliable what-if analysis helps users phrase instructions better next time. It also helps designers see which intents are fragile. The work brings counterfactual thinking to everyday agent control. A guess with no bounds is just a guess.
arxiv-2601-20590:
Nathanaël Hassler builds a bijection, an exact one-to-one pairing, between two objects in combinatorics. On one side are the edges of the Turán graph, a classic extremal graph. On the other side are the meet-irreducible elements of a lattice. That lattice holds compositions of a number, where parts are bounded and the order is the dominance order.

A bijection proves the two collections have the same size by matching their members directly. Such pairings often reveal structure that counting alone hides. Hassler's matching links extremal graph theory with the theory of ordered sets in a concrete way.
arxiv-2601-20690:
Yuto Sugimoto, Shinichiro Akiyama, and Yoshinobu Kuramashi study the strong nuclear force under extreme cold and density. Their 2026 paper uses a tool called the tensor renormalization group. The setting is QCD, the theory of quarks and gluons, in its strong coupling limit. They work in three space dimensions plus time.

The team tracks two changes as the chemical potential is varied. One is the chiral transition, tied to how quark mass appears. The other is the nuclear transition, tied to matter filling up with quarks. They compute the chiral condensate and the quark number density to follow both. Such work helps map how matter behaves under conditions no lab can hold for long.
arxiv-2601-21190: A large particle physics collaboration reports a search for a rare particle decay in this 2026 paper. The target state is sought through its decay into an eta meson and a psi(2S) state. The search channel produces two eta mesons plus the psi(2S) from electron-positron collisions. The author list is headed by M. Ablikim, with a long list of colleagues from the collaboration. Searches of this kind test how quarks bind into exotic states.
arxiv-2601-21590:
Xiaotong Ji, Rasul Tutunov, Matthieu Zimmer, and Haitham Bou Ammar make power sampling practical for language model reasoning. Training with reinforcement learning improves reasoning, but growing evidence says the gain mostly sharpens the spread of answers the model already gives. It does not add brand new skills.

If gains are sharpening, a training-free sampler might reach the same place. Power sampling draws answers from a sharpened version of the model's own distribution. The authors make that sampling efficient enough to use. Skipping the training run saves large costs while keeping the sharper, more reliable reasoning.
arxiv-2601-21690:
Qinglun Li, Anke Tang, Miao Zhang, Mengzhu Wang, Quanjun Yin, and Li Shen build a unified theory for merging trained models. Merging blends several fine-tuned models into one, working only on their weights. It needs no original data and no costly retraining, yet it often works surprisingly well.

A general theory for why it works was missing, above all when the merged models were tuned with different settings. Learning rates and batch sizes vary widely in practice. The authors' framework explains merging across that heterogeneity. A firm theory tells builders when a merge is safe and when it will quietly average away the very skills they wanted.
arxiv-2601-21790:
Luqman Mustafa and co-authors study a family of crystals where the same material can form in two different atomic patterns. These patterns, called pyrite and marcasite, are model systems for crystal chemistry. In cobalt selenide, theory says marcasite is the stable ground state, yet labs normally make the pyrite form.

The 2026 study reports synthetic control over which pattern forms across a series that mixes iron and cobalt with selenium. Gaining that control had not been achieved for cobalt selenide before, though the two forms had been seen in tiny particles. Being able to choose a crystal pattern on purpose matters, because structure shapes how such materials conduct, react, and store energy.
arxiv-2601-21890:
Laura Mack introduces a software toolbox for scientists who measure how land and air exchange gases and heat. The eddy-covariance method infers those exchanges from fast wind and gas measurements above a surface. It began as a way to track ecosystem-scale exchange between air and vegetation.

The method now also serves to test theories of atmospheric turbulence, with the aim of improving weather and climate models. Reddy, the open-source toolbox in this 2026 preprint, is built for analyzing such measurements in heterogeneous environments. Where the land below is a patchwork rather than one uniform field. Shared tools matter because flux data feed the carbon budgets that climate policy relies on.
arxiv-2601-21990:
Nicolas Blin and co-authors speed up a core routine inside mixed-integer programming. Solvers for such problems repeatedly solve related linear programs, for instance when testing branches in strong branching or tightening bounds. Solving them one by one wastes the power of modern graphics processors.

The team presents a batched first-order method that solves many linear programs in parallel on GPUs. It extends the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm to handle whole batches at once. Their 2026 preprint targets the inner loop of industrial solvers. Faster linear programming batches translate directly into faster logistics, scheduling, and energy planning, where mixed-integer models decide real operations every day.
arxiv-2601-22090:
Runsheng Wang and co-authors help stroke survivors' hands obey them again. Surface electromyography reads muscle signals from the skin, a promising control signal for assist-as-needed hand rehabilitation. Detecting intent from weakened, stroke-affected muscles is hard, though: calibration is long and subject-specific, and detection stays brittle.

Their 2026 preprint, ReactEMG Stroke, adapts intent detection from healthy users to stroke patients with only a few examples from the patient. Few-shot adaptation could make rehabilitation devices practical in clinics, where long calibration sessions are unaffordable. A device that reads intent reliably can assist movement at the right moment, which is how retraining a hand is thought to work.
arxiv-2601-22390:
Chanwoo Park and Chanwoo Kim attack voice ID systems with a mask tuned to fool them. Speaker systems check who is talking from the sound of a voice. Their 2026 preprint uses an energy mask to hide the cues such a system reads, so it names the wrong person.

Work like this probes a real risk, as voice checks guard bank and phone access. The team frame the attack as an evasion test, meant to expose weak points. A known weak point can be patched; a hidden one cannot. Their results can help builders harden voice ID. They also warn users of its limits.
arxiv-2601-22890:
Christina Schenk and Ignacio Romero review how to tune complex computer models when data are scarce. The method, Bayesian calibration, adjusts a model's settings so its output matches real measurements, with honest doubt attached. It matters most when each simulation run is costly and experiments are few.

The authors gather many existing calibration methods into one unified framework. A shared frame helps engineers pick the right tool for fields like climate, energy, and design. It also shows where the methods agree and where they rest on shaky ground. The unified framework is presented as a review, gathering scattered calibration approaches into one place for comparison and reuse.
arxiv-2601-23190:
G. De Cillis and seven co-authors blend physics models with machine learning for sea ice forecasts. Their hybrid treats the learning component as a state-dependent fix for forecast errors in a sea-ice column model. Snow thermodynamics and the ice's radiative properties are key error sources.

They train dedicated neural networks for each model configuration and test transfer to new ones. Transfer learning matters because Arctic conditions vary by season and place. Better sea-ice forecasts serve shipping, climate science, and northern communities. State-dependent parameterization is the key mechanism, letting the learned correction change with the ice and snow conditions.
arxiv-2602-00490: Chia-Ming Lee and colleagues fuse hyperspectral data by joining spectral detail from a low-resolution image with spatial detail from a high-resolution multispectral image. Deep methods suffer narrow receptive fields, redundant bands, and the quadratic cost of self-attention, so the team proposes HSSDCT. One block widens windows for multi-scale aggregation, while a correlation layer splits spatial and spectral dependence, cutting self-attention to linear cost. Tests show top reconstruction quality at lower cost, a new state-of-the-art result for hyperspectral fusion.
arxiv-2602-00690: Christian Rosenke and colleagues introduce Miniature Painting, inspired by miniature painting. A graph must be coloured to match a template with the fewest strokes, each recolouring a connected set. The problem equals a reversal of Free Flood-It, where a coloured graph is reduced to one colour in as few moves as possible. That equivalence transfers results, including NP-hardness for grids, trees, and split graphs. The result is a polynomial-time algorithm for co-gem-free graphs, a class generalising cographs, so Free Flood-It is also tractable there.
arxiv-2602-01090: Yang Liu and co-authors build FALCON, forcing language models to give only workable answers to hard combo tasks. Such models crack combo tasks in words yet lack any guard that answers truly work, as real use demands. FALCON pairs grammar-locked decoding and a fix layer for rule breaks, and smart best-of-N draws spending compute well. Its train rule weights like pairs by score gaps, giving dense teaching, no hand marks. On seven hard combo tasks, it hit full feasibility while matching or beating top solvers.
arxiv-2602-01190: M. Laczkovich proves a shift result for measurable sets on the real line. When two compact sets meet a density rule, with the second set dense at each of its points, a closed null slice of the first can be picked. Its sum with the second set then fills the whole sum. A spin-off says if every null slice of one measurable set can shift into a second set, some null slice can be dropped so the rest shifts in. The theme links to consistency lore on additive reals.
arxiv-2602-01490: Timothee Leleu and co-authors reshape global loop structure to speed local optimization. Frustrated graphical models trap optimization in rugged landscapes shaped by local and loop structure. Bethe approximation views the graph as a tree, ignoring it. The M-layer construction copies the graph M times, reconnecting edges randomly, from the original graph to Bethe at large M. The team generalizes it with a mixing kernel Q setting layer connection probabilities, shaping loops, and layer fluctuations decay, raising the odds of reaching the global minimum. Costs fall across Ising benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-01590: Shaohan Wang and colleagues challenge deep research agents to write at the level of expert Wikipedia articles. Current benchmarks lean on machine generated references or machine derived scores, which lack expert verification and fine grained objectivity. Their live benchmark, Wiki Live Challenge, uses one hundred recent Wikipedia Good Articles as references, judged by Wiki Eval across thirty nine criteria for writing quality plus strict factual checks. Experiments show a wide gap between present agents and human expert articles, confirming the benchmark as a demanding target for agent research.
arxiv-2602-01790: David Lancashire shows that incentive compatibility under informational decentralization cannot be achieved with the direct and revelation equivalent mechanisms usually studied in the field. He argues those impossibility results are conditional, since a narrow set of mechanisms outside the revelation equivalent class can sustain enforcement. Enforcement works by reading wants via parallel games that cannot be correlated with each other. The paper thus recasts a known limit as a line that new designs can cross, rather than a wall that blocks all design.
arxiv-2602-01990: Zhen-Hao Xie and colleagues propose SAME for multimodal tuning, where routing drifts. A query that activated place experts may route to irrelevant experts, while place experts get overwritten, losing function. These failures show router drift, shifting selection, and expert drift. SAME stabilizes selection by splitting routing, updating relevant paths. Expert updates use curvature aware scaling with past covariance, plus adaptive freezing to cut redundant computation and clash. A new long task benchmark shows SAME at top performance.
arxiv-2602-02090: Yikai Zeng and colleagues present LEC-KG, a two-way design mixing language model sense with graph vector logic for building domain graphs from raw text. Building domain knowledge graphs from raw text is hard. Their approach has three parts: layered link pull easing long-tail bias; source-backed Chain-of-Thought feedback; and meaning start. The two modules boost each other in turns, with vectors giving feedback, while triples improve models. Tested on Chinese SDG reports, LEC-KG shows gains over rivals on rare links.
arxiv-2602-02390:
Samyak Jain and 2 co-authors ask how much of the diffuse rain of high-energy neutrinos comes from active galactic nuclei, in a 2026 arXiv paper. These nuclei are bright centers of galaxies powered by supermassive black holes. IceCube, a detector buried in Antarctic ice, has already caught neutrinos from two such objects.

Using ten years of public IceCube data, the team tests whole populations of X-ray-bright and gamma-ray-bright nuclei. Gamma-ray-bright blazars can supply at most sixteen percent of the total flux. Several nearby Seyfert galaxies, including NGC 1068, show evidence of neutrino emission before trial corrections. Because these sources are gamma-ray dim, their neutrinos likely form in dense, hidden regions near the black hole. The class could supply anywhere from about a tenth to all of the diffuse flux.
arxiv-2602-02590:
Xubo Luo and 6 co-authors give generative navigation planners structured starting guesses instead of random noise, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Visual navigation in cluttered, uncertain environments demands paths that are safe, efficient, and varied enough to offer alternatives. Models that start from unstructured noise often produce unsafe, inefficient, or single-mode plans too slowly for real-time use.

StepNav first learns a geometry-aware success probability field that finds every feasible navigation corridor. Those corridors form an explicit multi-modal mixture prior, a structured starting spread. A conditional flow-matching process then refines candidates, framed as optimal control with smoothness and safety costs. Starting from physically grounded candidates yields safer, more efficient plans in far fewer steps. Simulation and real-world benchmarks showed steady gains in robustness, speed, and safety over leading generative planners.
arxiv-2602-02690:
Chenxi Huang and 9 co-authors build a living benchmark for AI agents that fix Linux kernel crashes, in a 2026 paper. Kernel fuzzers surface crashes constantly, and language-model agents have begun attempting repairs. Static benchmarks age badly against an evolving kernel and risk contamination, since models may already know the fixes from training.

Live-kBench continuously scrapes freshly discovered bugs and evaluates agents only on new material. Its companion environment standardizes compilation, execution, and feedback, decoupling agent logic from heavy infrastructure so frameworks compare fairly. The inaugural dataset holds five hundred thirty-four bugs. Agents scored notably higher on bugs fixed before their knowledge cutoffs, quantifying the contamination gap. Three leading agents resolved most crashes with plausible patches, yet only about a fifth closely matched developer fixes. Feeding back crash results improved resolution substantially.
arxiv-2602-02790:
Hyunsung Cho and 4 co-authors model how people search with eyes and ears jointly, balancing effort against accuracy, in a 2026 paper. Finding a car in a crowded lot or a speaker in a virtual meeting requires coordinating movement with hearing and vision under uncertainty. Existing models treat perception and action separately, missing that coordination.

Their computational model, Sensonaut, assumes searchers deploy body and senses as they believe will most efficiently raise the chance of finding the target. Search becomes resource-rational choice-making under partial observability, where the world is only partly visible. Validated against newly collected human data, the model reproduces how search time and effort scale with complexity, occlusion, and distraction. It also reproduces characteristic human errors. The authors aim the simulation at interface design: audiovisual systems should minimize search cost and cognitive load.
arxiv-2602-02890:
Anthony Fuller and 2 co-authors extend a training trick to unlabeled data in a 2026 paper. The trick, called model soups, averages the weights of several fine-tuned models into one better model. All earlier soups needed labeled data and the same training objective. Their version works with self-supervised learning instead.

Self-souping can use new unlabeled sources, such as data from a shifted setting. Souping on corrupted test data, then fine-tuning on clean training data, improved robustness on corrupted image benchmarks. Ingredients could even use different self-supervised algorithms, a first for soups. Mixed soups of four different methods beat every single ingredient model on accuracy.
arxiv-2602-03290:
Any continuous functional can be built from linear measurements plus scalar nonlinearities, proves a study by Andrey Krylov, together with 1 co-author. Their setting is compact subsets of products of Hilbert spaces, a general home for inputs such as fields and signals. A functional maps such an input to a number, and universal approximation asks whether a simple model class can approximate every continuous example uniformly well on the compact set.

The proof shows finitely many continuous linear measurements suffice as the first stage. Continuous scalar nonlinearities then combine those measurements into the approximation. The principle extends to maps valued in a Banach space, yielding finite-rank approximations. The results justify a common design pattern in operator learning and imaging, where systems measure, apply scalar nonlinearities, then combine.
arxiv-2602-03390:
Slot-based models try to split a video scene into separate objects without any labels. Hyun Seok Seong and 2 co-authors diagnose why training such models stalls in a 2026 paper. The encoder produces sharp attention maps, while the decoder returns blurry reconstructions, and each side's weakness keeps reinforcing the other in a vicious cycle.

Their method, Synergistic Representation Learning, turns that cycle virtuous. The encoder's sharpness cleans up object boundaries in the decoder output, and the decoder's spatial consistency removes noise from the encoder's features. A warm-up phase with slot regularization gives each slot a distinct entity early on. The approach reaches state-of-the-art results on standard video object-centric learning benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-03490:
How does a brain keep track of where things are while the eyes jump from place to place? Linda Ariel Ventura and 3 co-authors explore that question with a small neural network in a 2026 paper. The network reads tokens from two-dimensional scenes one at a time. It must predict the next token, given the current one and a saccade-like jump.

On fresh scenes, predictions improve as the sequence proceeds, showing in-context learning. Decoding the network's activity reveals path integration, a running tally of position, and dynamic binding of each token's identity to its location. Interventions show new bindings can form late in a sequence, even for unusual combinations. The results offer a concrete mechanism for sequential world modeling.
arxiv-2602-03890:
Moving point clouds, not just still ones, are the target of Xindan Zhang and 7 co-authors. Their 2026 paper presents a multimodal language model built to answer questions about dynamic 3D scenes. Because no suitable dataset existed, the team built one with more than forty thousand moving object sequences.

Their model uses a Mamba-based module to track long-range motion across frames. A bootstrapping strategy then finds the model's own failures and generates extra training questions aimed at those weak spots. On action and timing questions, the system clearly beats earlier models.
arxiv-2602-04090:
Fifty years after the J/psi particle announced the charm quark, Bing-Song Zou reviews what charmonium taught us about hadrons. His 2026 paper traces the quark potential model that grew from the charmonium spectrum, a QCD-inspired picture of quarks bound by a rising potential.

Zou then argues the simple picture is not enough. Unquenching dynamics, where quark pairs pop in and out, and multiquark components inside ordinary hadrons reshape the spectrum. Exotic multiquark states, once heresy, are now central evidence. Charmonium-like states remain the sharpest laboratory for hadron structure, because their heaviness makes theory cleaner.
arxiv-2602-04290:
A verifier that only grades the final answer lets early errors snowball. Lingzhuang Sun and 7 co-authors propose a Guided Verifier that co-solves tasks beside the policy model in a 2026 paper. Their target is multimodal reasoning, where one hallucinated detail can poison every later step.

During rollouts, the verifier checks consistency in real time and steers the policy toward valid trajectories. A data pipeline builds process-level supervision targeting multimodal hallucinations. Dynamic process supervision replaces the noisy signal of terminal rewards alone. The collaboration pattern, solver plus live guide, mirrors how careful humans work through problems with a checker at their shoulder.
arxiv-2602-04390:
Counting patterned triangles leads, unexpectedly, to derangements. Natasha Blitvić and 1 co-author study colored interlacing triangles in a 2026 combinatorics paper. These objects frame a central limit theorem for measures from LLT polynomials and depend on a color count and a triangle depth.

Prior work settled three colors at arbitrary depth. The authors take the complementary regime: depth two, arbitrary colors. Up to relabeling of colors, the triangles biject with Dumont derangements, so their count equals the Genocchi medians. The bijection links a probabilistic model to a classical hierarchy of combinatorial objects, with a decomposition that promises further structure.
arxiv-2602-04890:
Four researchers, Lucas de Magalhães Araujo and 3 co-authors, built this 2026 dataset paper for geophysics. Their subject is seismic imaging, which uses sound waves sent into the ground to map rock layers, often in the search for oil and gas. The team drew on a public United States archive of marine seismic surveys collected over decades.

The result is the Unicamp-NAMSS dataset: 2,588 cleaned seismic cross-sections from 122 survey areas around the world. The team balanced the set so no single survey dominates, and split it by region so models must prove themselves on unseen geology. Tests with neural networks show the images vary widely yet keep a coherent structure. The authors offer the set for training and benchmarking machine learning models that read seismic data.
arxiv-2602-05090:
Regular primes have been studied since the nineteenth century through the class groups of cyclotomic fields. Evan Chen and 20 co-authors prove a density result about a weaker property in this 2026 number theory paper. A prime is called partially regular when certain eigenspaces of the class group's p-part vanish across a range of characters, equivalently when p avoids dividing the numerators of many Bernoulli numbers.

The team proves that almost all primes, a set of density one, are partially regular in this sense. A reflection argument converts the result into a partial form of Vandiver's conjecture for the same primes. Consequences reach p-adic L-functions, congruences between cusp forms and Eisenstein series, and torsion in algebraic K-groups. Notably, the proof was fully formalized in the Lean proof assistant, produced automatically by a system called AxiomProver from a plain-language statement.
arxiv-2602-05490:
Tensors are multi-way arrays of numbers, and software that contracts them sits at the heart of quantum chemistry and physics codes. Jan Brandejs, Trond Saue, and 3 co-authors report on the second Toulouse Tensor Workshop, held in Toulouse in September 2025. The meeting followed a 2024 workshop that led to a working group and a draft low-level standard for tensor operations, shared freely on GitHub.

The report records the program and sums up the main points of debate among application developers and tensor software experts. Users of the draft standard gave feedback on how the basic interface should be refined. Talks also turned to what should come next, such as higher-level interfaces, tensor decompositions, symmetric tensors, and support for structured sparsity. For readers in scientific computing, the report shows a community trying to agree on shared tools. It also maps open questions that the standard has yet to settle.
arxiv-2602-05690:
Grouping items by asking noisy yes or no questions about pairs is the task of active clustering, where each answer costs time. Rachel Teo and 3 co-authors study how few queries can suffice when the number of groups is unknown. At each step an agent picks a pair; the answer is biased toward yes for pairs in the same group and toward no otherwise.

Using a change of measure argument, the authors derive a lower bound on the queries needed for a target confidence. They then design an algorithm whose stopping rule uses a generalized likelihood ratio statistic against a threshold. A cheaper variant keeps the method practical, with a gap to the bound within a constant factor. The work speaks to learning theorists and to practitioners who cluster with costly judgments.
arxiv-2602-05790:
Storing the weight matrices of large language models in low precision saves memory, and the best compression depends on the statistics of the inputs the weights will meet. Alina Harbuzova, Or Ordentlich, and Yury Polyanskiy ask whether one universal codebook can serve all possible input statistics at once. An input adapted codebook follows a waterfilling allocation along principal directions, which is near optimal but impractical to rebuild for every use.

The authors prove a universal codebook exists that is simultaneously near optimal for all input statistics. The price of universality is small: at most a tenth of a bit per dimension against the adapted codebook, in the case of Gaussian weights. Equivalently, a single net can cover a sphere nearly optimally under every Hilbert norm at once. The existence proof is non constructive, so the codebook is an ideal candidate for a storage format rather than a ready recipe.
arxiv-2602-05990:
Jonathan Davies extends a known kind of graded category to a wider setting. In the earlier work of Sözer and Virelizier, objects and morphisms carry compatible degrees graded by a character. Davies replaces the character with a general group homomorphism, so the grading follows any map between groups rather than one special kind.

Inside this wider frame he proves a half-enriched version of the Yoneda lemma, a basic tool that links objects to the maps around them. He also gives a structure theorem for the semisimple case, where objects split into simple parts. A third result reframes these graded categories as pseudofunctors into the category of categories. The paper widens a tidy grading scheme so it can travel with any group map.
arxiv-2602-06090:
Bug reports often carry key clues in pictures, such as broken layouts or missing buttons on a screen. Jincheng Wang and 7 co-authors built SVRepair, a repair system that actually reads those pictures. Most automated repair tools work from text alone and miss this evidence.

SVRepair first turns screenshots and flow charts into a scene graph, a tidy map of parts and their links. A coding agent then uses that map to find the fault and write a patch. A narrowing trick focuses the picture bit by bit on the buggy region. On standard repair benchmarks, the system fixed a solid share of the reported bugs.
arxiv-2602-06790:
Nathan Moses, Marcus J. Clark, Alex S. Clark, Siddarth K. Joshi, and Imad I. Faruque optimize single-photon sources built from tiny ring resonators on a chip. Efficient, bright sources of this kind are a key ingredient for scaling up quantum technologies. In these rings, a process called four-wave mixing splits pump light into pairs of photons, one of which can herald the other.

By tuning how strongly the pump, signal, and idler modes couple into the ring while pumping in pulses, the team mapped the trade-off between brightness and heralding efficiency. They recorded over 93,000 detected photon pairs per second in a moderately over-coupled setting, and a high intrinsic heralding efficiency near 98 percent close to maximal over-coupling. The measured curves matched theory closely, confirming the predicted trade-off.
arxiv-2602-07090:
Yu-Che Tsai and three co-authors defend text embeddings against inversion attacks. Embeddings power many language applications, yet attacks can expose sensitive attributes or rebuild raw text from them. Old privacy defenses assume every embedding dimension is equally sensitive. That forces excess noise and degrades utility. Their system, SPARSE, gives concept-specific privacy protection shaped by user-defined concepts.

Two parts work together. Mask learning that can be differentiated finds the dimensions that are privacy-sensitive for each concept. A Mahalanobis mechanism then applies shaped noise tuned by dimension risk, perturbing sensitive dimensions while sparing non-sensitive meaning. Tests span six data sets, three embedding models, and several attack scenarios. SPARSE cut privacy leakage while beating top privacy methods on downstream scores.
arxiv-2602-07390:
Survey tests draw units at random and assign treatments at random, yet finite samples still leave covariate imbalance that muddies results. Pengfei Tian and two co-authors study a stratified approach to covariate balance in survey tests.

They propose stratified rejective sampling plus rerandomization, and they build design-based large-sample theory for the stratified difference-in-means estimator of the average treatment effect. The result is an estimator with better balance and known large-sample behavior. Economists and social scientists running population-based tests get a design that locks in the balance chance alone only promises on average.
arxiv-2602-07590:
Mapping rock joint traces from images is essential for geotechnical work, but real labeled data is scarce and imbalanced.  Jessica Ka Yi Chiu and three co-authors combine geological modeling, synthetic data generation, and supervised segmentation to automate the task.

Discrete fracture network models generate synthetic jointed rock images at field scales, preserving persistence, connectivity. Node-type spreads, and models trained with mixed training and fine-tuning are tested on real box and slope data sets.  Synthetic data supports joint trace detection when real labels are thin, with mixed training winning where labels are consistent and fine-tuning proving more robust where labels are noisy.  Geologists get a useful recipe for scarce-label rock mapping.
arxiv-2602-07790:
Vision-language models train on many data domains, but choosing how much of each to mix is usually manual and expensive. Wanyun Xie and two co-authors propose MaD-Mix, a principled method that derives data mixtures from modality-aware domain alignment, computed in closed form through inter-modal coupling variables.

The framework handles domains missing a modality, including language-only data, and costs under one GPU-hour to compute. On models of 0.5 and 7 billion parameters, MaD-Mix matches human-tuned mixtures with 22 percent fewer training steps for image-text tuning, and improves accuracy over uniform mixing in harder video-image-text settings. Training teams gain a scalable, cheap replacement for mixture guesswork.
arxiv-2602-07890:
The Burau representation of braid groups has a famous flaw: its kernel, the set of braids it sends to the identity, is not fully understood. Vassily Olegovich Manturov and Igor Mikhailovich Nikonov approach the problem through groups called G_n^3, which encode the dynamics of point configurations and, in particular, braids.

They modify the group G_n^3 and construct a representation of the modified group whose induced braid representation is strong enough to detect the Burau kernel. In other words, the new representation sees exactly the braids that Burau misses. Braid theorists and topologists gain a fresh algebraic tool for a long-standing question about what linear representations of braids can capture.
arxiv-2602-08090:
Self-driving cars need outer screens that tell walkers what the car will do, and shaping those screens usually uses small, costly workshops. Ronald Cumbal and four co-authors test a scalable crowd work method that mixes crowd ideas, set hands-on rules, and expert feedback across rounds.

User concepts evolved from simple signals to multi-sense systems, including custom tracking lights and open haptic feedback, growing more context-aware over rounds. Two representative designs, one popular and one innovative, were compared against a benchmark in video models, with the popular design performing best on both measured outcomes. Designers gain evidence that broad crowd input can complement, not just imitate, expert-led hands-on design.
arxiv-2602-08590:
Federated prompt learning lets parties adapt vision-language models without sharing data, but one fixed prompt shape fits no client well. Yicheng Di and four co-authors propose SDFed, a framework that keeps a fixed-length global prompt for aggregation while letting each client learn a variable-length local prompt. Their arXiv paper targets heterogeneity in data and device capacity.

A subspace refinement method shapes local prompts, while an information-retention and divergence-control strategy preserves key local knowledge and keeps global and local representations properly separated. Tests across several datasets show consistent gains in performance and robustness under heterogeneous federated settings. Readers get a flexible design for privacy-sensitive, multi-party adaptation.
arxiv-2602-09390:
Coronal mass ejections drive much of space weather, and many carry cooler prominence material tangled in their magnetic fields. That cool component holds neutral atoms that shine in permitted lines, and researchers have hoped such lines could reveal the magnetic field inside an eruption. Chloe Pistelli and three co-authors report observations from the Upgraded Coronal Multi-channel Polarimeter that test that hope directly.

In helium light at a near-infrared wavelength, the instrument clearly shows neutral helium in eruptive prominences as they cross the lower and middle corona. Eruptions remain detectable out to about two solar radii, the edge of the instrument's view, adding spectral detail that extreme-ultraviolet and white-light imagers lack. The data also allow line-of-sight velocity estimates. The authors argue the capability could flag Earth-directed eruptions earlier and more accurately.
arxiv-2602-09990:
Fractional calculus extends derivatives to non-integer orders, and the Wiman-Valiron method tracks how fast analytic solutions can grow. A 2026 paper by Igor Chyzhykov carries that method into the fractional setting for linear equations with chained Caputo-Djrbashian derivatives. It extends an earlier result showing that solutions exist and are unique for the Cauchy problem.

For coefficients built from polynomials, where one term outweighs the rest, the paper pins down the exact growth order of solutions. That result matches the classical ordinary-differential-equation picture in full. It also shows the sharpness of an earlier result by Kochubei and extends it, carrying Wiman-Valiron theory over to fractional derivatives.
arxiv-2602-10290:
Primaries add a multi-stage twist to voting. Voters first shape intra-party picks before a general election names the final winner. A 2026 paper led by Colin Cleveland, with two co-authors, studies how hard strategic play is in primary elections under first-past-the-post with set tie-breaking. Where earlier work judged primaries by welfare distortion, this paper examines their game-theory traits.

Figuring out whether a pure Nash equilibrium exists proves complete for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. Computing a best response is NP-complete, while subgame-perfect equilibria in sequential primaries prove PSPACE-complete. Primaries thus sharply raise the hardness of strategic thought, marking them as a rich well of complexity-theoretic challenges for computational social choice.
arxiv-2602-10390:
Full world models demand immense detail, and using pre-trained large models directly in search is inefficient and inaccurate. A 2026 paper led by Khimya Khetarpal, with seven co-authors, asks whether large models can instead serve as partial world models. Partial models predict well only for a subset of states and actions linked through affordances that achieve user intents. Their formal answer: agents meeting task-agnostic, language-conditioned intents must hold predictive partial-world models shaped by affordances. In multi-task settings they introduce distribution-robust affordances and show partial models can be pulled out to make search faster.

Empirical tests in tabletop robotics tasks back the theory: affordance-aware partial models cut the search branching factor and earn higher rewards than full world models. The work thus reframes large models not as complete world simulators but as sources of focused, intent-linked predictions.
arxiv-2602-10690:
Meysam Mohseni and two co-authors map how extreme strain reshapes a diamond quantum emitter in a 2026 paper. The neutral silicon-vacancy center combines inversion balance with optical emission, making it resilient to stray electric fields. Its response to isotropic strain, from strong compression to strong tension, had not been quantified from first principles.

Using density-functional theory across strong pressures from roughly minus eighty to plus one hundred eighty gigapascals, the authors trace a rich response. Compression blue-shifts the zero-phonon line nearly linearly and stiffens a key phonon mode, suppressing vibronic instability. Tensile strain enhances other effects. The results guide strain building of diamond emitters for quantum technologies that demand stable, tunable light sources.
arxiv-2602-10790:
Paula Carolina Lozano Duarte and two co-authors harden flexible-gadget circuits against manufacturing defects in a 2026 paper. Indium gallium zinc oxide thin films enable wearable sense and large-area systems. But their analog-to-digital circuits face high defect counts and spread compared with mature CMOS. Defect weakness in these one-pole tools remains poorly known.

The paper presents a layered fault planting system for binary search circuits in n-type-only tools. Switch-level defect portrait joins with system-level fault spread study, letting fast search of single and multiple fault cases across the change ladder. The system names key fault-weak points, guiding fault-tough design for flexible gadgets where defects are the norm, not rare.
arxiv-2602-10890:
Daniele Di Pietro and Aurelio Spadotto develop hybrid discretizations for Friedrichs systems in a 2026 paper. Friedrichs systems transfer beyond the standard hyperbolic-elliptic sorting, suiting problems mixing spread and advection. The new arbitrary-order schemes use hybrid spaces with unknowns on elements and faces.

The methods support general meshes, conserve locally, and yield smaller algebra systems than older discontinuous Galerkin discretizations after static condensation. The paper carries out a complete steadiness and settling analysis, the first of its kind for this family. Results illustrations on scalar and vector solid spread-advection-reaction problems show the schemes handling the mixed physics they were built for.
arxiv-2602-10990:
Energy forms on rough spaces come in local and non-local kinds. Meng Yang, writing alone, studies how a local energy can pass its good traits to a non-local one through subordination. The setting is metric measure spaces, where shape is loose but still workable.

He starts from a local regular energy that meets a Poincaré inequality and a cutoff Sobolev inequality with a given scaling. Then a jumping-kernel non-local form above that scaling inherits matching non-local versions of both inequalities. Its new scaling is fixed by the two inputs. Cases with light polynomial tails are covered too. The result extends a classic subordination idea beyond Dirichlet forms into curved territory.
arxiv-2602-11590:
Masked diffusion models can generate tokens in parallel, but they suffer a one-way flaw: once a token is unmasked, it stays fixed, so early errors pile up and drag quality down. Yair Schiff and eight co-authors teach a model to do both jobs, unmasking and correcting, by reusing the denoiser output as training input for a corrector. During generation, extra refinement steps sit between unmasking steps so decoded tokens can still change.

The method, named Progressive Self-Correction, is tested across conditional and unconditional tasks. It reaches better quality-for-speed trade-offs, sampling up to about four times faster while still beating the best accuracy baseline, and it gains further from extra compute at inference time. Letting a model fix its own mistakes, the authors show, beats locking in every early guess.
arxiv-2602-11890:
Vessel activity at sea matters for route planning, logistics, safety, and eco watching, and the AIS vessel-tracking system follows hundreds of thousands of vessels daily. Large gaps in vessel paths, from coverage limits or planned gaps, harm the quality of results. Existing filling methods target vehicle paths, but sailing vessels move differently, with smooth turns, port moves, and rough-weather sailing. Giannis Spiliopoulos and six co-authors propose HABIT, a lightweight, flexible grouping-based filling system for vessel paths.

The data-driven system fills missing segments by pulling, checking, and sorting motion patterns from past vessel data. A study across varied periods, crowding levels, and vessel types finds HABIT matches baseline methods on score while beating them on latency, while handling vessel traits and motion patterns. For sea analysis, that mix of comparable score and faster response makes the system practical for real watching workloads.
arxiv-2602-12390:
Most neural networks use fixed activation functions, from ReLU to sigmoid, but trainable rational activations may do more with fewer parameters. Maosen Tang led this work with one co-author, Alex Townsend, studying networks with low-degree rational activations. They prove such networks can uniformly approximate any standard fixed-activation network on compact domains, with only polyloglog overhead in size for a given error target.

The reverse direction provably needs far more parameters, on the order of log inverse error in the worst case, an exponential gap that holds for full networks, gated activations, and transformer-style nonlinearities. In practice, rational activations slot into standard architectures and training pipelines, matching or beating fixed activations under identical setups and optimisers. The result is a leaner, more expressive activation choice.
arxiv-2602-12590:
Event cameras encode dynamic scenes as asynchronous spikes called events, but conventional pipelines need frames, and binning events into frames breaks gradients. Jinze Chen led this work with six co-authors, noting that binning functions are discontinuous, truncating gradients at frame level and forcing most event algorithms to rely solely on frame features. Learning directly from raw events avoids that restriction but suffers biased gradient estimation from binning discontinuities, limiting learning efficiency.

Their frame gives unbiased gradient estimation for arbitrary binning functions by synthesising weak derivatives during backpropagation while keeping forward output unchanged. Integration by parts lifts target functions to functionals, yielding an integral form of the binning derivative where the cotangent function naturally arises. Reconstructing that cotangent from sampled vectors gives weak derivatives matching long-range finite differences for smooth and non-smooth targets. Tests show lower errors and faster convergence on egomotion, optical flow, and SLAM tasks.
arxiv-2602-12690:
Knocking a nucleon out of a rare nucleus is a standard way to learn how single particles sit inside it. Yet measured rates fall below theory for deeply bound nucleons, a puzzle called quenching. Jin Lei traces this gap to the theory itself rather than to the nucleus. He derives an exact three-body description for reactions with composite projectiles. The method is a two-step projection that keeps track of what simpler models leave out.

The missing pieces are two induced effects: one from brief excitations of the target, and one from projectile states that the usual model excludes. Leaving them out inflates the predicted stripping rate, which makes real data look quenched. The same mechanism explains why the shortfall grows with separation energy, and checks against four-body calculations for lithium-6 support the new reference frame.
arxiv-2602-12890:
Kink oscillations of coronal loops are a key test for solar seismology, but gravity's effect on their frequency in curved loops has been unclear. Mingzhe Guo, Bo Li, and Mijie Shi run ideal magnetohydrodynamic mock runs of a curved, gravitationally stratified loop, studying other polarisations and harmonics. Frequencies read off from Lagrangian displacement are set against WKB forecasts.

For the vertical basic mode, the frequency misses the WKB value by about 18% yet matches the Alfvén frequency at the loop apex itself. The horizontal basic mode deviates only 7% and matches the Alfvén frequency near a quarter of the loop. First overtones follow WKB well for both polarisations. The results enable spatially resolved seismology, probing magnet field strength at other points along a loop.
arxiv-2602-13090:
Arthur packets organise representations of p-adic groups, and a natural question asks how many packets contain a given representation. Alexander Hazeltine, Aarya Kumar, and Andrew Tung determine that count for a fixed tempered representation of classical p-adic groups. Starting from a tempered extended multi-segment supported on the integers, they count all extended multi-segments reachable from it through operators from the theory of packet intersections.

The result is a precise enumeration rather than a bound: for the specified representation, the number of containing local Arthur packets is determined. For representation theorists, such counts clarify how tempered representations sit inside the larger Arthur classification, and the operator-based method offers a route to similar counts in related settings.
arxiv-2602-13190:
Spinodal splitting shapes tiny grains in alloys, but calling it without settings has been hard, since local energy terrains are hard to capture. Simon Divilov and four co-authors propose fixing bulk free energy for mess thickness, worked out from small, finite, typical cells. The fix stands in for the energy penalty for joining a messy state, calming locally concave free-energy regions needed for edges while taming long-range crowding swings.

That stand-in avoids full ab initio setting of edge traits and suits high-throughput and machine-learning workflows. The approach captures the physics behind spinodal motion, giving a scalable route for calling where spinodal regions form in alloys with tangled make-up and high chaos. For alloy builders, it offers faster screening of splitting conduct without pricey edge sums.
arxiv-2602-13290:
Running a mobile network means juggling speed, user satisfaction, and energy use, yet most self-managing network designs take no plain-language sustainability goals as input. AGORA closes that gap for beyond-5G networks. It places a local tool-using language model agent inside the control loop. It turns natural-language goals into telemetry-grounded actions, steering traffic through the User Plane Function to save energy.

Tests show a tight link between latency and energy in tool-driven control. Compact models kept a low energy footprint while still carrying out policies correctly, even migrating workloads under stressed edge conditions. The design points toward operations where human sustainability goals drive executable network choices. Rodrigo Moreira leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13390:
Some systems settle only partway, lingering in long-lived quasi-steady states before true equilibrium arrives. In open quantum systems, that dynamical metastability can spring from the spectral shape of a non-Hermitian operator, producing edge modes that live long and grow with system size. This paper carries the idea into the nonlinear, interacting regime, using magnetic heterostructures as its test bed.

An interacting spin model maps onto a metastable Hatano-Nelson chain, seeding size-dependent spin dipping and attraction to unstable equilibria, while topologically protected edge states survive nonlinearity and disorder. Classical multilayer modeling adds multistability and limit cycles absent from the quantum model, and the authors identify interaction, damping, and torque as control knobs. Vincent P. Flynn leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13490:
Trions, charged excitons with spin and charge degrees of freedom, were mainly studied in doped systems where extra charges were thought indispensable. This paper finds another route: exciting trions in two-dimensional tungsten-diselenide donors and transferring them into one-dimensional carbon-tube acceptors within mixed-dimension stacks, sidestepping the usual carrier requirement and intrinsic Auger-quenching limits.

A reservoir effect from the dimension mix lifts trion emission efficiency more than a hundredfold over conventional doping-based approaches, robustly across diverse doping conditions. Extending exciton transfer to three-body particles opens a new platform for excitonic physics and trion-based light and spin uses. N. Fang leads the work with twelve co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13590:
Altermagnets combine zero net magnetism with strong spin splitting that varies with momentum, arising from composite real-space and spin-space symmetries. This review centers angle-resolved photoemission, with spin-resolved and circular-dichroism variants, as the tool that directly images nonrelativistic band splitting and spin textures in these materials. Within the spin-group framework, ferro-, antiferro-, and alter- orders are distinguished and the symmetry origin of spin polarization explained.

Systems reviewed include the debated d-wave case ruthenium dioxide, layered d-wave cases, g-wave compounds such as manganese telluride and chromium antimonide, and the tilted magnetic case manganese ditelluride. Future micro-beam and in-situ methods, strain and domain tuning, and layered-device design are expected to advance the field toward spin-based and linked quantum research. Jiayu Liu leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13690:
Magnetic navigation offers an alternative when GPS is out or broken, but an aircraft's own magnetism corrupts the field signal, and the old Tolles-Lawson model handles random noise poorly. This paper imposes two physics constraints. Divergence-free vector fields are built by learning a vector potential whose curl defines the field, and E(3) symmetry is built from tensor products of geometric tensors via sphere functions. Together they enforce Maxwell's equations and correct shifts with sensor position and orientation.

Keeping the field true to physics restricts the function space, acting as a quiet guard that improves time-space performance, with the Contiformer, combining continuous-time dynamics and memory. Made-up data from the World Magnetic Model and time-series GANs eases scarcity. Experiments show embedding these constraints greatly improves forecast accuracy and physical plausibility, beating old and unconstrained deep learning approaches. Aritra Das leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13790:
Sign language lexicographers build bilingual dictionaries by mapping words to signs, but polysemous and homonymous words mapping to different signs across contexts are often underrepresented. A usage-based approach examining how word senses map to signs can identify novel mappings absent from current dictionaries, enriching lexicographic resources. This paper analyzes German and German Sign Language, manually annotating 1,404 word-use-to-sign mappings. They come from 32 words in the German Word Usage Graph and 49 signs in the Digital Dictionary of German Sign Language.

Three correspondence types are identified: one-to-many, many-to-one, and one-to-one, plus No Match cases. Computational evaluation finds semantic similarity using SBERT embeddings substantially outperforming exact match, 88.52 percent against 71.31 percent. Gains for one-to-many cases are dramatic at 52.1 percentage points. The work establishes the first annotated data set for cross-modal sense correspondence. Melis Çelikkol leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-14390:
Bahar Mojtabaei Ranani and two co-authors apply a 2026 arXiv Q-learning method to car fog computing. A three-tier build serves smart car clients, and the paper guesses goods needed by each client. Q-learning tunes sharing on the fly, learning from past runs to make wise choices as settings shift.

Through steady training and updates, the agent tunes to real-time facts and guesses best values for memory, bandwidth, and processor. Those guesses aim to cut goods use while meeting score needs of the fog setting. Test results show the method deftly tunes sharing, weighing thrift against the service needs of linked cars.
arxiv-2602-14690:
Coding agents are now steered by files in the repo itself, from context files to skills. Matthias Galster, with five co-authors, maps how developers configure agentic coding tools across Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini, and Codex. Eight mechanisms are identified, from static context to executable integrations.

A study of 2,853 GitHub repos finds context files dominate, often as the sole mechanism, with AGENTS.md as an emerging standard. Few repos use advanced tools like skills and subagents, and skills lean on static text over scripts. Claude Code users employ the widest range of mechanisms. The results give the first empirical baseline for harness engineering.
arxiv-2602-14790:
Weiliang Yao and colleagues tune the magnetism of hexagonal iron sulfide, a candidate altermagnet with a spontaneous anomalous Hall effect and only a tiny net magnetisation. In-plane compressive strain effectively suppresses both the Hall effect and the magnetisation, the team reports, offering a mechanical knob on a quantum material.

Neutron diffraction shows the strain mainly shifts the in-plane domain population, leaving the in-plane magnetic structure itself unchanged, so the effect runs through domains rather than through a rebuilt order. Altermagnets promise ferromagnetic-like transport without net magnetism, and strain now joins the tools for steering them. A squeeze changes what the material signals.
arxiv-2602-14990:
Cigna gives a formula for the Euler class of foliations carried by a cooriented branched surface. From the dual graph of such a surface, he builds a simplicial 1-cycle that stands for the Poincare dual of the Euler class relative to the boundary. The construction turns a geometric invariant into a concrete cycle that can be read off the surface data.

As an example, the formula completes the classification of homology classes in the Whitehead link exterior that occur as relative Euler classes of taut foliations. Cigna also shows the formula extends prior results of Lackenby and Dunfield. A final observation notes that cooriented branched surfaces whose complement is a union of balls satisfy a Combinatorial Transverse Surface Theorem in the sense of Landry, Minsky, and Taylor.
arxiv-2602-15190:
Ullrich and Drchal present their third-place system in the AVerImaTeC shared task for image-text fact checking. It joins last year's retrieval-augmented generation pipeline with a reverse image search module. Despite its simplicity, the system performs competitively with a single multimodal language model call per fact-check, costing just over one cent on average via GPT-5.1 on the OpenAI Batch API.

The system is easy to reproduce and tweak, built from only three decoupled modules. A textual retrieval module runs similarity search. An image retrieval module uses API-accessed reverse image search. A generation module uses GPT-5.1. The authors suggest it as an accessible starting point for further experiments, publishing code, prompts, vector stores, and insights into running costs and improvement directions.
arxiv-2602-15590:
Campos Rozo and colleagues study how magnetic fields reshape solar granules, the convective cells that rise to the Sun surface. They track granule area, shape, and brightness against field strength in observations of active region NOAA 11768 from the Swedish 1-metre Solar Telescope. A segmentation routine picks granules out of continuum images, while CRISP spectropolarimetric data supply the field vector and line-of-sight speed.

Granule area falls steadily as field strength rises, with the largest granules in field-free regions and a mean area near 1.58 square arcseconds. Mean brightness and size both drop in stronger fields, confirming that magnetism damps convective energy transport. Near-circular granules occur only where fields are absent, stretched granules occur everywhere, and granule long axes line up with field direction where the horizontal field is strong.
arxiv-2602-16090:
Ankur Mahesh leads a team of thirteen climate researchers testing whether machine-learned weather emulators can capture fast climate responses. Climate reacts to greenhouse gases through both slow feedbacks, tied to ocean warming over decades, and fast feedbacks, driven by rapid atmospheric processes over weeks. Fast feedback physics already lives in the historical weather records used to train modern emulators.

Without retraining on future Earth conditions, the team uses historically trained emulators to measure the fast precipitation response to lower and higher carbon dioxide levels. Their responses match those from full-physics Earth system models, even for conditions with no recent historical precedent. The paper argues that such emulators, alongside full models, can help study fast processes and the global water cycle, opening a cheaper route to probing radiative responses.
arxiv-2602-16490:
Ferdinand Kapl leads four coauthors on looped and depth-grown language models. Looping reuses one block of layers across depth, while depth growing trains shallow-to-deep models by copying middle layers. Both tricks have been tied to stronger reasoning, but how they relate was unclear.

The authors find the two share depth-wise signatures, such as heavier use of late layers and repeating patterns tied to the looped or grown block. These point to a shared form of iterative computation. The tricks also combine. Looping the middle blocks of a depth-grown model at run time lifts accuracy on some reasoning tasks by up to twofold, even though the model never trained to loop. Both adapt better than baselines with more examples or tuning data, and depth-grown models gain most from high-quality, math-heavy training mixes.
arxiv-2602-16990:
Yan Wang and co-authors bring in Conv-FinRe, a conversational and longitudinal benchmark for utility-grounded financial recommendation. Most benchmarks judge how well a model copies user behavior. In financial advice, however, what users do can be noisy or short-sighted when markets swing, and can clash with their long-term goals. Treating what users chose as the only truth mixes copying with good decisions.

Conv-FinRe tests language models beyond copying behavior. Given an intake interview, step-wise market context, and advisory dialogues, models must rank options over a fixed investment horizon. Multi-view references separate descriptive behavior from normative utility grounded in investor-specific risk preferences. That lets researchers see whether a model reasons well, copies user noise, or follows market momentum. Built from real market data and human decision paths, the benchmark shows a lasting tension between rational decision quality and behavioral alignment.
arxiv-2602-17890:
Krishna Neupane identifies a friction in the SEC Form 144 disclosure regime, called predictive decoupling. On welfare economics grounds, the reporting inversion violates Pareto efficiency by inducing one-sided pricing. Trade execution on Form 4 often precedes notice of intent on Form 144. The analysis uses an event-study frame. It examines insiders who file a notice of proposed sale but fail to execute within ninety days.

A machine learning audit reveals an opacity rate of about fifty-two percent. Aborted signals stay the same as trades, creating an information ceiling that blocks the market from exhausting the signal's content. Against the small-firm effect, higher odd returns appear in small-cap funds, yet significant alpha concentrates in large-cap firms. Prior volatility amplifies the signal, with gauges finding a cash crunch up to about two and two-thirds. The paper proposes mandatory execution receipt, Form 144-A, to restore informational balance.
arxiv-2602-17990:
Madhav Kanda and colleagues address a headache for teams shipping multi-agent language-model systems that turn plain-language requests into structured workflows. Updates such as rerun inputs, model swaps, or prompt refactors often yield workflows far from validated references. Engineers then lack a principled way to judge whether a change is safe to ship. Scores from automatic metrics are weakly calibrated, and a numeric shift rarely shows how bad the damage is.

WorkflowPerturb is a controlled benchmark applying realistic graded perturbations to golden workflows. It holds nearly five thousand golden workflows and nearly forty-five thousand variants across Missing Steps, Compressed Steps, and Description Changes at ten, thirty, and fifty percent severity. They benchmark several metric families for sensitivity and calibration with expected score paths and per-case alert rates. Their results map systematic differences across families and support severity-aware readings of evaluation scores in change review.
arxiv-2602-18090:
Takahiro Sanada and colleagues present a coding language for building neural networks within algebraic effects and handlers for arrows, plus its category theory. The language constructs networks with symbols, in the same manner as effects, and assigns code such as backpropagation runs through handlers. Network plans stay abstract and high-level, while code can be freely set.

The authors ground the language firmly with a type system, running rules, category theory, and soundness and fit theorems. The core is reverse handlers, a novel handler trick for arrows that runs backpropagation, plus new systems of strong promonads on reverse differential restriction categories. The string diagrams of those systems provide a formal picture syntax and meaning for neural networks.
arxiv-2602-18190:
Jorge Melegati argues that job role shapes how software workers remake their professional selves around generative AI. His 2026 paper starts from a gap. Studies show AI adoption triggers identity work, the quiet process of forming, adapting, and rejecting work identities. But they rarely separate developers from testers and other roles.

Melegati reviews role-specific studies and recent work on adopting generative AI in software engineering, then lays out a research agenda for tracing how role steers identity work. The agenda also aims at new tools to support adoption, tuned by role rather than one-size-fits-all. The paper closes by spelling out what such findings would mean in practice for teams bringing AI into daily engineering work.
arxiv-2602-18290:
Boris Daszuta and six co-authors present GR-Athena++, a code for neutron star mergers with neutrino transport. Their 2026 paper runs full relativity simulations of merging neutron stars with light, magnetism, and neutrinos included. Neutrinos are tracked with a moment-based scheme that sums over energies, plus a count of neutrino numbers. A wide set of standard tests checks the code as grids refine.

First tests include a collapsing magnetic, spinning neutron star, where light flow stays stable through horizon formation thanks to a new cut-out method that tapers the state inside the horizon. Two merger cases follow: a long-lived remnant with one matter law and a collapse case with another. Both stay stable over long runs on neutrino cooling times, including infall after collapse in three dimensions with magnetic fields and neutrino light.
arxiv-2602-18690:
People can rehearse a catch in their heads before they move, which suggests the brain keeps a map-like model of the world rather than a bare list of states. Joshua Nunley, writing alone in 2026, proposes world models that preserve that spatial layout, so predicting physics becomes motion across a map instead of a jump between abstract states.

The implementation uses motor-gated neural fields, where local links spread activity and motor commands scale selected channels. In three tests the same design predicted ballistic motion without teleporting, improved a catching policy offline by passing error through a frozen model, and grew body-selective channels without body labels. The work is early evidence for one shared basis behind prediction, offline learning, and body sense.
arxiv-2602-18790:
Hidden constants of motion are the secret symmetries that make some orbits solvable. The Carter constant is the classic example for spinning black holes. Christopher de Firmian, with one co-author, asks in 2026 whether two such constants survive for a charged spinning test particle. The setting is a simpler electromagnetic analogue, the square-root Kerr field on flat spacetime.

The particle obeys Mathisson-Papapetrou-Dixon equations. Its moments are generic, adiabatic, and conservative, covering spin- and field-induced types. The authors investigate analogues of the Carter constant and of Rüdiger's linear-in-spin constant. They exist only for special Wilson coefficients. Those coefficients match spin-exponentiation of effective Compton amplitudes through second order in spin. The result draws a sharp line around when hidden symmetry holds.
arxiv-2602-18890:
In twisted bilayer graphene, one number matters greatly. The Hubbard U sets the strength of on-site Coulomb repulsion. Yet measuring it in moiré systems is hard. Nachiket Tanksale, with one co-author, shows in 2026 that scanning tunnelling microscopy images can reveal it.

STM images show the local density of states in real space. Those images encode the material's electronic structure. The authors train machine learning to regress U directly from Fourier-transformed LDOS images. Accuracy holds despite very high visual similarity between images for different interaction strengths. Analysis hints at a gradual redistribution of spectral weight, with a possible turning scale near unity. Augmentation with physically motivated perturbations improves robustness to noisy, symmetry-broken images.
arxiv-2602-19290:
Regression discontinuity designs usually report an average effect at a cutoff. That habit holds even when a treatment reshapes the whole outcome distribution rather than shifting its mean. Kyle Schindl and Larry Wasserman argue that the mean alone can hide the story. They build a framework that measures the full distributional change at the boundary where treatment assignment jumps.

Their core measure is the Wasserstein distance between the outcome distributions just on either side of the cutoff. It is a single scale for how far apart the two distributions sit. That distance weakly bounds the average treatment effect. Equality holds exactly when the effect is purely additive, shifting every outcome by the same amount. The framework shows not just whether a policy moved the average, but how it rearranged outcomes.
arxiv-2602-19690:
News readers often meet stories that lean one way in politics, and judging that lean is hard to do at scale. A 2026 arXiv paper by Qile Wang and seven co-authors asks whether large language models can sort United States news by political slant. It also asks whether the reasons those models give change how people judge the news themselves.

The team first set model predictions against standard supervised methods on a large public set of articles. It then ran a study in which people annotated news with help from model explanations, short ones and longer ones. Help from the models raised the readers' confidence, and the longer reasons proved more likely to shift a decision. The paper closes with advice for building model explanations that support, rather than steer, human judgment.
arxiv-2602-19990:
Internet of Things systems pour out heterogeneous, high-velocity data streams from sensors, machines, and smart devices, but most stream architectures still integrate them syntactically, limiting flexibility and interpretability. A 2026 arXiv paper by Monica Marconi Sciarroni and Emanuele Storti proposes a context-aware platform for stream management built on meaning-based models.

The platform unifies diverse data sources through a knowledge graph that represents in formal terms streams, devices, agents, roles, rights, and conversion pipelines. That model supports gathering that adjusts easily, pipelines for stream processing that compose, and access by role that shifts with agent context, running on Kafka and Flink for real-time processing. SPARQL and SWRL-based rules enable context-dependent stream discovery. Tests show that joining semantic models with context-aware reasoning and distributed stream handling yields data workflows that interoperate for Industry 5.0 settings.
arxiv-2602-20390:
James Chen and two co-authors attack a famous numerical linear algebra question: how large can the growth factor get in Gaussian elimination with complete pivoting? The question is hard because many polynomial inequalities must hold at once. The authors combine numerical and exact computation via JuMP, Groebner bases, discriminant polynomials, and interval arithmetic. That marriage lets them pin down exact values where pure numerics could only guess.

For size five, the best value seen since 1988, about four point one three two five, is exactly the root of a sixty-first degree polynomial supplied in the paper. It is a maximum under the equality constraints found by JuMP. The authors conjecture that this lower bound is the true maximum. They also apply the technique to sizes six, seven, and eight, and slightly lower a 1969 upper bound for size five to four point eight four.
arxiv-2602-20690:
First stars ionized and enriched host galaxies and seeded black holes. Yet models assume one universal initial mass function across minihaloes. Shingo Hirano and two co-authors test it with one hundred thirty-eight simulations mapping masses across redshift, halo mass, and streaming velocity. A dense-cloud merger tree assigns star masses from gas accretion-rate profiles, yielding per-halo mass functions with no prior.

High-mass tails and multiplicity rise with redshift, halo mass, and streaming speed. Low-mass, low-streaming haloes form one or a few stars. Massive, high-streaming haloes host clusters and produce stars of one to ten thousand solar masses. Halo-to-halo scatter stays substantial in fixed settings, yet average mass functions converge to forms, ruling out one universal mass function. High-streaming haloes populate the heavy-seed regime for luminous sources. Low-streaming settings fit single-event enrichment marks in poor stars.
arxiv-2602-20890:
How far apart can two faces sit inside a strongly connected simplicial complex? Stefan Glock, Olaf Parczyk, Silas Rathke, and Tibor Szabo answer that question in this 2026 arXiv paper. For any fixed dimension and large enough vertex count, they determine the maximum possible diameter exactly.

The result improves a run of earlier bounds and settles a problem posed by Santos in 2013. Along the way, the authors also characterize when an extra-tight Euler tour exists in the complete uniform hypergraph. Readers get a sharp extremal answer plus a neat side result in hypergraph theory.
arxiv-2602-20990:
Entanglement reveals what ordinary order parameters miss in quantum matter. Min-Chul Cha, Hoon Beom Kwon, Ji-Woo Lee, and Myung-Hoon Chung study entanglement in the one-dimensional dimerized Fermi-Hubbard model in this 2026 arXiv paper. Using a matrix-product-state approach, they compute the ground state and find two insulating phases plus a metallic phase.

The two insulators are genuinely distinct: the half-filling phase has a charge gap from the band gap, strengthened by repulsion, while the three-quarter-filling phase has a Mott gap from particle interactions. That difference shows up in how the half-chain entanglement entropy scales and how the entanglement spectrum is distributed. Readers get entanglement fingerprints that separate phases other probes might confuse.
arxiv-2602-21290:
Waves from a neutron star face can steepen into monster shocks, near-light magnet shocks driving high-energy glow. Michael Grehan, Bart Ripperda, Andrei Beloborodov, Christopher Thompson, and Elias Most model them across the board in this 2026 arXiv paper with magnet-fluid math in dipolar shape, for calm and wrinkled backgrounds.

Runs back by-hand calls for equator shocks and light up slanted shocks off the equator. Shocks formed by Alfven-to-fast-mode switch show the engine's broad nature. Extra magnet-sphere waves can split the shock front, cut magnet strength, boost local Lorentz factors, and off and on spawn extra shocks along a line of sight. Readers get a global picture of shocks around magnet stars, mergers, and falling-in stars.
arxiv-2602-21390:
Gabriele Farina and one co-author study Defensive Generation. The goal is to produce generative models online, one outcome at a time, that cannot be falsified by observed data plus a preset set of computational tests. The models cover scalar, multiclass, and vector-valued outcomes, not just yes-or-no events.

The paper first links online high-dimensional multicalibration over a reproducing kernel Hilbert space to recent work on expected variational inequality problems. That link yields fast algorithms for the former. Applied to outcome indistinguishability, the method is the first to efficiently produce online models that pass infinite test classes. Those classes include tests of higher-order moments. The method runs in near-linear time, with generation error falling at the optimal rate of one over the square root of T.
arxiv-2602-21590:
Kart Leong Lim and two co-authors offer a physics-informed neural network using finite differences for its PDE loss. Physics-informed networks exploit hidden physics of building systems, with partial differential equations forming the loss.
