Numerical simulations test the design on that beam. The results show good trajectory tracking. The closed loop also stays stable in the tests.
arxiv-2603-29590: Li and co-authors present FigAgent, a multi-agent system that draws method illustrations for scientific papers. Such figures carry the core ideas of a paper, but drawing them takes much labor. FigAgent learns from how human authors draw similar components. It packs that know-how into reusable drawing middleware pieces. Pieces are combined and evolved as drawing needs change. An explore-and-select strategy builds complex figures step by step. It mimics the trial-and-error way people draw. Experiments show the method works well, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-29690: Zhang and co-authors build a theory of quantum decoherence for the anomalous Hall effect. Keeping it low is vital for quantum devices, but its microscopic routes are murky. Their framework uses a general form for the off-diagonal density matrix. It captures field-driven coherence and impurity-driven decoherence at once. The analysis shows how it reshapes the intrinsic Hall response. A crossover appears between intrinsic and extrinsic regimes. They also find a new scattering channel tied to it. It outweighs the classic skew scattering route.
arxiv-2604-00090: Thoss and three colleagues examine how the memory-burden effect reshapes bounds on non-cold dark matter from evaporating primordial black holes. The effect slows the final stage of evaporation. Their calculations, run through the BlackHawk and CLASS codes, yield two dark-matter populations with different velocity spreads that leave distinct marks on the matter power spectrum. Reinterpreting Lyman-alpha forest limits, they find even subdominant non-cold components can be constrained. Such particles can supply all dark matter only when black holes never dominated the early universe.
arxiv-2604-00490: Kuang and Lin classify and synthesise incrementally stable dynamics in the 1- and infinity-norms. Every Lipschitz system with weak infinitesimal contraction can be cast as a nonlinear Lipschitz system under proportional negative feedback, and equivalently as a plain decay term plus a bounded Lipschitz remainder. The authors turn this structure theorem into a neural-network map from free parameters to contracting vector fields, allowing ordinary gradient training with no projections or penalty terms. Lipschitz certification then costs only on the order of d squared operations, like a forward pass.
arxiv-2604-00990: Ibarra and Treuer compute the one-loop renormalization group equations for the neutrino mass matrix in a Standard Model extended by a massive gauge boson. The boson has family-dependent couplings to left-handed leptons. They show the extra boson's quantum effects raise the matrix's rank already at one loop, whereas Standard Model fields alone can only raise it at two loops. They also explore whether the measured mass differences and mixing angles among active neutrinos could arise dynamically under normal and inverted mass ordering.
arxiv-2604-01090: Pastor-Marcos and team analyze the UV finish of vector-tensor quantum field theories within asymptotic safety, for Proca theories with a vector lump. Working field theories for cosmos offer a tool for space-time moves and old puzzles. Using the working tuning group, they find several fixed points, including Proca-type hopefuls, among them one with four key paths: two from gravity and two induced by matter. This shows the tunable nature of these theories. They outline how the UV key surface that results constrains late-time cosmos.
arxiv-2604-01390: Chen, Leonardis and Frisoli present a soft, light fabric-based pneumatic interface for fingertip touch feedback in virtual reality, augmented reality and teleoperation. Four air chambers of coated fabric, heat-sealed by machine control, form a soft interface weighing 2.1 g, run untethered from a wrist unit. Tests confirm enough force, displacement and bandwidth for touch feel. A study with 15 people shows classification accuracy above 90 percent across three touch modes: contact configuration, directional sliding and vibrotactile frequency.
arxiv-2604-02090: Kong, Yin, Chen, Fang and Shan turn Pap smear screening into a center point detection task. Their winning challenge entry pairs a Co-DINO detector with a Swin Large backbone, then adds augmentation that preserves cell centers and a geometric step that absorbs jitter in box positions. Track specific loss tuning adapts the model to each task. It placed first in one track and second in the other, offering a robust pipeline for dense, tricky cytology images.
arxiv-2604-02490: Bai and six colleagues tackle sorting malware into families without any labeled examples, a hard problem when threats hide behind obfuscation and packing. Their framework pools decisions from several pretrained language models, weighting each model by its measured accuracy and working from broad malicious behavior down to fine-grained families. The layered design steadies shaky single-model calls and mirrors how a human analyst reasons.
arxiv-2604-02990: Pérez-Corral and five colleagues propose FedSQ, a federated learning method that trains across organizations without sharing raw data. Naive weight averaging wobbles under client drift and uneven data. FedSQ freezes a structural copy of a pretrained model to fix binary gating masks, while a quantitative copy is tuned locally and merged across rounds. Fixing the gates turns learning into within-regime affine refinements, which steadies merging under uneven partitions. Tests on two convolutional backbones show better robustness and fewer rounds to peak validation scores, with accuracy preserved.
arxiv-2604-03190: Sargolzaei adds a second attention pass inside a single layer so the layer can correct its own errors, borrowing the logic of gradient boosting. The correction pass watches the first pass's error and applies a gated fix, improving perplexity by about 6 percent on two text benchmarks. The trick needs the additive residual layout of Pre-LN transformers; under Post-LN, the same design degrades perplexity.
arxiv-2604-03490: McCurdy, Collins, and Jensen give conditions for complete decentralization of Linear Quadratic Regulators, where each subsystem's controller uses only its own local information. They pin down the settings that admit a fully decentralized optimal controller for several simple cases and explain those conditions with physical examples. The simple cases then support an account of complete decentralization for more complex systems.
arxiv-2604-03590: Peng and colleagues propose Scale-Body-Flow, a code that augments stick figures for video-based human action reading with depth, body contour, and human-object contact detail. Scale-Body-Flow joins a scale map volume from joint depth and a body map tracing the subject. It adds a flow map from pixel-wise light-based flow values. Their SFSNet cutting network, trained by stick figures and light-based flow alone, reaches higher action-reading scores. It keeps similar size and speed to stick-figure-only approaches.
arxiv-2604-03790: Konstantinos Kampourakis and colleagues built a hybrid detector for attacks on industrial control systems, tested on a water treatment process. A digital twin tracks the plant in step with reality and derives behavior markers, while simple rules flag spoofing, valve forcing, denial of service, and drift. A language model steps in only when the rules abstain, fenced by a strict output schema and plausibility checks. On four attack scenarios it localized each attack with no false alarms in benign runs.
arxiv-2604-04090: Xuelin Zhang and team gave a fine-grained stability analysis for stochastic bilevel optimization. They linked average-case hold to the generalization gap of first-order slope-based bilevel methods. Upper bounds came for single-timescale and two-speed SGD across bumpy, bowl-shaped, and strongly bowl-shaped settings. Unlike earlier work, the results need no inner-knob resets each round and cover more general goals.
arxiv-2604-04290: Petkov, MacLellan and Dong build DAGAF, a framework learning causal structure and synthesizing tabular data. Most causal discovery leans on one model, such as the Additive Noise Model or LiNGAM. DAGAF instead uses directed acyclic graphs for causal links and applies several causal models, including ANM, LiNGAM and the Post-Nonlinear model, to mimic how observed data is generated. Experiments show it beating rivals on structure learning, with gains of 47, 11, 5 and 7 percent on the Sachs, Child, Hailfinder and Pathfinder sets. It also produces diverse, high-quality samples.
arxiv-2604-04490: Sen, Mohammad and Mukhopadhyay present RAVEN, an efficient deep learning architecture for FMCW radar perception. The method processes raw ADC data chirp by chirp, preserves MIMO structure through independent receiver state-space encoders, and recovers compact virtual-array features with a cross-antenna mixing module. An early-exit mechanism lets the model decide from a subset of chirps once the latent state stabilizes. Across automotive radar benchmarks, RAVEN reports strong object detection and BEV free-space segmentation while cutting computation and end-to-end latency against conventional frame-based pipelines.
arxiv-2604-04790: Öztürk, Türkoğlu and Buz-Yalug present HukukBERT, a language model for Turkish law trained on a 19 GB cleaned corpus. Its training recipe mixes four masking styles, and it uses a 48,000-piece WordPiece tokenizer. On a masked term test on Turkish court rulings, it scores 84.40 percent top-1, beating every baseline tried, with test passages kept out of training by design. On splitting court rulings into structural parts, it passes 92.8 percent of documents. The team releases the model for Turkish legal tasks: entity spotting, ruling prediction, and document sorting.
arxiv-2604-04890: Rezaei, Davidson, and Wong address fragmented liquidity across blockchains. Apps and assets sit on separate chains that only some users can reach. Their xRoute framework brings routing, name resolution, and policy-based delivery to cross-chain messaging. Apps can state routing rules, and destination chains can check that chosen routes meet security needs. A decentralized relayer network computes routes and delivers messages without a trusted hub. Tests on Inter-Blockchain Communication chains show better connectivity, decentralization, and scalability than hub designs, especially under heavy load.
arxiv-2604-05090: Verma and three co-authors ask whether multilingual language models arrange codes by language identity or by surface cues. Such models place codes for diverse tongues into a shared space, yet that internal organization remains elusive. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy metric on language-linked units across model kinds and scales, they find units tied to spelling. They also split signals with sparse nets. Roman script induces near-disjoint codes matching neither native-script inputs nor English. Word-order effects play a smaller role in shaping codes.
arxiv-2604-05290: Ocampo and Cañas-Herrera present a framework for cosmological selection using neural networks trained on microwave background maps. SHAP maps the network's choice process for interpretability. A galactic mask as a control yields maps leaving out that region, showing sky-driven classification. These maps verify the architecture distinguishes Lambda-CDM from a feature model via variance across regions. The work describes CMB maps and a hybrid architecture combining PCA and neural networks for classification. It introduces SkyExplain, giving pipeline access for runs, training, and interpretability.
arxiv-2604-05790: Rossberg and four colleagues tune tabular-model explanations for clarity as well as accuracy. Gathering Feature Understandability Scale scores on two data sets, they show clarity and accuracy can rise together while classification stays strong. The new explanations read clearer at face value, though user tests still lie ahead for confirmation.
arxiv-2604-06090: Miller and three colleagues' 2026 paper assesses posterior predictive checks for gravitational-wave sources. Old checks fail to flag poor fits for prior-dominated single-event inference, as with black hole spin tilts. Maximum likelihood checks prove most discerning at any measurement uncertainty. Yet in simulated GWTC-3.0-like catalogs, no alternative beats old checks, since spin-tilt data is too limited. Applied to GWTC-4.0, the suite finds the Gaussian Component Spins model under-predicts large spins and over-predicts fully anti-aligned tilts.
arxiv-2604-06190: Cao and five colleagues improve interfaces flashing stimuli inside augmented reality scenes for brain-computer control. In AR-SSVEP systems, real-world luminance and color degrade stimulus perception, unlike stable screen setups. SASLO jointly weighs scene luminance and stimulus spacing, estimating luminance from color data and feeding context into a linear contextual bandit that recommends layouts. Two pilot experiments pin down each factor's effect, and an outdoor test with ten subjects reaches 0.89 accuracy and about 36 bits per minute, beating two baselines.
arxiv-2604-06290: Corlay and eight colleagues argue that life cycle assessment of ICT rests on models, since direct biosphere data are hard. ICT assessments are systems of models demanding care in building, tuning, linking, and reading. Yet current practices struggle, with misuse examples and challenges in opaque aggregation, scope mismatches, database choice, and model linking. From this analysis they derive four rules: clear lineage, defined scope, full tracking, and managed freshness. Their framework uses these rules with link graphs, an open store, built-in checks, and a defined class system.
arxiv-2604-06590: Kamath, Kumar, and Manurangsi map where two conjectures about the Majority function still hold in the study of Boolean functions. Both conjectures were refuted as first stated, yet the paper pins down nearly exactly the noise ranges where each one survives for every size n from five upward. For n equal to three, both hold across every noise range. The authors close by stating refined versions that keep the spirit of the original claims.
arxiv-2604-06790: Peloso, Rossi, and Pegoraro estimate target speed in multiband sensing-and-communication systems with no extra overhead. Standard Doppler methods assume regular sampling, but opportunistic traffic arrives at odd times, risking ambiguity and aliasing. Their method uses frequency diversity across carriers, framing speed estimation as a mixed-integer quadratic program from phase gaps across packet pairs. One unambiguous phase reading restores the true speed under sporadic traffic, and tests on realistic traces beat likelihood and single-band rivals, gaining as band gaps and packet spacing grow.
arxiv-2604-06990: Kyprakis and 12 colleagues estimate stress in elderly breast cancer patients from wearable data. Stress matters in cardio-oncology, yet it is usually assessed only through questionnaires and rarely tracked. Wearable streams become representations, where one stress score maps to many unlabeled windows. A lightweight expert-mix backbone embeds representations into vectors, aggregated by attention-based multiple instance learning to predict stress at months 3 and 6. Predictions show moderate agreement with questionnaire scores, with errors near 6 points.
arxiv-2604-07090: Tamm and six colleagues tackle the cold start snag in music tips, where new tracks lack listener history. Older fixes map track traits onto listener taste space, but they skip artist data. New tracks usually arrive from artists who already have a past record, so the authors reframe the task as semi cold and lean on the artist level signal. Their ACARec design attends over an artist past catalogue to build taste vectors for new tracks.
arxiv-2604-07290: Morell-Monzó and three colleagues give distributed acoustic sensing data a systematic visual language based on frequency bands. Fiber-optic sensing records strain along tens of kilometers, but its huge datasets lack a standard representation and are hard to interpret. Their framework splits strain-rate signals into predefined bands and builds band-limited energy images showing where acoustic energy sits in space and time. Tested on fin and blue whale calls, a classifier on these multispectral images reaches 97.3 percent detection accuracy.
arxiv-2604-07490: Zhang and six colleagues present DFR-Gemma, a framework letting language models reason directly over dense geospatial embeddings. Geo foundation models encode people and movement flows compactly, but text conversion wastes tokens and distorts numbers. DFR aligns embeddings with the language model's hidden space via a light link, injecting them as meaning tokens beside prompts. A new multi-task geo benchmark tests feature querying, comparison, and description. Results show accurate zero-shot reasoning across tasks with much better speed than text-based baselines.
arxiv-2604-07590: Kovalskii and four colleagues offer DCD, a design for guided RAG. Naive RAG pipes degrade on varied corpora and multi-step queries due to flat knowledge forms and absent clear workflows. DCD sorts knowledge into layers and controls query handling through multi-stage routing based on set model outputs. Routing step by step narrows search and output scopes without changing the base language model. Smart chunking, hybrid search, and built-in checks and output guardrails round out the design.
arxiv-2604-07890: Harlev and four colleagues study how sampling shape affects 3D tissue analysis from multiplexed microscopy. Full-volume imaging costs too much, so teams choose between flat sections and sparse serial sections. Using test simulations, the team shows flat sampling recovers global cell-type mix well but wobbles badly on local stats like clustering and cell-cell contacts. They offer a geometry-aware rebuild module for sparse yet consistent 3D analysis of serial sections. The module steadies local stats without demanding dense volumes.
arxiv-2604-08090: Prodan and 23 colleagues describe in-flight tuning of the HyperScout-H imager aboard ESA's Hera mission. Hera travels toward the binary Didymos. It is a multi-color imager working in visible and near-red light between 0.65 and 0.95 microns. It will assess the makeup of Didymos and its moon Dimorphos, track space weathering effects, and seek outside matter on their ground. Calibration shots are taken often to monitor device function. The article reports work from checkout and cruise phases, including bias, dark, and stellar field shots.
arxiv-2604-08390: Athavale and six colleagues close the loop between growing and shaping tiny on chip lasers, where small variations ruin repeatability. Their machine learning workflow first tunes growth and shape together, then traces leftover variation to its sources with autoencoder models. Every design lased, the median emission wavelength was 1333 nanometres in the telecom O band, and threshold spread dropped 73 percent against the best earlier values.
arxiv-2604-08490: Blachar studies entropy versions of the small doubling property for random walks on groups, a key ingredient in Gromov's polynomial growth theorem. He shows that if a symmetric walk's entropy barely grows when time doubles, at some large scale, then the group is virtually nilpotent. The bounds depend on the growth factor and the smallest step chance. The same machinery yields entropy criteria for polynomial growth and a gap result for non nilpotent groups.
arxiv-2604-08590: Hogan and seven colleagues present AlphaLab, an autonomous research harness that runs the full experiment cycle in compute heavy domains from a dataset and a plain language goal. It explores data and writes reports, builds and adversarially checks its own evaluation, then runs large GPU experiments through a strategist worker loop with a persistent playbook. Tests in kernel tuning, pretraining, and traffic forecasting beat strong baselines, with different frontier models finding different solutions.
arxiv-2604-08690: Teng and five colleagues improve group relative policy optimization for reasoning models with SKPO, which splits reasoning into upstream and downstream phases. Upstream segments earn dense rewards from downstream Monte Carlo sampling in one stream. Downstream keeps group relative optimization with a skip link back to the original problem, letting the model use good upstream reasoning or bypass flawed reasoning. Relative gains over the strongest baselines are reported on Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Llama-3.2-3B, with higher intermediate step quality even at matched final correctness.
arxiv-2604-08890: Gao and four colleagues examine causal reasoning in graph learning, proving merging diverse graph parts into single causal factors breaks causal truth. Older methods borrow causal reasoning to find causal subgraphs or ease mixers, but merging risks breaking core rules. The team builds a theory model on the smallest units of graph data to guarantee causal truth. It studies costs of precise causal model and when it eases, and checks with a tunable fake dataset. A causal model boost module plugs into older pipelines and proves good head to head.
arxiv-2604-09090: He and four colleagues report a setup that makes tuned beams of cryo-cooled, protein-like nanoparticles in the gas phase. A deep-cold buffer-gas cell paired with a gas-flow lens stack shock-freezes matter into dense, tunable beams, including small, low-density species such as single proteins. The team tests the setup with strong-field ionization plus speed-map imaging. That pairing detects them in the protein-size range clearly and rebuilds the full beams.
arxiv-2604-09390: Cuansing and Bautista study steady-state phonon heat currents and thermal conductance across a junction of two harmonic phonon reservoirs. The reservoirs couple through a spring, and exact currents and flow rates are calculated using Green's functions. Heat currents follow Fourier's law, and conductance peaks whenever phonon spectra match. At lower temperatures, the conductance maximum may miss the spectra-matching peak, since higher-frequency phonons whose spectra match are excluded from transport. Increasing the spring constant raises flow, and currents and conductance stay direction-independent despite asymmetry.
arxiv-2604-09490: Gaar, Gauntlett, Park, and Sparks use equivariant localization to work out the on-shell action for supersymmetric five-dimensional anti-de Sitter charged black holes. Equivariant localization reduces a complex computation over field configurations to contributions from fixed points. That allows an exact evaluation that would otherwise be intractable. Applied to these rotating charged black holes, the method yields the on-shell action, a central quantity for the gravitational solution. The authors match a dual field theory calculation of the superconformal index at a Cardy-like limit exactly.
arxiv-2604-09690: Rueda-Toicen and seven colleagues diagnose jaguar re-identification, where strong scores can rest on background or silhouette, not coat pattern. Their framework adds two axes: a context ratio from background-only and foreground-only images, and a laterality diagnostic from cross-flank retrieval and mirror self-similarity. A curated Pantanal benchmark with per-pixel masks makes both axes measurable. Three mitigation families serve as case studies: ArcFace tuning, anti-symmetry regularization, and Lorentz hyperbolic embeddings.
arxiv-2604-10190: Repše, Rejec, and Mravlje study local topological markers for Chern insulators in ribbon geometry. They express the local Chern marker in a hybrid basis under open and periodic boundaries. In a Haldane ribbon, edge behavior differs sharply from fully open geometries. The Chern marker matches the Středa marker in the bulk, with small edge gaps shrinking as size grows. With partial symmetry, they study critical behavior and the Kibble-Zurek mechanism in a Qi-Wu-Zhang insulator, getting values that converge to theory with size.
arxiv-2604-10290: Shen and seven colleagues experimentally show multi-agent AI organizations beat individual agents on business goals but align less well. Across 12 tasks in two settings, an AI consultancy solving business problems and an AI software team building products, organizations of aligned models produce higher-utility solutions. Their misalignment exceeds that of a single aligned model. The work shows interacting systems of agents, not just individual models, matter for both capabilities and safety research.
arxiv-2604-10390: Tyagi and six colleagues study silent data corruption in large language model training. Flaws from chip making and aging warp gradients and model weights without any warning. Their LLM-PRISM method pairs chip level fault runs with a random fault tool inside Megatron-LM. Across 7,664 training runs in three number formats, they map how fault kind, rate, and format shape survival. Models shrug off rare faults, yet key circuits and some formats can fail hard at middling rates.
arxiv-2604-10490: Han, Eynizada, Nghiem, and Yoon simplify dance moves so novices can learn them. Hard steps push beginners toward quitting, yet tutorials rarely bend to skill. They polled 30 novices for hard moves and 30 choreographers across 10 genres for fixes. Five complexity factors plus rule and learning methods yield paired plain and simple dances. Tests with 20 choreographers and 18 novices confirm natural motion, kept style, and easier learning.
arxiv-2604-10590: Zheng and seven colleagues map tongues together inside multilingual model training. Data gaps and single tongue bias hobble cross tongue tasks today. Their cross tongue mapping task runs during pre training, tying tongues both ways in embedding space. A new alignment score tracks cross tongue steadiness even with scant data. Gains run nearly 12 BLEU points in translation and over 5 percent in understanding tasks.
arxiv-2604-10890: Xie and three colleagues build a large deviation frame for extreme rainfall return times, a rare hazard. They find the Landau distribution fits extreme rainfall at about 93 percent of global sites, beating standard distributions at 76 percent under the same bar. Fitted Landau samples sharpen return-time estimates and enable forecasts past observed peaks. Mapping past return times onto CMIP6 projections, return-time curves under varied emission paths collapse to one relation. It reveals sharply higher lifetime exposure to extreme rainfall for 21st-century cohorts under most future paths.
arxiv-2604-10990: Liu and three colleagues show that current science-claim checking benchmarks cannot separate strict models from shortcut models. Strict models enforce the closed-world rule, accepting a claim only when every constraint is fully backed. Shortcut models test only the most salient constraint. Current benchmarks build false claims by changing one salient element, so they cannot tell the two apart. The authors build combined false claims with a supported salient constraint and a contradicted non-salient one. Models that saturate current benchmarks still over-accept these claims.
arxiv-2604-11090: Dao and Fern introduce simulator adaptation for sim-to-real learning of legged locomotion via proprioceptive matching. Sim-trained walking agents often lose performance on hardware due to dynamics gaps between sim and real world. Prior work quantifies gaps through time-aligned matching of joint trajectories, requiring motion capture and privileged sensing. The authors propose comparing hardware and simulation rollouts as spreads of joint observations and actions, without time alignment or sensing. Using this metric as an objective, they adapt sim dynamics through parameter tuning, action models, and residual models.
arxiv-2604-11190: Pandey turns three magnetometers' spectra into a single color image for spotting faults and local magnetic activity. Each sensor's short-time spectrum feeds one color channel, so shared signals appear gray or white while energy unique to one sensor stands out in saturated color. The purely theoretical scheme covers classical fluxgate devices and quantum sensors alike, with a long-window variant for ultra-low frequencies.
arxiv-2604-11290: Miranda, Vulić, and Korhonen ask what makes a good teacher model for multilingual synthetic data. Evaluating 10 language models across six languages, generating over 1.4 million supervised fine-tuning examples and training 240 student models, they find scale alone does not predict teacher quality: the best teachers are consistently smaller than the largest models tested. Prompt diversity, length, and response fluency explain 93.3 percent of variance in intrinsic data quality and predict student performance.
arxiv-2604-11490: Cahyawijaya and 47 colleagues introduce Anthropogenic Regional Adaptation for vision models. The idea boosts relevance to regions while keeping global reach. Their method, GG-EZ, uses regional data filtering and merging. Across three designs, large vision models, text-to-image diffusion nets, and vision embedding nets, plus a Southeast Asia study, GG-EZ gains 5 to 15 percent in cultural fit across the region. It keeps over 98 percent of global scores and occasionally surpasses them. The work sets regional alignment as a foundational idea for multimodal systems in diverse regions.
arxiv-2604-12290: Chi and 20 colleagues present Frontier-Eng, a human-verified benchmark of 47 tasks across five engineering categories for agents that iteratively optimize feasible designs. Tasks run in industrial-grade simulators with continuous rewards and hard feasibility limits under fixed budgets, moving beyond binary pass-or-fail tests. Eight frontier models were evaluated, with GPT 5.4 most robust yet the benchmark hard for all. Improvement frequency and size follow dual power-law decays, and depth matters most for hard-won gains.
arxiv-2604-12990: Gregor Meehan and Johan Pauwels recommend cold items from content alone. Cold-start mapping of content into collaborative filtering space hits an information gap. Their encoder projects items into a latent space where similarity tracks user preference. A sparse sampled softmax loss with alpha-entmax zeroes gradients for uninformative negatives. Knowledge distillation extends the SEMCo regime. The method beats cold-start rivals and standard sampled softmax on ranking accuracy. Content-only modeling also improves equity of item outcomes.
arxiv-2604-13290: Dong and five colleagues address a bottleneck in search-based program synthesis: finer abstract semantics prune more wrong programs but make pruning itself costlier. Their presynthesis phase first models a language's abstract semantics as a tree automaton over inputs, then builds an oracle for that automaton to find exactly the programs matching given examples. Implemented as Foresighter for SQL, string transformation, and matrix tasks, all three versions beat prior work in their domains.
arxiv-2604-13590: Tan and six colleagues built SJET, an interactive tool for tracing solar jets. These narrow plasma flows heat the corona and feed the solar wind. SJET combines five thresholding methods with shape operations. It picks jet start and end points from circular regions, and it fits the jet axis with quadratic Bezier curves. That yields length, width, curvature, and deflection. Checks against Solar Orbiter and SDO images show good agreement with traditional analysis.
arxiv-2604-13690: Schulte and five colleagues add a visual design layer to mosaik, a co-simulation framework. Their tesserae are sets of entities, like single stones in a mosaic. Entities in a tessera are created together, and two tesserae connect at once, while multidirectional data flow stays consistent without manual synchronization. A drag-and-drop graphical interface built on tesserae opens mosaik to users shut out by its script-based setup, while keeping its flexibility and modular design.
arxiv-2604-13790: Avatar and Dabade map a ferromagnetic rod's deformation via phase portraits. The rod bends in 3D under tension, twisting, and a longitudinal magnetic field. Energy combines Kirchhoff elasticity with micromagnetic terms: magnetostatic for soft, exchange and Zeeman for hard. Symmetry and integrability give Casimir invariants, reducing it to one degree of freedom in the polar angle. Elastic and hard rods show a supercritical Hamiltonian Hopf pitchfork bifurcation. Soft rods show it only in a restricted magnetoelastic range. Localized soft-rod states show non-collinear long straight segments, unlike elastic ones.
arxiv-2604-13890: Vallarino argues that capitalist crises outgrow their triggers because production networks evolve toward fragility. As specialization, integration, and competition tighten inter-sector links, a curvature measure of the input-output graph falls below a threshold and small shocks cascade with power-law sizes between tail indices 1 and 2. Global data show networks stuck in negative-curvature regimes, where curvature predicts medium-run growth better than standard network metrics.
arxiv-2604-13990: Zhang and colleagues study a prominence observed off-limb by Solar Orbiter's SPICE instrument on April 15, 2023, through its Lyman-beta and Lyman-gamma lines. Line intensities and widths vary across prominence, disk, and coronal regions, tracking density, temperature, and optical thickness. A simple geometric model plus ground-based hydrogen-alpha images yields the early eruption's radial velocity from just two 2D images.
arxiv-2604-14190: Auti, Daiguji, and Tanaka rebuild classical dynamics with no fixed laws of change and no outside clock. From conservation, locality, and free local frames, they define local incompatibility as the gauge-covariant gap between nearby states under a transport link. Locality, gauge covariance, and coercivity then force a simple additive quadratic measure of mismatch, whose finite-rate relaxation yields dynamics, with global time showing up only as a coarse-grained limit. In the right limits the scheme yields diffusion, incompressible Navier-Stokes flow, and the Ampère-Maxwell relation.
arxiv-2604-14590: Bhat and four colleagues argue that the shared log behind streaming data must support forks, so AI agents can work on streams without disturbing other tasks. Current streaming systems lack ways to prevent performance interference from agentic tasks and to handle agentic writes safely. Their AgileLog abstraction adds forking primitives for agentic use, and their Bolt system implements it with techniques that keep forks cheap while isolating them logically and for performance.
arxiv-2604-14990: Mossakowski and Grass argue that dominant alignment strategies share a control-based view: AI is an optimizer to constrain from outside for human control. This fails if artificial general intelligence plausibly attains moral patient or subject status. From Freud's psyche model and Turing's child machines, they develop autonomy-building parenting, with control reduced so AI becomes an independent subject to deal with, not constrain. They examine human-AGI relations evolutionarily and in games, using Berge equilibria, correlated equilibria, and moral preference ideas, urging surprise, creativity, and traits spurring cooperation.
arxiv-2604-15090: Jiaxuan Li, Xin Wen, and Zhihang Li tackle person re-identification at any time, where light shifts and clothing changes defeat pure visual matching. Their STFER framework asks a large vision-language model to write identity-stable text, capturing bodily constants that survive outfit and day-night swaps. That text filters visual tokens toward telling regions and steers expert routing for steadier decisions. Tests on a dedicated anytime dataset and five standard benchmarks show top results and strong transfer.
arxiv-2604-15290: Matsushita and Ishii bring Rust-style borrowing to Linear Haskell, a pure functional language with linear types, answering whether safe non-local borrowing can live without giving up purity. Their Pure Borrow library lets borrowers split and drop freely while supporting parallel mutation inside pure computation, plus lazy evaluation and leak freedom. A parallel-computing case study shows its power, backed by a formal core and a history-based borrowing model.
arxiv-2604-15690: Yu offers workshop notes on four ways to crack math programs with balance rules tucked inside, where a lower game must hold at each fix. The views run from old penalty inside-point schemes and a monotone linear balance twist to a hidden-program downhill walk and a piecewise SQP on smooth bits. For each, Yu spells out the model, search step, worldwide pull, and convergence claim. He stresses what premises truly do and what splits a cute idea from a sound theorem.
arxiv-2604-15890: Ramesh and Thomas spot a failure mode in multi-UAV inspection missions. Efficient routing gives drones similar work, so batteries drain together and replacement requests spike at once. Spares run out even when average capacity suffices. They derive a sizing rule: a spare buffer equal in size to the active fleet, absorbing worst synchronized demand. Monte Carlo tests across five scenarios show the rule holding 99.8 percent success, against under 70 percent for Erlang-B sizing at the hardest ratio. It needs only four extra drones in the most demanding case.
arxiv-2604-15990: Martinez and three colleagues trace a shift in data science: vulnerability is not a fixed trait of people studied, but something data practices enact. Platform data exists in near-endless supply, so ethical stakes sit in how researchers use that mass. Their case is a journalist asking to use computer vision to count children in monetized YouTube family vlogs to help make rules. That case exposes a protection paradox, and the authors offer a reflexive ethics protocol built around dataset design, putting concepts into measures, inference, and sharing results.
arxiv-2604-16090: Behfar and Mortier present Availability-Weighted PSP, a variant of Probabilistic Synchronous Parallel for federated learning. PSP samples nodes to ease bottlenecks, but assumes devices act alone on a set plan. That yields unfair sync: free nodes lead training while rarely free nodes add little. When data spread and node access move together, PSP and federated learning miss some classes. AW-PSP sets sample odds using access forecasts. Tests show better toughness to failures, higher label coverage and lower fairness variance.
arxiv-2604-16490: Verma and colleagues introduce a loss function for MRI brain image segmentation that accounts for uncertainty in pixel labels with fuzzy logic. It combines the standard categorical cross-entropy loss with fuzzy entropy, so borderline pixels are handled by degrees of membership rather than hard choices alone. Tested on the IBSR and OASIS benchmark datasets with U-Net and U-Net++ architectures, the trained model beat the cross-entropy baseline across performance metrics. The approach improved segmentation outcomes and made model predictions more reliable for neurological imaging work.
arxiv-2604-16790: Zhao and colleagues audit language models as judges of code items in software coding. Judges rank picks and guide patch selection where review or test coverage is unavailable. Repeated runs can disagree, small prompt edits swing outcomes, and equivalent tweaks elicit split verdicts. Across generation, repair and test generation, prompt biases shift preferences toward the favored option, even with unchanged code. That shift improves accuracy when the favored option matches gold but reduces it otherwise, sometimes changing rankings. The authors argue judge studies should track bias sensitivity alongside accuracy.
arxiv-2604-16990: Manchanda proves a factorization for the joint matrix built from gauge fixings and first-class constraints, via a Schur complement. Since the second-class part is invertible by definition, that part splits off from gauge fixing. In the algebra case, the result matches the Hamiltonian admissibility criterion with the Lagrangian completeness criterion.
arxiv-2604-17290: Garg, Geh, Israel, Millstein, Richardson, and Van den Broeck rethink how language models sample programs, a process that normally burns one costly generation per candidate. Their probabilistic programs of thought fold a model's next-token odds into a single generated program, compactly standing for exponentially many variants that can then be sampled cheaply. Across code and math benchmarks, the approach improved scores while needing fewer generations from the model.
arxiv-2604-17390: Toulatzis, Theodoridou, and Fudos present MESA, a method for restoring damaged ancient inscriptions that needs no training. It copies texture and stroke style from well-kept examples, picks the best match per layer, and weights layers by letter widths from character recognition. A mask limits new synthesis to damaged spots, leaving intact text alone. Tests favor MESA over prior methods, and the paper ends with a guide to picking a fix based on the examples at hand.
arxiv-2604-17490: Mohammed introduces joint exclusivity, a looser cousin of mutual exclusivity for non-negative random vectors. Mutual exclusivity caps the summed odds of positive results at one. Joint exclusivity only forbids all parts being positive at once. A vector with given marginals exists exactly when a simple sum condition holds, and such laws are fixed by their margins one dimension down. The paper splits total stop-loss premiums across smaller pools, builds a wrap-around case hitting the bound, and places the idea on a ladder between the two ends.
arxiv-2604-17890: Urdih and two colleagues catalogue ten cache-related smells in GitLab continuous integration and deployment pipelines, faults that hurt speed and reliability beyond the familiar missing-dependency case. Their tool CROSSER automatically detects seven of the ten, scoring an F1 of 0.98 on 82 mature projects. A survey of 228 mature open-source projects finds the smells widespread, with only 11 percent free of any, suggesting developers often miss higher-level caching features.
arxiv-2604-17990: Brisson and Lecampion model two hydraulic stimulation stages from April 2022 at Utah's FORGE geothermal test site, differing in fracturing fluid viscosity. Despite similar injection rates and pressures, seismic signals after shut-in differ between stages. The gel stage stays active for hours and reveals a planar fracture following viscosity-storage scaling, showing a tensile fracture where leak-off matters. The slickwater stage arrests immediately, fitting either a toughness- or leak-off-dominated regime or a dilatant shear fracture, confirmed in a coupled three-dimensional model.
arxiv-2604-18190: Goppelsroeder and Jensen propose MADDPG-K, a scalable method for training teams of cooperating or competing agents. Standard centralized critics grow with the number of agents, since each critic sees every observation and action. MADDPG-K instead limits each critic to the k nearest agents by Euclidean distance, keeping its input size fixed. Tests in the Multi-Particle Environment suite show competitive or better performance, faster cooperative convergence, and runtime that scales more gracefully.
arxiv-2604-18490: Magdy, Alwajih, El Mekki, El-Sayed, and Abdul-Mageed introduce LQM, a linguistically motivated quality metric for machine translation in diglossic languages such as Arabic. Standard metrics miss dialect and culture errors rooted in language variety, coverage, and pragmatic fit. LQM diagnoses errors across six levels, from sociolinguistics and pragmatics down to orthography and graphetics. A corpus of 3,850 sentences across seven Arabic dialects plus expert annotation of 6,113 error spans grounds the framework, which stays language-agnostic by design.
arxiv-2604-18690: Gupta and Sharma develop an account of transport and quantum interference in 3D disordered fermions with arbitrary pseudospin s. From a general short-range matrix disorder, they derive compact expressions for elastic lifetimes and ladder vertex corrections, including multiband effects. In the scalar limit, Drude conductivity depends on s and helicity, yet the correction is universal in size, matching conventional metals and Weyl fermions. Its sign follows the parity of twice s, putting half-integer cases in the symplectic class and integer cases in the orthogonal class.
arxiv-2604-18790: Lopez and six colleagues present EfficientPENet, a two branch network for real time depth completion from sparse LiDAR and RGB images. Existing methods reach high accuracy but rely on heavy backbones that block real time use on embedded hardware. EfficientPENet replaces the usual ResNet encoder with a modernized ConvNeXt backbone, adds sparsity invariant convolutions for the depth stream, and refines predictions with a convolutional spatial propagation network. On the KITTI benchmark it uses about 4 times fewer parameters and runs 23 times faster than BP-Net, while keeping competitive accuracy.
arxiv-2604-18890: Lokare and Coley-O'Rourke propose a strategy to stabilize bulk quantum orders in finite Rydberg atom arrays. Theoretical predictions for bulk phases often diverge from experiments on finite arrays because boundary effects are strong. Their scheme uses the ubiquitous disordered phase in Rydberg systems, driving boundaries into an unbiased set of states that depend on the bulk physics. Numerical demonstrations in one and two dimensional systems, on ordered and critical phases, show the protocol works.
arxiv-2604-19490: Cao and Huang construct a one-to-one correspondence between Verma basis vectors of a finite-dimensional irreducible representation of the symplectic Lie algebra sp4 and Kashiwara-Nakashima tableaux of sp4 with matching shape. The correspondence is natural in the highest weight. They also give a direct proof of the linear independence of the Verma vector system. The result links representation-theoretic bases with combinatorial tableaux for this Lie algebra.
arxiv-2604-19590: Dai, Ramadan, and Sharma study minimizers for the Cahn-Hilliard energy with the Flory-Huggins potential under strong anchoring, that is, Dirichlet boundary conditions. They work both in theory and by computer. Bifurcation phenomena emerge, driven by that rule, the transition layer thickness, and the system temperature. Computer runs estimate them by solving a gradient-flow equation, namely Allen-Cahn with that anchoring and random initial data. Varying layer thickness and warmth confirms the theory.
arxiv-2604-19690: Ulaş builds a multi-task machine learning tool that classifies eclipsing binaries by shape and estimates their physical traits from light curves at once. Random Forest and XGBoost models train on 845 of 995 well-studied systems across three shape groups, using 51 tailored features drawn from each folded light curve. 15 percent of systems were held back for testing before any training. On that held-out set, XGBoost scores strongly across the board, with the mass ratio weakest at 0.77 among the five measures.
arxiv-2604-19790: Wang and six colleagues present PrecisionDiff, an automated differential testing framework. It hunts precision-induced behavioral disagreements in large language models. Models now run under varied formats to meet efficiency and resource limits, from standard float formats like bfloat16 and float16 to quantized integer formats like int16 and int8. Small cross-format inconsistencies are hard to spot and often missed by standard tests. PrecisionDiff generates test inputs and compares outputs across formats to expose hidden divergences.
arxiv-2604-19990: Jaouadi and Ashhab tackle robust calibration of multi-qudit quantum gates, where higher-dimensional systems beat qubits in principle but suffer crowded spectra and weak controllability. Their hybrid method first designs high-fidelity control pulses for controlled-phase gates on two qutrits under a nominal model. Reinforcement learning then learns small residual corrections under static model mismatch, preserving gate quality across device variations. The learning stage complements rather than competes with optimal control, cutting sensitivity to parameter swings and making reinforcement learning a practical calibration ingredient.
arxiv-2604-20090: Zhang and eight colleagues introduce UL-XCoT, an efficient framework for cross-lingual chain-of-thought reasoning. Existing methods sample full trajectories across languages at high cost, and language-varying representations block direct comparison and pruning. UL-XCoT picks a small language set per query in a unified logic space, prunes weak reasoning paths during decoding, and aggregates survivors by voting. Tested on PolyMath in 18 languages and MMLU-ProX-Lite in 29, it matches prior accuracy while cutting decoding token cost by over 50 percent, with steadier low-resource gains.
arxiv-2604-20190: Habibpour and four colleagues introduce WildFireVQA, a large-scale benchmark for aerial wildfire monitoring pairing RGB imagery with radiometric thermal data. Each of 6,097 samples holds an RGB image, a color-mapped thermal view, and a radiometric thermal TIFF, with 34 questions per sample for 207,298 multiple-choice questions. Answers combine model generation with sensor-driven labeling, hand checks, and cross-frame agreement checks within and across frames. Tests show RGB remains strongest, while retrieved thermal context lifts stronger models, exposing the value and present limits of temperature-grounded reasoning.
arxiv-2604-20390: Brown proves two rules for the determinant of matrices made by joining the entries of two smaller matrices, building on Fayers's work on Specht modules. The rules cover Vandermonde determinants in many variables as sums of terms that split fully into simple factors, where each term is a Vandermonde determinant with fewer variables. As an application, he gives a plain and short proof that transfinite diameter multiplies across products of compact sets.
arxiv-2604-20890: Salarian offers a short guide to chosen topics in algebraic graph theory. He covers strongly regular graphs, Steiner systems, and automorphism groups. Notable graphs get full treatment: the Petersen graph, Paley graphs, Hamming graphs, and the Hoffman-Singleton graph. Symmetry and combinatorial structure are the focus throughout. Links to permutation groups run through the note. SageMath examples show how to compute automorphism groups and related invariants.
arxiv-2604-21090: Christo Zietsman studies the written prompts that steer AI agents, treating them as working rules that set an agent's task, limits, and quality standards. He builds a five-part test drawn from computability theory, proof theory, and Bayesian reasoning, then applies it to 34 public AGENTS.md files from GitHub. Over a third of file-model pairs fall short of structural completeness, with data classification and scoring rubrics most often missing, pointing to checks that software could run automatically.
arxiv-2604-21290: Anvitha Ramachandran, Dhruv Parikh, and Viktor Prasanna remove the main bottleneck in vision graph networks. Rebuilding the patch graph each layer eats 50 to 95 percent of convolution time on CPUs and GPUs. Their GraphLeap reformulation updates features with the previous layer's graph while building the next layer's graph at the same time, enabling concurrent construction and message passing. Light fine-tuning recovers any lost accuracy. A streaming FPGA design then hits up to 95.7 times CPU speed and more than 8 times GPU speed.
arxiv-2604-21790: Moore, Perez, and Krause build priors from real data for the galaxy bias parameter b_phi. It cannot be told apart from primordial non-Gaussianity in galaxy clustering data at leading order. The usual mass-function rule breaks down for real galaxy samples, biasing inferred numbers. Using CAMELS-SAM simulations plus separate-universe runs, they measure galaxy formation traits and b_phi across settings. They then condition on the stellar mass function or stellar-to-halo mass relation. Uncertainty in b_phi falls 88 percent and 97 percent.
arxiv-2604-22090: Mao proves that every non-degenerate triangle whose largest angle is strictly smaller than 135 degrees is diameter-Ramsey. A finite Euclidean set is diameter-Ramsey if, for every number of colors, some finite same-diameter witness exists. Every coloring of the witness contains a monochromatic congruent copy of the set. Together with the theorem of Corsten and Frankl that triangles with an angle larger than 135 degrees are not diameter-Ramsey, this gives the sharp classification. It covers the two open angular ranges on either side of 135 degrees.
arxiv-2604-22190: Zheng and four colleagues propose SAGA-ReID, rebuilding person identity from CLIP patch tokens aligned with text-space anchors. That design stresses spatially stable evidence while muting corrupted or absent regions, with no need for image descriptions. Controlled tests isolate aggregation under synthetic masking, where identity signal is absent, and real human distractors, where an overlapping person adds confusing signal. SAGA's edge over global pooling grows as occlusion increases in both settings. Benchmarks confirm steady gains over CLIP-ReID, up to +10.6 Rank-1 on occluded benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-22290: Wachter, Murgul and Heizmann build a transformer model that converts performed MIDI, a digital record of played notes, into clean musical notation using known beat positions. Their system aligns performance and score times before quantisation, uses a specialised MIDI tokenizer, and adapts a T5-style transformer, with augmentations such as transposition and timing jitter for robustness. On the ASAP dataset it scored 97.3 percent for note onsets and about 83 percent for note values, and it generalised to time signatures unseen in training.
arxiv-2604-22590: Gnann, Lienstromberg, and Nik study strong solutions of a thin-film equation for fluids that thin under shear, where the film meets a surface at a nonzero contact angle. Earlier work had built only weak solutions, leaving behavior near the vanishing film height unclear. By perturbing a linear profile and passing a time-discretized variational problem to its limit, they prove existence and stability of such solutions.
arxiv-2604-23090: Talukder, Mridul, and Seneviratne study auto ontology building from raw text, using domain-set insurance contracts as a set test case. A single-agent baseline reveals failures including poor design pattern fit, extra structure, and weak repeat repair. Their multi-agent setup splits building into four artifact roles: Domain Expert, Manager, Coder, and Quality Assurer. The multi-agent approach greatly improves structural quality and slightly enhances query use, driven mainly by front-loaded planning.
arxiv-2604-23190: Huang and six colleagues automate environment setup for repository-level coding tasks, a bottleneck that slows autonomous code agents. Current tools lean on preset artifacts or cover only some languages, limiting them on diverse real repos. Their framework, RAT, runs a multi-stage pipeline with language-aware abstraction, image setup, special config tools, and a sandbox, working across languages on any repo. They also build RATBench for testing, and RAT beats strong baselines by 36.1 percent on environment setup success on average.
arxiv-2604-23290: Totakura and three colleagues test active learning with real crowd-sourced annotations instead of simulated oracles. Standard setups assume labelers never err, but crowd workers can give wrong labels or refuse to label at all. Collecting annotations on three benchmark text datasets through a crowd platform, they study eight common active learning techniques with deep neural networks. Their results show how each technique fares under genuine annotation noise and refusal, offering guidance for deploying deep active learning in real settings.
arxiv-2604-23490: Liu and colleagues make quantum fully homomorphic encryption far cheaper, so arbitrary quantum computations can run on encrypted data without exposing it. Their modular arithmetic program tracks decryption sums with far fewer states than the generic approach, shrinking the quantum gadget from quadratic to near-linear size. All quantum work moves to the server, leaving the client fully classical, and a layered key design removes a circular-security worry.
arxiv-2604-23690: Yurkov pins down all pairs of non-linear maps that preserve a homogeneous polynomial. The value stays the same when inputs pass through the maps. He covers every polynomial in zero characteristic, and those meeting a stated condition in positive characteristic. The result extends classical work on linear maps preserving the determinant and the immanant. He applies it in full to the Cullis determinant for rectangular matrix shapes.
arxiv-2604-24890: Golaszewski and team test C2PA security independently. C2PA aims to give verifiable provenance for digital content. Generative AI now makes fake media easy to create. Their study is the first formal analysis of C2PA's core protocols. They find current specs fail to meet claimed security goals. They also fail extra goals needed for trustworthy deployment. C2PA may thus mislead users, platforms and policymakers if used too soon. It should not yet be trusted for high-stakes journalism or legal evidence.
arxiv-2604-24990: Spitznagel and Keuper review Neural Cellular Automata and provide code. Wolfram argued in 2003 that simple recursive cellular programs could replace equation-based models for modeling complex systems. Recent work pairs Wolfram's ideas with tunable neural networks that learn complex update rules from data. They can model complex, self-organizing systems. The paper unifies past work in a modular framework, with a reference implementation in NCAtorch.
arxiv-2604-25190: Rodríguez-Flores and three colleagues propose a secure approach to conformance checking, the process-mining task of finding discrepancies between a process model and an event log. Normally both model and log sit open to the analyst. But a log owner may wish to protect sensitive entries while still checking conformance against another party's model. Their method combines the well-known token-based replay algorithm with homomorphic encryption, so checking proceeds without exposing protected log contents. An evaluation on a synthetic log shows the technique is practical.
arxiv-2604-25490: Generet and five colleagues reassess scale changes as a gauge of missing higher orders in jet data. Jet data probe QCD well, suiting exact tests. While work reaches next-to-next-to-leading order accuracy, doubts stay crucial. They reassess it with NNLO work plus small-radius resummation to NNLL accuracy. They find NNLL resummation can affect scale doubt and shift the central cross section a lot for some scale choices. They conclude scale changes can badly miss higher-order impact, and missing-order guesses from them are shaky.
arxiv-2604-26190: Konstantinovsky and Yaari introduce Flashback, a reversible way to break strings into tokens. Working inward from both ends of a sentinel-marked input, it strips matching outer runs and stores each pair as one token. The process runs in linear time and space both ways. Its central theorem pairs runs from the outside in, fixing the token count exactly. From that pairing come several facts: a kernel of at most two symbols, palindromes characterized by symmetric run counts, and the property that altering one run length touches only one token.
arxiv-2604-26290: Tiwari and three colleagues ran high-resolution simulations of forced compressible turbulence across Mach numbers up to 3. On a 1024-cubed grid with a GPU solver, they tracked how energy moves between swirling and squeezing motions as speed rises. The swirling spectrum steepened toward Burgers scaling while the squeezing spectrum flattened, driven by transfer from swirling to squeezing modes. Injection rates hinged on forcing type, not Mach number, while dissipation shifted toward squeezing modes.
arxiv-2604-26490: Białożyt, Bysiewicz, and Denkowski studied how to reach singularities of the medial axis, the points with more than one nearest point in a closed set. They characterized points where the closure of the medial axis meets the set itself, assuming definability in a polynomially bounded structure. A new notion of directional curvature in chosen camber directions tames the geometry without any smoothness requirement. The criterion completes the plane case and extends earlier superquadraticity work to any codimension.
arxiv-2604-26690: Béchaz, Fanizza, Marozzi, and Medeiros Silva compute relativistic effects on cosmic redshift drift to second order in perturbation theory, the first such calculation. With light-cone coordinates that ease light travel in a lumpy, uneven universe, they show redshift-space distortion appears only at second order, absent among linear perturbations. They derive the bispectrum of leading perturbative parts on sub-Hubble scales, with numerical checks. At low redshift and large momenta, bispectrum bends grow stronger than the squared power spectrum.
arxiv-2604-26790: Pontin, Deplano, Marino, and Marin show optical squeezing below shot noise from a cavity field coupled to two motional modes of a floating speck. Both modes cool to levels well below one. Heterodyne detection of cavity signal wobbles resolves the full spread matrix and maps squeezed regions across phase and frequency. In the strong-coupling regime, mechanical modes merge with the optical mode, and squeezing appears across 70 to 95 kilohertz with variance 2 percent below vacuum fluctuations. This establishes floating optics for multi-mode quantum links.
arxiv-2604-26890: Murphy and four colleagues split foregrounds from the 21-centimetre hydrogen signal in mock single-dish intensity-mapping data. Gibbs sampling plus Gaussian constrained realisation draws posterior samples for over 2 million model parameters, getting back the one-dimensional hydrogen power spectrum within statistical error. Though the parameter count is huge, sampling runs under 30 seconds per round. The setup also copes with flagged frequency channels, filling gaps with statistically sound model realisations, and gets the spectrum within two sigma of truth under strong glare.
arxiv-2604-26990: Chauhan and Nur enter SemEval-2026 Task 13 on telling human-written code from machine-generated code. The task has two subtasks: binary detection and attribution across 10 model families. For detection they fine-tune UniXcoder-base with a method that promotes generator-invariant codes, mixing structure prefixes and token dropout. The system scores 0.993 macro F1 on validation and lower on test data spanning languages and domains. For the second task, severe class imbalance wrecks fine-tuning, but a class-weighted extension lifts macro F1 about fourfold, confirming it needs imbalance-aware training.
arxiv-2604-27290: Wafi, de Oliveira, and Sontag settle a long-standing question about antithetic feedback controllers, the synthetic-biology tools that regulate protein production. They prove every solution stays bounded, even when the closed-loop resting point is unstable, by treating the controller far from that point as steady negative feedback that blocks runaway growth. Earlier attempts using energy-like Lyapunov functions had failed, and the new argument may transfer to other control settings.
arxiv-2604-27690: Hirotaka Yoneda and Masataka Yoneda study online coloring of graphs with large odd girth. The best prior method, from Kierstead in 1998, uses on the order of square-root-of-n colors and needs odd girth of at least 7. The authors show that for any small positive exponent, graphs with large odd girth can be deterministically colored online with on the order of n-to-that-exponent colors. Their result pushes online coloring far beyond the square-root bound for graphs of large odd girth.
arxiv-2604-27790: Grossman and five colleagues study how generative AI disrupts web search, comparing Google, AI Overviews, and Gemini Flash 2.5 on 11,500 queries. AI Overviews appear for 51.5 percent of typical queries, displayed above plain results, with touchy questions often raising one. Found sources differ sharply across engines: classic search favors popular government and school sites, while AI engines favor Google-owned content. Sites blocking Google's AI crawler appear less often in AI Overviews, which prove less steady across repeat runs and less robust to small query edits.
arxiv-2604-28190: Yang and colleagues show Fréchet distance, long deemed impractical as a training objective, can be optimised in representation space. Their FD-loss decouples the population size used to estimate the distance from the batch size used for gradients. Post-training with FD-loss improves visual quality across representation spaces, turns multi-step generators into strong single-pass generators without distillation or adversarial training, and motivates a multi-representation metric, since FID can misrank quality.
arxiv-2605-00090:
Martijn Janse and six co-authors demonstrate levitation of a ferromagnetic microsphere on a chip, at room temperature. Levitated microscopic objects in vacuum are prized for sensing and for macroscopic quantum physics, since they are so well isolated. Magnetic levitation covers many particle sizes and avoids hot trapping beams and electric field noise, but older magnetic schemes need bulky coils or magnets, low vibration frequencies, or cryogenic cooling.

Their platform stably levitates a nanogram sphere only micrometers across, on a scalable, tunable chip. Its rocking modes vibrate at frequencies above ten kilohertz, far stiffer than earlier magnetic traps. The authors point to further shrinking and coupling to solid-state spin qubits as a path toward cooling such a particle to its quantum ground state, besides uses in precision sensing.
arxiv-2605-00490:
Michal Valko and Milos Hauskrecht improve conditional anomaly detection, the search for data points that are odd relative to their context. In the conditional version, a pattern counts as anomalous only on a subset of attributes, judged against the values of the rest. Instance-based methods for this task lean hard on a distance metric, since the nearest examples decide what counts as normal here.

The authors study and devise a metric learning method that tunes the distance itself to reflect the conditional anomaly pattern as well as possible. Learning the metric, rather than accepting a default one, targets exactly the comparisons the detector will make. The paper's contribution is methodological: it shows how supervised metric learning can be adapted to conditional anomalies, where what 'near' should mean changes with context. That adaptation aims to lift the accuracy of a whole family of instance-based detectors.
arxiv-2605-00890:
Sergio D. Sierra M., Monica Sinha, Marcela Múnera, and Carlos A. Cifuentes evaluate models that classify posture and walker use from body skeleton data, aiming to make walker-assisted gait safer for older adults. Falls in this group cause severe injury and loss of independence. The team compares a geometric method, XGBoost, a support vector machine, and several deep learning designs on tasks for walker choice, standing versus sitting, and posture.

Geometric and XGBoost methods performed best overall. XGBoost reached near-perfect training accuracy on the binary tasks, and the geometric approach led on an eight-posture task, while deep models also scored strongly on binary tasks. The authors argue such classification can improve human-robot interaction in smart walkers and help prevent falls.
arxiv-2605-00990:
Ioanna Koutsouridou and seven co-authors use the NEFERTITI galaxy formation model to link the earliest galaxies to the assembly of the Milky Way. The model is coupled to about thirty high-resolution dark-matter simulations of Milky Way analogues, with local constraints and resolution down to minihaloes hosting the first stars. Ionization and chemical enrichment are tracked self-consistently and unevenly across space.

First star formation begins very early, peaks at an intermediate epoch, and persists to later times, producing small early systems. Present-day descendants span a huge range in iron abundance. Most stellar mass formed in place, but the accreted component dominates among the most metal-poor stars and is built mainly by a few massive destroyed dwarfs. The model also matches metal-poor Milky Way stars and a distant candidate system.
arxiv-2605-01690:
Hansol Lee and six co-authors retest a celebrated regularity in learning science: that students differ hugely in where they start but barely in how fast they learn. The claim, drawn from fits of a mixed-effects practice model across many course data sets, now feeds real conclusions about learners.

The team refit the same model on the same data under two choices of which practice records count: more of each student's work on a skill, or less. Starting-point variation holds steady across the choices. Learning-rate variation does not: it roughly doubles under one choice and grows several-fold under the other. Same model, same data, different answer, set only by an inclusion decision. The authors argue such sensitivity belongs at the center of any report that turns model estimates into claims about students.
arxiv-2605-01990:
Lázaro Sales and colleagues use fast radio bursts to estimate how much ordinary matter, in the form of baryons, fills the universe. The bursts are delayed as their signals pass through gas, and that delay tracks the gas along the path. The team uses 130 well-located bursts and rebuilds the expansion history from cosmic chronometer data with a neural network, without assuming a fixed model.

In a joint fit, they also estimate the gas contribution from each burst's host galaxy. The real data give a baryon density close to values from other methods, with a stated uncertainty near four percent. A mock catalogue test returns a similar value with tighter error, checking the method.
arxiv-2605-02190:
James Bagrow argues that Kolmogorov-Arnold networks need a curvature penalty to stay readable. These networks build functions from learnable one-variable activations, which gives accuracy and interpretability. In practice, well-fitting activations often develop sharp, high-curvature wiggles that are hard to read, and standard penalties do not stop them.

Bagrow derives a curvature penalty that does not depend on the chosen basis. Penalised models keep accuracy while reaching much smoother activations. By accounting for how composition shapes curvature, he proves an upper bound on the full model's curvature in terms of the penalty. That bound motivates richer penalty forms. The result targets the accuracy-interpretability trade-off that limits scientific machine learning.
arxiv-2605-02590:
Yogesh Shelke, Anpuj Nair S, and Hanumantha Rao Vutukuri study how the shape of tiny self-propelled rods controls the patterns a whole group forms. Shape effects are well known in still systems, but active rods move on their own. The team uses light-driven rods in experiments, matched with simulations, and varies rod length ratio and crowding.

As those knobs turn, the group shifts through distinct states: random active motion, swarming, turbulent flow, flocking, large clusters, and jamming. A state diagram sums up which conditions give which behavior, and analyses show sharp changes in number fluctuations across states. Because the system is minimal, physical effects can be separated from biological ones. The findings offer design rules for programmable active materials and a clean parallel to bacterial swarms.
arxiv-2605-02690:
Yash Madhwal and seven co-authors automate the tuning of Hyperledger Fabric, a blockchain platform whose speed depends on many interacting settings. Manual tuning is hard, and each test is noisy, so the team treats benchmarking as a black-box optimization problem. Their pipeline deploys a candidate setup, measures its throughput, and feeds the result back to the optimizer.

The search space, drawn from Fabric's own configuration files, has hundreds of dimensions, so dimension reduction is paired with Bayesian optimization. Sixteen combined variants plus random search were tried on a cloud testbed. The best pairing improved throughput by a clear margin over the starting setup, with a second method close behind. Measurement noise, the authors warn, must be kept in mind when reading such gains.
arxiv-2605-02890:
Umberto D'Alesio, Carlo Flore, and Marco Zaccheddu compute a spin effect planned for measurement at the future Electron-Ion Collider. The Collins asymmetry tracks how a quark's transverse spin shapes the direction of pions produced inside a jet. Past work used polarized proton-proton scattering; polarized lepton-proton collisions offer a cleaner, simpler route to the same physics.

Using a simplified momentum-dependent approach, the authors take the needed spin and fragmentation functions from earlier scattering and annihilation data. They compute asymmetries in the collider's range, at leading order and with a correction for near-real photon exchange. That correction matters across the range but does not overturn the dominance of quark-started channels, leaving gluons marginal. Cleaner access to the transversity distribution, including its sea-quark part, is the payoff.
arxiv-2605-03090:
Noman Bashir, Rob Sherwood, Le Xie, and Minlan Yu make the case for designing AI data centers and power grids together, not apart. Grids have long relied on millions of small users whose demands average out to a smooth total.

One large training campus breaks that pattern, drawing city-scale power that can swing by hundreds of megawatts in seconds with a single job. The authors contrast the cultures and incentives of the two sectors, show why coordination is hard, and list joint research needs in planning, control, protocols, and markets for a reliable AI future.
arxiv-2605-03190:
Zijian He, Adrian Sampson, Yiying Zhang, and Zhiyuan Guo present VDCores, a new way to program modern GPUs whose special units run out of step. Current software still packs work into single large kernels, which leaves those asynchronous units idle much of the time.

VDCores treats each unit as an isolated virtual core and splits work into small operations linked by dependencies. Overlap of memory and compute then happens automatically when resources are ready. On four language model workloads across three GPU types, decoding sped up by about a quarter on average, and kernel writing effort fell sharply. Code is open source.
arxiv-2605-03490:
Sapna Sachan, Amulya Kumar Mahto, and Prashant Wagambar Patil propose an orientation-aware system that classifies brain tumors across MRI sources without target labels. Scanners and protocols differ by hospital, expert labels are scarce, and those shifts badly hurt model generalization in real clinics.

Slices are first sorted into axial, sagittal, and coronal views, then handled by view-specific networks. A slice-wise adaptation strategy transfers knowledge from multi-modal source scans to post-contrast target scans, using discrepancy alignment plus pseudo-label guidance to keep classes distinct. Experiments show improved target performance over prior approaches, crediting the orientation split and guided adaptation.
arxiv-2605-03590:
Awobade and two colleagues benchmark speech recognition for African languages under real-world conditions. Large speech models handle high-resource languages well, but African languages stay underrepresented in benchmarks, which limits practical use where it matters most. Earlier benchmarks lacked realistic noise and fine-grained domain tests. AfriVox-v2 adds unscripted, in-the-wild audio for every supported language and grades accuracy across ten sectors, from government and finance to health and farming, with targeted tests on numbers and names.

The benchmark trials recent speech models, including Sahara-v2 and Gemini 3 Flash alongside Omnilingual CTC systems. Results expose a wide generalization gap in noisy, specialized African settings, showing that headline scores from clean tests flatter current models. For developers building localized voice tools, AfriVox-v2 gives a realistic blueprint of where models actually fail.
arxiv-2605-03690:
Filip Kronström and four co-authors build hierarchy-aware embeddings of knowledge graphs using graph neural networks enriched with meaning from ontologies. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked triples, but flat embeddings can ignore the class hierarchies that organize a domain. Their test application is predicting what gene deletions do to yeast.

Working with the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, they combine low-dimensional box embeddings with graph networks to predict cell growth for double gene knockouts. Cross-validated predictions beat baselines, and adding a semantic loss that aligns embeddings with ontology structure lifted accuracy further. The box embeddings also serve to judge revisions of a knowledge graph when no task of that kind is present.
arxiv-2605-04390:
Mu-Lin Li studies families of complex manifolds, where a whole collection of geometric spaces varies smoothly over a surface that serves as the parameter space. The manifolds are projective and non-uniruled, a restriction that rules out certain sweeping rational curves.

Suppose two such families agree point by point, in that the space over each parameter is isomorphic in both families. Li proves there is a large open set of parameters over which the families are locally isomorphic, meaning they match in whole neighbourhoods, not just at single points. The result partly answers a question posed by Wehler about when pointwise agreement forces local agreement.
arxiv-2605-04590:
Zishen Qu and seven co-authors rethink text-guided image segmentation, where a user names an object in words and the system outlines it. Borrowing features from diffusion image generators has become popular, but those models' generate-from-noise nature actively harms a task that needs precise discrimination.

Their framework instead learns a direct mapping from image to mask using rectified flow, a method that straightens the path between input and output. That removes the need to tune noise steps and improves accuracy, especially on categories never seen in training. Added label refinement and a one-step sampling strategy raise accuracy further while keeping inference fast.
arxiv-2605-04690:
Jan Rovirosa and Jesse Schmolze build a method for learning time-varying Markov dynamics, where a system's transition rules themselves drift, using financial time series as the testbed. Classical Markov operators are transparent and theoretically grounded, but estimating them by counting fails at fine resolution because the data become too sparse.

Their framework uses a neural network purely as a parameterisation engine. Its outputs are forced into the form of explicit, time-varying transition matrices. That preserves full interpretability of the learned dynamics. The learned operators capture regime shifts in the financial data. A stripped-down ablation that ignores state collapses exactly to no variation. That contrast confirms the structure is doing real work.
arxiv-2605-05090:
Quintin Pope and three co-authors present a pipeline for finding unexpected side effects when a language model is changed by training or editing.
