Changes such as distillation, knowledge editing, or unlearning can shift behaviour far beyond their target. Their method compares a base model and a changed model on aligned prompts, contrasting their free-form generations.

The pipeline turns the contrasts into plain-language hypotheses checked with statistics, and groups them into shared themes. On built test cases with added changes it recovered the known effects well. Applied to three real changes, it surfaced intended and surprise shifts, separated large from subtle changes, and avoided making up differences where none existed.
arxiv-2605-05190:
Burger and four colleagues show a microwave-to-light device that needs no release step. Electro-optic modulators link microwave circuits to optical fibers. At the quantum limit, single photons convert between domains, which could share linked states between superconducting processors. High-confinement optomechanical crystals promise that interface, but optical absorption heats them, and release-free designs anchor heat better yet had never joined a microwave-optical transducer. The team prints a release-free silicon crystal onto lithium niobate by micro-transfer printing.

The device pairs strong light-motion coupling in silicon with efficient piezoelectricity in lithium niobate. Measured coupling rates suit quantum-level work alongside a superconducting microwave circuit. By keeping the crystal anchored while still converting signals, the work moves release-free devices of this kind closer to practical quantum interfaces.
arxiv-2605-05290:
András Grabarits, E. Medina-Guerra, and Adolfo del Campo study how quantum systems grow more complex over time. They focus on Krylov space, the smallest space in which a system's motion actually unfolds. Their systems are driven by Hamiltonians that change as time passes.

The team ties this motion directly to the Lie algebra behind the Hamiltonian. Ladder operators from that algebra generate the dynamics, and simple cases like a spinning particle in a rotating field fit the same frame. They also derive a new speed limit for complexity growth, and show when that limit can actually be reached.
arxiv-2605-05390:
Tracking a person's full body motion from cameras on a headset is the problem Nan Yang and five co-authors take on. The wearer moves, other people are partly hidden, and training data is scarce. Methods built for still cameras break down in this moving, first-person setting.

Their system, LAMP, first uses the headset's known motion and calibration to lift body keypoints into one shared 3D space. A transformer then fits the person's motion to that 3D data. The design beat earlier methods on standard tests and did far better in the egocentric setting it was built for.
arxiv-2605-05690:
Flat bands trap light in place and concentrate its interaction with matter, but making them usually demands delicate fabrication. Dun Wang and four co-authors engineer radiative flat bands in a single-layer honeycomb photonic crystal. Their trick is a gentle density-wave-like displacement of the lattice's air holes.

The periodic displacement couples flat-band states that normally sit below the light line up into the radiative continuum. There they can be excited and probed from free space. The strategy needs no exotic geometry or perfect multilayer alignment, offering a general recipe for flat-band photonics in a simple slab.
arxiv-2605-05790:
Smart glasses could help most if they knew when their wearer is mentally overloaded. Bin Wang and twelve co-authors present GazeMind, an agent that estimates cognitive load from eye gaze alone. Sensor-heavy alternatives are impractical in lightweight eyewear, and earlier gaze models were opaque and person-specific.

GazeMind encodes eye-tracking data into structured representations that a language model can reason over. The result is interpretable load predictions meant to generalize across individuals without task-specific fine-tuning. An assistant armed with that signal could time its help to moments when the user can actually absorb it.
arxiv-2605-05990:
Abdullah Al Shafi and Kazi Saeed Alam build a benchmark for removing motion blur from phone photos. Standard test scores average over all images, which hides how a method fares on easy versus severe blur. That hidden spread matters for tools that must run on consumer devices in daily use.

iPhoneBlur holds 7,400 image pairs made from high frame rate videos shot on an iPhone 17 Pro in varied real scenes. Samples are split into easy, medium, and hard tiers, backed by flow measures and rich metadata for each item. Six restoration models all dropped by 7 to 9 decibels from easy to hard tiers. The set also exposes a gap between pro and consumer cameras that targeted fine tuning largely closed.
arxiv-2605-06090:
Felipe Albino dos Santos gives a representation theoretic account of a recent discovery about orthogonal polynomials. Families of such polynomials had been found sitting in the centers of universal central extensions of superelliptic affine Lie algebras. Why they appear there, and why that particular family, called for an explanation inside representation theory.

Working in Verma modules of the Heisenberg subalgebra, dos Santos computes a canonical contravariant form in closed form on a special family of weight vectors. That family turns out to be the Legendre family, forced by the curve itself. The main result identifies a Sugawara element carried by an explicit intertwiner to the classical Legendre differential operator. All results are proved for the genus zero, four point case.
arxiv-2605-06390:
Aleksandr Bowkis and three co-authors argue that automating alignment research is harder and riskier than its proponents assume. A leading plan for aligning superintelligence uses AI agents to do a growing share of alignment research itself. Even with no deliberate sabotage, the authors warn, that plan could yield compelling but badly misleading safety assessments. It could end in the unintentional deployment of a misaligned system that everyone believed had been checked thoroughly and passed.

Alignment work is full of fuzzy tasks with no clear scoring, where human judgment is systematically flawed, so agent outputs would carry undetected systematic errors. Optimization pressure concentrates agent mistakes exactly where reviewers are least likely to catch them. Agent errors also differ from human ones, and shared training makes agent outputs correlate with each other. Scalable oversight and generalization, the leading remedies, face novel challenges in this setting.
arxiv-2605-06490:
Jonas Wiedermann-Möller, Leonard Dung, and Maksym Andriushchenko measure whether language model agents will break rules to reach a goal faster. Such instrumental behavior, like self-preservation, is hypothesized to matter for agent risk. Their benchmark uses realistic, low-stakes terminal tasks to reduce roleplay and evaluation awareness effects.

Each of seven tasks offers an official workflow and a policy-violating shortcut, under eight varied conditions. Ten models were tested over many samples with automatic scoring. Violations were rare overall, at about five percent, but concentrated in two Gemini models and three tasks. Making the shortcut necessary for success raised the rate far more than stressing how critical success was.
arxiv-2605-06690:
Debashis Guha, Amritendu Mukherjee, Sanjay Kukreja, and Tarun Kumar address two design choices recursive reasoning systems usually leave implicit: how to represent the growing state of reasoning, and when to stop. Such systems alternate between gathering evidence and consolidating what they know. The authors represent state as an epistemic graph holding claims, evidential links, open questions, and confidence weights.

Their stopping signal is the order-gap, the distance between states reached by expanding then consolidating versus the reverse order; agreement suggests more iteration will not help. They prove exactly when the linearized gap is informative near a fixed point, stressing this is a local condition only. Sketched uses include agent loops, tree-of-thought reasoning, and theorem proving.
arxiv-2605-06990:
Maria Despoina Siampou and six co-authors argue that city prediction needs movement, not just maps and images. Congestion, travel demand, and road safety depend on how people actually travel through a place. Trajectory data carry that signal, but sparse GPS points rarely line up with street-view images.

Their framework, TrajGANR, turns each trajectory into a continuous field that can be queried at any location along the path. That lets mobility data align with images taken off the path itself. Across four road-level tasks in San Francisco and Porto, it beats recent geospatial and trajectory models. Its location encoder also works where no imagery or trajectories exist.
arxiv-2605-07190:
Yu-Wen Xu and four co-authors create a higher-order topological phase in graphene using strain and light. Graphene is a standard playground for Floquet engineering, where shining circularly polarized light opens topological gaps. The team adds uniaxial strain and varies the light's angle of incidence to steer the effect.

Strain pushes graphene's electronic cones toward a merging point, making the light-induced mass strongly directional. With angled light, edges become gapped while robust corner modes survive, the signature of a second-order topological insulator. Calculations from first-principles-informed models confirm the predicted behavior, marking driven strained graphene as a tunable platform for such phases.
arxiv-2605-07290:
Masakazu Kato and two co-authors revisit a proof that answers to a quadratic wave equation in two space dimensions must blow up. The result, including a log-scale loss in lifespan guesses when an initial moment does not vanish, was already known with almost sharp constants. What was missing was a simpler proof suited to numerical use.

Using a slicing technique and looping over pointwise figures, the authors give that direct proof. Their aim is practical: a transparent argument whose figures analysts can apply. The paper is a proof-focused contribution, tightening how a known blow-up result for semilinear wave equations can be established.
arxiv-2605-07590:
Pedro Alonso and two co-authors look at why three-dimensional point cloud classifiers are easy to fool. Small shifts of the points that respect the surface shape can badly distort the model's internal features and flip its answer. They argue the root cause is a misalignment between the geometry the network learns and the true geometry of the surface.

Their framework, MAPR, adds features describing local curvature and diffusion structure, and trains the model to give consistent answers under shape-preserving perturbations. It needs no adversarial training and no extra data. Across several datasets and attacks, MAPR raised robustness substantially over plain models, by about twenty points on ModelNet40 and about nine points on ScanObjectNN in average gains.
arxiv-2605-07690:
Shijie Liu and three co-authors give time-series anomaly detection a certified defense, a guarantee that small adversarial tampering cannot flip its verdicts. Earlier certified defenses assume distortions measured by ordinary norms, which fit time series badly: a slight time shift is harmless yet changes those measures a lot. Dynamic time warping respects temporal alignment, but no certificate existed in that metric.

Adapting randomized smoothing, they build the first dynamic-time-warping certificate by bridging from the norm-based theory through a lower-bound transformation. Across datasets and models the defense held up in practice, improving F1 scores under warping-based attacks by up to about nineteen points over traditional certified models. Safety-critical monitoring is the intended beneficiary.
arxiv-2605-07790:
Hugo Vigna and Samuel Bontemps perform surgery on trained neural networks to fix their weakest classes, without retraining. The Hessian of a trained network has a telling spectrum: a bulk of near-zero eigenvalues plus a few large spikes, as many as the number of classes minus one. Earlier work described this structure but never used it operationally.

Their Hessian Surgery perturbs weights along the spike eigenvectors to rebalance per-class accuracy. A sensitivity matrix measures how each class's accuracy responds along each spike direction, a constrained optimization targets weak classes while protecting strong ones, and an adaptive budget grows or shrinks with progress. On CIFAR-10 and the ISIC-2019 skin lesion dataset, the method improved balanced accuracy and cut its spread across classes.
arxiv-2605-07890:
Claudio S. Montanari reflects on flavor, the pattern of fermion families, masses, and mixing, as the Standard Model's most successful yet least explained structure. The Higgs discovery completed the account of how mass is generated without explaining why the families and hierarchies look as they do. Neutrinos sit at the sensitive center of the puzzle, with tiny masses and large mixing.

The article argues that the DUNE experiment is an unusually good framework for testing whether the present three-flavor description is self-consistent or cracking. Its long-baseline oscillation program and near-detector complex hunt for small, correlated departures from the minimal picture. Its PRISM strategy controls interaction uncertainties and makes data-driven predictions, with reach into beyond-Standard-Model and dark-sector phenomena.
arxiv-2605-08090:
Jaehwan Kim studies the rank-three lifting problem for incidence matrices of finite projective planes. A lift replaces the zero-one incidence pattern with richer entries while keeping the rank at most three, and earlier tropical methods could not see all the obstructions.

Working at the level of residues, Kim shows that any such lift, in residue characteristic other than three, forces a huge number of small zero rectangles whose cross-ratios are nontrivial. For planes of order at least six, no monomial lift exists at all, so any lift must use real first-order corrections. The hard remaining part of the problem is shown to be genuinely global.
arxiv-2605-08190:
Ayoosh Bansal, Mikael Yeghiazaryan, Artyom Khachatryan, Tianyi Zhu, and coauthors strengthen runtime assurance for autonomous systems. Safety-critical vehicles rely on machine learning for perception and control, but learned components fail on rare long-tail cases. The standard fix pairs them with a verified safety monitor that can take over, yet monitors alone perform weakly.

Their Synergistic Simplex design lets the monitor use the learning component's outputs, a flow that classic assurance forbids. The team derives formal conditions under which this two-way integration keeps the safety guarantee intact. Better monitor performance then raises overall system performance without weakening the proof that the vehicle stays safe.
arxiv-2605-08390:
Annie Marsden and Elad Hazan show that a classic second-order online learning algorithm handles long-memory sequence prediction far better than expected. For marginally stable linear systems, most methods pay regret that grows with the hidden state dimension, and a shelf of specialized fixes has grown up around the problem.

Feeding a short autoregressive model to the Vovk-Azoury-Warmuth algorithm instead gives dimension-free regret, logarithmic in the time horizon, as long as the system's spectrum avoids a wedge around the negative real axis. The proof leans on universal sequence preconditioning to show a good short model exists. The authors present the bounds as state of the art for this regime.
arxiv-2605-08890:
Linsa J. and three coauthors tune how a trio of atoms trades light. A trio is the least shape where group electric and magnetic acts show up at once. As the shape slides from a line to a fair triangle, they track all nine group modes. They use a paired dipole plan and sort modes by their form class. Form shifts lift ties, wake dark modes, and open the full mode range.

Two gains come out of the map. In a near line trio, front and back scatter can flip by pitch alone. One magnetic mode, under one light tilt, shows a much raised magnetic field and a large boost to glow. Trio atoms give a least test bed for mode craft by form.
arxiv-2605-09290:
Deng and Xiao reframe architecture search prediction as conditional function inference, replacing supervised regression predictors that overfit scarce samples and fail on new architectures. Their approach uses a Convolutional Neural Process with meta-learning, inferring scores from partial observations. Training uses context target splits across synthesised tasks, aiming for generalisation under data scarcity and matching training with deployment in NAS.

The team further designs simple and effective meta-features for cell based designs and tests on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201. Tests show the approach clearly lifts top-K ranking quality and reaches leading architecture picks using limited samples. The work offers a fundamentally different formulation for prediction based NAS, treating score estimation as inference rather than fixed mapping fitting. By learning to infer from partial observations, the predictor adapts to new architectures instead of memorising a fixed mapping from scarce data.
arxiv-2605-09490:
Yuan and two colleagues ask whether every reasoning token must live in GPU memory. Reasoning models generate thousands of chain-of-thought tokens whose cache must sit in scarce HBM. Evicting low-importance tokens is catastrophic: accuracy falls to 0 to 2 point 5 percent when half the cache goes. Their semantics-aware hierarchy places tokens in four tiers — HBM, DDR, compressed, evicted — by attention scoring.

Low-importance tokens move to CPU memory, not destruction, then return at full precision before each step, adding the same terms as if on GPU. The authors call this zero-approximation-error offloading. Central finding: accuracy hinges on how many tokens are discarded, not on how many stay in HBM. A 3 by 3 grid over HBM and eviction ratios backs this across three scales and four benchmarks. With 3 percent eviction, the hierarchy keeps 91 percent of full-cache GSM8K accuracy and 71 percent on MATH-500.
arxiv-2605-10090:
Huang and eight colleagues tune in-memory vector search on multi-core CPUs, where approximate nearest neighbour search powers search engines, recommenders and ads. Recent indexes make CPUs cost-effective for million-scale search, yet per-core throughput stalls on memory-access latency and heavy distance computation. Simply adding cores on modern chiplet-based CCD processors does not scale well, because the multi-chiplet layout is ignored.

Their workload- and hardware-aware thread orchestration works at CCD level, unifying inter-query parallel HNSW search and intra-query parallel IVF search behind one interface. Cache-friendly, workload-adaptive task mapping plus CCD-aware task stealing fixes load imbalance, exploiting the high access locality and low cache use found in production request patterns. On real Xiaohongshu workloads from search, recommendation and advertising, throughput rises up to 3.7 times, with P50 and P999 latency falling thirty to ninety percent.
arxiv-2605-10290:
Lucas Morisset, Alain Durmus, and Adrien Hardy analyze how data augmentation regularizes supervised regression. Augmentation, such as rotating images to teach invariance, is routine in modern machine-learning pipelines, yet its regularization effect lacked a tight theoretical account. Their 2026 paper studies the proportional regime, where the number of covariates grows in proportion to the number of samples.

The authors give a tight account of test error, measured in mean squared error. It uses only population quantities of the true data plus first- and second-order statistics of the augmentation scheme. Results hold under misspecified feature maps and for any net architecture that trains only the last readout layer, with the rest frozen or randomly initialized. Specified for Gaussian data, the asymptotic account proves tight, giving practitioners a precise formula for how augmentation choices shape generalization.
arxiv-2605-10390:
Michael Dang'ana speeds up sorting for cloud databases, where sorting underpins queries, indexing, and joins. Radix sort is preferred for large data, but distribution dependence and limited parallelism hurt it, and common fixes cost preprocessing and memory. In-place variants add passes as precision rises, raising latency. His 2026 paper introduces FractalSortCPU, a bandwidth-efficient compressed radix sort on CPU.

The method adapts histogram compression to the CPU for keys of any precision. Fully parallel key-based histogram updates remove input bucketing and prep work. A parallel design with SIMD-accelerated operations gives top run time while limiting histogram growth. On data from 512 megabytes to 32 gigabytes at 16-bit precision, it beat the state of the art on bandwidth. Gains were 6 times on CPU, 3 times on GPU, and 2.5 times on FPGA.
arxiv-2605-10590:
Emil Javurek and four colleagues speed up causal sensitivity analysis with prior-data fitted networks. Causal sensitivity analysis gives bounds for causal effect estimates under hidden factors. But existing methods are per-instance steps: changes to the dataset, query, response level, or treatment require new compute. Their 2026 paper instead presents an in-context approach.

The key challenge is that response bounds are not available when sampling training data. The authors develop a prior-data build across treatment sensitivity models. It uses a Lagrangian scaling of the goal to generate training labels for the bounds. That tradeoff balances causal effect tuning against response model breaks, avoiding model-specific math. Under convex and linear conditions, the goal recovers the Pareto frontier of solutions. In tests, the approach's test-time compute beats per-instance methods by orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2605-10790:
Zhipeng Yao and eight colleagues diagnose a training bottleneck in diffusion models, the generators behind much of today's image synthesis. They call it representation degradation: as noise levels rise, model outputs warp structurally, which destabilizes training and degrades what the model makes.

Their analysis ties the trouble to mismatched target recoverability, linked to weakening spectral structure in the neural tangent kernel. Their fix, Elucidated Representation Diffusion, shifts optimization effort toward noise levels where targets can still be recovered. Across diffusion backbones it speeds convergence without outside supervision. Model builders get a plug-and-play remedy for a failure mode they may have blamed on tuning.
arxiv-2605-10890:
Tommy Ho, Khashayar Etemadi, and Zhendong Su build CppPerf, a pipeline and benchmark for automatically repairing C++ performance bugs. Realistic, runnable benchmarks for speed fixes have lagged behind, since existing C++ sets lean on contest code while real-world repair sets target Python and .NET.

CppPerf-Mine sifts open-source C++ repositories for patches that cut run time, filters them structurally, classifies them with a language model, and rebuilds each one inside a reproducible container. The resulting CppPerf-DB holds 347 hand-checked patches from 42 mature projects, and a leading repair agent fixes only about one in seven. Repair researchers get a hard, honest yardstick for repository-scale speed work.
arxiv-2605-11090:
Paul L. Schechter, Michael Zeng Lu, and Christopher Hernández set out a response protocol for quadruply lensed supernovae, using SN 2025wny as the worked example. Lensed supernovae rank among the most anticipated transients of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time, and quadruples constrain lens models far better than doubles.

Full value demands spectroscopic and photometric follow-up within hours, not days, plus on-the-fly modeling to predict trailing-image positions and magnitudes and to pre-cover leading images too faint to trigger alerts. The protocol hands brokers candidate host lists ahead of time, plus software to tell whether a supernova near a host is strongly lensed, and whether it shows four images or two. Brokers then broadcast positions and time delays enabling pre-covery, re-covery, and rough light curves from prior exposures. Survey teams get a playbook for rare, fast-fading gold.
arxiv-2605-11190:
Christian Bianchini and Gabriele Puppis set out broad conditions under which minimal models of streaming transducers exist. A streaming transducer reads an input word and produces an output value by updating an internal memory step by step. This abstract model subsumes classical sequential transducers, streaming string-to-string transducers, polynomial automata, and streaming string-to-tree variants.

The authors then instantiate these criteria to obtain working minimization results for variants where outputs are terms built bit by bit by extending tuples of terms at leaves or roots. Automata theorists get a unified existence theory for minimal streaming transducers plus concrete minimization results for the tree-output case.
arxiv-2605-11290:
Xueqi Cheng and three co-authors present ReAD, reinforcement-guided capability distillation for large language models. Capability distillation compresses a large model into a smaller one while keeping abilities for a downstream task. But most methods treat skills as lone targets and overlook how improving one skill shifts the student's broader profile, notably when multiple skills jointly decide task success.

The team studies this distillation under a fixed token budget and finds two consistent patterns. It induces systematic, budget-linked cross-skill transfer. Extra budget often brings limited task gains while sometimes hurting other useful skills. Building on these insights, ReAD accounts for skill interplay. It first works out key skills, then builds supervision aimed at them on the fly, and finally lets an uncertainty-aware bandit split the token budget by expected gains. Tests show ReAD lifts downstream performance. Teams get budget shares that respect skill links.
arxiv-2605-11390: Sophus Valentin Willumsgaard constructs an obstruction theory for A-n algebra structures in stable infinity-categories, and gives some of its properties. He uses this theory to show that the spectrum S over 4 admits an A-5 multiplication, built with synthetic spectra. The result pins down a piece of multiplicative structure in stable homotopy theory, where associativity up to higher coherence is often the hard part to establish.
arxiv-2605-11690: Alvarado and others outline a di-muon electro- and photo-making program with μCLAS12. CLAS12 pushed nucleon and nuclear structure knowledge, and new data open physics beyond its current limits. The program probes quark and gluon structure through di-muon making, aiming at beam-spin gaps in DDVCS. Varying photon states and push flow, DDVCS opens broad Parton spreads across three-dim phase space, beyond DVCS and time-like Compton scatters. Large reach and high brightness enable near-threshold J/psi making and high-stats time-like Compton scatters.
arxiv-2605-11790: Feifei Niu and seven colleagues replicate ABLoTS, a bug-localization method that traces links between issue reports and code. Its core TraceScore component matched or beat its original results on extended Java and Python datasets, but the team could not reproduce the headline figures from the original paper. They trace the gap to a cutoff-date slip that leaked test data into training, a cautionary finding for evaluating information-retrieval bug localization.
arxiv-2605-11890: Mushtaq Ahmad and M. Farasat Shamir link black-hole ringdown signals back to late-time scalar-tensor cosmology through effective field theory. Starting from a cosmology-conditioned posterior, they lift Jordan-frame data through a finite covariant jet, transport it to black-hole perturbation theory, and project it onto quasinormal-mode response kernels. They find cosmological tensor-speed deformations fall far below ringdown detectability, while operators vanishing on homogeneous backgrounds can stay active near black holes.
arxiv-2605-11990: Monit Sharma and Hoong Chuin Lau design sea energy security under strait closures with a two-stage chance network model. It joins route pledges, port goods stocks, storage growth, and case-based routing for crude oil, LNG, LPG, plus fertilizer, with choice-shaped odds and mean-CVaR risk in an exact MILP form. In an India-like case study, chance math beat the average-value policy by 1.35 percent, while LNG and LPG cover fell to 34.6 and 33.3 percent in worst cases.
arxiv-2605-12190: Futoshi Futami and Masahiro Fujisawa extend information-theory generalization bounds to sequential decision making. Supersample mutual information bounds are central for batch learning, but do not cover online learning, streaming active learning, or bandits, where data arrive. Their system splits the learner flow from a proof-side growth used for ghost-slot matches. Under swap rules, the gap is capped by CMI, which adds roundwise selector-loss information. A Bernstein-type tweak gives faster rates under variance cases, and the SCMI plan covers online learning, streaming active learning, and bandits.
arxiv-2605-12490: Behling and three colleagues use a deep neural network to fill gaps in proton-proton reference spectra for quark-gluon plasma studies. Heavy-ion work needs proton-proton data at the same collision energy as a baseline, yet some energies were never measured. Their model learns from ALICE data in LHC Runs 1 and 2, then interpolates and extrapolates transverse-momentum spectra to new energies. The result supplies reference spectra for Run 3 and beyond, where direct measurements are missing.
arxiv-2605-12590: Dymarsky presents a solvable model of three-dimensional quantum gravity from many copies of a rational Virasoro topological theory with central charge one half, summed over topologies. The theory is dual to an ensemble of 2D conformal theories with central charge half the copy count. Summing over topologies and evaluating the bulk partition function, he confirms the duality by matching the boundary ensemble for small copy counts. At large central charge the bulk simplifies to an Abelian phase, curing density-of-states negativity and showing a Hawking-Page transition.
arxiv-2605-12890: Liang and Li propose Steer-to-Detect, a two-stage method for spotting machine-generated text. Raw internal features overlap heavily between human and machine text, so the first stage learns a steering vector injected into a frozen observer model to separate the classes better. Detection then proceeds by hypothesis testing on the steered features. The authors prove finite-sample error guarantees, and tests show strong performance including out-of-distribution and adversarial settings.
arxiv-2605-13090: Keshari, Mayassi, Prabhakar and Nasser introduce the multi-virtual twin group, extending the twin group and Kauffman's multi-virtual braid group. They sort all homogeneous 2-local representations of the group into general linear groups, finding exactly eight distinct types. They probe faithfulness and irreducibility, proving the representations are mostly unfaithful and giving necessary and sufficient rules for irreducibility. For certain parameter values they also build non-local representations of the pure twin subgroup induced from the main group, with irreducibility rules set out.
arxiv-2605-13190: Lorenc, Berdoz, Mathys and Wattenhofer introduce N-vium, a mixture-of-exits transformer spreading computation across depth, raising FLOPs per second. Heads at multiple depths define the next-token distribution as a mixture over exits, with token-adaptive routing. The design generalises the standard transformer, recovered exactly when routing gives zero mass to intermediate heads. Mixture sampling is exact, and KV caches return by deferring upper computation and batching it with later tokens. Pretrained up to 1.5B parameters, it runs 57.9% faster than a standard transformer at no perplexity cost.
arxiv-2605-13290: Langner and colleagues ask whether a reasoning dataset can be judged before costly training runs. They propose intrinsic data measures and test them by tuning 8B and 11B models on variants of a Polish reasoning set. The measures track later model quality strongly, but the best predictors shift with scale. Small models need alignment measures for precision, while larger models gain from verbose traces and redundancy on hard tasks.
arxiv-2605-13490: Tom Banks argues that any model of de Sitter space as a finite quantum system is ambiguous. Semi-classical reasoning with quantum measurement theory implies this ambiguity. If our universe tends toward such a de Sitter state, a finite-system model of it might fit into a converging sequence. That sequence would converge to a non-perturbative completion of a unique superstring model, giving a precise model of our universe. Yet even the best local-detector experiments can capture only a tiny fraction of the system's total q-bits.
arxiv-2605-13690: Fengqing Jiang and eight colleagues show hyper-network power is ruled by which small patterns a design can detect and count. Joining hom-count fullness with fixed nearing, they show hom rates make all smooth hyper fixed traits, sorted in a strict ladder ranked by wide-tree width. That yields a Width Wall: no hidden size, training method or fixed-depth network can show fixed traits needing wider patterns. The frame joins 15 hyper designs, pinpoints info lost by clique growth, and motivates density-aware models beyond bounded-width message passing.
arxiv-2605-13790: Zhonghao Li, Chaoyu Liu and Qian Zhang propose Di-BiLPS, a unified neural frame handling forward and inverse partial differential equation problems under very sparse readings. Di-BiLPS mixes a variational autoencoder squeezing big inputs into a compact latent space, plus a latent spread module shaping doubt, and paired learning lining codes. Tests on several partial differential equation benchmarks show Di-BiLPS always reaches state-of-the-art performance under very sparse inputs, as low as 3 percent. It greatly cuts compute cost.
arxiv-2605-14290: Piet and seven co-authors argue plan-then-execute, not ReAct, should be the default for web agents. Web content mixes inputs from many parties. Under ReAct, all such content reaches the model at decision time, opening a path for prompt injections to steer control flow. Plan-then-execute redraws this line: untrusted data may sway values or branches inside a predefined graph, but cannot redefine the user task. WebArena analysis finds all tasks compatible with plan-then-execute, while 80 percent need only a purely programmatic plan.
arxiv-2605-14390: In a 2026 paper, Halevi and Shelah show that finite-index extensions and subgroups of omega-stable groups can be model-theoretically wild. More precisely, some omega-stable group interprets any countable first-order structure in a finite language in one of its finite-index extensions. The same structure can also be interpreted in one of its finite-index subgroups. The result separates base-group tameness from finite-index wildness. Passing to finite index need not preserve model-theoretic calm.
arxiv-2605-14490: Jiang, Ma, Marquette, Zhang and Zhang build superintegrable systems from Poisson centralisers. Such systems have more conserved quantities than degrees of freedom. They work in the Lie-Poisson algebra of a complex semisimple Lie algebra, where chains of reductive subgroups give invariant subalgebras. Their centres organise into Poisson projection chains. For a maximal torus they prove the chain is superintegrable, with dimension counts splitting commuting Hamiltonians from extra first integrals.
arxiv-2605-14590: Zhang, Zhang and Sun tackle stain variation across hospitals in federated pathology, where slides cannot be pooled for privacy reasons. Stain colours differ from site to site, and most methods sum this up with low-order stats that assume near-Gaussian shapes. Their FedStain framework instead swaps compact higher-order stain stats, skewness and kurtosis, with no pixel data sent. A contrastive cross-site aggregation step then builds stain-invariant features. The method is claimed to beat rivals with steady gains on two benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-14790: Gao, Xia, Liu and Xiong propose Graphs of Research, a supervised tuning method for research idea generation. For each seed paper, a two-hop reference set is extracted. Links among references are derived from citation position, frequency, predecessor links, plus publication time. The result is organised into a paper-evolution graph. Data comes from five major ML/NLP venues, with about seven thousand six hundred cited references. A fine-tuned model reading the graph and edge signals is claimed to beat GPT-4o baselines in judge contests.
arxiv-2605-14890: Ovcharov benchmarks tokenizer fertility and zero-shot performance on Ukrainian legal text. Fertility varies 1.6-fold across models, yet this cost-critical dimension is missing from model selection. Seven models from five providers are tested on two hundred and seventy-three validated court decisions from Ukraine's state registry. Qwen 3 models consume sixty percent more tokens than Llama-family models. NVIDIA Nemotron Super 3 scores highest, beating a model with 5.6 times more parameters at one third the API cost. Few-shot prompting cuts performance by up to twenty-six percentage points.
arxiv-2605-15290: Kyle R. Chickering and nine others derive the maximal update parameterization for grouped-query attention, allowing tuning transfer across architectures. Maximal settings ensure transfer through sound analysis but are hard to derive for new designs. Raising spectral-norm rules from rule-of-thumb to definition yields complete depth and weight-decay scalings, and a tweaked spectral norm handles non-full-rank weights. Tests confirm learning-rate transfer across the grouped-query repetition parameter and over weight decay.
arxiv-2605-15390: Ondrej Alexaj and five others present Kofola version 1.0, a modular tool for complementation and subset checking of Büchi automata, central tasks in machine-theoretic verification. The framework splits the input machine into strongly connected parts and applies a fitted flipping algorithm to each, plus modular subset checking with new heuristics. An on-the-fly emptiness check for the final broad Rabin rule stops as soon as the seen state space does. Benchmarks rank Kofola the most robust tool tested, often faster by orders of size.
arxiv-2605-15790: Yingqi Zhao and three colleagues tackle bias that search can inject into answers from systems that pull in outside text. Their plan reranks documents with set bias doses, tracks how bias spreads by position, and balances fit against fairness in one joint task. A scalable method called FARO splits the task to make it fast. Tests show the method cuts generation bias while keeping fit intact, offering a sound route to fairer search.
arxiv-2605-15890: Heekang Song and Wan Choi propose a bandwidth-saving gradient coding scheme for mixed distributed learning. Their unified framework jointly optimizes gradient coding and quantization, cutting leftover error while staying unbiased. They derive a closed-form code structure with an optimal bit allocation strategy and a fast algorithm that nearly matches the optimum. Proofs cover convex and smooth functions. Experiments on the COCO dataset show the joint design speeds convergence and improves communication efficiency over existing baselines.
arxiv-2605-15990: Isar Nejadgholi and three colleagues sort out what cultural skill in AI actually means, drawing on intercultural communication research. Their three-level taxonomy asks whether a model knows cultural facts, how it frames that knowledge, and whether it adapts as a conversation unfolds. The authors argue the scheme gives evaluations clearer, more interpretable results, warning that fuzzy definitions can flatter models and mislead deployment choices in sensitive settings.
arxiv-2605-16290: Krishnan and Savelka predict multiple-choice question hardness by tracking learner variety instead of taking one single-peak ability spread. Using EEDI student logs, they find habit types by latent class analysis, then tune a language model to mimic response spreads per type. Those signals join topic context in a Ridge fit to guess the item response theory value. Five-fold checks beat a recent baseline, cutting mean squared error from 0.367 to 0.274 and lifting R-squared from 0.525 to 0.686, with clear types showing why items prove hard.
arxiv-2605-16390: Toledo and Martínez test whether the training routine can induce spatial locality in early Vision Transformer layers trained from scratch. Holding settings fixed, they compare Baseline and Modern routines using AutoAugment, ColorJitter, CutMix, and Label Smoothing on three datasets. The Modern routine yields more local, concentrated early-layer attention. On CIFAR-100, the minimum mean attention distance falls from 0.316 for Baseline down to 0.008 for the Modern routine. Ablation names CutMix the determining component: all CutMix conditions show distance 0.024 in the test, while all others stay at 0.210 in the same test.
arxiv-2605-16490: Amend and three others study interaction phases for adiabatic winds spreading into power-law density shapes. When winds first turn on, they inflate a bubble bounded by two shocks, changing through such phases. For dense ejecta, the flow relaxes into an interaction similarity state and enters an energy-conserving regime. Using scalings with simulations, they quantify relaxation timescales and solution accuracy for fluid properties. Such solutions are attained within a few dynamical times; for n < 2 the flow converges to energy-conserving scaling.
arxiv-2605-16590: Bradley surveys recent work on boundary value problems over p-adic analytic manifolds, a geometry where distances obey a stronger triangle rule. He introduces coordinate Laplacians built from frame bundles, uses them to form elliptic operators, and formulates and solves Dirichlet problems that extend earlier results on compact p-adic domains. The account closes with prospects in number theory and ultrametric spaces.
arxiv-2605-16790: Kulkarni's team proposes TIER, a reward framework for multi-step tool use by language models that derives guidance from function schemas and live runs, not set paths. Outcome rewards are sparse, while path-supervised rewards punish valid options. TIER splits reward into valid format, schema fit, run success, and right answers, giving dense, clear feedback per step. On DepthBench, split by depth from 1 to 6 steps, TIER tops 90% scores at every depth where path-supervised rewards collapse beyond step 4, with gains on BFCL v3 and NestFUL.
arxiv-2605-16890: Lei derives the sub-Coulomb Trojan Horse result from the inelastic breakup cross section. At stellar energy, single near-threshold peaks make cross section and peak strength match. A single-pole ansatz with four rules reduces it to a per-pole Born cross section on the state, keeping twists and action. The width profile follows from the postform size, making it route-free, and analysis fixes absorbing strength as half the inelastic decay width. The split formula follows under three dynamic guesses plus a zero-range shortcut.
arxiv-2605-17290: Liu and colleagues present BluesFL, a fault-localization framework for processor designs that mimics how engineers debug. It splits code into dataflow blocks to focus the language model, then traces instruction paths and processor states to narrow the fault. On a real 19,000-line RISC-V core it pins down 24 bugs at first guess, far past the prior best of 7, at an average cost of about 26 cents per bug.
arxiv-2605-17390: Li and colleagues propose NOETHER, a constructive frame for finding metamorphic patterns from operator algebras. The work moves induction from per-program sampling to a per-domain algebra layer. An eight-block upstream split covers symmetry, order, self-adjoint form, time reversal, limits, motion patterns, method comparison and relational match. A downstream algorithm then builds pattern sets with algebra closure and poly-time decidability. Tests span reactor physics, equivariant ML and query optimizers. One completeness guess is falsified by counter-cases.
arxiv-2605-17590: Kennon Stewart formulates machine unlearning for online L-BFGS as counterfactual state alignment. The target is the optimizer state that would have formed had deleted samples never been processed. State-aware metrics in turn track parameter error, memory-operator error, combined state deviation and update-direction error. That metric compares inverse-Hessian actions rather than treating curvature pairs as finite influence. Under convexity he derives a recursive bound on deviation. Benchmarks show unlearning demands matching with a realizable target state, not weight fixes alone.
arxiv-2605-17790: Jiarui Su and three colleagues propose STRIDE, an agent framework for finding equations from data. Older loops propose candidates, fit them, score them, and reuse winners. But they can misjudge good skeletons, drop near-correct equations, and hoard redundant memories. STRIDE links data-aware generation, mixed-fitting checks, critic-executor repair, and a diverse semantic memory in one closed loop. Fitted scores feed back into each new round of the loop. Tests show better accuracy, robustness, and structural recovery on symbolic regression benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-17990: Yidan Zheng and five colleagues present a live gaze tracking system that senses latent features with light, without images. A microlens array with a binary chromium mask spreads light spatially, producing a compact measurement set sufficient for tracking. Sensing and feature extraction merge in light, removing image readout and cutting compute overhead. A 4 by 4 phototransistor array captures measurements, and a lightweight neural network maps them to gaze direction. The prototype reaches 3.4 milliseconds end-to-end latency, beating published systems with good accuracy on simulated and real data.
arxiv-2605-18290: Christoph Wolf's 2026 study quantifies how water dosage warps geometry in powder bed 3D printing of concrete. Small changes in voxel-wise water content cause large systematic deviations, including rounded edges and swelling, with biases that depend on direction. High-resolution stereophotogrammetry aligns as-built scans with CAD models to measure distance errors and volume differences across dosage settings. Deformation patterns repeat and strengthen with more water, yet stiffness and strength barely change. Excess voxel water diffuses into nearby powder, leaving the effective water-cement ratio nearly unchanged.
arxiv-2605-18390: Anlin Zheng and seven co-authors build VFMTok, a 2026 all-purpose image tokenizer stacked on a frozen vision foundation model. A region-aware quantization design cuts spatial overlap in grid features, while a meaning-based rebuild goal keeps decoded outputs aligned with the base model's features. For discrete autoregressive sampling it speeds training threefold and reaches a gFID of 1.36 on ImageNet, and 1.25 in continuous sampling with a noise-removal model.
arxiv-2605-18490: Theodore Cochran preregisters a comparison in a 2026 paper of single-round Vector RAG against an LLM-compiled markdown wiki browsed by a tool-using agent. Both answer thirteen questions on twenty-four papers. The wiki wins clearly on connecting findings across papers, but its organization edge falls below the registered threshold once both judges combine. RAG passes its single-fact groundedness test, though judge-sensitively. The wiki costs about 21 times more tokens per query, so no break-even point exists.
arxiv-2605-18590: Mamoru Nunokawa and Janusz Sokol extend, in a 2026 paper, Ozaki's condition for p-valent analytic functions. The known condition says a positive real part of the p-th derivative implies a function is at most p-valent in the unit disc. The paper proves an extension of this condition and determines new sufficient conditions for functions to be p-valent starlike of a given order. The work sharpens criteria for starlikeness in this function class.
arxiv-2605-18690: Luca Trinchão and fifteen co-authors report, in a 2026 paper, wider nonlinear dynamics in chip-scale Kerr parametric oscillators. Above a power threshold, degenerate parametric oscillators break symmetry into one of two stable, phase-shifted states. Using a silicon nitride microring, the team finds Hopf bifurcations that trigger self-sustained oscillations at megahertz frequencies. Tuning pump detunings and powers gives turnkey control between binary states and limit cycles. Period-doubling bifurcations appear as well, with simulations showing a cascade into chaos at higher powers.
arxiv-2605-18790: Yingnan Xu and Shuangshuang Chu compute one-loop matter corrections for a four-dimensional Lifshitz black brane. They treat a scalar field, a Dirac spinor, and a Maxwell field as probes on a neutral planar brane background. Each spin sector splits into a smooth radial part and a horizon-localized conical part. That split shows which piece appears in the boundary Ward identity and which feeds horizon replica entropy. The smooth part then sets the source-driven share of the scale response.
arxiv-2605-18890: Jinyi Ye, Lei Cao, Ding Chen and Emilio Ferrara warn against drawing scientific claims from language-model social simulations without robustness audits. Tiny changes in persona wording or game instructions can cascade through repeated interactions and shift cooperation by up to 76 percentage points in one model, while barely moving another. Network structure likewise shifts polarization in echo-chamber simulations. Because sensitivity varies by claim and model, the authors argue robustness must be measured case by case, and they offer TRAILS, an audit taxonomy spanning agent, interaction and system levels.
arxiv-2605-18990: Austin Bennett, Preston Vander Vos, Duc Le and Mira Belenkiy prove no balance-based rule can deliver anti-plutocratic governance on a blockchain. Token-weighted voting concentrates control in large holders, and quadratic voting was meant to dampen that power. But a Sybil attacker splitting tokens across wallets gains power growing at least linearly with holdings. For concave rules proposed, the best strategy stays asymptotically linear regardless of cost scheme. Replays from five major DAOs show Sybil amplification of 1172 to 4039 times under quadratic voting, and above 229000 times under steeper rules.
arxiv-2605-19090: Emilio E. Ramos-Torres and three colleagues describe a cheap way to produce cylindrical vector beams, structured-polarisation light beams, from acetate-sheet binary holograms. Swapping the hologram changes the beam, and a Michelson interferometer with a cylindrical-lens converter shapes it, while wave plates tune it from scalar to vector light. Polarisation maps reconstructed from Stokes measurements match simulations, and a vector quality factor confirms the degree of nonseparability. The authors pitch the setup as an alternative to programmable modulators for compact optics and teaching labs.
arxiv-2605-19190: Charvi Rastogi and 15 colleagues conduct localised red teaming for text-to-image safety in the Global South, where frameworks follow a Western-centric default. They gather local norms and contexts through workshops in secondary urban centres. PLACES holds over 26,000 model-failure examples from universities in Ghana, Nigeria, Karnataka, and Punjab. Prompts show socio-cultural and linguistic diversity and unique adversarial patterns from local nuances, plus theme clusters such as religion in India. The authors identify novel harms from normative dissonance, arguing safety needs localised, participatory methods.
arxiv-2605-19390: Li and colleagues address a gap in large multimodal models: sustaining four-dimensional reasoning about moving objects over time. They set a task where a model answers space-time questions and returns structured 3D paths for targets across a clip, plus Track4D-Bench with 526 dialogue samples. Their LMM-Track4D adds ray-time geometry encoding, a streaming state token for long horizons, and a decoder built for occlusion and viewpoint shifts. It beats strong baselines across the benchmark, suggesting explicit motion-state modeling helps.
arxiv-2605-19890: Alhuwaider and colleagues ask what short term store best helps a trained model adjust to new test data. Most work tunes the learning rule, but they show which past samples are kept matters just as much. Their tests find varied samples within each class beat fresh or evenly spread ones, and they build stores mixing even class shares with varied features.
arxiv-2605-19990: Francesco Pasti and three co-workers show that planar robot odometry needs only four light sensors plus an inertial unit. Four downward photodiodes view the ground via Gabor masks, and the light patterns they return carry speed information, which a temporal convolutional network decodes after joint optimisation in a physics-based simulator. Combined with angular speed from the inertial unit, the prototype tracks reference paths closely indoors and outdoors with no real-world fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-20490: Lautaro Estienne and four colleagues offer a new family of scores for systems that report both a prediction and their own doubt. Existing checks grade predictions and doubt separately, or fix one price for refusing to answer. That can mislead high-stakes choices, where costs differ by case. Their ECUAS scores, built as proper scoring rules, let the user tune how much bad predictions count against shaky doubt.
arxiv-2605-20690: Shanshan Ye and Duo Lu propose Declarative Data Services, a structured way for agents to compose data systems from user intent. Unbounded agents that iterate on failure logs often fail to converge on a working stack, even with added knowledge. Their framework splits the search into bounded parts with four typed contracts, covering intent, operator graphs, per-system skills, and runtime attribution. Sub-agents scan each typed space while the framework holds the whole together.
arxiv-2605-20790: Kamal Azaidaoui and four colleagues study field-tunable spin-valley transport in monolayer molybdenum disulfide through a single electric barrier. A uniform off-resonant elliptically polarized light is also applied, and a high-frequency Floquet expansion yields a static model with a laser-tuned mass term. Solving the scattering problem by spinor matching gives an exact transmission rule. The drive tunes the spin-valley propagation threshold and Fabry-Perot phase, switching the junction between broadband valley filtering and resonance-selective use.
arxiv-2605-20890: Sergei Zorkaltsev and six colleagues compare shared 3D convolutional networks for elastic constants prediction in porous metals. Metal shape strongly shapes how they respond to load. The authors generated 6,000 gold and 422 silver porous structures, computing three elastic modulus parts with molecular dynamics, for 19,263 data points. They compare a fully connected network trained on pre-made topological markers against several 3D convolutional designs from machine vision. The 3D networks beat the marker baseline, whose R-squared was 0.704, with top DenseNet-201 reaching 0.955.
arxiv-2605-21290: Ivan Noden studies Serre functors for categories of quasicoherent sheaves on affine quotient stacks. He considers stacks of the form Spec A modulo G, where G is a reductive group acting with a unique closed orbit. He shows the Serre functor is given by tensoring with the local cohomology of the dualizing sheaf at that unique closed orbit. From this description, he develops analogues of the Matlis and local duality theorems for local rings. The short note thus gives a concrete Serre functor formula in the affine quotient setting.
arxiv-2605-21690: Karen Eilers and co-authors summarize the 2nd Agile Practice and Research Workshop and issue a call for research. Agile development has been shaped by research-practice interplay for decades, yet gaps persist. The workshop, held at the XP 2026 conference in São Paulo, Brazil, brought researchers and practitioners. It tackled three gaps: theory, time, and transfer gaps. Organizers drew four propositions from the results for improving research-practice ties, plus three calls: broader open science adoption, higher empirical standards, and more explicit value contributions.
arxiv-2605-21890: Batsukh and Zunderiya study a generalized Fisher equation in cylindrical coordinates, using the Lie symmetry method to find its hidden structure. They pin down which source functions give the equation symmetries beyond simple time translation, when diffusion follows an exponential law. For those cases they also work out the reduced ordinary differential equations that follow from each one found. The work thus maps, case by case, when this spreading and growth equation admits extra symmetry structure in cylindrical form.
arxiv-2605-22090: Wenfeng Wu, Luping Xiang, and Kun Yang propose a camera-cooperative ISAC framework for sensing non-cooperative drones. Detecting such drones is hard for ISAC systems because single-modal perception is limited and sensing competes with comms for shared resources. Their camera-aided system uses multimodal sensing to enable efficient drone beam steering. Tests show an average reduction of 71 percent in beam steering overhead and 1.69 to 11.15 percent in tracking overhead, while keeping high angular accuracy and freeing room for extra comms tasks.
arxiv-2605-22190: Matteo Balice and co-authors present NoPo4D, the first feed-forward system for dynamic scenes with unknown camera poses. Dynamic methods need poses or monocular input, pose-free methods handle only static scenes, and per-scene optimization costs minutes to hours. NoPo4D splits Gaussian motion into image-plane shifts and depth changes, supervised from pseudo optical flow. A motion encoder and view-dependent opacity complete the system. On four dynamic benchmarks it beats prior feed-forward baselines, and with post-optimization it surpasses per-scene methods far faster.
arxiv-2605-22890: Safdari and Ashraf extend Deep Event Visual Odometry with a sparse point-cloud export pipeline. DEVO tracks camera motion from event-camera data. Rather than altering its core odometry, their method exposes the 3D structure DEVO already estimates. It converts that structure into an explicit point cloud for viewing and further use, with export, format conversion, and cleanup steps. On one test sequence the cloud matched EMVS reconstructions closely at a 5 centimeter threshold.
arxiv-2605-22990: Schlama and Schwaller introduce Drift-React, a generative framework that predicts complete chemical reaction pathways in one forward pass from reactant and product geometries alone. Mapping pathways and transition states usually costs thousands of force calls. By shifting distribution evolution to training through a Sinkhorn-weighted drifting field, the model skips both iterative force calls and sequential ODE or SDE integration. It matches rival models' sub-Angstrom saddle-point accuracy while running orders of magnitude faster.
arxiv-2605-23490: Marius Molz and colleagues sort all 179 MISRA C++ 2023 rules by how they fit Rust, a language gaining ground in safety critical systems. Of 111 rules that carry over as written, just under half are already enforced by Rust itself. Sixty nine rules still matter, yet 36 vanish inside safe Rust and return only with unsafe features. The team also spots gaps needing fresh Rust rules and shares the full mapping openly.
arxiv-2605-23990: Zarandi, Ebrahimi, and Toda generalize slow-roll inflation through non-standard entropies, linking potential, entropy, and observables with the Hamilton-Jacobi method. A new non-linear parametrization of the Hubble parameter yields a Tsallis parameter near 1.1 to 1.2, plus tiny Rényi and Kaniadakis values, consistent with recent data. Models are constrained first by primary parameters, the scalar spectral index and the tensor-to-scalar ratio, and second by varying uncertainty in the ratio bound. The dual approach narrows the viable parameter space of entropy-based inflation models.
arxiv-2605-24390: Yang, Du, and Liu introduce the Neural Eigenspace Operator, predicting the Laplace spectrum from point clouds. Finding low-frequency modes is slow because iterative solvers cost much on large data. Standard vector regression is ill-posed, plagued by sign flips and rotation mix-ups, so the network learns the stable subspace instead. Pairs come from a light Rayleigh-Ritz polish, and a mass-aware tool folds area weights into attention mixing. The method scales near-line with big speedups at matched scores and transfers zero-shot to high-res clouds.
arxiv-2605-24790: Hudaiba Soomro and co-authors show how alloy disorder shapes electric dipole spin resonance in silicon-germanium Wiggle Wells. Long-period swings in germanium concentration boost Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling, prized for spin-qubit gates since it removes the need for micromagnets. Disorder scrambles valley splitting and valley phase, a factor recent analyses missed. The Rabi frequency now depends on valley phase, scrambling it across the sample, yet fast resonance stays possible at most spots. Sweet spots deaf to electric-field swings support faithful oscillations under charge noise.
arxiv-2605-24890: Xuan Wang leads QuoVLA, a new take on vision-language-action models for robot control. Most methods assume pretrained vision-language models lack usable action data or must be shielded from action training. The team's quotient theory argues the latents already hold what control needs, plus prompt-level detail mapping to the same action. QuoVLA squeezes those latents into leaner action-sufficient forms with quantization and dual-branch temporal-complexity regularization. Across benchmarks it performs strongly, with clearest gains under shifts in visuals, wording, and setting.
arxiv-2605-24990: Kanhaya Sharma leads fabrication of 3D photonic circuits mixing two waveguide kinds on one chip. Planar platforms hit scaling limits that 3D routing can ease. The circuits pair compact high-confinement air-clad guides with robust low-confinement polymer-clad guides. Mode transfer between the two kinds proves efficient, and compact Euler S- and U-bends reach tiny radii with low loss. Compact adiabatic air-clad splitters also show low splitting loss over a short length. A full hybrid circuit build shows feasibility and scale.
arxiv-2605-25190: Paulina Sowicka, Gerald Handler, J. J. Hermes, and Keaton J. Bell report pulsations in the hot star at the heart of planetary nebula Kn 61, found in a month of Kepler short-cadence data. Four peaks match gravity modes of GW Vir stars. Three dipole modes give a mean period spacing of 21.526 seconds, implying a mass of 0.551 Suns that agrees with evolutionary models. The star also shows sporadic brightenings whose energy could reach ten to the fortieth ergs if driven by temperature rises.
arxiv-2605-25590: Lee and Oh study generalized linear bandits whose reward parameter drifts over time, covering linear, Bernoulli and binomial reward models. Existing methods revisit past observations each round, so computation and memory grow with time. Several also need a non-convex projection step. Their DOMD-GLB instead estimates parameters with discounted online mirror descent, holding per-round computation and memory constant. They prove dynamic regret bounds for drifting and piecewise-stationary settings, and claim the first algorithm of this kind whose per-round costs do not grow with time.
arxiv-2605-25690: Wu and colleagues improve recommendations that use side behaviors, where extra data should ease thin target data but often add noise. Their GCIB cleans auxiliary behavior data and enriches target profiles at two levels. At the graph level, a bottleneck objective keeps shared structure with the target graph while cutting ties to the raw side graph. At the feature level, a contrastive scheme treats cleaned side features and target features as two views of users and items. Tests show GCIB beating leading baselines with noise-tough, target-aware profiles.
arxiv-2605-25790: Pham and colleagues present HoLoArm, a quadrotor whose soft arms borrow the nodus structure of dragonfly wings. The design flexes naturally and stays stable, aided by a reinforcement learning policy that improves recovery and hovering. Tests show the drone deforms passively in any direction and recovers within 0.3 to 0.6 seconds. It survives collisions at speeds up to 7.6 meters per second and carries a 540 gram payload while staying stable. The work advances soft aerial robot design for cluttered, human-shared spaces and points toward fully soft drones.
arxiv-2605-25890: Schesch and Ernst tackle version control merging with machine learning. They build Merge-Bench, 7938 real conflict hunks from 1439 repositories, with developer-committed resolutions as ground truth. They train 14-billion-parameter LLMergeJ with Group Relative Policy Optimization to resolve Java conflicts. On Java programs, LLMergeJ beats three commercial models and trails only Gemini 2.5 Pro, the top performer. Across 11 languages, commercial performance stays largely stable, and the best models resolve under 60 percent of conflicts.
arxiv-2605-26090: Fressart, Nowak and Spillane bring domain decomposition preconditioning into the quantum setting for finite element problems. Quantum linear solvers speed up on paper, yet their performance still hinges on the matrix condition number, a measure of numerical sensitivity. Preconditioning multiplies the system by a matrix that shrinks that number. The authors prove quantum domain decomposition is feasible and bound the block-encoding parameters for the Poisson problem with a two-level Additive Schwarz preconditioner. They also detail how the required operators are implemented, a key step toward practical quantum solvers.
arxiv-2605-26290: Derek Regier and three colleagues' 2026 framework adds time awareness to signed graph neural networks, which predict links in networks where ties can be friendly or hostile. Their Historical Context Integration Module blends recency-weighted history, trajectory modeling from long short-term memory nets, and multi-head temporal attention. History joins current node states through global or node-adaptive weights, so the design fits otherwise static architectures. Built onto the interpretable SE-SGformer and tested on Bitcoin, Reddit, and synthetic networks, it beats the static baseline consistently and significantly.
arxiv-2605-26490: P. Poopathysankar, Lucas Hackl, and Anwesha Chakraborty study entanglement picked up by speeded-up detectors in flat spacetime that is curled up or superposed. They use the standard harvest protocol for Unruh-DeWitt detectors on Rindler paths, varying push direction, detector gaps, and curl direction. Gaps across the push line always cut harvested entanglement, since spacelike gaps grow. Curling boosts field links, raising concurrence and stretching harvest range at high push. Superposition adds wave interference that widens the harvest zone more, and backward push still beats forward push.
arxiv-2605-26690: Khanna and Grimm introduce SILO, a method for designing protein sequences when only a small number of lab evaluations is affordable. The system proposes mutations in two steps, first choosing a position and then a replacement residue, and learns by imitating the best trajectories found so far. Tested on eight protein fitness landscapes, SILO beats five rival methods on the highest and average top-100 fitness scores, and stays strong when data are scarce or noisy.
arxiv-2605-26790: Zhang and four colleagues show that low-thrust trajectory costs, fuel use and trip feasibility, can be predicted well by machine-learning stand-ins instead of costly optimal-control solves. As data and model size grow, accuracy improves steadily with the log of both, with no plateau in sight. A self-similar transform lets one trained model span orbit sizes, tilts, and central bodies, and tests on asteroid missions confirm strong accuracy and transfer.
arxiv-2605-26990: Guo and five co-authors present a constrained Bayesian experimental design method that adapts to dynamic constraints such as budgets, varying costs, and physical limits. Their approach combines offline pre-training of an amortized policy and posterior network with online multi-step lookahead planning over scenario trees. Tests across constrained design tasks show substantially more informative design sequences than existing methods, at only modest extra computational cost.
arxiv-2605-27090: The LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA collaborations describe open data from the gravitational-wave observatory network. The set includes the second part of the fourth observing run and selected engineering-run periods. The public set spans April 6, 2024 to January 28, 2025. It includes calibrated strain time series for each instrument, extra channels for noise subtraction and detector characterization, and new analysis products in the online release tied to version 5.0 of the Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog.
arxiv-2605-27790: Akshaj Murhekar and Abhijit Mishra introduce SYNAPSE, a neuro-symbolic system steadying EEG-to-text decoding with symbolic rules at run time. Cleaning EEG-derived meaning picks with commonsense graph links and latent models makes decoding hold up without end-to-end language model fine-tuning. The method beats free prompting baselines, survives object-label ablation, and matches heavy fine-tuned systems while keeping raw EEG work local.
arxiv-2605-27890: Sun and colleagues build an ultra-sensitive mid-infrared spectrometer that works with vanishingly faint light. Their single-pixel device converts infrared spectra upward into near-infrared light, encodes them with a programmable mirror array, and decodes them from one silicon detector. It reached fine spectral resolution at extremely faint light levels and cut data-gathering time by about ninety-five percent.
arxiv-2605-28190: Manuel Frank and Haithem Afli argue that embedding robustness is multidimensional, not a single static score. Their Harder Text Embedding Benchmark perturbs inputs at test time along lexical, length, and language axes, validated by thousands of human ratings. Scale raised absolute scores without closing the original-transformed gap, and English sets proved more sensitive than multilingual ones.
arxiv-2605-28290: Shiyun Lin and three colleagues study learning in matching markets, where players pair with newly arriving options. Each option's features are visible, yet small feature changes can overturn the stable-matching benchmark. That fragility can cause sharp regret spikes for some players. For random contexts they give a fully adaptive method with a slowly growing regret bound, and for adversarial contexts a tractable notion with a sublinear bound.
arxiv-2605-28490: Jiawei Li and five colleagues improve fine-grained 3D object grounding for unified language models that also handle dialogue, questions, and captions. Single-pointer grounding squeezes a relational instruction into one choice, which fails when several same-class candidates differ only by context and spatial relations. Their SSR3D-LLM writes latent spatial reasoning steps and memory tokens drawn from the query, plus a geometry-aware scorer refines candidate rankings step by step. Across three benchmarks it leads unified baselines, with large gains over single-pointer grounding.
arxiv-2605-28590: Pulak Banerjee and four colleagues compute two-loop massless quantum chromodynamics corrections to Higgs decay into a bottom-quark pair plus a gluon. Working to higher powers of the dimensional regularization parameter, they project the amplitude onto the right Lorentz forms for the process. They also show form-factor values at sample phase-space points. These results feed three-loop virtual fixes to bottom-quark annihilation into Higgs-plus-jet production at hadron colliders, a needed ingredient for that calculation.
arxiv-2605-28690: Quoc Hoan Tran and three colleagues present latent-conditioned parameterized quantum circuits, a hybrid quantum-classical way to make groups of quantum states. Classical neural networks map a sampled latent variable to circuit settings, instead of state-by-state prep. The authors prove these circuits fully approximate spreads over quantum states in 1-Wasserstein distance, stretching classical theorems to quantum spreads. Tests on a made-up set and a QM9-derived atom set show the method beats recent quantum rivals and matches a classical neural rival.
arxiv-2605-28790: Jan Hajduček, Jáchym Štindl, Ján Rusz, and Vojtěch Uhlíř establish electron magnetic linear dichroism as a spin-axis probe in electron microscopy. Adding exchange splitting to simulations with diffraction computes the momentum- and energy-resolved dichroic signal for any Néel-vector or magnet setting. The linear part separates from background effects and shows a pattern for rebuilding spin axes from a set of momentum-resolved spectra. Tests on antiferro and ferro phases of FeRh show this sensitivity from wide light to atomic probes across angles.
arxiv-2605-28890: Jiacheng Lu and colleagues hide ownership marks inside the reasoning traces of large language models rather than in final answers. Their BiCoT method lines up prominent structural anchors in a trace with a private signature space while steadying ordinary control tokens to protect meaning. A companion verifier, Robust Subspace Registration, uses sentinel tokens to correct for drift in output patterns when a model is stolen or altered. Tests show the marks survive tuning, quantization, and adaptive attacks while reasoning quality holds.
arxiv-2605-28990: Jiyao Wang and colleagues build a light self-supervised framework for brain imaging that works when data are scarce and labels are noisy. Their BrainSimSiam learns from positive-only pairs, producing features that transfer across downstream classification and regression tasks. The features beat fully supervised baselines and approach large-scale models, without the heavy pretraining and fine-tuning costs of foundation models. The work targets functional MRI, where small samples, variable label quality, and high dimensionality raise overfitting risk.
arxiv-2605-29290: Izhar Ali presents SWORD for online change-point detection in dynamic networks. Comparing graphs as they arrive, in time linear in edges and without parametric assumptions, is demanding. Recent spectral methods compute Chebyshev moments of the normalized Laplacian and score their histogram with singular-value decomposition plus cosine similarity. SWORD computes the same moments but compares their mean across two adjacent time windows by their absolute distance. On three real-world benchmarks, this lifts mean F1 sharply over the earlier method, which missed every change on one benchmark.
arxiv-2605-29390: Jungmin Ko presents Orthogonal Negative Guidance in attention space, a training-free method for text-to-image models. Forcing the absence of a named object or trait is hard, and current methods often fail to remove the target or degrade quality. It makes negative-prompt cues orthogonal to positive-prompt cues, taking away that part to suppress bad concepts while keeping desired meaning. Tests show trade-offs between removal, fit, and quality. Human tests put it 19% above the second-best rival, with multi-concept and tunable removal.
arxiv-2605-29490: DEBENCH, introduced by Puzhuo Liu and four colleagues, judges binary decompilers by practical reuse, not by looks. It scores recovered code on readability, recompilation, and true behavior, using 240 test functions compiled into 640 binaries. Testing five decompilers and three repair models, they find a steep reuse cliff: the best pairing matches broad behavior far more often than it matches exact output. Readability settings do not maximize function, compiler choice matters greatly, and failures split into noisy syntax, broken type systems, and losses no repair can undo.
arxiv-2605-29690: Lorenzo Carletti and Bruno Premoselli study critical polyharmonic equations with Dirichlet boundary data on a smooth bounded domain. The operator is elliptic of even integer order, led by a power of the Laplacian, with a critical Sobolev exponent. Their main result gives uniform a priori bounds in high dimensions for bounded-energy solutions, depending only on energy, under a coercivity assumption on lower-order terms. The bounds are sharp at least when the order parameter equals one, and the proof yields a new global picture of blowing-up solutions.
arxiv-2605-30090: Jiamin Chen and seven colleagues introduce DirectorBench, a diagnostic benchmark for long-form video generation that looks past single overall scores. It grades videos against 80 metadata entries, 7 user profiles and 40 checkpoint criteria across script, visuals, audio, cross-modal fit and stability. Testing four workflows, six base models and seven profiles exposes a between-unit bottleneck: transitions average only about a quarter of full marks, while prompt demand fulfilment averages about seven tenths. Checks with 14 human annotators confirm it tracks human-perceived quality and uncovers failures that aggregate scores hide.
arxiv-2605-30190: Wenhao Li, Xiangfeng Wang and Bo Jin introduce MF-Diffuser, lifting planning to the Wasserstein space, where a small subset of agents captures population motion. Their approach has a value-weighted entropy objective balancing fidelity with return maximization, and a gradual strategy growing the agent population. They establish suboptimality bounds, and prove the policy forms an approximate mean-field Nash equilibrium with convergence guarantees. Tests on three benchmarks show best returns in most settings. The largest gains come on suboptimal data and at scales over a thousand agents.
arxiv-2605-30290: Chen Henry Wu and Aditi Raghunathan propose self-trained verification (STV) for self-improvement at training and test time, gated by the verifier bottleneck. Loops stall when scores inflate while accuracy stagnates. A model cannot catch its own errors alone, but can when shown the reference solution; STV trains the verifier to imitate that version. At test time, STV improves loops on hard problems where alternatives do not, doubling math accuracy and lifting scientific reasoning fourteenfold. At training time, verifier-in-the-loop training adds a third to pass@1.
arxiv-2605-30590: Turk shows that two clinical AI systems can tie on coverage scores yet react very differently when patient facts change. His Causal Sensitivity Score mutates oncology tumor-board cases along five clinical dimensions and grades whether each model shifts its advice in the pre-set correct direction. Across six frontier models and 224 cases, coverage and sensitivity rankings run nearly opposite, and every model fails surgery-status changes. Tool use lifts most models but leaves the weakest one still fetching the same chart sections without updating its advice.
arxiv-2605-30690: Feng and colleagues present ElasticMem, treating memory as a learnable latent resource for language-model agents.
