Old approaches fix memory allocation: text methods stuff memories into context, while latent methods still use rigid retrieval. ElasticMem builds a latent memory bank and retrieves from the reasoner's hidden state. It assigns each memory a budget through a learned policy, and injects selected states as soft tokens. Optimized through group-relative policy optimization, it improves question-answering accuracy and control success on two backbones while using the fewest tokens on ALFWorld.
arxiv-2605-30790: Ross and colleagues study how retrieved content should be represented for a language model rather than a human reader. Holding retrieval fixed, they vary only document representation across thirteen transformations. Across fourteen representations, they measure accuracy for four generators, plus answer retention: whether an answer-bearing document still supports its answer after transformation. They find answer retention drives generator accuracy; when retention is high, wording, structure, length, and query-dependence have limited effect. Gains attributed to specific mechanisms may reflect how well they preserve answer-bearing content.
arxiv-2605-30890: Lyu tackles a gap in Marx's labour theory of value: reducing complex labour to simple labour, the step keeping the transformation problem unsettled. First, he proves that when the economy yields a surplus, reduction coefficients respecting a reproduction floor form a bounded feasible region. Inside it, two macro equalities can hold. Second, he builds a linear mapping from wages and the floor to construct those coefficients, preserving boundaries. A calibration on China's 2017 input-output table shows these coefficients beat homogeneous-labour and wage-proxy methods on profit share.
arxiv-2605-31290: Van Son and colleagues compile a living catalog and unified review of binaries shaped by mass transfer. Mass transfer defines binary star evolution, yet its physics stays poorly understood and its products are studied by scattered communities with different methods and terms. The review covers 16 observational classes and a curated sample of 5,452 systems in a public community-driven catalog. Trends show non-zero eccentricities common at all periods, period distributions broad and overlapping, and Gaia black-hole and neutron-star systems extreme only in mass ratio.
arxiv-2606-00090:
Or surveys a safety gap in physical AI in this 2026 arXiv review: systems that act on the world can fail without warning. Robots, drones, and vehicles driven by foundation models may issue consequential actions that look confident and plausible while resting on sensor drift, occlusion, or hallucinated affordances. Ordinary content filters cannot catch them, and older robot safety was not built for black-box learned models. The review spans embodied models, world models, simulation, safe control, and verification literature.

Its finding: no single research stream provides a runtime authorization boundary between a black-box model and physical execution. He defines silent physical-action failure as its own category. The paper offers a taxonomy of runtime guardrail functions that could allow or block actions before hardware moves. It sets testing requirements for comparing guardrails as assurance tools. It targets researchers and engineers building approval layers for autonomous systems.
arxiv-2606-00290:
Bodnár and co-authors map how dense a small graph can sit inside huge host graphs. The key gauge asks for the top share of a form a host can hold as a true part. Hosts grow vast in this gauge, called inducibility. Graphs with six points hold 78 forms in all, up to flips and mirror swaps.

The team works through the six-point case in a set way. Flag math gives the sharp cap in 36 of those forms. Most of those caps are fresh finds, they note. For each solved form, they sketch the shape of near-peak hosts. In 32 forms, that shape stands firm with no loose parts. They set firm guesses for 12 more forms. In those, top and floor marks sit close but not yet met.
arxiv-2606-00390:
Shapourian and co-authors report Zamba2-VL, a line of sight-word models on a mixed base. The base, Zamba2, blends state-space layers with a few shared watch blocks. Past kin tools built on such bases lagged plain watch-based tools. This line aims to close that gap.

Tests span image sense, thought, text reads, point marks, and counts. Scores tie top open tools of like size in most tests. They beat past state-space and mixed sight tools by clear spans. The base gives near-flat start cost and a small state to hold. First-word wait thus drops near tenfold next to watch tools at like size. Gains swell most at the two small scales, apt for edge gear. Three sizes ship free with run code.
arxiv-2606-00490:
Hossain and Ahmed allot HPC network room by bids, not by queue place. Big compute hubs face floods of data from more and more fields. Plain first-come rules clog the pipes and slow lab work. Their plan weighs each stream's worth as bids state it.

Two sale tools are built for the task at hand. A greedy tool picks by worth per room in a fast pass. A knapsack sale tool, of VCG type, holds strong proof marks. Bids state data needs and the worth of the work. Sims pit both tools next to first-come rules. Done-time lags fall by vast shares at high load. Spread of lags shrinks, and load swings calm as well.
arxiv-2606-00590:
Alam, Salemi, and Zamani close the loop twixt a search agent and its hunt tool with a critic. Agent search steps through found proof to crack hard asks. Tuning the hunt tool for that loop most oft needs dear tags or joint training. Their frame, Critic-R, grades each step as it goes.

A critic reads the agent's own thought trace past each found batch. It calls if that batch can bear the next step of thought. One part, Critic-R-Zero, rewrites asks and hunt rules at use time in a loop. One part, Critic-Embed, trains hunt tools on good and bad loop paths. No hand tags are a must for that train. Tests on four sets lift hunt grade and reply truth.
arxiv-2606-01090:
Adly measures how much data a symmetry prior is worth in this 2026 paper. Theory says a built in symmetry cuts the samples a model needs by the size of the symmetry group. The claim is widely cited but rarely measured as a scaling law. Confounds blur past tests: the prior, its fit, and its compute all shift at once.

His testbed is a controlled task with cyclic symmetry. A wrong group control, with the same orbit size and matched compute, does worse than no constraint at all. A mismatched prior harms, not merely fails to help. An augmentation baseline with test time orbit averaging matches the symmetric model bit for bit. The measured exchange rate is 1.28, near the predicted 1.0 in sign and scale in his main test. Wider bootstraps soften that match, and a finer replication is inconclusive. He supplies an estimator that cancels the shared difficulty confound.
arxiv-2606-01190:
Groot Koerkamp introduces a new anchor scheme for sampling string positions in this 2026 paper. Minimizer schemes pick one k-mer from each window by a fixed order. They sample sparsely when the window is short against the k-mer length. For very small k, plain minimizers fail, and richer schemes are needed. Bidirectional string anchors are one such scheme.

His scheme looks at suffixes inside the window. It keeps those that occur nowhere else in the window: the unique substrings. From them it samples the start of the smallest suffix under a new anti-lexicographic order. That order minimizes the first character and maximizes the rest. A linear time streaming algorithm computes all such anchors in window sized memory. For the DNA alphabet at the smallest k, the scheme's density sits within one percent of the lower bound.
arxiv-2606-01390:
Spears introduces and solves Limit Continuous Poker, a stylized game. It builds on Von Neumann's Continuous Poker model. Bet sizes vary, but limits cap how large they can get. The variant keeps key features of real poker. Information asymmetry, bluffing, and balancing all survive. The game stays simple enough to solve analytically. Spears derives the Nash equilibrium strategy profile.

Bettor and caller strategies hinge on the bet size limits. As limits move to extreme values, strategies converge. They approach those of other continuous poker variants. Links to real-world play close the analysis. Limited bet sizing shapes optimal play in concrete ways. The work serves game theory readers and poker modelers.
arxiv-2606-02290:
Fring and Marquette study a ghostly model in three dimensions. The model is a sixth order Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator in its fully resonant form. At the classical level, its flow in phase space cannot be diagonalized. It splits into two Jordan chains of length three. Those chains are complex conjugates of each other. That split explains why solutions oscillate with secular terms.

When the system is quantized, the authors build intertwining operators. Quadratic mixes of those operators generate a hidden u(2,1) algebra. That algebra acts as a spectrum generating symmetry. The descendant spaces are finite dimensional and invariant. They carry Jordan structure of their own. An sl2 subalgebra splits them into irreducible modules. That split need not match the Jordan form of the Hamiltonian.
arxiv-2606-02490:
Oswald and Massart study neural networks that classify positive-definite matrices. Such matrices appear in imaging and signal data. A key layer type multiplies the input on both sides. The matrix is hit by a weight matrix and its transpose. This congruence-like layer sits at the core of SPDNet. A common rule forces the weight matrix to be semi-orthogonal.

The authors show that this rule limits what the network can express. For some activation functions, the whole design collapses. It equals a network with one hidden layer. The cause is a loss of spectral diversity in the layers. That loss follows from Poincaré's separation theorem. The team also compares final classifiers. Several Riemannian classifiers are weighed against the feature maps. Their fit with congruence layers is discussed in depth.
arxiv-2606-02590:
de Saxcé synthesizes a family of variational principles for dissipative mechanics. The work draws on ideas from Brezis, Ekeland, and Nayroles. It spans plasticity, friction contact, and fracture mechanics. These are hard problems in the study of how solids bend, rub, and break. A unified framework for dynamic dissipative systems is built on that base. The result is a space-time variational principle of minimum. Convex analysis and symplectic geometry supply the tools.

The paper stresses the essential ideas behind the principles. Worked examples, both in theory and in numbers, show how they are used. Readers get one frame where three hard problem classes meet. Plastic flow, frictional contact, and crack growth share a variational root. The synthesis aims to guide both theory and computation in mechanics and in physics at large.
arxiv-2606-02690:
Haberland and Buonanno speed up gravitational waveform models for long neutron star signals. Binary neutron star inspirals are long. Parameter inference needs waveforms that are faithful and cheap. Wrong or slow models risk false claims about nuclear matter. Their work implements the SEOBNRv5THM model in the frequency domain. The frame is effective-one-body theory for quasi-circular, spin-aligned systems.

A hybrid method does the work. The stationary-phase approximation covers the early inspiral. A fast Fourier transform treats the late and post-inspiral parts. The split is applied mode by mode. Accuracy near merger, where matter effects peak, is preserved. Mismatches against the baseline model stay excellent. Real and synthetic data tests agree. Generation speed can drop further with multibanding and relative binning. Faithful estimation within days of runtime becomes practical. The procedure extends to binary black holes.
arxiv-2606-02790:
Raipat and co-authors track how a disaster rewires the social networks of a community. Displacement after disasters fragments ties and weakens cohesion. Social capital shapes resilience, but its restructuring is poorly quantified. The team builds a spatially embedded, dynamic network framework. Social capital becomes a network of repeated encounter chances. Large-scale mobility data supplies the encounters. Temporal co-presence networks at third places track the change. The test case is the 2021 Marshall Fire in Colorado.

Displacement contracts the networks sharply. Mean weighted degree falls by 48 percent. Two counterfactual models isolate the mechanism. One removes nodes at random. The other removes people by their estimated chance of evacuating. Both predict lower connectivity than observed. The residual connectivity concentrates in bonding ties between similar people. Bridging ties prove fragile. Interaction also clusters more around third places. Those places anchor social persistence under disruption. Behavior, not just displacement, shapes community resilience.
arxiv-2606-02990:
Meng, Bao, and Xiao recast quantum purification as a task that unfolds over time. Noise is the main obstacle to quantum advantage. It degrades the states that quantum technology relies on. Purification tries to extract high-fidelity resources from noisy ensembles, but standard methods act only after noise has struck.

Their spatiotemporal framework spreads interventions across the noise process itself. This opens capabilities that static methods cannot reach. The resulting forward-assisted purifications extend what performance is achievable. In some regimes, a single-copy protocol already beats what up to 50 copies achieve under standard purification. The framework also circumvents known no-purification theorems, including for Bell-state ensembles. Cases once thought impossible become feasible. The authors present this as an efficient route to fighting noise in quantum systems.
arxiv-2606-03390:
Yuan, Wan, and Harada stretch how far a robot arm can travel along a straight path. Extreme motion generation seeks the longest Cartesian path a manipulator can follow on a set line inside its workspace. Path following is core to tasks such as coating and welding.

The catch is safety: the arm must dodge its joint limits through the whole run, a long-horizon problem. The team's hybrid controller splits the work by distance to those limits. A learned policy runs the far zone, where it can maximize reach. A classical model-based controller takes the near-boundary zone, where learned policies thin out for lack of data. The start pose is sampled by a conditional diffusion method, which lengthens the path further. On ten thousand straight-line tasks with a Franka arm, mean rollout length rose by about 27 percent over the model-based baseline.
arxiv-2606-03690:
Lei and co-authors design a secure drone-assisted system that senses and communicates at once. Integrated sensing and communication is a key tech for future wireless networks. A UAV platform serves legitimate users with data links. It jams eavesdroppers at the same time. An extended Kalman filter predicts and tracks the paths of both user types.

Secrecy rate is the score to maximize. Beamforming and the drone's own path are designed jointly. Practical limits cover sensing beamwidth, transmit power, and propulsion energy. The joint problem is highly non-convex. An iterative algorithm mixes block coordinate descent, successive convex approximation, and the Kalman filter. It yields a high-quality suboptimal design. Simulations show the scheme beats benchmark rivals clearly. Wireless engineers get a workable plan for secure aerial sensing networks.
arxiv-2606-03890:
Li and co-authors benchmark streaming spatial intelligence in multimodal models with OVO-S-Bench. Robots, AR systems, and self-driving agents reason from continuous first-person streams. Evidence often sits outside the current view. Offline video tests and event-focused sets miss that spatial demand. This benchmark is fully human-annotated: 1,680 questions over 348 videos. Each question carries a time stamp and an evidence window.

At test time the model sees only the video prefix before the query. Four levels rise in abstraction, from instant perception to allocentric mapping. Thirty-eight models face the set. The best trails human experts by 33 points under the same access rules. Allocentric mapping is the dominant bottleneck. Streaming-tuned and spatial-tuned models even trail their own backbones. Ungrounded chain-of-thought makes spatial errors worse. The testbed sets a demanding bar for next-generation systems.
arxiv-2606-03990:
Dravid and co-authors ask if neuron groups change in set ways with scale. Scaling laws tend to track broad values like loss. They study Rosetta Neurons, whose firing patterns match across trained models. Language models up to 30B and vision models up to 5B were tested. The shared neurons form a small, clear test case.

Their count grows slower than model size, in a sublinear power law. So their share of all neurons shrinks as models grow. These neurons also grow more selective and more single-meaning with scale. Other neurons stay less selective, a split they call polarization. A simple model of feature value versus neuron capacity explains both trends. A data-filtering case study shows the neurons' domain focus at work.
arxiv-2606-04090:
Daniel Kynoch leads a large collaboration in 2026 mapping the gas around extreme coronal line emitting galaxies, rare nuclei that shine with unusually strong high-ionization lines. Several of these galaxies are linked to stars torn apart by their central black holes.

The team assembled optical spectra of thirty-three such galaxies and split them into changing, disruption-linked sources and steady, active-nucleus systems. In the changing ones, the highest-ionization iron lines flared and faded first, followed by lower lines, while oxygen brightened, suggesting the ionizing light softened or the illumination front moved outward. Line widths placed the glowing gas between the fast broad-line zone and the calm outer region. Gas distance grew with black hole mass in both groups alike.
arxiv-2606-04190:
Andrea Bonito and co-authors, including Ronald DeVore, settle a basic question in 2026. How well can a convex function of several variables be rebuilt from point samples? And what shape must the sampling take?

They prove matching upper and lower bounds for the best possible recovery. The lower bound shows no method can do better, no matter how clever. The upper bound gives a method that reaches the limit. Nonlinear sampling schemes reshape the problem in a helpful way: points cluster where the function bends most. Tests in simulations matched the theory. The result closes a gap in the theory of function recovery from data. It also guides how to place sensors for curved fields.
arxiv-2606-04690:
Lyu and coauthors hunt for a disputed particle state called Sigma 1380 in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. A resonance, in this setting, is a very short lived particle that shows up as a bump in data. Two experiments, Belle and BESIII, measured a decay of a heavier particle that might reveal it.

The team built a model where some particles form through interactions after the decay happens. They added both a known nearby state and the disputed Sigma 1380, then compared model curves with data. Adding the disputed state improved how well the model matched the measured mass and angle patterns. They also mapped which parts of the data react most strongly to that extra state. Better future measurements of this decay, they argue, could settle whether the Sigma 1380 exists. The claim stays open for now, since other work has explained the data without it.
arxiv-2606-04890:
Dobzinski and Shaulker break a barrier in the theory of trade between a buyer and a seller, in a 2026 arXiv economics paper. Both parties' values are drawn from independent distributions, and the goal is maximizing social welfare. The best fixed price guarantees at least 72 percent of optimal welfare, and none can guarantee more than about 73.8 percent. No other incentive-compatible mechanism was known to beat them.

The authors study the buyer-offering mechanism with a reserve price: the buyer makes a take-it-or-leave-it offer no lower than the reserve. They show some reserve price always guarantees 74.6 percent of optimal welfare. This improves the best known guarantee and proves fixed-price mechanisms are not optimal for bilateral trade.
arxiv-2606-05790:
Todorcevic and Jing Zhang build extreme colorings of pairs from any uncountable set in a 2026 arXiv paper. A coloring paints each pair of elements with one of countably many colors. Ramsey-style theorems hope for large calm sets where few colors appear. Strong colorings dash that hope as hard as possible. Their method rests on oscillations, counts of how walks between ordinals cross.

For any uncountable cardinal, their coloring hits every color on every large rectangular grid. The test sets need only be stationary, a weak form of largeness, near their shared top. Two hoped-for principles fall at once: a stationary Erdős-Rado theorem and a higher-dimensional Friedman property. Both are shown inconsistent with standard set theory. The authors also prove the result is optimal in several directions. The construction extends a line of work on walks that began in the early nineteen eighties.
arxiv-2606-05990:
Guolin Qin and Zhang prove a Harnack inequality for a critical nonlinear equation, with fine print stated up front in a 2026 arXiv paper. Harnack inequalities bound how wildly a positive solution can vary across a ball. For the critical p-Laplace equation the tools fail: Kelvin transforms and moving spheres need conformal invariance that the linear-like case enjoys. The authors assume critical Sobolev growth and a monotonicity condition on the nonlinearity.

Their result rests on two inputs from earlier work. Blow-up limits must classify as the Aubin-Talenti bubbles, and necks need a preliminary decay control. The heart is a Pohozaev-type neck argument. It upgrades the preliminary singular decay rate to the sharp rate of the p-harmonic fundamental solution. That upgrade delivers the Schoen-type estimate with a dimensional constant. Conditional progress is still progress: the neck argument supplies the missing step for general exponents.
arxiv-2606-06090:
Yaoqi Chen and a team argue an agent's memory should store execution state, not similar text in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long tasks chain interdependent decisions, and one bad step cascades. Similarity-based memory fragments those trajectories and mixes good traces with erroneous ones. Mage stores interactions in a hierarchical state tree instead. The agent's state is the path from root to current node, blending subgoal summaries, recent traces, and hints from sibling branches.

Four operations maintain the tree. Grow records new steps; Compress summarizes finished subgoals; Maintain validates the summaries; Revise rewinds to a clean boundary and branches anew. Context growth stays bounded while flawed segments are quarantined off the active path. On the MemoryArena benchmark, task success rose by eight to twenty points over baselines. Token consumption fell by over half at the same time. State integrity, not retrieval volume, is the paper's measure of memory quality.
arxiv-2606-06290:
Irem Topal and co-authors examine the physics style patterns of brain activity in early psychosis in this 2026 arXiv paper. Healthy large scale brain activity shows scale invariant dynamics, patterns that look similar at every zoom level, suggesting the brain works near a critical regime. That regime is prized for long range links and efficient processing. Earlier studies of such disorders used scattered measures, so it was unclear whether they pointed at one shared change.

The team combined three analyses on resting state fMRI scans from patients and healthy controls: a phenomenological renormalization group method, power spectral density, and detrended fluctuation analysis. Controls showed the expected critical like scaling. Patients kept the same overall scale invariant pattern, so criticality was not simply lost. Instead, their scaling exponents shifted across several measures at once. The authors read this as a reshaping of collective brain activity within a preserved critical regime.
arxiv-2606-06890:
Vision language models often answer from what text usually says, not from what the picture shows. Zhou, Zhang, Wang, and Wang diagnose that habit in this 2026 arXiv paper. They call it visual ignorance: confident answers with weak grounding in the image. Their study looks both inside the model and at the benchmarks judging it.

Inside, they swap layers and probe each layer's signals. Visual meaning often fades in the middle layers. Later layers can bury what survives under text biases. Outside, they blur test images step by step. Many questions stayed answerable even when the image was nearly destroyed. That held across twelve benchmarks and three models. So current tests can reward ignoring the picture. The authors urge training and testing on counterfactual data. Such data would force models to actually look.
arxiv-2606-06990:
Fake patient records let researchers share medical data without exposing real patients. Jalen Jiang and co-authors build the arena where generators of those records compete fairly in this 2026 arXiv paper. The field's code bases clash with each other. Data loaders, library versions, and scoring rules all differ. Head to head comparisons have been nearly impossible.

Their framework runs one pipeline from data intake to final scores. It reimplements four known generators under one roof. A plain GPT-2 baseline joins them as a reality check. All models produce diagnosis code histories at full vocabulary size. A shared privacy utility suite grades every model the same way. Bootstrapped confidence intervals accompany all metrics. The analysis exposes weak performance on rare, long tail diagnoses. A simple general model proved surprisingly competitive. Specialized designs, the authors imply, must now earn their complexity.
arxiv-2606-07090:
A mostly real video with a few fake seconds is a nastier forgery than a fully fake one. Umur, Guslu, and Delibasoglu study that scenario in this 2026 arXiv paper. Existing data sets cover deepfakes and object removal well. They poorly model a short manipulated clip spliced into authentic footage that then resumes.

The authors review those data sets and pinpoint the gap. They curate a custom test set for the spliced case. Two detectors establish the first benchmark on it. A supervised probe on modern visual features classified frame by frame. It missed most manipulated frames, struggling to generalize. An unsupervised method compared consecutive frames by feature similarity. It found the tampering boundaries far more reliably. On one hundred untouched control videos it held a near zero false alarm rate. Video level accuracy reached ninety five percent.
arxiv-2606-07190:
Judging a partial solution by whether each step is correct misses the point: does it make success more likely? Zhou, Cao, and Ye build a grader around that question in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reasoning prefixes are the opening stretches of a model's chain of thought. Their value, the authors argue, is the gain in solve rate they cause.

A lightweight student model measures that gain directly. Conditioned on a good prefix, the student finishes more problems. The Prefix Utility Model learns to predict these gains from paired comparisons. It can score both finished attempts and prefixes still in progress. Across best of many sampling, beam search, and reinforcement learning on math tasks, the signal proved strong. Benefits grew with larger candidate pools and tighter reward sparsity. The utility scores also transferred to stronger policies than the student. Correctness is a proxy; outcome gain is the thing itself.
arxiv-2606-07690:
Ning Wang and co-authors present HARP, a cheaper way to choose finetuning data for large language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Picking the right training examples matters, but the most faithful selection methods retrain models many times to score each candidate, which is costly. Cheaper proxy methods are fast yet often miss what the target task actually needs.

HARP organises the training pool into a hierarchy of regions and leaves, then measures only representative leaves by actually finetuning on them. Statistical estimates fill in the value of unmeasured examples, and two selection rules balance caution about redundancy against rewards for complementary regions. In experiments the variants took the best results, beating the strongest baseline by up to about nine points. They did so while using roughly seven times fewer training examples, which cuts the selection bill sharply.
arxiv-2606-07790:
El Mir, Takáč, and Lahlou probe how language-model agents cooperate when one of them betrays the group, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is a four-player Stag Hunt, a game where cooperation pays best only if everyone commits. Talk between rounds is cheap talk, messages that cost nothing and bind no one. Byzantine agents signal cooperation, then defect.

Across six model families and seven hundred twenty trials, honest agents spotted betrayal within one round yet failed to adapt together. Many kept cooperating while being exploited, because the game's unanimity payoff blocks collective recovery. Restricting who can talk to whom collapsed cooperation when the restriction was announced, yet the same restriction applied silently left cooperation nearly perfect. Failure therefore comes from reasoning about hidden information, not from losing it. Two archetypes appeared in every cohort: models that defect forever after betrayal, and models that keep cooperating at cost.
arxiv-2606-07890:
Jaewook Lee and Zrnic study prediction when the world reacts to the predictor and drifts on its own, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Performative prediction covers feedback loops: a deployed model changes the population it predicts, as when disease forecasts trigger interventions that slow the disease. Classical distribution shift treats change as external. Real deployments mix both: partially performative prediction.

Their framework lets the data distribution evolve partly in response to the deployed model and partly through an outside process. The field's two central targets, performative stability, a model that remains best for the distribution it creates, and performative optimality, are extended into online versions tracking the moving environment. The authors analyse practical heuristics, especially repeated retraining, and characterise when it adapts and when it falls behind. The work gives learning systems a language for settings where fighting the drift and causing it are both part of the job.
arxiv-2606-08090:
Kyoungmin Kim, Martin Catheland, and Anastasia Ailamaki speed up a workhorse of data processing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The subject is the semantic filter: asking a language model a yes-no question about each document in a corpus. Calling the model on everything is the gold standard but prohibitively expensive, so systems cascade: a cheap proxy scores documents, and uncertain ones escalate.

The authors catalogue four structural weaknesses in current cascades. Each family commits to one representation and one fixed pipeline, winning only in a narrow regime. The strongest online proxies ignore established representation-learning tools and miss token-level evidence. They train on binary labels, discarding the big model's confidence exactly at the boundary documents that matter most. And their calibration is over-conservative, escalating far more documents than needed. Against this diagnosis they present a unified framework and an adaptive two-phase fix.
arxiv-2606-08190:
Chandia studies a question in string theory in this short 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is the heterotic pure spinor superstring, a form of string theory that treats supersymmetry, the symmetry between matter and force particles, in a clean algebraic way. Chandia asks when a curved ten-dimensional background still allows conserved worldsheet charges, quantities that stay fixed as the string moves and that match supersymmetry in ordinary spacetime. The charges must also respect a symmetry condition known as BRST invariance.

In flat space, these conditions reproduce the familiar generator of ten-dimensional supersymmetry, confirming the construction is sound. In curved space, they organize into a tidy set of constraints on the background geometry. The key object is a normalizable spinor superfield, a field with well-behaved size whose lowest part is the spinor used in standard treatments of compactification, where extra dimensions curl up small.
arxiv-2606-08390:
Kuskova, Zaytsev, and Coppedge ask when an interaction found by a neural network is real, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neural time-series models sometimes report that one variable modulates another's effect on a target. The authors argue this is a question of identifiability: whether the data could pin down one explanation at all. They study a model where source contributions are gated, meaning scaled up or down, by other lagged variables.

The analysis shows that capacity is not identifiability. Dependent inputs cause leakage between interaction terms, and low-dimensional support permits distinct decompositions that agree on all observed data while differing elsewhere. The authors then prove an identifiability theorem for normalized minimal decompositions under explicit support conditions. They package the theory into a pre-fit diagnostic, a check practitioners can run before training.
arxiv-2606-08790:
De Valois-Franklin and Bogdan specify RAILS, a clearing system for commerce between autonomous software agents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents now negotiate, buy services, and move money for their users. Yet no neutral mechanism decides whether an agent actually met its obligation, who is at fault when it did not, and what payment should follow. They call this the agentic clearing problem, arguing that paying, authorizing, and judging are each different from clearing.

RAILS combines a per-output reliability score, a published reliability record, and a clearing function that consumes both. Its protocol rests on seven primitives, from an Obligation Object stating the duty to Finality Rules closing the case. The central guarantee is a soundness property: no financially material settlement is issued on evidence weaker than the floor the obligation itself sets. The property can be checked against the specification, making the design falsifiable.
arxiv-2606-09090:
Treude and Baltes name a quiet decay creeping into AI-assisted programming: the instruction files guiding coding assistants drift out of sync with the code, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Developers now maintain persistent configuration files, such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, describing architecture and conventions to their AI tools. As software evolves, these files go stale, a phenomenon the authors call context rot, and stale context misleads every AI session trusting it. Documentation researchers spent decades building consistency checkers for exactly this class of problem.

The paper maps that toolbox, built for READMEs, comments, and API docs, onto the new artifacts as a roadmap. As evidence, the authors applied a README and wiki consistency checker to a representative sample of 356 repositories. It found stale code-element references in 23 percent of them. The result shows existing tools already surface context rot unmodified, giving the field a running start.
arxiv-2606-09290:
Xu and colleagues split visual reasoning across a team of agents that are all the same model wearing different hats, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A single chain of thought commits early to one reading of an image, then defends it, hallucinations included. Visual Para-Thinker++ instead instantiates one shared multimodal policy as three roles. A Main Agent decomposes the task, Worker Agents reason in parallel under context isolation, and a Summary Agent reconciles the full worker traces.

Training matches the structure: Multi-Agent Capability Injection teaches the shared policy its roles, and Role-Decoupled Optimization assigns role-specific rewards to each role's tokens, cutting conflicts. A native engine reuses the shared visual prefix and key-value cache across agents. Across six benchmarks, from counting to RefCOCO grounding and HallusionBench, it beat single-trajectory and parallel baselines. Gains were strongest exactly where single chains fail, on hallucination-sensitive questions.
arxiv-2606-09390:
Alina Marcu and her colleagues study whether a robot can read human intent from body pose alone in this 2026 arXiv paper. In rescue work and other long-distance settings, a person's face and voice may be unavailable, yet their movements still carry messages. Existing datasets mix body motion with speech and facial cues, so the body-only signal has never been isolated.

The team releases a dataset of real full-body poses covering ten communicative intents. They benchmark models from skeleton graph classifiers to motion-forecasting networks, reporting speed on an embedded processor as well as accuracy. Average recognition recall on their real data reached about eighty-seven percent across twelve recognisers. They also show that a model's agreement with its own earlier predictions works as a reliability signal, and prove that the chance such a prediction is correct grows with each consistent step.
arxiv-2606-09490:
Gyeongseob Song and a large international team study how turbulence in stratified fluids transports buoyancy in bursts rather than steadily in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stratification, the layering of fluid by density, shapes the atmosphere and oceans. The authors ran direct numerical simulations of the Boussinesq equations, the standard model for such flows, sweeping the key control parameters across the geophysical range.

They varied the Froude number, which measures stratification strength, from one hundredth to one, and the Prandtl number between one and six. The buoyancy flux showed strongly non-Gaussian tails, with kurtosis reaching about one hundred. Its skewness grew as a power law as stratification weakened, following an exponent near zero point two eight, then saturated in the passive-scalar limit. The team traces the strong events to an energy defect between vertical and potential energy.
arxiv-2606-09590:
Sasha Ronaghi and a large team test how much patient data a medical language model can be made to spill in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such models train on real clinical notes and may memorise private facts. Most privacy tests just check if training text can be pulled back out.

Their framework grades attacks by access, from facts anyone can guess to leaked scraps of a note. At each tier they check word-for-word recall of patient text and leakage of sensitive diagnoses. The test model had trained on about three hundred seventy-eight thousand notes. Plain visit details, like name, birth date, and provider, drew out high recall across a patient's whole timeline. Recovery of abortion and HIV status scored well above chance. Yet over a third of the recalled tokens were mere form templates, so raw recall overstates true disclosure.
arxiv-2606-09890:
Hainiu Xu and a large team test whether a model can smell trouble before any bad act lands in this 2026 arXiv paper. Safety checks today judge a full run after the harm is done. Their PreAct-Bench instead serves a cut-off trace of clean-looking steps. The judge must call if the path will end in an unethical act. One thousand paired good and bad paths span five domains.

The bench scores calls at set slices of each path, so early skill counts most. Humans did well on the task. Strong models did not, even guardrail tools and hidden-state probes. One odd find: turning on a model's own reasoning made its calls worse, not better. The gap shows that seeing risk ahead is a skill apart from spotting it in full. The team release the data and code so others can chase that skill.
arxiv-2606-10290:
Michael Bommarito catalogues one of the Linux kernel's broadest attack surfaces, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer security. Drivers define thousands of such commands themselves, parse arguments in kernel context, and are catalogued in no central place, so a handler that trusts an unvalidated argument length can corrupt kernel memory. His census builds a queryable inventory of that entire surface from source code.

A deterministic analysis pass over an all-modules kernel build recovers hundreds of ioctl dispatch entry points, over a thousand decoded command codes, thousands of controlled-input sinks, and over a thousand permission gates. A second pass encodes the kernel's documented threat model, separating capability-ungated commands reachable by unprivileged users from gated ones. Backtesting against twenty-two recent in-tree ioctl vulnerabilities validates the census, which is released publicly for security researchers and kernel auditors.
arxiv-2606-10390:
Gao and his team at Tsinghua University propose a CT scanner design that spends detector resolution only where it matters, in a 2026 arXiv paper on medical imaging. Their foveated-imaging geometry design mixes a local portion of high-resolution data into a mostly low-resolution capture, described by two indices: the high-resolution data fraction and the pixel-size ratio between detector types. A seeded diffusion rebuild then extends the sharp region to the full field of view.

The diffusion method injects the measured high-resolution information into in-between image estimates in both projection and image domains during reverse diffusion, improving fit with the measured data. On a public grand-challenge clinical dataset and swine lung scans, the method beat other super-resolution approaches on image-quality and fidelity metrics. That supports foveated capture as a cheaper route to high-resolution CT.
arxiv-2606-10490:
Albert Civit-Bertran, Suzuki, and Futatani compare two codes for fusion plasma equilibria in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is the Large Helical Device, a stellarator that confines hot plasma in a twisted magnetic field. VMEC, the standard solver, assumes perfectly nested flux surfaces. HINT makes no such assumption and can represent magnetic islands and chaotic edge regions. The authors run both codes on three magnetic-axis configurations as plasma pressure, measured by beta, rises.

At low beta the two codes agree closely, so the nested-surface picture holds. Above a critical beta that depends on the configuration, the solutions diverge, showing the assumption failing. In the HINT results the enclosed plasma volume shrinks at high beta because the field near the edge turns stochastic, an effect VMEC cannot represent by construction. The effect strengthens from inward- to outward-shifted configurations, driven by Pfirsch-Schlüter currents.
arxiv-2606-10590:
Abhrojyoti Sen and Siltakoski extend the regularity theory of a two-speed diffusion equation in this 2026 arXiv paper in analysis. The parabolic double phase equation blends two gradient growth rates via a coefficient that can vanish on part of the domain. They model anisotropic composites and are notorious for the Lavrentiev phenomenon, an energy gap that breaks naive arguments. The authors prove local higher integrability: the gradient of a Hölder continuous weak solution is more integrable than the energy class guarantees.

The advance is the price of admission. The result holds under a relaxed gap condition on the two exponents, a bound purely parabolic in nature, stricter than the optimal elliptic one. The coefficient's weak regularity, growing from its zero set only in a one-sided way, motivates a new mollification, the slanted Steklov average. Sharper gap bounds widen the class of composite models with such well-behaved solutions.
arxiv-2606-10690:
Anguiano-Arteaga and colleagues publish a data set from a famous flyby in this 2026 arXiv paper on planetary science. En route to Saturn, Cassini swung past Jupiter in late 2000 and early 2001, its Visible and Infrared Mapping Spectrometer recording spectral cubes of the giant planet. The team now presents a calibrated catalogue of those observations plus its processing workflow. The workflow revises both channels' calibration, fixing cases the standard pipeline handled badly, corrects pointing misalignments between cubes and geometry data, and applies dark-signal corrections.

The products are radiometrically consistent cubes with geometry backplanes and wavelength data, validated against reference spectra from the literature. Together the channels span the near-ultraviolet to the thermal infrared, giving a uniform record of Jupiter under many viewing geometries, from approach to nightside crossings. The catalogue is public through a Zenodo archive, ready for analysis twenty-five years after the data were taken.
arxiv-2606-11090:
Sheshadri proves a lower bound in algebraic complexity theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. A polynomial's symmetric determinantal complexity is the size of the smallest symmetric matrix of affine-linear forms whose determinant equals it. His target is the diagonal power sum, the sum of each variable raised to the number of variables.

He proves its symmetric determinantal complexity is at least a constant times n squared, the constant approaching one over twice Euler's number. The engine is a general theorem about smooth hypersurfaces, surfaces cut out by one equation. It ties the top polar degree, a count of special tangent points, to the matrix size through a binomial bound. The proof redoes a rank-one kernel incidence analysis in the symmetric setting, with a local normal form at polar points and a multihomogeneous Bézout count. It is the symmetric companion to his earlier non-symmetric work.
arxiv-2606-11190:
Kamai and four co-authors map when multimodal learning helps and when it hurts in a 2026 arXiv paper. Two paradigms dominate: cross-modal alignment, pulling data views into a shared representation, and cross-modal prediction, predicting one view from another. Which will succeed on a given dataset, or whether combining views beats the best single view, is not systematically understood.

In a unified linear framework, the authors derive separation ratios for both objectives. Alignment whitens each modality and fails when nuisance variation is strongly correlated across views. Prediction uses one-sided whitening, hinging on the source modality's quality. The ratios carve problems into four regimes: both work, alignment only, prediction only, or neither, where cross-modal training actively harms. A data-driven procedure locates a dataset in the diagram from a small labeled subsample, before any training. Experiments on synthetic, stereo-vision, image-caption, and astrophysical data confirmed the regimes.
arxiv-2606-11490:
Chu, Zhang, Serbetci, Katiyar, Modad, and Molisch build a foundation model for indoor localization in a 2026 arXiv paper. Locating user equipment indoors from wireless signals is hard: building geometry varies, the set of detectable access points changes, and signals are heterogeneous. Learning-based methods often work only in limited settings and degrade under environment shifts. OmniLoc is, to the authors' knowledge, the first foundation-model approach built directly on wireless data for this task.

Three designs carry it. A unified tokenization module converts varied wireless signals into a common form. A geometry-aware Transformer emphasizes dominant access points while pooling evidence from supporting ones. A location head conditions regression on geometric embeddings for stable predictions. On a large in-house dataset and a public benchmark, OmniLoc clearly outperforms existing methods. Its components also improve other backbones when integrated, and it transfers well to unseen buildings.
arxiv-2606-11590:
Dapeng Jin is the named author on a 2026 arXiv paper about keeping clocks in step at the Circular Electron Positron Collider, a planned accelerator in China. Its clock must reach 192 control nodes along a tunnel 100 kilometres long, with timing spread under thirty picoseconds, each a trillionth of a second. The design builds on White Rabbit, a proven network method for precise timing.

The redesign replaces a noisy analogue tuning chain with a digital chip controlling phase directly. Restart uncertainty falls from nearly eighty-nine picoseconds to twelve, peak to peak. Measured precision stays under four picoseconds over both one metre and fifty kilometres of fibre. In a twelve-level chain, the far end stays near seven picoseconds even through a thirteen-degree temperature swing. Jitter stays below one picosecond, and a four-level chain ran steadily for twenty-five hours, well inside the budget.
arxiv-2606-11690:
Chitral Patil argues that public cost calculators badly misprice self-hosted language models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Every calculator surveyed treats hardware utilisation as a fixed input, sometimes silently assumed total. In reality the request rate an operator receives sets how busy the hardware stays, through a queueing relationship called Little's Law.

On identical H100 hardware, effective cost ranges from well under a quarter to over fifteen dollars per million output tokens, purely by varying the load. Underuse multiplies cost by roughly two and a half to twenty-four times at ordinary enterprise loads, and up to about thirty-six times near idle. Forty-two benchmarks across three model families validate the method, and an open-source meter reports real costs against an operator's own traffic. A larger sparse model can even beat a smaller dense one on cost at full load.
arxiv-2606-11990:
Amir El-Ghoussani and three colleagues predict machine failures with a borrowed brain in this 2026 arXiv paper. Useful-life prediction forecasts when factory kit will fail, enabling planned upkeep. Task-specific models usually need much feature work or large labelled datasets, both scarce in factories. Their approach freezes a pretrained time-series foundation model, Chronos-2, as a feature source.

Sensor windows pass through the frozen model, and a small network learns to map the resulting features to remaining life. Experiments use real factory sensor data from two device types. The model's features beat recurrent and transformer baselines. A context-length test shows longer histories improve results clearly. The authors argue this offers a practical route to failure prediction. Future work targets error bars and robustness when sensors go missing.
arxiv-2606-12090:
In this 2026 arXiv paper, Li and Rudge ask why a predicted peak in seismic energy loss is missing from lab tests on dry olivine. Olivine is the main mineral of Earth's upper mantle. The suspect process is elastically accommodated grain-boundary sliding, where mineral grains slide past each other while the grains stay elastic, meaning they spring back. Classic theory predicts a sharp loss peak, yet dry olivine shows almost none.

The team runs finite-element simulations, which solve a rock sample cell by cell, on patterns of irregular grains. Changing grain shapes alters the baseline response. A wider spread in grain size alone brings only modest changes and little broadening. Giving grain boundaries a broad spread of viscosities, or flow resistances, flattens and widens the peak into a weak background across many frequencies. So a missing peak can still hide real sliding.
arxiv-2606-12290:
Zeming Fei and co-authors show that the defense for AI agent memory guards the wrong thing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents store memory as a graph of linked facts. Provenance defenses check the origin of whatever facts get retrieved, rejecting tainted records. The flaw: retrieval itself is a global selection over graph structure that anyone can write to. An attacker who adds harmless structure, no fake facts at all, can steer which facts get picked.

In one test, a sourceless structural write misdirected twenty-eight irreversible ledger transfers across 499 live actions. Faithful provenance checking allowed every one; the authors' AuthSelect stopped every one. Their criterion: a selector is exposed only if its structural scoring can shove facts across the top ranks, as PageRank's walk mass allows but content-only reranking forbids. AuthSelect recomputes selection on the authenticated subgraph alone, with no over-blocking and 2 to 3 percent added latency.
arxiv-2606-12390:
Merten and co-authors follow cosmic rays escaping from bubbles blown by stellar winds, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Massive stars and clusters inflate wind bubbles with an inner termination shock where rays accelerate. Standard theory expects escaping rays to follow a familiar energy spectrum. But bubbles evolve: the forward shock moves, and transport inside changes with time. The team solves the time-dependent transport equation by converting it into stochastic equations inside the CRPropa simulation framework.

During the wind-driven phase, escaping spectra come out harder than the conventional expectation, richer at high energies. The turbulence model matters greatly at low energies. Some settings strongly suppress the lowest-energy escapees, trapping them inside the bubble. Pure Kolmogorov turbulence, by contrast, barely changes the spectrum yet caps energies near twenty teraelectronvolts. Trapped low-energy rays pile up grammage, material traversed, with possible multi-messenger radiation signatures.
arxiv-2606-12690:
Zhou and Miao present EWAM, an enhanced world action model that lets a robot adapt while it works, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A world action model predicts how the scene will change and generates actions from that prediction. Static versions fail through collisions, empty grasps, and confident but wrong perception, and cannot learn from what just happened. EWAM keeps a pretrained Cosmos policy backbone frozen and adds 4 trainable layers.

The layers retrieve past experience, detect anomalies when predicted and real states diverge, route situations toward direct execution, cautious replanning, or rollback recovery, and correct outgoing actions. On a banana-into-bowl task run with no new demonstrations, EWAM matches the backbone's success rate while cutting completion time from 25.60 to 9.27 seconds in the test. Path length falls from 1.81 metres to 0.83 metres across the same runs, and faults drop from 13.5 to 2.2 per episode on average.
arxiv-2606-12790:
Namuduri and colleagues propose Genie, a fine-grained metric for measuring how novel a language model's response is, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models are known to produce uncreative, repetitive outputs. But existing creativity scores are holistic: a single number, often based on distance from other responses, that cannot say what makes one answer original and another mundane. Novelty is task-specific, resting on plot and character in stories, or on motivation and methodology in scientific proposals.

Genie instead extracts task-relevant features automatically, by generating questions whose answers reveal each feature, and measures novelty feature by feature against a population of responses. The authors show holistic metrics struggle to capture this high-dimensional structure and give no insight into which properties they reward. Applying Genie to methods designed to boost creativity then shows where those methods improve novelty and where they do not.
arxiv-2606-12890:
Naveen and colleagues propose RepMT-SAC, a representation-based reinforcement learning framework for multi-task skill transfer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is a family of tasks that share system dynamics but differ in rewards or reference objectives, as when one quadcopter must track many trajectories.

RepMT-SAC uses spectral decomposition of the Markov decision process to capture the transferable dynamics. The value function is structured as a task-agnostic core, standing for what all tasks share, plus a task-specific adjustment. This split supports zero-shot results on in-distribution tasks and rapid few-shot adaptation to out-of-distribution tasks, because a new task mainly needs learning the adjustment rather than a policy from scratch. RepMT-SAC beats the baselines by up to 30 percent, showing that splitting shared dynamics from task objectives lifts both sample efficiency and generalisation.
arxiv-2606-13090:
Stanish and MacTaggart investigate the field line slippage rate as a physics-weighted proxy for magnetic reconnection in force-free field extrapolations of the corona, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The slippage rate measures the deviation of magnetic field lines from ideal evolution due to non-ideal terms in Ohm's law.

For these extrapolations, the authors show that the resistivity-induced slippage rate is governed by cross-field gradients of the field-aligned twist, establishing a connection between current structure and reconnection signatures. They then examine the relationship with the squashing factor Q, used to locate quasi-separatrix layers. A scaling estimate shows strong squashing amplifies slippage only insofar as it produces small transverse length scales. So large Q alone does not guarantee reconnection. Applied to extrapolations of NOAA active region 11158 around the X2.2 flare of 15 February 2011, the slippage rate reveals reconnection signatures tied to phases of the region's evolution.
arxiv-2606-13690:
Zou and Zou present a computing model built around indirection in this 2026 arXiv paper, framed as the basis for shared intelligent computing systems. The paper reviews how basic results shaped the mainstream digital computer paradigm. They include Turing's computability theory, Kleene's formal theory of small strings, von Neumann's stored-program design, and Turing's hypothesis on machine judgement in artificial intelligence. Against that background the authors introduce an indirect computing model and an indirect formal method compatible with both large and small strings of symbols.

Using Chinese information data as the running example, they sketch the design of a collaborative intelligent computing system prototype combining a human-computer interface with shared computing programs. The claim: optimised cloud computing, in their vision, evolves from data centres toward knowledge centres. The paper sets out a programme rather than experiments, with principles and a prototype concept.
arxiv-2606-13790:
Chen and colleagues present a new sampling method for lattice field theory, the grid-based approach used to compute how particles interact. Standard Markov chain methods slow down badly near phase changes, where each new sample looks much like the last. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds the Stochastic Path Sampler, which learns paths that carry random field arrangements from a simple starting spread toward the target spread described by the theory.

Two neural networks learn the forward and backward paths, guided by a variational free energy score drawn from nonequilibrium thermodynamics, the physics of systems pushed between states. An independence Metropolis Hastings correction step then fixes the remaining bias in each proposed sample. On the two-dimensional phi-four theory, a standard test case, the sampler matches Hybrid Monte Carlo quality for magnetization and susceptibility. Its samples also decorrelate much faster near the critical region, where older methods struggle most.
arxiv-2606-14090:
Kumari's team designs a signature scheme letting whole org trees sign data, checked as one compact bundle. In identity-based cryptography, an email-like name is the public key, removing certificate paperwork. A hierarchy delegates key-making downward from a root authority, and an aggregator merges many signatures into one. Their 2026 arXiv paper gives the first lattice-based construction of such a scheme, HIBS-DA, with post-quantum security from lattice hardness.

Users at different levels sign alone; a designated aggregator combines them, cutting message and verification costs. The analysis proves correctness, unforgeability, and consistency. The scheme is non-interactive, with zero round complexity, and every step has a stated cost. Target settings are large structured organizations: universities, firms, and government agencies. The authors argue it suits spread-out systems needing tiered authentication.
arxiv-2606-14290:
Siddiqah, Vasim, and Nabi derive one closed-form formula for the gluon content of a fast proton at small momentum fraction, valid from the saturated core to the dilute tail. At small Bjorken x, gluon densities soar and nonlinear effects cap growth; the color dipole gluon distribution encodes this regime. Its analytic form across all transverse momenta was open. Their 2026 arXiv paper starts from a general solution of the Balitsky-Kovchegov equation of saturation physics, written with the dilogarithm function.

Substituting that S-matrix into the definition and evaluating the Fourier-Bessel transform yields, at leading logarithmic accuracy, a closed formula. An ultraviolet-divergent piece vanishes identically. At x values for the future Electron-Ion Collider, it shows an inversion of the x-ordering at the saturation scale: curves for different x cross there. The same inversion appears in the BGK model: a model-independent signature of gluon saturation.
arxiv-2606-14490:
Prinoth and co-authors reanalyze ten hot giant planets in a 2026 arXiv study. Hot and ultra-hot Jupiters are gas giants close to their stars. Iron and titanium in their air trace heat and chemistry. The team used high-resolution spectra from two large telescopes. They searched in a uniform way for neutral iron and titanium absorption.

They found iron in seven planets and titanium in four. Each find passed a five-sigma confidence bar. A new metric compares the two elements head to head. That metric dropped sharply toward cooler planets. Flat temperature models could match this only with odd assumptions. They needed titanium loss growing toward cooler worlds, as cold-trapping would cause. Models with inverted temperature profiles fit the trend well on their own. In those models titanium turns into an oxide in deep cool layers. It then condenses out of the visible gas.
arxiv-2606-14690:
Aznag, Cummings, and Elmachtoub measure the difficulty of active learning across groups in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting estimates the mean of several groups, like treatment arms. A sampling budget is spent adaptively to cut the worst group's uncertainty. The learner chooses which group to sample next based on results so far.

The authors develop a local minimax framework. They prove the first general lower bound for this max-risk objective. It holds across any finite-variance hypothesis class. The bound splits difficulty into three orthogonal factors. One is a budget term. One is a heteroscedasticity index for how unevenly uncertainty spreads. The third is a new complexity measure called variance local curvature. It captures how much information a small variance change creates. Comparisons with the best known upper bound show near-optimality, except in highly heterogeneous cases.
arxiv-2606-14790:
Li and co-authors turn multi-agent workflows into runnable protocols in a 2026 arXiv paper. Language-model agent systems coordinate planning, tool use, and human input. Trust suffers at the vague edge between prompts and the harness running them. Nobody has a principled way to choose which promises belong in prompts. Nor which should become binding structure.

Their system, XFlow, gives a protocol language. It reads like a written protocol yet compiles and runs as a program. Loose meaning work stays inside actors. Chosen promises move into harness structure that can be checked and enforced. At run time, lifecycle-governed symbols act as typed state cells. They carry checks and commit states. Actor outputs are screened before becoming shared state. Tests in tight dialogue, long-context reasoning, and software work show gains in trust.
arxiv-2606-14990:
Yin and Yu replace the fixed activation inside sparse autoencoders with a learnable rational function in a 2026 study. Sparse autoencoders split a language model's activations into readable features for probing how models work. Standard designs hard-code one sparsity gate, such as ReLU, JumpReLU, or TopK, each with flaws.

Their Rational Sparse Autoencoder starts from a pretrained baseline, fits rational coefficients with a Remez-style procedure, then fine-tunes under the standard objective. Theory shows rational gates can mimic those gates on compact domains with few parameters. Tests use residual-stream activations from three open-weight language models across all three baseline families. After fine-tuning, the rational version improves reconstruction measures and downstream behavior measures alike. Feature interpretability under sparse probing does not suffer. The upgrade adds only a few scalar parameters per unit and runs in minutes on one graphics card.
arxiv-2606-15190:
Bödeker and coauthors detail a lattice surgery teleportation protocol for surface code qubits in a 2026 quantum computing study. Surface codes store one logical qubit across many physical qubits on a two-dimensional grid. Lattice surgery merges and splits patches to entangle or teleport logical states. The protocol suits superconducting chips, where only neighboring qubits interact. They weigh design choices that near-term experiments must settle.

Variants differ in how many stabilizer readouts the surgery needs and where they sit. The team tests adaptive readouts, where later checks depend on earlier outcomes. Adaptive schemes trade latency against error rates, winning only in certain regimes. They vary the size of the interface region joining the two patches. Simulations with a Pauli error model bring a surprise there. Enlarging the interface never raised the teleportation success probability in any tested scenario. The results give experimentalists a map for first logical entanglement demonstrations.
arxiv-2606-15290:
Deme and coauthors settle which generalized Pell numbers are concatenations of two others, in a 2026 number theory paper. The k-generalized Pell numbers extend the classical Pell sequence with a recurrence. Concatenation glues the decimal digits of two numbers into a number, like one and two making twelve. The question is which members arise as such gluings. Similar puzzles were solved for Fibonacci and Lucas numbers. The authors set up the Diophantine equation and solve it.

For the classical case k equals two, one solution exists. The fourth Pell number, twelve, is the concatenation of one and two. For every k of three or more, they prove no solutions exist at all. The proof works through the sequence's dominant root and recurrence structure. The result closes the Pell entry in a catalogue of concatenation problems. It shows digit-gluing phenomena in these sequences are rarer than they first appear.
arxiv-2606-15390:
Wang and coauthors present Assay in a 2026 machine learning paper, a method for auditing the skill libraries that AI agents accumulate from experience. Agents increasingly store natural-language skills, short rules learned from past tasks, for reuse on new ones. Libraries are usually curated by model judgment, with no check that a kept skill actually helps. Assay instead measures each skill's causal effect by randomly masking skills and watching task outcomes.

The audit exposes strong heterogeneity: over ninety percent of skills help on some tasks and hurt on others, so their effects cancel in averages and global pruning misses them. Assay restructures the library offline and suppresses, for each new task, the skills predicted to hurt it. On the hardest split of the AppWorld benchmark, one model sets a new best score. The bottleneck, the authors show, is matching skills to tasks at run time, not deleting bad skills outright.
arxiv-2606-15590:
Nakhli and colleagues improve zero-shot image segmentation in 2026 by mining the internal features of text-to-image diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion. Current methods extract features at one fixed timestep, forcing a trade-off between fine detail and rich context. The team instead builds Contextual Similarity Maps, fusing high-resolution attention maps with encoder features from the network for each pixel.

Their second advance rests on an emergent pattern they identify inside the denoising process: early timesteps carry part-level abstractions, while later ones carry whole-object abstractions. A new mechanism picks the best timestep for each pixel, so parts and objects are each read at the stage where they are clearest. Across experiments the method consistently beats existing zero-shot segmentation baselines. The result turns a quirk of diffusion internals into a usable signal for segmenting images the model was never trained to label.
arxiv-2606-16090:
Zhang and colleagues ask in 2026 whether particle exchange statistics, a quantum property rarely used in learning, can improve quantum machine learning. Quantum kernels measure similarity between data states inside a quantum feature space. Bosons bunch symmetrically, fermions avoid each other antisymmetrically, and anyons take fractional phases in between. The authors build one kernel framework spanning all three.

Three analyses support the fractional case. Mean dimension results show fractional phases reach feature-space directions that the symmetric and antisymmetric limits cannot. The resulting matrices separate further from the baseline for distinct particles and show lower label-linked complexity. On learning benchmarks, anyonic kernels beat their bosonic and fermionic counterparts in the reported tests, with stronger target alignment. Exchange statistics thus become a tunable design resource for quantum kernels. The simple model keeps the fractional phase while reducing braid structure to permutations.
arxiv-2606-16490:
Chen and co-authors teach two robots to collaborate in 2026 from one human operator's demos. Joint mobile manipulation couples two bimanual robots through shared rigid and deformable objects. Failures come less from poor local skill than from mistimed waiting, yielding, pulling, releasing, or repositioning. Synchronized two-operator demos are impractical to collect, and explicit communication is disallowed.

Sequential Asymmetric Imitation first trains Robot A from one-sided demonstrations with a compliant human partner. Robot B then trains against the deployed Robot A policy. Finally, Robot A is refined with sparse human help near coordination failures. The curriculum exposes the pair to delay, phase mismatch, weak yielding, and interaction conflict. Across deformable spreading, shared-workspace collection, and rigid transport tasks, the method improves task success, phase sync, and partner-contingent yielding over independent imitation, per the report. Teamwork, it suggests, can be curriculum-designed rather than communicated.
arxiv-2606-16590:
López and co-authors borrow exploration noise from babies in 2026, and find deep RL agents learn faster for it. Exploration is usually white noise, jitter with no memory. Correlated colored noise explores more smoothly and covers state space better. Measuring infants, the team finds babies' end-effector speed spectra follow colored noise whose spectral exponent grows with age.

Their mechanism raises the correlation of the agent's noise during training by steps, tracking the infant statistics. Across several RL tasks, the infant-inspired noise produces structured exploratory behavior and improves learning efficiency over standard strategies, per the report. The result adds motor development to the list of curricula agents can steal: not the goal, not the reward, but the texture of the flailing itself. Sometimes the best search strategy is the one evolution debugged in the nursery.
arxiv-2606-16690:
Zhou and colleagues introduce a safety monitor for robot manipulation in a 2026 robotics paper. Learned robot policies can act well in calm settings, yet open workspaces bring moving objects, brief occlusions and bumps near the planned motion. Older monitors watch the whole camera view or the policy's uncertainty, so they often cannot tell real execution risk from harmless visual change.

Their monitor, PATCH, works from the robot's active action chunk, the short block of motion now running. It projects an execution corridor, predicts how image patches inside should evolve, and filters out change caused by the robot itself. Persistent unexplained change becomes a local alarm signal. A router can then pause the policy, switch to a recovery source, and resume once the disturbance subsides. On real robot data and live deployments, PATCH gives steadier, better-targeted triggers than rival monitors, with fewer false alarms on clean runs.
arxiv-2606-16890:
Sanjay Basu tests how clinical AI fails in a 2026 paper on question answering over electronic health records. Headline accuracy hides the pattern of errors. Drawing on theory about transformer limits on composing steps, Basu predicts that questions needing more reasoning hops should fail far more often.

A pre-set taxonomy counts the distinct reasoning steps each question needs, across three hundred clinician-written record questions in the MedAlign collection. Three models from two providers are tested, in plain and extended-thinking modes. Every model declines steadily as hop count rises from one to four, with accuracy roughly halving in some cases. Statistical trend tests confirm the slide in each model, and reasoning-specialized models checked later show the same ceiling. The finding matters practically: a single accuracy number can hide a model that handles simple lookups yet breaks on the multi-step questions clinicians actually ask.
arxiv-2606-16990:
Grlj and Lauda compress persistent Laplacian spectra for learning in a 2026 paper on topological data analysis. Persistent homology tracks how holes in data appear and vanish across scales, but it ignores geometry that keeps changing after a hole is born. Persistent Laplacians add that geometric information through their spectra, yet full spectra are long and vary in length between scales.

The proposal distills each spectrum into three invariants with clear meaning. They are Betti numbers, which count holes, the spectral gap, and analytic torsion, a quantity borrowed from geometry. On benchmarks spanning handwritten digits, molecular data and protein binding data, this fixed-length summary captures the core signal of the full spectrum. Sometimes it beats the full spectrum, since dropping high-frequency eigenvalues also drops noise. The summary removes the hand-tuning that spectral feature engineering usually demands.
arxiv-2606-17090:
Bryngelson writes a Python route straight to Apple's neural accelerator in a 2026 software paper. Every recent Apple device carries the Apple Neural Engine, a fixed-function chip for neural computation. Normally it is reachable only through CoreML, which treats it as a scheduling hint: nothing guarantees the engine runs your model, and work can silently land on the CPU or GPU instead.

ANEForge compiles a lazy tensor graph, built from dozens of fused and bridge operators, into one engine program dispatched through Apple's own daemon stack. It goes beyond inference: fused attention, streamed compressed weights, resident optimizer state, and even training's forward, backward and update steps run on the engine. Small programs complete near the hardware's dispatch floor, and standard networks validate end to end. The catch is fragility: the private interfaces carry no contract, so each release is verified against a recorded system version.
arxiv-2606-17490:
Sakai, Inoue, and Owen present a 2026 arXiv paper revisiting whether winds blown off the accretion disks of active galaxies can explain the cosmic gamma-ray and neutrino backgrounds. Both backgrounds are diffuse glows whose sources remain unsettled, and disk winds were a live candidate. Earlier estimates swung widely because wind power and surrounding densities are poorly pinned down, so the authors rebuild the model with fresh calibration data from nearby Seyfert galaxies and new X-ray constraints.

Cosmic rays accelerated at the wind's forward and reverse shocks produce the modelled light and neutrinos through several channels. Spread over a full population of active galaxies, the winds supply only a small share of either background at the energies checked. The authors conclude disk winds are unlikely to dominate both glows at once. Nearby Seyfert galaxies with ultrafast outflows are flagged as sharp future tests.
arxiv-2606-17690:
Wach and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper cataloguing the very-high-energy gamma-ray environments of pulsars, gathered from every major ground-based observatory. Pulsar winds inflate nebulae and halos whose shapes and spectra change as the pulsar ages and moves through its surroundings. Until now the observations sat scattered across five instruments' separate publications. The catalogue merges them into one homogenised record and cross-matches each source with the pulsar data held in the radio and satellite catalogues astronomers use.

The final list covers well over a hundred gamma-ray sources tied to a few dozen pulsars at all life stages. Young, powerful pulsars near the Galactic plane dominate, but middle-aged halo systems are a growing share. Luminosity correlates only weakly with age, pointing to environment and particle transport as the real drivers. Five pulsars are flagged as prime targets where a nebula should be detectable next.
arxiv-2606-18090:
Elsner and colleagues add a missing piece to simulations of charge flow in rubrene, a star material for organic electronics, in a 2026 paper. Rubrene carries electric holes with striking ease, but predicting that ease from first principles is hard. Direct dynamics can track the carrier wave as it moves, with no set mechanism assumed. Past large runs, though, skipped the shifting electric fields made by the molecules themselves, since rubrene is apolar and the effect looked small.

With a fast method for those fields inside surface-hopping runs, the team shows the skip was not safe. The fields raise the energy a hole must repay to hop along both crystal axes, by clear margins over the no-field baseline. That reshapes the path the hole must cross. Even apolar crystals, they argue, need their own electric fields counted for honest mobility values.
arxiv-2606-18190:
Niloy and colleagues build the missing training data for catching multi-stage cyberattacks, in a 2026 dataset paper. Real attacks sprawl across system, network, and browser logs, and detectors must correlate all three. Public datasets cover one source at a time, or label whole traces merely malicious or benign. None combined all three sources with per-event MITRE ATT&CK technique labels, so the team captured their own.

Recording Windows endpoints during controlled attacks with real trojans, tunnels, and cloud exfiltration, they assembled eight hundred seventy sessions. The haul came to about two point three million events, tagged across twelve tactics and fifty-three techniques. Fine-tuning three small language models on the data transformed them: session accuracy leapt from under a tenth to above ninety percent.
