Technique-level identification stayed hard, with the best exact match under half.
arxiv-2606-18390:
Wang and colleagues present MOLAR, a framework for learning molecular representations when the training labels themselves are noisy, in a 2026 bioinformatics paper. Molecular labels often come from assays, curated databases, or weak annotation pipelines rather than clean observation. Models that trust them blindly can memorize corrupted entries, with graph and text fusion spreading the errors further.

MOLAR keeps two things apart: a latent clean property for each molecule, and the recorded label actually observed. Graph and text views each add residual evidence toward the clean property, while a learned observation channel maps that clean distribution to the noisy records used in training. The setup also yields a reliability score for each label and shows how much each view contributed. On naturally noisy benchmarks and on controlled label-flipping tests, MOLAR beat representative baselines, and its diagnostics helped explain which labels and modalities were driving predictions.
arxiv-2606-18490:
Machuca and colleagues test which style of stellar wind theory fits the light of B-type stars at different stages of evolution, in a 2026 astronomy paper presenting the ISOSCELES project. Radiation-driven winds shape how these stars evolve, but the standard fast wind solution does not always reproduce the optical fingerprints of giants and supergiants.

The team analyzed fifty Galactic B-type spectra spanning luminosity classes, fitting hydrogen, helium, and silicon lines with synthetic spectra computed from hydrodynamical wind models rather than assumed velocity laws. A clear split emerged: nearly all supergiants and most giants were better matched by the slower wind solution, with denser outflows and top speeds. Most dwarfs and subgiants fit the classical fast solution. Parameter trends with temperature supported the divide. The authors caution that optical lines barely probe the outer wind, so ultraviolet data are needed before the verdict is final.
arxiv-2606-18690:
Pang, Ping, and Wei analyze how polarization flows through charmonium decays into baryon-antibaryon pairs, in a 2026 particle physics paper. The charmonium states decay into pairs of spin-half baryons. The observables for it respond to the production and hadronization dynamics. They offer tests of helicity rules and quantum chromodynamics models.

Working in the spin density matrix formalism, the authors trace it from polarized electron-positron beams through the production chain, into the final baryon pair. Their helicity analysis confirms an angular distribution parameter for the spin-one state, fixed by a charge-conjugation selection rule. For the spin-two state, the parameter and transverse value depend on two amplitudes, with quark-model work agreeing with data. They show longitudinal beam polarization changes the spin values of both states. That gives facilities such as the Super Tau-Charm Facility new handles on decay mechanisms.
arxiv-2606-18790:
Prokopiou and the team bring feedback control theory to steering AI music making, in a 2026 paper on controllable generation. Activation steering adjusts a model's inner states to control traits with no new training. In symbolic music, a sparse-autoencoder variant gives readable control. But it fails at gradual change. When a steering strength ramps slowly, tiny values fall below the sparsity threshold that keeps the largest features. The intervention is gone until it switches on.

Their Temporal PID steering closes the loop at each autoregressive step. It uses a proportional-integral-derivative controller, whose integral term builds up the error of features failing to survive re-sparsification. It does so until the threshold is overcome. On the Multitrack Music Transformer, it enabled smooth pitch and duration transitions, with much less intervention strength and better quality than static steering. It allowed round-trip steering trajectories that static methods cannot express.
arxiv-2606-19090:
Du and colleagues test whether early dark energy can resolve the Hubble tension in 2026, using new JWST and DESI data. The tension is the mismatch between expansion rates inferred from the early universe and measured locally. Early dark energy adds a brief extra energy component near recombination that can raise the inferred rate. JWST high-redshift galaxy data and DESI expansion data now challenge the standard model more sharply.

Within a canonical axion-like early dark energy model, the team combines microwave background data from Planck, ACT, and SPT with DESI and JWST results. The inferred expansion rate rises enough to cut the tension to about the one-sigma level. The model also fits the JWST data better and beats the standard model by clear statistical margins. The findings show how early- and late-time data together can test early dark energy as a serious answer to the tension.
arxiv-2606-19290:
Gupta and colleagues derive the operator product expansion for a spin-orbit coupled bosonic system in 2026. Ultra-cold bosonic systems can be tuned through quantum phase transitions. Rabi-coupled systems show ferromagnetic and paramagnetic phases, while spin-orbit-coupled systems show richer phases such as supersolidity. Probing those phases needs sharp many-body tools. The operator product expansion is one, expressing the product of two separated operators as a series of local operators.

The authors derive the expansion for two operators at two points. They focus on the contact density term in that expansion. That term controls much of the universal physics of the underlying bosonic system, linking short-distance data to observables. A clean contact term for the spin-orbit case extends classic contact physics, developed for simpler gases, to a system where spin and motion are locked together. Contact probes can then read phase behavior in these gases.
arxiv-2606-19790:
Jiechao Gao and five colleagues argue in 2026 that process automation stalls on orchestration, not model power. Agent systems shine on digital-native tasks with clean interfaces. Logistics, health operations, and construction spread work across unlike tools and many hands instead.

Value there comes from a runtime that coordinates multi-step workflows. Such a runtime enforces hard domain rules, manages human approval, and bridges legacy systems. The authors supply an operational test for which workflows are orchestration-bound. A decomposition splits workflow tangles from coordination effort and its worth. Today's multi-agent frameworks leave a specific feature gap against that yardstick. The right path is staged, they claim, with the key guarantee set by each sector's friction. Rule enforcement carries regulatory settings; explainability carries liability settings. A research program follows from the frame.
arxiv-2606-19990:
Pu Li, Zhigang Lin, Qiang Wu, Yongxuan Lv, Fei Wang, and Shan You rethink reinforcement learning for embodied world models in 2026. World models predict how scenes evolve, and reinforcement learning can refine them, but cautious rollouts near the training data limit what the model discovers. Wider exploration invites reward hacking, where policies game flawed rewards. The team's answer pairs broader sampling with an active verifier.

Reward as an Agent judges generated behaviour directly, supplying robust reward signals under distribution shift. A companion method, DynDiff-GRPO, diversifies rollouts across the action space to widen state-action coverage. Across several open-source world models the combination mitigates hacking while delivering clear accuracy gains. Embodied AI gets evidence that bold exploration scales when verification keeps pace.
arxiv-2606-20690:
Felipe González and three colleagues describe a noise-driven electroacoustic string instrument in 2026, built from ideas shared between quantum physics and sound synthesis. Recent work at that boundary treats quantum concepts not only as metaphors but as working frameworks for new musical tools. Building on theory about stochastic string excitation, meaning random rather than fixed plucking, the team designs and fabricates a custom instrument for sonic exploration.

The system uses open-loop stochastic electromagnetic actuation, driving the string with magnets under random signals, without feedback or pitch stabilization. Its spectrum shows a dense, evenly spread regime unlike set plucking. The result is a playable instrument whose sound comes from controlled randomness.
arxiv-2606-20990:
Yiqi Zhao and many colleagues introduce DUET in 2026, a framework for teaching two robots to work together on mobile manipulation tasks. Two robots can carry loads and reach places one robot cannot. Training them is limited most by data collection. A unified virtual reality teleoperation system gathers synchronized data from two different robots. A tracking pipeline also records human pairs coordinating on the same kinds of tasks.

A transformer policy is first pretrained on human pair demonstrations. It is then fine-tuned on a small set of real robot trajectories. Four collaborative tasks form the benchmark. Robots used are a humanoid and a mobile manipulator. Results show human coordination data helps robot policies learn joint work with less costly robot time. Data-efficient teaching matters because dual-robot teleoperation is slow to stage, yet real teamwork needs many examples of timing, handover, and shared load control.
arxiv-2606-21490:
Yixuan Pu and five colleagues show in 2026 that how graphene sheets are stacked can rewrite the behavior of water squeezed between them. Water in nanoscale channels already acts strangely, and such effects are usually blamed on confinement size alone. Using machine learning potentials with first-principles accuracy, the team computed the phase diagram of water inside bilayer graphene capillaries. Two stackings, AA and AB, differ by a sideways shift of just 1.4 angstroms.

That tiny shift stabilizes different ice forms under AA stacking, raises the melting point by over one hundred kelvin, boosts proton transfer, and moves the onset of superionic behavior. The cause traces to changes in the hydrogen-bond network and the lateral energy landscape set by the walls. Angstrom-scale wall details, not just gap size, govern confined fluids.
arxiv-2606-21590:
Andreas Schliebitz, Heiko Tapken, and Martin Atzmueller swap a standard part of self-supervised learning in 2026: the projection head that sits on top of an image encoder during training. These heads are usually small perceptrons thrown away afterward, leaving costly labeled probing as the only way to grade the encoder. Their replacement is a radial basis function network, whose learned centers and shapes are readable directly, unlike perceptron weights.

From a trained head's centers and shapes they derive Scale-Normalized Separation, a label-free score of representation quality. Across five self-supervised architectures and four image datasets, the new heads match the old ones as drop-in replacements, with a three-layer Gaussian design recommended. The new score tracks logistic regression quality strongly, so a trained projector can certify its own backbone without labels.
arxiv-2606-21890:
Zhang and colleagues investigate, in 2026, whether giving a language model hundreds of examples in its prompt can replace fine-tuning for named entity recognition. That task finds names of people, places, and organizations in text. Earlier work used only a handful of examples, and models still trailed fully supervised systems. The team asked what changes when demonstrations scale into the hundreds.

Across several domains and models, scaling to hundreds of in-context examples let the models match or even surpass fully supervised BERT performance. The authors then used the same setup to annotate data for low-resource settings. With about one hundred human-labelled examples as demonstrations, the model generated training data good enough to lift fine-tuned BERT scores by roughly ten F1 points over prior state-of-the-art approaches. Many-shot prompting thus serves both as a recognizer and as a data factory.
arxiv-2606-21990:
Ugan and Waibel tackle code-switching in speech recognition in 2026, the everyday habit of mixing two languages inside one conversation. Large multilingual recognizers stumble on such speech, yet fine-tuning them on synthetic mixed data usually damages their strong single-language performance. The goal was to add switching skill without overwriting what the models already do well.

Their method, Bayesian factorized adaptation, learns how to fold switching-relevant knowledge into a pretrained model efficiently, guided by Bayesian principles. It needs only a small amount of synthetic code-switched data. Transcription errors on code-switched words fell by 32.87 percent, while overall word error rate improved by 5.31 percent across the test material. Monolingual performance stayed intact throughout. The authors conclude that effective adaptation depends more on how new knowledge is integrated than on the complexity of the added data.
arxiv-2606-22190:
Mufakharov and colleagues present, in 2026, three decades of multiwavelength variability for the blazar PKS 0735+178, a candidate source of the high-energy neutrino event IC211208A. Light curves span radio frequencies from one to 230 gigahertz, optical bands, and Fermi-LAT gamma rays. The bands vary together, with the emission region's structure read from how the signals lag one another.

Delays run from zero to 1,200 days and grow toward lower frequencies, consistent with an opacity-stratified jet. A bright flare after the neutrino event points to a compact, optically thick region with enhanced particle acceleration. Short optical and gamma-ray bursts occurred within days of the neutrino event, and a roughly twelve-day gamma-to-optical lag was detected for the first time. A ten-to-eleven-year variability timescale is robust in the radio bands. Jet precession alone cannot explain the modulation, since its required viewing angles clash with VLBI constraints.
arxiv-2606-22790:
Vyom Agarwal, Mokshda Gangrade, Siddharth Pal, and Jerry Wu map how speech models spend a fixed compute budget in this 2026 study. They vary three things together: model size, input length, and representation resolution, meaning how finely the audio is encoded. Two tasks anchor the work, automatic speech recognition and speech emotion recognition.

Experiments on LibriSpeech and CREMA-D show strongly non-linear returns. Growing a recognizer from 39 million to 244 million parameters cut word error far more than the next jump, to 769 million, did. For emotion recognition, about four seconds of audio was the sweet spot. Cutting encoder token resolution roughly halved the compute of a large model while raising word error by under three percent in relative terms. Fine-tuning with LoRA adapters also adapted models cheaply with little loss. Together these results give practical rules for designing efficient speech systems under real compute limits.
arxiv-2606-22890:
Aaditya Baranwal, Md Jahid Hasan, and Shruti Vyas build a benchmark for identifying bacteria in microscope images in this 2026 paper. Phase-contrast microscopy images live bacteria quickly without labels, but real samples mix species, including ones a system never saw in training. No computer-vision benchmark had tested multi-label identification on such mixtures.

Their dataset, PHOEBI, holds 120,000 wet-lab-prepared images covering forty combinations of six rod-shaped species. Its evaluation protocol holds out entire species combinations, mimicking deployment on unseen mixtures. Every gradient-trained aggregator they tested dropped sharply there, losing between 0.39 and 0.57 F1 from in-distribution to held-out data, a failure they trace to the aggregator rather than the visual features. A probe across thirteen encoders spread only about six F1 points. Their three lightweight anchor-based decoders scored higher on held-out combinations than on in-distribution validation.
arxiv-2606-22990:
S. E. Nikitin studies controlled random motion with resetting boundaries in a 2026 probability paper. A diffusion is a particle that drifts while being buffeted by random noise. In this model, whenever the particle reaches a marked boundary point, it instantly restarts from a prescribed distribution. The goal is ergodic control, meaning the best long-run average cost over time. Managers of such systems need rules that stay good indefinitely, not just over short horizons.

Nikitin derives a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, the standard equation whose solution gives optimal cost, here with boundary conditions that link distant points. A verification theorem then confirms that stationary Markov controls, which decide from the current state alone, can be optimal. For one resetting and one reflecting boundary, an existence result holds under weak assumptions. For renewal diffusions, the regenerative structure yields explicit cost formulas and concrete optimal drift choices.
arxiv-2606-23590:
Jiang and colleagues read the internal geometry of a language model to spot questions that cannot be answered as posed, in a 2026 paper on language model reliability. Ill-posed questions are ambiguous, underspecified, or contradictory, so they admit no valid answer or several plausible ones. Most detectors study model outputs and handle only one flaw type at a time. The authors ask whether all these flaws share one signature inside the model itself.

They treat hidden states of prompt tokens at each layer as a point cloud. Persistent homology, a topology tool, measures its shape across scales. Three compact numbers per layer summarize that shape, forming a fingerprint of the question. The fingerprint classifies ill-posedness far better than prompt-based or pooled-state baselines on three benchmarks. Feeding similar examples back as steering signals then raises acceptable responses, clarifications or abstentions, by about nine points.
arxiv-2606-23690:
Maharaj, Saxena, and Tamilselvam survey alternatives to left to right generation for AI code assistants, in a 2026 survey paper on software engineering. Autoregressive models write code one token at a time, never revising earlier choices. That rigidity hurts programming, where a decision late in a file can demand changes near the top, and an early mistake poisons everything after it. Human developers instead draft, sketch, and refine in loops.

The survey covers three emerging paradigms. Diffusion models generate code by denoising a whole draft at once, capturing long range structure that next token prediction misses. Code world models simulate program execution states, grounding reasoning in what code actually does. State space models process very long contexts in linear time, suiting massive codebases. Drawing also on cognitive neuroscience, the authors sketch directions toward deliberative, System 2 style code generation agents that plan before they write.
arxiv-2606-23890:
Maheshwari, Kisuryna, and Dodson measure a reaction that may explain how the only known interstellar chiral molecule becomes neutral and detectable, in a 2026 paper on astrochemistry. Propylene oxide is the sole chiral molecule so far observed between the stars, in the cloud Sagittarius B2. Its presumed precursor is its positively charged cation. Something must neutralize that cation for the observed molecule to accumulate, and ammonia is abundant in the same cloud.

Using a glow discharge source and an ion trap, the team measured charge transfer from ammonia to the propylene oxide cation. The reaction proceeds far more slowly than capture theories predict, yet ammonia's abundance makes it worth including in astrochemical models. Many chiral molecules, the authors suggest, may spend much of their interstellar lives as cations.
arxiv-2606-24190:
Shao and Shao open a series on running quantum dynamics cheaply, with dynamical low-rank approximation. The approach tracks a squeezed, low-rank shadow of a huge changing system. Their target is the Wigner equation, a phase-space form of quantum mechanics. Its collision term uses a nonlocal pseudo-differential operator that resists standard compression. This first part assumes the difference potential separates into simpler pieces.

That assumption, combined with two standard truncations of the operator, yields a separated representation the algorithm can chew on, with a cost analysis attached. Test problems are hard: harmonic oscillators, scattering from a Gaussian barrier, electron-electron scattering, and a helium-like atom. All of them fit it. Across them the new algorithm cuts the work needed ten to a hundred times over. The Shao team's 2026 start sets up later parts aimed at harder terms.
arxiv-2606-24390:
Bhatia and colleagues analyse uterine MRI scans while the patient is still in the scanner. Standard uterine assessment suffers from body variation, observer dependence, and a shortage of software tools in clinical workflow. Their 2026 framework, Female-RHINO, talks inline with the MRI scanner. It runs deep learning analysis during the scan. Measured results and a structured report come out with no manual interaction.

Segmentation and landmark-detection models measure uterine volume from sagittal images. They were trained and evaluated on more than five hundred multi-centre datasets, spanning diverse protocols, vendors, and patient groups. The system finds and measures common incidental findings, such as fibroids and Nabothian cysts. Six body landmarks are extracted for body measurement. Everything compiles into a doctor-oriented report with built-in images. Evaluation on independent past data accompanies the design. Bhatia's team aims to move measured reproductive-health imaging into the scan session itself.
arxiv-2606-24790:
Anand Kamat, Daniel Blake, and Brent Werness present Grad Detect, a method that predicts when a large language model is hallucinating. Language models produce fluent but false text often enough to endanger high stakes uses. Most detectors watch the model's outputs, through confidence scores or repeated sampling. Grad Detect instead reads the model's internal gradient patterns. One forward and backward pass during inference supplies the signal.

Across several question answering benchmarks, Grad Detect beats confidence based and sampling based baselines. It also predicts when a model should abstain from answering. Layer ablation studies span eleven models from four architecture families. They show the final five layers hold over 97 percent of the useful gradient signal. Detection can therefore run on a small slice of the network with little loss. Kamat and colleagues offer the method as one framework for several dimensions of model reliability, with clues about where failures begin.
arxiv-2606-24890:
Jasmine Brazilek, Maria Navas, and Alexa Gnauck test whether a small group of Wikipedia editors can shift what language models say about animal welfare. A volunteer group, the Pro-Animal Wikipedians, adds sourced animal welfare content to relevant articles. Their footprint is tiny: 125 edits across 115 pages. The question is whether such a footprint can measurably steer model behaviour on a contested topic.

Gradient based data attribution traces the influence of those edits inside trained models. On Llama 3.1 8B, sections the group edited dominate the top attributed documents for animal welfare queries. They take 68 percent of the top spots, against 52 percent for unrelated queries about the same companies. A second attribution method, run across five training seeds, sharpens the picture. In every seed, the ten documents most influential on animal welfare queries were all group edits. Small edits, the authors conclude, can indeed shape large models' values.
arxiv-2606-24990:
Borja Medina and Jon Paul Janet make reinforcement learning for molecule design honest about uncertainty. Chemical language models propose candidate molecules while RL steers them toward high property scores. Standard frameworks treat the scoring functions as exact oracles. In truth each property score carries uncertainty, and the search can chase highly scored molecules that the training data barely support. Optimisation then destabilises, with true values far from predictions.

First, uncertainty can enter as an objective, letting the policy trade raw score against reliability. Second, uncertainty can scale policy updates, down weighting molecules far outside the scorers' confidence domain. Three testbeds are used: a controlled model system with error growing with distance from training data, ChemProp models, and a conformal wrapper around a random forest. Across settings, uncertainty aware RL explores chemical space more robustly. The lesson is practical: a generator rewarded for confident predictions wanders less into fantasy chemistry.
arxiv-2606-25090:
Some Schrödinger equations are strongly indefinite: their energy splits into a positive and a negative part of equal standing, so ordinary minimisation fails. Bartosz Bieganowski surveys recent variational methods for such equations when the nonlinear terms can change sign and compete. The machinery he reviews includes a generalised linking theorem and a multiplicity theory for critical orbits in dislocation spaces.

The survey closes with a new ground state result of his own. For the competing pure power case, with the weaker power above two and the stronger below the critical exponent, a small positive coupling is enough. Its functional then has a critical point of least energy among all its nontrivial critical points: a ground state for an equation whose energy is unbounded both above and below.
arxiv-2606-25290:
Set theory meets the philosophy of probability in a short note by Yuanshan Li, forthcoming in Philosophy of Science. The part whole principle says a proper part should not measure the same as the whole. Li connects that principle to a quantity built from Dedekind cuts, which count the ways a linear order can be split into two pieces with no largest element below. The quantity generalises an older cardinal characteristic studied in the foundations of probability.

Establishing the connection sharpens a result by Mancosu and Massas about generalised probability functions, which assign values in ordered structures richer than plain numbers. Li also proposes follow up questions the link suggests. The argument shows how a purely combinatorial measure of order complexity can decide which exotic probability assignments are even possible.
arxiv-2606-25790:
Shift all data and all parameters by the same amount, and a fair comparison of two distributions should not budge. Frank Nielsen and Kazuki Okamura make that intuition a theorem in 2026 for transformation models, where a group acts on both data and parameters and densities adjust by a multiplier. Every f divergence, the broad family containing Kullback Leibler, Hellinger, total variation, and chi square, stays fixed under such actions. One proof covers them all. Such a measure then depends only on the pair's maximal invariant.

When the group sweeps the whole parameter space, that invariant is a double coset, a purely relative position. Multidimensional location scale families supply the worked application. The Fisher Rao distance, geometry's own measure, obeys the same reduction. Symmetry, properly used, collapses comparison problems to their relative core.
arxiv-2606-26090:
Thiago Bergamaschi proves fast mixing for quantum systems where every part touches every other part. Gibbs samplers prepare thermal states of quantum systems. At high temperature, known samplers mix fast on lattices, where geometry limits interactions. Many real systems lack that geometry, though. Electronic structure, mean-field models, and some quantum codes all interact at long range. Bergamaschi removes the lattice assumption entirely.

Arbitrary k-local Hamiltonians with bounded interaction strength are covered. At high enough temperature, a known quantum Gibbs sampler keeps a spectral gap that does not shrink with system size. A constant gap means mixing time stays tame as systems grow. Fully polynomial quantum algorithms follow as a consequence. Partition functions and global expectation values become efficiently approximable. The result extends the fast-mixing frontier from geometric systems to the all-to-all world, where many chemistry and coding Hamiltonians actually live.
arxiv-2606-26190:
F. Jörg, G. Eurin, and H. Simgen fight a ghostly background in rare-event physics: radon. Detectors hunting dark matter or neutrinoless decay sit deep underground, shielded from nearly everything. Radon gas still leaks from the detector materials themselves. It often dominates the background. Their countermeasure is a coating. A copper layer, electroplated onto the material, seals radon inside.

Method development drives the report. The team electroplated copper onto a stainless steel sample that had been implanted with radium, radon's parent. Emanation measurements then compared coated and uncoated behaviour. The coating cut the radon-222 emanation rate a thousandfold. That scale of suppression matters for experiments counting single events per year. Surface treatments could join shielding and material selection as standard tools in the rare-event toolkit. The work appears in a European physics journal devoted to such instrumentation questions.
arxiv-2606-26390:
Yohan Beugin, Paul Barford, and Patrick McDaniel review the life and death of Google's Privacy Sandbox, a set of browser APIs meant to replace tracking cookies. Google launched it in 2019, then cancelled the project and deprecated most APIs in late 2025.

Using seven years of web crawls and Chrome usage data, the authors track each API's adoption across the top 100,000 sites. Uptake stayed limited and uneven: only a few actors implemented a few APIs, each in different ways. They trace the failure to mismatched incentives and risks, and close with recommendations for the next attempt at web privacy reform.
arxiv-2606-26490:
Wen Fan and seven colleagues test whether language models can write formal specifications for a program verifier. Verifiers prove that code behaves correctly, but humans must write the specifications they check against. For VeriFast, a verifier based on separation logic, those specifications are complex and slow to write. Separation logic reasons about how programs use memory. Earlier model-based help mostly targeted simpler verifiers.

Coverage spanned three hundred three C functions. The authors tried eight prompting approaches, ten language models, and three input types. Models preserved correct behaviour in code and specifications more than nine times in ten. Full verification success was much lower, at under one third of cases. Stronger models and formal contracts in the prompt helped. Most errors, the great majority, came from missing domain knowledge about separation logic verifiers.
arxiv-2606-26890:
Buddhadev Hajra and Mohit Upmanyu prove a cancellation theorem for Brieskorn-Pham varieties, a family of algebraic shapes defined by simple power-sum equations. The Zariski cancellation problem asks a seductive question. If two shapes become identical after multiplying both by the same third shape, were they identical to begin with? For general shapes the answer can be no.

For Brieskorn-Pham varieties over the complex numbers, the authors prove yes. The result holds even when the multiplying factor is any separated complex scheme with a smooth point. The shapes are recovered not just as varieties but with their circle-action structure intact. The proof joins a general cancellation theorem for shapes with one singularity to an exponent rigidity theorem. That theorem says the defining exponents alone fix the shape's identity over any field of characteristic zero.
arxiv-2606-26990:
Schneider and colleagues argue that judging uncertainty estimates in machine learning needs a link to real decisions. Standard scores like negative log-likelihood reward matching true frequencies on average. Good scores there need not help a doctor, banker, or engineer choose better actions. The team defines decision-alignment, a test of whether a score ranks uncertainty methods the same way actual decision gains do. Many popular scores fail that test in their 2026 study.

Some failing scores also hide odd prior beliefs, meaning built-in guesses about which decisions will matter later. As a fix, the authors propose prior-weighted utility metrics, a family of proper scoring rules tuned to decision gains. Proper rules reward honest probability reports. Across benchmark tests and real case studies, the new scores track realised decision utility closely. Widely used scores do not, which exposes a flaw in current evaluation habits.
arxiv-2606-27390:
Tawfik and colleagues ask whether general relativity's curvatures are the only ones around a spinning, charged black hole. Their approach quantises the metric tensor itself through a geometric ansatz, rather than quantising matter on a fixed background. A conformal change of the standard metric keeps relativity's principles while extending them toward quantum scales. The Kerr-Newman spacetime, with its rotation and electric charge, is the arena. In the 2026 gravitation paper, field equations follow from the quantised metric.

Two families of Riemann curvature emerge. Alongside the positive curvatures of classical relativity, notable negative curvatures appear at lower, quantum scales. The authors read those as hints of quantum sources of gravitation that classical theory cannot reach. Analytic and numeric checks cross-check the picture. Whether the ansatz describes nature remains open. The work maps what metric quantisation would make visible around extreme black holes.
arxiv-2606-27490:
Makarov, Gepner, and Belavin tie two constructions of the heterotic string's Calabi-Yau sector together: one built from free fields, one from minimal models. Compactifying the heterotic string on Berglund-Hübsch type Calabi-Yau manifolds yields four-dimensional theories with the desired supersymmetry. The minimal-model construction realises the compact sector as a product of supersymmetric conformal field theories, with modular invariance checked explicitly. A free-field construction exists too, but its consistency needed the correspondence the authors now establish in this string theory paper from 2026.

For Fermat-type polynomials, Calabi-Yau vertex operators written in free fields correspond exactly to products of primary fields of the minimal models. Modular invariance of the free-field construction follows through the correspondence. The result extends to Berglund-Hübsch Calabi-Yau orbifolds, with conditions on complete vertex operators that parallel the minimal-model side.
arxiv-2606-27690:
Atanas Stefanov studies travelling kink waves in 2026. The setting is the dissipative Boussinesq problem. That model extends the good Boussinesq equation by adding viscosity effects. It supports monotone decreasing kink solutions. A kink is a wave that travels while keeping a step-like profile. The question is whether these kinks survive small disturbances over long times.

Stefanov reports two stability results. First, the kinks are orbitally stable in the H1 space. Orbital stability means nearby solutions stay near the kink's family of shifts. Second, stronger decay holds in other measures. The kinks are asymptotically stable in the homogeneous H1-type space. They are also asymptotically stable in Lp spaces for p between two and infinity. Asymptotic stability means disturbances not only stay close but fade away. Together the results cover both persistence of the wave shape and long-time settling toward it.
arxiv-2606-27790:
Peter Haine, Mauro Porta, and Jean-Baptiste Teyssier build moduli spaces for sheaves in 2026. A moduli space parametrises a family of mathematical objects as a space in its own right. Their objects are constructible sheaves. The varieties involved are complex algebraic ones and compact real analytic ones. The construction uses higher derived Artin stacks. Derived structure keeps extra homological information that classical spaces discard.

Perverse sheaves receive special attention. Every perversity function gives an open substack of perverse sheaves. That substack is a 1-Artin stack, locally of finite presentation. It generalises the usual character stacks familiar from representation theory. A sample application shows the derived structure at work. New examples of cohomological Hall algebras are constructed. They are associated to punctured Riemann surfaces. The paper thus links moduli theory, perverse sheaves, and Hall algebra constructions in one framework.
arxiv-2606-28390:
Hao Li, Chen Chu, Filip Biljecki, Cyrus Shahabi, and Wenwen Li automate quality checks for geospatial vector data, the points, lines, and polygons behind digital maps. Rule-based checkers struggle with varied city shapes and enormous data volumes, and checking native vector geometry with artificial intelligence remains largely unexplored.

Li and colleagues built Topo4Vec, which first simulates topological errors, overlapping polygons and street segments that overshoot or undershoot their junctions, to spare humans the labeling work. Representation learning then encodes real geometries so that errors sit apart from valid shapes. Across Los Angeles, Munich, and Singapore, the system caught overlapping building footprints with near-perfect accuracy, and street overshoots and undershoots less reliably. The authors draw lessons toward autonomous quality monitoring at ecosystem scale.
arxiv-2606-28590:
Kiyoaki Christopher Omori, Marcin Sawicki, Rosa M. Mérida, and ten colleagues catch galaxies in the act of colliding when the universe was young. Using Webb telescope imaging of a spectroscopically confirmed sample at redshift near five, they visually classify which galaxies sit in close interacting systems. They find nearly half of the forty-eight in pairs or groups.

Fitting each component's spectrum yields its star formation history. Interacting components show brief bursts, about two hundred million years long, of strongly enhanced star formation. These bursts multiply their stellar mass several-fold, forming far more new mass than undisturbed growth would predict. Assuming the components eventually merge, the team attributes roughly two fifths of all stellar mass growth at that epoch to mergers. Half of it is inherited stars and half stars born in the interaction itself.
arxiv-2606-28690:
Shenghan Zheng, Qifan Zhang, Zheng Zhang, Haonan Li, and Christophe Hauser audit the protocols that let artificial intelligence agents use tools and hand work to one another. These protocols state their security requirements in part and enforce them unevenly, and nobody had traced a requirement from the specification text all the way into running software.

Their AgentThread framework links sources end to end. It turns protocol-derived checks into logical invariants, compiles the specs into model-checkable form, and replays counterexamples against real development kits through adapters. Across five emerging protocols it logged thirty-five spec-level findings, backed by eighty code tests. It also found thirty more failures that appear only when protocols are composed. Only one protocol enforced a security-relevant control in practice, and none took charge of cross-protocol behavior, a responsibility gap the authors call the core problem.
arxiv-2606-28790:
Mu, Li, Luo, Wang and Zhao reanalyse a large quasar survey to squeeze more cosmology from data already collected. Their sample holds 343,708 quasars, distant bright objects, spread across a wide range of redshifts, meaning distances and look-back times. A single average redshift wastes the change across that range, so they weight each quasar optimally, giving more say to the ones most informative for each quantity they want to measure.

Both the standard and weighted analyses rest on a thousand mock catalogues that mimic the survey for checking errors. In the standard cosmology model the two approaches agreed, as expected. In a model where dark energy can change over time, the weighted version cut the uncertainty on the expansion rate by 43.3 percent, with smaller gains on other quantities. A parameter that was previously only bounded on one side became a proper two-sided estimate.
arxiv-2606-29190:
Wang builds a unified geometric framework connecting three structures that arise around BPS states in supersymmetric gauge theories. BPS states are special, stability-protected configurations whose charges determine much of a theory's spectrum. The three structures are the split attractor flow, the Hessian flow of a phase-rotated charge function, and the spectral network drawn on an underlying curve.

He proves concisely that the attractor flow and the gradient Hessian flow are orthogonal, using only the Kahler geometry. A lift-projection duality shows the spectral network projects to a characteristic Hessian flow. He also proves the Kontsevich-Soibelman equivariance, a consistency law for how BPS counts jump, by induction on the attractor tree's depth. Examples cover several gauge groups and quiver theories. For one Argyres-Douglas theory he derives a closed-form spectrum, a new result. In a tropical limit he obtains a generating function for disk counts.
arxiv-2606-29490:
Kumaran examines what a language model's stated confidence actually means. Models often report a number meant to estimate the chance their answer is correct. Kumaran uses a two-stage abstention test borrowed from neuroscience studies of perceptual decisions. The model first answers and reports confidence. It then decides whether to hand that answer to a user or abstain.

Over four non-reasoning models and varied prompts, verbal confidence predicts the later commit-or-abstain choice far better than it predicts correctness. Calibrated token log-probabilities behave differently: their power to predict abstention tracks their power to detect correctness, the signature of an evidence signal. Removing the part of verbal confidence shared with log-probabilities leaves the commitment link intact while correctness prediction falls to near chance. The split generalizes to four reasoning models and four benchmarks, and analyses inside Gemma models point to a commit-readiness state.
arxiv-2606-29590:
Bakhti studies critical gravitational collapse, the borderline between matter dispersing and a black hole forming, with an eye on primordial black holes. The formation threshold and mass-scaling laws near it depend sensitively on the equation of state. Most primordial black hole studies assume a radiation fluid. Real dense matter may stiffen as it nears a maximum density, a feature called saturation.

As a tractable stand-in, Bakhti uses the closed-form equation of state of a single-occupancy lattice gas, with a density-dependent sound speed. General-relativistic simulations of spherically symmetric collapse follow. The nonlinear pressure feedback raises the black hole formation threshold slightly compared with the radiation case, within the model's causal regime. The critical mass-scaling exponent, however, stays consistent with the radiation-fluid value. At low density the lattice gas approaches the radiation fluid, so near-critical behaviour changes only mildly.
arxiv-2606-29890:
Wiggins studies a Kerr-cat qubit, a quantum bit stored in the two wells of a driven nonlinear oscillator, where a logic gate briefly changes the drive. The worry is that the same pulse that performs the gate can corrupt the stored bit.

Comparing classical phase-space diagnostics with the quantum outcome over a disk of starting states, Wiggins finds the corruption depends on the full time course of the pulse, not just its strength. A sudden quench, an abrupt change, erases the bit, while a smooth ramp of the same peak height largely preserves it. A sensitivity field marks the classical transport boundary, and a Loschmidt echo, measured near the gate's end, predicts the much later quantum result.
arxiv-2606-30390:
Y.-Z. Cai leads a large international team reporting a bright, slow-fading supernova of the interacting Type IIn class. SN 2019vxm peaked at an absolute magnitude near minus twenty. It took thirty-five days to reach that peak brightness. Its light curves and spectra evolved unusually slowly afterward. Early spectra showed flash-ionisation lines of carbon, nitrogen, and helium.

A mid-infrared excess appeared seven months after maximum light. It signals a small amount of newly formed dust. Comparison with interacting supernova models bounds the progenitor's mass loss. The star was shedding at least a hundredth of a solar mass yearly. A weak absorption feature reveals slow unshocked gas nearby. That gas moves at only about sixty kilometers per second. The bolometric light curve fits a simple power law well. Together the signs point to a massive, compact progenitor. A luminous blue variable in a clumpy environment fits best.
arxiv-2606-30690:
Seamus Lavine answers a question in additive combinatorics, the study of set growth under sums and products. For a finite set of real numbers, a Minkowski polynomial applies a polynomial to the set in a sum-product sense, mixing sums and products of its elements. A folklore hope said such expressions always grow almost as fast as the degree allows. For the simplest case, products plus sums, earlier authors had already disproved the strongest version and asked whether the weaker one survives.

Lavine shows it does not. Take any monic polynomial of degree at least two. A monic polynomial has leading coefficient one. Lavine constructs arbitrarily large finite sets whose image under it falls short of maximal growth by a fixed power. The shortfall exponent depends only on the polynomial. The result covers the products-plus-sums case and closes the question raised by Roche-Newton, Ruzsa, Shen and Shkredov.
arxiv-2606-31190:
Li and Simchi-Levi characterise how efficient causal estimates can be in sequential experiments. Modern trials assign treatments adaptively or under rollout, fairness, and budget limits, so samples are no longer independent draws. The classic efficiency benchmark from independent sampling then needs a new form before designs can be judged.

Every design that does not peek ahead induces an average propensity score, the mean chance of treatment. Precision for regular locally unbiased estimators is capped by the independent benchmark scored at that induced value, so one number benchmarks all such designs. The authors then build batched adaptive designs that reach the cap in two ways: regression adjustment with efficient influence functions, and adaptive covariate balancing that lets simple moment estimates do the job.
arxiv-2606-31490:
Usman and two colleagues redesign the adder trees at the heart of ultrasound beamforming for small FPGA chips. Delay-and-sum beamforming adds signals from many channels on every sample. Full-precision adder trees eat lookup tables, stretch timing paths, and burn power. Real-time imaging on cheap hardware suffers for it.

Their tree uses left-to-right arithmetic. It works most-significant-digit first, so it can emit a good image before full precision finishes. On a Xilinx Zynq chip with a 64-channel dataset, the design uses far fewer lookup tables than the smallest rival tree. It also meets timing and draws 23 percent less dynamic power. Stopping the clock early selects precision at runtime, and fifteen parallel copies reach 67 frames per second.
arxiv-2606-31690:
Zakeri, Nguyen and Juntti make WiFi sensing cheaper by paying attention to how old each measurement is. Channel state information, the per-packet record of how a radio signal was distorted, lets systems recognize human activity and identity without any worn device. But sensing must share airtime with data traffic, so fresh samples arrive sparsely and irregularly.

Their framework encodes the age of each retained sample and fuses that freshness signal with the channel embedding by multiplication, under both deterministic and random sampling policies that respect a sensing budget. On the NTU-Fi activity recognition and person identification datasets, the age-aware model beats both a channel-only baseline and the leading time-aware attention model. It gains up to ten percentage points on identification, with the largest gains under the strictest budgets.
arxiv-2606-31790:
Altwlkany and four colleagues ask whether robocalls are a global problem or mainly an American one. Automated scam and spam calls cost United States victims a reported 1.1 billion dollars in 2025 alone. Fighting them is hard because campaigns cross borders, languages and legal systems, and public data have been scarce.

Over nine months the team gathered reports from 65 countries across all inhabited continents. They release an open dataset with 8.7 million call records, 839 transcripts from 28 campaign clusters, and 677 recordings. Analysis covers calling patterns, shared campaigns, callback numbers and language differences between regions. Robocalls prove international, but the threat is far more severe in the United States than elsewhere.
arxiv-2606-31890:
Sierra Miranda and Studer prove uniform Lyndon interpolation for GLS, Solovay's provability logic, using non-wellfounded proofs. GLS tells what the provability predicate of arithmetic satisfies under true arithmetic. It was known to enjoy uniform interpolation, but whether the Lyndon refinement, which also tracks the polarity of variables, held was open.

Non-wellfounded sequent calculi had delivered Craig, Lyndon and uniform interpolation one at a time for other logics, never the combination. New notions of Lyndon fixpoints and Lyndon equational systems make the interpolant built by the proofs respect polarity. A second proof of cut elimination for GLS falls out of the same tools. The method adapts to other provability logics with non-wellfounded calculi.
arxiv-2608-00390:
An, Balram, and Murthy study skyrmion excitations in monolayer graphene at filling factor minus one. The ground state is an SU(4) quantum Hall ferromagnet there. Short-range anisotropic interactions compete with Zeeman coupling and a sublattice potential. Four distinct spin-valley-ordered ground phases result. Their framework joins effective field theory with Hartree-Fock approximation.

A variational method treats Coulomb interaction and symmetry-breaking terms on equal footing. Minimization fixes the best skyrmion texture, radial profile and spinor structure alike. They map the phase diagram of skyrmion excitations. Thirteen distinct skyrmion phases appear under varied field conditions. Textures, energies, and sizes are determined for each. Robustness across radial ansätze backs the approach. The frame extends to wider SU(4) quantum Hall systems.
arzneikunst-und-alchemie-im-siebzehnten-:
Printed at Hamburg in 1890, this German lecture pamphlet belongs to the popular science series founded by Rudolf Virchow and Franz von Holtzendorff. Its subject is healing and alchemy in the seventeenth century, a period when doctors still worked inside an older cosmos of planets, metals, and secret signs. The surviving scan is hard Fraktur type, and its title-page byline is barely legible in machine reading.

Pages move from the alchemist's way of treating sickness to the old Roman names of the weekdays, each tied to a planet god: Luna, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn. Secret writing gets close attention, with its many shifts and codes across the centuries. Readers meet a medicine that mixed remedy, star lore, and coded books long before chemistry split away from alchemy.
ashton-curious-creatures-in-zoology-1890:
John Ashton fills a cabinet of strange beasts in Curious Creatures in Zoology, his book of 1890. Ashton was a scribe who loved old prints and tales. He draws on sea logs, priest books, and fair tales. His hoard holds beasts that sit twixt lore and life. The kraken drags ships down. The sea serpent haunts a score of ships.

Each beast gets its tales, dates, and draws in Ashton's wry, rich prose. He grants doubt, yet loves the hoard too much to scorn it. The book is a joy for fans of strange life.
blake-marriage-heaven-hell-1790:
William Blake printed The Marriage of Heaven and Hell around 1790 by his own method of illuminated printing, words and designs etched together on copper plates. The work mixes prose argument, proverbs, and vision into one prophetic book. It stands as the founding text of Blake's mythic system.

Blake attacks the tame religion of his day and praises energy, desire, and creative fire against cold reason. His Proverbs of Hell, like the road of excess leading to the palace of wisdom, still get quoted worldwide. The book remains a landmark of visionary Romantic religion and of poetry as picture.
bohm-bawerk-capital-interest-smart-1890:
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk was an Austrian economist and finance minister who took on Marx's theory of value head-on. His Capital and Interest, in Smart's 1890 translation, is the Austrian school's great statement on why interest exists. It mixes close criticism of rival theories with a positive account of his own.

Bohm-Bawerk argues that people value present goods above future goods of the same kind, and that interest prices that gap. Roundabout methods of production, which take longer, yield more, and interest helps coordinate them. His demolition of exploitation theories of interest set terms of debate for a generation.
burnet-sacred-theory-of-the-earth-vol2-1:
Volume two of Burnet's Sacred Theory, in English in 1690, holds the two last books. The third book treats the burning of the world to come. The fourth treats the new heavens and new earth after that fire. Burnet closes with a review of his theory and its proofs.

His Earth passes from smooth Paradise, through the Deluge's ruin, to final flame and renewal. Prophecy and natural philosophy march together through the scheme. Readers of the age praised the sweep and the prose alike. The two English volumes complete his famous system. Modern geology grew partly by arguing with Burnet. His questions about Earth's past outlived his answers.
carnot-motive-power-heat-thurston-1890:
Sadi Carnot was a young French engineer who asked a simple question: how much work can heat do? His short memoir first came out in 1824, when he was only in his twenties. Robert Thurston's English version, issued in 1890, is the form most readers meet here.

Carnot argues that a heat engine works best when heat moves from hot to cold in a smooth, reversible cycle. No engine can beat that ideal, no matter how it is built. His reasoning gave later scientists the seed of the second law of heat science, and the cycle still bears his name.
cia-0000009190:
Allen W. Dulles, director of central intelligence, addressed the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in a statement dated April 1960. Dulles was the CIA's best-known chief, a lawyer turned spymaster from the Second World War's secret services. Open testimony by a sitting director was still unusual.

The statement lays out the director's case before the Senate's senior foreign policy body. Such appearances shaped how Congress funded and watched over secret work. Weeks later, the U-2 shootdown would test Dulles and his agency severely. The file preserves his public footing just before that storm, in his own official words.
cia-0000009590:
France's postwar industrial recovery is surveyed in a CIA paper dated July 1948. France was rebuilding factories, mines, and railways wrecked or worn down by war and occupation. The Monnet Plan guided that effort, and American Marshall Plan aid began flowing the same year.

Recovery figures carried political weight, since communists led many French unions and strikes could halt production. Analysts read output statistics as signs of stability or trouble. The paper shows economic reporting serving strategy in the early Cold War. France's rebirth as an industrial power can be watched here at its measured, uncertain start.
cia-0000009690:
A possible American prisoner of war camp in Ha Tay province is located in a July 1972 CIA item. Ha Tay wraps around Hanoi's western side, close to the capital's known prisons. The word possible does heavy work in the heading: the site was reported, not confirmed.

Unconfirmed camps posed a lasting dilemma for the accounting. Chasing every rumor wasted effort, yet ignoring one could abandon a living man. Analysts recorded the location and its uncertainty together, honestly. Later evidence might promote or kill the lead. This file is that honest record: a place on the map with a question mark kept beside it.
cia-0000009790:
Two Americans were seen with Viet Cong units in Quang Ngai province, an activity report from September 1974 states. Quang Ngai, on South Vietnam's coast, remained contested ground in the war's last phase. Americans with enemy units could be prisoners, defectors, or misidentified altogether.

Activity reports followed such men over time rather than in a single sighting. Patterns could show whether a man moved freely or under guard. That difference decided how officials treated his case. The file preserves the watching, not a verdict, which suits a subject where verdicts were so often wrong or late.
cia-0000009990:
International connections of American peace groups are examined in a January 1968 CIA paper, the third in its series. Antiwar activism was then swelling, driven by the Vietnam War's escalation. The paper maps the movement's foreign ties as the agency understood them.

Domestic subjects made this file different from the foreign reports around it. Watching Americans at home later became one of the CIA's great scandals of the 1970s. Read now, the paper shows that watch in progress, numbered and routine. It preserves evidence for a lasting argument about where secret intelligence work should properly stop.
cia-0000011590:
National Intelligence Estimate 34-61, excerpted here, gave Washington's coordinated judgment on the prospects for Iran at the start of 1961. The Shah ruled Iran with American backing, eight years after the coup that restored his power. Yet opposition stirred beneath the surface, and oil politics still shaped every question about the country's future.

The estimate weighs the Shah's hold on his throne and the strength of those who opposed him. It also treats Iran's place in the contest between the West and the Soviet Union. The pages preserved here show the intelligence community's shared view of a key ally whose stability it rarely doubted aloud.
cia-0000012090:
National Intelligence Estimate 36.1-66, issued in April 1966, is the community's yearly judgment on the outlook for the United Arab Republic. Egypt still bore the union's name, though Syria had left it five years before. The annual estimate took stock of Nasser's state at a moment of growing strain.

Yemen's war and the economy's troubles dominate the analysts' pages. The estimate weighs how those burdens pressed on the regime's strength and choices. It stands in a long series of yearly reckonings, each one testing the same questions about the Arab world's leading state and its ruler's staying power.
cia-0000012390:
An operational plan for a subject blacked out in the title fills a CIA paper from 1961. The plan lays out an operation's steps in order, the tradecraft's choreography written down. Parts of it are blacked out in the released copy, as such plans usually are, since the same methods might still serve somewhere in the world.

What survives shows the script: who moves, who watches, what happens if things go wrong. Every covert action began as pages like these before it became risk. For readers, the plan's blacked steps are their own reminder that the most interesting parts stay hidden.
cia-0000014790: The Atom Spies, a book by Oliver Ramsay Pilat, is noted in a CIA file dated July 3, 1969. The file says the book deals mainly with the networks behind the atomic cases. Pilat wrote as the cases were still fresh public wounds. A 1969 note shows the agency still shelving new takes on its oldest spy story.
cia-0000015290: A letter to Gordon Scherer from John Warner fills a CIA file dated July 1, 1953. It concerns a letter of August 24, the title notes. Scherer sat in Congress, where saucer mail from voters piled up. The file shows the agency answering the Hill on a topic the public would not drop.
cia-0000015490: People still interested in UFO phenomena are the subject of an untitled CIA record dated in 1976. The record also forwards related material, judging by its clipped title. By 1976 the great official studies had closed, yet public interest had not. A late file like this shows the subject living on in small corners of the government long after its heyday.
cia-0000020390: Letelier's release from prison and his petition to the United Nations are discussed in an untitled CIA record dated in 1976. Orlando Letelier had been held by Chile's junta after the 1973 coup, then freed and sent abroad. A petition to the UN carried his case to the world. The record shows his fight moving from a cell to open diplomacy.
cia-0000022790: Photo comparison case number 12,410 has its results kept in a CIA record dated in 1971. The subject's name does not appear in the title, so none is guessed here. By 1971 the matching cases ran into the twelve thousands, a count of loss in itself. Each result was filed so that no lead, however small, was ever lost twice.
cia-0000024390: The situation in South Vietnam is surveyed in a CIA paper dated in 1963. That year President Diem's government faced Buddhist protests, a coup, and his own death in November. A situation paper in such a year tried to fix a moving target on paper. It stands as a snapshot of a regime coming apart while the war around it grew.
cia-0000028290: Iran is the single word title of a CIA record dated in 1969. Country files under a bare name usually held basic reference material on the state. In 1969 Iran was ruled by the Shah, rich on oil and close to Washington. A plain country file from that calm decade reads differently after the revolution that no forecaster placed on its pages.
cia-0000028490: Rightist terrorism in El Salvador is studied in a CIA paper dated in 1980, tagged Truth Commission in the catalog. Rightist terror meant death squads linked to the far right, killing union men, teachers, and priests. Naming it plainly in an official paper mattered in a year when such killings peaked. The tag ties the study to the later inquiry into that war.
cia-0000034690:
Allen W. Dulles had run the CIA, and a declassified record dated January 6, 1966 holds his calendar schedule. The schedule covers January 1 through January 27, 1966, well after his years in office had ended. It is a diary-style record rather than a report or a study.

Inside are the planned days of a retired spymaster, set down in the plain form of appointments. Small records like this fill in the human side of a famous intelligence career. They show how even a former director's routine was kept, filed, and later released to the public. Dulles had led the agency through much of the 1950s, at the height of the Cold War.
cia-0000048990: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee received a briefing on violence in El Salvador in 1981, and a CIA item from that year preserves the session's record. Senators deciding American aid wanted the war described plainly, away from public debate. Briefings like this one shaped how much money, and how many conditions, Congress attached to the war.
cia-0000049090: Members and collaborators of ARENA, El Salvador's Nationalist Republican Alliance, are listed in a CIA item from 1984. The list reaches into the party's paramilitary side, the zone where politics and armed groups overlapped. Rosters like this one let later investigators draw the right's organization as a chart of names and ties.
cia-0000095090: Estimated date and Mexican economic situation frame declassified CIA document 0000095090, dated September 6, 1976. The heading flags its own date as estimated before naming Mexico's economy. Readers get a short declassified assessment record on that subject, notable for the dating caution built into its title. It is a companion to the other Mexico items filed that month.
cia-0000096490: The City of Rams-III is the cryptic title of declassified CIA document 0000096490, dated June 5, 1967. The heading gives a place-like name and a numeral and nothing more. Readers get a short declassified item whose meaning cannot be settled from its title alone, preserved as one of the catalog's most opaque headings.
cia-0000098090: Cuba, A Status Report is the title of declassified CIA document 0000098090, dated November 4, 1963. The heading promises a general status account of the island. The brief file is a declassified status report in that plain form. It is a companion to the Guantanamo policy item. It also sits near the Cuba options paper in the same cluster.
cia-0000105890: Sukarno's Action and Plans to Balance the Power of Forces in Indonesia is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000105890, dated April 5, 1965. The title describes a balancing effort by President Sukarno among forces inside his own country. It names the actor and the method, balancing, in one line. The brief record is a political maneuvering item from 1965 Jakarta.
cia-0000107290: No U.s. Soldiers in Cambodia is the short heading on declassified CIA document 0000107290, dated June 6, 1991. The title states a flat denial about American soldiers in Cambodia. No source for the denial is named in the heading itself. The brief record is a denial item, filed among the June 1991 Southeast Asia items in the release.
cia-0000108490: Dated January 6, 1983, with that date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000108490 reports the arrest of American and Spanish citizens. Its catalog heading notes the original title was deleted, then breaks off at the word In. The place of the arrests is cut off in the surviving heading text. The brief record preserves the deletion note and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000115490: Situation in Nicaragua -- Interagency Intelligence Memoran is the heading, cut off mid-word and with its date estimated, on CIA document 0000115490, dated August 2, 1981. The title marks a shared paper: an interagency memorandum on the situation in Nicaragua. Memorandum breaks off at Memoran in the released heading. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the break.
cia-0000118690:
This February 1977 analysis covers Latin America as a region, its politics country by country and trend by trend. It was written weeks after a new American president took office. Much of the continent was then ruled by military governments, and Washington was rethinking how to deal with them.

Regional surveys like this one gave policymakers a single map of a crowded field. The analysis weighs the strength of the generals' regimes and the pressures building against them. It also captures a turning point. The new administration's stress on human rights was about to clash with the habits of America's anti-communist partners in the hemisphere.
cia-0000119590:
Dated around January 1964, this CIA document warns that a drastic austerity program is about to be announced. The heading never names the country concerned. Harsh budget cuts and price rises were the kind of news that could shake a weak government.

Warnings like this one were meant to reach policymakers before the headlines did. An austerity package could spark strikes, riots, or a cabinet's fall, and Washington wanted no surprises. The document captures that alert as it was filed. Without the country's name on its face, it stands as an example of the agency's watch work, flagging trouble whose setting the heading alone does not give.
cia-0000126890: A CIA situation report gives the state of affairs as of 1 p.m. local time on February 17, 1968, during the Tet Offensive in Vietnam. Hourly reports tracked a fast-moving crisis that winter. The paper freezes a single hour of that emergency as the agency saw it. The filing date in the record sits oddly before the hour the report covers, a clerical quirk preserved in the release alongside the crisis reporting itself.
cia-0000132290: Situation Report 599 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series, dated January 6, 1991, covers Iraqi political developments under a headline cut short in the record title. Inside Iraq, the regime was tightening its grip as the deadline over Kuwait drew near. The short report records Baghdad's internal politics at that moment, as analysts understood them from outside a closed police state.
cia-0000132490:
Dated April 4, 1960, this CIA briefing sums up Cuba's political situation for American officials. Castro had been in power for just over a year. Relations between Havana and Washington were sliding downward month by month.

A summary paper like this one pulled the main facts together in one place: the new government's course, the mood on the island, and the friction with the United States. It belongs to the steady flow of Cuba reporting the agency produced that spring. Declassified years later, it lets readers watch a Cold War crisis build in near real time.
cia-0000132590: Yugoslavia failing to win Cuba's friendship fills a CIA item dated September 1, 1960. Havana chose Moscow's camp over the middle path that Belgrade offered to new states. Tito's road held little appeal for Castro's government at that point. The short item reports the failed courtship and what Belgrade had hoped to gain from a Cuban tie.
cia-0000135690: One more Spanish document from the 2506 Brigade files is dated 4 November 1960, a busy week in the surviving record. The brigade, exiles armed and trained by the CIA, was preparing in secret for Cuba. The catalog assigns this item no subject. Its description can honestly carry only its date, its Spanish text, and its place in the declassified brigade collection, which is how it is presented here.
cia-0000135890: A CIA planning paper from 1 May 1954, now declassified, deals with planning papers with an attached briefing, the names on both layers deleted by the censors. PBSUCCESS was the code name for the CIA effort to bring down President Jacobo Arbenz of Guatemala, which ended with his fall in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136290: Urgent steps at the United Nations Security Council are recommended in this June 1954 LINCOLN cable. The station advises that the United States, or preferably another delegate, submit all the facts about Guatemala's armament so the Council can judge its defensive or offensive character against neighboring armies. The aim was to answer Guatemala's complaint about the PBSUCCESS invasion on legal ground. It shows the diplomatic front being scripted from the field station.
cia-0000136990: Field reports from CALLIGERIS's forces fill this June 1954 cable to the Guatemala City station, though the text is tangled. Headquarters and LINCOLN received two reports that day stating government vehicles and trains had been located, and a request was passed urging an embassy to forward information. A man named Holland telephoned urgently, without reference to the names reporting, and attaches were to observe. The cable shows headquarters chasing battlefield sightings through diplomatic channels in the invasion's last days.
cia-0000139490: Prisoner movements in North Korea are recorded in this October 1953 report, three months after the armistice. In July 1953 all South Korean prisoners were transferred from the Kangso camp to another camp near Tokchon. An American army sergeant was transferred from Kanggye to the area that formerly housed the South Korean prisoners. A United States Air Force captain was also at the Kangso camp, and on 10 August additional United Nations prisoners arrived, the excerpt continues. Coordinates are given for each camp in the one-page report.
cia-03178390:
Soviet planning opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 25 December 1956. After central committee criticism, the short-range planning commission is rebuilt under Pervukhin. Five senior officials join him, shedding deputy premier posts. The plenum communiqué claims the 1956 industrial plan overfulfilled and consumer goods up nine percent. Coal, metal, cement, and timber are still scolded for missing their targets.

Poland needs prompt American aid, an official warns in the second item. Israel faces a final decision on further Sinai withdrawals. An army revolt in Indonesia follows: a Sumatran commander pledges loyalty to Sukarno but demands an honest government in Djakarta. The cabinet's answer is equivocal, relieving him temporarily while sending negotiators. Ishibashi forms a new Japanese cabinet. Pravda attacks the Polish idea of national communism. Turkey and Greece shift tactics on Cyprus.
cinq-traites-d-alchimie-des-plus-grands-:
Cinq traités d'alchimie des plus grands philosophes, edited by Albert Poisson and followed by a glossary, was published in Paris in 1890 in the Bibliothèque Chacornac. The five treatises are ascribed to great names of the old art: Paracelsus, Albertus Magnus, Roger Bacon, and Ramon Llull stand among them in the book's credits. The text is in French.

Poisson's preface argues that today's sciences are daughters of mysterious older ones. Alchemy mothered chemistry, he writes, as astrology went before astronomy. The treatises then speak in the old coded tongue of the work. Putrefaction, the black stone that hides whiteness within it, and the reddening that follows are set out as stages. They are stages of the one Pierre, the stone.
constitution-benin-1990:
Benin adopted this constitution in 1990, after a national conference ended years of one-party rule. Title one covers the state and sovereignty, declaring a republic with French as the official language. Title two lists the rights and duties of the individual, including rights to life, liberty, education, and work, and a ban on torture.

A president leads the executive and is elected for a set term. The National Assembly makes laws, and a Constitutional Court guards the charter; Benin's court became famous for bold rulings in defense of rights. Other titles cover the courts, local communities, and a council for economic and social affairs. The 1990 text launched one of Africa's more open democracies.
constitution-micronesia-1990:
The Federated States of Micronesia works under a constitution adopted in 1979, before full independence, and the hosted text is the version through 1990. It joins four island states, Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae, scattered across a vast stretch of the Pacific. Early articles found the federation and divide power between the national government and the states, much as the United States model does.

A president heads the executive and is chosen by the Congress from among its state-elected members. The Congress is a single chamber where each state holds an equal voice through at-large seats plus seats by population. Later articles protect rights in a declaration, cover the courts, and handle finance. Island custom and clan life get explicit respect in the text.
contributions-of-alchemy-to-numismatics-:
Contributions of Alchemy to Numismatics, by Henry Carrington Bolton, Ph.D., was read before the New York Numismatic and Archaeological Society on December 5 and printed at New York in 1890 in an author's edition of one hundred and seventy-five copies. A prelude sets the lure in figures: lead is worth about five cents a pound, gold about three hundred dollars. The conversion of the one into the other would yield a fabulous profit.

Such was the creed and goal of the alchemists for more than five centuries, Bolton writes, needing only industry and piety. His subject is the medals that creed left behind. One, of four ducats' weight, was struck for the baptism of Prince Christian Ernest on May 14, 1679: a two-headed bird, part eagle, crowned, with the words protection of the prince.
donnelly-caesars-column-1890:
Ignatius Donnelly imagines a twentieth century ruled by giant trusts in Caesar's Column, from 1890. His traveler tours a New York of splendor above and misery below. Wealth glitters in the air while the poor seethe in cellars, until revolt brings a violent and terrible reckoning on all.

Donnelly, a populist orator, wrote the best-selling dystopian novel of its age. The column of the title, built of the dead, chills every reader who reaches it. His nightmare of plutocracy warned America where greed might lead. The book helped invent American dystopian fiction, and its anger at monopoly still feels close to home.
dorian-gray-1890:
Oscar Wilde's sole novel first ran in Lippincott's Magazine in July 1890, in this form of thirteen parts. The text here stands as the magazine printed it, from page scans of that print. Wilde made it longer and more soft for the book form of 1891.

Dorian Gray keeps his youth while a portrait of him grows old and foul in his place. The magazine form is more raw and more bold than the book that most readers know. It holds lines and scenes Wilde cut or toned down when the first storm broke on the tale.
europmc-pmc10281990:
Lynch and co-workers show that strains of a gut bacterium, Turicibacter, change bile acids and body fats in different ways, in a 2023 study. Turicibacter species are common gut residents whose levels track with dietary fat and body weight. What they actually do to the host was poorly understood when the team began.

They compared strains in mice and found clear differences in how each strain altered bile acids and blood lipids. The results show that even close strains can push host metabolism in opposite directions. That nuance matters for probiotic design.
europmc-pmc10404590:
Fan and co-authors reviewed tiny drug carriers for cancer care in 2023. Most cancer drugs hit healthy cells as well as tumours, which causes harsh side effects. Carriers built at nano scale aim to fix that. They wrap a drug and steer it toward the tumour, sparing the rest of the body.

Good aim needs three steps, Fan explains. The carrier must reach the tumour, enter its cells, and release the drug at the right spot inside. Most carriers today manage just one or two of those steps. New designs try to chain all three steps in one trip. The review weighs what blocks use in clinics and what may clear the path.
europmc-pmc10448590:
Durante and a panel of thyroid experts wrote the 2023 European guide on thyroid nodules. A nodule is a lump in the thyroid, the gland in the neck that steers body fuel use. Sharp scans now find such lumps in vast numbers of adults. Most are harmless and need no treatment at all.

Even when a lump is cancer, it is often small, slow, and safe to watch. Durante sets out first tests and next steps for adults with a nodule. The guide pushes care that fits each person's risk, at lower cost where safe. Patient wishes form part of each choice. The guide does not cover care of thyroid cancer itself.
europmc-pmc10484790:
Brandes and co-authors used a deep AI model in 2023 to predict the effect of every gene variant in humans. A missense variant swaps one protein building block for another. Such swaps can be harmless or can cause disease. Past tools could score only some swaps, due to gaps in kin data or software caps.
