Their model, ESM1b, learned from protein sequences alone. It scored all roughly 450 million possible missense swaps. Brandes found it beat past tools on 150,000 known disease-linked swaps. It also matched lab measures across 28 large test sets. About 2 million swaps harmed just one form of a protein, not its kin forms.
europmc-pmc10601490:
Li Manni led a huge author team in 2023 to report growth in OpenMolcas, a free chemistry software pack. The pack simulates how electrons behave in molecules, which sets how they react. Users world-wide add tools to it in an open, shared model. The report covers new work since spring 2020.

Fresh skills span light spectra, shape tuning, and atom motion runs, Li Manni notes. Links to outside packs widen what the core can do. The team groups the gains by topic, from electron theory to dynamics. Each part shows the kinds of chemical puzzles the pack can now solve. The authors cast it as a strong base for top-tier atom studies.
europmc-pmc10618090:
Moncrieff and co-authors ran a broad evidence check in 2023 on the serotonin theory of depression. The theory holds that low serotonin, a brain signal chemical, causes low mood. It still shapes public views and drug ads. The team pooled past reviews across six key proof areas, to December 2020.

Seventeen studies met their bar, most of them pooled reviews. Two checks of a serotonin waste product in body fluids found no link to depression, Moncrieff reports. Blood serotonin showed no link either, though drug use may lower it. Brain scans of serotonin targets gave weak, mixed results. A check of draining its raw stock found no effect in most healthy people. The team found no firm support for the theory.
europmc-pmc10620090:
Klein and a large team profiled the immune systems of people with long Covid in 2023. Long Covid is a set of lasting symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Common signs are deep fatigue, crashes after effort, and foggy thought. What drives the state has stayed unclear.

The study enrolled 275 people with or without long Covid. Blood tests showed clear gaps in immune cell mixes versus matched controls. Klein reports stronger antibody responses to the Covid virus, and to other viruses such as Epstein-Barr. Levels of the stress hormone cortisol ran lower in the long Covid group. Machine learning picked the traits that best flagged the condition. The marks may guide tests and future care.
europmc-pmc11004190:
Zhang and colleagues review the largest family of drug targets on cell surfaces in this 2024 paper. G protein-coupled receptors are proteins that span the cell membrane and relay outside signals inward. They help run many body processes, so drugs often aim at them. Their action is complex, with signals that can be switched fully, partly, or in a biased way.

The review covers new 3D shapes of these receptors and how they switch on. It then dissects drugs approved in the US in the past five years that bind the main pocket. A fresh analysis covers drugs that bind side pockets and tune the receptor gently. Such side sites are widespread, the authors note. They propose hybrid drugs that grip both pockets at once as a future route.
europmc-pmc11701590:
Perez and a large team present the 2025 update of the UCSC Genome Browser in this 2025 paper. The browser is a web tool for visualising and analysing genomic data across more than 4,000 genome assemblies from diverse organisms. Released in 2001, it has become a core resource for genomics research. Annotation tracks come from the team itself and from community track hubs.

The year's updates include more than 25 new tracks for annotations. One is the gnomAD 4.1 population variant track on the human reference assembly. Three new public hubs were added, and the Genome Archive system for handling assembly variety expanded significantly. Interface work includes a new popup dialog that shows item details without leaving the main page. Gene track displays gained right-click zoom and precise navigation options. Custom tracks remain a core feature.
europmc-pmc11701690:
Perez-Riverol and colleagues mark 20 years of the PRIDE proteomics repository in this 2025 update. PRIDE is the world's leading archive for mass spectrometry proteomics data, and a founding member of the ProteomeXchange consortium. Submissions to its archive now average around 534 datasets per month.

A new transfer tool, Globus, handles very large datasets, making that volume possible. A new resubmission pipeline and automatic checks of datasets were added. New activities include a PRIDE chatbot built on open-source large language models. Support improved for crosslinking datasets, which capture protein-protein contacts. The team also reanalyses stored data and feeds the results to UniProt, Ensembl, and other added-value resources.
europmc-pmc1241790:
Birnbaum and Staskal asked whether brominated flame retardants warrant concern in 2004. These chemicals cut fire deaths and property damage for decades. Yet several types now turn up in nature and in people. Production is wide, contamination is rising, and effect data are thin.

Three chemical groups get close review for data gaps. They include tetrabromobisphenol A and two other major products. Fires kill over 3,000 Americans yearly, so benefits are real. Still, the toxicology record is incomplete and often conflicting. Birnbaum concludes the available data raise concern for certain classes. One is tetrabromobisphenol A; the others are hexabromocyclododecane and the PBDE mixtures.
europmc-pmc1434790:
A gene that fights viruses may also raise prostate cancer risk when faulty. Urisman and co-authors explored that link in 2006. Men with two copies of a weak form of the gene, called R462Q, face higher risk. The team reasoned that a virus might drive cancer in these men.

A virus-hunting chip found a new retrovirus in tumors from seven of 11 men with the weak gene pair. A wider check of 86 tumors found it in 40 percent of such men, but in just one other case. Urisman named the virus XMRV. It sits in about one percent of support cells near the tumor.
europmc-pmc1488890:
A trial result may not travel well to other patients or places. Rothwell examined that problem in 2006, called external validity: whether trial findings apply beyond the trial. He shows how the setting of a trial can bend its results.

In one carotid surgery trial, slow UK centers waited over two months to enroll patients, fast Dutch and Belgian centers three weeks. The delay shrank the treatment benefit, since stroke prevention has a short window. Rothwell also cites TB vaccine trials whose benefit faded toward the equator. He urges readers to weigh health systems, patient selection, and local disease patterns before applying any trial result.
europmc-pmc1557990:
A root bacterium helps peas and beans pull nitrogen from the air. Young and co-authors sequenced its genome in 2006. Rhizobium leguminosarum lives in root nodules and fixes nitrogen, letting crops grow without nitrogen fertilizer.

The genome splits into a core and an accessory part. The core holds the steady housekeeping genes shared with kin. The accessory part carries genes for partnership with specific hosts, since strains specialize on peas, clover, or beans. Young places the genome among the larger plant-linked bacterial genomes. The split design shows how one species adapts to many legume partners.
europmc-pmc1564390:
Counting virus plaques under a gel overlay is slow and fiddly. Matrosovich and co-authors tested a runnier overlay in 2006, made from microcrystalline cellulose called Avicel. Plaque assays measure viruses and antiviral drugs by the clear spots they leave in cell layers.

Plaques under Avicel grew larger than under agar or methylcellulose. Even a 0.3 percent mix kept plaques localized. The low viscosity made work in 96-well plates easy, and the overlay could go on without removing the virus first. With a flu drug, the assay measured drug strength well. Matrosovich calls it faster and more sensitive for large screening runs.
europmc-pmc1934390:
Servin and Stephens introduced in 2007 a statistical framework that lets genetic association studies test variants nobody directly measured. A study usually genotypes marker variants, called SNPs, in a candidate region. The causal variant may sit between markers, weakening the signal and clouding which variant is to blame.

Their method borrows correlation patterns among variants from reference projects such as HapMap. It then imputes, meaning it estimates, each person's unmeasured genotypes from their measured ones. Testing those estimates beat standard single-marker tests in power, even when the causal variant was in fact measured. Gains were greatest when several causal variants lurked in one region. The method also scores, for each variant, the evidence that it rather than a correlated neighbor is causal. Software named Bim-Bam implements the approach.
europmc-pmc1976390:
de Jonge and co-authors mined in 2007 more than thirteen thousand human gene array samples to find better reference genes. Gene activity readings must be scaled against housekeeping genes assumed to run at a steady level. The classics, such as ACTB and GAPDH, in fact swing widely between conditions, quietly corrupting results.

Their meta-analysis ranked genes by expression stability across many cell types and experimental setups. Novel candidates, including RPS13, RPL27, RPS20, and OAZ1, showed enhanced stability. None of the commonly used housekeeping genes reached the top 50 most stable genes. A parallel analysis of 2,543 mouse array samples confirmed the same candidates in another mammal. The authors recommend these genes as the right normalizers for gene expression work, replacing habit-based choices with evidence.
europmc-pmc2092390:
McClintock and colleagues reported in 2007 that a protein behind a rapid-ageing disease also marks normal ageing in skin. Hutchinson-Gilford progeria makes children age fast and die early, often from stroke or heart disease. Most cases carry a mutation that produces a faulty lamin A protein, called progerin. The team screened 150 skin biopsies from healthy people aged from newborn to 97 years.

The same splicing event occurred at low level in normal skin at all ages. Progerin messenger RNA stayed low, but the protein built up with age. It appeared in some skin fibroblasts and a few surface skin cells. Positive cells sat near the basement membrane in young adults. In elderly skin they spread deeper and grew more numerous. The authors call progerin a biomarker of normal cellular ageing.
europmc-pmc2125190:
William Thalhimer and M. A. Rothschild of Mount Sinai surveyed the Aschoff nodule in 1914, the tiny heart-muscle focus named for Aschoff, and asked what it proves in rheumatic fever. In rheumatic heart inflammation the nodules are present and characteristic. They favor the left ventricle's walls, while the auricles usually escape.

The diagnostic weight comes from the comparisons. Nodules appeared in three cases of chorea with no joint signs at all, tying that movement disorder firmly to rheumatism. They were absent in fourteen cases of subacute bacterial endocarditis caused by Streptococcus mitis, and in endocardial infections by four other named germs. Where an old rheumatic infection has burned out, the nodules may be gone, but their healed scars, dense sclerotic patches, remain. Readers get a microscope finding promoted to a court of appeal for diagnosis.
europmc-pmc2126690:
Ernest W. Smillie, Ralph B. Little, and Laura Florence interpreted the agglutination blood test in seventy-five cases of bovine abortion. Their 1919 Journal of Experimental Medicine paper checks test readings against bacteriological proof in each case. The test measures clumping power against Bacillus abortus, the abortion bacillus, across a full range of serum dilutions.

Run to its limit, the test is delicate, but it mirrors several tangled conditions at once. Timing matters: a uterus infected in the eighth month gives agglutinins little time to build. Infection lasting three or four months lets them accumulate far more. Bacilli living in the udder also drive the reaction's strength in many cases. So no fixed reading rules can be laid down. As a rough guide, a low titer suggests the cow is not infected at testing time, without ruling out past infection.
europmc-pmc2128090:
H. W. Graybill charted how the eggs of Heterakis papillosa, a worm of chickens, develop and survive outside the bird. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1921. He cultured the eggs at set temperatures, froze and dried them, and stored them in salt solution and in outdoor soil.

The eggs failed to develop in near-freezing cold and developed slowly a few degrees higher. At warm room temperatures they reached their final stage in seven to twelve days. Undeveloped eggs survived four days of freezing, and developed eggs survived a week outdoors. Drying killed undeveloped eggs somewhere between sixteen and forty-one days. Embryos in salt solution stayed alive a little over twelve months. Eggs in outdoor soil still held living embryos after eight months, a warning about how long poultry ground stays infested.
europmc-pmc2128190:
James B. Murphy, Raymond G. Hussey, Waro Nakahara, and Ernest Sturm tested whether the cell reaction X-rays stir in skin can defeat a cancer graft planted there. Their paper is the sixth in the X-ray effects series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1921. Small groin skin areas got a reddening dose, and a week later grafts went into the treated skin and the shielded opposite groin.

Grafts in the X-rayed skin took only rarely, while grafts in normal skin took at the usual high rate. Grafts planted deeper grew equally well on both sides. Tissue study explained the split: days after treatment the skin layers were thick with round lymphoid cells, and the reaction reached no deeper. This local lymphoid gathering, the authors suggest, controls skin grafts. They note the match with human cases, where skin metastases often melt under mild doses while deeper growths resist.
europmc-pmc2128290:
Francis G. Blake and Russell L. Cecil produced pneumonia in monkeys with the hemolytic streptococcus, in the eighth paper of their experimental pneumonia series. It appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1920. Normal monkeys received the germ by injection into the windpipe. The resulting disease was then compared, feature by feature, with the human illness.

Pneumonia followed in every case, matching the human disease in its signs, its complications, and its tissue changes. Two tissue patterns occurred, one spread through the lung framework and one filling whole lobules, sometimes in the same animal. Dose seemed to decide the pattern: small amounts gave the first form, a mark of strong resistance, while large amounts gave the second. Early study showed the germs breaking in through the walls of the larger air passages. From there they spread along the lung's framework and lymph channels.
europmc-pmc2128390:
Nathan Chandler Foot traced which cells build the tubercles of tuberculous meningitis in the rabbit's brain. His paper is the sixth in an endothelial reactions series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1922, from Harvard's comparative pathology department. The tubercles were produced experimentally in the brain and its membranes.

The tubercles form from cells of endothelial origin, the lining cells of vessels and organs. Those cells do not come only from the capillaries nearby. The blood's own wandering macrophages, large eating cells, are drawn into the building work, and in this case they can even divide while still free in the blood. Removing the spleen did not materially cut the supply of these cells. Liver and bone marrow lining may contribute, but the lung, Foot reports, plays a much larger role as a source than anyone had suspected.
europmc-pmc2128590:
Hobart A. Reimann counted blood platelets through the course of pneumonia in patients, and in rabbits infected with pneumococci. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. Platelets, the small clotting elements of blood, had no settled place in the pneumonia story when he began counting.

Once infection is established, the platelet count begins to fall, and the low count lasts through the fever. At the crisis of lobar pneumonia, or as the temperature drifts down, platelets climb again. After the fever they overshoot, rising well above the normal count, and settle back only after about two weeks. Later feverish complications bring a fresh fall, then another overshoot on recovery. During the low stage the platelets run smaller and more granular than usual. Antipneumococcus serum given by vein ordinarily made no difference to the count.
europmc-pmc2131290:
David Smith reported part ten of a rabbit respiratory infection series in 1927, describing an outbreak at Saranac Lake, New York. A stock of rabbits there was hit by pneumonia and snuffles, a nasal infection, caused by Bacterium lepisepticum. His laboratory studied tuberculosis at Saranac Lake, and the outbreak offered a natural test of how such epidemics begin.

Mucoid strains of the germ, of moderate and even strength, set off the epidemic. The germ had not grown stronger; rather, virulent germs reached a group of rabbits that had never met them before. Resistance varied by animal. Some died of pneumonia and blood infection, while others held the infection to the nose alone. The outbreak thus turned on contact and host weakness, not on a changed germ.
europmc-pmc2140590:
Hoagland and Davis, with the assistance of Martin, analyzed the cell sap of the alga Nitella in a 1923 paper. Plant cells draw minerals from very dilute water. The pair pressed out sap and measured its main inorganic elements. They compared them with the pond water the plants grew in. They also tested whether the elements sit in the sap as free ions.

Every principal element, potassium, sulfate, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, chloride, and sodium, sat in the sap far more concentrated than in the growth water. Conductivity showed nearly all of it in ionic form. The wall and protoplasm held bound calcium chiefly, and no bound potassium. Healthy sap kept a steady acidity even as the outside water swung wide. Nitrate entered the sap far faster from a slightly acid solution than from an alkaline one.
europmc-pmc2246290:
Marygold and a large team systematically linked ribosomal protein genes to Minute loci in the fruit fly in 2007. Ribosomes, the cell's protein-building machines, need dozens of ribosomal proteins. Minute loci are genome positions where mutations cause a classic dominant trait: small bristles and slow development. Many were suspected to be ribosomal protein genes, but no systematic check existed. The team combined bioinformatics with genetic experiments.

They identified 64 Minute loci that correspond to ribosomal protein genes. The fly's cytoplasmic ribosomes contain about 78 to 80 ribosomal proteins, while its mitochondrial ribosomes hold up to 80 more. Some ribosomal proteins also do extra jobs, including DNA repair and triggering cell death. The inventory gives fly genetics a firmer map for studying ribosome defects and their striking visible effects.
europmc-pmc2267490:
Lutz, Brefczynski-Lewis, Johnstone and Davidson scanned meditators' brains in 2008 during compassion meditation. Loving-kindness meditation cultivates wishes for others' happiness and relief from suffering. Novice and expert practitioners generated that state inside a functional MRI scanner while emotional and neutral sounds played. The team tested whether compassion training heightens affective processing, especially for sounds of distress, in brain circuits tied to empathy.

Emotional sounds raised pupil size and activated limbic regions, the insula and cingulate cortices, more during meditation than at rest. In experts, insula activation was greater for negative sounds than for positive or neutral ones, exceeding the novice pattern. Activation strength tracked self-reported meditation intensity in both groups. Experts also showed extra activation in the amygdala and in regions for understanding others' minds. Expertise in cultivating positive emotion thus reshapes empathy circuitry.
europmc-pmc2363790:
Hanks and an expert working group updated European guidance on morphine for cancer pain in 2001. The group belonged to the European Association for Palliative Care, which covers care for people with incurable illness. Morphine is the standard strong painkiller for moderate to severe cancer pain, but newer alternatives had appeared.

The recommendations keep morphine as the first-choice strong opioid, the class of powerful pain drugs derived from opium chemistry. They note oral morphine doses can vary a thousand-fold between patients for the same relief, so dosing must be fitted to the person. The group addressed public and professional fears of addiction and slowed breathing, calling them largely unfounded in proper pain care. Guidance also covers alternative opioids and hard situations where trial evidence is thin, marking how strong the evidence behind each point is.
europmc-pmc2525690:
Cirelli and Tononi asked a blunt question in this 2008 essay: is sleep actually essential? No theory yet explains why animals sleep, yet every studied species does it and lost sleep does harm. The authors test the null hypothesis, the idea that sleep has no core function and is just safe idleness when nothing better presses.

They check three predictions that idea makes. If sleep were optional, some animals should skip it entirely, some should need no catch-up sleep after staying awake, and going without should carry no serious cost. The evidence fails each test: all species examined show sleep, recovery sleep follows deprivation, and the consequences of missing sleep are severe. The authors conclude sleep is essential, most likely for a cellular function science has yet to pin down.
europmc-pmc2586090:
Gresham and colleagues evolved yeast in nutrient-limited tanks for about 200 generations in 2008 and then read the genomes of the winners to catalogue adaptation. Experimental evolution lets scientists watch evolution happen, but finding the responsible mutations was once the hard part. They ran 24 cultures of baker's yeast limited by glucose, sulfate, or phosphate and used microarray methods to detect every class of genetic change.

They found frequent gene amplifications and rearrangements and new jumping-gene insertions, plus 32 point mutations across ten clones. Fitness rose by 5 to 50 percent. Glucose- and phosphate-limited cultures found several distinct genetic routes to success, while sulfate-limited ones were tightly constrained. Many mutations hit genes never before linked to the nutrient's metabolism, teaching new physiology.
europmc-pmc2636790:
Heled and Drummond presented in 2008 a new way to read the past size of a population from its genes. Their method, the Extended Bayesian Skyline Plot, works back from DNA samples to estimate how numbers rose or fell over time. Unlike earlier tools, it can combine data from many genes at once.

The pair tested the method on made-up data where the true history was known. Many genes together recovered sharp past crashes in numbers, called bottlenecks, that one gene alone would miss. They then tried real data: one gene from hepatitis C virus in Egypt, and ten genes from fruit flies across 16 populations. Even small mistakes in reading the DNA lowered accuracy a lot, so clean data matter as much as more data.
europmc-pmc2642990:
McBride and colleagues showed in 2009 that a cell energy sensor called AMPK also senses stored fuel, not just fuel in use. AMPK switches cells to making energy when supplies run low. One part of it, the beta subunit, carries a patch that grips glycogen, the body's stored form of sugar, but the purpose of that grip was unclear.

In lab tests, glycogen slowed AMPK down, and highly branched glycogen, with many chain ends, slowed it most. The team built small branched sugars to test the effect precisely. Sugars with a single branch point blocked AMPK and also blocked the enzymes that switch it on. Cutting the grip patch by mutation removed the effect. The sensor, it seems, reads both the fuel gauge and the fuel tank.
europmc-pmc2660690:
Erlanger and colleagues reviewed in 2009 the past, present, and future of Japanese encephalitis, a mosquito-borne virus disease across Asia. Some 3 billion people live where the virus circulates. Each year it strikes an estimated 30,000 to 50,000 people, kills 10,000 to 15,000, and leaves many survivors with lasting brain damage.

The virus breeds in a mosquito that favors flooded rice fields. Water birds carry it in nature, and it spills into pigs, horses, and people. The disease is rising where populations grow and rice irrigation spreads, but falling where vaccination and changed farming cut exposure. The authors stress how sharply the yearly burden swings, which makes single-year figures unreliable. Control, they argue, must join vaccines with attention to farming and water, the forces that set the mosquito's numbers.
europmc-pmc2680990:
Mehling and co-authors reviewed in 2009 the questionnaires that claim to measure body awareness, a person's sense of signals from inside their own body. Noticing heartbeat, breath, and gut feelings can help or harm: it guides care for chronic pain and trauma, yet anxious over-focus can worsen symptoms. Dozens of scales existed, but no one had checked them side by side.

From 1,825 papers, the team kept 12 scales that fit their scope. Only two earned top marks for consistency, and four for measuring what they claim. Reading every question closely, the team sorted body awareness into four domains with eleven parts, covering noticing, attention style, and trust in body signals. No single scale covered them all, and the parts that separate healthy awareness from harmful were exactly the ones missing. Better tools, they argue, are needed before therapy can target this skill.
europmc-pmc2712090:
Pesquita and co-authors reviewed in 2009 semantic similarity, a way to compare living things by the meaning of their labels in a biomedical ontology. An ontology is a formal schema that names traits and how they relate. When genes or diseases share that schema, their label sets can be scored for how close in meaning they are.

Their review sorts measures into node-based and edge-based forms, and into pairwise and groupwise forms. It also surveys tests that compare the measures and the software that runs them. Uses include checking gene groups, gene activity studies, and hunting for disease genes. The authors expect such measures to grow as central as sequence matching already is.
europmc-pmc2719090:
Sun, Huang, and Zhang tested in 2009 whether MAP kinases, a family of signaling enzymes, control the antioxidant master switch Nrf2 by tagging it directly. Nrf2 turns on many protective and detox genes when oxidative stress hits. It is normally held down by Keap1, which marks it for destruction, and stress frees it through changes on Keap1.

They proved Nrf2 is tagged by these kinases in living cells and mapped the main tag sites on the protein. Mutating all those sites lowered Nrf2 activity only modestly, mainly by slightly reducing its entry into the nucleus. Its stability, set by Keap1, did not change. Direct tagging thus plays only a small part, and the kinases likely act indirectly.
europmc-pmc2777390:
Chasman and co-authors ran in 2009 a genome-wide association study of plasma lipoprotein measures in over seventeen thousand women from the Women's Genome Health Study. Standard cholesterol tests sum up whole fractions, while NMR measures count particles by class and size, traits that may track heart disease risk more closely. They tested seventeen NMR measures plus the standard lipids and two carrier proteins against genome-wide markers.

Thirty-six regions reached genome-wide significance in their main analyses. Ten of them had never been tied to blood lipids before. Some regions shaped particle size without changing cholesterol content, for LDL at four places and HDL at one. Adding regions already known from standard lipid studies brought the total to forty-three loci. Many hits clustered at genes for the machinery that builds and clears lipoprotein particles.
europmc-pmc2836990:
White, Biérinx, Gnocchi, and Zammit charted how mouse muscle fibers grow after birth in 2010, using a fast leg muscle that is set in fiber count before birth. A growing fiber can enlarge only if new nuclei join it, and those come from satellite cells, the muscle's resident stem cells. Two reporter mouse lines let the team count fiber nuclei and satellite cells separately.

Fiber number never rose after the first week, yet fiber volume grew about fourteen-fold by adulthood. Nuclei per fiber rose roughly five-fold in the first three weeks, then stopped, while fibers kept swelling, so each nucleus served a much larger territory. Satellite cells per fiber fell from about fourteen to the adult five over the same three weeks.
europmc-pmc2847190:
Alaux and colleagues tested in 2010 whether a gut parasite and a common insecticide together hurt honeybees more than either alone. Bee colonies have been vanishing across Europe and North America, and single-cause explanations keep falling short. The team exposed bees to Nosema, a microsporidian gut parasite, to the neonicotinoid imidacloprid, or to both, and tracked survival, energy stress, and immune measures.

The combination produced the highest death rates and the strongest energy strain in the short term. Individual immune counts stayed untouched, but glucose oxidase, the enzyme bees use to sterilize colony and brood food, fell only in the combined group. The synergy, the authors argue, leaves colonies open to further infection over time.
europmc-pmc2851690:
Ma, Liu, Che, Yu, Dai, and You tested in 2010 whether the flavor of immune cells inside lung tumors predicts how long patients live. Macrophages in tumors come in two broad forms: M1 cells that attack tumors and M2 cells that abet them. The team stained tumor samples from one hundred non-small cell lung cancer patients, half short survivors and half long survivors, counting each form separately.

About seventy percent of the macrophages were the tumor-friendly M2 form, and their numbers matched survival not at all. The anti-tumor M1 cells told another story: long survivors carried roughly ten times more M1 cells inside their tumor islets than short survivors did. M1 density inside the islets independently predicted survival, making it a candidate prognostic marker.
europmc-pmc2866690:
Herbstman and a large team followed New York children from birth in 2010 to test whether flame retardants met before birth affect brain development. The chemicals, called PBDEs, were added to foam and electronics and build up in body fat. The cohort began after the September 2001 attacks and enrolled mothers who delivered at three lower Manhattan hospitals.

Cord blood from two hundred ten newborns carried measurable levels of several PBDE types. Children with higher levels of the three most common types scored lower on mental and motor tests given between ages one and six years, after other influences were accounted for. The pattern matched animal findings and added human evidence that these widespread chemicals can quietly shape early development.
europmc-pmc2891790:
Lee and Zheng reviewed in 2010 PDZ domains, small protein modules that grip the tails of other proteins to organize cell signaling. A PDZ domain reads a short amino acid motif at a target's very end, docking it into place at membranes, junctions, and channel clusters. Hundreds of human proteins carry these modules, so their binding rules shape transport, ion channel behavior, and many signal pathways.

New tools such as peptide libraries and protein arrays have measured the grip preferences of whole PDZ families at once, replacing one-at-a-time studies. The binding turns out to be choosier than the simple tail code suggests. Chemical tagging by phosphorylation, either on the tail or on the domain itself, can switch a pairing on or off, adding a regulatory layer.
europmc-pmc2912890:
Novák, Neumann, and Macas adapted in 2010 a graph-clustering trick to catalog the repetitive DNA that fills most of a plant genome. Repeats are too numerous and varied to assemble conventionally, yet a single light round of shotgun sequencing samples every major family. Their method compares the short reads to each other and groups them into clusters, where reads from one repeat family clump together into a recognizable graph shape.

Cluster sizes estimate how much of the genome each family occupies, and the graph's shape reveals the family's internal structure. Tests on pea and soybean, two legumes with very different genome sizes, recovered their known repeat landscapes faithfully. Species with no sequenced genome can now get a repeat census from one inexpensive sequencing run, a door into genome evolution studies.
europmc-pmc2935890:
Smith and colleagues ran a randomised trial called VITACOG, reported in 2010, testing whether B vitamins slow brain shrinkage in older people with mild memory trouble. Raised homocysteine in blood is a known risk marker for shrinkage and dementia, and B vitamins lower it.

Over two years, volunteers past seventy took high-dose folic acid plus vitamins B6 and B12, or a dummy pill. Among those who finished brain scans, yearly shrinkage ran clearly slower in the vitamin group than in the placebo group. The gap suggests a cheap dietary approach worth testing further against decline.
europmc-pmc3002190:
Reif and co-authors ranked environmental chemicals for hormone disruption risk using the United States ToxCast screening data in a 2010 study. Hundreds of chemicals had been run through hundreds of fast lab assays, and regulators needed a fair way to choose what to test deeply first.

Focusing on estrogen, androgen, and thyroid pathways, they built profiles for each chemical and merged many data sources into a weighted priority index. The combined score gave sturdier rankings than any single source alone. Their approach offers the national screening programme a transparent decision aid for ordering follow-up testing.
europmc-pmc3023790:
Chen and coauthors examined in 2010 how three related plant genes shape responses to stress and to a key plant hormone. The genes, named WRKY18, WRKY40, and WRKY60, make proteins that switch other genes on or off in the small plant Arabidopsis. The hormone, called ABA in short, helps plants handle drought, salt, and other hard conditions.

Using plants with one, two, or all three genes knocked out, plus plants with extra copies, the team found the genes pull in opposite directions. Two of them made seeds and roots more sensitive to the hormone and to salt stress. The third worked against them and also turned the second group down. Together they form a small control network. It fine tunes how plants answer both attack and harsh weather.
europmc-pmc3042390:
Thomée, Härenstam, and Hagberg followed in 2011 more than four thousand Swedish young adults to test whether heavy mobile phone use harms mental health. Participants aged twenty to twenty four answered surveys at the start and again a year later. The team counted not just call volume, but also felt demands to be reachable, stress from constant access, night waking by the phone, and self judged overuse.

Heavy users reported more stress, worse sleep, and more depressive symptoms at the same point in time. Looking ahead, heavy use predicted new sleep trouble and depressive symptoms a year later among those free of them at the start. Feeling stressed by constant reachability was the strongest warning sign for both sexes. The authors suggest prevention should help young adults set limits on availability, their own and others, rather than only cutting minutes.
europmc-pmc3042690:
Das and Chandran reviewed in 2011 how microbes can clean up oil pollution, one of the most stubborn environmental problems from the petrochemical industry. Spilled petroleum contains compounds that can cause cancer and damage nerves, and common fixes such as burning or burying waste grow very costly at large scales. Many soil and water microbes, by contrast, can eat hydrocarbons as food.

The review explains how these microbes break complex oil compounds down, sometimes fully into carbon dioxide, water, and cell material. It surveys which organisms do the work in different settings, from seawater to soil. Because living cleanup is cheaper and can finish the job completely, the authors present it as the most promising route for large contaminated sites. They note that success depends on matching microbes and conditions to each spill.
europmc-pmc3047790:
Coutinho and Chapman reviewed in 2011 how glucocorticoid drugs calm inflammation and suppress the immune system, and why their long term use is a bargain with harm. Since the nineteen forties these drugs have been among the most effective treatments for inflammatory and autoimmune disease. Their costs include bone thinning, high blood pressure, disturbed blood fats, and raised diabetes risk.

Drug hunters have long tried to split the benefits from the harms, with limited success so far. The review gathers recent, sometimes surprising findings on how the drugs actually work inside cells. One local enzyme that boosts or cuts the drugs' strength inside tissues gets close attention. Better maps of these pathways, the authors argue, are the route to safer versions. The paper is a status report for researchers chasing that split.
europmc-pmc3098090:
Matsen, Kodner, and Armbrust introduced in 2010 pplacer, a program that slots new short DNA reads onto a fixed family tree of known species with proper statistical rigor. Environmental sequencing produces mountains of short reads with no names attached. Name matching by simple similarity can mislead badly for distant relatives, while building a fresh tree for every read is far too slow.

Placement instead asks where each read best fits on an existing, trusted tree, using likelihood methods. The program places tens of thousands of reads per hour, with time and memory growing only in step with the reference tree. It also reports how uncertain each placement is, edge by edge, and draws trees whose branch thickness and color show placements and doubt. Tests on simulated reads showed high accuracy. The tool is free as code, binaries, and a web service.
europmc-pmc3116190:
Chia-Yen Lee and colleagues surveyed tiny devices for mixing fluids in a 2011 review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Lab-on-a-chip tools handle drops far too small for stirring, so blending samples quickly and fully is a core design problem. At that scale, blending depends mostly on molecules spreading between streams on their own.

The review sorts designs into two families. Active designs shake or push the fluids with outside energy, such as sound, heat, or electric force. Passive designs instead stretch the contact between streams through winding or split channels, needing no extra power. After a decade of proposals, the authors compare the main designs so engineers can match a mixer to their device and task.
europmc-pmc3117990:
Tamas Varga, Zsolt Czimmerer, and Laszlo Nagy reviewed a family of fat-sensing gene switches in a 2011 paper in Biochimica et Biophysica Acta. Cells meet many kinds of fat daily, and these switches read fat signals and turn genes on or off in response. They sit at the crossing point of energy handling and immune activity.

The switches govern how the body stores and burns fat and sugar, and they were already targets of diabetes drugs. Newer work shows they also dial inflammation up or down, linking rich diets and clogged arteries to immune overreaction. The review gathers fresh findings on how the switches are controlled and how they keep balance in health, plus where that balance fails in disease.
europmc-pmc3153290:
Irina Pinchuk, Ellen Beswick, and Victor Reyes surveyed a family of bacterial super-toxins in a 2010 paper in Toxins. The source germ is carried by about a third of people and causes illnesses from food poisoning to toxic shock. Its gut toxins, more than twenty in number, survive heat and stomach acid that would destroy most proteins.

Two members are the best studied. They latch onto immune cells and force huge numbers of T cells to fire at once, releasing a flood of signal chemicals that can tip into shock. In food, the same hardiness lets them survive preparation and trigger sudden vomiting illness. The review also flags drug-resistant strains as a rising hospital concern, tied to diarrhoea in patients on antibiotics.
europmc-pmc3257290:
Brenna Henn and colleagues used genome-wide data to reconstruct the ancestry of North Africans, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Genetics. People north of the Sahara differ from sub-Saharan Africans in culture, language, and appearance, but when and how much their genes diverged was poorly understood. The team genotyped hundreds of thousands of sites in seven North African populations and one Spanish group.

They found a gradient of Maghrebi ancestry rising from east to west, strongest in groups with Berber identity. That ancestry appears to descend mainly from a back-to-Africa migration more than twelve thousand years ago, before the Holocene. Most populations also carry ancestry from the Near East. Smaller shares come from sub-Saharan Africa and from Europe. Dating DNA tracts placed a west African migration into Morocco roughly twelve hundred years ago and a Nilotic one into Egypt about seven hundred fifty years ago.
europmc-pmc3411490:
Karastergiou, Smith, Greenberg, and Fried reviewed in 2012 why fat settles differently on women and men, the biology behind the pear shape. Women carry more body fat overall, yet the hip-and-thigh pattern typical of women brings lower metabolic risk than men's belly-centered pattern. The review compares the fat cells of each depot and sex.

Evidence points to built-in differences in the precursor cells that make fat, shaped further by sex hormones, the local tissue setting, and early development. Women's lower-body fat may simply be a safe storehouse for spare energy. Or it may actively steer body-wide metabolism through signals it releases. The authors weigh both possibilities and the experiments behind them.
europmc-pmc3427890:
Carruthers led an international consensus panel that published new diagnostic criteria for myalgic encephalomyelitis in 2011. The panel argued the older label chronic fatigue syndrome undersells a disease marked by widespread inflammation and nervous-system pathology. Its members, from thirteen countries, had treated roughly fifty thousand patients between them and reached full agreement through a structured Delphi process.

The criteria center on a crash after exertion, called postexertional neuroimmune exhaustion, as the required core feature. Around it they organize symptoms across nerve, immune, gut, and energy systems, with working notes to sharpen each judgment. The authors present the name and the criteria as a truer map of the illness. Clinicians and researchers get a shared standard for diagnosis and study.
europmc-pmc3530590:
Dog gut microbes shift with illness, and Jan S. Suchodolski leads a fourteen-author team profiling feces across health and disease in 2012. They sequence the 16S gene in samples from 32 healthy dogs, 12 with non-bloody acute diarrhea, 13 with bloody acute diarrhea, and dogs with active or controlled inflammatory bowel disease.

Acute diarrhea, especially the bloody form, scrambles the microbiome most. Bloody diarrhea dogs lose Blautia, Faecalibacterium relatives, and Turicibacter while gaining Sutterella and Clostridium-like groups. In active IBD, Faecalibacterium and the Fusobacteria phylum fall, then recover when disease is controlled. Diversity trends lower in sick groups. The catalogue gives veterinarians a baseline for what dysbiosis looks like in dogs.
europmc-pmc3532190:
Cells export microRNAs in tiny vesicles, and Jasenka Guduric-Fuchs and five colleagues test whether that export is selective in 2012. They sequence small RNAs from HEK293T cells and their extracellular vesicles, before and after forcing the cells to overproduce one microRNA, miR-146a.

A definite subset of microRNAs is enriched in the vesicles, and their predicted target genes cluster around regulating endocytosis, the cell's uptake machinery. Checking other cell types and public data shows many of these microRNAs are preferentially exported widely, not just in this line. Overproduced miR-146a, by contrast, is handled differently. Export looks like a sorting process, a point that matters for future therapies built on vesicle cargo.
europmc-pmc3567190:
Xiang Zhou, Peter Carbonetto, and Matthew Stephens presented a hybrid statistical model for genetics in PLoS Genetics in 2013. Genome studies face a split problem. Traits may be shaped by thousands of tiny gene effects spread everywhere, which linear mixed models handle well, or by a few large effects, which sparse regression catches. For any real data set, no one knows in advance which picture fits, and choosing wrong costs accuracy.

Their Bayesian sparse linear mixed model contains both approaches as special cases and lets the data shift weight between them. A new sampling algorithm makes the heavy computing practical. On two jobs, estimating how much of a trait genes explain and predicting trait values for new cases, the hybrid matched the strengths of each parent method. For prediction it beat both, along with several other large-scale tools. Free software accompanies the paper.
europmc-pmc3580690:
Dimitri Gusmao-Flores and colleagues weighed two bedside tools for spotting delirium in Critical Care in 2012. Delirium, a sudden failure of attention and thinking, strikes many intensive care patients and worsens their outcomes. Two structured checks were designed for the unit: CAM-ICU, a short algorithm-based test, and ICDSC, a checklist scored over a shift. The review pooled studies that judged both against formal psychiatric criteria.

Nine studies with 969 patients covered CAM-ICU; four studies with 361 covered the checklist. CAM-ICU caught about eighty percent of true cases while wrongly flagging few healthy patients, with specificity near ninety-six percent. The checklist was a little less sharp on both counts, catching about seventy-four percent. Quality scoring of the studies accompanied the pooling. For busy units, the numbers support CAM-ICU as the stronger default screen.
europmc-pmc3606290:
Ryo Kurita and colleagues grew immortal human red blood cell factories in PLoS ONE in 2013. Transfusion depends on donated blood, with shortages and infection worries built in. Making red cells in the laboratory could ease both. The team had already built everlasting mouse cell lines for this. Here they report a reliable recipe for human versions, starting from blood-forming stem cells. They switch on selected growth genes to keep the starter cells dividing forever.

The lines made hemoglobin that works and carried the markers of red cell precursors, strengthening those markers when told to mature. Most importantly, after maturation signals the cells expelled their nuclei, the defining final step of a true red blood cell. Output efficiency still needs work, the authors note. Even so, this is the first showing that immortalized human lines can serve as a renewable source of finished red cells.
europmc-pmc3819990:
Judith A. Finegold, Perviz Asaria, and Darrel P. Francis chart heart disease deaths worldwide in the International Journal of Cardiology, with the record dated 2013. They use death records from the World Health Organisation and population data from the United Nations. The years covered run from the mid-1990s to the late 2000s.

Blocked heart arteries form the single largest cause of death on Earth, the study finds. Rates differ more than twenty-fold between countries. Eastern Europe and Central Asia sit at the top, rich nations at the bottom. Age-adjusted rates have fallen by more than half in rich countries, yet stay flat or rise in some poorer ones. Most deaths now occur in low- and middle-income countries.
europmc-pmc3882890:
Enola K. Proctor, Byron J. Powell, and J. Curtis McMillen give reporting advice in Implementation Science in 2013. Implementation strategies are the how-to steps that change health care practice. Studies of them often label and describe the steps so poorly that no one can reuse or test them.

The authors propose that each strategy be named, defined, and spelled out on seven points. Who acts, what they do, who or what they target, when and how often, how much, which outcomes they aim at, and the theory behind the choice. Vague package labels should give way to those parts. Precise reports would let clinics copy what works and let science test strategies head to head, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc3984790:
Laurent Dortet, Laurent Poirel, and Patrice Nordmann review the worldwide spread of NDM carbapenemases in BioMed Research International in 2014. These bacterial enzymes, first flagged in New Delhi, destroy nearly all beta-lactam antibiotics, including the last-resort carbapenems, leaving only a few older drugs standing. The main reservoir is the Indian subcontinent, with a second established in the Balkans and the Middle East.

The resistance genes travel mostly on plasmids, DNA circles bacteria swap freely, within gut bacteria families, and they have also landed in Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter, the latter possibly a bridge species. Variants keep multiplying. The authors argue that containing this threat rests on rapid tests, such as the Carba NP assay, and on screening carriers before the genes seed new hospitals.
europmc-pmc3990490:
Natacha Bodenhausen, Miriam Bortfeld-Miller, Martin Ackermann, and Julia A. Vorholt test whether plant genes shape the microbes that live on leaves, in PLoS Genetics in 2014. Leaves form a vast home for bacteria and fungi, yet host control of that mix was not known. The team used the small plant Arabidopsis thaliana in a clean, germ-free set-up.

Plants were dosed with a simple mix of seven bacterial strains drawn from the main leaf groups. A screen of fifty-five mutant plants, changed in surface, wall, defence, or scent traits, found a few that shifted the mix or its size. Mutants with faults in the leaf skin, named lacs2 and pec1, showed the strongest shifts and held more bacteria. A gene for a growth signal, ein2, also shaped the mix. Plant type alone changed the community too, so genes do guide leaf microbes.
europmc-pmc4003790:
Pasupuleti Visweswara Rao and Siew Hua Gan review the health effects of cinnamon, in Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine in 2014. Cinnamon bark is among the world's most used spices, in food and in folk care alike. Its scent and much of its action come from oils in the bark, chiefly a compound called cinnamaldehyde.

Reports credit cinnamon with a long list of effects. It can fight oxidation and inflammation, kill microbes, and lower blood sugar and blood fats. Studies also link it to lower heart disease risk and to action against some cancers. Work on brain disorders such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's is noted too. The review gathers the evidence for these claims, sets out the spice's main compounds, and shows how a daily kitchen spice came to be studied as a many-sided medicine.
europmc-pmc4035690:
Navdeep S. Chandel reviews mitochondria as signallers, not just power plants, in BMC Biology in 2014. Textbooks cast these cell parts as makers of energy and building blocks. That view cracked when a protein spilling from them was found to start a cell death cascade.

Since then, modes of mitochondrial talk have piled up. The parts release reactive oxygen as a signal and host signal teams on their outer skin. Faulty mitochondria raise stress answers in the rest of the cell, reporting their own state. Newer finds add more channels: shared metabolites, movement and shape change of the parts, and direct contact with other cell parts that tunes signals. Chandel traces this history from the first shock to the present web. The upshot is that cell fate in health and disease often turns on messages from these former power-only parts.
europmc-pmc4057290:
Jack E. Zimmerman, Andrew A. Kramer, and William A. Knaus tracked hospital deaths for patients admitted to intensive care units across the United States. Their study, published in Critical Care in 2013, covers admissions from 1988 to 2012. It asks whether death rates changed even as patients arrived older and more severely ill.

Using clinical records for more than four hundred eighty thousand admissions, the authors found a large relative fall in hospital mortality over the period. The drop differed sharply by diagnosis, with the steepest falls for some lung, seizure, and surgical conditions. More patients also left for post-acute care rather than home. The authors link the gains mainly to better care, while noting that discharge patterns may also play a part.
europmc-pmc4103590:
Anthony M. Bolger, Marc Lohse, and Bjoern Usadel created Trimmomatic, a tool that cleans raw Illumina sequencing reads before analysis. Their software note appeared in Bioinformatics in 2014. Adapter pieces and low-quality stretches left in the data can easily spoil downstream results, yet spotting them without cutting good data is tricky.

Existing cleaners, the authors found, lacked the mix of flexibility, speed, and correct handling of paired-end reads they needed. Trimmomatic was built to fill that gap. Tests on both reference-based and reference-free tasks showed its output at least matched rival tools and often beat them. The program is cross-platform Java, released under a free licence, with supplementary data online. It became a standard first step in many sequencing pipelines.
europmc-pmc4142390:
Ayla Valinezhad Orang, Reza Safaralizadeh, and Mina Kazemzadeh-Bavili reviewed how tiny RNAs called microRNAs steer genes, and how they can at times turn genes up, not just down. Their review came out in the International Journal of Genomics in 2014. Found in 1993, these RNAs are now seen as one of the big gene-steering groups, with tens of thousands known.

The stock view is one of cuts: a microRNA binds the tail of a target note and brings its end, or blocks the making of its protein. Newer work shows the same RNAs can boost output too. Which way they act rests on cell type, state, and the partners at hand. That two-way power lets cells react fast to new states with no waste of fuel. The team sums up how these RNAs are made, how they cut, and what is known of the boost path.
europmc-pmc4151090:
Silvia Galván-Peña and Luke A. J. O'Neill reviewed how a macrophage's fuel choice decides its behaviour. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Immune cells' metabolic state and their function are tightly linked, and macrophages show the pattern clearly.

Attack-style M1 macrophages, first responders to bacteria, run on fast sugar burning. Repair-style M2 macrophages use slower oxidative metabolism to sustain long-term healing work. Intermediates are not just fuel: in M1 cells, a Krebs cycle product called succinate steadies a factor that drives lasting output of an inflammatory cytokine. In M2 cells, a sugar-pathway enzyme proves critical to their programme. Targeting these metabolic switches, the authors say, is an exciting route to steer disease.
europmc-pmc4167990:
Paul Geeleher, Nancy Cox, R. Stephanie Huang, and Jason D. Barbour presented a software package named pRRophetic in PLoS ONE in 2014. Their earlier work showed that a tumour's gene activity pattern can hint at which chemotherapy drug will work on it. Those models were trained on drug tests run on large panels of cancer cell lines.

pRRophetic wraps that method in the R language so other labs can build and apply such models with ease. The team shows it can predict response for many drugs, and that training on blood cancer cell lines sharpened forecasts for the drug bortezomib in myeloma. The package also works with several kinds of input data, widening who can test the approach.
europmc-pmc4175590:
Nicolas Stransky, Christoph Lengauer, and three co-authors charted kinase gene fusions across cancers in Nature Communications in 2014. Fusions form when genes break and rejoin wrongly, and some create overactive kinase proteins that drive tumours. Such fusions can be ideal drug targets, as shown by drugs for certain leukaemias and lung cancers.

The team built rules for spotting fusions in RNA sequencing data and ran them on nearly 7,000 tumour samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas. They found several new and repeated fusions involving kinases, across both blood cancers and solid tumours. Because approved or test drugs already exist for many of these kinases, the catalogue points to treatment options that could be matched to patients by their tumour's fusion profile.
europmc-pmc4183590:
Terence N. Bukong, Gyongyi Szabo, and four co-authors showed a new route of hepatitis C spread in PLoS Pathogens in 2014. Antibodies that block the virus from entering liver cells give limited help, which suggested another way in. Exosomes, tiny sacs shed by cells, can carry genetic material between cells, and the team tested their role.

Exosomes taken from the blood of infected patients carried hepatitis C RNA, including the negative strand that proves the RNA can copy itself. Those sacs infected fresh liver cells without using the normal entry receptors. Inside the sacs the viral RNA rode with three host helpers, Ago2, HSP90, and miR-122. Blocking any of those helpers, or the pumps that load the sacs, sharply cut the spread, which names possible drug targets.
europmc-pmc4226890:
Johannes Attems and Kurt A. Jellinger reviewed the mix of vessel disease and Alzheimer's in BMC Medicine in 2014. Brains of older people rarely show one clean disease: Alzheimer's changes and blood vessel damage usually arrive together. The pair asked how the two pathologies interact in the tissue itself.

Up to 84 percent of aged subjects show vessel disease signs alongside Alzheimer pathology, most often amyloid in vessel walls and small vessel disease. In early Alzheimer's, small strokes and vessel lesions seem to push thinking downhill and bring dementia forward. In full-blown disease, small infarcts add little, swamped by the Alzheimer damage. Mixed dementia brains hold more large infarcts. The authors call for studies that separate the stages at which vessel damage matters most.
europmc-pmc4234490:
Haibao Tang, David C. Schwartz, and ten co-authors released an improved genome for a model legume in BMC Genomics in 2014. Medicago truncatula, a small clover relative, stands in for beans, peas, and other legumes in research. Its earlier genome build left much sequence unplaced.

The new version, Mt4.0, rebuilt the assembly from fresh shotgun reads and pinned the pieces to chromosome maps using an optical map and a genotyping map. About 360 million letters now sit in place, against roughly 250 million in the prior build, and most genes once stranded off-chromosome moved onto the map. Re-annotation counts 50,894 genes in total. The sharper reference should speed gene discovery for the whole legume family.
europmc-pmc4310190:
Amy E McCart Reed, Jamie R Kutasovic, Sunil R Lakhani, and Peter T Simpson review invasive lobular carcinoma, a distinct form of breast cancer. Their review appeared in Breast Cancer Research in 2015. It is the most common special subtype, making up to about fifteen percent of breast cancers, and on paper its outlook looks good: low grade, slow dividing, hormone sensitive.

In practice the tumor hides from screening, spreads in single file strands, and seeds distant sites widely, so long term outcomes can be worse than the standard form. The review covers its look under the microscope, its marker profile, and its gene level features. The contrast between tame markers and invasive behavior frames the open questions in care.
europmc-pmc4383390:
Caren Chancey, Andriyan Grinev, Evgeniya Volkova, and Maria Rios reviewed West Nile virus worldwide in BioMed Research International in 2015. The virus was first isolated in Uganda in 1937 and has grown into a major cause of human and animal disease. It cycles naturally between birds and mosquitoes, spilling over at times into people and horses. Most human infections cause no symptoms, but severe brain disease can follow, with lasting effects or death.

The review traces how the virus's range kept expanding over 77 years, as its mosquito carriers are found nearly worldwide. Outbreaks grew more frequent and severe from the mid-1990s, reaching the Americas in 1999. Because no vaccine or specific cure anchors control, surveillance and prevention carry the load. The authors stress steady monitoring wherever transmission is possible, since the virus rarely announces itself before severe cases appear.
europmc-pmc4394490:
Delphine Antoni, Hélène Burckel, Elodie Josset, and Georges Noel reviewed three-dimensional cell culture in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2015. Cells grown flat on plastic, the classic lab method, behave unlike cells in the body, where they touch neighbors and scaffolding on all sides. Three-dimensional culture grows cells in gels or scaffolds that mimic that setting. Across many studies, such cells match living tissue more closely in shape, growth, and gene activity.

The review lists where the difference matters: cell survival and division, movement and invasion of tumor cells, blood vessel growth, immune evasion, drug metabolism, and response to stimuli. Gains rest on progress in materials science, cell biology, and bioreactor design. Better mimicry should improve how well dish results predict drug effects in patients, a chronic weak point of cancer and drug research.
europmc-pmc4436290:
Virginie Lecomte and seven co-authors, including Pratibha Nerurkar, compared gut bacteria in rats fed a high-fat diet in PLoS ONE in 2015. Gut microbes are now counted among the factors behind obesity, but most past work described diet effects only at broad group level. The team used high-throughput gene reading on fecal samples from rats fed fatty food or normal chow for weeks.

At species level the two groups differed markedly. A Lactobacillus species that dominated in chow-fed rats fell sharply on the fatty diet, while species that make the short-chain acids propionate and acetate rose. Abundances of several species tracked body measures tied to obesity, such as weight and metabolic markers. Three kinds rose or fell with every measure tested. The results link specific gut species, not just broad groups, to the obese state in this model.
europmc-pmc4454990:
Gurpreet Singh Dhillon and seven co-authors, including Paul Tchounwou, reviewed the antiseptic chemical triclosan in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2015. Triclosan is added to many soaps, toothpastes, and household goods to kill microbes. Wide use gives it many routes into water and soil, and it has been found in sewage outflow, rivers, groundwater, and even drinking water.

Its chemistry suggests it can build up in living tissue and persist in the environment. Standard water treatment does not remove it fully and can even create more toxic byproducts. Evidence of harm to water organisms worries the authors, who note that monitoring data are still scarce. They argue triclosan should be classed as a priority emerging contaminant and its use in consumer products should be regulated.
europmc-pmc4460190:
Nicola Wilson and a large team of co-authors combined single-cell tests to sort out blood stem cells in Cell Stem Cell in 2015. Adult blood-forming stem cells differ in how long they can keep renewing themselves, which muddies studies of pooled cells. Gene studies of bulk samples mix true stem cells with several subtypes and stray non-stem cells, blurring the signal.

The team linked three single-cell approaches in mouse cells: a function test for each cell, a sorting method that records each cell's surface profile, and single-cell gene readings. Merging these data let them design a sorting scheme that separates true stem cells from the rest without prior bias. Transplant tests then confirmed which enriched cells renew long-term, and gene data named molecules tied to durable renewal. They show the same linking strategy works in another stem cell system too.
europmc-pmc4501690:
Claire Webster and a large team of co-authors catalogued the viruses of the fruit fly in PLoS Biology in 2015. Drosophila melanogaster, the standard lab fly, is a valuable model for virus infection and antiviral immunity, and for how insects and viruses evolve together. Yet the full set of viruses that naturally infect it was far from known, limiting that work.

Searching sequence data from wild flies with a metagenomic approach, the team found more than twenty previously undetected RNA viruses and a DNA virus, including entirely new virus groups. Small RNA profiles showed these were active infections, and revealed both defense-related small RNAs and a novel microRNA from the DNA virus. Surveying thousands of individually collected wild flies, they found more than a third carried a detectable virus. The catalogue transforms the fly into a richer model for natural virus ecology.
europmc-pmc4515490:
Rinaldo Florencio-Silva and four co-authors review how bone tissue works in BioMed Research International in 2015. Bone is not fixed; it is rebuilt all through life. Osteoclasts break old bone down, osteoblasts lay new bone, and osteocytes, cells buried in the bone, sense strain and direct the work.

Signals from inside the body and from local growth factors keep breakdown and build-up in balance. When build-up lags, diseases such as osteoporosis follow. The review describes each cell type's shape and job, and the talks between them that link removal of bone to its replacement. It also covers signs that bone exchanges signals with other organs, making it a dynamic tissue rather than a passive frame.
europmc-pmc4560790:
Sergii Yakunin leads a ten-author team making tiny perovskite crystals lase, in Nature Communications in 2015. Perovskite semiconductors have surged as light materials, but almost all work used films or bulk crystals. What uniform nanocrystals of the caesium lead halide family would do with light was nearly unstudied.

The crystals, about 10 nanometers across, amplified light at room temperature across the whole visible range, from 440 to 700 nanometers. The energy needed to start was low, and the gain high. Two laser forms were shown: light whispering around coated silica spheres, and random lasing from crystal films. The results extend perovskites toward cheap, color-tunable light sources.
europmc-pmc4562190:
Paula T. Trzepacz and four co-authors translate between two bedside thinking tests, in BMC Geriatrics in 2015. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment was built to catch mild cognitive impairment earlier than the older Mini-Mental State Examination. Clinics switching tests need to know how scores on one map onto the other.

The team analyzed 219 healthy controls, 299 people with mild impairment, and 100 with Alzheimer's dementia from a national imaging study database. Dementia cases scored abnormal on both tests, while mild cases overlapped heavily with healthy scores. Most mild cases scored 17 or above on the Montreal test. The paper supplies a conversion grid between the tests and weighs which test sections separate mild impairment best.
europmc-pmc4597190:
Alan Serrels and colleagues brought out a 2015 cancer study on focal adhesion kinase, or FAK, a protein that helps tumour cells evade the immune system. Working with squamous cell carcinoma, they asked what FAK does when it sits inside the cell nucleus. The work appeared in Cell and used mouse tumours plus cell experiments.

Nuclear FAK switched on chemokine genes, above all one called Ccl5. Those signals drew in regulatory T cells and wore down the killer T cells that attack tumours, so FAK-bearing tumours kept growing. A drug that blocks FAK, named VS-4718 in the study, cut the regulatory T cells and let killer T cells respond. The findings suggest FAK blockers may work partly by freeing the immune system.
europmc-pmc4648090:
Amit M. Oza and colleagues reported final survival results in 2015 from ICON7, a phase 3 trial in newly diagnosed ovarian cancer. Adding the drug bevacizumab to chemotherapy had earlier delayed disease progression, especially in high-risk patients. The open-label trial ran at 263 centres in eleven countries. The work appeared in The Lancet Oncology.

A total of 1,528 women with high-risk early-stage or advanced disease were assigned to standard carboplatin and paclitaxel, with or without bevacizumab given during chemotherapy and then as maintenance. Earlier reports showed the progression benefit concentrated in women at high risk of progression. The final analysis reports overall survival by intention to treat for the whole group and subgroups. The results complete the picture for judging where this added drug earns its place.
europmc-pmc4668290:
In 2015, Chintan Parmar and colleagues' study that pitted machine learning tools against each other for reading survival odds from head and neck cancer scans appeared. Radiomics pulls hundreds of measures from a scan and treats them as a portrait of the tumour. Clinics need tools that are both sharp and steady before they can trust such scores.

A training group of 101 patients and a test group of ninety-five were used, with 440 measures pulled from CT scans. Thirteen ways to pick key measures and eleven ways to class patients were run through a fair test frame. Three of each kind paired high scores with high steadiness. The choice of classing tool drove more of the swing in results than any other step. The study hands radiomics teams a short list of tested methods.
europmc-pmc4702890:
Chih-Hung Chou, Nai-Wen Chang, Sirjana Shrestha, and nine colleagues updated miRTarBase in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that dial genes down after their messages are made. Knowing which genes each microRNA truly targets, proven by experiment, is the database's whole purpose. The 2016 update folded in results from 138 large crosslinking datasets produced by twenty-one studies, on top of hand-curated papers.

Holdings reached about five thousand articles and several thousand strongly proven interactions, with hundreds of thousands more from the crosslinking sets, a sevenfold jump since 2014. Cancer genome expression profiles were layered in to give the data context. The authors argue the resource now stands among the most complete of its kind. For microRNA researchers, it replaces scattered literature hunts with one validated shelf of target claims.
europmc-pmc4705690:
Martin Fischer, Marianne Quaas, Lydia Steiner, and Kurt Engeland mapped a gene-shutdown pathway of the tumor suppressor p53 in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. p53 halts the cell cycle, partly by switching genes off, but the route was unclear. A chain running from p53 through p21 and the DREAM complex to specific promoter sites was known for a few genes. The team asked, genome-wide, how many genes it governs.

Combining binding data, expression data, and conserved promoter elements, they predicted 210 target genes. Detailed checks on nine cell cycle genes confirmed the pattern of p53-driven repression. Most targets run the late phases of cell division, the G2 and mitosis stages. Shutting them down, the authors argue, is a main way p53 freezes dividing cells. The list gives cancer biology a fuller map of one guardian pathway.
europmc-pmc4709190:
Catharina Missailidis, Jenny Hällqvist, Abdel Rashid Qureshi, and six colleagues studied a gut-microbe chemical in kidney disease, in PLoS ONE in 2016. The chemical, TMAO, forms when gut microbes process certain foods, and high levels track with heart disease in the general public. The team measured it in 179 patients across stages of chronic kidney disease and in 80 controls, asking what drives its level and whether it predicts death.

Kidney function was the dominant driver: worse filtration meant higher TMAO. Dialysis did not lower it, but a kidney transplant returned it to control levels. Higher TMAO also tracked with inflammation markers, and patients with high levels died at notably higher rates even after adjustment. The study ties a microbe-made chemical to kidney failure's risks and suggests the transplant result as a clue that the level itself is movable.
europmc-pmc4766490:
Yuko T. Sato leads eight authors in Scientific Reports in 2016 on a way to custom-build drug carriers from cell parcels. Exosomes are tiny bubbles cells release, and their natural build makes them attractive as drug couriers. The catch is steering them: plain exosomes go where biology sends them, not where a doctor aims.

The team fused exosomes with lab-made fat bubbles, liposomes, using a freeze-thaw cycle. Exosomes that carried a chosen surface protein kept it through the fusion. By swapping the fats in the partner bubble, they changed how the hybrids entered cells. The work shows two design levers, genes and membrane mixing, can be stacked. That opens a path to couriers tuned for a target tissue.
europmc-pmc4819590:
Timothy Matthews leads seven authors in Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology in 2016 separating two states that are often confused: being socially isolated and feeling lonely. Their data come from a British twin cohort of over a thousand pairs, assessed at age eighteen. The twin design lets them split the roots of each state into genes and lived experience.

Isolation and loneliness overlapped only moderately: many isolated young adults were not lonely. Both tracked with depression, but loneliness held the stronger link when the two were weighed together. Genes explained about forty percent of each state, and the genetic overlap between loneliness and depression was large. Help for young people, the authors argue, must target the feeling of loneliness itself, not just add social contact.
europmc-pmc4865890:
Pramod Shah and co-authors built HuMiX in 2016, a chip-based lab model where human gut cells and gut microbes grow together. Animal models of the gut differ from humans in key ways, which limits what they prove. HuMiX stacks tiny flow chambers so gut lining cells meet microbes under gut-like conditions, including low oxygen for the microbes.

Human cells grown with a friendly bacterium, Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, answered with gene, chemical, and immune shifts much like those seen in the body. Adding a second strict anaerobe, Bacteroides caccae, gave a distinct response again. The device lets researchers watch host and microbe talk directly, step by step.
europmc-pmc4873990:
Lyudmila F. Gulyaeva and Nicolay E. Kushlinskiy reviewed how microRNA levels are controlled, in the Journal of Translational Medicine in 2016. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces, 18 to 22 letters long, that tune gene activity after a gene is read. Their seed part binds target messages, mostly at the tail end, and lowers protein output.

Disease studies often report changed microRNA profiles, above all in cancer, yet why the levels change gets less attention. Control acts at gene reading, at several trimming steps, and at decay. Faults at any step can skew the whole set. Knowing the control layers helps turn microRNA profiles into sound tests and, later, into treatments.
europmc-pmc5193490:
Kira M. Holmström, Rumen V. Kostov, and Albena T. Dinkova-Kostova review what the transcription factor Nrf2 does for mitochondria. Nrf2 is the master regulator of the cell's redox balance. Its target genes make antioxidant enzymes, clear damaged proteins, and calm inflammation. Glutathione, the cell's main small antioxidant, is one product of that network and counters the reactive oxygen species mitochondria produce. Nrf2 activity is suppressed in disorders such as Parkinson's disease and Friedreich's ataxia.

When Nrf2 is missing, mitochondria burn fatty acids poorly, respire less, and make less ATP. Small-molecule activators of Nrf2 protect mitochondrial integrity, partly by promoting the cleanup of damaged organelles. The review also reaches into stem cells, where Nrf2 bears on self-renewal and survival. The authors frame Nrf2 as a link between the cell's defense program and its energy supply, with implications for both degeneration and regeneration.
europmc-pmc5222290:
H. J. Hutchens, professor of comparative pathology and bacteriology at Durham, opened a two-part clinic on so-called ptomaine poisoning in The Hospital on August 19, 1911. The phrase was a popular label for sudden gut illness blamed on a particular food, in which most people who ate the item fell sick. Hutchens argues the name misleads, because it blames ptomaines, substances that are not in fact the cause.

Ptomaines were chemical products found in rotting meat, named by the Italian toxicologist Selmi and later studied by Brieger and others. Once Pasteur proved that bacteria drive putrefaction, these substances were understood as bacterial products. Pasteur and Koch then showed that microbes cause infective disease largely through chemical products they release. Pasteur proved the point in 1880, when filtered, germ-free cultures of the fowl cholera organism still reproduced the disease in birds.
europmc-pmc5240090:
Kiera Murphy and eight colleagues ran a pilot study of human milk and infant gut microbes in Scientific Reports in 2017. Milk carries helpful compounds and is also a source of bacteria that may seed the baby's gut. The team followed ten mother-infant pairs over the first three months of life, profiling bacteria in milk and in infant faeces.

Sequencing found wide diversity in milk, more than 207 bacterial genera, with twelve core genera making up 81 percent of the milk community in the early weeks. Genera shared between a mother's milk and her baby's faeces accounted for 70 to 88 percent of the baby's gut community. In one pair, identical strains of Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus plantarum turned up in both milk and faeces, direct support for live transfer through breastfeeding. The authors note each pair's mix was distinct, unlike sterile formula or pasteurized donor milk.
europmc-pmc5309790:
Yingying Zhang and co-authors studied a form of cell death called necroptosis in Nature Communications in 2017. This planned death is set off by the signal TNF and plays a part in infection and injury. Two proteins, RIP1 and RIP3, form a death complex called the necrosome. Harsh oxygen forms made inside cell powerhouses help drive the process, but the link was unclear.

The team found that three key sulfur sites in RIP1 sense the harsh oxygen. That signal makes RIP1 add a phosphate tag to itself at one spot, site 161. This tag is the main job of RIP1 in the death path. With the tag in place, RIP1 can pull in RIP3 and build a working necrosome. Since RIP3 also helps make the oxygen signal, the loop feeds itself and locks in cell death.
europmc-pmc5318690:
