Mitchell R. McGill reviewed liver injury blood tests in EXCLI Journal in 2016. Two enzymes, called ALT and AST, are the most used markers of liver harm. They leak from hurt liver cells into the blood. Doctors lean on them to find and track liver disease. Yet reading their levels can be tricky.

Both enzymes can rise for reasons outside the liver, and they say little about how a grave case will end. McGill traces the history of these tests and explains how the enzymes act and rise. He then looks at new markers now in growth. Health agencies in the United States and Europe have backed some of them for use in drug trials. The new tests may one day sit beside ALT and AST, or even take their place.
europmc-pmc5320690:
Andrew J. Page and co-authors presented a software tool called SNP-sites in Microbial Genomics in 2016. Cheap gene reading has swollen microbe studies to thousands of samples at once. A routine step is to pull out the single letter changes, called SNPs, from a large aligned set of genomes. Older tools were slow, ate memory, and were hard to install.

SNP-sites pulls the changes fast on modest gear. On a huge test file with close to two thousand microbe genomes, it finished in a few minutes using a small slice of memory and one processor core. Results can come out in several formats for later study steps. The tool is written in C, is free and open to all, and installs through standard package systems. The authors tested it on more than twenty operating systems.
europmc-pmc5437690:
Rhouma and co-authors review how pig farms can beat post-weaning diarrhea without leaning on colistin. Their review appeared in Acta Veterinaria Scandinavica. The disease strikes piglets in the first two weeks after weaning. Toxigenic E. coli bloom in the gut. Piglets die suddenly or fall behind in growth. Colistin has long controlled the disease. It is given by mouth across the swine industry.

That reliance now carries a cost. Colistin is a last-resort drug for human infections. Resistant E. coli are rising in pigs. A plasmid gene, mcr-1, can pass that resistance between bacteria. The review first maps the risk factors for the disease. Weaning stress, diet change, and mixing all play roles. It then surveys control options that spare colistin. Feed, vaccines, and gut health measures feature. The authors end with a phase-by-phase plan for farms.
europmc-pmc5445790:
Gerhardt and Boccaccini review bioactive glass scaffolds for growing new bone. Their review appeared in Materials. Bioactive glasses bond directly to living bone. A bone-like mineral layer forms at the surface. The classic mix, 45S5 Bioglass, dates to a 1969 discovery. Such glasses once served as simple defect fillers. Tissue engineers now shape them into porous scaffolds. Cells can grow through the pores.

The review starts with the field's history and scaffold needs. It then surveys melt-derived silicate glasses and glass-ceramics. Common making methods get a full rundown. Structure is tied to strength and function. The authors compare scaffold traits with real human bone. Dissolving glass releases silicon, calcium, and other ions. Those ions can spur bone growth and vessel growth. Composite builds that mix glass with polymers also feature. The authors end by marking open research paths.
europmc-pmc5461490:
Shi and co-authors uncover a signal from immune cells that feeds stem cells in a deadly brain tumor. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The tumor is glioblastoma, the most lethal kind. Immune cells called macrophages flood into it. Their presence predicts poor survival for patients. The team screened one type of these cells for secreted factors.

One factor stood out. The cells release large amounts of a protein called pleiotrophin. Its receptor sits in high levels on glioma stem cells. In patients, more of the protein meant more immune cells and worse outcomes. Adding the immune cells to tumors sped stem-cell growth in mice. Silencing the protein in those cells removed the boost. Blocking the receptor stripped stem cells of their tumor-forming power. Blocking the signal in animals slowed tumors and lengthened survival. The authors name this signal path a target for new drugs.
europmc-pmc5536290:
Usmani and co-authors describe a database paper in PLoS ONE called THPdb. Peptide and protein drugs form a fast-growing market share. Details on approved products were scattered across papers and patents. THPdb gathers them into one curated, free repository. Its sources include 985 publications and 70 patents.

The database holds 852 entries, they report. They cover 239 FDA-approved therapeutic peptides and proteins plus 380 variants. Each entry lists sequence, chemistry, disease area, and target. Toxicity, dose route, and drug action details come along too. Browsing tools, a web interface, and a mobile app serve users.
europmc-pmc5553090:
Weirather and co-authors present a comparison study in F1000Research. They test two long-read DNA sequencing platforms head to head. Pacific Biosciences and Oxford Nanopore both read single molecules at great length. The team used RNA data from human embryonic stem cells.

The authors compared error patterns, read length, and mapping quality. PacBio gave better data quality overall. Nanopore gave a higher yield of reads. For finding and counting gene isoforms, PacBio also led by a small margin. Combining either long-read set with short Illumina reads beat long reads alone. Readers get a practical guide for choosing a platform for transcript studies.
europmc-pmc5624990:
Shaffer and Ginsberg survey heart rate variability in Frontiers in Public Health. A healthy heart is not a metronome. The gaps between beats shift from moment to moment. That wobble reflects how well the body adapts.

The overview sorts the measures into three families. Time-domain indices count the spread of beat intervals. Frequency-domain values split the signal into bands. Non-linear measures capture how complex the pattern is. Recording length changes what each number means. A day-long trace and a five-minute trace are not interchangeable. The authors compile normal values from many studies. Age, sex, and setting all move the baselines. They urge professionals to build norms for their own groups too. Readers get a field guide for using HRV in clinics and performance work.
europmc-pmc5645390:
Chen and co-authors report a sampling study in Nature Communications. It maps bacteria along the female reproductive tract. Whether sites beyond the vagina hold distinct microbes was debated. The team sampled 110 women of reproductive age. Sites included the cervix, uterus, fallopian tubes, and peritoneal fluid. Methods combined gene sequencing with bacterial culture.

Each site held a distinct microbial community. The pattern formed a continuum from vagina to upper tract. That result points to a non-sterile environment. Some microbes tracked the menstrual cycle. Others were over-represented in adenomyosis or endometriosis-linked infertility. The authors suggest vaginal or cervical surveys could flag upper tract disease. That would give clinicians a simpler test route.
europmc-pmc5733390:
Brancucci and co-authors study how the human malaria parasite decides to make sexual forms. Only those forms, called gametocytes, can infect mosquitoes. Rates of making them shift with host conditions, for unclear reasons. The team hunted for a signal in human blood.

They find a host fat, lysophosphatidylcholine, holds the sexual switch off. When that fat runs low, parasites build a key membrane fat from it less. That shortage turns on sexual stage genes and gametocyte growth. The work links parasite diet sensing to its life cycle, and hints at ways to block spread.
europmc-pmc5753190:
Harding and co-authors report the 2018 update of the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY. This expert checked database logs how drugs and other ligands act on targets. It has grown from work dating back to 2003. Content choice rests with 96 subcommittees of scientists and in-house curators.

The guide now holds about 9,000 ligands and 15,000 binding constants. It links roughly 1,700 human proteins to 6,000 papers. Ten releases since 2015 added content and features. A new sister project, the Guide to IMMUNOPHARMACOLOGY, forks from the same model. It adds immune targets, pathways, cell types, and diseases.
europmc-pmc5761190:
Munn and co-authors propose a typology to help reviewers pick the right kind of systematic review. Reviews are the base on which evidence based healthcare rests. Their methods have grown to fit many question types. New reviewers often skip the step of matching review type to question.

The paper defines a set of review types in one scheme. For each type it sets out how the question should be framed. Inclusion criteria for each type are also spelled out. The aim is one shared language for review kinds. Both new and seasoned reviewers are the target readers.
europmc-pmc5807490:
Cage and co-authors survey autistic adults on acceptance and mental health. Autistic adults face high rates of depression and anxiety. Feeling accepted as autistic may protect them. The team tests that link with an online survey.

A total of 111 autistic adults took part. They rated acceptance from others and from themselves. Both kinds of acceptance predicted lower depression. Acceptance from others also predicted lower stress. It did not predict anxiety. Hiding autistic traits, called camouflaging, tied to more depression. Readers get early proof that social acceptance shapes autistic well-being.
europmc-pmc5876990:
Kondo and co-authors review urban green space and human health. Their systematic review appeared in an environmental and public health journal. Over half of humanity now lives in cities. Prior reviews rarely focused on that urban setting. Most also leaned on cross-sectional studies, which cannot show cause. This team kept experimental, quasi-experimental, and longitudinal work. They asked whether green space exposure links to better health.

More green space tied consistently to lower mortality, they report. It also tied to lower heart rate and less violence. Attention, mood, and physical activity rose with exposure. Results were mixed for weight, depression, and stress measures. Too few studies covered birth outcomes or cancer. The authors urge stronger designs for firmer answers.
europmc-pmc5886390:
Alikhan and co-authors give a genomic overview of Salmonella population structure. Their article appeared in PLoS Genetics. Salmonella was long split into serovars by antibody tests. A newer scheme grouped strains by seven housekeeping genes. That scheme lacked detail for outbreak tracing. Its claim to mark natural populations also lacked proof.

The team built on EnteroBase, a web platform for Salmonella genomes. It already held over 100,000 assembled genomes. Gene-based groupings matched across two typing schemes, they report. That match supports them as natural populations. A finer core-genome scheme gave the detail tracing needs. Readers get tools for study at every scale of diversity.
europmc-pmc5907490:
Li and Yang review manganese, oxidative stress, and metabolic disease. Their review appeared in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Manganese is essential for many enzymes in the body. It helps regulate glucose and lipid metabolism. It is also a core part of a key antioxidant enzyme. Both too little and too much can harm health.

Low intake can raise reactive oxygen and oxidative stress. High exposure can do the same, the authors note. Metabolic diseases linked here include diabetes, obesity, and fatty liver. Workers in mining and welding face extra exposure risk. How manganese helps or harms metabolism remains unclear. Readers get the known links and open questions.
europmc-pmc5915590:
Peeken and co-authors show Arctic sea ice traps and carries microplastic. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Plastic bits have reached even remote polar waters. Ice held high levels, but their spread inside ice was unclear. The team sampled ice from different growth regions. Drift paths were tracked for each floe.

Plastic makeup varied sharply between ice layers, they report. Each region left a distinct polymer pattern. That points to local sources even in the far Arctic. Ice growth and drift shape what each floe carries. More Arctic activity will likely raise the load. Melting zones will then release stored plastic.
europmc-pmc5959890:
Marioni and co-authors run a genome-wide association study using family history of Alzheimer's disease. Their study appeared in Translational Psychiatry. The team used self-reported parental history in UK Biobank. That covered 314,278 participants. They asked whether such reports can stand in for real cases. The answer was yes for genetic study purposes. Meta-analysis with consortium data widened the search further.

Three new Alzheimer's-linked loci turned up, they report. The genes include ADAM10, BCKDK/KAT8, and ACE. Gene-based tests flagged the drug target VKORC1 as well. Signals near TOMM40 may work through gene expression and methylation. Some loci hold targets already used in other diseases.
europmc-pmc5979390:
Itatani and co-authors review resistance to anti-angiogenic therapy in cancer through changes to the anti-VEGF pathway. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Blocking blood vessel growth is a proven strategy against solid cancers. Bevacizumab, an antibody against VEGF A, won approval in 2004. Other VEGF pathway drugs followed, from kinase blockers to decoy receptors. Many patients gain longer survival from them.

Some patients gain little or nothing, the authors note. Resistance can be present from the start or grow over time. The review sums up backup routes for vessel growth. Those routes bypass VEGF and drive resistance.
europmc-pmc6060790:
Capper and co-authors describe how Heidelberg put DNA methylation testing into brain tumor diagnosis. Their report appeared in Acta Neuropathologica. A machine learning classifier sorts central nervous system tumors by their methylation pattern. The center ran the test on more than 2,000 tumors between 2015 and 2018.

About half came from local neurosurgery departments. The rest arrived from outside institutions. The authors explain how results merge with classic microscope findings. They give a catalog of copy-number changes for each tumor class. Hard cases where methods disagree get special attention. Pitfalls and practical fixes fill much of the text. Readers get a working model for molecular tumor boards.
europmc-pmc6096490:
Terwilliger and co-authors automate the sharpening of cryo-EM and crystal maps. Their article appeared in Acta Crystallographica Section D. Sharpening weights a map's detail by resolution. The right amount reveals structure without noise. No formula could pick that amount in advance.

Their method scores maps on detail and connectivity together. It then tunes sharpening to raise both scores. The team applied it to 361 deposited map pairs. Models shipped with the maps allowed checking. The approach needs no model of its own. It works for both electron and X-ray maps. Readers get a practical step toward clearer structural images.
europmc-pmc6107290:
Song and co-authors present a research article in PLoS Pathogens on the spike of the SARS coronavirus. The spike sits on the virus surface. It locks onto a host cell protein called ACE2. That step lets the virus enter cells.

The team used cryo-electron microscopy to image the spike bound to ACE2. They found that just one of its three binding parts grips the receptor. That part lifts into an up pose. They also watched spikes under varied lab setups. The work shows how binding may free part of the spike. That could start the shift that fuses virus and cell.
europmc-pmc6109690:
Soares and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Chemistry on nanomedicine, the use of very small particles in drug products. Working at the nanoscale gives materials new traits. Those traits can change how a drug acts in the body. They also raise hard questions for testing and approval.

The review covers basic concepts for these nanosystems and the methods used to study them. It then turns to the hurdles of bringing such products to market. Much of the focus is on rules in the European Union. The authors close with current uses and likely future paths. Readers get both the science and the regulatory picture in one survey.
europmc-pmc6141690:
Mason and co-authors present a research article in Frontiers in Chemistry on plastic particles in bottled water. Bottled water is sold as a pure product worldwide. Reports of microplastic contamination raised doubts. The team tested major brands bought across the globe.

They processed 259 bottles from eleven brands, bought in 19 locations in nine countries. About 93 percent showed signs of microplastic contamination. After subtracting lab background, they found an average of 10.4 large particles per liter. Fragments were the most common shape. Polypropylene, the plastic used for bottle caps, was the most common type. The study raised wide questions about plastic packaging and drinking water.
europmc-pmc6235890:
Wu and co-authors studied a chemical mark on RNA that steers bone forming stem cells. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The mark is called m6A, and the enzyme Mettl3 adds it. The cells sit in bone marrow and can become bone cells or fat cells. Balance between those fates keeps bones strong. In ageing, the balance often tips toward fat, and bone is lost.

Removing Mettl3 in mouse stem cells caused bone loss signs like those in osteoporosis. Bone formation fell, and marrow fat rose. Adding Mettl3 back guarded mice against bone loss after hormone loss. The team traced the effect to a hormone receptor pathway in the cells. Without the mark, that receptor was made less well. The work names a new control layer in bone health.
europmc-pmc6292890:
Darvin and co-authors review immune checkpoint inhibitors, a new class of cancer drugs. The review appeared in Experimental and Molecular Medicine. Tumors can switch on immune checkpoints to hide from attack. Antibodies that block these checkpoints have changed cancer care. Two main targets are PD-1 and CTLA-4.

The authors report strong gains for some patients with these drugs. Yet many patients do not respond at all. Others suffer immune side effects. The review thus focuses on biomarkers that could predict response. Candidates include PD-L1 levels, new antigens, and gene signatures. Better tests would help doctors pick the right patients for treatment.
europmc-pmc6355990:
Baxter and co-authors test how three fermentable fibers change gut output in people. Their study appeared in mBio. Gut bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids. Butyrate, one of them, guards gut health and immunity. Not all fibers raise it equally, though. The team ran dietary interventions with three fibers.

Responses depended on each person's starting microbes. Some people raised butyrate, others did not. Two bacterial species seemed required for the resistant starch effect. They are Ruminococcus bromii and a Clostridium species. Bifidobacteria broke down fibers well in the tests. Yet they did not drive the butyrate rise short term. The authors stress personalization in fiber advice. A supplement only works if the right microbes are present.
europmc-pmc6389790:
Gurevich and Gurevich review how cells switch off a major receptor family, in Frontiers in Pharmacology. G protein-coupled receptors sense many signals outside cells. About a third of clinical drugs target them.

An active receptor is first marked by kinases called GRKs. Arrestin proteins then bind the marked receptor and stop its signal. Arrestins also start fresh signals of their own. The review explains these steps and the odd cases that break the pattern. Knowing the switch-off system matters for designing drugs with fewer side effects and longer, cleaner action.
europmc-pmc6403190:
Vermassen and co-authors review bacterial cell wall hydrolases in Frontiers in Microbiology. Bacteria build a wall of peptidoglycan to hold their shape. As they grow and split, enzymes must cut that wall in exact places without killing the cell.

Three enzyme groups do the cutting, each aimed at a distinct bond. Amidases, glycosidases, and peptidases are sorted in the review. Their roles run from wall growth to cell death. Tight control keeps the balance between building and cutting. The authors show how varied these enzymes are across bacterial kinds.
europmc-pmc6441890:
Verduci and co-authors review the circRNA-microRNA code, the web of interactions through which circular RNAs tune gene expression in cancer. Circular RNAs form closed loops that resist breakdown far better than straight RNA strands. They bind microRNAs, long noncoding RNAs, and proteins, and their abundance makes them plausible biomarkers.

Cancer examples run through the survey: some circles fall in gastric tumors and behave as suppressors tied to spread and stage, while others rise and track survival. Because circles appear in body fluids and stay stable, diagnostic use is a recurring theme. The authors close with treatment designs that target the code directly.
europmc-pmc6509190:
Haran and co-authors compare the gut microbes of nursing home elders with and without Alzheimer's disease, writing in mBio. They enrolled 108 elders and took monthly stool samples for up to five months, 300 in all. Of the group, 24 had Alzheimer's, 33 had other dementias, and 51 had none.

Deep sequencing showed the Alzheimer's group carried a distinct mix of gut bacteria, and machine learning used microbe plus clinical data to sort the groups. In lab tests, stool from Alzheimer's patients disturbed the P-glycoprotein pathway, a calming system in the gut lining. Losing that control can drive gut inflammation. The authors frame the finding as a link between gut microbes, gut inflammation and this brain disease.
europmc-pmc6512290: After colon cancer surgery, tiny traces of tumor DNA floating in the blood can reveal whether cancer remains. This study used extremely sensitive sequencing to hunt for those traces in patients with early-stage colorectal cancer. The test could help doctors decide who needs extra chemotherapy after surgery and who can safely skip it.
europmc-pmc6548990:
Wajant and Siegmund review how two receptors for the signal TNF steer macrophages between life and death, writing in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. Macrophages guard tissues and fight germs, and most danger sensors make them release TNF. That same signal then acts back on the macrophages themselves.

TNFR1 carries a death domain. Its default output is inflammatory gene programs, but when safeguards fail it can trigger apoptosis or the bursting death necroptosis. TNFR2 lacks the death domain and mainly boosts survival and activation signals. The review maps how the two pathways intertwine, including cross-talk with germ sensors, interferons and the inflammasome. The balance they set decides whether a macrophage works on, or dies, at an infection site.
europmc-pmc6567490:
Oliphant and Allen-Vercoe review what gut microbes make from the food that reaches them, writing in Microbiome. Complex carbohydrates, proteins and some fats escape digestion and land in the colon, where bacteria ferment them into a crowd of small molecules. Those by-products act on the gut wall and, once absorbed, on the whole body.

Carbohydrate fermentation yields mainly short-chain fatty acids, which feed colon cells and calm immunity. Protein breakdown is rougher, producing ammonia, phenols, indoles and sulfur compounds alongside useful acids. Fat processing adds glycerol and choline derivatives. The same molecule can help or harm depending on dose and place. The authors map each family to its microbes and disease links, and mark where the evidence still runs thin.
europmc-pmc6585590:
Eddie and co-authors systematically review peer recovery support for substance use disorder, writing in Frontiers in Psychology. The model hires people who have lived through addiction and recovery to mentor, teach and support patients now in treatment. Hospitals and clinics are adopting it fast, ahead of solid proof that it works.

The evidence so far is encouraging but thin. Studies report less substance use and fewer relapses, better ties with providers, longer treatment retention and higher satisfaction. Yet null results are common, and the literature is hampered by shifting definitions of the peer role, mixed populations and weak comparison groups. The authors also flag boundary and training questions that clinics must settle, and call for rigorous trials of benefit and cost.
europmc-pmc6604390:
Teng and co-authors build a DNA test from the CRISPR enzyme Cas12b. Their research article appears in Genome Biology. Fast, exact DNA detection matters for clinics and quarantine checks. Earlier CRISPR platforms traded sensitivity against single-base accuracy. The team aimed to gain both at once.

Their method, named CDetection, uses the enzyme AaCas12b. On binding its target, the enzyme shreds reporter molecules and gives a signal. The authors tuned the guide RNA for sharper discrimination. CDetection beat the earlier Cas12a platform on sensitivity. It reached sub-attomolar detection levels. It also separated targets that differ by one single base. The authors present it as a practical platform for SNP genotyping.
europmc-pmc6714090:
Lu and co-authors reviewed the immune-suppressing surroundings of liver cancer. Hepatocellular carcinoma is rising as chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis spread. Surgery and chemotherapy exist, yet death rates stay high. The tissue around a tumor helps it grow by holding the immune system back.

The review describes the cells that do this work. They include tumor-linked macrophages, suppressor cells from bone marrow, neutrophils, fibroblasts, and regulatory T cells. Each type helps the tumor in its own way. The authors then survey current treatments aimed at these cells. They close with open questions for future immunotherapy research.
europmc-pmc6717890:
Stratoulias and co-authors argue that microglia come in distinct subtypes. Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells and its first active barrier. The standard view holds that one cell type bends to fit each situation. The authors say that view misses built-in differences between microglia themselves.

They review subtypes found in health and disease, each with its own traits and jobs. Some appear only in the embryo or in the first days after birth. Others gather near fiber tracts. The authors propose sorting subtypes by function, not just by state. That shift, they argue, would sharpen research on brain immunity.
europmc-pmc6761190:
Fu and co-authors report that CAR-T cells release exosomes with anti-tumor power of their own. CAR-T therapy engineers T cells to attack cancer. It can work fast and durably, but it brings sharp toxicities. The engineered cells shed tiny vesicles, mostly exosomes, that carry the CAR receptor on their surface.

These exosomes are loaded with killing molecules and stopped tumor growth in tests. Unlike the parent cells, they carry no PD1 receptor. Added PD-L1, which normally blunts T cells, could not weaken them. In a mouse model of the therapy's worst side effect, cytokine release syndrome, the exosomes proved safer than the cells. Cell-free treatment may follow from this work.
europmc-pmc6769590:
Guillin and co-authors review selenium and viral infection. Viral infections produce reactive oxygen species, which can help or harm cells. When these molecules overwhelm defenses, oxidative stress follows and can even speed viral growth. Infection also raises the body's need for trace nutrients while draining them. Selenium stands out among those nutrients for its role in defense.

Most selenium activity runs through a family of proteins that carry a rare amino acid. These proteins defend against oxidation and keep redox balance in cells. Low selenium, the main controller of their levels, has been tied to worse outcomes in several viral diseases. Hepatitis C offers a documented case, where viral proteins drive liver oxidative stress.
europmc-pmc6786290:
Yeager and co-authors ran a national experiment on growth mindset and school achievement. A growth mindset teaches that intellectual ability can be developed. Short interventions exist, but none had been tested in a sample that represents a whole nation. Their online lesson took under one hour. U.S. secondary students across the country took part.

Grades improved among lower-achieving students. Enrollment in advanced mathematics courses rose overall. Effects lasted only where peer norms matched the lesson's message, a school context effect the study was designed to catch. In one analysis, the share of low achievers off track for graduation fell from 46% to 41%. Independent data handling and pre-registered analyses back the findings.
europmc-pmc6800990:
Chen and co-authors review tumor-associated macrophages as accomplices in solid tumor progression. In many cancers, these macrophages fill the tumor microenvironment. Heavy infiltration tracks with poor patient survival. Their state is set by signals from the tumor surroundings. The review describes where they come from and how that state is dictated.

These macrophages promote tumor growth in many ways. They help cancer cells resist chemotherapy and radiotherapy. They grow new blood vessels for the tumor. They drive migration, invasion, and metastasis, and they suppress immune attack. STAT3 signaling inside them proved necessary for gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer models. The authors then survey treatments that clear, block, or reprogram them in the clinic.
europmc-pmc6872490:
The One Thousand Plant Transcriptomes Initiative reports a vast survey of plant evolution in Nature. Green plants span roughly 450,000 to 500,000 species and shape nearly every land and water ecosystem. Their family tree, though, has resisted resolution at its deepest branches. The initiative sequenced the active genes of plants chosen to span that diversity.

In all, 1,124 species were sampled, reaching beyond green plants to red algae and glaucophytes. Family trees built from the data mostly agreed across methods. A few key nodes still conflicted between plastid and nuclear genes, a sign of ancient rapid splits and genome doubling. Flower genes of the MADS-box family traced back about 300 million years.
europmc-pmc6873690:
Hinz and Jücker review the AKT protein family in breast cancer, in Cell Communication and Signaling. AKT is a central switch in a pathway that drives cell growth and survival. It comes in three forms, AKT1, AKT2, and AKT3. The forms share about 80 percent of their makeup. Yet they do not simply back each other up.

Across many studies, the three forms show distinct, sometimes opposing, effects on tumour growth, spread, and blood vessel formation. In HER2-positive breast cancers, changes were reported in AKT3 in 10 percent of cases and in AKT1 in 2.5 percent, in one study cited. The review weighs each form against therapy response and patient survival.
europmc-pmc6889290:
Pittenger and co-authors take stock of mesenchymal stem cells, in NPJ Regenerative Medicine. These multipotent cells, called MSCs, were first isolated about 30 years ago. The literature on them now exceeds 55,000 publications. They can mature into bone, fat, and cartilage in the dish. Their stronger clinical draw is their calming effect on inflammation and immunity.

The authors trace the field from basic cell biology to current trials. How a cell is grown shapes what it becomes: soft gels favour fat, stiff surfaces favour bone, and long culture locks the choice in. Most human testing leans on the anti-inflammatory powers. The perspective weighs what the cells can and cannot yet do.
europmc-pmc6891890:
Huhn and co-authors compare schizophrenia drugs in The Lancet. Antipsychotics are the standard treatment for schizophrenia, one of the most burdensome mental illnesses. Dozens of agents exist, and which to choose first is contested. Trials usually test one drug against placebo or one rival, leaving the full field unranked.

The team ran a network meta-analysis, which links trials into one web of comparisons. It covered 32 oral antipsychotics from placebo-controlled and head-to-head randomised trials. Drugs were ranked on symptom relief and on side effects such as weight gain and sedation. All-cause dropout data covered 42,672 participants. Differences between agents were real but often modest, the authors found.
europmc-pmc7005290:
Sutton and co-authors survey clinical decision support systems in modern medicine. Their overview appeared in NPJ Digital Medicine. These computer tools feed clinicians patient-matched knowledge and advice at the point of care. First used in the 1980s, they now ride inside electronic medical records, whose spread has made them routine.

Success stories from the past decade show real gains in care quality and documentation. Setbacks show the risks just as clearly: bad fits to workflow, alert fatigue, and harms when advice misfires. What these systems do to clinicians, patients, and costs is still partly unknown. The authors sort the tool types, gather use cases with proven benefit, and catalogue common pitfalls. They close with evidence-based advice for safe design, rollout, evaluation, and upkeep. Tools that read data humans cannot interpret are flagged as the next wave.
europmc-pmc7012990:
Briganti and Le Moine survey artificial intelligence in medicine as it stands and as it may become. Their perspective appeared in Frontiers in Medicine. Deep learning systems now chew through data from wearables, phones, and home sensors. A few narrow uses have reached the clinic: spotting atrial fibrillation, seizures, and low blood sugar, and reading scans and tissue slides.

Patients await this augmented medicine for the autonomy and personal care it promises. Many doctors resist, untrained for the shift. The authors weigh gains, future chances, and risks for doctors, hospitals, teaching, and ethics. New tools, they argue, still need old-fashioned clinical trials to prove themselves. Medical schools must add digital skills, perhaps even doctor-engineer tracks. Who owns patient data is shifting toward patients themselves. Connected monitoring raises ethical questions that the field has barely begun to debate.
europmc-pmc7022790:
Fernández-Bravo and Figueras update knowledge of the bacterial genus Aeromonas in the journal Microorganisms. These Gram-negative bacteria live widely in water, and some species infect humans, fish, and other aquatic animals. Naming species in the genus is tricky, because appearance-based methods often misidentify them while gene-based methods work better.

So far 36 species have been described, and at least 19 can cause human disease. Among 1,852 strains from recent clinical cases, 95.4 percent belonged to just four species. Gut infection, blood infection, and wound infection dominate the case reports. The review covers naming, spread, and the mix of virulence factors that make these bacteria harmful, giving labs and clinicians a current reference point.
europmc-pmc7037090:
Genchi and co-authors review nickel and health in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Nickel is a metal spread through air, water, and soil. Industry, fuels, and waste add to natural sources. No clear nutritional role for nickel in humans has been shown.

The review describes nickel's chemistry and how it harms the body. Contact can cause allergy, heart and kidney disease, and lung damage. Lung and nasal cancers are also linked to it. The authors point to faulty mitochondria and oxidative stress as likely key mechanisms. Nickel-driven changes to gene marks may aid cancer growth. The review ends with clean-up options. Plants can pull nickel from soil, a method called phytoremediation.
europmc-pmc7054990:
Larios and co-authors uncover a sorting route into exosomes in the Journal of Cell Biology. Cells package selected proteins into tiny internal vesicles inside endosomes. Some vesicles are destroyed; others are released as exosomes carrying cargo such as tetraspanins. How cargo gets chosen was only partly understood. The protein ALIX and the ESCRT-III machinery turn out to run a dedicated pathway.

ALIX recruits ESCRT-III onto endosomes without help from the other ESCRT complexes, but it needs a late-endosome lipid called LBPA, a requirement the team showed both in cells and in reconstituted systems. This route builds the internal vesicles and steers tetraspanins into them for delivery to exosomes. The pathway runs parallel to the classical one that uses other ESCRT components. The findings explain a separate loading dock for exosome cargo, relevant wherever exosomes carry signals between cells.
europmc-pmc7083890:
Ashraf and co-authors looked for signs of ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, in Alzheimer's disease brain tissue, in Redox Biology. They combined protein tests, element analysis, and metabolite profiling on post-mortem samples. Seven Alzheimer's brains were compared with seven from cognitively normal donors of similar age.

The Alzheimer's tissue showed disturbed iron handling, with raised ferritin but no rise in total iron. A cystine and glutamate transporter part was increased, and fat damage markers pointed to ferroptosis. The balance between excitatory glutamate and calming GABA also shifted. The authors suggest drugs that block ferroptosis could be worth testing against the disease.
europmc-pmc7119290:
Wang and co-authors review the current understanding of metal ions in Alzheimer's disease, in Translational Neurodegeneration. The brain must keep iron, copper, zinc, and calcium in careful balance. In Alzheimer's, that balance fails, and misplaced metals gather in the wrong regions.

Imbalanced metals generate oxidative stress and push the disease's two signature proteins, amyloid-beta and tau, toward harmful forms. They switch on enzymes that make more amyloid and add phosphate groups to tau, while damaging mitochondria and other cell parts. The damage then worsens the metal imbalance, closing a vicious cycle. Correcting metal levels by adding or removing specific ions is discussed as a possible treatment direction.
europmc-pmc7140590:
Eubank and co-authors comment on the influential Imperial College model of COVID-19 control measures, in the Bulletin of Mathematical Biology. The Ferguson team's report on non-pharmaceutical interventions, such as distancing and isolation, drew wide attention in March 2020. The commentary places that work among the standard tools of outbreak modelling.

Compartmental models, which sort people into susceptible, infectious, and removed groups, have been the field's workhorse for a century. The authors build a coarse taxonomy of model types and weigh what each can and cannot show. They discuss the context and significance of the Imperial College results and similar studies for judging how interventions cut deaths and hospital demand.
europmc-pmc7144090:
Challis and co-authors present BlobToolKit, software for spotting contaminant DNA in genome assemblies, in G3: Genes, Genomes, Genetics. Sequencers cannot tell which species a DNA fragment came from, so stray DNA from handling or co-extraction can end up inside a published genome. Such mixtures mislead later studies.

The toolkit processes assembly and read files into interactive browser plots that separate target DNA from foreign sequences. It can filter assemblies during production and audit public ones. The team runs it automatically on eukaryotic genomes in the public archives and posts the results in an open viewer, with quality views being linked from the European Nucleotide Archive record pages.
europmc-pmc7164390:
Shi and co-authors tested which domesticated animals SARS-CoV-2 can infect, in Science. The virus likely came from bats, but its route into humans is unknown, and a good animal model was needed for drug and vaccine work. The team exposed ferrets, cats, dogs, pigs, chickens, and ducks to the virus.

Ferrets caught the virus in their upper airways but passed it to each other poorly. Cats supported replication in the nose and throat, suffered inflammation deeper in the airways, and did pass the virus through the air to other cats. Dogs showed low susceptibility and poor replication. Pigs, chickens, and ducks were not susceptible at all in these tests.
europmc-pmc7174390:
Tsukui and co-authors build an atlas of collagen-producing cells in mouse and human lungs. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. These cells hold lung structure together in health. In fibrosis, they drive harmful scarring of lung tissue. The team used single-cell RNA sequencing to find every such cell type. They sampled healthy lungs and fibrotic lungs. Human samples came from patients with lung fibrosis and scleroderma.

The authors report several distinct cell subsets. Each subset sits in a different lung compartment. One subset appears only in fibrotic lungs. It expresses a gene called Cthrc1 and makes the most collagen. Staining showed these cells cluster inside fibroblastic foci. Tests on purified cells confirmed disease-linked traits. The atlas gives researchers a map for studying each subset. It may guide work on how fibrosis starts and worsens.
europmc-pmc7238190:
Manzanares and Ceña review endocytosis, the main gateway nanoparticles use to enter cells. Their article appeared in Pharmaceutics. Tiny particles increasingly serve as carriers for medicines. Getting inside the cell is the first step of delivery. Most particles enter by endocytosis, where the cell membrane wraps and swallows them.

Several distinct uptake pathways exist, each with its own machinery. A particle's size, shape, and surface chemistry steer which route it takes. Sugar-based carriers called cyclodextrins enter mainly by one classic pathway. Adding certain chemical groups can raise uptake sharply. Targeting decorations can switch the entry route altogether. Understanding these choices helps designers deliver more drug to the right place. The review maps the options for nanomedicine builders.
europmc-pmc7277690:
Johnson and co-authors review the role of interleukin-6, a signaling protein, in skin wound healing and scarring. Their review appeared in Biomedicines. Healing skin must switch from inflammation to repair at the right time, and IL-6 helps govern that switch. It activates immune cells, skin cells, and the fibroblasts that build new tissue.

When IL-6 signaling runs off balance, wounds either scar excessively or fail to close. A feedback loop between IL-6 and another signal, TGF-beta, drives fibrosis, the overgrowth of scar tissue. In old age, diabetes, and obesity, disturbed IL-6 responses help explain chronic wounds that linger. The authors also survey treatments that adjust IL-6 activity, weighing its helpful and harmful faces in skin repair.
europmc-pmc7319590:
Jalili and co-authors update the state of Galaxy, the web platform that lets biomedical scientists analyze large datasets without writing code. Their update appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Since 2005, Galaxy has grown into a global community project serving tens of thousands of scientists, built around accessible, reproducible, and collaborative research.

Over two years, every side of the project grew: code, integrated tools, users, and training material. The interface improved for handling large dataset collections and for interactive exploration. The framework gained federated identity support and better ways to send jobs to remote computers. New large public servers opened in Europe and Australia, regional communities multiplied, and the Galaxy Training Network expanded its teaching resources substantially.
europmc-pmc7347890:
McKay and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on a COVID-19 vaccine candidate. The vaccine uses self-amplifying RNA that codes for the virus spike protein. The RNA sits inside tiny fat particles for delivery. The team tests the approach in mice.

Mice got two shots one month apart, at doses from very low to high. The authors report strong, dose-linked antibody levels in mouse blood. The antibodies blocked both a lab-made virus and the real virus. Levels topped those seen in people who had recovered from COVID-19. The response leaned toward the Th1 type, with no sign of antibody-driven harm. Immune cells also reacted to virus pieces. Readers get early mouse evidence for a vaccine design built for fast, large-scale use.
europmc-pmc7392190:
Atyeo and co-authors profile early antibody responses in hospitalized COVID-19 patients in Immunity. Why some patients recover while others die quickly was unknown. The team studied 22 hospitalized people in depth, then checked their conclusions in a larger group.

Total levels of virus-specific IgG did not separate the outcomes. Quality and target did. Survivors carried richer antibody responses against the spike protein, while patients who died showed stronger functional responses against the inner nucleocapsid protein. In other words, where antibodies aim matters more than how many there are. Early antibody signatures, the authors argue, point to the disease's trajectory and to the mechanisms that protect.
europmc-pmc7468890:
Corrò, Novellasdemunt, and Li give a brief history of organoids, lab-grown mini organs. Flat cell cultures have long served as research tools. Yet they lack the structure and mix of real tissue, so they miss true body processes.

Organoids grow in three dimensions from stem cells. They copy the cell variety, layout, and work of primary tissues. That lets teams recreate human organs and diseases in a dish. The review traces how the method arose and grew. It weighs strengths and limits of the models. Uses span regenerative medicine, drug discovery, and precision medicine. The authors see organoids as a shift in what lab culture can show about health and disease.
europmc-pmc7490390:
Xu and co-authors build a hybrid photocatalyst that turns carbon dioxide into solar fuels with light. The hybrid joins titanium dioxide with perovskite quantum dots of CsPbBr3. A simple charge-driven self-assembly makes the material.

Theory and tests show electrons move from the dots to the titanium dioxide. That move builds an inner electric field across the junction. Light then drives electrons back in an S-scheme path, which splits electron-hole pairs well. The fibers cut carbon dioxide at a higher rate than plain titanium dioxide fibers. Isotope tracing proved the products came from the gas, not from dirt. The work shows how junction design can lift solar fuel output. It may guide other light-driven carbon recycling tools.
europmc-pmc7509090:
Rose and co-authors review PARP inhibitors, their clinical place, how they work, and how tumors resist them. The PARP family runs key cell tasks, from gene control to DNA damage response. PARP1 adds chains that call repair crews to single-strand breaks.

PARP inhibitors were the first approved drugs to target the DNA damage response. They struck BRCA-mutated breast and ovarian cancers first. Since then, use has spread to more cancer types. The review covers the proposed ways these drugs kill tumor cells. It lists markers that may predict response in patients. Pairing PARP drugs with other treatments gets close attention. Resistance paths, and ways around them, close the survey of this fast field.
europmc-pmc7540790:
Wise and co-authors track risk perception in the US during the first COVID-19 week. Behavior change can slow a fast-spreading pandemic. Early awareness of risk was still unclear at that stage.

The study followed 1591 US-based adults over that week. Awareness of risk grew across the period. People reported more protective acts over time. Still, many rated their own risk below average. Belief about personal infection best predicted distancing and hand washing. A subgroup saw low risk and acted less. The authors stress risk perception in early response. Clear risk messages may help close that gap.
europmc-pmc7602490:
Yoo and co-authors review interactions between gut microbiota and the immune system. Gut microbes help digest food and make vitamins. Their products carry signals between gut and immune cells.

A mucosal barrier keeps microbes apart from immune tissue. It also limits gut leakiness in healthy people. Faulty interplay can raise harmful gram-negative bacteria levels. Their products can cross the barrier into the body. That can raise infection risk and inflammation over time. Chronic imbalance links to type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Bowel and autoimmune diseases also link to it. Short-chain fatty acids get focus as key signals. The review highlights gaps in this fast field.
europmc-pmc7710390:
Doraiswamy and co-authors scope the early literature on telehealth in the COVID-19 pandemic. Telehealth use surged as clinics shut and patients stayed home. The team searched PubMed and Embase for work from January to June 2020, under a set protocol.

The review kept 543 articles from 331 journals. Most, 61.3%, were opinions or commentaries rather than studies. Authors from rich nations wrote 86.6% of the set. Writings used 39 unlike definitions for telehealth terms. Only 7.7% dealt direct with COVID-19 care itself. The authors map a field that grew fast but lacks shared terms and hard data.
europmc-pmc7804290:
Kokic and co-authors work out how remdesivir stalls the SARS-CoV-2 copying enzyme. Remdesivir was the only FDA-approved drug for COVID-19 at the time. Its active form mimics a building block of RNA. The viral polymerase inserts it into new RNA chains. Three more blocks can follow before copying halts.

The team used synthetic RNA chemistry, biochemistry, and cryo-electron microscopy. Adding the fourth block after remdesivir proved hard. A barrier blocks the RNA from sliding forward. The last RNA block stays stuck in the enzyme's grip site. The next building block then cannot enter, so synthesis stalls. The stalled shape may also block the viral proofreading enzyme. These details should aid the hunt for better antivirals.
europmc-pmc7820290:
Lu and co-authors study how the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein forms droplets with RNA. The N protein binds the viral genome, about 30 kb long. It helps pack that genome into new virus particles. The protein mixes binding and pairing parts with loose regions.

Its middle loose region drives droplet formation with RNA. Nearby chemical edits change how those droplets behave. Inside cells, the droplets pull in a host protein called G3BP1. That may blunt the cell's stress and defense response. The viral membrane protein M starts droplets of its own. Mixed droplets split into separate zones. One zone holds N with M, the other N with RNA. The authors link this sorting to genome packing.
europmc-pmc7820390:
The GBD 2019 Blindness and Vision Impairment Collaborators chart 30 years of world vision loss. The work supports the WHO push called VISION 2020: The Right to Sight. The team updated estimates of the global burden. Fresh figures cover the year 2020.

The analysis spans 1990 to 2020. It also forecasts the picture in 2050. The team reviewed population surveys of eye health. They pooled the data with meta-analysis. Rates of blindness fell as a share of population over time. Total case counts still rose as populations grew and aged. Distance and near vision loss are both covered. The results give health systems a base for planning eye care.
europmc-pmc8029490:
Louis and co-authors set out consensus guidelines for folding molecular data into nervous system tumor classification. Big discoveries in tumor biology had outrun a system built on microscope appearance alone. The International Society of Neuropathology convened experts in Haarlem to decide the way forward. Their white paper speaks to the next update of the WHO classification.

The meeting agreed that molecular information should enter the classification, under clear rules. Diagnostic entities should be defined as narrowly as possible. Each diagnosis should be layered: histologic type, WHO grade, then molecular findings, under one integrated diagnosis. Some pediatric tumors should stand apart from adult counterparts. For each entity, testing may be required, suggested, or unneeded. Standard formats for testing and reporting complete the scheme.
europmc-pmc8036490:
Ulanowska and Olas review the biological properties of eugenol and where it might be used. Eugenol is a phenolic compound drawn mainly from clove oil. It has served for years in cosmetics, medicine, and pharmacology. Its known actions include fighting bacteria, viruses, and fungi. It also shows antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. High doses, though, can be toxic.

The pair set the safe dose at 2.5 mg/kg of body weight. They gather recent work on eugenol and its derivatives from the PubMed database. Derivatives such as isoeugenol sometimes beat the parent compound against microbes. Anticancer findings feature as well. The review weighs eugenol as a candidate ingredient for future drugs. Its many actions in one molecule keep researchers interested.
europmc-pmc8198390:
Oura and co-authors review the immune setting of liver cancer and suppressive therapy for it. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the main form of liver cancer. It resists drugs and often returns after treatment.

New immune therapies have lengthened survival for some patients. A checkpoint inhibitor paired with a VEGF inhibitor now leads first-line care. How well these drugs work depends on the tumour immune setting. The review sums up that setting's parts and states. It aims to help doctors match patients to the right immune drugs. Resistance paths get close attention too.
europmc-pmc8219590:
van Doorn and co-authors give guidelines for Bayesian analysis with the JASP software. Bayesian methods grow more popular in research each year. Yet practical guidance on running and reporting them stays thin.

The guidelines cover four stages of work. They run from planning through execution to reading and reporting results. A single running example shows each step. Most advice extends beyond JASP to Bayesian work in general. JASP itself is open-source software. The paper aims to make sound Bayesian practice routine, not rare. Clear reporting checklists form part of the advice given.
europmc-pmc8280690:
Davis and co-authors characterise long COVID in a large international cohort. Many patients face symptoms for months after infection. Few studies had mapped this group in depth, above all outside hospitals.

An online survey reached people through support groups and social media. Data came in from September 6 to November 25, 2020. The analysis covered 3,762 participants with confirmed or likely COVID-19. It tracked symptoms over 7 months and their effect on daily life. Return to prior health was slow for many. The study gives the condition a detailed human profile. The point of the count is to show which groups face the most risk and so need the most care and help.
europmc-pmc8290290:
Mascher and co-authors test long-read sequencing for assembling the barley genome. Big, repeat-rich plant genomes resist assembly. Older work needed huge computing and several methods at once.

The team compared current long-read platforms on barley. Circular consensus sequencing on the PacBio platform led the gains. Most long-read assemblies clearly beat the short-read reference. Accurate long reads gave the most continuous results. The study weighs speed, cost, and quality per platform. Pan-genome projects in crops stand to gain most. Barley serves as the test case for wider plant work. Barley stands in for other large crop genomes here.
europmc-pmc8298890:
Veerman and co-authors compare five methods for isolating extracellular vesicles. Vesicles are tested as therapies and biomarkers. Subtypes remain poorly defined, and pure samples are hard to get.

The team ran all five methods on cell medium and plasma. Sample volumes were 250 microlitres or 3 millilitres. Methods spanned precipitation, membrane affinity, and size-exclusion routes. A density gradient and a phosphatidylserine affinity route completed the set. Each method yielded vesicles of different origin and purity. Clinical fit varied just as much. The comparison helps labs pick a method honestly. Plasma work shows the small-volume case most clinics face.
europmc-pmc8440190:
Blomberg and co-authors follow Long COVID in patients who stayed home during their illness. Lasting harm after COVID-19 is well known in hospital cases. The symptom range after mild disease needed closer study.

The cohort held 312 patients from Bergen's first pandemic wave, most of them home-isolated. At 6 months, 61 percent still had symptoms. Risk rose with worse early illness, higher antibody levels, and past chronic lung disease. Among home-isolated adults aged 16 to 30 years, about half still had symptoms. Loss of taste or smell, fatigue, and breathlessness led the list. Memory and focus problems also appeared. The authors stress infection control for the young.
europmc-pmc8495390:
Fan and co-authors review immunotherapy for colorectal cancer, its wins so far and its next steps. Immune drugs have changed care for many solid tumors. Colorectal cancer joined that story through a defined subgroup. Those tumors lack mismatch repair and show high microsatellite instability.

Two PD-1 blocking drugs won approval for that subgroup, with lasting remissions. Trials since moved the drugs into first-line and earlier-stage care. The bigger prize is the majority group, whose tumors repair DNA well. New work hints that immune gains may reach them too. Vaccines and adoptive cell therapy draw attention as well. The review also covers markers that predict response.
europmc-pmc8507690:
Usman and co-authors place vimentin at the heart of cancer spread through epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Vimentin is a filament protein that supports cell structure and function. Its levels are low early in cancer growth. They climb as tumors begin to invade nearby tissue.

The review traces vimentin's many roles in growth and spread to distant sites. EMT lets epithelial cells gain the traits they need to invade. Damage to the vimentin gene shows up in cancers, though its effect is not yet known. The authors urge new technology to target vimentin with drugs. Blocking it could slow spread and lift patient survival.
europmc-pmc9022290:
Chen and co-authors review CD36, a cell-surface protein that both senses signals and pulls fatty acids into cells. It sits on macrophages, dendritic cells, and some T and B cells, plus many non-immune cells. By shaping how immune cells fuel themselves, CD36 steers their growth, activation, and fate. The review covers its roles in innate defense and in adaptive immunity.

Dysfunction of CD36 feeds common diseases, including artery hardening and tumor growth. The authors draw out shared themes across cell types. They argue that tuning CD36 could become a way to reset immune cell metabolism in disease.
europmc-pmc9127490:
Tang and co-authors update progress on human organoids for basic research and clinical use. Organoids are tiny three-dimensional structures grown in the lab from stem cells. They mimic the cell mix, shape, and jobs of real organs. Organoids from patients also carry that person's genetic makeup.

The update covers methods for growing brain, retinal, kidney, liver, lung, gut, and heart organoids. It compares organoids from pluripotent stem cells with those from adult stem cells. Uses span disease study, drug testing, gene repair, and transplant work. The authors also name current limits that hold the field back. Readers get a broad guide to a tool that brings human biology into the dish.
europmc-pmc9465090:
Li and co-authors review the System Xc-/GSH/GPX4 axis as a shield that blocks ferroptosis in solid tumors. Ferroptosis is an iron-driven cell death caused by lipid peroxide buildup. Triggering it is a new hope against drug-resistant tumors. Tumors that resist standard drugs may still fall to this route.

The axis joins a cystine transporter, glutathione, and the enzyme GPX4. Together they stop lipid damage before it kills the cell. The review explains each part of the axis in turn. It then covers how each part is regulated. Blocking the axis can force ferroptosis in tumor cells. Case sections cover lung, breast, liver, and gut cancers. Pancreatic cancer gets its own section. The authors close with how tumors build resistance to ferroptosis itself.
europmc-pmc9646490:
Islam and co-authors present SigProfilerExtractor, a tool for pulling mutational signatures out of cancer genomes. Signature study is a standard part of cancer genomics work. Each mutagen leaves a pattern of changes in tumor DNA. Finding those patterns from scratch is the hard step.

The team benchmarked their tool against 13 other programs. Tests ran across 34 scenarios with 2,500 simulated signatures. The sets held 60,000 synthetic genomes and 20,000 synthetic exomes. Their tool found more true signatures than rivals found. It also raised far fewer false signatures in the runs. Applied to real data, it covered 4,643 whole genome cancers. It also ran over 19,184 whole exome cancers in the study. Four novel signatures came out of that sweep. One of them was tied to tobacco smoking in bladder tissue.
europmc-pmc9795790:
Kolb asks whether inflammation in obese belly fat starts as protection and only later turns harmful. Fat tissue hosts resident immune cells even when lean. Obesity brings a slow, low grade inflammation to that tissue. The trigger is fat cells losing their metabolic balance.

At first, extra fat and sugar are met by cell growth. Immune cells wake up to help restore tissue balance. Their early signals are tissue protective in this account. Fat cells swell, strain, and start to die over time. Worn out cells of several types pile up in the tissue. Their debris draws in waves of new immune cells. Scarring and vessel growth then intensify in the fat. Senescent cells may spread their state to neighbors nearby. Kolb frames the fire as a rescue that overstays. Late stage inflammation adds damage instead of repair.
europmc-pmc9825490:
Deutsch and co-authors mark ten years of the ProteomeXchange consortium with a 2023 update. Mass spectrometry drives most high-throughput protein studies today. The consortium was set up to standardize sharing of that data. Six member resources now run the exchange together.

Submissions have climbed every year of the decade. By mid 2022 over 34,233 data sets had been submitted. More than half of them arrived in the last three years. A universal spectrum identifier system was rolled out. Metadata capture for experiments got sharper as well. Reuse of public data sets keeps growing each year. That reuse links proteomics to other data resources. It also seeds new studies and new databases. Handling of sensitive human clinical data gets guidance here. The authors sum up where open proteomics now stands.
europmc-pmc9825590:
Davis and co-authors report the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database update for 2023. The database ties chemical exposures to their biological fallout. Curators hand gather the links from published papers. Chemicals, genes, traits, anatomy, and diseases are interwoven.

Content grew by a fifth in this update round. It now spans 17,100 chemicals and 54,300 genes. Phenotypes number 6,100 and diseases 7,270 in the set. Exposure statements reached 202,000 curated records in total. A new tool called Tetramers builds four part blocks. Each block links a chemical, gene, trait, and disease. Those blocks sketch testable paths of harm. Exposure records now tie to anatomy pages directly. Users can survey chemical traces by body tissue. Page designs were streamlined across the site. The resource serves both lookup and hypothesis building.
europmc-pmc9826790:
Jiao and co-authors review ribosome biogenesis in disease, naming new players and drug targets. Ribosomes are the cell's protein building machines. Making them drives growth, division, and cell change. Three signal systems jointly steer that production line.

The mTORC1 and Myc pathways lead the control set. Noncoding RNAs form the third steering arm. The review compares our ribosomes with bacterial ones. Human ribosomes carry four RNAs and 80 proteins. That contrast explains how antibiotics hit bacteria selectively. Resistance tricks bacteria use get their own survey. Frameshifting, stalling, and collision events are explained. Disease links range from blood ills to brain decline. Heart disease and cancer feature strongly in the tour. Trials and therapies aimed at ribosome making are summed up. Vaccine angles for COVID-19 close the disease survey.
europmc-pmc9863490:
Saez and co-authors examine the innate immune system in inflammatory bowel disease. The disease group includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, both marked by chronic gut inflammation. The cause remains unclear. Innate immune cells give a fast, broad first response in the gut.

The review covers neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, innate lymphoid cells, and NK cells. These cells guard against pathogens while tolerating resident gut microbes. When that balance breaks, inflammation can follow. The cells drive defense, healing, and inflammation through cytokines, chemokines, phagocytosis, and antigen presentation. The authors argue that this system offers targets for future bowel disease therapies.
fouillee-evolutionnisme-idees-forces-189:
Alfred Fouillee built his name on one striking claim: ideas are forces. His French work L'evolutionnisme des idees-forces, from 1890, states that claim in full. An idea, once held, pushes toward act and change in the world. Fouillee joined that claim to the theory of evolution.

He traces how ideas grow, spread, and reshape both minds and societies over time. Thought is no idle picture, on his account, but a real power at work. The doctrine let him link mind, morals, and social life in one scheme. French readers took the book as his core statement. It still marks his place in French thought.
france-thais-1890:
Anatole France published Thaïs in 1890, here in the Library Edition English rendering of 1924 in print. The novel tells of an Alexandrian courtesan-saint and the monk who loves and converts her in Egypt. Its irony about desire and holiness made France famous well beyond France in the 1890s of his prime.

Paphnutius, a desert monk, enters Alexandria to save Thaïs, the actress whose beauty ruins men in droves. She converts, burns her treasures, and enters a convent to die in odor of sanctity and peace. The monk, meanwhile, is consumed by the desire he denied, and demons mock his wasted, burning soul in dreams. At her deathbed he confesses his love and is thrust aside as she sees heaven open above her. France balances pity for both, and judges neither, in prose of classical calm.
frus-1861-d190:
Mr. Stockton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 September 1861. The dispatch is document 190 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Stockton's September report answers, across a long gap, the April letter from Seward. The record gives no post for him in either heading. His page joins the file as a lone report, its value lying in its date and its place in the year's run. A lone report still earns its place, as one dated point in the year's wide record. One dated point, honestly kept, can anchor a whole chapter of the year's tale.
frus-1861-d290:
Writing on 25 July 1861, Mr. Harvey sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 290 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d90:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 11 October 1861. The dispatch is document 90 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By mid October, Adams had held his post for five months of war. His reports kept their even tone through praise and blame in the press. The letter shows the worth of a steady man in a post where a hot word could cost a country its cause. A hot word in London could have undone a year of care in a single week. Steady men in hot posts are the quiet heroes of this whole record.
frus-1862-d190:
Two Seward letters to London bear the date 18 November 1862, and the first is Document 190 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, received it from Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Mid-November mail crossed an Atlantic growing calmer on the war question, since Britain had declined the French truce plan. Other business filled the gap: Confederate ships in British yards, trade, and the treatment of Union vessels. This dispatch is part of the shift from crisis management to the daily grind of holding neutrality in place. Earl Russell, the British foreign secretary, was the minister Adams dealt with most in London.
frus-1862-d290:
On 21 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to William L. Dayton in Paris, in a dispatch printed as Document 290 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Three letters in two days mark a heavy mail.

A steamer's sailing explains such clusters: the Department cleared pending business before the bag closed. Seward's June letters to Dayton went out while Stuart handled Britain's legation in Washington and Lee prepared to strike near Richmond. The cluster shows a government working several channels at once, each letter a small part of a larger design. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d390:
Two Seward dispatches to Simon Cameron are dated 6 September 1862, and the first is Document 390 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Cameron was the American minister in Russia, at St. Petersburg.

Seward wrote six days after Bull Run, with Lee entering Maryland. His September mail to St. Petersburg carried Washington's account of a hard month to the court least likely to doubt it. The pair of letters that day shows the Department keeping even its quietest channel current in a crisis week. The legation's quiet year was the exception in a volume full of friction. Cameron, a Pennsylvania political chief, had run the War Department before going to Russia.
frus-1862-d490:
Dated 16 March 1862, this report from James Shepherd Pike at The Hague reached Secretary of State William H. Seward out of strict order in the printed file. It is Document 490 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The volume's editors grouped letters as they were received and printed, so a Hague report of mid-March can sit behind one dated days later. Pike's subject in those weeks was the Netherlands itself: its ministry's caution, its merchants' losses, and its colonial stake in the Caribbean. His dispatch adds one more layer to the Dutch record for March, a month in which Seward wrote to The Hague four times. The file's density is the point: Washington watched even friendly small powers closely.
frus-1862-d590:
On 7 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to Thomas Corwin in Mexico City. It is Document 590 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the annual message.

June orders to Mexico went out as the armies closed on Richmond, and Washington's mind was necessarily divided. Seward still kept the Mexican brief exact: support for the republic's independence, protest against the French design, and no step that risked war with France. Corwin, on the ground, had to make that limited brief feel like friendship to a government under invasion. The instruction is one of the year's clearest statements of how the Union rationed its strength abroad while its own survival was undecided.
frus-1862-d690: Dated 20 March 1862, this dispatch from a Mr. De Long went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 690 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the last of his run of letters that winter. The title and record name him and the date only, so his post and subject stay unstated here.
frus-1862-d90:
A letter home from Charles Francis Adams, dated 3 July 1862, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 90 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d190:
Reporting on 7 May 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 190 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d290:
A dispatch dated 10 September 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 290 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in early July 1863 weakened the case for aiding the South. British leaders grew more careful, and Adams's post grew a little less tense. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d390:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 11 February 1863. It stands as document 390 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Read together, these letters trace a slow cooling of the crisis mood of 1861 and 1862. Recognition of the South grew less likely with each month the channel stayed open. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d490:
Under the date 4 May 1863, the record holds a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d590:
Secretary William H. Seward directed a letter to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington on 17 July 1863. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d690:
William H. Seward wrote once more to Lord Lyons on 11 November 1863. Lyons, the British minister in Washington, was his most frequent foreign contact that fall. The letter is document 690 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863.

Three notes in this run bear the same date, which tells its own story about the load of work. The Union wanted trade kept open and the South kept isolated. Britain wanted its ships and goods kept safe. Seward's mail walked that line in short, firm steps. This dispatch is one such step, and its worth lies in the full sequence it belongs to.
frus-1863p1-d90:
On 24 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 90 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It opens a three-day run of Seward letters in the file.

Seward's late-February sheets set the brief anew as spring neared. The war at home was stuck in winter mud, and the talks abroad moved by small steps. His letters told Adams which claims to press and which to let rest. This one begins that run, a sign that Washington meant to keep its London hand tight as the season turned.
frus-1890:
Central America fills the front of the 1890 volume. Its file runs far past any other country's. Harrison's message stresses clean administration at home. Revenues above four hundred fifty million dollars, he reports, show no defalcation. Mexico and Turkey take the next-longest runs. China adds its main file and legation papers. Persia earns a solid section.

The mid-volume testimony comes from cold waters. A sealing witness recalls fifty years in the trade. His family worked South Shetland, South Georgia, and the Diegos. Seal life had recovered there, he says, over decades. Some 40,000 skins were taken in six good years. The Bering Sea quarrel stands behind such evidence. Britain and America argued from men's memories. This volume preserves the sealing case in sworn form.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d190:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent President Roosevelt a long personal review from Moscow on 4 November 1943, and it sums up what the foreign ministers' conference had shown him about Soviet thinking. It runs to several parts and mixes praise for new cooperation with warnings about hard issues ahead.

Harriman says the Soviet leaders had decided to try working with Britain and America on war and postwar problems. Molotov grew more open as he saw no united front against him. Their acceptance of China as a signer of the Four Nation Declaration proved the point, he argues. Against that, Moscow was stung by Western caution on Turkey and Sweden, and still awaited a firm answer on the Italian ships.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d290:
