The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 401/1 at Cairo on 23 November 1943, on airfields for very-long-range B-29 bombers in the China-Burma-India area. It answers the American paper C.C.S. 401, after President Roosevelt's telegram to Churchill asking for help in building the bases.

The British chiefs accept the American recommendations in full and are issuing orders to their authorities. Churchill has already told the commander in chief in India to give every help with the four Indian bases. One warning is attached. If the work is to finish in time, the American units and equipment must reach Calcutta by 15 January. Otherwise the deadline of 1 April will slip. The building effort may even have to stop for the Ledo road.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d390:
Louis Dreyfus, the American minister in Iran, wrote a secret letter to General Patrick Hurley at Tehran on 29 November 1943. It reports a morning call from Iran's prime minister, Mohammad Sa'ed Soheily, about the statement the conference might issue at its close.

Soheily told Dreyfus he had seen Foreign Secretary Eden that day and raised the idea of a joint communiqué built on three lines. The Allies would recognize that Iran has given them every possible help. Iran's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity would be confirmed, as already set out in the Tripartite Treaty. And Iran's economic needs would be considered when the peace treaty came to be negotiated. Eden agreed in principle, Soheily said, but asked him to approach the Americans and the Soviets for their agreement to go ahead.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d490:
President Roosevelt sent a message to Prime Minister Churchill on December 5, 1943, while both men were at the Second Cairo Conference. They were meeting daily, yet still exchanged written notes, which the State Department later printed in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Written messages between the two leaders matter because they fixed points that conversation left loose. Roosevelt and Churchill's wartime correspondence runs to hundreds of items, and the Cairo notes belong to its most intense stretch, right after Tehran. A reader finds the alliance's two heads communicating in their own words at the moment of decision, not filtered through staff summaries or later memoirs.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d90: John Winant, the American ambassador in London, wrote to President Roosevelt on November 2, 1943. His dispatch is Document 90 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Winant was close to Churchill's circle and reported British thinking with a sympathetic ear, which made his letters a valued channel. The record gives the date and the two men and no topic. The dispatch is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d190:
For this September 14, 1944 meeting, the editors print Eden's diary. Eden and Cadogan found Churchill with Roosevelt, Morgenthau, and Cherwell conferring about lend-lease. The visitors were welcomed as an interruption, and talk ranged over Russians, Poles, and Dumbarton Oaks until it was time to dress for dinner.

White, who was not present, adds the scene's famous line. Roosevelt delayed initialing the lend-lease committee memorandum by telling stories, while Churchill grew nervous and eager. At last Churchill burst out: "What do you want me to do? Get on my hind legs and beg like Fala?" Fala was the president's dog. The anecdote survives because Morgenthau retold it to White the next day.
frus-1944-quebec-d290:
The companion message to Chiang Kai-shek, sent September 16, 1944, over Leahy's name, hastens to inform the Generalissimo of plans for the mutual effort, particularly in Southeast Asia. Roosevelt and Churchill declared themselves determined to employ all available resources toward the earliest practicable invasion of the Japanese homeland, and were expediting redeployment after Germany's defeat to that end.

Mountbatten's operations in north Burma would continue and extend, securing the Myitkyina air bases and opening overland communications between India and China. The message asks continued cooperation from Chinese troops in Burma and the Salween armies. Success by next spring would let the Ledo Road advance with its pipelines. Mountbatten was also directed to prepare a large-scale amphibious operation in the Bay of Bengal.
frus-1944-quebec-d90:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to Secretary Hull on September 9, 1944. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. It came three days before the Quebec Conference opened. Stimson and Hull led the two great wartime departments.

Letters between cabinet secretaries settled positions before summits began. The War Department ran the armies nearing Germany's border. The State Department handled the alliance and the coming peace. For readers, Stimson's message shows those two worlds meeting on paper. Their agreement, or friction, shaped what Roosevelt could promise at Quebec. The conference opened at Quebec City on September 12.
frus-1945-50-intel-d190:
A letter dated 13 March 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg). The reader was the Chairman of the Joint Research and Development Board (Bush). It stands as document 190 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

Letters between senior men often carried the real weight of a matter, since a signed letter put the writer's name and office behind the words. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d290:
A memorandum dated 17 June 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) and Secretary of State Marshall. The State Department prints it as document 290 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d390:
On 25 July 1949, the Executive Secretary (Souers) sent a memorandum to the National Security Council. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 390 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d90:
McCormack wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 23 April 1946, his last letter in the volume's State thread. He had led the department's intelligence office since its birth the previous September. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A last paper by a founding chief carries a summing-up quality, whether the writer intends it or not. McCormack's office had begun as the heir of the OSS analysts and the seed of a State-led intelligence system. By April, that hope had passed to the central group. Readers who have followed his thread from the first hopeful exchanges of October will find this letter a fitting close. The man who built the office writing to the chief who let it go.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d190:
The new Bonomi government took office with allied blessing, this press release announced on 14 December 1944. Reprinted in the Malta and Yalta volume, the statement closes the public phase of the Italian cabinet crisis. It speaks in the name of both wartime partners.

The American and British ambassadors in Rome, it says, have stayed in close contact through the recent developments. Ambassador Kirk reports that Italy's new government rests on a majority of the political parties, those of the Committee of National Liberation among them. It thus keeps a representative character. The United States, in accord with the British government, is happy to see the new government under Signor Bonomi take office.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d290:
The cruiser Quincy carried Roosevelt into Grand Harbor, Malta, on 2 February 1945, and the President's log records the morning by the clock. The log entry, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, comes from the official booklet of the trip. It is the plainest kind of sea record.

At midnight the ship was in the Mediterranean, steering from Gibraltar. Sicily was sighted at ten past six, and Gozo and Malta soon after. At twenty-five to ten the Quincy passed the submarine net gate into Grand Harbor at Valletta. The President stood on deck as crowds lined both sides of the channel. The ship moored at Berth 9 an hour later. The total run from Newport News stood at 4,883 miles. Churchill watched the arrival from the cruiser Sirius across the channel.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d390:
Admiral Ernest King, the Navy's chief, set down the Soviet questions put to him on February 8, 1945, with his answers. Admiral Kuznetsov had asked what had been settled about transferring ships to the Russians under the Milepost program. King answered that firm dates were hard to give. Much depended on the U-boat offensive in the Atlantic.

Deliveries, King said, could be worked out step by step, though later ones might slip. On the transfer port, Dutch Harbor might not suit. Kodiak was the second choice, and King gave his view. The memo shows sea power changing hands by schedule and training class.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d490:
Yugoslavia and Rumanian oil lead the excerpts of Grew's cable of February 10, 1945, his thirty-third message of the series. The British Foreign Office held that Subasic, rather than Tito, had opposed Simovic. Subasic would likely leave soon for Belgrade even without agreement on the regents. King Peter's approval, London felt, was essential, above all for the air and naval forces.

On oil, the Moscow embassy had been instructed to welcome the decision to stop removing equipment from Rumania. It was also to renew America's unwillingness to accept the Soviet contention on the matter. The digest shows the home department fighting Yalta's side battles in parallel.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d90:
Gromyko's mind was not closed on voting, the Secretary of State told the President in this draft memorandum of 20 January 1945. The draft, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, reports two long talks between the Soviet ambassador and Leo Pasvolsky. It was prepared for Roosevelt on the eve of his trip.

The ambassador had asked many questions and seemed to be getting the American arguments into his mind. Pasvolsky gained the firm impression that Gromyko wanted to present the matter fully to his government. Speaking personally, Gromyko had even floated a distinction between discussion in the Council and formal action by vote. The draft calls that a move in the right direction, though not enough.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d190:
Acting Secretary Grew staked out a hard line on the Balkan satellites in a telegram extract dated July 6, 1945. The extract is document 190 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full message appears later in the volume.

Winant may tell the Foreign Office that at the coming high-level talks the United States intends to press strongly for carrying out the Yalta Declaration on Liberated Europe. Washington also wants the Allied Control Commissions in all three ex-satellite states reorganized. And it will oppose proposals to establish diplomatic relations with, or conclude peace with, the present governments there. The position put Romania, Bulgaria, and Hungary near the center of the Potsdam fight over Soviet control in Eastern Europe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d290:
Acting Secretary Grew asked the field missions to judge a British shortcut in a telegram dated June 21, 1945. The message to Maynard Barnes in Bulgaria is document 290 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The same questions went to the American representatives in Romania and Hungary.

The British Foreign Office had proposed that the two governments work for an early conclusion of peace treaties with Hungary, Bulgaria, and Romania. London's reasons follow. Moscow is not likely to give the Western members a fuller voice on the control commissions. And peace would bring the withdrawal of Soviet troops. That would free the countries to decide their own destinies. Grew asks for urgent views on two points. First, does ending the armistice early outweigh the weak Western position meanwhile? Second, what would peace with the present governments mean for free choice and for the Yalta pledges?
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d390:
German warships and merchant ships are treated separately in an extract from a State Department memorandum of June 30, 1945, later forwarded to President Truman. On the battle fleet the extract makes no recommendation at all. Disposal of the German fleet, it says, is a military problem, and one the Joint Chiefs of Staff were already considering.

Merchant ships are another matter. Subject to the military authorities' approval, the extract recommends agreeing to the Soviet claim to one-third of these ships. The short extract shows the Department leaving guns to the soldiers while it bargained over cargo hulls, the shipping Europe needed to recover and America needed against Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d490:
Bierut's promises are reported in an extract of Harriman's cable from Moscow of June 26, 1945. Harriman had discussed with the Polish leader, point by point, the assurances Washington sought in its cable of June 22. Bierut said American representatives would be given every opportunity to travel within Poland and see what they wished.

Rapid communications between the Warsaw embassy and Washington mattered greatly, Harriman stressed. Bierut said his government was working on it and was anxious to establish direct radio communication with the United States. Air links could be arranged after the ambassador's arrival. Harriman closes with a doubt: he cannot predict how far the Russians will try to brake Polish desires for open contact with the West.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d590:
A top secret briefing paper of July 3, 1945, takes up military government in a beaten Japan. It is document 590 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its central question is what the occupying forces should do about the Emperor.

One part suggests that any talk of the Emperor be sent to a Far Eastern advisory body. An appendix then gives the State Department's own approved line. On surrender, the Emperor's powers should be suspended at once. He and his close family should be held in a detached palace outside Tokyo, in seclusion. He should be made to proclaim the surrender himself and to order all forces to lay down their arms. He should also sign the surrender instrument with Japan's top commander.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d690:
Ambassador Harriman reported the Turkish ambassador's private fears from Moscow on June 25, 1945. His secret wire is document 690 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. A member of Harriman's staff had talked with Ambassador Sarper the day before.

Sarper said there were no new developments in the Soviet demands. Turkey's flat replies, he thought, had given Moscow pause. Had Turkey yielded, he believed, fresh demands on its inner affairs would soon have followed. Their aim would have been to bring Turkey, in his words, like Poland under direct Soviet sway. The rebuff had only postponed the joining of the issue, he warned. The Russians, he said, are not bluffing. Sarper saw Turkey lying in a Soviet security zone taking shape from Finland to China, and he expected the pressure to go on.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d90:
Churchill passed Stalin's answer on the conference site to President Truman on June 23, 1945. Telegram number 98, document 90 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam, repeats Stalin's reply to Churchill's proposal that each delegation run its own closed enclave, as in the Crimea.

Stalin agrees to the plan and names the ground. The delegations will be housed at Babelsberg, southeast of Potsdam, each on its own closed territory. Joint sessions will meet in a fourth building, the palace of the German Crown Prince in Potsdam. Advance parties should arrive around June 28, when Zhukov returns, and a good airfield sits at nearby Kladov. Churchill adds that he has ordered Montgomery to send his party in as soon as possible.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1090:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew sent this memorandum to Potsdam on July 18, 1945. Italy's ambassador had called that morning, leaving papers for the President and Byrnes. Rome fears Britain and the Soviet Union want the harshest possible peace terms for Italy. Harsh terms, the ambassador warned, would crush Italian morale and block her recovery.

Two letters from Ambassador Tarchiani are enclosed. One thanks Washington for pledging not to sign an unfair or oppressive treaty, and for promising Italy a full hearing before any treaty is final. The other carries Foreign Minister De Gasperi's views. Italy's first need, he writes, is release from the armistice terms and standing restored among nations.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1190:
Staff of the United States Chiefs of Staff wrote this memorandum on 18 July 1945. Papers from the chiefs' staff gave the American team the armed forces' formal view of the questions at Potsdam. This one dates from the second day of the talks.

The chiefs spoke for the services that still fought Japan and now held half of Germany. Their staff work turned that weight into advice the envoys could use. A memorandum like this is the Pentagon's paper, filed for the diplomats. It shows the military house putting its knowledge on record at the start of the bargaining.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1290:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 18 July 1945. It came from the summit's second day, early in the British staff's run of papers. The note shows the military view being worked out before it hardened into stands.

London's chiefs had to weigh a shrinking purse against a world-wide set of duties. Their papers brought that hard math to the envoys' table. This memorandum is one of the early pieces. Read beside the American notes of the same date, it shows two allied staffs at work. They started their Potsdam labors in step, each in its own voice.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1390:
Instead of a memorandum, Mikołajczyk's paper of 28 July 1945 is a diary entry. The Polish deputy prime minister kept a private record beside his formal papers during the Potsdam period. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Diary entries differ from memoranda in one great way: they are written for the writer, not for a reader in office. That freedom often brings candor about moods, meetings, and men. Readers can set this entry beside Mikołajczyk's formal papers of the same days and watch the public and private voices diverge. The volume gains depth from printing both, and the diary is among its most human pages.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-90:
A second set of Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 24, 1945 survives in the Potsdam record. The chiefs met more than once that week as the conference pressed on. Each session dealt with live war business while peace terms were debated nearby. The set was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Having two records for one day shows the pace of work at Potsdam. Military questions could not wait for the plenary sessions to end. The minutes let readers track what the chiefs settled among themselves. They also show what was passed up to President Truman for a final call.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d790:
Nikolai Novikov, secretary of the Soviet delegation, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on July 25, 1945. Document 790 is a formal Soviet-American exchange inside the conference machinery. Delegation secretaries ran the paper flow between teams. Novikov later became a noted Soviet envoy. His letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

Secretaries' letters look minor and are not. They move texts, set meetings, and fix the record of what passed between sides. Readers see the conference's clerks doing the work that let leaders lead. The document also shows courtesy holding under strain. Even hard rivals kept the forms, and the forms kept the talks alive.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d890: Emilio Collado wrote to Assistant Secretary of State William Clayton on August 1, 1945, about one word in a presidential letter. The letter told the War Department its duties on German financing. Collado had spoken with Admiral Leahy, who did not know if Truman had signed it yet. Collado argues the word facilities should not appear in the first charge sentence, given the shape of the reparations deal. He prepared a substitute page without it. The editors note the swap was never made.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d990:
The American military attaché in Sweden, Kessler, cabled the War Department on July 24, 1945. His subject is a group of interned German aircraft in Sweden. The planes had come there from the German-Soviet front during the war.

A Russian delegation in Stockholm has surveyed the aircraft. The Russians propose to fly them out shortly as war booty. Their plans, Kessler reports, have been aired in the newspapers. He notes that neither Britain nor the United States has made any request about the remaining aircraft. The message reached the American delegation at Potsdam the next day, by retransmission from the War Department.
frus-1977-80v12-d90:
A telegram from the U.S. Embassy in Afghanistan to the State Department, sent December 20, 1979, weighs why Soviet troops have come. It is document 90 in Volume XII of the 1977-1980 series. Three battalions of Soviet combat troops had reached Bagram Air Force Base. The embassy notes that the insurgency had not grown sharply worse. Kabul's regime did not face a clear threat to its survival. The cable offers several motives, alone or mixed.

Moscow and Kabul may hope to stiffen the regime before a threat can grow. The troops may guard Soviet citizens if Kabul's safety fails. They may also shape palace politics, or lead a larger intervention. The embassy judges the last unlikely, on the evidence then at hand.
gao-gaoreports-b-296490:
Johnson Controls Security Systems protested a Treasury award for guard systems work in GAO decision B-296490, dated August 29, 2005. The winner was Quanta Systems. The site was the Bureau of Engraving and Printing plant in Washington. The work was to run, watch, and fix the security systems. The firm hit the marks and the pick.

GAO sustained the protest on two grounds. The winner had claimed it had set up needed training and papers for staff before award. That claim was false and the agency had leaned on it. The agency also treated bids as just pass or fail. It failed to weigh the firm's stronger tech bid, as best value rules required.
gao-gaoreports-b-297890:
PDS Consultants protested a Veterans Affairs award for eye care in GAO decision B-297890, dated April 4, 2006. The winner was Caribe Opti Lab. The work was eye exams and eyeglasses. The buy was set aside for small firms. The firm said the winner would not give home-made goods. The Buy American Act was thus at stake.

GAO denied the protest. A bid is a pledge to give home-made goods. The agency had no facts to doubt that pledge. A claim that a firm will breach its pledge needs facts, not fears. No facts showed the goods would be foreign. The award thus stood on the pledge in the bid.
gao-gaoreports-b-298390:
Dismas Charities protested a Federal Bureau of Prisons award to Bannum, Inc. The contract covered Comprehensive Sanctions Center services for federal offenders in Austin, Texas. The center work aids job search, housing, and self-improvement. GAO ruled in B-298390 on August 21, 2006.

Dismas argued that the agency scored proposals in a flawed way. It also said the award did not rest on best value. GAO reviewed the scoring and the source selection. It found both fair and in line with the stated terms. The challenge gave no basis to upset the award. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298590:
General Injectables & Vaccines, Inc. protested its removal from a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention competition. The contract covered vaccine stockpile management and distribution. The work runs under the Vaccines for Children Act. GAO ruled in the B-298590 series on November 15, 2006.

The firm claimed panel members were pressed to change scores. It also said the agency held unfair talks with the winner on a pass-fail point. GAO found the final scores well backed by the record. No real flaw in the last scoring round was shown. Talks with all offerors followed the first round. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298790:
SCS Refrigerated Services, LLC protested a Defense Commissary Agency award to Spokane Produce, Inc. The contract covered fresh fruits and vegetables for stores in the west region. The buy was set aside for small firms. GAO ruled in the B-298790 series on November 29, 2006.

The firm attacked the scoring of its proposal. It also faulted the best-value award call. GAO tested the record against the stated terms. It found the review fair at each step. The pick tracked the terms and the rules that govern such buys. No ground to upset the award was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310790:
C&H SERVICE Srl lost its protest (GAO decision B-310790, dated February 5, 2008). The Air Force sought air units for sites near Aviano Air Base, Italy. The units had to cool and heat rooms. The call asked that units sit on a named test site list. The award went to Sanson Bruno. C&H units were not on that list.

GAO denied the protest. The toss of C&H's bid was fair on the call's terms. C&H said its unit was the twin of a listed one. Proof for that claim came from C&H and its own supply chain. Self-made proof of that kind can be set aside.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-190:
Equal Employment Opportunity, GAO-05-190 of February 18, 2005, brings data on fair treatment at six Energy Department labs. In April 2002, GAO urged tighter fair-job watch at three weapons labs. It told Energy and the Labor Department's contract watch office to work as a team there. Congress then asked for a fresh look at six more labs.

GAO compares pay, merit raises, exits, and step-ups for women and minority staff next to men and white staff. It lists the fair-job fears lab staff raised. It checks what the two departments did with the 2002 advice. The text is data first, built for hard oversight talks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-290:
Indian Child Welfare Act, GAO-05-290 of April 4, 2005, studies how a 1978 law works when states place Native children in care. In the 1960s and 1970s, Native children were about six times more apt to enter foster care than others. Many went to non-Native homes. The act gives tribes a voice in each such case. It tells states to tell the tribe and let it step in.

GAO asks what shapes each placement call. It asks if the act has slowed placements. It asks how Washington watches the states' work. Facts in hand could aim state help with more care, the title holds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-490:
Oversight of charter schools in the District of Columbia is covered in GAO interim report GAO-05-490, issued on May 19, 2005. Two bodies approve and watch the city's charter schools: the Board of Education and the Public Charter School Board. The 2005 D.C. Appropriations Act ordered this early look. GAO set out what the School Reform Act asks of both bodies and how each does the work.

The act requires the authorizers to review school applications and approve those that qualify. It also requires them to monitor schools and decide whether charters should be renewed or revoked. Each body must issue a yearly report on its work. GAO found both had built processes to meet those duties, in different ways. Both run yearly reviews and deeper checks every 5 years. One board had revoked charters of failing schools. The other was moving to revoke one. Full study results were due in fall 2005.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-690:
Tax breaks as shadow spending anchor GAO-05-690, a report dated September 23, 2005. Since 1974 the count of tax expenditures has more than doubled, and their real cost has tripled, to nearly $730 billion in 2004. The 14 largest breaks take 75 percent of the loss, led by the tax-free status of employer health cover. Counted as spending, the total topped yearly discretionary outlays for most of the past decade and runs near 7.5 percent of the economy.

Yet no routine review asks whether each break still earns its keep. GAO's 1994 plea for regular scrutiny has seen little progress, it finds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-790:
Guarding national icons and federal buildings is the charge of GAO-05-790, dated June 24, 2005. Terror risk made site security a top concern. Two bodies face a hard balance: keep sites safe, yet keep them open. One runs parks and monuments. The other owns or leases office buildings. GAO named the challenges each faces and the steps each has taken.

GAO found shared strains: open access versus safety, clashing claims among parties, and remote sites that are hard to guard. The parks body has raised security at famed sites and set up a central security office. It built a shared way to rank risk. GAO said the next step is to tie those ranks to where money goes. The buildings body faces the same strains, plus a guard force moved to a new department.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-190:
Postal Service purchasing reform is weighed in GAO-06-190, a report dated December 15, 2005. Buying is a large share of the Postal Service's yearly costs. The agency has just rewritten its purchasing rules to act in a more businesslike way. Small suppliers, some of whom live on postal work, voiced worry about the shift. GAO described the changes and the agency's reasons for them. It judged the changes against reform principles and the habits of leading buyers.

The changes look promising, GAO found, but two needs stand out. The agency's ombudsman setup needs revision so suppliers have a fair channel for disputes. Steady oversight must also continue as the new rules bed in. Past GAO work faulted the agency for missing savings targets. The report presses the agency to keep small firms in view as it chases savings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-290:
The Capitol complex and its caretaker's management make up GAO-06-290, dated February 21, 2006. The Architect of the Capitol runs upkeep, renovation, and new building across more than three dozen sites. In 2003 GAO reviewed the office and urged fixes in seven areas. It wanted the office run in a more strategic and answerable way. GAO reported on progress in January and August 2004.

This report sums up how far the earlier advice has been carried out. It also covers project and facilities management, where big builds meet daily upkeep. Remaining challenges get their own plain list. The stakes are practical: cost, schedule, and safety on the nation's most symbolic ground. The review reads as a progress report on a slow reform. Some habits have changed; deep management problems, the title says, remain. Congress asked for the tally, and the office works under its eye.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-390:
Sewage plants serve every town, and their pipes can also be a weak point. GAO decided GAO-06-390 on March 31, 2006, on securing wastewater facilities. Large underground sewers could be reached by terrorists. Devices placed there could damage buildings or streets above. GAO asked what laws and directives govern protection of these plants.

GAO then checked steps key facilities took after September 11, 2001. It also reviewed help from the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of Homeland Security. Utilities had made important upgrades, GAO found. More gains on key parts may be limited by costs and other constraints. Readers see both progress and limits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-590:
Two Pacific island nations depend on U.S. aid compacts, yet growth stays slow. In GAO-06-590 (June 27, 2006), GAO reports on Micronesia and the Marshall Islands. The United States began aid under a Compact of Free Association in 1987. Amended compacts in 2004 commit over $3.5 billion until 2023. Joint committees must monitor progress toward development goals. They also address policy reforms to spur investment. Law requires GAO to report on conditions in both nations from time to time.

GAO examined each country's political and social setting. It reviewed the economic setting as well. It checked the status of economic policy reforms. Development prospects remain limited, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-290:
A federal housing program keeps rents within reach for poor households, if owners stay in. GAO reviewed preservation efforts in GAO-07-290, issued April 11, 2007. The project-based Section 8 program signs long contracts with landlords. Congress feared the housing department was letting the stock slip away. GAO analyzed contract data from 2001 through 2005. It asked owners and managers what drives their choices.

Most owners stayed, GAO found. Some 13,218 contracts covering 931,570 units were renewed in the period. That is 92 percent of contracts up for decision. Only 8 percent ended, and 6 percent were owner opt-outs. Market pull drove most exits, not agency pressure. Owners left for higher rents or condo sales in hot markets. Family properties left more often than elderly ones. Nonprofit owners renewed at higher rates. GAO said the department's tools and rules lag the market.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-90:
The personnel office's reform leadership is examined in GAO-07-90, dated January 19, 2007. The Office of Personnel Management guides human capital change across government. It must certify agency pay systems before they can use new flexibilities. A 2004 performance-based pay system for senior executives tests that role. GAO used the pay system as a model case. It drew lessons for future reforms. This is the second report in a planned series.

Agencies' trials with the pay system exposed a knowledge gap at the office, GAO found. Staff lacked depth in some skills that reform demands. GAO advised the office to reexamine its agencywide skills. It also urged sharing of best practices among agencies. Progress toward reform goals should be tracked and reported. The office said it has made headway on its goals. It neither agreed nor disagreed with the advice. The report aims the lessons at the next round of change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-990:
Contractor support near the core of government is probed in GAO-07-990, dated September 17, 2007. Homeland Security spent $1.2 billion in fiscal year 2005 on four support service types. Over half of 117 work statements cover planning, policy, and buying support. Those tasks sit close to duties reserved for officials. Coast Guard fleet planning used contractor help. A credential program drew on contractor strategy work. Nine cases were studied in close detail. In none did officials weigh the sway risk first.

Speed and scarce staff drove the choices, GAO found. Long policy warns against contractor sway over public calls. Contractors sometimes did the same work as federal staff beside them. Intelligence analysis and budget work appear on the list. Oversight of these deals runs thin in places. GAO urged stronger risk checks before signing such deals. It also urged tighter control once work starts. The department broadly agreed with the advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-590:
Individual retirement accounts are studied in GAO report GAO-08-590, issued June 4, 2008. Congress created these accounts so workers without job plans could save, and so savers could keep plan money when changing jobs. GAO weighed their size, employer barriers, and federal oversight.

In 2004, the accounts held about $3.5 trillion, more than the $2.6 trillion in defined contribution plans or the $1.9 trillion in pension plans. Rollovers, not new contributions, supply most of the money flowing in. Small firms still rarely offer payroll-deduction accounts, citing plan costs, promotion limits, and contribution rules. Payroll-deduction accounts sit outside the Labor Department's reach, GAO notes. It urged better data sharing and ways to spur employer offers. Neither agency took a position.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-90:
American Indians and Alaska Natives have the third highest rate of HIV/AIDS diagnosis in the United States, and they tend to enter care later and die sooner. GAO-08-90, issued in December 2007, reviews the prevention and treatment services the Indian Health Service offers them. GAO checked what prevention work the service's 12 areas provided and where patients actually got treatment.

Prevention services were broadly available but uneven across areas. Every area offered HIV education and testing, though the type and reach of services varied, and some areas added efforts such as condom distribution. Treatment was a different story. Only five IHS-funded hospitals, such as the Phoenix Indian Medical Center, treated patients regularly. Most facilities sent patients to outside providers because they had few known cases, limited staff and resources, or both.
gower-confessio-amantis-1390:
John Gower, a friend of Chaucer, finished his Confessio Amantis, the Lover's Confession, around 1390. It is a great Middle English poem of some 33,000 lines. Gower frames it as the confession of a lover, Amans, to Genius, priest of Venus.

Under the seven deadly sins, Genius tells tale after tale drawn from Ovid, the Bible, and old chronicles. The story of Apollonius of Tyre is the longest and finest of them. Gower's smooth couplets and moral care made him Chaucer's peer for centuries. The poem remains a rich storehouse of medieval storytelling. Kings and courtiers prized it, and fine copies survive with painted scenes.
hamsun-hunger-1890:
Knut Hamsun published Hunger in 1890, a novel about a young writer with no money in Kristiania, now Oslo. The narrator wanders the streets hungry and proud. He tries to write, pawns his few goods, and refuses steady help. Hunger clouds his thoughts and twists how he sees other people.

Little happens in terms of plot, yet the inner life is intense. Pride, shame, and sudden joy follow one after another. Hamsun broke with the calm realism of his time to show a mind under strain. The book made his name across Europe. It is now seen as a first step toward the modern psychological novel.
hartmann-in-the-pronaos-of-the-temple-of:
Franz Hartmann told the tale of the Rosy Cross in In the Pronaos of the Temple of Wisdom, out in 1890. The long title names the porch of the shrine of truth. Hartmann traces the band of the Rose and Cross from dim roots through the age of print and craft guilds.

He casts the band as keepers of a deep cure for souls. Tales, signs, and chief names fill the tale. The book came from the heart of the new occult wave. It links the old band to the new creeds of his day. The porch in the title marks a first step, not the shrine's heart. Hartmann hints that true lore lies past what print can hold.
hartmann-magic-white-and-black-1890:
Franz Hartmann laid out the rules of magic in Magic, White and Black, his primer of 1890. Hartmann was a healer and a sage of the occult from Bavaria. He sorts magic by its aim. White magic seeks truth and help for souls. Black magic seeks gain and power for the self.

Chapters deal with signs, rites, faith, and the risks of the path. Hartmann warns that pride dooms the mage. The book was the chief school text of magic in English in its age. It taught a whole crop of new mages. Hartmann had roamed the world as a healer and a seeker. That broad trek feeds the calm, wide view he takes of rite and creed.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's first volume, in the David Reed transcription of Milman's edition, begins with the introduction and both prefaces before measuring the empire at its height. Chapter one gives the extent and military force of Rome in the age of the Antonines. Chapter two describes the union and internal prosperity of that golden age.

Chapter three explains the constitution, and the narrative proceeds through the Antonine and Severan emperors toward crisis. Northern peoples cross the Danube and Dacia against relaxed Roman discipline in the later chapters. This transcription duplicates the library's other first volume; keeping both reflects Gibbon's importance and lets readers pick a text. The whole six-volume story starts here.
holland-treatise-against-witchcraft-engl:
Henry Holland, a Cambridge man, published his Treatise Against Witchcraft in 1590. The work takes the shape of a dialogue, the era's favorite teaching form. Its speakers work through the greatest doubts concerning witchcraft, question by question, in a university spirit.

Holland affirms the crime while sifting what may truly be believed about it. Spells, charms, and the devil's compact each face examination. The treatise counts as an early Elizabethan demonology, earnest and learned. It shows Cambridge debating the devil in the decade of the great Essex trials. For students of the period, Holland's dialogue catches Protestant England thinking its way toward a settled doctrine of witchcraft.
howells-hazard-new-fortunes-1890:
A Hazard of New Fortunes, published in 1890, is William Dean Howells's largest and most searching novel. Basil March, a figure from Howells's earlier books, moves with his wife from Boston to New York. There he helps run a new literary magazine backed by a blunt, rich dry-goods man.

Around the magazine Howells builds a wide city panorama of artists, editors, and strivers. A labor strike in the city pushes private lives toward crisis and tragedy. An old German socialist becomes the moral center of the tale. The novel weighs wealth, art, and justice against each other, and it stands as a founding work of urban realism in America.
ibsen-ghosts-archer-1890:
Henrik Ibsen wrote Ghosts in Norwegian, and William Archer made this English version in 1890. The play scandalized London when a single club performance drew howls from the press of the day. Heredity, hypocrisy, and the sins of the fathers drive its grim, compact plot to ruin.

Mrs. Alving built an orphanage to bury her late husband's vile memory for good. Pastor Manders urges duty while she confesses the truth she hid for thirty years. Her son Oswald returns from Paris with his father's disease in his brain and body. The orphanage burns uninsured, and Oswald begs for morphine as the sun rises on stage. Ibsen shows old lies poisoning the young in one of drama's starkest works.
james-principles-psychology-vol-1-1890:
William James published The Principles of Psychology, Volume 1, in 1890, after twelve years of work. The book founded modern psychology in America. James describes consciousness as a stream, not a chain of separate ideas. Habit, attention, and the self receive deep and lively treatment.

He writes as a biologist of the mind, asking what each faculty does for life. Famous chapters treat the emotions and the sense of self. The prose mixes science with literature in a way few textbooks match. Teachers used the Principles for decades. Volume 1 can be read alone with profit. Its chapters on habit and attention are still assigned.
james-principles-psychology-vol-2-1890:
William James completed The Principles of Psychology with Volume 2 in 1890. This volume treats sensation, perception, instinct, and the will. James also covers hypnotism, reasoning, and the production of movement. His theory that emotion follows bodily change appears in this part of the work.

We feel afraid because we tremble, he argues, not the reverse. The claim, shared with Carl Lange, still sparks debate. James ranges over animal minds, insanity, and genius with equal curiosity. The two volumes together run to nearly fourteen hundred pages. They remain a founding text of psychology and a pleasure to browse.
jewett-strangers-wayfarers-1890:
Strangers and Wayfarers, printed at Cambridge in 1890, is dedicated to a painter of New England folk and fields. The contents open with A Winter Courtship, then The Mistress of Sydenham Plantation and The Town Poor. The Quest of Mr. Teaby follows among the later tales.

Travelers stir settled village lives in these stories: a peddler, a lost child, a summer boarder. Jewett builds on the clash between the rooted and the rootless. Each side learns something it lacked from the other. Tender and closely watched, the tales show her doing what she did best, at the height of her art and fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-samuel-be: Aaron Samuel ben Moses Shalom of Kremnitz wrote "Nishmat Adam," printed at Hanau in 1611. The short entry lists the book's themes and gives nothing about his life. Its dissertations treat the nature of the soul and the purpose of man's existence. They also treat the future world, and rewards and punishments. Those four themes are the whole record kept here under his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdallah-ibn-sa:
Abdallah ibn Salam was a Jewish convert to Islam in the time of Mohammed, who died in 663. Among Moslems he holds a high place, and books of tradition give whole chapters to his fine qualities. He stands as the model of Jewish converts of that age. Born Al-Husain, of the Banu Ḳainuḳa'a, he claimed descent from Joseph and took his new name at his conversion.

The entry warns that the tales of his conversion can not be trusted. He in fact converted late, two years before Mohammed's death, so the belief that he shaped the Medinian part of the Koran is false. He could still feed Mohammed facts from Jewish sources in that late period. On that ground the entry calls him one of the fathers of the Hadith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abele-zion-mour:
Abele Zion, the Mourners for Zion, are a group whose home and root the entry argues over. One view, held by Jost, makes them Karaites. After the Crusaders took Jerusalem, they left the Holy City, settled in Constantinople, and took the name in grief for their lost home. Frankl rejects that account outright.

Frankl points to Benjamin of Tudela, who found Mourners for Zion and Jerusalem in southern Arabia. Those men dressed in black, lived in caves, fasted on week-days, and ate no meat or wine. They prayed without pause for Israel's return. Zunz sides with Jost, though Benjamin also names German Jews in black for Jerusalem. Hadassi, the entry adds, called himself the Mourner from grief at exile, not as a refugee's son.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abigdor-ben-mos: Abigdor ben Moses, also called Abigdor Sofer of Eisenstadt, lived in the sixteenth century in Cracow. He worked as a translator there. The entry records one task of his by name. He turned certain parts of the prayer-book into German. That task, that city, and that century are the whole of this very brief notice. It cites Steinschneider's catalogue and Michael's work for the record, and gives no birth year, death year, family, or other book under his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-ged: Abraham ben Gedaliah ben Asher, called Aba, was a commentator born at Safed in Syria. He held rabbinical office at Aleppo in the second half of the sixteenth century. He had studied under Joseph Caro, who lived from 1488 to 1575, and later swapped learned letters with him. Abraham wrote a commentary on the Midrash Rabbot. Only the Genesis Rabbah part was printed, at Venice in 1567, as Ma'adanne Melek. The rest still rests in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-solomon:
Abraham Solomon of Saint Maximin was a physician of the fifteenth century in high favor with René of Anjou, count of Provence. Caesar of Nostradamus calls him very learned and widely known in medicine, and a celebrated philosopher as well.

René kept him in service and excused him from the taxes usually laid on Jews. Through his Jewish physicians René learned of the poor state of Provence's Jews and did what he could to ease it. Abraham probably belonged to the Abigdor family, as the Abraham Abigdor of 1433-48 in a Marseilles doctors list. His father may have been Solomon ben Abraham Abigdor, a translator of some repute.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abudarham-david:
David ben Joseph Abudarham was a writer on synagogue prayer who lived at Seville about 1340. He had learned under Jacob ben Asher. He saw that common folk lacked sound knowledge of the prayers. So he set out to explain the prayer book in a plain, full way. He drew from both Talmuds, from the Geonim, and from notes down to his own day.

His work runs through the whole order of prayer. Three first parts treat the Shema, the daily prayer, and the blessings. Then come the night, morning, and feast day prayers. He also gives a clear account of the Jewish calendar. The entry praises his mix of grammar, good sense, and deep learning. It calls the book all but a must for students of the old rite. Nine prints of it came out over the years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-addison-lancelo: Lancelot Addison was an English churchman and author. He was the father of Joseph Addison. He was born in Westmoreland in 1632 and died on April 20, 1703. He studied at Queen's College, Oxford. From 1662 to 1670 he served as chaplain at Tangiers. There he took a close interest in the Jews and their ways. Back home he wrote on what he had seen. His book on the Jews of Barbary came out at London in 1675. It rests, he says, on talk, not on report.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agde-890: Agde is a town in the Hérault district of France, two miles from the Mediterranean Sea. Jews most likely lived there before the sixth century. A church council at Agde in 506 barred Christians from eating with Jews. That bar proves the two groups had been on good terms. Agde was a hub of sea trade, and Jews shared in it. A pact of 1195 set all its merchants on an equal foot. Its Jews had no grave field and buried their dead at Béziers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahinoam-brother: Ahinoam, meaning "Brother is Pleasantness," is the name of two women here. The first was a daughter of Ahimaaz. She became the wife of Saul, the first king of Israel. The second came from Jezreel and was taken by David during his war with Saul. She became his wife. Amalekites later seized her from Ziklag, but David soon rescued her. At Hebron she bore Amnon, David's first-born son.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alcan-felix-109:
Felix Alcan was a French publisher and scholar, born at Metz on March 18, 1841. He was the grandson of Gerson Levy and the son of a known Metz publisher. He entered the Ecole Normale Superieure of Paris in 1862. On leaving in 1865 he lectured on mathematics for four years. Then he took over his father's business at Metz.

In 1872 he moved to Paris and joined the old house of Germer-Bailliere. He became its head in 1883. In 1880 he launched a set of school-books for the lyceums, covering science, history, and philosophy. His firm issued the weightiest French works of philosophy of the day. In 1895 he was made a knight of the Legion of Honor. He also sat on the central committee of the Alliance Israelite Universelle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfarabi-abu-na:
Abu Nasr Mohammed Alfarabi was an Arabian philosopher born in Farab, Turkestan, about 870. He died in Damascus about 950. He studied at Bagdad and traveled in Syria and Egypt. His writings shaped Jewish thought for centuries. Some of his works survive only in Hebrew versions.

Much of the entry covers his book of principles on the six grounds of all being. It also covers his work on the logic of Aristotle. Later pages trace his reach among Jewish writers. Judah ha-Levi and Moses ibn Ezra both drew on him. Maimonides praised his logic in strong terms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almon-1290: Almon was a city in the land of Benjamin. The book of Joshua lists it among the towns given to the priests. The entry gives the verse as chapter twenty-one. It says the place is now called Almit. A twin list in First Chronicles uses a second name. There the town is called Alemeth. The entry is only two lines long. It gives no past events or people for the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-american-jewish:
American Jewish Historical Society was formed in New York City. The date was June 7, 1892. Cyrus Adler called the first meeting to order. About forty persons came to that meeting. Oscar S. Straus was picked as president. Adler took the post of secretary. The group set out to gather and keep records. Those records bear on the past of Jews in America.

Nine volumes of its papers had come out by 1900. The papers print old records new to print. One line of work shows Jews held rights in the colonies. Home rule had barred those same rights in Europe. Other papers treat Texas, Ohio, and New York. One set treats Jews in the war for freedom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ancient-of-days:
Ancient of Days is a poetic name for God. The entry calls it a poor rendering of an Aramaic phrase in Daniel, chapter 7, which should read 'an aged one.' The phrase stresses either God's contrast with new idols or his venerable character.

In rabbinic writing, the entry explains, the name marks God as old beside all created things, which are of yesterday. Commentators pictured him as a venerable sage and judge, stern yet mild in judgment. Mystic circles, where Daniel and kindred books arose, heard in the title both majesty and tenderness. The phrase also passed into the Book of Enoch and the Book of Revelation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antiochus-v-eup:
Antiochus V Eupator, the Well-born, was king of Syria, son of Antiochus IV. Born in 173 B.C., he died in 162. He came to the throne at twelve, by some accounts at nine, and reigned two years, 164-162 B.C. Lysias ruled as his guardian and regent.

Lysias marched on Judea with a huge army to win back what Syria had lost. Judas Maccabeus and his small band could not hold the field at Beth-Zechariah, and hunger pressed the Temple Mount hard in a Sabbatical year. Then revolt at home forced Lysias to make peace. He granted the Jews full religious freedom, the very prize they had fought for.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-armleder-persec:
Alsace in 1338 and 1339 saw the Armleder persecutions, attacks by armed bands that killed large numbers of Jews. A Franconian nobleman began the killing in 1336, claiming an angel had sent him, and his men called themselves Judenschlager, Jew-beaters. John Zimberlin, an innkeeper in Upper Alsace, copied him. His men tied leather bands round their arms, which gave the movement its name.

Under their leader, called King Armleder, the bands besieged Colmar, whose citizens sheltered Jews who had fled there. Emperor Louis of Bavaria drove them off once, but they returned. On May 17, 1338, Alsatian lords allied to hunt Armleder down. A knight instead granted him amnesty for a pledge of ten quiet years. The entry calls the attacks a prelude to the Black Death massacres of 1349.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aschaffenburg-1:
Aschaffenburg, a leading town on the right bank of the Main in Bavaria, first names Jews in the thirteenth century, when a Rabbi Abraham of Aschaffenburg appears. The town stands in the reports of the Black Death persecutions of 1349. Jewish settlements are also recorded across the diocese towns, from Seligenstadt in 1292 to Miltenberg, where a large cemetery stood by 1336.

Documents of 1344 and 1345 mention the town's synagogue. A scholar of Aschaffenburg is quoted in the fifteenth century, and named rabbis follow in the sixteenth and seventeenth. A new synagogue rose in 1698 with the prince-elector's consent. By the early eighteenth century the congregation had shrunk to twenty members. From that point the entry can list its religious leaders one by one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-samue:
Samuel ben Elieser Ashkenazi wrote new readings on the Talmud. He lived at Opatow in Poland in the second half of the sixteenth century. He had studied under Meir ben Gedaliah of Lublin. His Hiddushim treat the treatises Ketubot and Kiddushin, with close attention to Rashi and the Tosafot.

His readings were not printed as his own book in his lifetime. They were culled, the entry says, from the responsa literature and printed at Prossnitz in 1602. The record rests on Furst's Bibliotheca Judaica and Benjacob's catalogue. It gives his town, his teacher, his two treatises, and the late printing, and nothing of his birth or death years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-atlas-elazar-la:
Elazar Atlas was a literary critic. He was born on March 5, 1851, in Beisegola, in the government of Kowno, Russia. His father was David Atlas. Elazar spent his early years at Novo Zhagory studying the Talmud. In 1884 he reached Warsaw and became a chief writer for Sokolow's yearbook "Ha-Asif." By trade he was a bookkeeper, settling at Byelostok in 1895.

While still unknown, Atlas was trusted to review major works in "Ha-Asif." His review of Herzberg on ancient Jewish trade became a sketch of that trade in its own right. His notice of Weiss on Jewish tradition showed him at home in Talmudic writing. In 1888 he edited the yearbook "Ha-Kerem," which ran to one number. The entry praises his wide learning, sharp judgment, and clear style. It ranks him among the foremost living critics in Hebrew letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ayyas-jacob-mos:
Jacob Moses Ayyas was a son of Judah Ayyas. He lived at Jerusalem and was sent abroad to gather money for the poor of Palestine. In 1783 he visited Algiers and was received with great honor.

A call then took him to Ferrara, where he settled as rabbi and teacher. One of his pupils was Nepi, a joint author of a biographical work on Israel's great men. Ayyas wrote "Derek Ḥayyim," The Way of Life. It treats the annulling of vows and the ceremony called Tashlik, among other topics. It was printed at Leghorn in 1810.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baca-the-valley:
Baca is a valley named in the eighty-fourth Psalm. Pilgrims passing through it, the Psalm says, turn it into a land of wells. Old translators took the name to mean a valley of weeping. The entry argues for a plainer sense: any valley short of water.

Support comes from Samuel and Chronicles. There the plural of the same word names a tree much like the balsam. A dry valley, it is held, could take its name from that tree. König drew the word from an Arabic root and read it as lacking in streams. The Psalmist, the entry holds, had one real valley in mind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bakri-joseph-co: Joseph Coen Bakri was chief of the Algerian Jews and a financier, born at Algiers in the middle of the eighteenth century. He died at Leghorn in 1817. He founded the famed firm Bakri Brothers, which shaped Algerian politics for half a century. At his son David's death he took over the firm. The dey then made him chief of the Algerian Jews, an honor that brought him ruin. In 1816 he was banished and his goods seized. He ended his years at Leghorn in poverty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bar-giora-simon:
Simon bar Giora was a Jewish leader in the revolt against Rome, born about the year 50 at Gerasa. Strong and reckless, he gathered a band after Cestius was put to flight and harried the Idumeans. Driven off, he held Masada. His troops grew to many thousand Sicarii, and he took Hebron and came to the gates of Jerusalem.

The Idumeans and Zealots, at war in Jerusalem in April 68, called Bar Giora in. He made himself lord of the city and fought John of Gischala without pause. When Titus closed in, the rivals made peace and struck the Romans in sallies. After the Temple burned, Bar Giora held the upper city, then fled through tunnels. Hunger drove him out in a white shroud. At the triumph in Rome he was dragged through the streets and hurled from the Tarpeian rock.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraita-of-r-is: Baraita of R. Ishmael sets out the thirteen rules of R. Ishmael and shows their use with Bible examples. The name is also given, wrongly, to the first part alone, which only lists the rules. The Baraita forms the introduction to the Sifra and stands before it in all editions. The rules get their working use in the Sifra itself. The entry judges that it likely arose in R. Ishmael's school, so the name is not wholly wrong.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-yavan-ca:
Baruch Yavan was a Polish financier who served as agent to Count Brühl, the Polish prime minister. He was born at Starokonstantinov, in Volhynia, early in the eighteenth century. He knew Talmudic literature and spoke Hebrew, Polish, and German.

Baruch used his place at court to defend fellow Jews. He acted against followers of Shabbethai Ẓebi and the Frankists, and he sought help when copies of the Talmud were seized and burned. He also argued against a blood accusation brought against Jews. The entry draws much of its account from letters by Jacob Emden.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berlin-jacob-ca: Jacob Berlin, called Yokob, was a German Talmudist born in 1707, most likely at Berlin. He died in 1749 at Fürth, in Bavaria. A pupil of Jacob ha-Kohen, he settled at Fürth by 1734 and lived there as a well-off private citizen. Of his seven works, two came out after his death. One holds a set of his responsa with a part on Talmudic terms. The other is a homiletic commentary on the Pentateuch. The entry notes he was not kin to the famed Berlin family of Fürth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bigthan-3290: Bigthan was a eunuch of King Ahasuerus. With Teresh, he plotted against the king. Mordecai discovered the conspiracy. On his word the two eunuchs were put to death. Esther tells the story twice. In the later passage the name reads Bigthana. The entry is only a few lines long. It adds nothing beyond those Esther verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bikayim-meir-be: Meïr ben Halifah Bikayim was a Cabalist in Turkey. He lived in the eighteenth century. The entry lists six of his works. "Golel Or" treats metempsychosis, or the soul's rebirth. It follows Luria, Vital, and Azariah of Fano. It appeared at Smyrna in 1737. "Meore Or" comments on the Pentateuch in cabalistic style. Other works explain the 'En Ya'aḳob and Pirḳe Abot. One treats atonement for sexual impurities. His books appeared at Smyrna and Salonica.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-josef-sam:
Josef Samuel Bloch was an Austrian rabbi and deputy. He was born at Dukla on November 20, 1850. Poor parents raised him for the rabbinate. He earned a philosophy doctorate at Zurich. He served pulpits from Rendsburg to Floridsdorf. About 1880 anti-Semitism peaked in Austria.

Bloch attacked Professor Rohling's blood-accusation offer head-on. Rohling withdrew rather than swear to it. In 1883 Bloch founded the "Oesterreichische Wochenschrift." It defended Jewish political rights weekly. Voters sent him to parliament three times. A second ritual-murder frame-up fell to his lawsuit in 1893. Government pressure ended his career in 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bomberg-daniel-:
Daniel Bomberg was a Christian printer and publisher of Hebrew works, born at Antwerp. He died at Venice in 1549. He learned printing and type founding from his father Cornelius and worked in Venice from 1517.

Bomberg issued the first Biblia Rabbinica and the first Hebrew Bibles. Under Pope Leo X he printed the first complete Babylonian Talmud. His list runs to Bibles, grammars, rituals, and Midrashim over three decades. He spent so freely on paper, engraving, and type that he lost almost his whole fortune before he died. Skilled Jewish editors helped him choose and prepare the texts. Jacob b. Hayyim worked on the Talmud, and Baruch Adelkind worked on other volumes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boskowitz-hayyi: Hayyim ben Jacob Boskowitz was a Palestinian author who lived about the middle of the eighteenth century. He wrote Toze'ot Hayyim, meaning Life's Issues. It is a commentary on the Pentateuch. The book was printed at Amsterdam in 1764, together with the biblical text. It deals chiefly with the moral lessons that can be drawn from the Bible stories. The entry gives no birth or death dates and names no other work by him at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bresner-isaac-b: Isaac ben Elijah Levi Bresner, called Melammed, the Teacher, was an Austrian educator at Prague. He published Iggeret Yizhak, an order of confession, at Prague. That work was compiled from Gerundi's Sefer ha-Yirah and from Isaiah Hurwitz. It is now placed in many rituals, the entry says. He also published a compilation of maxims in Judaeo-German at Prague. Its title means The Words of Ethics. The entry's own dates for his life and books do not line up cleanly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buchsbaum-3790:
Buchsbaum names a family of Jewish physicians of Frankfort-on-the-Main whose work spanned a century. The entry profiles four men. Benjamin Levi, born in 1645, studied medicine and philosophy at four universities and graduated at Padua in 1669. He then practiced at Frankfort with a high standing among Jews and Christians alike.

His son Gutman Wolf graduated at Leyden in 1697 and also practiced at Frankfort. Gutman Wolf's brother Lipman took the same path that same year. Confined for a time on false charges, Lipman used prison to write a long medical treatise. The line ends with Amschel Gutman, who graduated at Giessen in 1729 and died in 1743.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cagliari-abraha: Abraham da Cagliari was a rabbi at Cagliari, Sardinia, in the eighth century. Two writers of that age mention him. One reports that Abraham read many Phoenician inscriptions gathered by the Sardinian king Gialeto. The other says that Abraham, with another Jewish scholar named Canaim, read Greek and Phoenician inscriptions. Those stones had been found in the palace of Masu. The entry is very short. It gives no writings by Abraham and no dates beyond his century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carvalho-carval:
Mordecai Baruch Carvalho, a rich Tunisian merchant, died in January 1785 at an advanced age. He gave part of his time to rabbinical study. In 1752 he followed his teacher Isaac Lumbroso as rabbi of the Leghorn congregation of Tunis. His name as a rabbinical authority stood high across the country.

His To'afot Re'em, a commentary on Elijah Mizraḥi, appeared at Leghorn in 1761. A second work, Mira Dakya, treats tracts of the Babylonian Talmud and Maimonides, and came out in 1792. Carvalho also printed an unfinished work by his son Isaac, who died in 1759 at age twenty-eight. That book joins a life of Isaac with notes on Mizraḥi and four funeral orations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cesena-4190: Cesena is a city of the Pontifical States with an early Jewish community. The tosafist Eliezer is named there in the thirteenth century. Moses de Rossi and Obadiah Sforno were born in the city late in the fifteenth century. A rabbi, Isaac Joshua de Lattes, served there in the sixteenth. Under papal rule the community faced special laws and the Inquisition. Jewish trade wealth grew so large that, in 1514, townspeople feared Jews would become masters of the city. Expulsion from the papal lands ended the community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chelod-4290: Chelod is a name in Judith i. 6, pointing, it seems, to the Chaldeans. The usual English rendering speaks of many nations of the sons of Chelod gathering for battle. A better rendering, from the Greek, speaks of nations joining the array of the sons of Cheleul. The Syriac version has them fight against the Chaldeans. Judith may mean Nebuchadnezzar's own army by the phrase. A link to Calneh is called improbable. The matter stays very uncertain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-levi-a-44:
Levi A. Cohen, a journalist and champion of the Jews of Tangier, was born at Mogador in 1844 and died at Tangier on Nov. 9, 1888. Raised partly in England, he settled at Tangier for life. Among Morocco's Jews he stood out as a protector, one of the few men ready to denounce any breach of their rights in plain terms.

To give that work reach he founded a French-language journal, the Reveil du Maroc. He also spoke for the American board of delegates and reported for the Anglo-Jewish Association. He made risky trips into the interior and to the Sultan's court to plead for Jews. Poor Arabs, the entry adds, found in him a kind advocate as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-connecticut-114:
Connecticut, one of the six New England states and one of the original thirteen, names a Jew in its records as early as Nov. 9, 1659. That was David the Jew. In 1670 Jacob Lucena was fined 20 pounds, likely for Sabbath breaking. The court cut the fine to 10 pounds since he was a Jew, then to 5 on Asser Levy's plea.

New Haven's tale gets a check from Ezra Stiles's diary. Against a claim of six Jewish families by 1770, Stiles records the first real Jewish family settling there in 1772 and holding the first Jewish worship in a lamplit room. Hartford follows, with its Beth Israel congregation of 1843 and newer Russian congregations. Civic and professional honors of Hartford Jews close the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-costa-emanuel-m: Emanuel Mendez da Costa was a librarian and fellow of the Royal Society of London. He was born in 1717 and died in 1791. His father Abraham had come from Normandy to England about 1696. Emanuel won fame as a botanist, naturalist, and collector of notes and manuscripts. He joined the Royal Society on Nov. 26, 1747, and later served as its librarian. His books include a natural history of fossils and two works on shells, from 1776 and 1778.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crescas-mordeca: Mordecai En Crescas, of Orange, was a leading member of the community of Carcassonne, France. He lived in the second half of the thirteenth century. As syndic for the Jews of the whole district, he won them a special jurisdiction. He also secured a decree from Philip the Fair. It assured the Jews quiet possession of their synagogues, cemeteries, and communal property. He may be the Talmudist of Carcassonne who wrote to Solomon ben Adret of Barcelona. Toward 1304 he lived in Carpentras, serving there as rabbi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-csillag-therese: Therese Csillag was a Hungarian actress, born at Duna-Adony on May 17, 1862. At thirteen she entered the dramatic school in Budapest. The National Theater engaged her in 1879. There she played young-girl roles up to 1898 and was a popular comedienne for years. Nearly all Hungarian playwrights of her day wrote parts for her. She excelled above all in the plays of Gregor Csiky. Since 1899 she has been engaged at the Vigszinhaz in Budapest. The entry closes by noting she has embraced the Christian faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-danon-joseph-be: Joseph ben Jacob ben Moses ibn Danon was a Hebraist and Talmudist. He was born at Belgrade about 1620 and died at London late in the seventeenth century. His family was Spanish stock, settled at Belgrade for generations. He served as secretary to its rabbi, Joseph Almosnino. When Belgrade fell in 1688, he was exiled with most of its Jews. He lived on charity in Moravian towns, then found a patron at Amsterdam. There he wrote on the three things the world rests on: Law, Worship, and Charity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davidsohn-leon-:
Leon Davidsohn was a Russian publicist and translator born at Kopil, in the government of Minsk, in 1855. Raised on Talmud and Hebrew, he could write Hebrew verse at nine and was ordained as rabbi at fifteen. He then turned to Russian and secular study at Minsk, writing for the Hebrew paper "Ha-Ḳol."

At Warsaw Davidsohn graduated as doctor of medicine in 1888, and he practiced at Pruzhany. The Polish writer Clemens Junosza asked him to translate Abramovich's works. He rendered one into Russian and another into both Russian and Polish. He kept writing articles for Hebrew papers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-denmark-5090:
Denmark is a kingdom of northwestern Europe, and this long entry follows its Jewish history. Old Jewish writing identified the Danes with the Bible's Dodanim on the strength of similar names, but Jews in Denmark in the Middle Ages are doubtful. The story really begins in Holstein, then Danish land.

In a letter of November 25, 1622, King Christian IV invited Portuguese Jews from Amsterdam to settle at Glückstadt with free exercise of their religion. Danish kings stayed friendly to their Jewish subjects in those provinces. The Jews of Denmark proper long kept close ties with Altona, whose chief rabbi also held civil authority over them. The article then follows emancipation and community growth in Copenhagen and the provinces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-diessenhofen-51:
Diessenhofen is a city in the Swiss canton of Thurgau, linked by a bridge to Gailingen in Baden. Its spot drew Jews early. In 1348 its Jews were accused of poisoning the wells. Their houses were plundered and some were burned at the stake. Over three hundred fled to the fortress of Kyburg under the Austrian governor's guard.

When the governor himself was threatened, the refugees were expelled or, by other accounts, burned on September 18, 1349. Jews returned within fifty years, but in 1401 a false murder charge brought new killings at Diessenhofen and nearby towns. Jews came back yet again by 1426. In 1865 a Jew was granted leave to settle there, and in 1902 about twenty Jewish families lived in the city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eagle-5390:
Eagle is the English Bible's rendering of the Hebrew nesher. The entry argues the nesher is not the eagle at all. It was bald, nested on high rocks, and lived in flocks. Those marks fit the griffin-vulture, the entry says.

True eagles of several kinds do live in Palestine. They may hide under another Hebrew term, ozniyyah, in the unclean-bird lists. The Talmud calls the eagle king of birds, yet afraid of the flycatcher. It also ranks the bird among the unclean. In rabbinic speech nesher could even name the Roman government as a title.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eisenstadt-5490:
Eisenstadt is a Polish family that took its name from the Hungarian town. Some of its members became rabbis there. The entry sketches many bearers of the name. First stands Abigdor Eisenstadt, who died in 1591. He rendered the festival prayers from Polish into German at Cracow in 1571.

The family's best-known scholar is Abraham Hirsch Eisenstadt of Byelostok. Born in 1812, he died at Königsberg in 1868. His Pithe Teshubah indexes later rulings on the Shulhan Aruk. The entry praises its near-complete gathering of responsa references. Parts appeared at Wilna in 1836 and at Lemberg in 1876. His own added novellae, the entry says, are of little value.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elkan-moses-569: Moses Elkan was a Russian doctor and Hebrew scholar. He was born at Tulchin in the government of Podolsk. He died at St. Petersburg on Jan. 31, 1822. His works mix verse, song, and school text. He wrote a hymn in Hebrew and French for Czar Alexander. He also wrote a school book on Jewish history in German. A sketch of the land of Palestine went with it. That book was later turned into Russian for schools. It came out at Moscow in 1880.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephod-5790:
The ephod is a thing named in two senses in the Bible. In one set of texts it is a priestly garment. In a second set it is most likely an image. As a garment it forms part of the high priest's dress. Exodus bids it be made of blue, purple, and scarlet threads. A girdle of the same work held it fast. Two shoulder pieces crossed the shoulders at the top.

The entry is frank that no clear shape can be drawn. The Bible text does not fix the length of the robe. Josephus adds words but no firm picture of it. Gold rings sat at the front above the girdle. The breastplate was tied to those rings by cords. The entry sorts the proof texts group by group. It then takes up the ephod as an image in the tales.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ethiopia-5890:
Ethiopia, as the Bible versions use the name, can cover three lands, the entry warns: Ethiopia proper, parts of northern Arabia, and regions east of Babylonia. The name renders Cush, son of Ham. Egyptians first used it for tribes south of the second cataract of the Nile. Greeks meant the Nile valley from Syene toward modern Khartum. Abyssinia took the name only late, confusing later scholars.

Pharaohs made the land a province, and its viceroys later ruled on their own from Napata and Meroe. Ethiopian kings held Thebes about 800 B.C. and took Egypt under Shabako about 700. Assyria then drove them back. Rome later punished a border raid by wrecking Napata. The Bible also uses Ethiopia as a byword for a far-off, wealthy land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-falero-abraham-: Abraham Aboab Falero was a Portuguese giver to charity who died at Verona in 1642. He settled at Hamburg late in the sixteenth century or early in the next. There he built a synagogue named Keter Torah for the Portuguese community. He founded study houses wherever he could, even reaching Palestine. He was famed for spending large sums to ransom captives. Near the end of his life he went to Verona to see his son, R. Samuel Aboab, and died there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ferrara-6090:
Ferrara, a city in central Italy, held one of Italy's richest Jewish communities, the entry says. Jews seem to have lived there in 1088, but numbers grew only in the thirteenth century. A decree of 1275 shielded them, barring pope, duke, or any power from lifting the town's duties toward them. The town drew fighters from both sides of the Maimonides quarrel.

Under the Este dukes in the fifteenth century the community grew fast. The dukes wanted settlers to build the economy, and Jews came first as lenders, then as traders and makers. They ran their own affairs under ducal leave. The long entry then follows the community's schools, presses, and leaders through later centuries of rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-flisfeder-d-i-6:
D. I. Flisfeder was a Russian physician and scholar born about 1850. He died in 1885 at Kishinev, where he had settled a few years earlier. He was best known for his writings in Russian on the Jewish question. At only twenty years old he wrote on the Jews of Kiev for a Russian paper in 1870.

He took up the same subject again in 1872 and in 1880. His two chief works came out at St. Petersburg. One, in 1874, treats Jewish teaching about people of other faiths. The other, in 1882, puts the Jewish question before the court of history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-ernst-6:
Ernst Fränkel was a German physician born at Breslau on May 5, 1844. He studied medicine at Berlin, Vienna, and Breslau, taking his degree in 1866. He served as assistant surgeon in the war of 1866 and again in the Franco-Prussian war of 1870-71. In 1872 he set up in his home town as a physician. His special work was in childbirth and women's diseases. In 1873 he began to teach at Breslau University. In 1893 he became an honorary professor there.

Fränkel took an active part in the politics of Breslau. In 1903 he was elected an alderman of the city.
