His medical essays include a study of the diagnosis and surgical treatment of pregnancy outside the womb, printed in 1882. Another, from 1898, treats appendicitis in its bearing on pregnancy and birth. His books cover questions of surgical gynecology, printed in 1896. A handbook chapter on the general treatment of women's diseases followed in 1898-99.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedmann-siegw:
Siegwart Friedmann was a German actor born at Budapest on April 25, 1842. He was a pupil of the actor Dawison, who trained him for the stage. Dawison even took him into his own home and family. He first acted at Breslau on October 18, 1863, as Ferdinand in Egmont. That start was not a success. In 1864 he came back to the stage with Dawison at the royal playhouse in Berlin. He stayed there until 1871.

After a year at Schwerin, Friedmann worked under Laube in Vienna from 1872 to 1876. He soon ranked among the best actors of the German stage. He went to Hamburg in 1876 and came back to Vienna three years later. His greatest work for the stage was helping found the German Theater at Berlin in 1883. In 1888 he toured as a star in Germany and Austria. He left the stage in 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gama-gaspard-da:
Gaspard da Gama, a German-Jewish mariner of the fifteenth century, said he was born in Posen and left in 1456 under pressure. He went by Jerusalem and Alexandria to India. There he was seized and sold as a slave. He rose high in Goa service and became admiral under the viceroy Sabayo.

In 1498 he met Vasco da Gama ships near Goa. The Portuguese bound and beat him until he took baptism and agreed to pilot them. He then sailed with Vasco and later with Cabral. Kings prized his knowledge of eastern lands and tongues. In 1503 he gained the title of knight of the royal house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gematria-4390:
Gematria is a cipher that gives a word by its number value, or swaps letters to form a new word. The term first shows in the twenty-ninth of the thirty-two rules of Rabbi Eliezer, about the year 200. The Bible itself names no such method. Yet letter swaps in Jeremiah hint that the swap form was known early.

Later writers find number matches in set texts. One case ties the number 318 in Genesis to the name Eliezer. Other rules take a word at face value, at minor value, or with letters changed. Parts of a word may be dropped or vowels left out. The entry sorts these forms and warns that proof for Bible use stays unsure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geomancy-6590:
Geomancy is telling the future by points made in sand, or by pebbles or grains set on paper. Some Muslim writers trace the art to Enoch, others to Daniel. It arose in northern Africa about the ninth century. From there it entered Jewish writing. Maimonides names it in his Mishnah comment. Nahmanides and Joseph Albo also speak of it.

Albo calls it the lot by sand, or the science of points. Books called Sefer ha-Goralot set out lot casting built on this art. One is ascribed to Ahithophel, one to Saadia Gaon, and one to Abraham ibn Ezra. Answers come by counting, but the counting rests on the points of geomancy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-girzites-or-giz: The Girzites, also read Gizrites, get only a single sentence in this entry. They are described as a tribe rich in cattle and apparel. Together with the Geshurites and the Amalekites, they held the land between the south of Palestine and Egypt. The entry's sole source for this is I Samuel xxvii. 8 and 9. Nothing further is said here about their history, language, or fate, so the notice stays a brief pointer to that one biblical passage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grossman-rudolp: Rudolph Grossman was an American rabbi. He was born at Vienna, Austria, on July 24, 1867. He took his B.L. at Cincinnati's university. He took his rabbi's title and D.D. at Hebrew Union College there. From 1889 to 1896 he was associate rabbi of New York's Temple Beth-El. From 1896 he led Temple Rodef Sholom in the same city. In 1902 he was corresponding secretary of the Central Conference of American Rabbis. He wrote essays for Jewish and other magazines. He served as grand chaplain of New York's Masonic grand lodge in 1898-1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habillo-chavill:
Elisha ben Solomon Ḥabillo was a Venetian Talmudist of the eighteenth century. He came from a well-known Palestinian family and studied under David Pardo. His entry is built around four books printed at Leghorn in the 1790s.

"Pat Leḥem" sets out the rules for blessings, above all the grace after meals. "Hamon Ḥogeg" comments on the Passover Haggadah. "'Abodat ha-Tamid" comments on the prayer-book in the Spanish rite, using views of Shabbethai Ḥayyim that he later dropped as heretical. "Shif'at Rebibim" prints liturgical poems by his teacher Pardo, with some of his own added.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hartog-levi-de-:
Levi de Hartog, born at Gorinchem in Holland on Nov. 6, 1835, was a Dutch jurist. He read law and Oriental tongues at Leyden, taking his doctorate in 1859. He taught history and politics at Haarlem and Utrecht. In 1877 he became professor of law at the University of Amsterdam.

His books cover Dutch state and local government and the constitutions of the Netherlands. He also wrote on the persecution of Jews in 1096. De Hartog gave much time to Jewish causes. He led the Dutch section of the Alliance Israelite Universelle and chaired the Jewish theological seminary from 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-joshua-p: Pheibel ben Israel Hayyim, also named Joshua, was a geographer of the eighteenth century from Tarnigrod. He wrote a geography of Palestine in Hebrew. Its title was "Kazwe Arez," and it came out at Zolkiev in 1772. A second edition appeared at Grodno in 1818. That printing bore a new title meaning the land of Israel with its borders all around. The entry is only a few lines long. It names no other work and gives no dates for his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heilbut-abraham: Abraham ben Judah Heilbut was a German Talmudist who lived at Altona in the middle of the eighteenth century. In July 1751 he wrote a commentary there on the Midrash Rabbah. It also covers the Midrashim on Psalms, Proverbs, and Samuel. He paid special heed to words missing from the standard word book. That work was never printed. Neither was his short Talmud word list. One book of his did reach print, a commentary on Pirke Abot issued at Altona in 1779.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heres-7590:
Heres is a biblical name the entry treats under three separate headings. The first is a city in Egypt named in Isaiah. The second is a mountain named in Judges. The third is a hill tied to Gideon's return from battle.

For the Egyptian city, versions differ between City of Destruction and City of the Sun. The entry judges the sun reading likely correct and points to Heliopolis. For the mountain, it suggests Beth-shemesh or Ir-shemesh between Judah and Dan. The hill's site is called uncertain, and its text is said to vary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hobab-7790: Hobab is a name found twice in the Bible, borne by Moses' father-in-law or by his brother-in-law. In Numbers he is son of Raguel the Midianite. In Judges Hobab himself is called Moses' father-in-law. Commentators split on the link. Rashi and Naḥmanides favor the Judges reading. Ibn Ezra read that phrase as brother-in-law. Whoever he was, Hobab knew the desert well. Moses asked him to stay and serve Israel as its eyes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horwitz-bella-c: Bella Horwitz, also called Bella Hazzan, was the daughter of the martyr Be'er ben Hezekiah ha-Levi Horwitz. She married Joseph ben Hayyim Hazzan, who died at Prague in 1713. In 1705 she published a history of the house of David. With Rachel Porges she edited a mostly legendary early history of the Jews of Prague. She also wrote a prayer for the ten penitential days. The short entry rests on a few named sources about Jewish women and Prague history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-ezra-solomo: Solomon ben Moses ibn Ezra was rabbi of Venice in the second half of the seventeenth century. He studied under Joseph Escapa. His work was chiefly that of an editor and preface writer. He edited the second part of his teacher's Rosh Yosef, printed at Smyrna in 1659. He also brought out works by Solomon Algazi in 1665 and by Jacob Berab at Venice in 1663, adding many responsa of his own to the second. He edited the responsa of Baruch Kalai as well, in 1660.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-muhajar-ahu: Ahub ben Meir ibn Muhajar was a Spanish-Arabian poet of the twelfth century. He was probably a brother of the poets Joseph ben Meir and Abraham ben Meir ibn Muhajar. Sources call him Ahub or Oheb, and which form is right is unclear. If Oheb is right, two signed poems may be his. Judah ha-Levi praised a certain Ahub in song, but the surname differs there, and the entry doubts the match. A further tag attached to his name has never been explained.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-immanuel-b-solo:
Immanuel ben Solomon ben Jekuthiel was an Italian scholar and satirical poet born at Rome about 1270. He died probably at Fermo about 1330. He came of a rich and leading family and held high place in the Roman community. He preached on the Day of Atonement. In 1325 he lost all his wealth and had to leave home.

Friends dropped him, and he wandered Italy in poverty and age until a patron at Fermo took him in during 1328. His studies ran from Bible and Talmud to mathematics, astronomy, and medicine. He commented on nearly all of Scripture in allegorical style. His lasting gift was verse, in Hebrew and Italian alike. Italian poets ranked him beside Dante, whom he knew. His poems mix wit and satire with true piety.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ha-kohen-: Isaac ha-Kohen of Ostrog was a Russian rabbi who lived in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The short entry records a single work of his, called "Mattenot Ani" or "Kizzur Mizrahi." It is a shortened form of Elijah Mizrahi's commentary on Rashi, with notes of his own added. The book was printed at Prague across the years 1604 to 1609. The entry gives no town where he served, no teachers, and no dates for his birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-amram: Jacob ben Amram was a polemical writer of the seventeenth century. In 1634 he wrote, in Latin, a book against the Christian religion. It bore the Hebrew title "Sha'ar Emet," the Gate of Truth, rendered in Latin as "Porta Veritatis." He borrowed much from Manasseh ben Israel. Wolf proved, though, that Manasseh was not the book's author, as some had thought. The English bishop Richard Kidder answered Jacob's arguments in his "Demonstratio Messiae," printed at London from 1684.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacques-heinric:
Heinrich Jacques, an Austrian deputy, was born in Vienna on Feb. 24, 1831. He studied at Heidelberg and Vienna, took a law degree in 1856, and settled in Vienna as an attorney in 1859. In 1879 the first district of Vienna sent him to the Reichsrath, where he joined the constitutional party. He shot himself on Jan. 25, 1894.

In parliament he won passage of a law that kept a basic amount of property free from taxation, and he pushed for full pensions after thirty-five years of service. He also directed railway and bank firms, founded the Wiener Handelsakademie, and wrote many books on law and Jewish life in Austria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeremiah-8590: Jeremiah, with no father's name given, was a Polish rabbi of the second half of the eighteenth century. He headed the study house at Mattersdorf in Hungary, where he gave his strength to the legal tractates of the Babylonian Talmud. Aaron Chorin sat among his pupils. His one named work comments on a section of a legal book about protests against forced acts. It was printed at Lemberg in 1795 by his son Joab, who wrote a matching work of his own and a second book of new readings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joachimsthal-ge: Georg Joachimsthal was a German physician born at Stargard in Pomerania on May 8, 1863. He took his medical degree at the University of Berlin in 1887 and set up in that city the next year. In 1890 he became an assistant in bone and joint surgery at the university clinic, and in 1898 a private lecturer. A French prize came to him in 1897 for an essay on changes that can be made in the moving parts of the body. He also wrote a book on birth defects of the upper limbs, printed in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jose-b-jacob-b-: Jose ben Jacob ben Idi was a Palestinian teacher of the fourth century. He worked beside Judan of Magdala and set out the story teachings of Aha the Lydian for others. A few sayings of his own survive. In one he argues that Jeroboam was made king in a Sabbatical year, when the nation's head had to read the Law aloud at Jerusalem. To dodge the shame of watching Judah's king read there, Jeroboam set up his own shrine with golden calves. Only one legal ruling of his is kept.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-solo: Joseph ben Solomon of Carcassonne was a French liturgical poet of the eleventh century. He wrote a yozer, a poetic piece for the morning service, for the feast of Hanukkah. Rashi names the poem in his notes on Ezekiel. Joseph built the piece from older haggadic tales and recast them in payyetanic style, the ornate manner of the synagogue poets. Its verses run three lines each and follow the order of the alphabet. The entry gives no other facts about his life or works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kanitz-felix-ph:
Felix Philipp Kanitz was a Hungarian scholar of old remains and of peoples. He was born at Budapest on Aug. 2, 1829. He died at Vienna on Jan. 8, 1904. At seventeen he entered the University of Vienna to study art. After 1850 he traveled widely in the west. In 1856 he settled at Vienna.

From Vienna, Kanitz made long trips through the Balkan lands. He crossed Dalmatia, Bosnia, Servia, Bulgaria, and Macedonia. Those trips made him the student of the Southern Slavs. The entry lists his books on Roman finds in Serbia. It also lists his travel studies of the Danube lands and the Balkans. They rest on trips made from 1859 to 1875.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kley-israel-or-:
Israel Kley, who called himself Eduard, was a German preacher and educator. He was born at Bernstadt, in Silesia, on June 10, 1789. He died at Hamburg on Oct. 4, 1867. He studied at Breslau and at Berlin, under Fichte and Schleiermacher. In 1817 he took charge of Hamburg's Jewish free school as its director. That school gave the impulse to the founding of the Hamburg Temple. Kley became the Temple's first preacher.

He held that pulpit for over twenty-one years, resigning in 1840. He directed the free school until 1848. Kley was a very prolific writer. He published a catechism, a hymn-book, and many volumes of sermons. His sermons covered all the festivals of the year. He is often called the Jewish Schleiermacher. An institution for aged and destitute teachers at Hamburg bears his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-korn-selig-frie:
Selig Korn, a German writer and mythologist born at Prague on April 26, 1803, died at Teplitz on Oct. 16, 1850. Thrown out of his gymnasium over a poem mocking a teacher, he tried trade and taught himself in spare hours. In 1829 he left for Leipsic and worked in several cities. After his parents died he converted to Christianity.

Writing under pen names such as Friedrich N. Nork, Korn produced satires and studies in myth. His books treat Persian myth, Bible myth, and word roots, dated from 1830 to 1843. The entry closes flatly: neither line of work brought him success, and most of the books are now forgotten.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ladier-dob-bar-: Dob Bär ben Shneor Zalman Ladier, a Russian Ḥasidic rabbi born about 1770, died in 1834. He was son of Shneor Zalman of Liady, founder of the Ḥabad sect. He followed his father as chief of that group. His books treat the way of life, repentance, and morals, dated from 1799 to 1821. Two short works build out his father's thought on reflection and on religious heat. One appeared first in 1831. His Zohar notes, printed about 1816, record only what he had heard from his father.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lamden-or-lamda: Lamden, or lamdan, is a late Hebrew word for a man well read in rabbinical books who is not a scholar in the strict sense. The entry says the term does not seem to appear before the eighteenth century. Ezekiel Katzenellenbogen, who lived from 1670 to 1749, used it in a tax ruling dated 1732. Jacob Emden also used a softer form for a Hamburg patron. Older writers in the sixteenth century marked the same gap with a different phrase instead. The entry is short and stays with word use and dated examples.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lazarus-moses-9: Moses Lazarus, an American merchant born in New York city on June 29, 1813, died there on March 9, 1885. Sugar refining held him until 1865, when he retired. In 1840 he married Esther Nathan of another leading New York family. Seven children survived him. Two daughters, Emma and Josephine, won fame as authors. He belonged to the Shearith Israel congregation. He also helped found the Knickerbocker Club, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-jonas-phil: Jonas Phillips Levy, an American merchant, was born in Philadelphia in 1807. He was a son of Michael Levy and Rachel Phillips. He died in New York in 1883. Peru granted him the freedom of the country for signal services in its navy. He commanded the U.S.S. "America" during the Mexican war. He carried troops to Vera Cruz, and General Winfield Scott made him captain of that port after it surrendered. He left three sons and two daughters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luperio-luperci:
Isaac Luperio, also spelled Lupercio, gets one of the briefest entries in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a Jew of Spanish descent, perhaps a Marrano, who lived at Smyrna. Almost nothing else about his life is recorded here. What survives is his writing, an apology aimed at a monk in Seville.

The article describes his work on Daniel's seventy weeks, a favorite topic of Jewish-Christian debate. His apology, written in Spanish, answered the Seville monk and explained his reading of the prophecy. It appeared in a Latin translation at Basel in 1658. The entry rests on bibliographies of Spanish and Portuguese Jewish writing. For modern readers it is a small trace of hidden Jewish scholarship. Such works answered church critics in print, in the language of their opponents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mahler-gustav-1:
Gustav Mahler, the Austrian composer and conductor, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Kalischt, Bohemia, on July 7, 1860, he studied at Vienna's university and conservatory. There Bruckner taught him composition and counterpoint. A string of theater posts followed, at Hall, Laibach, and Cassel.

The article climbs with his career. At Prague he succeeded Anton Seidl and conducted Wagner's Ring and Tristan. He reorganized the Royal Opera at Budapest after 1888. Hamburg took him in 1891, and Vienna's Royal Opera in 1897, where he soon became director. The entry notes his conversion to Christianity soon after. It also lists his growing work as a composer, including Das Klagende Lied and three symphonies. Written while Mahler still lived, the piece catches him ranked among the greatest conductors of the day, his composing just winning notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marble-10390:
Marble in the Bible is the subject of a brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. The stone, mostly calcium carbonate, appears in only three late passages. Chronicles says David prepared white marble stones for the Temple. The Song of Solomon compares the bridegroom's legs to marble pillars in golden sockets. Esther describes marble columns and pavement in the Persian king's palace.

The article doubts the stone's real presence in old Israel. The Kings account of the Temple building never mentions marble at all. Even the Esther passage may be textually unsound, the writers warn. The total silence of the older sources suggests the Hebrews did not know marble as a building stone. Its use was limited even among the Assyrians, they add. The short entry is a caution against picturing the biblical world in the white stone of later ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mattithiah-b-is:
Mattithiah ben Isaac of Chinon was a French scholar of the end of the thirteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and S. Kahn give him only a few lines in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. What the entry can say is soon told. He was a pupil of R. Perez of Corbeil. He belonged to the generation of Mordecai ben Hillel, who was martyred at Nuremberg in 1298.

The notice exists largely to prevent a confusion. Mattithiah of Chinon is sometimes wrongly identified with an earlier Mattithiah, the teacher of Eliezer ben Joel ha-Levi, author of the work “Abi Asaf.” For evidence the entry points to citations in the legal writings of Mordecai. It also points to “Gallia Judaica” by Gross, the standard geography of medieval French Jewry. The notice is a small but typical piece of the encyclopedia's housekeeping among hundreds of similar names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mequinez-10690:
Mequinez is a town of the Moroccan interior. It sits some thirty-five miles from Fez. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco give it a communal report in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. About six thousand of its fifty thousand people were Jews. Most of them were of Spanish stock, the article argues. At least eighteen of thirty family names are Castilian. Dress and cooking still show the Spain of the Middle Ages. Yet the town was founded about 940. It held a few Jews before 1492.

The documented history begins with disaster. The famine of 1878 brought relief missions from London and the Alliance Israélite. The drought and epidemic of 1879 brought them too. The Alliance bulletin counted forty-two Jews assassinated there between 1864 and 1880. The entry ends with the institutions of 1904. It names nineteen synagogues, two Alliance schools founded in 1901, and ten small Talmud Torahs teaching some eight hundred children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michaelis-johan:
Johann Heinrich Michaelis was a German Christian theologian and Hebraist born at Kletterberg on July 26, 1668. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He learned Ethiopic under Ludolf at Frankfurt. He joined the Halle faculty in 1699 and became professor of theology ten years later.

His chief work was an edition of the Hebrew Bible printed at Frankfurt in 1720. He built it by comparing nineteen earlier editions and five Erfurt manuscripts. It was reprinted all through the eighteenth century. He also wrote a Hebrew grammar and the standard work of his age on Hebrew accents. He made the Latin translation of the Ethiopic psalter that Ludolf published.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mizmor-le-dawid:
Mizmor le-Dawid, a Psalm of David, is the superscription of Psalm 29, and Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen describe its Sabbath music in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The psalm is chanted before the Sabbath evening service and again in the morning, while the Torah scroll is carried back to the Ark. The two rites treat it oppositely.

Among the Ashkenazim there is no recognized traditional melody, so modern composers' settings fill the morning service. The Sephardim keep an ancient Peninsular chant, built on the third and fifth degrees of the scale, which the article prints in transcription as characteristic of their traditional intonation. Two anthologies, De Sola and Aguilar's and Cohen and Davis's, are cited for the tunes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-isaac-jud:
Moses Isaac Judah Löb ben Naphtali Hirz, also called Löb Zunz, was a rabbi and cabalist born at Frankfort on the Main. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn. He studied Talmud under Aaron Samuel Kaidanover and Cabala under Jacob Temerles. He died at Pinczow in Poland in 1682.

In 1669 Löb became rabbi of Holleschau in Moravia, approving his old teacher Temerles' book that year. He was still there in 1675, and later moved to the rabbinate of Pinczow, where he stayed until his death. Many rabbis applied to him for approbations of their works. David Kaufmann later wrote his life for a book on the family of Leopold Zunz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahum-full-of-c: Nahum, whose name means full of comfort, was one of the Minor Prophets. The Jewish Encyclopedia gives him a brief notice by Emil G. Hirsch and J. F. McLaughlin. His book calls him Nahum the Elkoshite, but Elkosh has never been surely placed. The article takes him for a native of Judah. His feeling for Judah's suffering under Assyria, and his hatred of her oppressor, point that way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-navarre-11390:
Navarre was an old kingdom on Spain's northern edge. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there before the tenth century ended. King Sancho drew Jews in to refill emptied towns. They settled at Tudela, Pamplona, Estella, and elsewhere.

Early kings gave Jews full civil rights and town defenses. Later kings took back much of that safety. One gave Estella's synagogue to the Church in 1144. Theobald I refused a pope's demand for a Jewish badge. French rule brought fresh taxes and attacks on Jews. In 1328 mobs killed more than six thousand Jews. Estella's ghetto was burned with all its people inside.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ollendorff-henr:
Henri Ollendorff was a French teacher of tongues from Rawicz. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1802 in Posen, a Prussian land. He died at Paris on April 3, 1865. His name lives on in the Ollendorff method of teaching.

His method taught a new tongue as a child learns its own. It kept rules of grammar to the bare few. It began with short, plain lines of speech. It then moved step by step to hard forms. Ollendorff first used the plan while he taught in London. He moved to Paris about the year 1830. There he wrote books for German, then for English. His works spread to Italian, Spanish, and Greek as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-osprey-a-v-ospr: The osprey is a bird named among the unclean birds. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Hebrew name stands in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. The true osprey is not oft seen in Palestine. So the name may cover a set of like birds of prey. The gold, royal, and short-toed eagles may be meant. The last of these is the most seen eagle in that land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paperna-abraham:
Abraham Jacob Paperna was a Russian teacher and author. Herman Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Kopyl, in the Minsk land, in 1840. He had a fair schooling in his youth at home. It held the Bible, Hebrew grammar, and the Talmud.

In 1863 Abraham entered the rabbis' school at Jitomir. He read there till the year 1865 in that school. He was then moved to the rabbis' school at Wilna. He left that school with his full course done in 1867. In 1868 he was named a teacher at Zakroczyn. In 1870 he became the head of a school at Plotzk. He stood close to the Haskalah, the new learning move. He wrote books and pieces in Russian and in Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phasaelis-phasa:
Phasaelis was a city Herod founded in his brother's honor. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stood in the Jordan valley north of Jericho. The ground was barren until men worked it. Herod also raised a tower of the same name.

Herod left the city to his sister Salome. She passed it on to the empress Livia at Rome. The whole Jericho region was famed for fine dates. Phasaelis shared in that rich palm trade. Later writers still name the town. Its name survives today in Khirbat Fasa'il.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-portaleone-1229:
Portaleone is the name of a Jewish family of northern Italy. Gotthard Deutsch and Hermann Vogelstein wrote its history for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name likely comes from a quarter of Rome by the ghetto. In 1399 Elhanan Portaleone served as a judge in Lombardy. Many in the family worked as doctors.

Guglielmo Portaleone doctored Ferdinand the First of Naples. He later served Galeazzo Sforza of Milan. He then settled in Mantua and worked there until 1500. His sons and grandsons kept the family trade. Many of them doctored the Gonzaga rulers of Mantua. The Gonzagas held them in high favor for years. The article traces the house across those courts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prosbul-or-1239:
Prosbul is a court paper that shields a loan from the Sabbatical year. The Editorial Board and Julius H. Greenstone wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word is cut down from a Greek phrase. It means before the assembly of counselors, they say. A man spoke the paper in court before he lent money.

By that act, the law of release would not touch his loan. Debts fell due for release in the Sabbatical year. With a prosbul, this one debt stood safe from release. The article gives the very words of the paper. It then traces how rabbis used and stretched the device. Rich and poor both felt its effects on lending.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-ufran-: Rabbah bar Ufran was a Babylonian teacher of the third century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He passed on one tale-saying of Eleazar ben Pedat. That saying stands in the tractate Megillah. One fresh reading of a verse is his own. It treats a verse in the book of Jeremiah. Nothing more of his life is known.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ratisbon-12590:
Ratisbon is a Bavarian city onetime free in the German empire. Gotthard Deutsch and A. Eckstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Tradition says Jews lived there before the common era. It is the oldest Jewish settlement in Bavaria with records.

The article cites a document from 981 about the Jew Samuel. A Jewish quarter is named in the early eleventh century. That quarter is the oldest German ghetto in known sources. In 1182 Emperor Frederick I confirmed Jewish rights there. Jews held the status of chamber servants, the writers say. Later they were pawned to Bavarian dukes for yearly payment. The entry traces rights that shifted between rulers and city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rochester-12790:
Rochester is the county seat of Monroe County, New York. Cyrus Adler and Max Landsberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It was the state's third largest city. The 1900 census counted 162,608 inhabitants there.

The article estimates about five thousand Jews among them. A few Jews lived there as early as 1840. Community history properly begins in 1848, they say. Twelve young German men met to hold festival services. They gathered at one member's home that year. The day after the Day of Atonement they formed a congregation. It was called Berith Kodesh. A rented hall served them from 1849. In 1856 they bought a former Baptist church. A grand new temple was dedicated in 1894. It cost one hundred thirty thousand dollars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-safed-hebrew-ze:
Safed is a city of Upper Galilee, founded in the second century of this era. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. For centuries it drew rabbis, mystics, and Spanish exiles to its hills.

In the sixteenth century Safed became a great center of Jewish learning. Jacob Berab tried to revive ordination and a patriarchate there. Isaac Luria and Hayyim Vital renewed the Cabala in its streets. Joseph Caro, its rabbi, wrote the Shulhan Aruk, the standard code of law. Plague in 1742 and earthquake in 1769 then shattered the community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-alex: Samuel ben Alexander of Halberstadt was a German rabbi and scientist who died on July 6, 1707. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He perhaps lived at Frankfort-on-the-Oder. His one named work is Peri Megadim, an alphabetical index to the Hoshen Mishpat part of the Shulhan Aruk, printed there in 1691.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sapphire-hebrew:
Joseph Jacobs and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the sapphire. The Bible names this prized sky-blue stone often. It appears in Exodus, Job, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. The article warns that the ancients meant a different stone. Their sapphire was lapis lazuli. Gold-like specks of pyrite glitter in its blue depths.

Babylonians and Egyptians prized the stone as well. It was mined in Upper Egypt. In Exodus it sits among the stones on the high priest's breastplate. Isaiah pictures the new Jerusalem with sapphire foundations. Tobit gives the city gates of sapphire too. In Exodus and Ezekiel, God's throne rests on a floor like sapphire. That image stands for the dark-blue sky strewn with golden stars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shallum-13490:
Shallum is a biblical name borne by several men, and the entry treats them in turn. Emil G. Hirsch, E. I. Nathans, Wilhelm Bacher, and Louis Ginzberg wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia piece on the name. One Shallum ranked among the great men of Elisha's time. He still gave daily help to the poor himself.

That Shallum went outside the city gates each day. There he gave water to thirsty travelers passing by. God rewarded his kindness, tradition says, with prophecy for him and his wife Huldah. A son famed for piety was granted to them as well. The entry mixes Bible text with rabbinic tales that fill out these brief names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shishak-sheshon:
Shishak, or Sheshonk the First, founded Egypt's twenty-second dynasty as its first king. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His grandfather was a Libyan soldier who married royalty. His father held high military and religious offices.

Before taking the throne, Shishak commanded all Libyan troops. He ranked next to the sovereign in official standing. Clever marriages for his sons helped him gain power. He then founded the Bubastite dynasty of Egypt. Shishak knew Jeroboam, a fugitive from Solomon's court. He also knew Hadad of Edom, another exile. Those ties drew his eye to Palestine's troubles. Scripture remembers him as the pharaoh who later raided Jerusalem's temple treasures.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-lakish:
Simeon ben Lakish, called Resh Lakish, was a top Palestinian amora of the second generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Born about 200, he died about 275. His brother-in-law Johanan was his great legal opponent and partner.

Resh Lakish appears to have lived at Sepphoris from youth. There he studied under Johanan in that city. He treasured having seen the patriarch Judah ha-Nasi himself. That sight, he said, grounded his knowledge of Torah. Scholars debate who else taught the young Resh Lakish. Judah Nesiah, Bar Kappara, and Hoshaiah all have claims. He cites Hoshaiah often and calls him father of the Mishnah. The entry opens the life of one of the Talmud's most colorful debaters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sisterhoods-of-:
Sisterhoods of Personal Service were groups of women charity workers. Joseph Jacobs and Hannah B Einstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A sermon by Dr Gustav Gottheil in 1887 sparked the first group. He preached at Temple Emanu-El in New York city. Members were to do the work themselves, in person.

Each sister gave part of her time to a set task. The aim was to join rich and poor as friends. It was not to be patron and dependent, but friend and friend. Sisterhoods ran relief work, schools, nurseries, and kindergartens. They also ran job bureaus and workrooms for women. Soon almost every large New York congregation had such a group.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-sam: Solomon ben Samson was a scholar of Worms in the eleventh century. Gotthard Deutsch and S Mannheimer wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was a teacher and relative of Rashi. Rashi cites him as an authority beside Isaac ha-Levi. He is likely the Solomon ben Samson named as a native of Vitry. That name may point to Lorraine, where he is also cited among scholars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-star-worship-13:
Star-worship is perhaps the oldest form of idolatry among the ancients. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Wisdom says early peoples took planets and stars for gods. Egypt's religion consisted preeminently of sun-worship in its core. Moses sternly warned Israel against worshiping the host of heaven.

Israel still fell into this idolatry in early times. By Amos's day they carried images of Siccuth and Chiun. Judah later outdid the north in star-worship, the article says. Manasseh built altars to the host of heaven in the Temple courts. Altars stood on house roofs, with horses dedicated to the sun. Josiah abolished the public cult in 621 BCE at last.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stuhlweissenbur:
Stuhlweissenburg was the coronation city of Hungary's kings until 1527. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Its Hungarian name is Szekesfejervar and its Latin name Alba Regia. By the 1300s it held Hungary's most influential Jewish community. Royal visits made its leaders speak for all Hungarian Jews.

The community survived under Turkish rule in the 1600s. When the Turks left in 1686, the Jews left too. One Jewish family returned under Emperor Joseph the Second. A law of 1839 and 1840 let Jews settle in royal cities. A small congregation formed there by 1842. Rabbi Mayer Zipser organized it but split it over reform. The entry follows a community through expulsion and return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tabor-14190:
Mount Tabor is a dome-shaped hill in northern Palestine. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. It rises on the northern edge of the Jezreel plain. Modern Arabs call it Jabal al-Tur. It stands about 562 meters above the sea.

Tabor formed a border for Zebulun, Issachar, and Naphtali. Barak gathered his army there against Sisera. Judges tells that mustering in its fourth chapter. An ancient cult also centered on the height. Hosea names it in a warning to Israel. Its lone, rounded shape made it a far-seen landmark. Jeremiah and the Psalms praise it beside Carmel and Hermon. Other Tabors in scripture belong elsewhere, the entry warns. It sorts true mountain references from same-name places.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tien-tsin-14390: Tien-Tsin, a commercial city of China, had about 150 Jewish residents when Joseph Jacobs and N. E. B. Ezra wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Most were Russian and Polish merchants and hotel-keepers. They had not organized as a formal community. Services met only in the penitential season, in private halls, with Torah scrolls brought from Shanghai. In 1902 J. Dietrich bought land and gave it for a Jewish burial ground. A branch of the Anglo-Jewish Association formed in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trebitsch-abrah:
Abraham ben Reuben Hayyat Trebitsch was an Austrian scholar born around 1760. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Trebitsch in Moravia and died at Nikolsburg. In 1775 he attended a Prague yeshiva. He later served as secretary to Moravia's chief rabbi.

His chief work, Korot ha-Ittim, tells the times in Hebrew. It covers Europe's monarchs from 1741 to 1801. Austria's emperors receive close attention throughout. Jewish history and literature in Austria get special weight. The book continues an earlier chronicle that ended in 1740. A later editor extended it to 1830. Trebitsch also co-wrote a tale of an exorcism. It appeared in Hebrew and Yiddish in 1785.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-veszi-joseph-14:
Joseph Vészi was a Hungarian editor and member of parliament. He was born at Arad on November 6, 1858. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied philosophy, literature, and languages at Budapest. As a young man he wrote lyric poems. Two volumes of his verse appeared in 1880.

From 1877 Vészi worked in journalism with liberal views. He edited the Budapester Tagblatt and wrote for Pester Lloyd. In 1894 he became chief editor of Pesti Napló. Two years later he founded the Budapesti Napló. He led Budapest's journalistic club as its president. Voters sent him to parliament in 1899 and again in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wassertrilling-:
Hermann Wassertrilling was an Austrian Hebraist and epic poet. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Boskowitz, in Moravia. He taught at Hotzenplotz, in Silesia, about 1850. Later he served as rabbi of Bojanowo, in Posen. All his books appeared at Breslau.

His poems retell Bible stories in Hebrew verse. One epic sings the life of the prophet Elisha. It runs to nine cantos. Another tells Daniel's story in eight cantos. It ends with the return to Jerusalem and the Second Temple. A verse collection gathers Talmud legends in lesson order. He also wrote a treatise defending circumcision practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-widdin-14890:
Widdin is a Bulgarian fortified town on the Danube. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands where the Widd River meets the Danube. Its Jewish community began in the thirteen hundreds. Byzantine and Hungarian Jews were its first members. The town then belonged to Wallachia's ruler.

Two famed rabbis reached Widdin in 1376. Moses Yewani, called the Greek, came with R. Shalom. Shalom founded Bulgaria's first rabbinical school there. He became the community's first rabbi. After 1453 a Wallachian prince taxed rich Jews harshly. He threatened an eye or ear for nonpayment. The sultan revoked that cruel edict on appeal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolff-julius-14:
Julius Wolff (1836-1902) was a German surgeon known for work on bones and joints. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in West Prussia, he schooled at Berlin and took his degree in 1860. He then set up as a surgeon in that city.

He served in three wars and won the Iron Cross. In 1884 he became a teacher of surgery at Berlin. In 1890 he took charge of a new bone clinic there. He wrote more than one hundred pieces for medical journals. They treat bone care, joint ills, and the throat. His chief book states his law on how bones change shape. The Royal Prussian Academy brought that book out in 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yeshibah-12890:
Yeshibah is a high school and a college for rabbis in Jewish life. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It is the oldest school form in that life. It ranks above the grade school and the Talmud Torah.

The word first meant a sit or a meet of scholars. An elder led those meets in the old days. The patriarchs were all elders of such a school. In time the school met in a hall of its own. That hall stood by the house of study in the town. The head of the school gave a set talk each day. One or two meets were held on each school day. The talk had a set length, like a fixed measure of time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yishar-koheka-m: Yishar Koheka, or may thy strength be firm, is a common phrase of thanks. Cyrus Adler and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first word comes from a root that means to be firm. The phrase stands in the Talmud in Hebrew and Aramaic forms. Men say it to the preacher after a sermon. They say it to the prayer leader and to the priest as well. It serves as a warm word of thanks in each case.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zuckermann-bene:
Benedict Zuckermann was a German scientist who taught mathematics at the Breslau seminary. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Breslau on October 9, 1818, he died there on December 17, 1891. At the university he devoted himself to mathematics and astronomy.

When Zacharias Frankel took charge of the seminary, he put Zuckermann on its teaching staff. Zuckermann taught mathematics and calendar science, and ran the library and the stipend fund. His books cover the sabbatical year cycle, Talmudic coins and weights, and math inside the Talmud. Strictly Orthodox and modest, he fled town on his seventieth birthday to escape all celebration.
judge-bhagavad-gita-1890:
William Q. Judge put the Bhagavad-Gita in fresh English dress in his rendering of 1890. The Gita is the famed talk twixt Prince Arjuna and his guide Krishna on a field of war. Arjuna balks at the fight. Krishna urges him to act with a free, calm heart.

Judge adds notes that read the talk through his creed's lens. He stresses the soul's long growth and duty free of greed for fruits. His version was the creed's own Gita for years. It sits apart from the plain verse takes of its day. Arjuna's doubt at the brink of war gives the talk its charge. Krishna's reply has drawn fans for two thousand years and more.
judge-echoes-from-the-orient-1890:
William Q. Judge gave a brief sketch of his creed in Echoes from the Orient, a slim tract from 1890. The creed claims its roots lie in the old East. Judge sums up its view of God, man, death, and the soul's long road in a few short parts.

The tract was meant to be passed hand to hand. Its prose is plain and warm, fit for a first read. Fans in the United States used it as their hand book. It shows how the creed wished to be known by the crowd. The tract first ran in a tract press tied to the creed's own house. Cheap print helped it roam far on both sides of the sea.
kipling-the-mark-of-the-beast-1890:
Rudyard Kipling sets a wolf tale in India in The Mark of the Beast, his short tale of 1890. A drunk guest in a shrine mocks the monkey god and stamps a leper with a hot end of a smoke. The leper's touch marks his chest with a beast's print. Night past night, the guest sinks: he growls, craves raw flesh, and shuns the light of day.

His mates must force the cure from the leper at great risk. Kipling's prose is taut and grim. The tale, from Life's Handicap, is a hard gem of dread. It bites.
lavoisier-elements-of-chemistry-1790:
Antoine Lavoisier, the great French chemist, set out the new chemistry in full in his Traite of 1789. Robert Kerr turned it into English in 1790, with this title. The book threw out phlogiston and built the science on weight and proof. It was writ in a clear style that a new student could read with ease.

Lavoisier lists the true elements as he knew them and shows how acids, salts, and gases form. His balance sheet method tracks each stuff through a change, gram by gram. The book marks the start of modern chemistry, and its terms are in use to this day.
leskov-steel-flea-hapgood-1890:
A craftsman in Tula hears that English makers have built a tiny steel flea, and pride demands an answer. Leskov's tale The Steel Flea, in Isabel Hapgood's 1890 translation, follows Lefty, the cross-eyed smith who shoes the flea with microscopic shoes. The story unfolds in skaz, a yarn-spinner's voice full of twisted learned words.

Praise turns to neglect, and the fable cuts at how Russia treats its own gifted hands. Craft versus machine, home skill versus foreign shine: Leskov packs the argument into a comic, mournful tale. It remains his best loved story, a small masterpiece of Russian prose.
lewis-elementary-latin-dictionary-1890:
Charlton Lewis published his Elementary Latin Dictionary in 1890 as his own school abridgment of Lewis and Short. Where the great dictionary served scholars, this one served the classroom. It became the Latin student's standard dictionary for generations.

Lewis trims each entry to the senses a school author actually uses, with clear grammar help. An appendix covers the persons and places met in Caesar, Cicero, and Virgil. The definitions favor plain English over learned display. For over a century, students construing their set texts reached for Lewis first, and many scholars kept the habit for life.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Volume Five of Motley's Barneveld history spans the years 1609 to 1614. Its sixth chapter explains the shared rule of the Cleves duchies. Brandenburg and Neuburg, joint heirs, quickly became bitter rivals. Brandenburg forces, helped by the States-General, occupied Julich.

Spain and the Archdukes protested, and Spinola seized towns in reply. Wesel surrendered, and talks at Xanten tried to settle the dispute. A treaty finally divided the territory between the two houses. The chapter shows a local inheritance quarrel pulling in great powers. Spain's prohibition later tried to undo the Xanten settlement entirely. Delays and disagreements, Motley notes, followed the treaty for years.
mahan-sea-power-1890:
Alfred Thayer Mahan was an American naval officer who taught strategy at the Naval War College in Newport. His 1890 study of sea power covers the wars of England, France, Holland, and Spain from 1660 to 1783. It quickly became the most quoted naval book of its age.

Mahan argued that command of the sea decides the fate of nations more than armies on land. He praised large battle fleets, strong ports, and trade routes guarded by guns. Leaders in America, Britain, Germany, and Japan read him closely, and his ideas fed the battleship race before the First World War.
marlowe-tamburlaine-part1-1590:
Christopher Marlowe's Tamburlaine the Great burst onto the London stage around 1587 and changed English drama. Part One was printed in 1590. Marlowe, a Cambridge graduate and shoemaker's son, wrote in a new, thundering blank verse that audiences had never heard before.

Tamburlaine begins as a Scythian shepherd and rises by force of will to conquer Persia and challenge empires. He defeats kings, keeps them in cages, and marries the Egyptian princess Zenocrate. His speeches soar with longing for crowns and limitless power. The play made Marlowe famous and showed that blank verse could carry the grandest tragedy.
marlowe-tamburlaine-part2-1590:
Christopher Marlowe wrote Part Two of Tamburlaine because the first part's success demanded more. Both parts were printed together in 1590. The sequel follows the conqueror into age, grief, and death, testing how far his will can reach.

Tamburlaine now burns towns that resist, trains his sons for war, and rages against sickness itself. The death of his beloved Zenocrate breaks something in him that armies never could. He grows crueler and more desperate as his body fails. In the end the man who defied every power meets the one enemy he cannot defeat. The fall completes Marlowe's portrait of ambition.
marshall-principles-economics-1890:
Alfred Marshall taught economics at Cambridge and spent years writing the book that would train two generations of students. His Principles of Economics, published in 1890, set out the field as a calm, ordered science. For half a century it stayed the dominant textbook in the English-speaking world.

Marshall gives supply and demand their classic form, shown as two blades of one pair of scissors cutting price together. He adds tools like elasticity, the measure of how buyers respond when prices shift. His patient, balanced style made hard ideas feel like common sense carefully stated.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette:
Volume seven of Campan's memoirs opens at chapter nine, in the Revolution. The Queen has been robbed of her purse on a short walk. She passes from the Tuileries to the Feuillans when it happens.

She asks Campan's sister to lend her twenty five louis then. That loan, told under questioning, becomes a pretext for an arrest. The note breaks off in the sample at that charge's start. Campan's tale has reached the Queen's last, captive days by this volume. A note ties the loan to her sister's own sworn words. Small sums make large charges in a court turned to terror.
mizora-1890:
Mary E. Bradley Lane wrote Mizora in the year 1890. Its full title adds the word Prophecy to the name of a hid land. A Russian woman, cast out for her views, sails north and finds a hole to a world inside the Earth. That world holds women, and women alone.

The inner land has fine schools, clean towns, and science far past our own. Men died out there long past, Lane says, and peace came with their loss. The book was the first utopia of its kind by a woman. It holds a key place in both hollow Earth and women's tales.
moll-hypnotism-1890:
Albert Moll gives hypnotism its scientific synthesis in Hypnotism, from 1890, the field's foundational textbook. The Berlin physician surveys the whole subject with sober care. Charcot's Paris school, Bernheim's Nancy method, and Liebault's cures all pass under his calm, critical review in one balanced and thorough account.

He weighs crime, law, therapy, and stage abuse beside the cures. Myths are pared away, and solid fact is sorted from show. Doctors and jurists across Europe took the book as their guide. It marks the moment the subject grew up, when hypnotism gained a literature that universities could shelve without a blush.
mr-murray-s-list-of-new-and-recent-publi:
John Murray's firm issued this trade list from Albemarle Street in July 1890. It is a publisher's catalog of new and recent books, with prices and press praise. One lead item is a volume of speeches given in India. The speeches are by the Marquis of Dufferin and Ava.

Long review quotes sell each book to shops and readers. The Saturday Review calls the speeches light, gay, and wise on India. Other entries follow the same sales pattern. The list shows what a top London house pushed in 1890. It is a small window on Victorian books, prices, and taste.
nicholas-flammel-his-exposition-of-the-h:
W. Wynn Westcott signed the preface to this 1890 printing of Nicholas Flammel's exposition, limited to one hundred copies. Flammel, who died in 1418, had figures painted on an arch in St Innocents churchyard in Paris. The work first came out in London in 1624, per the record.

Flammel explains those painted figures, called hieroglyphical, sign by sign. His theme is the theory and practice of the philosophers stone. That stone, in alchemy, was held to change base metals and grant long life. The sampled pages are worn and hard to read, but the title states the aim plainly. Students of alchemy still seek Flammel's name.
openalex-w1975288090:
Jeremy Ledermann, Ann Powers, and co-authors studied this mosquito. The catalog record gives no author or year; the sample names them. A Zika outbreak struck Yap Island in July 2007. That outbreak prompted studies to find the transmitting mosquito. Aedes hensilli was the island's predominant species.

Field teams surveyed larvae, pupae, and adult mosquitoes on Yap. No virus was found in the field-collected insects. Lab studies then tested hensilli's ability to carry the viruses. Chikungunya and Zika viruses were the pair in question. Knowing the vector guides control on Pacific islands.
openalex-w2015450690:
Ana Luisa Sosa, Emiliano Albanese, Blossom Stephan and colleagues measured mild memory and thinking problems in older people. Their study appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2012. They worked in Latin America, China and India. Such problems may raise the risk of dementia. Little was known about them in poorer countries.

The team used surveys from the 10/66 Dementia Research Group. Over fifteen thousand people aged sixty-five and older took part. None had dementia at the time. A fixed rule identified amnestic mild impairment. Rates ranged from under one percent in China to over four percent in India. The condition was linked with disability and anxiety. It was also linked with apathy and irritability. The authors urged follow-up studies over time.
openalex-w2019456090:
Andrew Kirkpatrick, Derek Roberts, Jan De Waele and colleagues updated guidance on pressure inside the abdomen. Their paper appeared in Intensive Care Medicine in 2013. High pressure in the abdomen can harm organs. In its worst form it is called abdominal compartment syndrome. The guidance came from a world expert society.

The panel reviewed research in a systematic way. They updated the shared definitions doctors use. They also updated practical advice for care. The statements cover how to measure pressure. They cover how to spot the syndrome early. They also cover treatment steps for adults and children. A separate subgroup handled the child guidance. Common terms and steps help intensive care teams act alike.
openalex-w2078183490:
Andrew Steer, Adam Jenney, Joseph Kado and colleagues measured two common skin diseases in Fiji. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2009. Impetigo is a bacterial skin infection. Scabies is caused by a tiny mite. Both are widespread in tropical countries, yet poorly mapped.

The team ran three studies in 2006 and 2007. Two studies covered primary school children. One study covered infants. About a quarter of school children had impetigo. Nearly a fifth had scabies at checks. Rates in infants were also high. Simple survey methods made the studies repeatable. The results show a heavy hidden burden. Skin health deserves more attention in the Pacific.
openalex-w2114878190:
Chih-Lin Wei, Gilbert Rowe, Elva Escobar-Briones and colleagues mapped life on the world seafloor. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2010. Direct sampling of the deep sea is sparse. A global database offered a way forward. It gathered records from many research institutions.

The database came from Census of Marine Life projects. It holds seafloor abundance and biomass records. A machine learning method modelled the patterns. Depth and surface food supply shaped biomass strongly. The model predicted biomass for unsampled regions. Coastal and slope areas held richer life than abyssal plains. The maps guide deep-sea conservation planning. They also reveal where sampling remains thinnest.
openalex-w2152334290:
Ray Norris, A. Hopkins, J. Afonso, and colleagues published this survey plan in the Publications of the Astronomical Society of Australia in 2011. EMU, the Evolutionary Map of the Universe, is a wide radio survey planned for the new ASKAP telescope in Australia. Earlier radio surveys caught mainly the brightest radio galaxies nearby.

EMU will map the whole southern sky and part of the northern sky in radio light. It should catalogue about seventy million galaxies. Normal star-forming galaxies will show up across vast distances, plus active galactic nuclei near the edge of the visible universe. The paper defines the survey's science goals and settings, and the new techniques needed to handle its flood of data.
openalex-w2276139690:
Mauricio Retamal, Isaac García, Bernardo Pinto, and colleagues published this theory paper in Frontiers in Physiology in 2016. They propose that cysteine residues on the outer loops of connexin proteins act as redox sensors. Connexins build gap junction channels and hemichannels, the tunnels that let neighboring cells trade ions and signals directly.

Six connexins join to form one hemichannel, and its opening is tightly controlled. Early work showed that channel formation depends on the chemical state of those outer cysteines. Reducing agents could break the links they form. The authors argue these cysteines sense the cell's redox balance. They tune channel gating accordingly, with effects in healthy and diseased tissue alike.
openalex-w2621266390:
The LIGO Scientific and Virgo Collaboration reported this gravitational-wave detection in Physical Review Letters in 2017. The signal, named GW170104, came from two black holes merging far away. Advanced LIGO's twin detectors caught it on January 4, 2017, during their second observing run. The signal was strong, with a false alarm rate below one in seventy thousand years.

The merging pair totaled about fifty times the Sun's mass. Their distance was measured at roughly three billion light-years. The black holes' spins seemed not aligned with their orbit, though zero spin was not excluded. Each new event sharpens estimates of how often such mergers happen across the universe. The growing catalog also tests Einstein's general relativity in extreme gravity. Those are regimes no earlier instrument could reach.
openalex-w2895615590:
Soujanya Poria, Devamanyu Hazarika, and Navonil Majumder, with colleagues, introduced the MELD dataset at the 2019 ACL meeting. Emotion recognition in conversations is a prized, hard problem for artificial intelligence. Existing emotional dialogue databases held at most two speakers per conversation. Real conversations, though, are multi-party, and feelings unfold across turns and speakers.

MELD extends the EmotionLines dataset using dialogues from the television series Friends. It holds about thirteen thousand utterances from over fourteen hundred dialogues. Every utterance carries emotion and sentiment labels. Text, audio, and video are all included, so models can read faces and voices too. The authors supply strong multimodal baseline systems. Their results show context and multiple modalities both matter for accuracy. The dataset is public, giving the field a shared benchmark for conversational emotion.
openalex-w2901297890:
Hugo Rodrigues, Ricardo Ney Cobucci, and António Gouveia Oliveira measured burnout among medical residents in PLoS ONE in 2018. Burnout combines emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and shrinking personal accomplishment. It is very common in residency, medicine's grueling training years. How common, and in which fields, needed one pooled answer.

The team reviewed the literature through March 2018, following PRISMA rules. From thousands of papers, twenty-six studies with 4,664 residents in all made the cut. Overall burnout rate came to about thirty-six percent. Surgical fields, anesthesiology, obstetrics, and orthopedics grouped highest, near forty-one percent. Internal medicine, plastic surgery, and pediatrics sat near thirty percent. Otolaryngology and neurology were lowest, near fifteen percent. The gradient gives training programs concrete targets for reform.
openalex-w3040245690:
Gabriele Berg, Daria Rybakova, Doreen Fischer, and colleagues wrote this commentary in Microbiome in 2020. It revisits the definition of the word microbiome itself. Research on microbe communities has grown fast and draws wide public interest, yet the field lacks one agreed definition of its central term.

The article reports a workshop of about forty field leaders, held under a European project, plus an online survey of more than a hundred experts. From those discussions, the authors propose a definition meant to be compact, clear, and complete. They also note the missing consensus on best research practices. A shared definition, they argue, is basic housekeeping for a young and booming science.
openalex-w3112105690:
The GenOMICC Investigators and partner groups published this study in Nature in 2020. It searches for genetic mechanisms behind critical illness in COVID-19. In the sickest patients, lung inflammation driven by the patient's own immune system is what kills.

Earlier finds showed that rare gene faults in immune sensing and interferon signaling can cause severe disease even in the young. Genome-wide scans can expose further pathways and point to drug targets. The authors treat critical COVID-19 as its own condition, distinct from mild disease: steroid drugs seem harmful before breathing failure, yet help greatly once it sets in. Their scan hunts the human gene variants that tip patients into that critical state.
openalex-w3138893590:
Eun-Young Lee, Ajaypal Bains, Stephen Hunter, and colleagues published this systematic review in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2021. It synthesizes what shapes outdoor play and outdoor time in children aged three to twelve. Both are widely praised and widely declining.

Searching twelve databases in five languages, the team gathered one hundred seven studies covering nearly one hundred ninety thousand children in twenty-nine countries. Children played outside about one to three hours daily, by varying measures. Of hundreds of possible influences tested, a solid subset held up, from safety and space to parents' habits. Sorting them through a social-ecological lens shows change must work at home, school, and street levels at once.
openalex-w4311872390:
Humberto Arruda, Édison Silva, Marcus Lessa, and colleagues review two free tools for mapping research fields. Their review appeared in the Journal of the Medical Library Association in 2022. As publications pile up, researchers and librarians struggle to see a field's whole shape. The tools, VOSviewer from Leiden University and Bibliometrix from the University of Naples, build maps from citation data. Such maps connect themes, authors, venues, and institutions in one picture.

VOSviewer draws network diagrams that place related items close together on a page. Bibliometrix supports wider statistical analysis of a literature. Both are free, which lowers the barrier for small teams and libraries. The reviewers explain what each tool does so readers can pick the right one for strategy, publishing, or career decisions.
openalex-w7153077790:
Hasan Cenk Mirza led a 2026 study in the Journal of Antibiotics testing two drug options against Acinetobacter baumannii, a hospital bacterium that resists carbapenems, some of the strongest antibiotics. The team compared sulbactam alone with sulbactam joined with durlobactam, a partner drug that shields it from bacterial enzymes. Twenty-four resistant isolates carrying specific resistance genes were tested in the laboratory.

Almost all isolates were susceptible to the combination, while only one reacted to sulbactam alone. The two isolates that resisted the combination carried changes in a target protein gene, and one also lacked a brake on a pump that expels drugs. The authors conclude that the combination keeps working well against these strains, with resistance tracing to changes that can be pinpointed.
openalex-w7165480890:
Miyu Umebayashi and Mikio Eto, of Keio University, published a 2026 theoretical study of photon-assisted tunneling in a double quantum dot, a pair of tiny electron islands used in nanoelectronics. When one dot is bathed in an oscillating field, electrons can tunnel through it by absorbing or emitting photons, creating side peaks in conduction beside the main peak. The authors treat the process with scattering theory.

For a single dot they show conduction proceeds through combined light-matter states when coupling to the leads is weak, and follows the oscillating level itself when coupling is strong. Extended to two dots threaded by magnetic flux, the interference effect known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect appeared in the side peaks too, proving coherent travel. The theory also supports phase measurement in a three-terminal layout.
openalex-w7204272490:
Luzia Martins Pereira led a Portuguese-language paper, in Brazil in 2026, on the contemporary school's move from homogenization toward diversity. The modern school treated students as uniform; Brazil's society, marked by cultural diversity and historical inequality, no longer fits that mold. In dialogue with decolonial thought, the authors examine the school as a space that can reproduce or transform society. They question the coloniality of knowledge and the power relations inside curriculum and teaching practice.

The paper defines racism, prejudice, discrimination, and stereotype as core elements of social relations and looks for classroom methods that value ethnic-racial diversity. The contemporary school, the authors conclude, must take a key, transforming role committed to equity, social justice, and plural identities, through inclusive and thoughtful teaching.
openalex-w7207688590:
Agata Aparecida Soares and five colleagues test greens sold at street stalls and shops in south-central Rio de Janeiro state. In the towns of Tres Rios and Paraiba do Sul, the team took twenty lots of greens. They used a sink test that lets eggs, young worms, and cysts settle out for a look through the lens.

Four of each five lots bore some germ sign or trace of filth from dung. The team reads stall greens as a gauge of clean care down the whole chain, from field and hands to the stall. For those who shop and those who guard health, the find backs one plain rule. Greens from open stalls need a good wash, and their safety is set by clean hands long before they reach the home.
openalex-w7212126190:
Isadora Coutinho Ferreira de Almeida leads a team on irritable bowel syndrome, and on the mind-body links that shape life with it. The syndrome brings belly pain and changed bowel habits, with no clear fault to find on a scan. Its roots mix gut germ shifts, low-grade swelling, and a stress system set too high. Strain, worry, and low mood feed the whole loop.

Drugs alone, the team finds, help too few patients. Care that joins fields does more. A diet low in hard-to-digest sugars can ease bloat and pain. Talk therapy of a set kind can calm the gut-brain loop. So can care that resets gut germs with live cultures. The review backs a plan that treats gut and mind as one system, not two charts in two rooms.
openalex-w7212446490:
Marcello Phillipe Aguiar Martins leads a team that sets out the four legs of a school patrol run by a police unit in Amazonas, Brazil. The legs are: rounds to head off harm, calls at schools, class-like talks, and response when harm hits. The team read the rule that set the model up, and weighed it with crime and school science.

Joined, the legs form a loop: stop, learn, act, and plan anew. Each leg works on a new front: the chance to do harm, the weak spots of kids, the ties at school, and the real event. The talks leg adds a school soul to the scheme. There the force acts as a guide, not just a guard. One line holds the whole: the force must stay in its lane and talk with the school at all times, or trust will thin.
openalex-w7213418390:
Micheli da Cruz Leal and Elaine Reda da Silva review entrepreneurship training in nursing. Their 2026 integrative review searched health databases in July 2026 and kept thirteen studies. It asks what skills nurse entrepreneurs need, what blocks them, and what they add to health care.

Three themes emerged: views of nursing entrepreneurship, the profile of nurses drawn to it, and how it is taught. Entrepreneurship can widen and raise the value of nursing work, the review finds. Barriers include weak management training, money problems, and gaps in degree courses. New models and technology show promise. Creativity, leadership, and willingness to take managed risks need strengthening in training.
openalex-w7213648090:
Karla Maria Cordeiro Cabral and Maria Emília Camargo analyse telework at the Court of Justice of Pernambuco, Brazil. Their 2026 mixed-methods study surveyed 156 staff working fully from home. Court rules and regulatory acts were also reviewed, and results are read through a human rights lens.

Most staff said telework raised productivity, and over half reported good home conditions and work-life balance. Counterweights were sharp: many judged staffing insufficient and equipment inadequate. Over half reported work-related health problems. Many worked during rest time, and most saw no career growth. Benefits are real, the authors conclude, but depend on health, proper conditions, and protection of workers' rights.
openalex-w7213790390:
Giovanna Azevedo Rodrigues and co-workers propose a wider classification of mutism in children and teenagers. Their 2026 review, in English, follows PRISMA guidance and searches four sources to April 2025. Standard diagnostic manuals and a classic textbook serve as foundation sources.

Current systems reduce most mutism to selective mutism, an anxiety condition, they argue. Forms tied to severe mood, psychotic, and catatonic states stay largely absent from child literature. Six subtypes are proposed: oppositional, selective or phobic, depressive, perplexed, delusional, and catatonic. Each is characterised by brain basis, risk factors, and clinical meaning. The aim is sharper recognition and better matched care for silent young patients.
openalex-w7214201690:
Raquel Rezende dos Santos led a 2026 narrative review, written with colleagues in Brazil, on hyaluronic acid fillers used in cosmetic skin treatment. The review explains rheology in plain terms: how a gel flows, stretches, and holds shape. Those traits differ across products and affect how a filler behaves once injected.

Inside, the authors link gel traits such as thickness, elasticity, and firmness to product choice, injection technique, and how long results last. They also discuss problems like lumps, overfilling, and blocked blood vessels, and why the enzyme used to dissolve filler may act differently on different gels. For clinicians, the message is to match the product to the task and know its risks.
openalex-w7214800890: Priscila Cardoso Garcia led a ten-author systematic review, published in Brazil in 2026, on a class of diabetes drugs that block sugar reabsorption in the kidneys. The review asks whether these drugs reduce cardiovascular and kidney events in people with type 2 diabetes. The evidence sample for this entry contains only the title page and author list, with no abstract or synthesis results, so the review's conclusions are not described here.
openalex-w7216180590:
Amanda Clara Kaed Moura and a co-author reviewed, in 2026, surgical complications in implant dentistry, sorted by when they occur. The field rests on osseointegration, the bonding of titanium implants to bone described in the 1960s. The review searched three databases and read twenty-eight articles in Portuguese and English on complications, risk factors, prevention, diagnosis, and clinical management.

During surgery, problems include bleeding, nerve injuries, bone fractures, perforations of the maxillary sinus, and damage to nearby teeth. Early after surgery come swelling, pain, bruising, suture opening, and infection. Late problems center on inflammation around the implant, loss of the bone bond, and implant failure. Success, the authors conclude, depends on far more than correct implant placement: planning the operation, knowledge of anatomy, spotting risks early, and proper handling of problems decide outcomes.
openalex-w7221038790:
Marcelene Alves Duarte led a five-author study of mathematics teachers in Brazil and the gaps in their training, published in 2026. Working with twenty experienced teachers, the team tested how well they understood the math strands set by the national curriculum for elementary and middle school, and whether workshops could close the gaps.

Teachers first solved open problems, answered a digital questionnaire, then joined workshops built on games and hands-on materials. Weak early results and insecurity, the authors found, came less from hard content than from shallow initial training and traditional, context-free teaching. Games and concrete materials eased emotional blocks and deepened understanding, supporting a more inclusive and fair mathematics education.
plos-pbio-0020090:
Frances Crawford, Eric Huseby, Janice White, and co-workers built a screening tool for T cells in PLOS Biology in 2004. T cells react to peptide fragments shown by MHC proteins on cell surfaces. The team made a display library of such pairs to fish out reactive T cells, including rare ones that react to the body's own tissues.

Some T cells attack self tissue and drive autoimmune disease, yet they are hard to find and study. A library that presents many peptide-MHC pairs at once makes that search practical. The tool can reveal what these cells see and how strongly they respond. That knowledge may help design treatments that calm only the harmful cells and spare the rest.
plos-pbio-0020290:
Elizabeth A. Hadly, Uma Ramakrishnan, Yvonne L. Chan, and their team read climate history from ancient DNA in PLOS Biology in 2004. They used DNA from old specimens, paired with family-tree timing methods. With them, they tracked how animal populations rose and fell as the climate shifted.

Their approach, called phylochronology, turns fossils and museum samples into a time series of genetic change. It showed population crashes and rebounds tied to warming and cooling. That record is a guide for the present. Species facing rapid warming now may follow paths seen in the data. The paper helped launch a field that reads the past to forecast the fate of wildlife.
plos-pone-0000090:
Tobias Kalisch, Claudia Wilimzig, Nadine Kleibel, and their team studied handedness across age in PLOS ONE in 2006. Most right-handed people do skilled tasks far better with the right hand. The team found that this gap between hands shrinks in older adults, a change called attenuation of hand superiority.

The dominant hand loses its edge as age advances, likely because the brain and body systems that keep it special wear unevenly. That finding matters for stroke care and for testing older patients. A smaller gap is normal in old age, so doctors should not read it as damage by itself. The study gives aging research a clean baseline for a basic human trait.
plos-pone-0000190:
Akihiro Horii, Xiumei Wang, Fabrizio Gelain, and colleagues published this biomaterials paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It follows up on designer peptide nanofiber scaffolds, self-assembling protein fibers used to grow cells in three dimensions. This time the cells are osteoblasts, the builders of bone, and the title reports the scaffolds strongly boost their growth, maturation, and 3-D migration.

A scaffold that bone cells thrive on is a candidate material for repairing bone. The authors measure how much better the osteoblasts do on the designer fibers. The work is part of a push toward lab-made matrices that the body treats like its own tissue scaffolding.
plos-pone-0000290:
Rayna I. Kraeva, Dragomir B. Krastev, Assen Roguev, and colleagues published this molecular biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. When a gene is transcribed, its message can form duplexes, paired strands, with DNA or with other RNA. The authors show that the stability of mRNA/DNA and DNA/DNA duplexes affects how much mRNA gets transcribed.

Stability is set by sequence, so the DNA code itself can throttle its own reading. The finding adds a physical layer to gene regulation, beyond proteins that switch genes on and off. It matters for predicting expression from sequence, a basic task in genomics.
plos-pone-0000390:
Philipp Leucht and colleagues examined how bone heals, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study of skeletal regeneration. Healing bone must sense physical forces, a process called mechanotransduction, where cells convert pressure and strain into chemical signals. The work centers on FAK, a protein that helps cells register those forces.

Broken and regrowing bone is loaded and stressed as an animal moves, and cells use that input to shape the repair. If FAK carries much of that signal, then blocking or boosting it could change how well bone mends. The study speaks to fracture care and to the design of implants and scaffolds that work with the body's own repair signals.
plos-pone-0000490:
Dan Zhou and colleagues bred fruit flies to survive air with almost no oxygen, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007.
