The experiment used experimental selection: over generations, only flies that tolerated an extremely low oxygen environment reproduced. Drosophila became a test of how fast evolution can push a hard physiological limit.

Surviving near-zero oxygen matters medically, since human tissues face oxygen shortage in stroke, heart attack, and altitude sickness. Flies that crack the problem reveal which genes and pathways can be tuned. Selection experiments of this kind show evolution working in real time, on a trait with clear survival stakes.
plos-pone-0000590:
Johannes J. Le Roux and colleagues documented a plant clone that conquered the world, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper titled Super-Genotype. Against the odds of nature, a single genotype has spread across the globe. Vast numbers of plants are genetically one individual. They spread by cuttings and fragments rather than seed.

A clone that succeeds everywhere challenges the idea that genetic diversity is required for success. Such super-genotypes are often invasive species, where one tough genotype exploits many environments. Understanding how a clone wins helps predict and manage invasions, and it tests evolutionary theory's assumptions about sex and variation.
plos-pone-0000690:
Ryan J. Mailloux, Robin Bériault, Joseph Lemire and co-authors found a novel twist in one of metabolism's oldest pathways, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The tricarboxylic acid cycle, or TCA cycle, runs in all organisms that use oxygen. It supplies building blocks for growth and the reducing factors NADH and FADH2 that drive energy generation.

Textbooks treat the cycle as a closed loop of chemistry. The authors show this network is also an integral part of something more, in their words a novel twist on the ancient system. Discoveries inside such a well-mapped pathway are rare. They remind readers that even core metabolism still holds surprises.
plos-pone-0000790:
Fabien Burki, Kamran Shalchian-Tabrizi, Marianne Minge and co-authors redrew the top branches of the family tree of complex cells. Sorting out how eukaryotes, the group that holds animals, plants, fungi, and many microbes, are related is a long-running hard problem. Gene data had lately sorted all of them into five or six large supergroups. That scheme was the view being tested.

Using many genes at once, a method called phylogenomics, the team found the supergroups needed reshuffling. Some groups merged, and some ties between groups changed. Moves at this level shift whole kingdoms of life. The study shows how fast rich gene data can upset trees built from one or two genes.
plos-pone-0000890:
Simon Lacey, Andrew Peters and K. Sathian tested whether recognizing an object by sight and by touch depends on viewpoint, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Earlier work had suggested that both visual and touch based recognition suffer when an object is turned. Those studies, though, used objects stretched along one axis, which may have skewed the result.

Lacey and co-authors revisited the question with that flaw in mind. Their title gives the direction of the work: cross-modal recognition, matching what is seen with what is felt, can hold up across viewpoints. The finding matters for how we think the brain stores shape. It suggests shape knowledge is not tied to one fixed view.
plos-pone-0000990:
Natalia Komarova and Dominik Wodarz modeled how resting tumor cells affect leukemia therapy, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In chronic myelogenous leukemia, the most primitive cancer cells can enter quiescence, a state where they stop dividing for a time. Resting cells are hard for drugs to kill, since many therapies strike dividing cells.

Using mathematical models, the pair ask how that rest state changes the success of targeted treatment. A model can test schedules and combinations far faster than trials can. Their work helps explain why a therapy can clear most disease yet fail at the root. It also points to what a cure would have to handle.
plos-pone-0001090:
Martins Kalis, Per Leveen, Valeriya Lyssenko and colleagues linked variants in a fatty acid receptor gene to beta cell function, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The receptor FFAR1 sits mainly on pancreatic beta cells, the cells that release insulin. It is switched on by medium and long chain fatty acids and by a class of diabetes drugs, raising calcium and promoting insulin release.

Those properties make its gene a natural suspect in diabetes. The team report variants in FFAR1 are associated with beta cell function. A receptor that senses dietary fat and tunes insulin is a neat meeting point of food and hormone. The association supports FFAR1 as a drug target worth care.
plos-pone-0001190:
Influenza A viruses mutate constantly and swap gene segments, so new strains keep emerging from animal reservoirs, as the H5N1 bird flu virus did. A. T. Heiny and colleagues looked for the stable parts of the virus in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They searched avian and human influenza A viruses for protein sequences that stay conserved through all that change.

Conserved sequences are attractive vaccine targets because a vaccine aimed at them might work against many strains, not just one. The authors present such sequences as candidate targets. Their approach addresses the central problem of flu vaccination: the target keeps moving.
plos-pone-0001290:
Violence is a leading cause of illness and death in South Africa. Katherine Doolan, Rodney Ehrlich, and Landon Myer examined how the experience of violence relates to socioeconomic position. Theirs was a national study, reported in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Violence research usually treats social position as a confounder to control away; a social epidemiology approach treats it as part of the story.

The authors analyze who experiences violence across the social ladder in South Africa. Patterns by income, education, and employment shape where prevention should aim. Their national data give the public health approach to violence a firmer base.
plos-pone-0001390:
Marco Salemi and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on HIV in Albania. In west Europe, one subtype of HIV-1 drives most cases. Far less was known about the east, where other subtypes are more common. AIDS cases in Albania had risen fast in the prior six years. The team set out to map the local strains.

Using close gene reads, they traced the types of HIV-1 found in Albania and their past. Their map shows how the virus spread and changed in the country. Such maps help health teams plan tests, care, and vaccines. They also show how a local epidemic can differ from the pattern next door.
plos-pone-0001490:
Eiji Goto and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on watching tagged proteins enter cells. When a surface protein is tagged for removal, it is pulled inside the cell. That step is hard to see as it happens in mammal cells. The gap blocked work on how tagging drives the pull in.

The team built a system that makes this step easy to track and rate. With it, labs can watch the pull in live and in bulk. A clear view should reveal the parts that run the process. That in turn may expose drug targets on paths that many receptors share.
plos-pone-0001590:
Francine Grodstein and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on telomeres and dementia risk. Dementia takes decades to grow, so care must start early to have a chance. Marks that flag risk years ahead are thus prized. Telomeres, the caps on DNA ends, shrink with age and stress. The team ran a first check in 62 women from a large nurses' study.

Shorter telomeres went with higher early risk marks for dementia in this small set. The authors stress the work is a first look, not a verdict. Larger checks must test the link before any clinic use. Still, a cheap blood mark for dementia risk would be a major gain.
plos-pone-0001690:
Petter Minnhagen and Sebastian Bernhardsson questioned whether evolution shaped the layout of cell metabolism, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Their model is called the blind watchmaker network. Metabolic networks, which map how a cell's chemistry links together, are scale-free: a few compounds take part in very many reactions, most in few.

The authors suggest this pattern reflects plain randomness, implying natural selection pressed little on the network's degree distribution during evolution. The full text gives the model, its math, and the match to real metabolic networks of simple organisms. If the layout is mostly chance, the search for adaptive design in network shape needs sharper tests. If not, the model marks where selection's hand should show.
plos-pone-0001790:
Marta Luisa Ciofi degli Atti, Stefano Merler, Caterina Rizzo, and their co-authors modeled pandemic influenza in Italy in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Models that simulate spread person to person can give the most reliable estimates for disease planning. The question was what various control measures would achieve in an Italian pandemic.

The team paired a global SEIR model for cases from abroad with a detailed national model. They then tracked the spread of pandemic flu under different scenarios. The full text gives the scenarios and the forecast case counts. Plans written before a pandemic decide school shutdowns and vaccine priorities under pressure, so tested models are a core planning tool.
plos-pone-0001890:
Fumiaki Sato and colleagues built a scoring tool for a throat condition that can turn to cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In Barrett esophagus, acid harm changes the lining of the food pipe, and a small share of cases move on to cancer. Watching all such patients closely is costly, and doctors did not agree on its worth.

The team sorted patients into three risk tiers using both health facts and chemical marks on DNA that can mute genes. A clear tier score helps doctors watch high-risk patients closely and spare low-risk ones needless tests. Work of this sort turns a vague worry into a plan with steps matched to risk.
plos-pone-0001990:
Nicholas Cothros, Jeremy Wong, and Paul Gribble tested how the brain learns to reach against odd forces, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When people learn to move in a new force field, learning a second field often disrupts the first. A recent idea held that the brain treats such tasks as handling a novel object.

If so, a distinct feel in the hand, a haptic cue, might let the brain keep the two skills apart. As the title states, distinct cues did not reduce the interference. That null result trims a neat theory and pushes learning science toward other accounts of how skills collide.
plos-pone-0002090:
Shih-Hwa Chiou and co-authors found radiation-proof cells in a rare child brain tumor, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor is an extremely malignant tumor of the central nervous system that strikes infants and children. Recent work suggested that CD133 marks brain cancer stem-like cells, the seeds thought to regrow tumors.

The role of CD133 in this tumor was unclear. As the title states, the team identified CD133-positive cells that are radioresistant in these tumors. If a small seed set survives radiation, it may explain relapse, and it becomes the target that therapy must kill.
plos-pone-0002190:
Sonja Kleinlogel and Andrew White explored how shrimp see polarized light, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Animal eyes can detect brightness, color, and the direction of light waves, called polarization. Systems studied before theirs could sense up to four channels of linear polarization, paired against each other.

Mantis shrimps turned out to go further. The authors describe a visual system with a richer set of polarization channels than any known before. Such an eye can read patterns in light that are invisible to humans, and possibly to the shrimp's prey and rivals. The work marks one of the most advanced polarization vision systems found in nature.
plos-pone-0002290:
Keith Baverstock and Mauno Rönkkö wrote on how mammalian cells are regulated without changes to their DNA code, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Such epigenetic regulation decides which genes a cell uses to express its phenotype, its working form. Ionizing radiation can flip a normal cell into a genomic instability state, where copying the genome accurately becomes unreliable.

The authors set out a view of the mammalian cell as a regulated epigenetic system. In their account, that system, not DNA damage alone, explains how one radiation exposure can echo across many cell generations. The paper is a conceptual piece meant to reframe how instability after radiation is studied.
plos-pone-0002390:
Work from Yeka and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Adoke Yeka, Grant Dorsey, Moses R. Kamya, and others. Its subject is artemether-Lumefantrine versus Dihydroartemisinin-Piperaquine for Treating Uncomplicated Malaria: A Randomized Trial to Guide Policy in Uganda. Uganda recently adopted artemether-lumefantrine (AL) as the recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated malaria.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002490:
In 2008, Hubert and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Nicolas Hubert, Robert Hanner, Erling Holm, and others. Its subject is identifying Canadian Freshwater Fishes through DNA Barcodes. DNA barcoding aims to give a fast way to identify species with short molecular tags.

The tags come from one region of the mitochondrial COI gene, a standard marker for this work. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002590:
A research team led by Keil reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Matthias S. Keil, Agata Lapedriza, David Masip, and others. Its subject is preferred Spatial Frequencies for Human Face Processing Are Associated with Optimal Class Discrimination in the Machine. Psychophysical studies suggest that humans preferentially use a narrow band of low spatial frequencies for face recognition.

Here we asked whether artificial face recognition systems have an improved recognition performance at the same spatial frequencies as humans. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002690:
Steffanie A. Strathdee led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was differential effects of migration and deportation on HIV infection among male and female injection drug users in tijuana, mexico. Authorship is credited in the record to Steffanie A. Strathdee and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. HIV prevalence is rising, especially among high risk females in Tijuana, Baja California. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002790:
Xiao-Dong Fu led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was Extra-Nuclear signaling of progesterone receptor to breast cancer cell movement and invasion through the actin cytoskeleton. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Xiao-Dong Fu, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Progesterone plays a role in breast cancer development and progression but the effects on breast cancer cell movement or invasion have not been fully. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002890:
Shen Yon Toh, Jingyi Gong, Guoli Du and colleagues studied mice lacking the protein Fsp27 in PLOS ONE in 2008. Fsp27 sits on lipid droplets and helps fat cells store fat. The team wanted to know what it does for fat tissue growth, insulin response, and energy balance across the body.

In mice without Fsp27, white fat tissue gained traits more like brown fat, the kind that burns energy as heat. Mitochondrial activity, the cell's energy output, also rose. The paper links one storage protein to whole-body weight control, a topic with clear relevance to obesity research.
plos-pone-0002990:
Yan Cui, Ying Ying, Andrew van Hasselt and co-authors studied the tumor suppressor OPCML in 2008. Finding suppressor genes silenced by methylation helps reveal how tumors form and can yield biomarkers. Loss of DNA at chromosome region 11q25 is common in many tumors, including nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

OPCML sits in that region. The team reports it as a broad tumor suppressor across multiple carcinomas and lymphomas, frequently switched off by epigenetic means rather than mutation. Published in PLOS ONE, broad action across cancer types makes the gene notable for both biology and testing. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003090:
Marta García-Lecea, Igor Kondrychyn, Steven Fong and co-authors filmed choroid plexus development in zebrafish in 2008. The choroid plexus, part of the blood-brain barrier, makes cerebrospinal fluid. It protects and nurtures the brain and helps coordinate neuron migration during development, yet its own development was little studied.

In vivo analysis means watching formation in the living fish, made possible by zebrafish transparency. Published in PLOS ONE, the work fills a gap in how a vital brain structure is built. Disorders of cerebrospinal fluid start here, so the basics matter. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003190:
Bhavin R. Sheth, Davit Janvelyan and Murtuza Khan challenge a simple view of sleep and learning in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Emerging evidence suggests sleep plays a key role in procedural learning, in particular the continued growth of motor skill after first practice. The authors argue for a detailed look at the time course of performance across sleep on the finger-tapping task.

Their title, Practice Makes Imperfect, signals restorative effects of sleep on motor learning that are more complex than steady gains. Readers see performance tracked hour by hour rather than before and after alone. The work cautions against treating sleep benefit as a single simple boost.
plos-pone-0003290:
Debasish Sen, Thomas J. Deerinck, Mark H. Ellisman and colleagues test quantum dots for immune imaging in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Dendritic cells play a key role in initiating adaptive immune response by presenting antigen to T cells in lymphoid organs. The team investigate the potential of quantum dots as fluorescent nanoparticles for in vitro and in vivo imaging of dendritic cells, and as a particle-based delivery tool.

Readers get bright, stable labels for tracking cells that start immune responses. Tracking dendritic cells shows whether a vaccine reaches the right cells. Quantum dots could also carry antigens, linking tracking and delivery in one particle.
plos-pone-0003390:
Wenyun Zhou and co-authors linked diet and a gene to cancer protection in 2008. They studied mice fed diets with balanced or low methyl nutrients. Such nutrients feed chemical tagging that can switch genes off. The typical Western diet is often low in these nutrients.

Mice on the balanced diet were protected from cancer in these tests. That protection vanished when a gene called RIZ1 was missing. So the diet's benefit seems to need this gene in place. The study ties food chemistry to one named genetic gatekeeper. Food alone, in other words, did not explain the protection they saw in the mice.
plos-pone-0003490:
Manuel Comabella and co-authors scanned genomes for multiple sclerosis risk in this 2008 study. The disease slowly strips insulation from nerves in the brain and cord. Genes play a real part, with the HLA region the strongest known factor. The team pooled DNA to scan half a million markers at once.

Their pooled genome-wide scan flagged a new risk spot at 13q31.3. A locus is a fixed address on a chromosome. New addresses widen the search for disease mechanisms. Each one may point to a fresh drug target or test. MS strikes young adults and has no cure, so each new risk spot draws wide notice.
plos-pone-0003590:
Marie Åsberg, Åke Nygren, and Rosario Leopardi hunted blood markers of stress in women in this 2009 paper. Prolonged psychosocial stress is usually assessed through self-reports. The team aimed to find biochemical markers for screening and early help. They measured a panel of plasma compounds in the women.

The panel covered interleukins, interferon-gamma, and related immune signals. Novel markers could move stress detection toward lab tests. Objective measures may catch harmful stress before it deepens. The work targets women facing long-term psychosocial strain. Stress at work is the main target group the authors had in mind.
plos-pone-0003690:
Joset A. Etzel, Valeria Gazzola, and Christian Keysers published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Mirror neurons fire both when we act and when we watch others act. That finding supports simulation theory, the idea that we grasp others' actions by replaying them in our own motor system.

The authors tested the theory by sorting fMRI data across seeing and doing. If the same brain code serves both, a classifier trained on one should read the other. Their cross-modal test weighs a large claim about how social minds work, using data instead of debate.
plos-pone-0003790:
Isabelle Magalhaes, Donata R. Sizemore, Raija K. Ahmed, and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. BCG is the standard tuberculosis vaccine, and viral boosts might make its protection stronger and longer. The team tested a recombinant BCG prime followed by an adenovirus 35 vaccine boost.

In rhesus macaques, the prime-boost pairing drew strong antigen-specific T cell responses. Six animals received the recombinant priming vaccine in the skin, as the report describes. The strategy aims to broaden and prolong defense against tuberculosis beyond what BCG achieves alone. Monkeys are the closest test bed for human TB shots.
plos-pone-0003890:
Christiane Montag, Florian Schubert, Andreas Heinz, and co-authors linked a brain chemical to social thinking in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns the prefrontal cortex, at the front of the brain. Taking another person's view is a skill tied to that region. Weakness in that skill appears in disorders such as schizophrenia and autism.

The authors measured glutamate, a key signal chemical, in the prefrontal cortex. They compared those levels with how well people took mental perspectives. A link between the chemical and the skill hints at a biological base for empathy. It may guide later work on treatments for disorders of social thinking.
plos-pone-0003990:
Daria Osipova, Dora Hermes, and Ole Jensen linked two brain rhythms in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Brain oscillations in several frequency bands shape cognition. How those bands interact with each other stayed unclear. The authors focused on gamma power and posterior alpha activity.

They report gamma strength is phase-locked to the alpha rhythm at the back of the head. When alpha sits at one phase, gamma rises or falls predictably. Such coupling lets a slow rhythm organize faster local activity. The finding guides models of how brain regions coordinate. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004090:
Jason A. Pfister, Chi Ma, and Brad E. Morrison compared sirtuin enzymes in neuron survival in 2008. Sirtuins are seven NAD-dependent enzymes that regulate cell fate. SIRT1 was reported to protect neurons from death. SIRT2, in contrast, was reported to promote degeneration.

Their PLOS ONE article reports SIRT1 protection does not need its enzyme activity. The deacetylase function long defined SIRT1 proved unnecessary here. That surprise separates the protein's presence from its chemistry. Drug designers aiming at sirtuins must account for such effects. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004190:
Natalia Bondar and colleagues published this behaviour genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Repeated aggression can grow out of various psychiatric disorders. The team asked what repeated winning does to the brain of the winner.

They measured gene activity in the ventral tegmental area, a midbrain hub for reward, in male mice that had won fights again and again. Four genes tied to aggression were tracked: Th, Dat1, Snca, and Bdnf. The study shows how social victory itself can rewrite gene activity in the brain, possibly locking in more aggressive behaviour.
plos-pone-0004290:
Paweł Weber, Elżbieta Kula-Eversole, and Elżbieta Pyza published this circadian study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In the first optic neuropil of the fly's visual system, called the lamina, certain cells change size and shape across day and night. These are the monopolar cells L1 and L2, plus glial cells. The most pronounced changes are the daily size swings of these cells.

The authors examined the circadian control of dendrite morphology, the shape of the branching inputs of these neurons, in Drosophila. A visual system that rebuilds parts of itself daily must be tuned by the body clock, and this study maps that tuning.
plos-pone-0004390:
Saving species takes choices about which places matter most. One guide is how much shared evolution a place holds. Nathan Swenson's 2009 PLOS ONE paper works on that measure. It deals with phylogenetic diversity, the spread of species across the tree of life. It also deals with dispersion, how closely the species in a community are related.

Many family trees used in such work have unresolved branches. Swenson asked how that weak resolution bends the numbers. If a blurry tree gives the same answer as a sharp one, field teams can trust cheaper data. If not, they need care. The paper helps ecologists know how much tree detail their conclusions require.
plos-pone-0004490:
Brief starvation helped immune-deficient fruit flies survive bacterial infection, report Anthony Brown, Janina Baumbach, Peter Cook, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some people are born with immune defects that leave them open to life-threatening infections. These conditions show, by what is missing, which parts of immunity matter most. A key defense route is the Toll pathway and its relatives.

Flies with broken versions of that pathway are a model of such deficiency. Counter to intuition, a short period without food improved their survival against Gram-negative bacteria. The result suggests that the body's state, not just its immune parts, shapes the outcome of infection. It raises careful questions about nutrition and infection that animal work can now pursue.
plos-pone-0004590:
Mice missing an enzyme that chews up amyloid learned and remembered better in old age, a surprising result from Thomas Walther, Doris Albrecht, Matthias Becker, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme is neutral endopeptidase, also called neprilysin. It is considered one of the key enzymes in the initial degradation of amyloid beta, the protein that builds up in Alzheimer's disease.

Logic said removing the cleaner should worsen dementia-like symptoms. The team explored the impact of its deficiency on the initial development of such symptoms in mice. Instead, aged mice lacking it showed improved learning and memory, as the title reports. A paradox like that forces a rethink of how amyloid is handled, and warns against simple stories in Alzheimer's research.
plos-pone-0004690:
Géraldine Maro, Matthew Klassen, and Kang Shen studied how Wnt signals guide nerve fibers in a tiny worm, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Wnts are proteins that shape growth in many ways, from cell growth to cell fate. More work now shows they also steer growing nerve fibers in many species.

Yet how Wnt signals steer fibers in worms was still not clear. The team traced a Wnt path that needs a partner protein called beta catenin. They showed it guides fibers along the head to tail axis. The worm work helps explain nerve wiring rules shared across animals.
plos-pone-0004790:
Marco Thines argued that rare grass parasites connect Phytophthora and downy mildews, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Downy mildews and the root and leaf rots caused by Phytophthora rank among the most destructive plant pathogens. They have drawn much attention over the past two decades due to crop and forest losses worldwide each season.

A close evolutionary relationship between the groups was known, but a sharp divide was still drawn. Rare parasites of grasses bridge that gulf, Thines shows. The bridge reshapes the family tree of these pathogens. It may also hint at shared control strategies. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up.
plos-pone-0004890:
Yu-Wei Chang and colleagues reported three new structures of left handed RadA helical filaments, in PLOS ONE in 2009. RecA family proteins including microbe RecA, archaeal RadA, and eukaryotic Rad51 mediate homologous recombination essential for genome integrity. In presence of ATP these proteins bind single strand DNA forming right handed nucleoprotein filaments. Making the left handed RadA assemblies structurally surprising and mechanistically informative.

Flexibility of the N terminal domain is critical for activity. Alternative filament forms may store inactive protein. Recombination control prevents genome instability. Structures guide mutant design. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004990:
The gut moves food along with rhythmic squeezes. Nitric oxide is a key relax signal in that system. It passes messages between nerves and gut muscle. Hemant Thatte, Xue He and Raj Goyal imaged it directly. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They watched nitric oxide during neuromuscular transmission in the gut.

Impaired nitrergic signaling is implicated in gut disorders of all kinds. Until now, its role rested on indirect functional studies. Direct imaging confirms nitric oxide as the messenger. The pictures show where and when it acts. The work gives researchers a firmer basis for studying gut motility diseases.
plos-pone-0005090:
Peroxisomes are the cell's detox workshops. Small molecules must flow across their membrane constantly. The gates for that traffic were an enigma. Aare Rokka and colleagues identified one in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied the protein Pxmp2 in mice. Disrupting its gene revealed its role.

Pxmp2 forms a channel in the peroxisomal membrane. Solutes pass through it between the cell and the workshop. The finding names the doorway for small-solute traffic. It ends a long-standing gap in peroxisome biology. Channels like this decide what the organelle can process. The work may matter for peroxisomal diseases. When the workshop's gates fail, toxins build up.
plos-pone-0005190:
Cholera toxin is best known as the cause of cholera's severe diarrhea, but in small doses it is also a strong vaccine booster. Given through the nose, it was thought to push immunity toward one set type of response. Lee and colleagues reported a different result in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Nasal cholera toxin led instead to a response led by Th17 cells, a helper T cell type tied to defense at body surfaces. The response also covered other antigens given at the same time. The finding changes how vaccine makers should think about this booster for nasal vaccines.
plos-pone-0005290:
Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited disease that kills retinal cells and leads to blindness. Gene therapy could help if a healthy gene can be delivered to the retina safely. Cai and colleagues used compacted DNA nanoparticles for that delivery in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Earlier work showed these tiny DNA packets drive strong gene activity after injection under the mouse retina. Delivering a therapeutic gene this way partly rescued retinal structure and function in a mouse model of the disease. A partial rescue in animals is a step toward human trials.
plos-pone-0005390:
ALS, the most frequent adult motor neuron disease, involves hypermetabolism tied to faulty muscle energy use. Whether muscle faults are a side effect or a driver was unknown. Dupuis and colleagues uncoupled muscle mitochondria in mice and reported the result in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Uncoupling in muscle dismantled the neuromuscular junction, where nerve meets muscle. It also triggered distal degeneration of motor neurons, damage starting at the far end. Muscle-first damage reframes ALS research, suggesting the disease may begin outside the neurons that die. If the first harm starts in muscle, drugs that guard muscle may slow this disease. They may act at a stage when nerve drugs come too late to save the cells that move and breathe.
plos-pone-0005490:
Kusdiantoro Mohamad and colleagues traced the roots of Indonesian cattle in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Two kinds of cattle feed into the herds there: zebu from mainland Asia and the local banteng. Crosses between them can breed, though male offspring of one cross are sterile.

Local breeds were long thought to mix both kinds, but that had never been proven with gene data. The team read DNA from many breeds to test the old claim. Knowing the true mix helps protect rare local breeds and guides breeding for hardy cattle suited to the islands.
plos-pone-0005590:
Sebastian Schuck and co-authors hunted T cell targets of hidden tuberculosis in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many people carry the tuberculosis germ quietly, without illness. T cell responses to germ proteins made during sleep, waking, and regrowth could mark that hidden state.

The team built a test that boosts T cells twice in the lab, then reads their signals. The test picked out responses to proteins tied to the germ's life stages. A reliable marker of hidden infection would help target preventive treatment to those who need it. Hidden infection is common worldwide, and treating it wisely depends on tests that can truly find it.
plos-pone-0005690:
Mary Campbell and colleagues asked in 2009 whether people with HIV can catch a second strain of the virus on top of the first. This event, called superinfection, has been seen both early and late in infection. Its risks are still not well known.

The team followed couples in which both partners had HIV, during the era of modern drug therapy. They checked whether one partner picked up the other's strain over time. The answer matters for counseling: partners who share the same status may still face risk from each other's virus. Clear data helps clinics give honest, precise advice.
plos-pone-0005790:
Martin Brinkhof, Mar Pujades-Rodriguez, and Matthias Egger pooled studies in 2009 on what happens to HIV patients who vanish from treatment programs. In poorer countries, many patients lost to follow-up simply stop coming. Programs cannot tell whether they moved, stopped drugs, or died.

The review and meta-analysis gathered mortality data on those lost patients across studies. A fair share, it turns out, had died, which changes how programs should judge their success. Counting only patients who stay paints too rosy a picture. The paper pushes programs to trace the missing, and offers the numbers to plan with.
plos-pone-0005890:
Rebecca Robey and co-authors mapped in 2009 how T cells answer the herpesvirus behind Kaposi's sarcoma. This virus causes the most common cancer in untreated HIV and AIDS patients. How well T cells control it was only partly characterized.

Responses from both CD8 and CD4 T cells skewed toward the virus's early and late lytic proteins, the team found. That skew shows which viral parts the immune system sees best during its copying phase. Vaccine and therapy design can aim at those visible parts. The characterization fills a gap for a virus whose control fails catastrophically when immunity drops.
plos-pone-0005990:
Bladder and kidney infections are common in women, and habit alone does not explain who gets them. Thomas Hawn, Delia Scholes, Shuying Li and colleagues asked in 2009 whether genes play a part. Their PLOS ONE study tests variants in Toll-like receptor genes, the sensors that first spot germs, for links to urinary tract infection in adult women.

If a sensor variant weakens the first alarm, germs may gain a foothold more often. A genetic risk factor of this kind would sit beside known habit-based risks like sexual activity. The study opens the way to risk advice shaped to the person, and to a better grasp of why some women face these infections again and again.
plos-pone-0006090:
The retina's first layer talks back to the light catchers above it. Iris Fahrenfort, Marvin Steijaert, Trijntje Sjoerdsma and colleagues weighed two rival accounts of that talk in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies feedback from horizontal cells to cones in the vertebrate retina, a signal that shapes how the eye answers contrast and color.

One account credits channels called hemichannels; the other credits a change in acidity at the synapse that alters the cone's calcium current. The title backs both: hemichannel-mediated and pH-based feedback each play a part. Settling a two-camp dispute with room for both sides gives vision science a fuller circuit to work with.
plos-pone-0006190:
Australia has yielded far fewer dinosaur fossils than other continents of its size. Scott Hocknull and colleagues describe new dinosaurs from Winton in Queensland in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The bones date to the middle Cretaceous period, near its latest Albian stage, when dinosaurs still ruled the land.

Most Australian dinosaurs were known only from scraps with unclear family placement. The Winton finds add fuller material to that thin record. Richer fossils let scientists place Australian dinosaurs on the family tree with more care. They also hint at what lived in ancient inland Australia. Each solid find makes the continent's lost world easier to picture.
plos-pone-0006290:
When the transport protein transthyretin misfolds, it can pile into amyloid fibres that damage organs. Satheesh Palaninathan and colleagues designed blockers of that process in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Earlier work showed that holding the protein in its healthy four-part shape stops amyloid formation.

The team synthesised new inhibitor compounds, tested their biological activity, and solved X-ray structures of them bound to the protein. Seeing exactly how a blocker grips its target guides better versions. The compounds add options for amyloid diseases linked to transthyretin. Structure-guided design is the thread running through the work.
plos-pone-0006390:
Bats are famous for hearing, but their eyes carry a surprise colour channel. Brigitte Mueller and colleagues found ultraviolet-sensitive cone photoreceptors in bat eyes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Mammalian retinas hold rods for night vision and cones for daylight and colour; most mammals have two cone types with pigments peaking at short wavelengths.

Bat cones tuned to ultraviolet extend their colour range beyond human vision. UV sensitivity may aid navigation or foraging at dusk. The finding revises the picture of bats as purely sound-guided animals. Their visual world is richer than assumed.
plos-pone-0006490:
Bryan Glaser, Veit Bergendahl, Larry Anthony, and colleagues measured protein binding under salty conditions for PLOS ONE in 2009. Studying protein-protein interactions is increasingly important for understanding how cells regulate their processes. The team quantified how strongly bacterial RNA polymerase core enzyme binds two sigma factors, σ70 and σ32. Sigma factors guide the polymerase to the right genes.

They varied salt levels and used luminescence resonance energy transfer to measure binding. Salt dependence reveals what forces hold the complex together. That detail matters for models of gene switching in bacteria. It also shows how a physical method can give hard numbers on fleeting molecular contacts.
plos-pone-0006590:
Michael Gurven and co-authors studied artery aging in a lean farming people in PLOS ONE in 2009. Artery aging is well described in rich, industrial lands. It is hardly described in groups with little access to modern medicine or drugs. The team checked health and artery aging among lean forager-farmers who live in a very different way.

Their title says that inflammation and infection do not drive artery aging or heart risk factors in this group. That result challenges the idea that long-term inflammation must harden arteries. Way of life seems to change the rule. This group gives heart research a useful contrast to industrial life.
plos-pone-0006690:
Sylvie Faucher and colleagues built a blood test for a soluble immune receptor in PLOS ONE in 2009. The receptor is the alpha chain of the interleukin-7 receptor. Interleukin-7 is a cytokine that T cells need to develop and survive. It binds a receptor made of two chains on the cell surface. Levels of the receptor's shed alpha chain can reflect immune states.

The team developed a quantitative bead capture assay for human plasma. Their method measures soluble receptor alpha with beads that catch the molecule. A reliable measure matters because receptor levels often fall in illness. Doctors and researchers could use the assay to track immune health. It also supports studies of diseases where T cells decline.
plos-pone-0006790:
Jesus F. Dominguez and co-authors built new calorimetry for newborn rodent pups in PLOS ONE in 2009. Studying metabolism in newborn rodents was limited by technology. Pups breathe tiny volumes at rest. Measuring oxygen use and carbon dioxide output reliably is hard. Respiratory ratio calculations suffer from the same small signals.

Their indirect calorimetry technology analyzes metabolism in individual pups. Each pup can now be followed on its own. That allows developmental studies of metabolic function. Researchers can watch metabolism mature day by day. Better measurement may reveal how early metabolism shapes later obesity or disease.
plos-pone-0006890:
Jicheng Hu and colleagues examined how a fly protein controls a sex-deciding RNA cut in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is SNF, the fly version of general splicing factors U1A and U2B. SNF is essential in Drosophila sex determination. Splicing decides which exons a message keeps. Sex in flies hinges on splicing of the sex-lethal message.

Besides binding U1 RNA, SNF binds polyuridine tracts beside a male-specific exon. That second binding gives it a novel functional mechanism. The structure and mechanism explain how SNF steers the sex decision. It is a clear case of a general factor gaining a specific regulatory job.
plos-pone-0006990:
Anne-lie Ståhl, Lisa Sartz, Anders Nelsson, and colleagues studied clotting in a kidney syndrome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hemolytic uremic syndrome can follow infection with certain E. coli. Tiny clots form in small vessels and damage the kidneys. Clumps of platelets and white blood cells in the blood help drive that clotting.

The team exposed blood cells to Shiga toxin and bacterial lipopolysaccharide. Both triggered platelet-leukocyte clumps and release of tissue factor, a clot starter. The result names a concrete mechanism behind the syndrome's thrombosis. Blocking that pathway could protect the kidneys of affected children.
plos-pone-0007090:
Jun Sung Lee, Il Shin Kim, Jung Hwan Kim, and colleagues measured receptor uptake in cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. When a signal molecule binds its receptor, the receptor is pulled inside the cell. Adaptor protein 2 and a crew of endocytic proteins run that uptake. The team studied the epidermal growth factor receptor, EGFR.

They measured the kinetics of EGFR endocytosis. A protein called PLD1 regulated the process by associating with part of the adaptor. Self-regulating uptake keeps signaling from overshooting. Faulty uptake is a known feature of many cancers driven by EGFR.
plos-pone-0007190:
Abbas Shirinifard, J. Scott Gens, Benjamin L. Zaitlen, and colleagues built a three-dimensional computer model of tumor growth in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper simulates many cells at once. It also includes angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels that feed a tumor.

At first, simulated tumor cells multiply by taking oxygen from nearby vessels. As the tumor grows, its need for oxygen changes its shape and spread. The authors present a generic model that others can adapt to specific tumor types and host tissues. Cancer modelers get a flexible starting framework.
plos-pone-0007290:
Gloria Terrados, Jean-Pascal Capp, Yvan Canitrot, and colleagues characterized a risky variant of a DNA repair enzyme in 2009. DNA polymerase lambda helps repair DNA. It likely works in base excision repair and in joining broken DNA ends, two systems that keep chromosomes stable during cell life.

The authors describe a natural variant of the human enzyme. They report that the variant promotes chromosomal instability by compromising end joining. A single inherited variant can thus raise genome damage. Their finding matters for understanding why some people accumulate chromosome changes linked to cancer.
plos-pone-0007390:
Gregory M. Erickson, Oliver W. M. Rauhut, Zhonghe Zhou, and colleagues measured growth in the oldest known bird in 2009. Archaeopteryx is the oldest and most primitive known bird. Many scientists believed its growth and energy physiology were inherited entirely from non-avian dinosaurs, making it slow growing like a reptile.

That hypothesis makes testable predictions about its long bones. The authors examine bone growth in Archaeopteryx specimens. They reconcile its slow growth with bird ancestry. Their PLOS ONE analysis clarifies when faster, more bird-like growth physiology evolved in the dinosaur-to-bird transition.
plos-pone-0007490:
Fumio Matsuda and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on quality control in metabolomics, the science of naming small molecules in samples. Researchers match precise masses from a spectrometer against chemical databases. A match suggests an elemental composition for the unknown molecule. But different molecules can share nearly the same mass, so some matches are simply wrong. The team built a way to count those errors.

Their method estimates the false discovery rate of composition searches. Knowing the error rate tells researchers how much to trust each identification. Without it, long lists of named molecules can hide many mistakes. With it, studies can set honest thresholds for what counts as found. The paper is a measurement of measurement itself, and every metabolomics lab can use it.
plos-pone-0007590:
David Courtin and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how children in Africa gain protection from malaria. Antibodies aimed at proteins on the parasite's surface are thought to drive that slow-won protection. Some types of IgG, the kinds that help cells kill, seem to matter most. The team measured the antibody response of African children to those surface proteins. They tracked both how much antibody each child made and which types, then watched who stayed free of malaria.

Amount and type together matched real protection. Children with the right amounts of the right types fared better against the parasite. That pairing gives vaccine makers a clear target to aim at. A vaccine must copy not just any antibody response, but this one. Field work like this sets out what success should look like before trials start. The marks of natural protection are the blueprint.
plos-pone-0007690:
Irina Antonova and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks how brain cells strengthen their connections. In the hippocampus, a brain area tied to memory, lasting strengthening is called long-term potentiation. It unfolds in stages that mirror the stages of learning.

The authors focused on the late stage of that process in rat neurons. They found a fast and lasting rise in sites where new synapses, the junctions between cells, can be built. That growth in ready sites may be one way the brain makes a memory endure.
plos-pone-0007790:
Joost Kreijtz and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a vaccine against H5N1 bird flu in mice. Human infections with H5N1, reported often since 2003, are frequently deadly. A pandemic strain could emerge from these viruses, so vaccines are wanted.

The vaccine uses a harmless carrier virus, MVA, fitted with H5N1 parts. A single immunization at low dose protected mice. Protection crossed clades, meaning it covered differing virus branches. Cross-clade cover at low dose is exactly what pandemic stockpiles need. The study supports MVA as a platform for bird flu vaccines.
plos-pone-0007890:
Wayne Hancock and Engin Ozkaynak published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It maps how the protein Foxp3 gets into the cell nucleus in mice. Foxp3 is a transcription factor that regulatory T cells need to work. Those cells control self-reactive T cells and prevent autoimmunity.

When regulatory T cells are activated, Foxp3 levels rise. The protein must reach the nucleus to switch genes on. The authors found three distinct domains that contribute to that nuclear transport. Knowing the entry route in detail helps explain Foxp3 defects. Such defects sit behind severe immune disorders in children.
plos-pone-0007990:
Nicholas Haley and colleagues exposed deer to waste from sick herds and waited, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The illness is chronic wasting disease, a fatal prion disease of deer and kin. Prions are misfolded proteins that spread the misfolding to healthy ones.

Deer that took in urine and droppings from sick deer carried hidden infection long after standard tests read clean. The germ can thus lurk and spread while herds look healthy. The finding urges longer, sharper testing where the disease is known, and care with how waste from sick areas is handled.
plos-pone-0008090:
Fredrik Barrenas and colleagues mapped where complex disease genes sit in cell networks in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genome-wide scans had listed hundreds of genes tied to common diseases. Past network studies leaned on single-gene diseases or cancer and carried a bias toward well-studied genes.

The new map used the scan-based list, which is fairer, and charted how those genes link to each other. Their places in the network hint at how small faults add up to illness. The map also helps pick which genes in a crowded scan result deserve the next lab test.
plos-pone-0008190:
Frances E. Lock and Neil A. Hotchin studied skin cell development in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Human skin is built from layers of cells called keratinocytes. Healthy skin needs a tight balance between cell growth and final maturation. Two related proteins, ROCK1 and ROCK2, help control that balance. The authors asked whether each one has a distinct role.

Their work separates the jobs of the two proteins in keratinocyte differentiation. Knowing which protein does what matters for understanding skin repair and disease. It also matters for drugs that block these proteins. The study gives a clearer map of how skin cells mature.
plos-pone-0008290:
Lawrence Rajendran and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about white blood cells and how they move. These cells crawl to the scent of a wound or a germ. That crawl is key in a sore, in fights with germs, and as the blood system first forms in the womb. To crawl well, a cell must make a front and a back. In a cell at rest, most parts that drive this shape sit spread out in a plain way.

The team found that proteins named flotillins help both young and old blood cells take that front-back shape. When a call to move comes, these proteins shift to one side of the cell. That shift may set up the crawl. The work helps show how immune cells get where they are most in need.
plos-pone-0008390:
Sawsan Napthine and colleagues studied viral protein production in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Murine norovirus is a calicivirus that infects mice. Its minor structural protein, VP2, is believed to be made by an unusual mechanism. After finishing one reading frame, the ribosome restarts at the next instead of leaving. Scientists call the process termination-reinitiation, and it depends on the stop codon.

The team examined expression of VP2 through this strategy. Confirming the mechanism explains how the virus balances its proteins. Similar strategies appear in other viruses, making the work broadly useful. It adds detail to how viral genomes are decoded.
plos-pone-0008490:
Alexander Pasternak and co-authors study HIV that persists on treatment in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Standard care is combination antiretroviral therapy, or cART. Treatment counts as a success when virus in blood falls below detection. Yet therapy still fails in many patients after that apparent success. Virus hidden in cells may predict who will fail. The team measure unspliced HIV RNA inside cells.

Cell levels of that RNA predict therapy outcome in their patients. All had undetectable virus in blood at the start. A cell test thus adds warning that blood tests miss. It could flag patients who need closer watch or a change in drugs.
plos-pone-0008590:
Kamakshi Sureka and co-authors find a new control on germ cell division in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Germ cells divide with help of a multi-protein complex. Parts must bind each other for division to proceed well. Little was known about those bindings in mycobacteria, the TB germ group. The team find a binding between FtsZ, a core division protein, and FipA. That binding depends on a phosphate tag on one of the proteins.

The tag thus acts as a switch for division in these germs. When the tag is present, the two proteins bind as needed. That new role widens the known control circuit. It suggests fresh targets for drugs against TB germs.
plos-pone-0008690:
Amadou Diallo, Ndjido Kane, Zahra Agharbaoui, and coworkers moved a wheat gene into a small test plant. Their findings appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, TaVRN2, helps wheat hold off flowering until winter passes. Cold and day length control it in its home plant. The team placed it in Arabidopsis, a weed used widely in labs.

Plants carrying the wheat gene flowered later than normal plants. Surprisingly, they also survived freezing better. Salt, heat, drying, and wounding could switch the gene on as well. A flowering brake that doubles as a stress guard could interest crop breeders facing colder snaps.
plos-pone-0008790:
Irina Krasnova, Zuzana Justinova, Bruce Ladenheim, and colleagues let rats dose themselves with methamphetamine. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Meth is a widely abused stimulant. Forced injections in earlier studies drained dopamine and serotonin from brains. Self-administration is closer to human addiction, though. The team wanted the chemistry left behind by voluntary use. Brain regions for reward and habit were the focus.

Rats that self-administered meth showed lasting changes in dopamine terminals. Both striatum and cortex carried the marks. Persistent damage may underlie craving and relapse. The model helps test treatments for meth addiction's long shadow.
plos-pone-0008890:
Chia-Chien Hsieh, Blanca Hernández-Ledesma, Hyun Jin Jeong, and colleagues paired a soy peptide with a bodyguard protein. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Breast cancer rates are lower in many Asian countries than in the West. Soy-rich diets are one suspected reason. A soy peptide called lunasin shows cancer-preventive promise in the lab. Digestive enzymes, though, can destroy it before it works.

A soy protease inhibitor shielded lunasin from digestion. With the bodyguard present, more intact lunasin survived to act. Two soy parts thus play complementary roles in prevention. The pairing explains how whole soy foods may outperform isolated parts.
plos-pone-0008990:
Sylvie Tondeur and co-authors mapped gene messages in human blood-forming cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Blood stem cells, marked by the protein CD34, grow into all blood cell types. As they mature, the cells gain special skills like moving through tissue and fighting germs. Genes can be spliced in alternate ways to make varied protein versions.

The team charted splicing across the full set of genes these cells express. Movement and immune-response genes showed especially heavy alternate splicing. That editing helps a plain stem cell become a patrolling immune cell. The map is a reference for anyone studying blood diseases or bone-marrow transplants.
plos-pone-0009090:
Helen Jenkins, Rosie Woodroffe, and Christl Donnelly studied badger culling and cattle TB. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2010. Badgers carry tuberculosis that spills into British cattle herds. The Randomised Badger Culling Trial had tested widespread culling across large areas. Culling gave modest drops in cattle TB while it ran.

The team followed what happened after culling stopped. Benefits faded over time once the pressure was removed. Knowing the decay rate matters for judging culling's true value. Policy on badgers and cattle TB remains one of Britain's thorniest farm debates.
plos-pone-0009190:
Junwei Yang and co-authors published this sepsis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sepsis is a dangerous whole-body reaction to infection. A fat-like signal called platelet-activating factor, or PAF, helps drive that reaction. An enzyme in blood, PAF acetylhydrolase, breaks PAF down and calms the response.

In human sepsis patients, activity of that enzyme usually falls. The team asked whether the same drop happens in Mongolian gerbils given bacterial toxin to trigger sepsis. They found that enzyme activity in the blood decreased in this gerbil model. A matching animal pattern makes the gerbil a useful stand-in for testing sepsis treatments.
plos-pone-0009290:
Moran Valensi-Kurtz and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diseases of the peripheral nerves are hard to study without the right cells. No good lab model of human peripheral neurons existed. Human embryonic stem cells, which can become many cell types, offered a possible source.

The team coaxed those stem cells into peripheral nervous system neurons. They produced an enriched population of the cells in the lab. Such cells give researchers a platform for studying peripheral neuropathies directly. They could also serve to test drugs on human nerve cells instead of guessing from animal results.
plos-pone-0009390:
Nancie Archin and co-authors published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV hides in resting CD4 cells, untouched by standard therapy. One hope was valproic acid, a drug that can wake hidden virus so therapy can kill it. Stronger antiretroviral treatment was added in the same strategy, called intensification.

The team measured leftover virus in the blood and infection in resting cells. Neither intensification nor valproic acid produced a sustained drop. A negative result like this saves patients from regimens that add burden without benefit. It also redirects cure research toward stronger ways of waking the reservoir.
plos-pone-0009490:
Morgan Price, Paramvir Dehal, and Adam Arkin updated a widely used software tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. Biologists build family trees from DNA sequences to show how species relate. New data sets hold hundreds of thousands of sequences. Their tool, FastTree, builds near best trees at that scale. The new version aims for better accuracy at the same speed.

Changes to how the tool joins and refines branches raised the quality of its trees. Tests on large alignments showed gains without a loss of speed. FastTree 2 lets researchers handle data sets once thought too big for careful tree building. It has since become a standard tool in the field.
plos-pone-0009590:
Scott Widenmaier and co-authors tested a gut hormone mimic in diabetic rats in PLOS ONE in 2010. The hormone GIP is released after eating. It helps the pancreas's beta cells work and survive. It also promotes fat storage, which limits its use as a drug. The team used a shortened mimic of GIP. They gave it to rat models of diabetes and measured the effects.

The mimic protected beta cells from dying. It also improved their function and the animals' blood sugar control. Those gains came with the hope of fewer fat related drawbacks. The study offers a refined lead for diabetes care built on a natural gut signal.
plos-pone-0009690:
Nerve growth factors, called neurotrophins, do more than guide growing nerves. Fariba Rezaee and colleagues showed in 2010 that they also steer immune signals in bone marrow support cells. Their PLOS ONE study centered on IL-6, a signal protein tied to inflammation.

The team found that neurotrophins change how much IL-6 the marrow stromal cells release. The change ran through the MAPK pathway, a chain of signals inside the cell. That cross-talk links the nervous system with the marrow that makes blood cells. It suggests nerves help tune inflammation in ways doctors had not mapped.
plos-pone-0009790:
Brain imaging work by Lichan Liu and Andreas Ioannides, published in PLOS ONE in 2010, tracks how fast the brain sorts facial emotions. Seven men viewed happy, fearful, and neutral faces shown in the center or at the edges of sight.

Using a method that records magnetic fields from the brain, the authors found emotion sorting done well within a tenth of a second. For faces in the center, one groove area acted first, then the amygdala, the brain's alarm center, then a front area. Faces at the edges used a different order. The results suggest two linked routes, one for fast alarm and one for careful judgment.
plos-pone-0009890:
Computer simulations can watch a protein fold, but reading the flood of data is hard. Aruna Rajan, Lydia Freddolino, and Klaus Schulten pushed past the standard way of sorting that data. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The standard way is clustering, grouping similar shapes from a molecular dynamics trajectory. The test case was the villin headpiece, a small protein that folds very fast. Going beyond clustering revealed finer steps in how the headpiece folds. Better analysis tools help turn simulations into real folding stories. Folding decides what a protein can do.
plos-pone-0009990:
Small heat shock proteins guard other proteins when cells are stressed by heat. Pierre Poulain, Jean-Christophe Gelly, and Delphine Flatters examined the lone form of these guards. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Heat shock proteins were first found after heat exposure.

Detection and architecture means finding the monomers and describing their build. A monomer is a single protein unit, before it joins partners in a cluster. These proteins usually work in large clusters, so the lone form is easy to miss. Knowing the unit's shape explains how clusters assemble under stress.
plos-pone-0010090:
Julien Pelletier is first author on a 2010 PLOS ONE study of smell in the southern house mosquito, Culex quinquefasciatus. The species spreads West Nile virus and other diseases. Its smell receptors, proteins in the antennae that detect odors, were still unknown, unlike those of two other mosquito species.

The team found a family of about one hundred and fifty-eight candidate smell receptor genes. They tested one antenna receptor in frog egg cells and found it highly sensitive to indole, a scent that draws females to egg-laying sites. Its response matched a real nerve cell type in the mosquito. The receptor offers a target for screening new attractants or repellents.
plos-pone-0010190:
The authors were Luqing Zheng, Zhiqiang Cheng, Chunxiang Ai, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study targeted iron shortage through rice. Polished rice feeds more than half the world's people, yet holds little usable iron. Iron shortage harms health widely, and adding iron that bodies can absorb is hard through breeding alone so far.

The team identified nicotianamine, a plant compound, as an enhancer of iron availability from rice. They describe it as a novel promoter of iron use in humans. Enhancing the grain itself could prevent deficiency in populations that depend on rice daily.
plos-pone-0010290:
Dae Kim, Michel Tremblay, and John DiGiovanni studied skin cell responses to ultraviolet light in 2010. A signaling protein, Stat3, loses its phosphate tag quickly when skin cells meet UVB rays. Blocking that removal protected cells from UVB-induced death and restored Stat3 levels. That pattern implied an enzyme that strips phosphate was at work in the response.

The team showed three such enzymes cooperate in the rapid dephosphorylation of Stat3. They acted in keratinocytes, the main cells of the skin surface. Their PLOS ONE work maps an early step in how skin reacts to sun damage.
plos-pone-0010390:
Yo Shinoda and colleagues watched young rat brain cells lose connections on purpose, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Growing brains first make too many synapses, the links between nerve cells. Extra or wrong links are then pruned away, sharpening the network. Healthy pruning is needed for normal development. How a link is chosen for removal was not well understood.

Repeated weak signaling, a pattern called LTD, made synapses vanish for good in their tests. That offers a mechanism: links that keep failing may be deleted. The same process, if misdirected, could matter in brain disorders. Pruning is a quiet kind of brain construction. This study helps explain how the brain edits itself as it grows.
plos-pone-0010490:
Carina Cesar and colleagues studied early HIV drug changes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their sites spanned the Caribbean and Latin America. Treatment rollout there had grown fast, covering most eligible patients by 2007. No multi-country study had yet measured early regimen changes. Changes can signal side effects, drug shortages, or failing therapy. The team pooled patient cohorts from seven sites.

Rates and reasons differed across sites, showing local conditions matter. Knowing why regimens change helps programs fix the fixable causes, like supply gaps. Early changes carry costs and can limit later options. This regional snapshot gave health planners their first shared baseline. It also highlights where support for new patients is weakest.
plos-pone-0010590:
Qibin Qi and colleagues tested a known obesity gene in a Chinese Han population, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Variants in the gene PCSK1 had already been tied to obesity in European groups. The question was whether the same link held in a different ancestry.

The team typed two closely linked PCSK1 variants in a large community sample. They then compared the variants with weight and related traits. Checking findings across populations matters, because a marker that works in one group may fail in another. Results like these shape how genetic risk tests should be built and used.
plos-pone-0010690:
Thomas Geisbert and colleagues built a primate model of Nipah virus disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nipah is an emerging virus that causes deadly brain and lung disease. Between forty and seventy-five of every hundred known patients have died, and no vaccine or drug is approved for people.

The team infected nonhuman primates and tracked the illness closely. The animals developed fast, severe disease much like the worst human cases. A faithful model lets scientists test vaccines and drugs before human use. For a virus with outbreak potential and no treatment, that test bed is an urgent piece of preparation.
plos-pone-0010790:
Karen Beenken and colleagues mapped a tug-of-war between two regulators in staph bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Staphylococcus aureus builds biofilms, slimy fortresses that resist drugs and immune attack. Two regulators pull in opposite directions: sarA favors biofilm growth, while agr restrains it. Their interaction had therapeutic interest because blocking biofilms could reopen infections to treatment.

Mutant tests showed how each regulator's effect depends on the other. Changing one shifted what the other could do. The pair forms a coupled control circuit, not two lone switches. Any anti-biofilm drug must reckon with that coupling, or the circuit may route around the block.
plos-pone-0010890:
Claire Bertelli, François Collyn, Antony Croxatto and co-authors published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Waddlia chondrophila is a bacterium linked to miscarriage in women and abortion in farm animals. It belongs to the chlamydia family, whose members live only inside host cells and are hard to study because they cannot easily be genetically altered.

Using two sequencing technologies, the team assembled the first full genome for this bacterial family branch, a chromosome of about two million letters plus a small plasmid. Unlike classical chlamydia, its genome is peppered with repeated stretches, hinting at a more restless history. Bertelli and colleagues open a window onto how these hidden bacteria live and cause harm, giving researchers targets for diagnosis and future experiments.
plos-pone-0010990:
Haitske Graveland, Jaap Wagenaar, Hans Heesterbeek and co-authors published this farm health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A strain of drug-resistant staph bacteria, MRSA ST398, emerged in livestock and in the farmers who handle them. What drives carriage in animals and people was not fully known, so the team surveyed veal calf farms across the Netherlands.

About a hundred randomly chosen farms were visited over a year. Farmers answered questionnaires and gave nasal swabs, and thousands of calves were swabbed as well. Graveland and colleagues linked human carriage to how antibiotics were used on the farm and to hygiene practices. Their cross-sectional evidence gives regulators concrete levers: antimicrobial habits and farm cleanliness, rather than chance, shape whether a resistant germ colonizes both calves and the families raising them.
plos-pone-0011090:
Symmonds, Emmanuel, Drew and colleagues reported human behavior research in PLOS ONE in 2010. They tested whether being hungry or full changes the choices people make when money is at risk. The body state, they reasoned, might sway choices that seem purely mental.

Their results showed that metabolic state did shift choices under risk. Hungry and fed people did not judge the same bets in the same way. That link between body and mind matters for how scientists study choice. It also warns that lab tests of decision making should note when subjects last ate.
plos-pone-0011190:
Ahmed, Creanga, Gillespie and colleagues analyzed mothers' health care use in PLOS ONE in 2010. Across developing countries, they examined how wealth, schooling and a woman's say in decisions affect whether she uses maternal health services. Those services protect both mother and baby around birth.

All three factors shaped service use, with schooling and empowerment playing strong roles. That means clinics alone cannot fix low use; social conditions matter too. Raising women's education and standing may save mothers' lives as surely as new facilities. The analysis gives policy makers evidence to invest in women beyond the health sector.
plos-pone-0011290:
Xue, Liu, Gao and colleagues built a prediction tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. Proteins gain a nitric oxide tag at specific sites, changing their behavior in cell signaling. Finding those sites by lab work is slow. The team developed software, GPS-SNO, that predicts likely tag sites from protein sequence.

Their modified algorithm improved prediction accuracy for this tag type. Fast prediction lets biologists choose the most promising sites for lab checks. That speeds mapping of signaling networks that rely on this tag. The tool is freely useful to systems biology groups studying how cells switch proteins on and off.
plos-pone-0011390:
Cristiano Nogueira and colleagues surveyed Brazil's most range-limited freshwater fishes in 2010. Brazil holds an extraordinary variety of river fish, and many species live in just one stream system and nowhere else. Such narrow ranges make a species easy to wipe out with a single dam, farm, or pollution event, yet these fishes had never been mapped together.

By compiling where the most restricted species cluster, the team showed planners which waters hold the most irreplaceable life. Protecting those hotspots first gives the greatest return for limited conservation funds. The study also serves as a warning list: each mapped species is a candidate for urgent assessment. For Brazilian freshwater conservation, it turns scattered records into a clear order of priorities.
plos-pone-0011490:
Marcelo Kitahara and co-authors rebuilt the family tree of stony corals in 2010 from DNA evidence. Scleractinia, the stony corals, build the world's tropical reefs, but their classification rested on skeleton shapes that can mislead, since unrelated corals converge on similar forms. The team used mitochondrial CO1 sequences, a standard DNA barcode region, across a comprehensive set of corals.

The resulting tree sorts reef-builders into groups that reflect true evolutionary kinship rather than surface likeness. Several traditional groupings did not survive the DNA test. A reliable tree matters well beyond naming: conservation triage, reef ecology, and studies of how corals respond to warming seas all assume the groups are real. The paper gives those fields a firmer map of who is related to whom among reef's chief builders.
plos-pone-0011590:
Han-Ching Tseng and co-authors studied how natural killer cells treat stem cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Natural killer cells are immune guards that destroy abnormal cells. The team asked whether these guards attack stem cells more than the mature cells that stem cells later become.

They found that stem cells were indeed killed more readily than their mature offspring. When mature cells were pushed back toward a stem-like state, they again became targets. That pattern matters for stem cell therapy, since transplanted cells may be destroyed by the patient's own immune guards before they can help.
plos-pone-0011690:
Mark Bi and co-authors studied a single DNA variant in the ARIC population study, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The variant, in a gene that regulates the sugar-processing enzyme glucokinase, had been linked to higher blood fats and better blood sugar control in mostly European populations. Whether it also predicted future disease needed testing.

Using long-term ARIC data, the team related the variant to metabolic traits, new diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Their analysis connects one DNA letter to several chronic conditions over time. Such links help explain how a sugar regulator can raise one risk while lowering another.
plos-pone-0011790:
Hamady Dieng and co-authors documented a dengue mosquito moving indoors in Malaysia, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Aedes albopictus, the Asian tiger mosquito, is usually adapted to areas around homes and typically breeds outdoors. In northern peninsular Malaysia, however, the team found its larvae in most containers inside homes.

Their study anticipates what this indoor breeding means for disease spread. A mosquito that breeds indoors is harder to reach with outdoor spraying and bites people where they live. Dengue control in the region may therefore need to cross the threshold into homes.
plos-pone-0011890:
Andrew Miller and colleagues described in 2010 a microscope built for places that cannot afford or power a standard lab instrument. Their design covers both ordinary bright field viewing and fluorescence, which makes samples glow for study. It runs on batteries, uses an LED flashlight as its light source, and could be manufactured for about two hundred and forty dollars.

The team built and evaluated the device, reporting sharp imaging even at high magnification. A portable microscope at that price can serve field clinics diagnosing infections, classrooms, and survey teams far from labs. The study treats cost and power as design problems to solve, not as limits to accept.
plos-pone-0011990:
Haisheng Nie and colleagues surveyed in 2010 gene expression across chicken tissues and compared the patterns with genome structure. The chicken is both a farm animal of huge importance and a model bird for science, yet bird expression data were scarce. A normal baseline is needed before disease or breeding effects can be judged.

The survey ties expression levels to structural features of the chicken genome and finds transcription patterns conserved across land vertebrates. Birds and mammals last shared an ancestor long ago, so shared patterns mark deep rules of genome organization. The chicken baseline also serves poultry breeding, where gene activity underlies growth and egg traits.
plos-pone-0012090:
David Blackburn, David Bickford, Arvin Diesmos, and co-authors studied the flat-headed frogs of Southeast Asia for PLOS ONE in 2010. These odd frogs, in the group called Barbourula, live on islands in that region. Most island life there was thought to have spread during the recent ice ages, but the authors test a much older story for this frog line.

Their evidence points to roots that reach far back before those ice age movements. That would make these frogs rare survivors of a much older island world, not recent arrivals. The result changes how scientists read the deep past of the whole region, and it gives these little-known frogs a stronger claim on care and protection.
plos-pone-0012190:
Julien Textoris, Leang Heng Ban, Christian Capo, and co-authors compared Q fever infection in male and female mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. The disease, caught from animals, strikes men more often and more severely than women at the same exposure. The team asked whether gene activity during infection differs by sex, and whether the body's daily clock plays a part.

Their measurements link the sex gap to different gene responses, with daily-rhythm genes among the suspects. If timing and sex hormones shape this infection, treatment may one day be tuned by both. The study also adds to the wider lesson that male and female immune systems cannot simply be averaged in research.
plos-pone-0012290:
Hesham Tawfeek, Brahmchetna Bedi, Jau-Yi Li, and co-authors studied parathyroid hormone and bone loss in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Too much of this hormone, whether from disease or from continuous treatment, thins bones by shifting the signals that tell bone-building cells what to do. Recent work had shown T cells of the immune system are somehow required for the hormone's bone effect, a surprise bridge between immunity and skeleton.

Deleting the hormone's receptor only in T cells protected the mice from that bone loss. The protection proves the immune cell is not a bystander but a required middleman. It opens an unexpected treatment idea: quiet the T cell link and the skeleton may be spared.
plos-pone-0012390:
Julieta Acevedo, Lazaro Centanin, Andrés Dekanty and colleagues studied oxygen sensing in the fruit fly in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. When oxygen drops, cells switch on rescue genes through a factor called HIF. Enzymes named prolyl hydroxylases sense oxygen and mark HIF for destruction when oxygen is plentiful. The fly has one such enzyme, Fatiga, but it comes in several forms.
