The team found that the Fatiga forms differ in how well they control the fly's HIF partner, Sima. Some forms act strongly, others weakly, giving the fly tuned responses to low oxygen. The work clarifies a sensing system that also matters in human anemia, altitude illness, and tumor growth.
plos-pone-0012490:
Samah Abdel Baki, Ben Schwab, Margalit Haber and colleagues combined two drugs to treat brain injury in rats, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. No drug currently treats traumatic brain injury, and single drugs have failed trial after trial. The team paired the antibiotic minocycline with N-acetylcysteine, a common antioxidant, hoping their different actions would add up.

Together the drugs improved cognition and memory after injury more than either did alone, a true synergy. Combination therapy is standard in cancer and HIV care but rare in brain injury. The rat results argue for testing paired, well-known, safe drugs rather than hunting one magic molecule.
plos-pone-0012590:
Prabhakar Sripadi, Bindesh Shrestha, Rebecca Easley and colleagues read chemical changes in virus-transformed cells with mass spectrometry, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. When a virus transforms a cell, changes cascade from genes to proteins to the metabolome, the cell's full set of small chemicals. The broad metabolic side of that cascade was little documented, though it decides how the changed cell feeds itself.

Mass spectrometry detected diverse metabolic shifts directly in cells expressing the viral Tax protein. Distinct metabolic signatures of transformation could become diagnostic markers or reveal feed lines a transformed cell depends on. Cutting such a feed line is a classic strategy for selective cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0012690:
Nettle and Cockerill studied why the age at which women first have children varies so much by neighbourhood. In modern England the gap is striking, with first motherhood coming about eight years earlier in the poorest urban areas than in richer ones. Their 2010 study followed one English city area in detail.

They trace how these timing patterns develop over childhood and the teen years. Early childbearing shapes health, schooling and income for decades, so its roots matter for policy. Local detail shows national averages hide the real drivers. The authors argue place itself shapes these life paths.
plos-pone-0012790:
Wiese, Antebi and Zheng followed the amyloid precursor's worm cousin inside nerve cells. Alzheimer's disease is marked by plaques made from a fragment of the amyloid precursor protein. The worm C elegans carries a relative of that protein, called APL-1, whose travels can be watched in living animals.

Their 2010 study tracked where APL-1 goes inside cells and what it does at synapses. A worm model lets scientists test gene changes fast and cheaply. What APL-1 does in worms may hint at the human protein's normal job.  The worm work also flagged genes that shift APL-1 traffic.
plos-pone-0308190:
Simon Turner and colleagues ran a simulation study on a problem facing digital health. How do you prove a wrist or phone sensor's new measure is valid when no gold standard speaks the same units? Their simulated step counter was compared against a questionnaire about activity, both secretly driven by the same hidden physical ability. Two statistical routes, a simple correlation and a factor model, were tested on judging the relationship.

The simple correlation proved steadier, easier, and tougher against broken assumptions, especially with few participants, while the factor model gave less biased answers in every scenario. Using both together inspired the most confidence. Adding several questionnaire measures, collected more often, filled out the picture further. The authors offer device developers a practical validation playbook for measures with no direct ruler.
plos-pone-0330790:
Mauricio Domínguez-Castro and a large team measured quality of life in seventy-five Mexican women living with HIV during the months after childbirth. A standard World Health Organization questionnaire designed for people with HIV scored health, independence, social life, environment, and beliefs. The scores were set against medical and social details such as treatment use, symptoms, schooling, and marital status.

Nearly half the women rated their quality of life as low, with mental health, environment, and spirituality scoring below the middle. Using HIV treatment during pregnancy and after birth mattered, as did symptoms and education. Physical health, independence, and spiritual life best predicted a high overall rating. The authors call for care that hunts down these drag factors, for the sake of mothers and babies alike.
plos-pone-0341290:
Elise Doppenberg-Smit and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about people living with cancer. It examines the emotions these patients feel, both adaptive ones that help coping and maladaptive ones that make life harder. The authors take a network perspective on how those emotions connect.

In a network view, emotions are not treated as one mood score but as linked states that can trigger or calm each other. Seeing which feelings sit at the center of the web may show where support could help most. Psycho-oncology teams designing emotional support for patients are the readers most likely to use this map.
plos-pone-0341790:
When cancer spreads to bone, fractures and spinal squeezes can strike suddenly, and patients go home needing to watch themselves. Jing Shan and colleagues interviewed such patients at a cancer hospital in Hebei, China, about what teaching they wanted at discharge, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Five needs stood out. Patients wanted deeper bone knowledge, including warning signs of fracture and of the cancer advancing. They wanted hands-on guidance for daily self-management, from safe movement to pain control. Emotional and practical support themes followed. The authors turn the themes into a checklist for nurses building discharge education for this fragile group.
plos-pone-0343890:
Silvia Guerra and colleagues tested whether people literally fail to see plants, a tendency called plant awareness disparity. In three experiments, volunteers counted or compared sets of pictures showing trees, animals, or minerals. The researchers varied colour and even flipped images upside down, which scrambles recognition while keeping shapes and brightness the same.

People consistently undercounted the trees compared with animals and minerals, in both colour and black-and-white pictures. When images were flipped, the undercount largely vanished. That pattern suggests the blindness sits in meaning, not eyesight: once a tree stops reading as a tree, it gets counted fairly. The authors argue this quiet bias in basic perception helps explain why plants are so often overlooked in science and policy.
plos-pone-0344390:
Nawar Raad Hussein, Hayder B Sahib, and Zahraa Sabbar Omran tested a newly built molecule against two of cancer's favourite tricks: growing new blood vessels and multiplying without pause. The compound joins several ring structures known from other drugs and was aimed at the main receptor that summons new vessels. Activity was checked in rat tissue, in chick embryo membranes, and against vessel, colon, and breast cancer cells in dishes.

The molecule slowed vessel growth in both tissue tests and curbed cell growth across all three cell lines, with vessel cells most sensitive. At higher doses it also turned down the gene for its target receptor in a blood-vessel tumour line. Computer profiling suggested reasonable drug-like behaviour, with some flags for liver enzyme clashes. The authors present the compound as an early lead, far from a medicine, but mechanistically coherent.
plos-pone-0345190:
Aliocha Nkodila and colleagues checked how well treated mosquito nets are reaching young children in Congo, where malaria remains a major killer of the young. They surveyed children aged six months to five years at preschool health visits in one hundred fifty-six facilities across six provinces in 2025. Interviewers asked families about net ownership and use.

Among more than twelve hundred children, most families were poor and many guardians had little schooling, conditions linked to lower net use. Statistical models identified factors tied to children not sleeping under nets. Nets only prevent malaria when children actually sleep beneath them, so the gap between handing out nets and using them is where prevention succeeds or fails.
plos-pone-0345490:
Jiawei An and seven colleagues simulate a tunnel boring machine's cutting discs in this 2026 engineering study. The discs chew through rock, and the size of the fragments tells engineers how efficiently energy is being spent. Computer models of indentation tests varied the rock's joints: their angle, their spacing, and the squeezing pressure around them. Fragment size distributions were then correlated with the specific energy the cutting consumed.

Cracks preferred to run along the weak joint surfaces. Joint angle mattered in a wave: cracking first intensified, then eased as angles steepened. Closer joint spacing let cracks join up, lowering the energy needed. Higher confining pressure choked off clean tensile cracks. Failure turned to shearing, fragments grew finer, and energy costs rose. Fragment gradation tracked energy use with strong, straight-line correlations. Quarry the rubble, in other words, and you can read the machine's efficiency without instrumenting the cutter itself.
plos-pone-0346290:
Kristen M. Lucibello and co-workers measure how many Canadian teenagers feel unwelcome at school and for what reasons. A welcoming climate supports health and learning, but the specific reasons students feel shut out are rarely counted at scale. Their 2026 study uses survey answers from more than fifteen thousand six hundred students in forty-one Ontario secondary schools.

Nearly two in three students felt unwelcome for at least one reason. Appearance led the list, followed by school marks and emotional struggles. Race and culture were named by about one in ten. Students who saw themselves as overweight, gender-diverse students, and poorer students were overrepresented among the unwelcome. Fixing climate means tackling many doors at once, from teacher training to classroom materials.
plos-pone-0346490:
Qingpan Wen and colleagues ran a controlled trial of Wuqinxi, a traditional Chinese exercise built on the movements of five animals, in older adults with mild memory and thinking problems. Fifty-three volunteers in the 2026 study practiced either Wuqinxi or gentle stretching for twelve weeks. The researchers measured thinking skills, fall risk, and quality of life before and after.

The Wuqinxi group improved clearly on memory tests and moved more steadily, while the stretching group gained far less. Participants also reported better physical health, less pain, and better mood on a standard quality of life survey. Because lapses in thinking and falls often arrive together in old age, the authors argue this low-cost routine deserves a larger trial.
plos-pone-0346890:
Deborah G Smith, Luis Enrique Espinoza, and co-authors surveyed health care providers in North Louisiana about prescribing PrEP, the preventive medication that blocks HIV infection. Uptake of PrEP lags badly in the American South despite its heavy HIV burden. Their 2026 survey covered one hundred two providers at a medical school and its hospital, asking about knowledge, habits, and obstacles.

Only about a quarter had ever prescribed PrEP, and nearly half had never even discussed it with a patient. The commonest barriers were missing training, reported by more than eight in ten, and absent clinic guidelines. Providers who rated their own knowledge higher were far more likely to discuss and to prescribe. The authors call for targeted training and institutional policies that make prescribing the easy default.
plos-pone-0347690:
Qing Ma, Yao Peng, and Zhenwei Liu modeled a supply chain for innovative products where goods are sold, used, and then recycled, and where customers can regret two different things. Buyers may regret a purchase, or regret replacing a product too soon or too late. The model follows a manufacturer, retailers, and a third-party recycler competing over time, and solves for the best prices and recycling effort.

Purchase regret lowered sales and shrank long-term profits for makers and retailers, while replacement regret drew in more buyers and raised profits. Recyclers' profits were untouched by purchase regret. Both kinds of regret stretched how long products stayed on the market. The results show consumer feelings are a real force in how green supply chains perform.
plos-pone-0347790:
Jianwen Yang, Qiang Huang, and Yating Lin work on sending data when feedback keeps dropping out. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. A classic scheme uses instant feedback to fix errors with great accuracy. It assumes the feedback link never fails. Real wireless links fail often, though.

The authors adapt the scheme for feedback that arrives only at times. They cover clean feedback first, then noisy feedback. They work out how length, error odds, speed, and secrecy trade off. They also grade how well the schemes guard data from eavesdroppers. The math gives engineers clear targets. Satellite links, where feedback is patchy, are one use case.
plos-pone-0347990:
Exaud Tweve and three co-workers built a smart switch box for solar plants at work sites. Work sites draw sharp peaks of power when all kit runs at once. Old plans ask staff to turn things off, which is hit and miss. This box eyes power traits live. It fixes a waste trait on its own and cuts low-rank loads at peak times.

The team built a real box and checked it with past load data from a live site. The fix cut the waste trait's load by more than two fifths. Load cuts at peak trimmed true use by near a fourth. Power ran far more smooth all day.
plos-pone-0348290:
Ummer Shakeel and co-workers compare five deep learning designs for spotting diseases on rice leaves, adding an outlining step that shows where the sickness sits. Pakistan ranks among the world's top rice growers, and hand scouting cannot cover its fields. Their 2026 study trains the rival designs on a balanced public set of close to two thousand leaf photos.

Each design learned from pre-trained vision backbones rather than starting cold. After sorting, a guided cut-out method traced the diseased patches so farmers can see why the program flagged a leaf. The classification came from the networks alone; the outlines serve explanation. Clear visual proof could help skeptical growers trust and act on automated scouting.
plos-pone-0348590:
Hua Song and co-authors compared how four Chinese cities build high-tech industries, drawing on nearly forty thousand research papers and ten thousand patents from the past decade. Wuhan, Chengdu, Hangzhou, and Tianjin were profiled across artificial intelligence, fibre-optic communication, connected vehicles, and memory chips, using publication mapping plus language models to tidy keywords and label topics.

Each city showed a distinct personality. Wuhan paired universities with industry in optics and chips. Hangzhou raced ahead in artificial intelligence and smart vehicles under industry leadership. Chengdu published heavily but translated less into patents. Small-scale Tianjin held surprising pockets of strength. The authors argue that national innovation policy should be tuned city by city, since the machinery of invention differs so much between places.
plos-pone-0348790:
Hip replacements sometimes fail early, and catching warning signs within the first year could spare patients worse revision surgery. Sarah Galante and colleagues built a combined prediction model using X-rays, clinical scores, and other illness data, in this 2026 PLOS One study of two patient groups.

One group held four hundred patients and the other about one hundred fifty-five, each contributing hundreds of images with and without warning signs. Separate models read each data type, and their answers were averaged into one verdict. The blend performed better than any single source. The authors present the tool as automatic screening to flag patients for closer review after surgery.
plos-pone-0348890:
Md Ismail Hossain and Iftakhar Ahmad study schooling in the Haor wetlands of Bangladesh, where seasonal flooding shapes daily life. Their 2026 study gathers survey data from nearly two hundred secondary students across ten schools, plus talks with teachers and parents, to sort out what drives grades and attendance.

Family income and support from classmates predicted stronger school results. Parents' own schooling predicted better attendance, while a long trip to school hurt it. Bullying and harsh teacher behavior fed long-term absence. More teachers and kinder classrooms could help as much as family wealth does. The picture shows wetland children need support on several fronts at once, not a single fix.
plos-pone-0349090:
Tony Navas and co-workers build a lab test that measures an active cancer-related protein called MET inside tumor samples. MET can drive tumor growth, and drugs that block it need a reliable way to show they hit their target. Their 2026 paper describes a microscope method using glowing tags to count both total MET and its switched-on form in single cells.

The team checked the test in lab-grown cells, animal tumors, and patient tissue, and it matched an older test run on ground-up samples. The method can also tell whether the active protein sits on the cell surface or in the nucleus. In patient tumors from colon and lung cancers, surface and nuclear levels did not simply track each other.
plos-pone-0349190:
Na Wu and colleagues simulated how cracked rock breaks apart under pressure coming from several directions at once, as it does deep underground. Their models embedded three shapes of flaw, surface, through-going, and fully buried, inside uneven virtual rock. Then they squeezed the samples along different stress paths. They watched cracks sprout, link, and finally split the block.

New cracks grew mainly as wings from the original flaws, and the squeeze direction steered everything: rotate the middle stress and the failure switches from a pulling-apart pattern to a sideways one. Surrounding pressure made every sample stronger, and buried flaws behaved differently from surface ones under the same turn. The authors give engineers a sharper picture of which flaw shapes threaten tunnels and caverns under real three-way stress.
plos-pone-0349290:
Walking with poles gives older adults exercise plus balance support, and Mohsen Keramati and colleagues tested whether retirement homes could run such a program well. Their 2026 PLOS One trial took place in four Saskatoon care homes during the summer of 2022, with sessions offered three times a week for twelve weeks.

Nineteen residents joined and fifteen finished, with an average age near eighty-five. Attendance stayed high, staff and residents rated the program favorably, and no serious harm was linked to it. Balance, leg strength, and self-rated physical function all improved over the twelve weeks. The team now plans a larger, randomized trial.
plos-pone-0349390:
Wei Zheng and colleagues built a small timing device for hospitals that clean medical tools in acidic electrolyzed water, a disinfectant whose strength fades as dissolved solids change. Their gadget senses those solids, starts and stops its own timer, stores a record of each cycle, and warns staff with lights when timing goes wrong. It is sealed against water and charges without wires.

In one hospital supply department, the device was compared with ordinary kitchen timers over two months. Cycles were timed far more often with the new device, and nearly all disinfections ran for the right length of time. The authors pitch it as a cheap, simple way to make disinfection safer and easier to audit.
plos-pone-0349590:
Rebecca Linnett, Noelle Robertson, and Stephanie Hubbard reviewed ninety studies using the Intuitive Eating Scale-2. The questionnaire measures how much people eat by hunger and fullness cues rather than by rules or emotions. Intuitive eating is promoted as a healthier relationship with food, and this scale is its most common yardstick. The reviewers checked how sound the scale's measurements are beyond the student group it was built on.

The collected studies span community samples and people in treatment for eating or weight problems across three search rounds. The reviewers weighed the scale's structure, consistency, and links to other traits, and judged the risk of bias in how it has been used. For researchers choosing a measure, this audit shows where the scale is trustworthy and where caution is due.
plos-pone-0349690:
Hang Li and colleagues surveyed two hundred and seventy-two nurses who work in orthopaedic operating theatres in Shanxi Province, China, about staying safe around surgical power tools. Drills and saws used on bone throw up blood, fragments, and aerosols, yet protection habits vary widely. Their questionnaire scored what nurses know, how they feel, and what they actually do about protective gear and procedures.

Only about half the nurses scored well on each of the three measures, leaving the other half exposed in knowledge or practice. Nurses with degrees, senior titles, recent safety training, and a habit of reading the latest guidance scored far higher on knowledge. Training within the past year mattered most of all. The authors urge hospitals to make protection training frequent and routine rather than rare.
plos-pone-0349790:
Denise Sproul, Michael McCaul, and Gerhard Hanekom recorded what contraception women chose right after giving birth at Tygerberg Academic Hospital in South Africa, a setting serving mostly low-income, high-risk patients. The days after delivery are a prime moment to offer family planning. Their 2026 study reviewed discharge records for more than a thousand women over the first half of 2023.

Nearly every woman, about ninety-eight in a hundred, left with a family planning method. The three-month injection was the favorite, chosen by almost half, especially by younger women. Worryingly, almost half of those receiving methods fell into a World Health Organization caution category, almost entirely because the injection was given while breastfeeding. Two thirds of women had spaced pregnancies over two years apart. The authors flag the eligibility pattern for clinical attention.
plos-pone-0350090:
Wyatt H Bridgman, Cosmin Safta, and Jaideep Ray built a statistical method to track a hidden quantity during an outbreak: the infection rate itself. Daily case counts are noisy because of reporting errors, while the underlying rate shifts more smoothly with how people mix. Their 2026 study estimates that rate for whole regions at once, borrowing strength from neighboring areas so the picture stays coherent across a map.

A fast approximation method makes the heavy computation practical across many counties. Tested on COVID-19 data from all thirty-three counties in New Mexico during 2020, the method reconstructed infection rates and flagged the arrival of the autumn wave. The estimated rates also grouped counties with similar outbreak behavior. The authors offer the rate field as a steadier signal for spotting changes in an epidemic.
plos-pone-0350290:
Man Zhang, Jiabin Wu, and Yu Liu charted more than a thousand officially recognized traditional villages across China's Henan Province to see where they cluster and why. These villages carry the region's cultural heritage, yet urban growth threatens them unevenly. Their 2026 study combined geographic mapping tools, statistical detectors of influence, and historical records to trace the villages' spread across time.

Villages clustered strongly in the north, center, and south of the province, while the flood-prone east stayed sparse, a legacy of centuries of Yellow River flooding. Village locations went with moderate elevation, nearby water, and middling distance from county towns, but no single factor explained the pattern once spatial spillover was considered. The authors argue location reflects combined, layered causes, and they recommend protecting villages in clusters rather than one by one.
plos-pone-0350390:
Winsy Wing Sze Wong and co-authors published a trial plan in 2026 on virtual reality script training for Cantonese speakers with chronic aphasia after stroke. Script training rehearses useful everyday conversations, and immersion may make practice feel real. No results are reported yet.

One hundred twenty participants will be split among virtual reality training, the same training without virtual reality, and no treatment. In the virtual arm, practice happens inside scenes of daily life; the other training arm uses still photos. Before and after measures cover daily communication, language severity, and life quality. The design isolates exactly what the headset adds.
plos-pone-0350990:
Yong Yang and colleagues improve how drones spot very small objects from the air. Tiny targets fill few pixels, sit in busy scenes, and shift scale fast, so fixed window detectors miss detail. Their module feeds map coordinates into the detector at several scales, blends them with image features, and adds attention that favours small, sharp targets.

Tests on three drone image sets showed steady gains over strong rivals, with little added computing cost. A test on a general photo set also held up, which hints at wide use. Sharper small object spotting helps traffic watching, search work, and crop scouting, where the key detail is often the smallest thing in frame.
plos-pone-0351690:
Lambert Motilal and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One genetics study of cacao trees in Peru. The trees grow on indigenous farms and feed the fine-flavor chocolate trade. Peru's cacao roots are poorly documented. The team fingerprinted nearly four hundred farm trees from eight regions. They used almost two hundred DNA markers. They compared the trees with known types from across the Amazon.

Four new genetic groups emerged, each tied to a region. Other trees mixed ancestry from ten known groups. The ancestry of a famous farmed type was also pinned down more sharply. Its largest share traced to one of the new Peruvian groups. The authors say the map will strengthen Peru's gene banks. It will also help the fine-flavor trade certify and breed distinct local cacao.
plos-pone-0351890:
RETRACTION: The PLOS One Editors retract an article that used directional statistics to argue Earth's magnetic field murmurs may guide migrating birds. After publication, concerns were raised about the work's validity and about incomplete sentences and other oddities in the text. The editors judged the text problems came from typesetting code errors, and that part was resolved. The statistical problems were not.

A statistical advisor found the study's core assumption shaky: it treated each change in a bird's heading as independent, yet turns along one flight path are naturally linked in sequence. The corresponding author conceded the point as a weakness of the approximation. Because the assumption underpins the analysis, the editors withdrew the article. Its claims about magnetic guidance should not be relied on.
plos-pone-0351990:
Diane Some and colleagues field-tested a smarter way to read malaria rapid tests in febrile young children in Burkina Faso, where malaria surges with the season. The standard test hunts one parasite protein, but that protein lingers after cure, causing false alarms. Their algorithm read two proteins in sequence and used recent treatment history to sort true infections from leftovers, in a trial of nearly twelve hundred children.

Checked against expert microscopy, the standard test caught nearly all malaria but cried wolf often. The sequence method, on the cases it could settle, was both highly sensitive and far more specific, though about one case in eight landed in an undecided band needing the treatment-history rule. In clinics drowning in fever cases, fewer false malaria calls mean antibiotics and attention flow to the real cause.
plos-pone-0352090:
Zeynep Begüm Kalyoncu Atasoy and four colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One survey on air fryers and home cooking in Istanbul, Türkiye. Nearly four hundred adults living with a partner took part, half of them air fryer owners. The study measured cooking skills, how couples share kitchen work, and how closely diets matched the Mediterranean pattern.

Owners reported stronger cooking and food skills and more equal sharing of tasks like setting the table and washing dishes. Owning an air fryer, however, showed no link to Mediterranean diet adherence, which instead tracked with age, exercise, and not smoking. Women outscored men on skills and diet quality in both groups. The authors read the appliance as a marker of engaged home cooking rather than a cause of healthier eating.
plos-pone-0352190:
Mitiku and colleagues studied blood infections in newborns at a hospital in southern Ethiopia in a 2026 paper. Newborn sepsis is a leading reason for intensive care and antibiotic use, and blind treatment fuels drug resistance. Two hundred eighty babies suspected of infection gave blood samples over three months for germ testing.

Lab work named the germs present and tested which antibiotics still killed them. The team also looked for factors tied to confirmed infection, with attention to germs the World Health Organization lists as priorities. Local germ and resistance patterns help doctors choose first antibiotics wisely instead of guessing, which protects both the baby and the usefulness of the drugs.
plos-pone-0352590:
Lorrein Muhwava and seven colleagues ask whether wearable glucose sensors could work in South Africa's public clinics, in this 2026 PLOS ONE interview study. The sensors track blood sugar continuously, sparing people with type 1 diabetes constant finger pricks, but they are rare in poorer health systems. More than one hundred patients, caregivers, and health workers in Cape Town and Pretoria shared their experiences through group discussions and interviews.

Users welcomed the convenience and the clearer picture of their glucose patterns. Training and family support made the devices easier to adopt. Cost, low awareness, and hardships like food insecurity stood in the way. The authors argue the technology fits, provided policy tackles price and support together.
plos-pone-0352690:
De Van Nguyen and four co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One study of breast lumps at two hospitals in Vietnam. The lumps had high-suspicion imaging scores. The team asked how well needle sampling sorts them, and what predicts cancer. Just over one hundred women had ultrasound-guided needle tests. Surgery results served as the final check. The lab read the samples under a global standard system.

About half the lumps proved to be cancer. The needle test was highly accurate overall. It sorted the great majority correctly. After full adjustment, only two traits predicted cancer on their own. Older age added risk bit by bit. Larger lump size did the same. The top imaging grade lost force in that model, though its highest-risk subgroup was small. The authors advise weaving age and size into risk judgments, next to the lab result.
plos-pone-0352890:
Qingqing He, Shunyu Huang, and Jipeng Wang present this 2026 PLOS One methods study. It seeks a consistent way to measure one soil enzyme. The enzyme helps release nitrogen from protein in soil. Labs run the standard test under widely varied conditions. That makes results hard to compare. The team varied acidity, doses, heat, timing, and soil amount in a planned way. They used a purified enzyme and three contrasting soils.

They found a clear recipe. Mildly alkaline conditions worked best. A set dose kept the reaction steady. Readings stayed stable for at least three hours. Adding more soil, oddly, lowered the measured activity. Metal additions made little difference. The authors also suggest this enzyme matches one measured by an older color method. They offer their findings as a basis for a standard protocol.
plos-pone-0353190:
Maria Berikou and co-authors measured how much extra shoppers pay for meat carrying sustainability claims. Labels promising lower emissions, organic production, or grass feeding let producers stand out, but their shelf value was unmapped. Their 2026 study scraped prices and labels for beef, pork, and chicken across stores in forty-eight states.

Nearly every claim studied carried a real price premium. Organic and reduced-emission claims sat among the strongest. Geography also moved prices for the same products. Berikou and colleagues caution that a premium shows what shoppers pay, not what production costs. Still, the map of premiums tells producers which promises the market currently rewards.
plos-pone-0353390:
Murphy and colleagues validated a phone-based mental health screening tool for university students in a 2026 study. Long waits for assessment leave many young adults without guidance. The tool, adapted from a youth version, asks students about life pressures and points them to resources matched to need and urgency.

Students aged seventeen to twenty-nine at a Canadian university completed the tool, then received a standard counselor assessment for comparison. Close agreement would mean the tool can safely sort who needs urgent help and who can use lighter support first. A trusted self-check could ease pressure on campus clinics while still catching students in real distress early.
plos-pone-0353490:
Mirlashine Selvendran and colleagues survey in 2026 young shoppers in Sri Lanka who buy electronics in shops that blend physical and digital features. Nearly five hundred customers from the youngest adult generation answered a structured survey. Statistical modelling traced how the blended experience linked to loyalty, through steps such as satisfaction and felt value.

Blended experiences linked strongly and directly to loyalty in the model. Shoppers valued interactive, tech rich settings they could help shape, and skill with digital tools mattered for moving smoothly between shop and screen. Because answers were self reported at one time, the authors warn against reading the links as proof of cause.
plos-pone-0353790:
Monica Anona Rose, Andrew Robinson, and Antony Payton ask a genetics question. Do common variants in the brain's dopamine system explain why thinking slows with age? Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. More than fifteen hundred people took part. All belonged to a long-running Manchester ageing study. They were followed for twelve years. Processing speed and other abilities were measured along the way. Eighty-nine independent variants were tested. They spanned nine dopamine genes.

Nothing survived strict statistical correction. Not single variants. Not whole genes. Not a combined pathway score. Checks against brain tissue after death were also blank. The team had power to catch moderate effects. So the honest answer is clear. Common dopamine variation does not drive cognitive slowing in any large way.
plos-pone-0353990:
Piotr Żukowski and Marcin Naranowicz tested whether a good mood loosens word connections differently in a first and a foreign language. Positive mood is known to widen mental activation among related ideas at home. Their 2026 study put highly skilled Polish-English bilingual women into happy or sad moods with film clips, then measured brain responses to word pairs.

In Polish, a positive mood shrank the brain signal that marks unrelated words as hard to connect, meaning distant ideas became easier to reach. In English, mood made no such difference. Closely and weakly related pairs behaved alike across moods. Żukowski and Naranowicz conclude that mood's broadening effect may stop at the border of a second language.
plos-pone-0354290:
Kimihiko Mori and seven colleagues use motion-capture data to sort the walking patterns of stroke survivors, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. After a stroke, one-sided weakness distorts how the body's weight moves over the standing foot, and no two patients distort it alike. Seventy-eight community-dwelling participants walked through a three-dimensional gait laboratory while forces under their feet were recorded.

Measures of how the body's centre travelled relative to the pressure point under the foot lined up with braking and pushing forces, especially late in each step. Statistical grouping suggested four candidate walking styles. The authors offer the groups as a working map for tailoring rehabilitation, while cautioning that some groups were small.
plos-pone-0354590:
Wenjing Zhao led a team of seven authors on this 2026 study of a jelly-like scaffold for growing cells in three dimensions. Their injectable gel, built from chitosan and two helpers, stays liquid at room temperature and sets at body temperature. A small factorial screen weighed setting speed, ease of injection, and stability to pick the best recipes.

Two winning formulas kept liver cancer cells and stem cells alive and spreading for ten days, with the cancer cells balling into tumor-like spheres. Zhao offers the screening routine and gel as a dependable platform for laboratory cell culture.
plos-pone-0354890:
Coty Jasper and co-authors study in 2026 how gene activity in the inner ear of female midshipman fish shifts with breeding state. In summer, nesting males hum to attract females, and females hear better in breeding season through changes in two ear regions. One region adds new sensory cells, while the other sharpens without adding cells, so the controls likely differ.

Gene counting showed the two regions carry distinct profiles, with more target genes changing in the cell adding region across seasons. The results point to separate molecular routes for the same hearing gain. The framework may guide work on hormone driven hearing change in other animals.
plos-pone-0355190:
Zhilin Dong and co-authors propose in 2026 a graph learning method to locate the source of wide range oscillations in modern power grids rich in electronic converters. Such wobbles span many frequencies, shift quickly, and fade fast with distance, defeating methods built for slow, narrow wobbles. Their network splits signals into a smooth global branch and a local contrast branch, then fuses them adaptively.

Benchmark grid simulations showed the method beat several time based and graph based rivals, with the clearest gain at high frequencies where smoothing methods erase the source signal. A larger benchmark gave early support for scale. Real large grid testing is still needed, the authors note.
plos-pone-0355290:
Héctor Loyola Irizarry and four colleagues survey biology and biomedical undergraduates at two large public research universities about their mentoring, reporting in 2026. Mentoring helps science students persist, yet most research focuses on research-lab mentors and ignores where students actually find guidance. The team's questionnaire asked who mentors these students, where those mentors sit, and how supported students feel.

Most students at both universities reported having a mentor, but many mentors were peers or people outside the student's own institution, a reminder that support comes from several directions at once. Students felt best supported on degree and career guidance and on having a role model. Contact frequency mattered surprisingly little; longer relationships helped slightly. The authors give practical recommendations for mentors and program leaders, and note the field lacks shared tools for comparing mentoring across universities.
plos-pone-0355390:
YueXin Chen and co-authors followed teenagers wearing overnight reshaping lenses to slow short-sightedness, tracking vision quality for a year. Orthokeratology lenses flatten the cornea during sleep, but they can scatter light. Their 2026 prospective study measured optical quality, corneal shape errors, and corneal clarity at five time points.

Light scatter rose clearly by the third month and stayed up. A sharpness ratio fell significantly by the year's end. A resolution cutoff measure, however, did not change significantly across visits. Corneal shape errors shifted alongside the optical changes. Chen and colleagues give clinicians a fuller picture of the trade-off: daytime freedom from glasses, paid for with some night-time optical quality.
plos-pone-0355490:
Wenqiang Fan and colleagues survey in 2026 university students about using artificial intelligence tools during class and how that shapes their attitudes toward the tools. A few hundred questionnaires fed models that tested whether felt benefits for engagement carry the link. Engagement was split into thinking, feeling, and behaviour parts.

Classroom use linked to warmer attitudes both directly and through stronger thinking and feeling engagement, with the two paths about equal. Behaviour engagement benefits, though raised by use, did not carry a clear indirect link. Students were positive overall. The authors suggest the value of classroom tools lies in learning experience, not speed alone.
plos-pone-0355690:
Manoj Kumar leads a team of six building software to spot unusual human activity in real surveillance footage, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Many anomaly detectors are trained on staged or synthetic clips and stumble in messy real scenes. The authors instead combined transfer learning with a two part network. A proven image model reads each frame for spatial content. A bidirectional memory network then reads the sequence forward and backward for timing.

Fused together, the two views judge whether behavior in a clip turns abnormal. The team evaluated the system on real world crime surveillance recordings rather than simulations, and report performance ahead of established comparison methods. Applications range from station platforms to hospital corridors, anywhere a human watcher cannot stare at every feed. The authors stress that training on genuine footage, not synthetic stand ins, is what makes the detector plausible for deployment.
plos-pone-0356390:
Shuai Zheng and three colleagues investigate why Chinese university students engage, or fail to engage, in their English classes, in this 2026 study. Nearly four hundred students at one university reported how supported they felt by their teachers, how much they valued English learning, and how well they monitored their own learning. The analysis tested whether support works partly by strengthening those beliefs and habits.

Perceived teacher support predicted engagement directly. It also worked indirectly, twice over: students who felt supported valued English more and monitored themselves better, and each of those carried support's influence into engagement. A chain effect appeared too, with value beliefs feeding self-monitoring in sequence. The authors draw a practical lesson for language teachers: visible support is not mere kindness, it is the lever that builds students' conviction and self-management.
plos-pone-0356490:
Lambert Tetteh Appiah and colleagues gathered everything published on lipoprotein(a) in Africa. This is a cholesterol-like particle. Its blood level is set mostly by genes, and it independently drives heart disease. Their 2026 review found just seventeen usable studies. They were scattered across west, central, southern, and north Africa. The studies measured healthy adults with differing lab methods.

Elevated levels were common. In Ghana they affected between roughly three and six in ten people, depending on the group. Women consistently ran higher than men. Reported averages varied widely by country and assay. High levels traveled with hypertension and diabetes in several cohorts. Given Africa's genetic diversity, the authors argue this understudied risk factor deserves proper mapping. Heart prevention guidelines should not simply import cutoffs from elsewhere.
plos-pone-0356690:
Kristan Amendola and colleagues put twenty-three young women through two popular fasting styles in turn. One style meant eating only within a daily window for three days. The other meant alternate-day fasting for three days. The aim was to compare how each feels. Their 2026 crossover experiment collected daily noon ratings of mood, hunger, and diet satisfaction. It also collected sleep quality ratings, before and during each fast, with a rest interval between.

Alternate-day fasting disturbed mood more on its first day, though the effect faded by day two. Hunger climbed under both regimes but bit harder with alternate-day fasting. Participants were clearly more satisfied with the daily-window diet. Neither style harmed perceived sleep. For young women choosing a fast, the gentler daily rhythm looks easier to live with.
plos-pone-0356790:
Severine BSW Hex and Gerald S Wilkinson watch how greater spear-nosed bats treat each other inside two very different social worlds: harems guarded by one male, and bachelor groups of leftover males. The species is strongly polygynous, and females far outlive males, a gap social stress might help explain. Observations tallied friendly grooming and hostile encounters in both group types, noting who fought, how, and for how long.

Bachelor life proved rougher: fights were more frequent, longer, and almost entirely one-on-one brawls with highly physical moves rarely seen among females. Grooming appeared only between harem females, clustered around evening departure and return. Hex and Wilkinson propose that bachelor groups impose a heavier stress load, which may feed the survival gap between the sexes.
plos-pone-0356990:
Vladimir Đurišić and colleagues confronted a familiar retail analytics problem: software that mines shopping baskets for product pairings returns hundreds of thousands of rules, most of them redundant. Their 2026 study built a pruning method that keeps only rules adding real confidence, then turned the survivors into a product network and extracted its strongest backbone.

On a Montenegrin retail dataset of millions of baskets, the method cut rule counts by well over half while keeping the meaningful links. The backbone crowned delicatessen goods as the network's hub, with chains running into beauty products, fresh meat, and healthy produce. Retailers get a short, readable map for designing bundles, promotions, and shelf layouts instead of an unreadable rule dump.
plos-pone-0357090:
Mustafa Aziz Amen, Hourakhsh Ahmad Nia, and Amen Mustafa Aziz asked a forecasting question about Erbil, Iraq. Did the city's street layout in 2004 foretell which homes would become shops over the next twenty years? Their 2026 study rebuilt the old network of 279 intersections. It scored each street segment's importance in several ways. It then raced two prediction models against each other. One was a graph neural network that learns from neighbors.

Both models predicted conversions well. The graph model was slightly more precise. It produced smoother, more continuous commercial corridors. The simpler regression caught a few more true conversions. How straight a street ran proved the strongest single clue. City planners could use such forecasts to prepare corridors for commercial pressure before it arrives piecemeal.
plos-pone-0357290:
Sándor Hornok and a wide team screen blood from zoo and wild animals for insect molting hormones, substances known to boost growth in some animals. Insect-eating songbirds and bats carry these compounds naturally, but whether other partly insect-eating animals do was unknown. Samples covered water birds, hunting birds, carnivores, primates, and a reptile, drawn from zoos and from road-killed animals, and were tested with precise lab instruments.

Only two samples out of well over a hundred tested positive: a kestrel and a beech marten, each with a modest level of a molting-related compound. Hornok and colleagues note such traces do not prove any growth effect. The mostly empty result usefully bounds how common these compounds are outside true insect specialists.
plos-pone-0357490:
Nerea Tolón Zardoya and coauthors published a 2026 pilot study in PLOS ONE on teaching contact lens fitting with 3D-printed eye models instead of only on fellow students. Rigid gas permeable lenses give superb vision but are fiddly to fit, and practicing on classmates limits eye-shape range and raises discomfort and safety concerns. Optometry students first fitted lenses on peers, then one group trained on printed sclero-corneal surfaces, with questionnaires tracking expectations, confidence, and fluorescein-pattern skill.

After peer practice, students named reading the fluorescein pattern and adjusting the lens as the hardest steps, and eye discomfort as a demotivator. After the model session, nearly all in the experimental group judged the printed eyes realistic, and most prized practicing without a patient in discomfort. The printed kit, they conclude, is a safe rehearsal stage broadening the eye shapes students meet before real patients.
plos-pone-0357590:
Sulaiman Alamro presented a security model for future 6G networks in PLOS ONE in 2026. Quantum computers will one day break today's encryption, and networks that manage themselves, called zero-touch networks, must be ready before that day. Alamro's model, named QShield-ZTN, is built to be quantum-resilient while following current standards.

The model covers how security is orchestrated across an autonomous network, so protection does not depend on constant human control. Designing this in now is far cheaper than retrofitting after quantum machines arrive. Telecom planners face long lead times, so published models that meet standards give them something concrete to test. The study joins a wider effort to make post-quantum safety routine, not rushed.
plos-pone-0357790:
Xue Lei, Weilan Liu, Zongnian Luo, Bangyong Wu, Yu Meng, and Qiang Jiang published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents a bispecific T cell engager aimed at CD3 and CSPG4, a laboratory-built molecule that grabs a T cell with one arm and a cancer marker with the other. The platform is aimed at malignant melanoma, the deadliest skin cancer.

By forcing T cells against CSPG4-bearing tumor cells, the engager turns the patient's own immune system into the drug. Bispecific platforms are prized because their targeting arms can be swapped for other cancers. Immunotherapy researchers developing melanoma treatments are the readers for a new engager design.
plos-pone-0358190:
Xiaosi Song and colleagues published a 2026 computer vision paper in PLOS ONE on finding the red official seals stamped on invoices, a step that matters for automated financial review. Seals vary in size, sit on cluttered backgrounds, and the detector must stay light enough for modest hardware. Their model, ISD-YOLO, adapts a popular detection network with modules that sharpen features at several scales, focus attention on promising regions, and adapt to the seal's shape, behind a slim detection head.

Tested on a mix of public seal images and real invoices, the model beat its baseline and rival detectors on standard accuracy scores while using only a few million parameters. The authors say the balance of accuracy and lightness suits resource-limited settings such as office scanners or edge devices. Broader scenarios and real edge hardware still need testing before the design counts as field-proven.
plos-pone-0359090:
Yan Qian, Quanjie Song, Xinyi Xie, and Li Deng published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It works on metagenomic sequence classification, sorting DNA fragments from mixed samples of microbes. The method is codon-aware and uses multi-scale feature fusion, combining patterns at several sizes, with codon meaning the three-letter DNA words that code for protein parts.

Metagenomic samples blend thousands of species, so classifying each fragment is like sorting shredded books by scraps of text. Codon patterns carry species clues that raw letters may miss. Microbiome researchers identifying what lives in soil, water, or the gut are the audience for a classifier built on those clues.
plos-pone-0359290: Nguyen-Quang and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on a small antenna for home and office Wi-Fi. Their design uses a single flat layer yet sends a focused signal in three bands at once. It targets the Wi-Fi 6 and 6E standards, which use newer, wider channels. A compact three-band antenna could ease router design while keeping speeds high across bands.
plos-pone-0359790:
Solomon Gedfie and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It is a meta-analysis, built on a systematic review, of serum ferritin, a blood marker of iron stores, in children diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD. The question is what ferritin levels look like in these children across past studies.

Iron supports brain development and dopamine pathways tied to attention, which is why ferritin keeps being measured in ADHD. Pooling many small studies gives a steadier answer than any one clinic's sample. Child psychiatrists and pediatricians weighing iron testing in ADHD are the readers for this synthesis.
pmc-10654390:
Podocytes, the kidney's filter cells, are hard to source for research, so labs grow them from reprogrammed stem cells. Masahiro Yasuda and co-authors found a switch that makes the conversion work better. A growth pathway called mTOR, famous in cancer biology, turned out to be a brake on podocyte maturation. Blocking it helped the stem cells commit.

With the inhibitor added, the grown cells switched on nephrin and podocin, the signature proteins of the filter slits. The resulting cell layer behaved like the real filter: small molecules passed, albumin mostly stayed back. The protocol, published in 2023, gives kidney researchers a cleaner model for disease and drug testing.
pmc-10654890:
Yifan Xu, Miaogen Chen, Senjiang Yu, and Hong Zhou make stretch sensors from wrinkled silver films in a paper from 2023. The films sit on a silicone rubber that is liquid during coating. Silver atoms sink slightly into the surface, locking the film in place. Once the rubber sets, the wrinkle pattern is frozen. Pattern shape is tuned by film thickness, rubber mix, and applied strain.

The sensors respond strongly, with sensitivity above four thousand. They stretch to about eighty percent strain and answer in eighty milliseconds. Six thousand stretch cycles left them stable. The authors target health monitoring and motion tracking wearables. The trick is the interlocking layer that stops the film from peeling.
pmc-10675090:
Ben Baker and co-authors reported a first-phase trial of measles and rubella vaccine given by skin patch in twenty twenty-three. Patches promise a safer, simpler, cheaper route than needles. Sixty-three healthy adults were split by lot into four groups: a bare patch, a low-dose vaccine patch, a high-dose patch, or a standard under-skin injection of an approved vaccine.

The vaccine stayed potent on patches after two years in the cold, and a three-day heat spell cost little strength. Patch dosing was safe and well tolerated, with only mild or moderate reactions. Antibody levels after low-dose and high-dose patches matched those after injection. Conversion rates were modest in all groups, which the authors link to most adults already carrying antibodies at the start. The data back patches as a workable way to deliver this vaccine.
pmc-10691590:
Menghan Liu and co-authors test deep learning on multi modal images to identify a breast cancer subtype in a 2023 study. The Luminal A subtype guides personalized treatment choices. The team studied 158 patients with 170 lesions, split into training, test, and validation sets. Images came from mammography and several MRI modes, each also tested alone.

A combined multi modal model beat every single mode model on accuracy and sensitivity, with an overall accuracy measure well above the single modes. Its specificity was slightly lower than the best single MRI mode. Five single mode results are reported for comparison, all trailing the blend. Readers see why combining image types helps subtype prediction, while one trait still needs work.
pmc-10693890:
Traditional and complementary healing, from herbal medicine to acupuncture, is used worldwide, and the World Health Organization's ten-year strategy for it is ending. Tido von Schoen-Angerer and co-authors review progress and set out what the next strategy should fix. Their analysis works from WHO documents and stakeholder views.

They find research on these practices is growing but lags far behind their use, and needs funding priority. Training guidance sets useful minimums, yet rules should respect how formal and informal practice differ. Herbal products have gained oversight, but other products still need a risk-based approach. The reviewers also say disease plans often overlook what these practices could add. Finally, countries differ widely, some welcoming and some restricting such care. They urge a positive framework that ties it to universal health coverage.
pmc-10694090:
Ahmad Hosseinzadeh and five colleagues published a case report in two thousand twenty-three on a rare infection tearing into the body's main artery. A fifty-three-year-old man came in with belly pain and black stools. Scans showed an inflamed bulge in his abdominal aorta.

During surgery the team found a hole linking the aorta to the gut. They replaced the damaged stretch with a synthetic graft and closed the hole from inside the artery. A month later, blood tests revealed brucellosis, a bacterial infection from animals, as the hidden cause. Antibiotics for the infection followed. The authors urge doctors to consider this infection behind inflamed aortic bulges, and show one workable repair.
pmc-10694390:
Lesang Shen and colleagues compare the tiny sacs breast tumors shed with those from other sources, in a study from twenty twenty-three. The sacs carry messages between cells near the tumor. Sacs grown in culture may differ from tissue ones. The team collected sacs from tumor tissue, normal tissue, blood, and tumor organoids.

Tissue sacs carried a cancer-specific mark rich in adhesion and immune molecules. Fibroblasts linked to the cancer fed a large share of the tissue sac network. Organoid sacs missed much of the matrix and immunity character. Tissue sacs also stirred macrophages and killer T cells more strongly. Some blood sac markers from noncancer cells showed promise for finding the disease. The study argues real tissue sacs set the standard. Culture models only partly copy them.
pmc-10694990:
Emma Hansson, Venkat Ramakrishnan, and Mary Morgan present a 2023 systematic review on a surgical trick used in breast reconstruction. Surgeons rebuild breasts with the patient's own belly tissue. A common failure is venous congestion, blood pooling in the flap, blamed in many lost flaps. Venous supercharging adds an extra vein connection to drain the tissue. The team gathered and graded all studies on its effects.

Thirty-six studies qualified, but most carried serious limits and indirect evidence. Only one randomized trial appeared, and it found fewer complications with the added vein. Certainty ratings came out low or very low for key outcomes like complications and hospital stay. Deciding who needs the trick ahead of time also rested on weak evidence. The authors conclude the benefit is plausible but unproven. Better trials are needed before routine preventive use.
pmc-10696090:
Lisa Miller and co-authors study how past trauma shapes brain responses to self-control tasks across a military deployment, in this 2023 paper. Service members face heavy trauma loads, which can alter brain circuits and raise the risk of post-traumatic stress. The team gave 166 mostly male army combat staff a Go/NoGo task before and after deployment. Brain waves during the task were tracked.

People with heavy past interpersonal trauma showed changed signals for conflict monitoring and response holding across deployment. Trauma that began in the teen years shifted response signals in a different way. Trauma from childhood left its own pattern. Arousal symptoms tracked with the conflict signal. The authors say support plans should weigh both how much trauma a person carries and when it began.
pmc-10696890:
Gustavo Patow and co-authors model the whole brain to separate the effects of two proteins in Alzheimer disease in a 2023 study. The proteins, amyloid-beta and tau, build up in the brain and are tied to failing memory. Which one drives activity changes at each disease stage was unclear.

Their dynamic model of brain regions was tuned to match how each protein shifts the balance between excitation and inhibition in local circuits. In early impairment, amyloid-beta dominated the effect. In full disease, tau took over as the dominant influence. The authors say regional maps of the two proteins can define realistic brain models. The work offers a test bed for hunting biomarkers and drug targets in simulation before trials.
pmc-10698490:
When a virus spreads, the share of people who catch it often overshoots the level where the spread would naturally stall, and that overshoot fills hospitals. Maximilian Nguyen and co-authors pin down the worst case in a 2023 paper on the classic spread model. They derive an exact ceiling for the overshoot rather than a rough guess.

The ceiling lands at just under a third of the population past the stall point, at one sweet-spot mix of spread traits. Data from an early COVID-19 wave in a Brazilian city show how real that hazard runs when spread sits near the danger zone. The team then extends the frame to models with vaccination, giving planners a firm worst case to build surge capacity against.
pmc-10698790:
Priyanka Patel, Andrew Ellefson, and David Paul examine how a standard risk calculator's use of race may steer steroid treatment unequally in premature infants. The calculator predicts bronchopulmonary dysplasia, a chronic lung disease of prematurity, and includes race as an input. Clinicians use such predictions when deciding on postnatal corticosteroids.

In a cohort of two hundred seventy-three infants born before thirty weeks, Black and White babies had similar gestation and breathing support. Yet the calculator predicted lower risk for Black infants on both day fourteen and day twenty-eight. Applied retrospectively, that gap translated into different theoretical steroid administration by race. The authors join calls to remove race from clinical prediction tools.
pmc-10698890:
Ting Shi and co-authors hunt, in 2023, for what puts children with COVID-19 at risk of convulsions. Seizures are a worrying brain symptom in infected children. The study compared one hundred two children with convulsions, one hundred seventy-two without, and fifty healthy controls at a children's hospital.

Convulsions struck over a third of patients, mostly toddlers infected with the Omicron variant. Several inflammation ratios ran high in the convulsion group, while protective cell counts, including natural killer cells, ran low. Statistical modeling flagged a low natural killer cell count and a past history of fever seizures as strong risk factors. The authors urge close monitoring of children matching that profile.
pmc-10701790:
Kentaro Shirakura and co-authors report a two-stage repair of aortic dissection and arch aneurysm in a patient aged ninety-two, in a case report from 2023. A full arch replacement is the standard fix when a tear and a bulge occur together. For an older patient with other illness, that surgery can be too invasive to survive.

The woman first had a partial arch replacement by open surgery. A stent graft repair through a vessel followed as the second stage. The hybrid plan treated both the tear and the bulge with less strain. The case shows staged repair can suit very old patients who cannot face one large operation.
pmc-10703790:
Mariame Kane leads a team of thirteen authors showing that the heart's mitochondria keep a schedule, and that fasting rewrites it differently in males and females' daily cycles. Using electron microscopy, enzyme activity assays, and reporter mice that flag mitochondrial cleanup, they tracked heart mitochondria across times of day, sex, and fed or fasted states.

Mitochondrial numbers peaked at one point in the daily cycle in fed animals, a rhythm governed by the heart's own BMAL1 clock gene. Energy-chain activity did not oscillate but dropped sharply with fasting, alongside cleanup of mitochondria, more antioxidant protein, and more of a fission protein. Knocking out the clock gene abolished the fasting cleanup response. The interactions among sex, clock, and feeding are the paper's core claim.
pmc-10705090:
Light-activated cancer therapy can work better when the light dose is split in two, and Hongjing Sun, Weibing Yang, Yihong Ong, Theresa Busch, and Timothy Zhu measure how much better in mice. Tumors were dosed with the drug Photofrin, then lit twice with a two-hour gap, at three total light levels. The team tracked a dose measure based on reactive oxygen, the damaging species the light creates.

Ninety-day survival jumped under the split scheme at every level, reaching one hundred percent at the highest dose against fifty percent for one sitting. The split scheme also needed a lower oxygen dose to reach its best result. Splitting, the team concludes, buys lasting control at no extra drug cost.
pmc-10707390:
Takahito Suzuki and co-authors trace how a long non-coding RNA helps guard a tumor suppressor gene in lung cancer, in a study from 2023. The RNA, named LINC00173, does not build proteins but steers other genes. Its partner is a protein called SNAIL, which is known to switch genes off. The guarded gene, FHIT, slows tumor growth when it is active.

In a lung cancer cell line, the RNA was found bound to SNAIL. Removing the RNA lowered FHIT levels, while removing SNAIL raised them. Removing both restored FHIT, which proves the chain of control. Data from more than five hundred patients backed the same links. The authors say the axis may drive how this cancer starts and spreads. It could offer a fresh target for drugs.
pmc-10712890:
YanLong Li and Jin Peng measured how digital financial inclusion, access to finance through phones and platforms, changed welfare across Chinese provinces from 2013 to 2019. They built a welfare index from income, jobs, housing, education, and medical care. Digital inclusion raised welfare on every component, and the finding survived statistical cross-checks. The gains were larger in the central and western provinces than in the richer east.

Tracing the mechanism, the authors found digital finance improved welfare mainly by creating jobs, and secondarily by raising public welfare spending. One channel cut regional imbalance while another widened it: the job effect favored the interior, the spending effect favored the east. On balance, digital inclusion narrowed the welfare gap between regions and within the interior. The study maps where phone-based finance does the most social good, and warns that its side channels do not all push toward equality.
pmc-10713190:
Yudai Chen, Liping He, and Xiaoling Zheng published a study in 2023 on stomachs that grow more than one early cancer at once. Multiple early gastric cancers and their precancerous cousins are treated by tunneling under the lining to peel lesions away, but their patterns were loosely described. Reviewing twenty-three such patients treated over a decade at two Fujian hospitals, the team compared each patient's first and second lesions.

Multiples made up about five percent of early cases, mostly appearing together rather than years apart. The paired lesions sat close together and resembled each other: matching shape, depth, and tissue type, with strongly correlated positions in the stomach. The practical moral is vigilance: find one early cancer, and the endoscopist should scour the neighborhood for its twin.
pmc-10713590:
Rafael Porras and four co-authors test whether durum wheat's leaf rust resistance survives the hotter, carbon-rich air ahead. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Mediterranean wheat faces both climate stress and this fungal disease, and their interplay was unclear.

Greenhouse trials mimicked conditions forecast for Córdoba, Spain, late this century. One susceptible and two resistant wheat lines faced the rust under each climate. Heat and extra carbon dioxide left the lesions' outward look unchanged. Inside the tissue, though, the susceptible line formed fewer pustules yet lost more photosynthetic area. Heat drove most of the damage. Inoculating during heat cut infection sharply, hinting that heat waves themselves may suppress the fungus.
pmc-10714490:
Takahiro Tsukioki, Seema Khan, and Tadahiko Shien review the state of breast cancer prevention in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Breast cancer is rising worldwide and often strikes women in their thirties. Known risk factors range from diet and alcohol to hormones and genes, yet prevention remains hard to apply well.

Drugs such as tamoxifen can lower risk but carry strong side effects. Preventive surgery helps women with high-risk gene mutations, though timing and quality of life questions remain. The authors also highlight DNA methylation, a chemical marking of genes, as a promising path to better risk checks. They call prevention a health priority for high-risk women.
pmc-10716390:
Umakanta Sahoo and co-authors compared yoga practice between town and country India in a 2023 survey study. Yoga and mindfulness can help older adults stay active, keep their minds well, and hold on to daily freedom. Yet uptake may differ a lot between rural and urban life.

The team drew on a national survey of 72,250 middle-aged and older adults. They charted how many in each setting practice yoga or mindfulness and which traits go with practice. Town and country gaps in access, work, and custom all play in. The results can steer health drives to the groups least served by such low-cost habits.
pmc-10719890:
David Lawrence and co-authors explore, in a 2023 study, why people with HIV and a fungal brain infection reach care late in Botswana and Uganda. The infection is a major cause of AIDS deaths, and late arrival doubles the risk of death. The team interviewed fifty-eight patients and family decision makers inside a clinical trial.

Headaches, the key early sign, were brushed off by patients and health workers alike as common and usually harmless. Few people knew of the fungal disease at all. Paths to hospital sped up only once HIV was diagnosed or disclosed, which forced the issue. The authors urge social and behavior programs inside advanced HIV care to cut these delays.
pmc-10722190:
Victor Danelon and colleagues reviewed a nerve receptor with immune ties in 2023. The receptor belongs to a large immune receptor family. Yet it acts mostly in the nervous system, not immune cells. Its shape resembles its cousins, but its habits differ. It pairs with helper receptors to do its work. It also binds loose paired signals, unlike most cousins. The review compares these traits across the family. A recent finding gives the receptor a direct immune doorway.

An immune surface protein changed during primate evolution. In humans and other primates, it can now bind this nerve receptor. In lower mammals, it cannot. That binding lets immune signals reach nerve cells directly. It can trigger removal of synapses in the brain. The authors link this route to inflammation and injury responses. They argue the receptor truly shares immune family behavior. The review reframes a nerve protein as a brain-immune bridge.
pmc-10722990:
Rafael Gomes and Carlos Afonso design a teaching experiment that makes a nitrogen compound in flowing liquid in a 2023 paper. Aminals form when an aldehyde meets a ring-shaped amine, and they are handy building blocks. Making one continuously, rather than in a batch flask, shows students modern green methods.

The starting aldehyde comes from biomass, which underlines renewable feedstocks. A solid catalyst packed into a simple reactor does the chemistry as liquid flows through. The setup is cheap enough to build during class itself. Students meet flow chemistry, heterogeneous catalysis, and green principles in one session. The experiment was written for laboratory teaching, with the full procedure laid out for instructors.
pmc-10724090:
Sebastian Rock and co-authors report an experiment from two thousand twenty-three on stress and reproduction in an invasive flatworm. Animals under stress often cut reproduction to survive. The team tested whether physical or chemical stress changes how fast the planarian Girardia tigrina reproduces without sex, by splitting into pieces.

Three hundred twenty worms were kept alone and watched for twelve days. One group faced ammonia in the water, one was decapitated, one was starved, and one was fed freely. The stressed groups began splitting at once and produced the most offspring, while the well-fed group waited a week. The authors propose that rapid splitting under stress boosts survival odds, and may help the species invade harsh waters.
pmc-10725690:
Zhi-Hao Zhao and colleagues published a risk prediction study in 2023. They studied ruptured liver cancer, a dangerous emergency. The tumor bursts and bleeds inside the abdomen. Acute liver failure can follow and kill quickly. Predicting who will develop failure guides urgent care. Records came from nearly three hundred patients over a decade. The team built a visual scoring tool, a nomogram. Tumor size and blood tests fed the model. Standard liver scores were used for comparison.

About one in five patients developed liver failure. Four factors drove the new risk model. They were tumor size, platelets, clotting time, and a marker. The nomogram predicted failure with high accuracy overall. It beat all three standard comparison scores clearly. Calibration checks showed predicted risks matched reality well. Clinicians could triage ruptured cases more confidently.
pmc-10725990:
Liyuan Chen, Fen Liu, Danna Fang, and Jianwei Li reviewed real-world results for the drug nusinersen in children with spinal muscular atrophy, types two and three. The drug is still fairly new, and most data came from trials. The team studied records of eighteen children treated in twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-three.

After the loading doses, arm and hand scores improved in nearly half the children. Those who improved most also showed a bigger rise in a key protein in spinal fluid. Liver tests stayed steady. Blood platelet counts and urine protein dipped at times but recovered. The authors call the drug effective and broadly safe, with checks still needed.
pmc-10728290:
Ayushi Sharma, Anjana Goel, and Zhijian Lin test a traditional plant remedy for rheumatoid arthritis in rats and safety data. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. The plant, Nyctanthes arbor-tristis, has long been used against joint inflammation.

Leaf extract was made with a water-alcohol mix. Safety was checked in rats first: a mid-level dose showed no signs of sub-acute poisoning. Rats with induced arthritis then got the extract while the team tracked paw swelling, body weight, arthritis scores, pain response, blood tests, X-rays, and tissue slides. Key markers of inflammation and its counterweight were measured too. The work supports the plant's folk use with lab evidence. It also sets a dose that looked safe in this animal testing.
pmc-10728990:
Six researchers relate fitness to personality and risk attitudes in Spanish teenagers in a paper from 2023. Three hundred seventeen high school students took fitness tests and a sports risk questionnaire. Cardiorespiratory fitness came from a shuttle run, strength from handgrip. Sex differences appeared in fitness and every questionnaire factor. Fitter, stronger, and older students scored higher on several risk-related factors.

Younger and stronger students scored higher on the remaining ones. A mediation analysis delivered the key insight: once fitness entered the model, sex stopped predicting the factors directly. Fitness carried the sex effect. The authors suggest building strength and endurance may shape how teens judge sports risk.
pmc-10730390:
Victoria Parker and a large team of colleagues run a phase 2 trial of cotadutide, a dual hormone drug. The trial is in people who are overweight or obese with type 2 diabetes, with focus on the liver. Cotadutide activates both GLP-1 and glucagon receptors; the glucagon arm was the open question. People in the trial got the drug, a placebo, or the GLP-1-only drug liraglutide.

Cotadutide emptied liver glycogen stores more than either of the other arms and reduced liver fat. That is exactly what glucagon action should do, since glucagon triggers glycogen breakdown. Tolerability matched earlier reports. The authors read the results as human proof that the drug's glucagon activity works in the liver. That supports its development for fatty liver disease, diabetes, and kidney disease.
pmc-10732190:
Meaghan Flagg and co-authors study COVID virus variants in human lung organoids in a 2023 paper. People vary hugely in how sick the virus makes them, and the reasons stay partly hidden. The team grew mini lung tissues from several donors and infected them with an early strain plus the Delta and Omicron variants of concern.

Omicron grew weakly in the organoids overall. Organoids from one donor, though, let both Omicron and the early strain grow much better than the others. Gene activity scans tied that openness to low baseline interferon signaling, the resting hum of antiviral defense. The authors propose that each person's resting interferon level helps set their risk from new variants, and that organoids can model that spread.
pmc-10733490:
Wanci Wang and five co-authors weigh the death toll of a hard cold spell that swept China in late 2022. The spell began on November 26, the first of that winter. Its bite came from a stuck high-pressure block over the Ural range, which deepened a cold vortex in its path. Their 2023 study uses health math that ties cold to death risk across many provinces.

The mean extra death risk sat at about 2.75 percent for the spell. In sum, the team counts about 369,000 extra deaths. Risk split wide by place, from near zero to about 5.7 percent. Southern provinces, less used to cold, took a worse hit than the north. Eastern and central provinces bore the most deaths, and Shandong bore the most of any province. The team ties the maps to health plans for cold snaps.
pmc-10735390:
Andrea June and Carrie Andreoletti present a 2023 report on a study-abroad course that mixes generations to study age-friendly life in Scotland. Their university joined the Age-Friendly University network in 2017. The course, Global Aging and Age-Friendly Initiatives, takes younger and older learners abroad together.

Before travel, students study lifespan development and the World Health Organization's healthy aging ideas. They first examine livability efforts at home in the United States. Nine days in Scotland then expose them to city and country life. The group rates transit access, green space, and local attitudes toward older adults. The design seeks mutual gain: students see policy in flesh, and older participants share in the learning. Programs elsewhere can copy the template.
pmc-10736190:
