Jennifer Deal, Bryan James, and Alison Abraham lead a 2023 symposium session on how sensory health is measured in aging research. Hearing and vision shape how older adults think, move, and stay social, yet researchers measure them in very different ways. A lab test of hearing captures what the ear can do, while self-report captures how a person hears in daily life.

The session draws on a large national study of Medicare beneficiaries that recently added direct measures of vision and hearing loss. Talks cover how measurement choice changes estimates of how common sensory loss is, above all among the oldest adults. Other talks address how sensory loss can distort thinking tests, and how the choice of hearing measure changes estimates of the share of dementia tied to hearing loss.
pmc-10736390:
Jennifer Yee-man Tang and co-authors built a heart risk calculator in 2023 for Chinese patients with schizophrenia in Hong Kong. People with schizophrenia die early from cardiovascular disease, yet the standard Framingham risk model ignores psychiatric factors and overestimates risk in Chinese groups. The team mined an electronic health data store for nearly forty thousand patients diagnosed between 2005 and 2015 who had no heart disease at the start.

Using survival models, they weighed which psychiatric and medical factors forecast a first cardiovascular event within ten years. The likely factors included other psychiatric diagnoses, how long the schizophrenia had lasted, antidepressant use, and first- or second-generation antipsychotic drugs. The resulting model aims to give clinicians a locally calibrated tool that reflects the added risks carried by mental illness and its treatment, rather than borrowing scores fitted to other groups.
pmc-10736490:
Mark Espeland and a team of co-authors studied whether fine air particles help explain racial gaps in Alzheimer's risk, in two thousand twenty-three. Their group held older Black and White women who had no dementia when they joined in the late nineteen nineties. Health was then tracked for years.

Black women faced a higher risk of the disease than White women. That gap stayed after the team allowed for place, income, habits, and heart risks. Exposure to fine particles was higher for Black women, but it explained only a small part of the gap. The link between particles and risk was about twice as strong in Black women.
pmc-10736590:
Sumina Shrestha and Christine While study migrant nursing aides in aged care homes in Australia in two thousand twenty-three. Many aides come from other lands, yet they often get casual work and low pay. The team asked if aides whose first tongue is not English feel less sure in their care work. They also asked how well those aides serve older residents.

Aides whose first tongue was not English felt less sure of their skills. Residents still rated them high for care, respect, and warmth. Residents said character mattered more than background. The authors back the use of migrant staff but call for fairer hours, pay, and support.
pmc-10736690:
Amal Wanigatunga and co-authors present a 2023 study of tiredness and real movement in men with and without HIV. Near seven hundred men in a long AIDS cohort, mean age 59, wore motion trackers and rated their fatigue three ways. Two ratings, a can't-get-going feel and work strain from body health, were common, at about two fifths and one fifth of men. Rates looked alike by HIV state.

Men with those two ratings moved less per day by roughly twenty to thirty-five minutes on the tuned counts. The third rating showed no such link. Self words and wrist data thus agree in part. Fatigue screens could flag men whose movement is quietly sliding. Movement loss feeds other risks in aging with HIV.
pmc-10737390:
Lijuan Yin, Woojin Song, Jordan Skowronski, and Maria Caceres report on testing movement in frail older adults at home, in two thousand twenty-three. Movement skill lets older adults handle daily tasks and stay in their homes. Activity programs could help, but home-bound adults are often left out of trials for lack of safe test methods.

Their study held more than one hundred frail participants, assessed just before the pandemic. A third did not feel safe doing standard balance or chair stand tests. Many who tried needed support or extra movements to stay balanced. The team adapted their instructions and built a new measure suited to frail adults, with added safety steps.
pmc-10737490:
Truc Bui wrote this economics paper, published in 2023. It asks whether states with stronger laws against age discrimination shielded older workers from the job losses of the COVID-19 recession.

Bui compared older and younger workers in states with strong and weak laws, before and after the pandemic hit, using national survey and employment data. The paper finds very little sign that stronger laws protected older workers. In some cases, stronger protections were tied to worse outcomes, though higher hiring partly offset higher separation rates. The pattern matched what happened in the Great Recession. The results suggest that tougher state laws alone do not keep older workers safe in a downturn.
pmc-10737590:
Loneliness is a real health risk in later life, and friendship is one source of support that may ease it. Emily Lim and Jeffrey Burr used Health and Retirement Study data from 2006, 2010, 2014, and 2018 to ask how the number of friends relates to loneliness in older men and women. Their sample held 7,257 community-dwelling adults aged 50 and over. They modeled the link with multilevel methods, including curved terms for friend count.

More friends went with less loneliness overall, but the shape of the link was not a straight line. For women the pattern was more complex, with both quadratic and cubic terms mattering. For men only the quadratic term mattered, hinting at a threshold effect. The authors conclude that social programs may need to be tailored differently for older men and older women if they aim to build friendships and cut loneliness.
pmc-10737690:
Denise Orwig and co-authors study recovery at home in a 2023 paper on hip fracture in older Americans. Men fare worse than women after hip fracture, and dementia, which is spotted unevenly by sex, may drive part of that gap. The team used Medicare records from 2010 to 2017 for patients who survived the hospital stay.

Their measure counts days alive and spent at home in the year after fracture. Men with dementia averaged about one hundred sixty-one such days, the lowest of the four groups. Women without dementia averaged the most, near two hundred forty-eight. Adjusted models confirmed men lose more home days, and the gap widens with dementia. The authors suggest that spotting and supporting dementia could lift recovery for men in particular.
pmc-10738990:
Hope Vue and Kellie Agrimson build a gene-editing toolbox for studying testicular cells in a 2023 project report. Aging raises both cancer and infertility rates, and testicular germ cell cancers have been climbing. To learn what single genes do in male germ cells, the team set up a CRISPR system in testicular cancer cell lines, which stand in for germ cells in the dish.

They targeted two genes: one that brakes the cell cycle, and one induced by a stress hormone. Primers and guide RNAs were designed with online bioinformatics tools to cut each gene out cleanly. The readout is cell proliferation after the knockout. The project is groundwork: a tested editing kit that later studies can use to probe fertility and cancer genes one by one.
pmc-10739090:
Adelnia, Wang, and Gore build a scan method to gauge tiny vessel shifts in aging muscle in this twenty twenty-three paper. Small vessel harm is thought to feed a range of age-linked ills, from muscle waste to heart strain. No proven no-cut scan yet reads small vessel shape and count in live tissue.

Inside, the new method uses a weak hold field to catch how water spins shift near tiny vessels. The team ran it in full three-way form on the lower legs of five mid-age rats. Read values fell in a set way as the hold strength rose across the test range. The team plans checks in young rats and proof by tissue cuts next to firm the method up.
pmc-10739990:
Lukas Wehmeier and six co-authors present a 2023 paper on a detector upgrade that opens the terahertz gap to nanoscale spectroscopy. Near-field infrared tools characterize materials at tiny scales, but the single-digit terahertz range, where many excitations live, stayed hard to reach. The team cooled a mercury cadmium telluride detector with liquid helium instead of the usual milder cooling. Its threshold dropped sharply, noise improved, and its response sped past ten megahertz.

Mounted at a national synchrotron facility, the setup measured spectra from five to over fifty terahertz, a span long nicknamed the THz gap. Demonstrations captured vibrations in two crystals and exotic surface waves in a layered material. The authors offer the instrument as a user program for visiting researchers. They frame it as finally bringing broadband nanospectroscopy to this neglected frequency range.
pmc-10741390:
María José Sevilla-Sánchez and co-authors published this 2023 study on a snake venom enzyme as a possible cervical cancer drug, and on making it in a lab instead of milking snakes. The enzyme, a phospholipase called Pllans-II from a Central American pit viper, killed cervical cancer cells while sparing healthy ones in earlier work. Safety and supply were the open questions.

In mice, the native enzyme caused no bleeding at the injection site and no spikes in inflammation or liver damage markers, and organs stayed clean under the microscope. The team then brewed a recombinant copy in bacteria and checked it against HeLa and Ca Ski cancer lines: the copy kept the enzyme activity and the anticancer punch. The results clear two early hurdles toward therapy.
pmc-10741990:
Guoyu Li and five co-authors study reindeer hooves to design better robot feet for frozen ground, in a two thousand twenty-three bionics paper. Robots scouting icy or planetary terrain need grip that ordinary feet cannot provide.

The team prepared soft and hard frozen soils and measured friction and pressure using reindeer trotting data. The hoof's cusp, outer edges, and capsules carry the load, and microscopy revealed tight fur scales and ribs in fixed proportions. Four bionic foot designs followed. The foot combining ribs with a hoof-like capsule gripped best, raising dynamic friction by roughly eleven to thirty-two percent over a standard checkerboard foot. Fine surface patterns pressing into rough ice explain the gain.
pmc-10742390:
Özgür Eroğul and four co-authors scan the eye's tiny vessels in gout patients, hunting early damage from high uric acid. Their cross-sectional study was published in twenty twenty-three. A noninvasive angiography scan can map retinal vessel density without dye.

Thirty patients with gout were compared with thirty-two healthy people. The surface vessel density at the center of vision and around it ran lower in patients. Deeper vessel layers showed no clear differences. Higher uric acid levels tracked with thinner surface density and more gaps in the layer beneath the retina. The eye may reveal gout's vessel toll before symptoms appear.
pmc-10742690:
Vincenzo Ricci and co-authors propose a guide for ultrasound imaging of skin scars in a 2023 paper. Modern machines with high frequency probes can assess surface tissues accurately. Use of ultrasound for skin problems is growing, yet no standard protocol existed for pathological scars.

The guide starts from how scars look under the microscope, then builds a layer by layer scanning approach from surface to deep. The aim is a reproducible exam that different providers can perform the same way. A shared language for findings should also help clinicians compare results and follow scars over time.
pmc-10742890:
Neelam Vanjari and co-authors report a blood cancer case where a hidden gene swap hid behind confusing chromosome results, in a case report from 2023. The patient had a rare fused gene pairing, BCR with JAK2, formed through tangled chromosome breaks. Standard tests hinted at the swap but could not pin down its shape.

The team used optical genome mapping, a method that reads long DNA stretches for large changes. The method confirmed the fused gene and showed the exact break path. It also found extra swaps touching other genes, which may help explain a poor response to chemotherapy. The authors review past cases and urge deeper testing when this swap is suspected.
pmc-10744390:
Chenhao Xue and co-authors design and print springy lattice structures for sports gear, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. The lattice follows a smooth, repeating minimal-surface shape that can be tuned by formula. Flexible gear like insoles and helmets gains from light weight and shock uptake.

A design method based on the shape formula let the team set stiffness in advance. Printed samples were squeezed in tests and matched by computer models. Shape and solid share drove most of the behavior. Sloped and mixed lattice designs added gains in softness and shock uptake. Tests mapped the full squeeze curve of the printed parts.
pmc-10744690:
Chao He and co-authors survey in 2023 the fungi living inside cultivated medicinal plants in farmland in northern China. These internal fungi help plants grow and resist stress, yet their communities in farm settings were little known. The team used high-throughput sequencing across plant species, tissue types, and seasons to map who lives where inside the plants.

They found over a thousand fungal groups, dominated by one major class. Host species and tissue shaped communities more than season did. Diversity was higher in roots than leaves in summer, reversing in winter. Network links between fungi were mostly positive, and leaves showed more complex networks than roots.
pmc-10745390:
Animals pass immune memory to their young, and colostrum is one carrier of it. Mesfin Yimam and co-authors ask whether plants hide similar transfer factors. They screened 100 protein-rich plants. Extracts were tested on human blood cells set to attack cancer target cells. Any extract that boosted killing beyond a colostrum-based factor counted as a hit. The first pass gave an 11 percent hit rate.

Three extracts were confirmed protein-rich. Filtering split their proteins by size, and the mid and large fractions stayed active. Seeds of radish and mustard ranked as the top two hits. Their active fractions went forward for deeper study. The authors frame the hunt as a search for plant-based immune boosters.
pmc-10745490:
Tao Wang leads a team that tunes a glowing phosphor with indium swaps. Their study from twenty twenty-three deals with a chromium doped material. It was made by a high heat solid phase method.

Some gallium ions were swapped for indium in the matrix. The glow shifted red and held well at high heat. Inner and outer efficiency both rose with the swap. The tuned powder was packed into a near infrared LED. That LED told water from pure ethanol in tests. Such checks show promise for non destructive testing.
pmc-10746990:
Mafalda Miranda and co-authors study people who learn of their HIV infection late in a 2023 European paper. Late presenters may spread the virus for years before diagnosis, since they do not know their status. The team used a shared European database covering 2,679 people followed between 2008 and 2019. Virus gene trees grouped infections into transmission clusters.

Most people carried subtype B, and most were men in their late thirties. Clusters holding late presenters were compared with clusters of people caught early. The share of late presenters inside clusters tells health teams how much spread happens in silence. That share helps decide where testing drives would cut transmission most.
pmc-10747990:
Ana Gavilán and a team of co-authors test whether adding a second viral gene region sharpens mumps outbreak tracing in Madrid, in a two thousand twenty-three molecular epidemiology paper. Mumps keeps resurging despite high vaccine coverage, and standard surveillance sequences only the SH gene.

From nine hundred three cases in the two thousand fifteen to two thousand twenty wave, four hundred fifty-three were genotyped, revealing eight SH variants and thirty-four haplotypes. Geographic mapping exposed previously undetected clusters. Ninety cases then received combined SH plus non-coding region sequencing; the extra region failed to improve cluster discrimination. The authors judge the addition of limited resolution for local outbreak investigation and keep SH as the workhorse.
pmc-10748090:
Wei Chen and co-authors build a fouling-proof sensor for a cancer marker in blood in two thousand twenty-three. The marker, CA19-9, helps catch and track several cancers early. Blood is messy, though, and proteins coat sensor surfaces, blurring the read.

Their electrode wears a three-dimensional web of graphene laced with albumin, glued into a porous, conductive mat that resists fouling. Antibodies on the mat grab the marker, and an impedance read reports the catch without any label dye. In human serum the sensor read from near its floor up to a thousand units per milliliter and kept its signal clean. Checks against the standard lab assay matched. Selectivity and stability also held up.
pmc-10752490:
Kun Zhang and co-authors review mouse models of cancer spreading to the spine in a 2023 letter-style article. The spine is a common landing site for metastases. Patients suffer pain, fractures, and deformity as tumors invade spinal bone, and better treatments need better lab models.

The authors summarize the models in use and what each is good for. Human tumor cell lines from prostate, lung, melanoma, kidney, and breast cancers can all seed spinal tumors in mice. Mouse cell lines serve the same purpose in mice with working immune systems. Matching the model to the question helps researchers study how spinal metastases grow and test new therapies against them.
pmc-10753690:
Four surgeons, Aniket Wagh, Jignesh Tandel, Kapil Jagtap, and Sanjay Kantharia, report a case series from 2023 on full elbow joint replacement in young patients. The work follows four cases for eight years after surgery. Each case had a distinct cause of severe elbow harm.

The four causes were joint disease, a lasting dislocation, a stiff joint after injury, and a failed first replacement. All four patients got the same kind of linked implant through an approach from the back of the arm. At eight years, all showed strong function and lasting pain relief, with high scores on a standard elbow rating scale. The authors argue the surgery can suit some young patients well.
pmc-10754290:
Abhineet Ram and co-authors wrote a 2023 review on how cells read signals from a key pathway called ERK. The pathway helps control cell growth, death, and change into new cell types. This is the second part of a two-part guide, and it focuses on what happens downstream of the signal.

Cells turn the timing and strength of the signal into distinct changes in gene activity. The review draws on experiments and computer models, with a focus on studies that watch single cells with sensors. It groups the effects into four modes: changing cell counts, guiding patterns by gradients, spreading waves of change, and creating varied cell states. These modes break down in cancer, which makes them targets for new drugs.
pmc-10808490:
Jill McTavish and co-authors argue that case conceptualization is a neglected tool in child welfare work, in an article published in 2023. The method, also called case formulation, helps workers build a clear picture of a child's history and situation before choosing a plan. It is widely used in mental health care but rarely in welfare settings.

The authors lay out a step-by-step version of the method shaped for child welfare. They show it at work in a made-up case of a 10-year-old child referred for mental health and behaviour concerns. Standard services did not help the child, and further advice was sought. A careful formulation led to a sharper treatment plan and a better outlook. The authors urge welfare teams to use the method more often.
pmc-10834690:
Tian-Le Shi and fifteen co-authors published a plant genomics study in twenty twenty-four on how yellowhorn, a hardy oil tree, builds its valuable fats. The tree's oil serves as both food and biofuel and is rich in very long-chain fatty acids. The pathway making them was mostly unknown.

The team reconstructed the pathway and annotated one hundred thirty-seven enzyme genes. Four oleosin genes, active only in fruit, package the oil and likely anchor production. A time-ordered co-expression network across fruit and leaf development spotlighted key enzymes and regulators. Two transcription factors sat at the top of the fruit network, steering carbon into fatty acids. The results guide breeding and engineering of this stress-tough oil crop.
pmc-10863790:
Yoo, Kang, and Jung ask if pancreas surgery diabetes raises heart risk. Removal of pancreas tissue can cause a form of diabetes. Diabetes is a known risk for blocked heart vessels. No past study checked that risk in pancreas cancer patients.

The team used a national health database in South Korea. Records covered cancer patients who had surgery from 2002 to 2019. More than 30,000 patients were in the full pool. Matched pairs cut bias from unlike patient traits. Risk models weighed new diabetes against new heart illness. Their aim was to guide heart checks after pancreas surgery.
pmc-10899890:
Alegre, Suneeta Sharma, Farley Cleghorn, and Carlos Avila call for structural fixes to primary health care in poorer nations in work dated two thousand twenty-three. The hosted text dates the work to two thousand twenty-three. Primary care is the cheapest route to health cover for all, yet funding lags and systems stay weak, above all for the marginalized.

Forty-five years after primary care hit the global agenda, the pandemic exposed how fragile the platform is. The authors propose five game-changers: weave services around the client, digitize care, reinvest efficiency gains into essentials, sharpen district and clinic management, and deepen community voice. Each must be fitted to local ground, they stress. Advocacy alone, they argue, has spent its force.
pmc-10945490:
Wei Wang and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-three study building a prognosis model for bile duct cancer after surgery. The model rests on a gene regulator called SIRT2. Its levels differ between tumour and normal tissue in public data.

Tissue from dozens of matched pairs was stained to measure the protein. Patients treated surgically at one hospital over several years were followed. The team linked protein levels to tumour features and survival. A combined prediction model was then built and checked with standard accuracy curves. Clinicians get a biology-based tool for judging which patients need closer follow-up.
pmc-10956690:
Mohammad Mahdi Doust Mohammadi and co-authors published a review paper in 2023 on the social weak spots that put immigrants and refugees at extra risk in disasters and health emergencies. Culture, money, and legal status can all leave these groups exposed when floods, quakes, or outbreaks strike. Aid that ignores those weak spots often fails the people who need it most.

The team searched seven databases and kept fourteen studies for close reading. Across them, these groups ranked among the most in need of urgent care in epidemics. Language gaps, poor housing, and fear of officials came up again and again. The review ends with steps agencies can take to close those gaps.
pmc-11041490:
Arif Budiarto and co-authors scope the studies that use machine learning on health records to predict asthma attacks. A warning tool could let patients and doctors act before an attack turns grave. Records hold years of history on each patient, and learning models can mine them for risk patterns. Many teams have built such tools; this review judges how well the work has been done.

The team searched two databases for studies from 2012 to early 2023. Papers had to use health record data as the main source, predict asthma attacks, and compare model performance. Reviews, commentaries, and protocol papers were left out, as were papers with no detail on method or results. Seventeen papers made the cut. They were summed up across data cleaning, algorithms, validation, explainability, and real-world use. A model that clinics cannot read or trust will warn no one.
pmc-11065190:
Ishola and co-authors reported a rare newborn hernia case in a study whose head dates it to 2023, from Nigeria. In this condition, gut loops fail to return to the belly after their normal early herniation in the womb. It is rare and often mixed up with a small omphalocele, a close but distinct fault.

Their patient was a 4-day-old boy whose hernia was blocked. The cord stump was swollen, ringed at its base by a collar of normal skin, and the belly wall gap spanned about four centimeters. The team lay out the signs that split this fault from its twin and how they fixed it. The case warns delivery teams to look twice.
pmc-11110090:
Children with one paralyzed vocal cord risk food and liquid slipping into the airway, and clinicians sometimes feed them lying on their side to help. Neil Monaghan and co-authors check whether position really matters in a 2023 chart review.

Swallow studies from ninety affected children were examined, including twenty-three tested in both upright and side-lying positions. Across all liquid thicknesses, penetration into the airway and full aspiration occurred at similar rates in both postures. The paired subgroup showed the same flat pattern. The authors note their data set had gaps, so the question is not fully closed. Still, the expected protective effect of side-lying did not appear, which may free families from an awkward routine.
pmc-11460290:
Lim and five co-authors speed up cell-by-cell ray harm sims with a pre-made track bank in this twenty twenty-three paper. Such sims trace how ray cures scar DNA in each cell of a tumor. Full track math per cell is true yet far too slow for drug design runs.

Inside, lone-track harm files are made once and kept in a bank for reuse. Time stamps are hand-added to those files to catch dose-rate play. A cell-fate model then reads a drawn file and calls breaks, bad fixes, and death. Checks on break yield match lab facts from past work in the field. A test on tumor cells dosed with a ray drug gave scar counts in line with print.
pmc-11532390:
McCall Calvert, Maliha Hoque, and Corlett Wood measure how plant and microbe genes shape their mutual exchange, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Legumes trade sugars for nitrogen fixed by rhizobia partners. Outcomes of such mutualisms swing with context, and the traded traits themselves were little measured.

The team split trait variation by plant gene type, microbe gene type, and their pairing. Pairing and microbe effects dominated most traits, including how traded goods were used and produced. That reach surprised the authors, who expected plant genes to rule the use traits. The work grounds future tests of why fitness variation persists in mutualisms.
pmc-11533290:
Mursalin Habib and four co-authors study flat spots in evolutionary tree search in a 2024 paper. When data are missing for some species, many different trees can score exactly the same. Such plateaus, called terraces, confuse the hunt for the best species tree.

Earlier work defined terraces for single-gene analyses and later for species trees from gene collections. The older species version ignored how close the tied trees sit to each other in shape. This study characterizes true species tree terraces mathematically. It shows they do not depend on how much gene trees disagree. A new peak terrace type adds shape awareness to the picture. The results clarify when missing data makes tree choice genuinely ambiguous.
pmc-11535390:
Hideo Hagihara and Tsuyoshi Miyakawa published a review and pooled analysis in twenty twenty-four on a small shift in the brain: its acid level. Brains of people with schizophrenia and bipolar illness run a bit more acid, tied to changed energy use. The pair asked if the same holds in deep low mood.

They pooled thirty-nine data sets, close to eight hundred patients and over nine hundred controls. Brain pH was lower in the ill group, a small but clear gap. The gap also held when they checked for ties to how long the illness had lasted and how often it came back. Low mood, it seems, shares this quiet brain change with its sister illnesses.
pmc-11547390:
Cezary Kraskiewicz leads a team that tests tram track mats made from old tires. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with mats placed under track slabs. Town growth brings more noise from transport that must be cut.

Mats of many depths and weights were tested in the lab. Some had holes and some had none at all. The mats use shred rubber from waste car tires. Test rules came from a set German standard for such mats. Results were then used to design two track types. Rail bend and mat stress were worked out for each.
pmc-11548090:
Costanzo and co-authors work in 2024 on a light based sensor that can spot human blood at crime scenes without harming the sample. Current quick tests can mistake other fluids for blood and can spoil later DNA work. Their sensor uses short DNA strands that bind tightly to red blood cells.

The design pairs gold specks with tagged DNA strands that glow when freed. When red cells are present, the strands break away and the glow returns. Two blood binding strands were chosen for the design. The team tuned how strands join the gold, pair with tags, and break free, and they saw the glow return as hoped in tests.
pmc-11565790:
Verena Schäfer and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on how a breakdown product of 2-methylfuran reacts with DNA. The parent compound forms during food heating and is common in coffee. In the body it converts to 3-acetylacrolein, which was already known to react with amino acids. The team asked whether it also binds DNA building blocks.

The compound formed adducts with three of the four DNA bases tested, and the team built sensitive methods to measure them. In isolated DNA from rat liver cells, adducts grew with dose and time. In whole cells dosed with either compound, no adducts appeared, which suggests strong detox handling inside cells.
pmc-11573790:
Jeremy Balch and eight co-authors review machine prediction of patient-reported outcomes in a 2024 paper. The review feeds a bigger idea: an algorithm that predicts what an incapacitated patient would choose. Dozens of studies used learning models to forecast how patients rate their own outcomes after surgery or other events. Bone and spine surgeries dominated, and prior self-ratings were the strongest predictors.

Model performance was mostly poor to moderate, and fairness checks were rare. The authors conclude that values and preferences, not just demographics, must enter future preference predictors. Their scan maps what evidence exists for building one responsibly.
pmc-11574690:
Astrid Carton de Tournai, Yannick Bleyenheuft, and colleagues run a trial of intense two-hand play therapy for babies with one-sided cerebral palsy. The brain is most able to rewire in the first years of life, so early help may pay off most. The therapy trains both hands and the legs together through guided play.

Forty-six babies, six to eighteen months old, took part. Half got fifty hours of the therapy over two weeks; half kept their usual activities. The main test measured how well each baby used the weaker hand, with motor and parent-rated scores as backup. Babies were checked at the start, one month, and three months. The design aims to show whether a short, dense burst of therapy moves motor skills this early.
pmc-11575090:
York Kiat Tan and four co-authors test heat imaging for hidden joint inflammation in a 2024 study. Rheumatoid arthritis can inflame joints before they swell or ache. Ultrasound can spot that quiet inflammation, but it takes time and skill. A heat camera offers a quick, objective surface read.

The team compared wrist heat measures with ultrasound scores. Patients split into those with quiet wrists and those with sore or swollen ones. Among quiet wrists, heat values were checked against ultrasound signs of inflammation. Several raters scored both image types to test agreement. Links between heat and sound based measures were explored with standard statistics. The authors ask whether heat imaging can flag cases needing closer checks.
pmc-11580190:
Francois Cholette and a large team used virus family trees in two thousand twenty-four to find unmet HIV needs among men who have sex with men in Kenya. This group carries a heavy share of Kenya's HIV burden. Dried blood spots from three counties, collected across two survey rounds, supplied virus gene sequences from men living with HIV.

Closely related virus clusters showed where infections link together, hinting at ongoing spread and missed chances for testing, prevention, and treatment. Only a small share of samples sequenced successfully, limiting the view. Still, cluster patterns by partner-seeking setting help programs aim outreach where hidden transmission continues.
pmc-11580390:
Janina Leinberger and seven co-authors published a 2024 study of chemical signals made by a marine bacterium. The bacterium releases NAMEs, fatty compounds akin to the quorum signals many bacteria use, though NAMEs do not join that signaling. The team built a chromatography method to measure two major NAMEs and one true signal in cultures. The main NAME reached levels above the doses known to stop an alga and a fellow bacterium from growing.

Signal output ran all through growth, unlike the classic signal's pattern. Spiking cultures with each compound shifted gene activity in distinct waves, and stress genes answered differently to each. The authors read this as support for NAMEs serving as antibiotics in the wild. The method also enables dose-based tests of such chemistry.
pmc-11580690:
Samuel Schut and five co-authors wrote this 2024 review of how state boards in the United States treat extra training for chiropractors. After licensure, chiropractors must earn ongoing study credits to keep practicing. Whether long residency or fellowship training counts toward those credits was unclear.

Between February and April 2024, the team searched the websites and policy papers of all fifty states and the District of Columbia. Only four states clearly accept residency or fellowship training for credit. Six states have unclear wording on the point. The rest make no mention of such programs at all. The authors also noted the credit rules that apply to new license holders.
pmc-11583690:
Ha Nguyen Van and a large team load a cancer drug into soft-breaking silica particles to cut its harms. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The drug, docetaxel, works on breast, lung, and ovarian cancers, but it aims poorly and harms much. Its usual mixes add solvents that stir allergy and nerve ills.

Their carrier is a porous organosilica that breaks down inside cells, so it cannot pile up. It beats plain silica kin on size, surface, and drug load. Cell studies hint it can soften the drug's ill effects while it ferries the dose. The team frames it as a path to surer, gentler taxane care.
pmc-11586790:
Factories made of enzymes pinned to a solid support can be reused batch after batch, but they wear out in ways the eye cannot see. Javier Santiago-Arcos and co-authors watch that wear with a cryo X-ray probe in a 2024 study. Their catalyst pairs two metal-bearing enzymes that pass a helper molecule back and forth to keep a reaction loop turning.

Frozen snapshots show both the protein frames and their metal centers drifting within the support during use and heat stress. The pair moves as one unit rather than falling apart. That slow migration seems to tire the catalyst out, even while the proteins keep their shape. The authors say such maps should guide the design of tougher enzyme supports for industry.
pmc-11589590:
Yinghao Li and co-authors watched a mixed-metal catalyst make hydrogen, live, in a 2024 study. The catalyst is an ultrathin sheet mixing up to eight metals, called a high-entropy metallene. Such sheets are hard to shape and harder to understand while they work. The team made them in one pot and used X-ray tools during operation to see which atoms do the work.

One mix of five metals drove hydrogen making at very low extra voltage in acid, neutral, and alkaline water alike. The live view showed a division of labor among the metal sites. Manganese sites grab water parts and ease splitting at palladium sites. Rhodium sites hold hydrogen at just the right strength to speed its release. The study maps how the sites help each other.
pmc-11590190:
Jian-De Lu and eight colleagues tested whether a blood marker of nerve damage tracks with chronic kidney disease in the general population. Neurofilament light chain rises when nerve fibers are injured, and it is increasingly measured in blood. Its relationship to kidney function was controversial. The team analyzed 2,051 adults aged twenty to seventy-five from a United States national health survey cycle. Logistic and linear models linked the marker to kidney disease and two function measures.

Models adjusted for confounders, and results were checked separately by age and sex. The marker entered analyses on a log scale because of its skewed distribution. Population data of this size can settle whether the association is real or an artifact of small clinic samples. The twenty twenty-four study contributes to judging blood neurofilament as a kidney-relevant biomarker.
pmc-11592190:
Suhardi and co-authors build a mouse model of implant loosening that needs no wear debris in this 2024 study. Joint implants usually loosen in models because plastic wear particles inflame the bone. Real clinical loosening often happens without such particles, leaving a modeling gap.

Thirty-two mice received one of four implants in the leg bone. A rough press-fit titanium rod modeled healthy integration. A smooth plastic rod, a loose smooth rod, and a loose rough rod modeled three failure styles. Pull-out tests at two weeks measured interface strength. Tissue cell makeup matched samples from human revision surgery. The model lets researchers study quiet loosening, the kind patients actually present with.
pmc-11592890:
Caimei Wu and co-authors test whether selenium-fed yeast shields laying hens from cadmium harm to their ovaries, in work from 2024. Cadmium in feed can kill egg follicles and cut laying. The harm runs in part through excess self-eating in the cells that nurse the egg.

Sixty-four hens were split into four diet groups: plain feed, selenium only, cadmium only, and both. Hens on both kept better ovary health and laid more than hens on cadmium alone. Their hormone levels and follicle counts ran higher, and self-eating markers fell. Cadmium stored in tissue also dropped. The authors conclude the selenium dose used here blunts cadmium's ovarian harm.
pmc-11595090:
Julian Cheong Kiat Tay and a large team report early experience with pulsed field ablation for atrial fibrillation in Asia. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The method uses short electric pulses to scar small areas of heart tissue and block the stray signals that drive the faulty rhythm.

One hundred and one patients were treated from late twenty twenty-two to early twenty twenty-four. Most had the common short-burst form of the condition. About three in ten also had the back wall of the heart treated, and that extra step worked in every case. Success was judged by freedom from rhythm relapse after a three-month settling window, over a year. Safety checks covered death, stroke, and heart harm in the first month. The report adds Asian data where uptake of this new method was little known.
pmc-11597690:
Maria Amalia Taut and colleagues made tiny healing capsules for dental fillings in two thousand twenty-four. The capsules hold a liquid repair mixture. A thin polymer shell wraps each droplet. Cracks in a filling could break the shells open. Released liquid would then seal the crack.

The team tested several stirring speeds during production. Faster stirring gave uniform, round capsules. Slower stirring made mixed, uneven ones. Many lab methods confirmed size and structure. Controlled liquid release worked better in uniform batches. Dentists may one day use fillings that repair small cracks alone. That could extend filling life for patients.
pmc-11600490:
Chris D Fokkema and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on how Earth's orbital rhythms paced the climate of an ice-free Arctic some fifty-four million years ago. Sediment drilled from the Arctic seabed holds chemical and pollen records fine enough to resolve two thousand years per sample. Three cycles stood out, matching the known wobbles of tilt and orbit.

Sea surface temperatures swung by over a degree with tilt and about half a degree with the seasonal cycle. Warm peaks came with more pollen, spores, and marine productivity, meaning more rain washed nutrients into the basin. Because the warmth maxima line up with local sunlight maxima, the team concludes regional hydrology, not imported water, drove the pattern.
pmc-11603190:
Mohamed El-Kassas and co-authors compared blood-based scores for liver scarring in chronic hepatitis C in two thousand twenty-four. A biopsy can stage scarring, but it is invasive. Simple scores from blood tests could help sort patients, above all where resources are scarce.

The team checked six scores against biopsy results for nineteen thousand five hundred one patients in Egypt's national treatment program. All six scores predicted scarring stages. Four did best, and two led the pack. One, FIB-4, followed by King's score, best flagged advanced scarring and cirrhosis at the cut points they report. The authors back such scores for fast sorting of who needs specialist care.
pmc-11603290:
Yuan-Wan Sun and co-authors read saliva chemistry in mice dosed with a tobacco carcinogen in a 2024 study. Their long goal is a non-invasive early test for oral cancer. The mouse model they use mirrors the human disease well, and saliva is easy to gather without harm.

The carcinogen, a smoke compound found in the environment and tobacco, was painted into the mouths of mice three times a week for six weeks. A fine chemical read then set the saliva profile of dosed mice against that of controls. Shifts in small body chemicals stood out. Such shifts could form the base of a spit test for early oral cancer.
pmc-11603690:
Thi Quynh Anh Ho, Peter Lee, and Lan Gao published this epidemiology study in 2024. It measures the burden of leukemia and lymphoma, blood cancers, across Australasia and Oceania from 2010 to 2019, using Global Burden of Disease data. Six subtypes were tracked by age and sex, counting new cases, prevalence, deaths, and years of healthy life lost.

Acute myeloid leukemia and non-Hodgkin lymphoma carried the largest burden in both regions. Australasia's rates ran far higher than Oceania's, reflecting both detection and demographics. Over the decade, Australasia saw rising incidence and deaths for most subtypes. Oceania's trends were mixed, with some mortality measures falling even as incidence rose. Men generally saw worse trend lines than women. The authors argue that two neighboring regions need different strategies, and that wider access to modern treatments is the lever most likely to cut the burden.
pmc-11603890:
Olga Godovalova and co-authors present a 2024 study of how the human visual cortex folds before birth. The main sight field hides in a deep groove, and later fields share a second groove nearby. Fetal occipital tissue was stained for nerve and glia marks to watch the fields form. The main field, tied to the first groove, formed ahead of the shared bud of the next two fields.

Its working split began as input fibers from the deep brain grew in. At that same stage the first groove briefly smoothed out. Uneven timing, the team show, is the rule, not a flaw. Sight fields do not rise as one block. Fetal maps help doctors read early brain scans with better clocks.
pmc-11603990:
Aihan Wen and co-authors analyze hospital costs for lung disease patients in Yunnan, China, in a 2024 paper. The disease is COPD, a long-term breathing disorder that fills hospital beds. Records covered nearly seven hundred thirty thousand patients from 2016 to 2022. The team tracked spending trends and used path analysis to see what drives the bill, directly and through length of stay.

Total spending rose over the period, while the average bill per stay fell by about a fifth. Diagnosis and service fees grew as shares, while drug fees shrank. Age, hospital level, payment method, infections, and other illnesses all shaped costs, mostly by stretching stays. The authors argue that safely shortening stays is the surest lever for cutting patient costs and raising hospital efficiency.
pmc-11605590:
Masaki Tatano and co-authors study whether PET scans can predict how a common brain tumor will behave, in a paper from 2024. The tumor type, called meningioma, is the most frequent primary brain tumor. Most cases stay mild, but some grow back after surgery. The team compared scan results with lab findings from the removed tissue.

The study covered fifty-five patients treated with surgery over a span of years. Two tracer scans were checked against tumor grade and a marker of cell growth. Both tracers ran higher in higher-grade tumors. Both also ran higher in the twenty cases that later grew back. The authors conclude that scan values track how aggressive a tumor is. They say the scans can help flag patients at risk of return after surgery.
pmc-11607390:
Sanne Houben and four co-authors present a 2024 study of what legal professionals know about false memories at different ages. Judges, lawyers, and police must judge witness accounts, and memory errors change with age in ways that are not obvious. Young children, for one, can be more prone to planted memories in some setups, a pattern that reverses with age.

The team gave 102 legal professionals from three European countries a case story about a girl who saw her mother's murder. The story varied the witness's age, six versus twenty two, and whether her account came freely or after suggestion. Ratings showed the professionals leaned toward a false memory reading for the young witness.
pmc-11610490:
Mandeep K Chahal and co-authors review metal-free ring molecules as catalysts in a 2024 paper. The molecules, called tetrapyrrolic macrocycles, include porphyrins, the pigments behind blood and leaf color, and their cousins calix[4]pyrroles and corroles. Beyond their roles in life, lab-made versions serve in sensors, solar cells, and medical light therapy.

The review gathers cases where these rings speed reactions with no metal at their heart. They work as plain catalysts, as light-driven catalysts, and as electric-current catalysts. Changes to the ring, such as added side groups, bending out of flatness, or stiffening, tune how well they work. The authors present the family as a flexible base for green catalyst design.
pmc-11612190:
Hao Huang and co-authors compare ovarian tumors from Black and White women across gene, mark, and immune layers, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Tumors came from thirty-five Black and thirty-one White patients. The cancer type kills Black women at the worst rate ratio.

Near two hundred mark sites and near three hundred genes differed by group. Hit paths cover DNA repair, cell death signals, and fat handling. Silencing two named genes made cells drug-shy less and slowed growth. Black patients' tumors held fewer young and guard T cells. The authors urge work on how these gaps shape care response. Readers get hard biology behind a stark gap.
pmc-11613290:
Brielle Ruscitti, Caroline Kern, and Diana Bowser weigh the out-of-pocket costs of health plans for people with diabetes. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The health law in the United States widened coverage, but high fees and cost shares still strain those with long-term ills. They compare plans in many states for set user types.

They price the bench plan for a non-diabetic adult and for diabetic adults who engage much or little with care. Diabetics spend a far larger share of income past the fee than non-diabetics. Low-engagement diabetics can spend three times what high-engagement ones do. The upfront amount a patient must pay drives most of that spend. Town and country costs do not differ in a firm way.
pmc-11614490:
Lin leads a large team testing a mustard compound in toxoplasmosis, in work from twenty twenty-four. Allyl isothiocyanate is a natural product from mustard and horseradish, used in food preservation and medicine. Toxoplasmosis, caused by a widespread parasite, can be severe in acute form.

Mice were given the compound and then infected with a virulent parasite strain. Early in infection, the compound made the disease worse, not better. It suppressed inflammatory cytokines that the immune system needs to fight the parasite. The cautionary result shows a food derived compound can harm host defense, a point supplement claims often ignore.
pmc-11615190:
Álvaro Luna and Estel Blanch published a 2024 study of birds on a green roof in a Mediterranean city, Madrid, across a full year. Green roofs give city birds food and rest. How birds use them in such a climate was little studied. The team watched one green roof and the conventional roofs next to it, in all four seasons.

Seventeen bird species were seen in the area in total. Eight used the green roof. The feral pigeon led by far, and it used the roof all the time. The rest came only now and then. More species came at midday, and spring was the richest season. Most species live there all year, and most eat grain, or grain plus other foods. Feeding was the main activity seen on the roof. No nesting was confirmed. The team reads green roofs as a real benefit for city birds.
pmc-11616290:
Edmond Li and five co-authors ask patients what they think about shared electronic health records in a 2024 focus group study. When record systems cannot exchange data smoothly, patients may face errors and delays as they move between providers in Britain's National Health Service.

Eighteen patients with long-term conditions or many medicines, plus caregivers, joined five online groups in 2022. Most said record sharing falls short of their needs. Gaps in sharing led to wrong records, repeated errors, and poor choices by clinicians, forcing patients into workarounds. The group offered fixes: one central system, stronger data security, more staff training, and a bigger role for patients in keeping their own records accurate.
pmc-11616890:
Alison Skipper, Rowena Packer, and Dan O'Neill lead a 2024 consensus study on dog health research funding in the United Kingdom. More than fifty experts from research, veterinary work, and front line care ranked priority topics, future research approaches, and reforms to funding processes.

Most top issues concerned the human and dog relationship, such as ownership and behavior. Experts stressed how factors for dog and human welfare interlock. Topics judged most underfunded all concerned real world welfare, especially dog breeding and supply. A check of past funding for common chronic disorders added context to the gaps.
pmc-11618590:
Yan Song and co-authors build a camera system that films ultrafast events as a movie of two-dimensional frames, in this 2024 paper. Many fast processes, like the flight of a light pulse, need both fine time steps and full images. Standard cameras cannot do both at once.

Their design pipes the image through a fiber bundle that splits a square grid into four long lines. A streak camera records the lines in parallel, and software rebuilds the frames from the known fiber layout. The grid holds over four thousand picture points and resolves time near ten picoseconds. A light-flight test shows the system's promise for ultrafast science.
pmc-11618690: Xueqin Chen, Yangang Zhu, and Man Luo examine the link between poor vision and poor sleep in older adults in India, in this two thousand twenty-four study. The two problems often occur together in later life, but their tie has not been studied much. The authors set out to measure how visual impairment and insomnia relate in people who are middle-aged and older.
pmc-11619290:
Chen Jin leads a team of eight authors tracing chronic prostate inflammation to one chemokine circuit. That circuit recruits macrophages and pushes them to a hot state. The drivers of long-term prostatitis were not known. So the team screened a panel of forty-eight cytokines in men with prostatitis-like symptoms. They set those men against healthy controls. One signal, CCL5, stood out as much raised.

Tests in mice with autoimmune prostatitis confirmed the rise of CCL5. CCL5 binds its receptor CCR5 on macrophages. That push turns them toward the inflammatory M1 state. A phosphatase then keeps the Stat1 signal switched on. At the same time, the NF-kappaB pathway turns on, and cytokine output stays high. The team blocked the receptor with the drug maraviroc to test the value of this path as a drug target. The axis gives prostatitis a target it lacked before.
pmc-11621690:
Ingrid Bertin and colleagues studied ancient archery gear from a Spanish cave in two thousand twenty-four. The cave preserved organic materials remarkably well. Finds included arrows with feathers still attached. Tied fibers and sticky coatings also survived. Two probable bowstrings were part of the set. The gear dates to the early farming period.

Combined chemical and shape analysis identified the materials. The bowstrings are the oldest known made from animal sinew. Shafts used olive wood and reed, a first for prehistoric Europe. Birch bark tar coated the shafts. The burial setting hints at ritual meaning. Farming communities clearly prized skilled craft.
pmc-11622590:
Ying Luo and colleagues used gene sequencing of stool samples to study gut microbes in people with acute leukemia, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. They compared samples taken before and after chemotherapy. The team tracked which microbes were present, how varied the community was, and which antibiotic resistance genes the microbes carried. They also compared microbe patterns with blood test results and with the doses of antibiotics each patient received.

After chemotherapy, the gut community became less varied and more spread out between patients. Certain bacteria, including types known to carry resistance genes, became more prominent. Some antibiotic treatments were linked to resistant Klebsiella taking hold in the gut. The authors say these patterns can help doctors think about infection risk and antibiotic choice during leukemia care.
pmc-11624690:
A patch of tiny needles that melt into the skin can slip drugs past the skin's wall without a shot. Haonan Li and five co-authors review in 2024 the kind made from chitosan, a shell-born sugar with a kind face for flesh. The needles pierce the dead top layer, melt, and free their load where it counts, dodging the liver's first pass. The sugar's own hooks let builders tune its strength and tricks.

Uses in the works run wide: closing wounds, hauling big protein drugs, giving vaccines, and fighting skin tumors. The review sorts the builds by form and tells how each melts in the body. Gaps the team name include dose room and even needle strength. Their close maps a field mid-climb, with clinic goods in sight.
pmc-11628190:
Brenda Gati Mirembe and a large study team published an HIV prevention study in two thousand twenty-four on young African women. Young women account for two thirds of new HIV infections in Africa. Many start the preventive pill PrEP but take it poorly, which weakens protection.

The INSIGHT project enrolled over three thousand women aged sixteen to thirty at twenty sites in six countries. A quick urine test showed whether the drug had been taken in the past four days. Results were shared at once with tailored counselling at most visits. Nearly all women started PrEP. The study estimated recent adherence after accounting for missed tests, and checked whether earlier feedback raised later adherence.
pmc-11629990:
Francesco Ceccarelli and co-authors present AnnoGCD, a tool that labels cell types in single cell gene data, in a 2024 paper. Hand labeled training sets are costly, and new cell types keep turning up. A tool that only knows fixed labels misses them.

AnnoGCD mixes a small labeled set with raw data. A first block sorts the known types, and a second block hunts for new clusters on its own. Tests ran on five human data sets and a mouse atlas. The tool beat rivals on both known and new types, and it held up when some types were rare. Code and data are posted in public.
pmc-11631190:
Xyrus X Maurer-Alcalá and Eunsoo Kim present a 2024 journal article on TIdeS, a tool for finding true gene reading frames in transcriptomes. Samples from uncultured eukaryotes often carry contamination and mixed species, which breaks standard prediction tools. TIdeS was built to predict reading frames and sort real from foreign ones in a single stop.

Tested on transcriptomes from 32 taxa across the eukaryote tree, the tool beat the standard rival, finding more complete, in-frame sequences. It classified sequences well even under heavy contamination and from tiny inputs. The authors pitch it for family tree studies, host-symbiont work, and clean dataset building.
pmc-11632290:
Health care in Quebec is split across regions and sites, and that split breaks the path of patients who need chest surgery in more than one place. The authors tested a web platform, called Akinox, meant to smooth transfers between sites for cancer and non-cancer chest surgery. They ran the study in two regions and two sites, talking with 27 staff and managers, holding design workshops, and then surveying the 13 end users.

Every user agreed the platform helped. Most said it improved coordination between sites and continuity of care, and it helped with intake and with the flow of the process. Surgeons said it made the transfer of records safer and easier to track, including referrals and follow-up needs. Nurses praised its help before surgery, during surgery, and at discharge. Both sites chose to keep using it long term.
pmc-11634190:
Dae Hee Pyo and eight colleagues compared a bending laparoscopic instrument against rigid tools in colorectal cancer surgery. Straight tools limit wrist-like movement inside the abdomen. The ArtiSential device bends at its tip, which promises easier suturing and dissection. The study looked back at seven Korean hospitals, from twenty twenty-one to twenty twenty-two. Propensity matching paired 694 patients in the bending-tool group with 694 in the rigid-tool group.

Operating time was slightly longer with the bending tool, though not significantly so. No bending-tool case converted to open surgery, against one percent of rigid-tool cases. Overall complications ran about nine and a half percent in the bending-tool group. Baseline features were balanced after matching. This twenty twenty-four study sizes up whether a bending tip earns its place in cancer surgery.
pmc-11634390:
Kyoungdong Lee and co-authors set stomach cancer surgery results from before and during South Korea's 2024 doctor crunch side by side. In that year many young doctors quit training posts at once, and wards ran short. The fear was that care would slip. One top training hospital gave the team its surgery charts for the same weeks in past years and in the crunch.

Two hundred eighteen patients had surgery in the past span and thirty-one in the crunch. Cut counts fell by more than half in the crunch weeks. Ills after surgery came in about twenty-two of a hundred past cases and about ten of a hundred crunch cases. No bad ills at all arose in the crunch span, and cut time held near even. Sex and body mass, not the crunch, tracked who had ills.
pmc-11637490:
Yaguang Zheng and co-authors published a 2024 study of video telemedicine visits and medication adherence in patients with heart failure, a weak heart pump. Video visits grew fast in the pandemic years. Whether they hold adherence as well as office visits was not known. The team looked back at the records of one health center from a half year when both ways were offered.

Over nine thousand patients were in the analysis. The video-only group was small; the office group was vast. All were tracked for a half year from their visit. Adherence was measured as the share of days with medication in hand. Adherence above a set mark counted as sound. Statistical tools weighed the tie of visit kind to adherence, age, sex, and the rest. Most patients were old, in their late seventies, and most were White.
pmc-11637990:
Mélanie Ormancey and co-authors share design tips for plant peptides in a 2024 letter. Their topic is two peptide types: peptides encoded by microRNA genes, and partner peptides that boost a target protein. Both could help farming as chemical options shrink.

MicroRNA-encoded peptides raise the output of their own gene. Partner peptides instead help ribosomes reach a chosen protein, lifting its production. The authors explain how these peptides were found and why they suit farm use. The letter then lays out rules for designing active peptides of both kinds with ease. The goal is to help others create peptides that raise plant output safely.
pmc-11638290:
Nine authors present a case series from two thousand twenty-four on rebuilding the skull and eye socket in one operation after tumor removal. The tumors are benign growths where the sphenoid bone meets the orbit. Computer design now lets surgeons plan the cut and the implant together.

Eleven patients treated between two thousand nineteen and two thousand twenty-four were reviewed. Three-dimensional models of tumor, skull, implants, and cutting guides fed the navigation system, and models were printed at the hospital for planning. Most tumors were low-grade meningiomas. The custom implants are made of a strong medical plastic, PEEK.
pmc-11638390:
Milan Zimmermann and co-authors test whether a Huntington's gene also causes two other diseases in a 2024 study. Long repeats in the HTT gene certainly cause Huntington's disease, and a recent report found them surprisingly often in patients with ALS and frontotemporal dementia too. If the gene truly caused those diseases, carriers should appear in patient groups more often than chance allows.

The team screened 249 patients with genome sequencing and found exactly one repeat expansion, in a man with classic ALS signs and no hint of Huntington's. Brain tissue after death showed both diseases' marks side by side, motor damage from ALS plus Huntington-type protein clumps, but no Huntington-type shrinkage. The verdict: the two conditions co-exist rather than one causing the other.
pmc-11638690:
Jiakun Zheng and co-authors published this 2024 scoping review on using AI to measure what people eat. Standard tools like food diaries and recall interviews lean on memory and honesty, so their numbers often drift. AI offers a more automatic path, from photo-based logging to smart estimates of nutrients.

The team searched four databases for studies through mid-2023 and kept 25 that used modern AI on human food intake. The studies spanned 2010 to 2023 and a wide range of settings. The review sums up how well the tools work, where they beat the old methods, and where they still stumble. It gives nutrition researchers a map of a fast-moving field.
pmc-11639890:
Song Yang and co-authors search in 2024 for hub genes and drug targets in bile duct cancer using data from a chrysanthemum-based herbal formula. The cancer has poor outcomes and few treatment options. They combined gene expression, co-expression networks, and genetic causal analysis to find molecular drivers instead of relying on single data sources alone for the search.

Enrichment analysis pointed to cancer-related processes in tumor samples. Intersecting network modules with the herb's known targets gave four candidate hub genes. Docking tests showed the herb's compounds bind those genes. Genetic analysis also implicated fourteen immune-related genes as causal factors in disease risk.
pmc-11639990:
Mu-Long Lu and colleagues fed mushroom waste to sheep in two thousand twenty-four. Spent oyster mushroom substrate is produced in bulk. Most of it goes underused today. The team replaced corn silage at several levels. Young sheep were split into five feeding groups. Gut microbe changes in the small intestine were a focus.

One middle replacement level digested nutrients best. Blood liver enzymes shifted with inclusion level. Gut microbe richness stayed stable across diets. A few bacterial groups differed at the highest level. One fungus genus trended upward with feeding. Waste streams could become useful feed ingredients. Liver effects need watching at higher doses.
pmc-11640090:
Vivek Podder and co-authors present a 2024 review of immune therapy safety in brain metastases. Cancer spread to the brain is common in lung cancer, breast cancer, and melanoma. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs have become a core option there. They can be used alone or with chemotherapy and focused radiation. Their risk is immune side effects that can strike many organs. Brain patients face those risks on top of fragile neurology.

The review maps side effect mechanisms organ by organ. It grades safety across solo and combined treatment plans. Survival and control gains from the drugs are real, as the authors report. Neurologic side effects draw special care in the analysis. Oncologists get a balanced ledger for a hard trade-off. Brain spread once barred patients from such trials, so a dedicated safety record serves a group long left out.
pmc-11640190:
Hanin AboTaleb and colleagues tested metformin in a mouse fibromyalgia model in 2024. Fibromyalgia causes widespread chronic pain. Fatigue, poor thinking, and mood problems often follow. Metformin is a common diabetes drug. New interest focuses on pain relief beyond sugar control.

Treated mice showed less pain behaviour. One inflammatory signal fell in brain and cord. Brain chemical messengers also shifted under treatment. Male mice showed clear messenger changes. Glutamate fell while serotonin and norepinephrine rose. Female mice showed no such shift. The authors propose sex-specific mechanisms here. Pain relief is the main hope raised.
pmc-11641490:
Sonia Wardejn and co-authors tune plant-based wrap films that kill germs, for food packs that rot back to soil. The films come from starch, chitosan, seaweed gum, and two blends. Their 2024 work casts the films, then stirs in plant brews, softeners, link salts, burnt sugar, and fine plant threads. Four brews faced three test germs first.

Chestnut brew won and joined all films. Chitosan films beat Gram-high germs, tied less on Gram-low, and failed on a yeast. Fine threads lifted the strength and germ fight of chitosan both. Sea-gum films with a salt link hit the coli germ hardest. Two sea-gum kinds won the full card: wet feel, strength, and germ fight on all three germs.
pmc-11641590:
Diane Tshikudi, Hannah Hutchison, and Jean-Eric Ghia study a gut peptide blocker in mice in a 2024 paper. The peptide, pancreastatin, runs high in ulcerative colitis, a disease that scars the colon lining and shows sex-skewed patterns. A blocker of the peptide had calmed gut swelling before, but its effect on the lining cells themselves was untested.

The team gave the blocker to male and female mice, with and without induced colitis. In healthy females it cut lining cytokines and sped cell renewal through a named pathway. In sick females it worsened disease, while in males it guarded stem cells and eased colitis. The authors conclude the peptide steers gut upkeep in ways that hinge on both sex and disease state.
pmc-11644290:
Adrian Vicente and co-authors study fibres of a silicone made by electrospinning, as a stand-in with no fluorine for polymeric coatings. Their 2024 study deals with uses that call for a surface that sheds water and holds back ice, and with membranes that keep water out but let air pass.

Polymers with fluorine work well, but they raise worries for the world round us, and that drives a search for other choices. Polydimethylsiloxane has low surface energy and can bend with ease at very low heat, but it is hard to work into fibres. When a small amount of a second polymer was added, and the mats were treated with heat, they came out even and were made, for the most part, of the pure material. The porous coating shed water in tests. The team puts it forth as a choice to take the place of fluorine coatings.
pmc-11644390:
Sunglim Choi and co-authors improve, in 2024, the making of hyaluronic acid filler, the gel used in cosmetic injections. The standard process crosslinks the acid with a chemical partner, but quality varies. Their new method simply lets the solvent disperse through the dissolved acid at low temperature before reacting.

Dispersion homogenizes the mix, and in alkaline water the acid chains partly break down and rebuild at a target size, widening the crosslinking surface. The resulting gel was thicker, stiffer, and tackier than the old process at both bench and factory scale. The authors present the change as a simple route to more consistent filler.
pmc-11644690:
Zijin Jiang and co-authors toughen a polyurethane glue for structural work in this 2024 paper. Such adhesives must be strong, fast-curing, and hard to crack, yet the standard heat-set versions are brittle, age poorly, and cure slowly. The team attacked all three flaws at once.

They raised the glue's internal cross-linking by choosing richer building blocks, and stirred in rubber particles with a core-shell design using a solvent swap so the particles spread evenly instead of clumping. The cured composite's impact strength rose from fifty-two to ninety kilojoules per square meter, and it stretched more than twice as far before breaking. A catalyst let it cure at room temperature to high strength within thirty minutes. The glue also survived heat, cold, ultraviolet light, damp heat, and salt spray. The authors pitch it for transit manufacturing.
pmc-11646290:
Keith Skubitz reviews how a family of surface molecules shapes neutrophil behaviour. His literature review from twenty twenty-four covers CEACAM proteins. Neutrophils are best known for killing bacteria directly. They also steer immune cells, tumours, and inflammation in many directions.

Four CEACAM types appear on human neutrophils. Some rise from internal stores when cells activate. One works as a grab-and-eat receptor for microbes. Others send braking or go signals inside the cell. Pathogens including bacteria and fungi bind these molecules too. The review organises a confusing web of interactions. Understanding these switches may yield infection and cancer therapies.
pmc-11647190:
Manal Bawazeer and colleagues compare children with bronchial asthma in Saudi Arabia before and during the COVID-19 lockdown. Their 2024 study uses records from a specialist children's hospital in Riyadh.

The retrospective study included three hundred forty-three patients aged three to fourteen with moderate to severe asthma. Hospital admissions fell sharply in twenty twenty compared with twenty nineteen. Oral steroid use also decreased, and leukotriene inhibitor use declined slightly. Emergency visit patterns changed as well. The authors consider whether reduced traffic, air pollution, and social contact during lockdown may have eased asthma exacerbations in these children.
pmc-11647390:
Jarman and eight co-authors tested in twenty twenty-four which parts of cigar warning labels push smokers to quit. Near one thousand United States adults who smoke cigars took an online choice test. Each set showed three warnings that varied in health claims, cause words, and label terms.

Health claims, cancer and non-cancer alike, drove the picks most. Cause wording came next, then the marker word and verb choice. Naming the tobacco kind mattered least of all. A top warning from their math names heart disease and blood clots with a danger head. Strong health facts should lead cigar warnings, they find.
pmc-11648790:
Daisy Namirembe and four co-authors survey parasite spread among farm animals and wild mammals in western Uganda in a study from 2024. Liver flukes and blood flukes harm both livestock and people, and shared grazing and water may pass them between wild and farm herds. The team checked dung samples, inspected livers at slaughter sites, and spoke with local farmers and rangers.

More than half the cattle carried the liver fluke, and hippo dung showed the highest rate among wild animals. One blood fluke turned up in a small share of cattle and goats. Free grazing and shared open water were common risky habits, the interviews showed.
pmc-11649790:
Refah Alotaibi, Mazen Nassar, and Ahmed Elshahhat use rainfall data to test a new way of handling incomplete experiments, in a 2024 statistics paper. Long studies often end with some items untested, a setup called censoring. Their censoring scheme adapts as results arrive, gaining information without waiting for every item.

The authors suppose lifetimes follow a mixed Weibull-exponential model and estimate its parameters two ways. The classic likelihood route gives point and interval estimates. The Bayesian route adds prior beliefs and computes intervals by simulation. Simulated contests compare the two routes under varied plans. Two real rainfall datasets then show the methods at work, with checks to pick the best censoring plan. The work serves engineers and weather analysts who test under time limits.
pmc-11653090:
Dengue fever keeps surging in Bangladesh, and health officials need warning of how bad the coming months will be. Pratyay Hasan and co-authors trained two classic forecasting models on monthly dengue records from national health sources. The models, ARIMA and its seasonal sibling SARIMA, learn from the series' own past patterns: trends, cycles, and the yearly rhythm of the mosquito season. The team picked the best fitting version of each.

The two models parted ways in their forecasts for the next twelve months. The plain model projected a steady level of dengue. The seasonal model predicted strong swings across the year. The authors say both tools give planners useful guidance for staffing and supplies, provided they remember that weather, mosquito control, and other outside forces can bend the curve. Their overall expectation is that dengue in Bangladesh will rise in the future.
pmc-11654990:
María José Molina-Cando and co-authors measure how many Ecuadorian children meet the World Health Organization's daily activity guidance, and what predicts falling short. Wrist-worn motion sensors tracked activity in two contrasting regions: urban-leaning Cuenca and poorer, rural Quinindé. Together the studies covered more than 1,600 children.

Boys were far more likely than girls to hit the target in both settings. Richer children were much less likely to meet it than poorer ones, in both places. In Cuenca, a larger waist size also predicted missing the target. In Quinindé, non-Mestizo children met the guidance more often than Mestizo children. The authors argue that social and body factors shape activity in ways policy must respect. They note how little objective data exist for poorer countries, and they offer these two portraits as a base for action.
pmc-11656990:
Sayuri Iitaka and nine co-authors published a 2024 study of a urine test that uses worms to watch for returning stomach and food-pipe cancers. The test, called N-NOSE, exploits the sharp sense of smell of a tiny nematode worm, which moves toward or away from urine scent. It had already shown it can flag cancer, but not recurrence after surgery.

Forty patients at a Tokyo hospital gave urine samples before and after their operations, and were followed for two years. In patients whose cancer returned with spread into blood vessels, the worm-based index rose clearly at a strong dilution. The authors suggest the test could help monitor such patients after surgery. Larger studies would be needed before routine use.
pmc-11657390:
Fehlberg and co-authors study in 2024 how three ways of judging a new health practice link to each other. Staff views on whether a practice is welcome, fits well, and can be done are used to guess if it will spread. Yet the three views may blur into one another in real use.

The team surveyed gene health staff who gave patients extra gene results, then spoke with them in depth. Survey scores and talks were read side by side to map how the three views connect. Their work may help clinics pick shorter, clearer checks when they roll out gene services, instead of treating each view as fully apart.
pmc-11657890:
Bemrew Admassu Mengistu and co-authors give a full review of drug resistance in mammalian cancer stem cells. Their 2024 review sets out why these cells help tumours live through care, and what that means for therapy.

Cancer stem cells can renew themselves, turn into other cell types, and fix harm done to them. Those traits drive growth of a tumour and resistance to chemotherapy. The cells dodge drugs, radiation, and cell death. They do so by pushing drugs out at a higher rate, and by switching on paths that keep them alive. Some tumours gain resistance in their genes. Others shift through epigenetic change. The team talks through biomarkers, and paths picked as targets, such as Wnt, Notch, and Hedgehog. They also cover nanocarriers that bring drugs to the right spot. Bioinformatics, genomics, proteomics, and immunotherapy are put forth as more routes to take.
pmc-11657990:
Qinglu Tian, Shiqi Gao, Siying Li, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It shows how a metabolic pathway, the glutamine to alpha-ketoglutarate axis, steers stem cells from dental pulp toward making bone and dentin, the hard tooth tissue.

As these stem cells mature, their chemistry rewires. The team tracked small molecules during that change and found the axis rising steadily, along with the enzyme that feeds it. Adding alpha-ketoglutarate sped the cells' hardening program and helped repair clipped mouse incisors. Knocking down the enzyme slowed things. Gene reading traced the effect to a chemical mark on the message of a growth factor gene, which the metabolite helps set. The authors say the pathway links cell fuel to gene control in tooth regeneration, a possible lever for dental repair.
pmc-11658390:
Renu Sehrawat and co-authors designed new drug candidates from caffeic acid, a plant compound, aimed at an enzyme that cancer and microbes both depend on. The enzyme, DHFR, drives the folate chemistry cells need to grow and divide; blocking it is the strategy behind the established drug methotrexate. The team modeled, synthesized, and tested a series of derivatives against the enzyme, bacteria, and breast cancer cells.

One compound, CE11, blocked DHFR about four times more strongly than methotrexate and docked into the same pocket. It also killed breast cancer cells at low doses.
