Two sibling compounds beat standard antibiotics against several bacteria, including resistant problem species. Computer docking explained the grip: snug fits in greasy pockets plus a few well-placed hydrogen bonds.
pmc-11663390:
Sepsis can tear up the lungs, sending patients toward respiratory failure with few good drug options. Jiatian Zhang and co-authors test a compound called UMI-77 in mice with sepsis-driven lung injury. To see how it works, they read the activity of genes and the levels of small molecules in lung tissue at once.

The drug visibly eased the lung damage under the microscope. It shifted 124 genes, mostly in pathways for chemical signaling between cells, cell death control, and inflammation. Four genes and three small molecules stood out as the hubs of the effect. The altered chemistry pointed to purine and pyrimidine handling and signals between immune cells. The authors present this map as a base for developing UMI-77 further toward clinical use.
pmc-11663990:
Yang and nine co-authors tested a scan-based way in twenty twenty-four to tell whether a failed artificial joint is infected, one of the worst setbacks after joint replacement. Current checks for this infection can be slow or invasive, so a clear imaging sign would help surgeons act sooner.

The study enrolled one hundred twelve patients facing repeat hip or knee surgery. Before the operation, each had a dual-energy CT scan that measured the lymph nodes near the pelvis on the affected side. Swollen nodes proved a strong signal: node length sorted infected from non-infected joints better than two standard blood tests. Clear cutoff sizes gave both high catch rates and few false alarms. Using length and width together sharpened the result further. The authors propose node measuring as a practical add-on test when infection is in doubt.
pmc-11665790:
Rafaela Timoteo and co-authors test BREAST+, a 2024 augmented reality tool that helps surgeons plan breast reconstruction. In flap surgery, surgeons rebuild the breast with tissue from the belly and must first mark where tiny blood vessels pierce the muscle, a step usually guided by flat scan reports.

Worn on a headset, the system projects the vessel points onto the patient's skin and shows clinical data hands-free. Twenty-seven medical students and two breast surgeons tried it in a controlled study. Marking each point took under eight seconds on average, with errors of a few millimeters. Users found the system fast, though depth judgment through the headset biased some estimates.
pmc-11668990:
Cherith Jane Semple and co-authors test online training that helps staff support families at life's end, in work from 2024. When a key caregiver for children is dying of cancer, families often ask health teams how to prepare the children. Staff say they lack the training and confidence for that task.

Near one hundred staff finished both entry and exit surveys, and a dozen sat for talks a month later. Confidence scores rose by a clear margin after the course. Users rated the course clear, neat, and easy to read, and they said it would change their practice. The team blends count and talk data to judge the course as a whole.
pmc-11669790:
Myrofora Kakoulidou and co-authors present a 2024 study on bringing neurodivergent young people inside mental health research, not just asking their advice. Young people with ADHD or autism are usually consulted at arm's length. A program called RE-STAR instead built a framework with its youth panel to deepen their role.

Academics and youth researchers together wrote a protocol for participatory qualitative work. They then applied it to a study of emotion, co-designing and co-running interviews with twelve adolescents with ADHD or autism diagnoses. The paper evaluates how the approach worked in practice. Its aim is a reusable method for translational research where the studied community helps shape the questions, the fieldwork, and the meaning drawn from it.
pmc-11671690:
Andrew Mishin, Tobin Groth, Richard Green, and Christopher Troll published this study in 2024. It introduces a simpler way to assemble genes from short DNA pieces in the lab. Older methods demand highly purified pieces and enzymes that copy or glue DNA step by step.

Their method, named Splynthesis, works in one tube. Longer standard pieces, about 150 letters each, are lined up by shorter guide pieces called splints. The splints carry chemical blocks that stop wrong joins and stray copying. The team built a gene fragment of 741 letters and checked it with several standard tests, including long-read sequencing. The finished piece could be cloned like any lab-made gene. The authors say the approach suits synthetic biology and protein studies that need custom DNA fast.
pmc-11672590:
Ayooluwa Ojo and co-authors review how beef producers can breed and feed cattle that turn feed into beef more efficiently. Feed is the industry's biggest cost and footprint, but measuring each animal's intake was long impractical. New sensors now record individual intake precisely, giving breeders and nutritionists hard data.

Genomic selection can then spot efficient animals early, and pooling data across herds sharpens those predictions. Feeding models tuned to each herd's genetics promise further gains. The authors argue the two toolkits work best together: genetics sets the potential, nutrition delivers it. Their roadmap aims at lower input costs and a more sustainable beef supply as global demand grows.
pmc-11673390:
Woosik Jeong and co-authors build AI models to tell apart two spine conditions that look alike on MRI scans, in work published in 2024. Cancer that has spread to the spine and compression fractures from weakened bone can both cause pain and nerve problems. Telling them apart matters for care, yet scans can be hard to read.

The team used MRI data from a university hospital gathered over three years. Images were cleaned with two standard processing steps that sharpen edges and contrast. A deep network model and a support vector model were trained on the processed data. The deep model on one scan type reached near-perfect sensitivity and high accuracy for spotting cancer. The authors say processed MRI data can support AI-assisted diagnosis in the clinic.
pmc-11673590:
Maesako and six co-authors compare ways to measure shrinkage in dental composites, in work from twenty twenty-four. Flowable resin composites in a universal shade aim to match tooth color with less chair time. As they harden, they shrink, which can cause sensitivity and failure.

Two density based methods were used: a wet method under an international standard and a dry gas method. Several universal shade flowable products were measured both ways. Comparing methods matters because labs may report different shrinkage for the same material. A trusted common method helps dentists compare products fairly.
pmc-11674290:
Siyu Chen and six colleagues hunted for reference genes that stay steady when Arabidopsis plants face heat stress. Quantitative PCR needs such genes as fixed yardsticks, since their expression must not shift under the test conditions. The team measured seventeen candidate genes under high heat. Four were traditional housekeeping genes. Thirteen had never been reported as references before. Five statistical methods ranked how stable each one was.

Two genes, LHCB4.1 and LHCB5, from the light-harvesting complex family, came out most stable. The team verified them by measuring a known heat-response gene against each one alone and the pair combined. A poor yardstick can fake or hide real changes in gene expression. This twenty twenty-four work gives plant heat-stress researchers a tested pair for their PCR studies.
pmc-11674690:
Raffaella Candeloro and a team of co-authors test a blood marker for multiple sclerosis, in two thousand twenty-four. The marker is a small protein piece made by immune cells in the fluid around the brain and spine. It may show immune activity there as well as the current gold standard test.

The study held more than two hundred patients, some with the disease and some with other nerve conditions. The marker caught most true cases in both sexes. It was less exact in women than in men at ruling the disease out. Agreement with the gold standard was strong for men and moderate for women. The authors call for sex-specific cut-off values.
pmc-11674890:
Cabiati and co-authors probe in 2024 whether bone morphogenetic proteins help drive vascular calcification, using a dynamic lab model of the vessel wall. Calcification is an active, bone like process in artery cells. Their setup grows human coronary smooth muscle cells alone or with lining cells in a flow bioreactor.

A phosphate mix pushed the muscle cells toward a bone like state over seven days. Gene reads then tracked two BMP signals and their receptors. BMP-2 rose in calcified muscle cells under both still and flowing setups. BMP-4 and the receptors appeared in all settings, rising mainly under flow. Co culture results extend the picture in the full text.
pmc-11675190:
Lee Roosevelt and co-authors study fear of childbirth among pregnant people who feel they face anti-fat bias from providers, in a paper from 2024. Bias against larger bodies is common in health care and can worsen outcomes. Fear of childbirth can lengthen labor, raise the chance of surgical delivery, and color early bonding with the baby.

More than three hundred pregnant people were surveyed at three large academic centers and through social media. Standard tools measured how much bias they felt from providers and how strong their fear was. People who felt more bias reported stronger fear. The link was strongest among Black participants who felt bias. The authors urge training for providers on weight bias in pregnancy care.
pmc-11675390:
Juan Luis Santos and co-authors studied how an extra chromosome goes silent during sperm formation in a grasshopper in a 2024 paper. Some grasshoppers carry B chromosomes, extras beyond the standard set that often behave selfishly. During meiosis, the cell division that makes sperm, chromosomes must pair, swap parts, and stay active in a careful balance.

The team tracked pairing using a cohesin protein that marks chromosome axes, and watched DNA breaks and gene activity alongside. The B chromosome showed transcriptional inactivation, a shutdown of its genes, during sperm formation. Silencing may be the cell's defense against a disruptive passenger. The work shows how genomes police extra chromosomes, a question that reaches into fertility and evolution.
pmc-11675690:
Katharina Rippel and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, whether image reconstruction can rescue chest artery scans that came out too faint. Before valve replacement, surgeons need a clear scan of the aorta, but contrast dye sometimes fades badly by the lower arteries, ruining the picture. A new photon-counting scanner can rebuild the same data at chosen energy levels, and low energies make iodine stand out.

Fifty-five patients with fading contrast were studied. Reconstructions at forty and forty-five kiloelectronvolts beat the standard setting on both signal and contrast measures, and readers rated the vessels stronger with only a slight cost to overall quality. Half of the scans first judged non-diagnostic became readable at low energy. The authors note the practical prize: rescued scans mean fewer repeat scans, and less radiation for patients who can least afford delays.
pmc-11675790:
Janssen wrote a review in two thousand twenty-four arguing that fat stored in the wrong places helps cause metabolic syndrome. The syndrome bundles insulin resistance, blood sugar trouble, and related risks. Modern diets and overfeeding can push insulin high, and high insulin in turn drives fat into organs rather than into safe stores under the skin.

People born with too little fat tissue show a severe form of the syndrome, which hints at the mechanism. When safe depots cannot take more energy, fat lands in liver, pancreas, and muscle, where it blunts insulin action and harms insulin-making cells. Cutting that ectopic fat quickly restores liver sensitivity and pancreas function. Prevention of misplaced fat may thus cut risk.
pmc-11676690:
Tahia and co-authors test whether a drug called L-cycloserine can protect mouse retinas from light damage. The drug blocks new ceramide production, a fat linked to cell death in the retina. Earlier cell work showed it guards light-sensing cells from stress.

Given to albino mice thirty minutes before bright light, the best dose sharply cut cell death. The team tracked how much drug reached the retina and how long it stayed. They also measured fat profiles and genes tied to cell death. The results set up future work on ceramide as a treatment target.
pmc-11677990:
Marina Tihhonova and six co-authors test a machine that prints custom drug tablets in a study from 2024. The printer squeezes out a soft gel layer by layer to form tablets with exact doses. Their test drug was prednisolone, a steroid used here with pets in mind, since dogs and cats need doses that standard tablets do not match.

Printed tablets hit their target weights closely and had smooth, even shapes. The drug changed its crystal form inside the gel but released fast, with most of the dose out within thirty minutes. Drug content held steady over three months of storage. The method suits pet, child, and personal dosing.
pmc-11678290:
Alcohol vapors foul indoor air and harm health, and better sorbents than zeolites or activated carbons are wanted. The authors study zeolitic imidazolate frameworks, a sub-class of metal-organic frameworks, and focus on a brominated form called ZIF-8_Br. They test how well it captures aliphatic alcohols at low partial pressures, where capture is hardest. Experiments are paired with density functional theory and Grand Canonical Monte Carlo simulations.

Mixture calculations with ideal adsorbed solution theory gauge selectivity in equimolar alcohol pairs. The brominated framework shows a higher affinity for alcohols than the standard ZIF-8_CH3 form. The authors argue that this stronger pull could serve environmental cleanup or membranes for alcohol vapor sensors.
pmc-11678590:
Anna Geraci and co-authors present a 2024 study of essential oils drawn from mandarin peel waste grown in Sicily. Mandarins are a winter fruit from China and Southeast Asia, used widely in food and juice. Their rinds are a by-product that may hold useful oils, turning waste into a resource.

Five local cultivars grown in the Palermo botanical garden supplied the peel material. The team profiled each oil's chemistry with gas-based methods and tested the oils against bacteria. They also tested whether the oils slow the sprouting of other plants, a trait called allelopathy. Oils with such powers could serve farming as natural protectants.
pmc-11678790:
Min Sun and co-authors report two new compounds from a soft coral of the South China Sea in this 2024 paper. The coral was collected off Ximao Island, and its chemistry yielded a family of ring-shaped diterpenes. Two members were new to science, alongside two known relatives, and the team proposed that all four form through a folding reaction inside the coral.

Structures were pinned down with a battery of spectral methods, quantum calculations, and X-ray work. In lab tests, one new compound strongly slowed three bacteria that sicken farmed fish, including a strain resistant to a common antibiotic. Three of the compounds were also checked for activity on a cell receptor tied to metabolism. One known compound switched that receptor's beta form on selectively. The authors present the coral as a source of both fish-protecting leads and receptor probes.
pmc-11679190:
Venkata Ramana Yamani and co-authors report, in a 2024 study, on restoring the look and feel of hands thinned by Hansen's disease, the infection long known as leprosy. The disease damages nerves, wasting the soft tissue of the hand and twisting its shape. Tendon surgery can restore movement, but it leaves the hollow, aged look, and the shame that comes with it, untouched.

The team treated twelve patients who had already had tendon surgery, moving their own fat from the belly into the hand by a standard grafting method. Patients reported strong satisfaction, with fuller hand contours, better skin texture, and gains in self-esteem and quality of life. Social stigma eased as well. The authors argue that fat grafting is a safe, effective part of full care for these hands, treating the mind as well as the mechanics.
pmc-11679790:
Andrei Ratoi, Corneliu Munteanu, and Dan Eliezer wrote a study in twenty twenty-four on how polymers and glass could help store more hydrogen. Hydrogen burns clean, but keeping it in a small, safe space is one of the hard problems in the field. One design packs the gas into arrays of tiny tubes, which give much surface area in a small volume.

The three checked candidate polymers and glass for use in these tubes. They worked out the strength of each material under an inner pressure of seven hundred bar, the standard load for hydrogen tanks in cars. Their maths shows how much extra storage each material and design could add. Some choices, such as Zylon AS, Dyneema SK99, and S-2 Glass, came out ahead thanks to high strength and low weight. The gains ran from fifteen to thirty-seven percent by weight.
pmc-11679890:
Connor Dupuits and three colleagues review what consumers know and feel about eating sustainably, in a scoping review published in two thousand twenty-four. Today's food system harms both planet and people. Shifting diets could help, but only if consumers come along.

Forty-five papers met the review's criteria. Many participants misunderstood what a sustainable diet actually means. Willingness to adopt one was often low. Ignorance about sustainability and reluctance to cut meat were the twin barriers. Women formed the majority of participants across studies, a gender imbalance the authors flag. The review maps the knowledge-attitude gap that campaigns must close. Information alone, the evidence hints, rarely moves dinner plates.
pmc-11683490:
Taehyeong Lim and six co-authors craft ginger-based compounds to fight Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a hardy germ that infects chronic wounds and lungs, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. The germ talks to its kin through a signal system and builds slime shields called biofilms. Gingerol, from ginger, was already known to jam one of those signal readers. The team reshaped its middle and tail parts to make stronger versions.

One version, named 5a, bound the signal reader best, cut signal gene activity, and lowered the germ's harm factors. It also thinned biofilms and eased disease in tests, and it touched a second signal system too. The authors offer 5a as a lead for new drugs that disarm rather than kill the germ.
pmc-11688190:
Haijun Hu, Hongliang Luo, and Ziqing Deng review a long non-coding RNA called PCAT19 and its many roles in cancer. Their review was published in twenty twenty-four. RNAs of this class do not build proteins but steer cell behavior, and this one shows odd levels in many tumors.

Its levels track with patient features and outlook, which makes it a candidate marker for diagnosis and prognosis. It can act as a cancer driver in one tissue and a brake in another. It touches cell growth, death, spread, and energy use, often by soaking up smaller RNAs or binding proteins. Signals it feeds include growth and cell cycle paths. Fresh work even links it to nerve pain. The review gathers this scattered picture into one map.
pmc-11688890:
Brianna Soulie, Anne Barrett, and Hope Mimbs look at how older women meet and answer age-based beauty norms. Their 2024 study notes that past work stressed the beauty work women do to cope with aging. Less work looked at the day-to-day moments that push women to do that work. Less work still looked at the full range of ways women reply.

The team draws on deep talks with 20 women aged 57 to 83. Age-based norms came up in plain talks with co-workers, friends, and people they knew. The norms hold that faces and bodies past youth are not good to look at. They also hold that hiding signs of age is the right reply. Some women did that work, and some opted out.
pmc-11688990:
Baker and co-authors link poor sleep to later falls in older women in this 2024 study. Falls are the leading cause of injury in older American adults. The data come from the Study of Women's Health Across the Nation, a long-running multi-ethnic cohort.

Women reported their sleep in 2010-2011 and their falls five years later. Frequent trouble falling asleep raised fall risk by 27 percent. Frequent middle-of-night waking raised it by 24 percent. Trouble falling asleep also more than doubled the odds of repeated falls, with an odds ratio of 2.54. Sleeping under six hours raised those odds too, at 1.80. The authors present sleep as a changeable fall risk factor.
pmc-11689190:
Coaching nursing home staff to talk with residents as people, not tasks, takes groundwork, reports Natalie Douglas in a 2024 study. Her team used a planning framework called PRISM to scout three urban nursing homes before rolling out a dementia communication coaching program.

Twenty seven staff, from executives to aides, joined five focus groups. They named the barriers plainly: weak dementia care overall, thin leadership support, short staffing, and confusion over federal rules. They also backed the program and wanted a home wide plan to keep it alive. Outcomes they cared about were fewer incidents and falls, and residents joining in more.
pmc-11689490:
Ronald Shorr and six co-authors link nurse staffing to as-needed sedative use in veterans' hospitals in a 2024 study. Drugs given for sudden agitation act like a chemical restraint, and their safety is debated. Whether thin staffing pushes teams toward those drugs was unclear.

Data covered 166 nursing units across five years of records. Two staffing gauges were tracked monthly: total nursing hours per patient day and the share given by registered nurses. Units were grouped into staffing quartiles for comparison. Patients were mostly older men, with many at high clinical risk. The analysis tests whether leaner staffing months show more sedative use. Results can inform staffing policy as a safety lever beside restraint reduction programs.
pmc-11690390:
Seven researchers study discrimination and care access among LGBTQIA+ older adults in a paper from 2024. By 2030, millions of older adults in the United States will identify as LGBTQ+. Fear of discrimination keeps many from seeking aging and long-term care services. The team ran a national survey with a partner advocacy group, gathering six hundred forty-three responses.

Over two fifths of respondents reported lifetime discrimination or violence tied to their identity. Large shares worried about future access to services, medical care, and inclusive caregivers. Those who had faced discrimination worried significantly more. Few had concrete long-term care plans. The authors urge inclusive care efforts and more research on these barriers.
pmc-11690490:
Jasmine Santoyo-Olsson and co-authors adapt a virtual medical planning program for care partners of people with cognitive impairment, in a research paper from 2024. Care partners want to help with advance care planning before decision capacity is lost. They report needing more support and better virtual access to guidance.

A video-based website already helps care partners plan for others. The team explored turning it into live, facilitated online classes. Interviews with facilitators and care partners surfaced barriers such as topic complexity, tech limits, fear of death, and low readiness. Experience and home access helped. The study gives design advice for virtual planning classes.
pmc-11690690:
Tongxin Sun and seven co-authors study how to draw older adults into design work for goods and services made for them. Their study, from two thousand twenty-four, compares work in China and the United Kingdom.

The team used surveys, talks, and time spent with the people they studied. They argue that the act of asking people to join should itself be treated as a service to them. Five sets of facts shaped how older adults felt about joining: who they see themselves as, their region, their values, their use of tech, and their social ties. The paper shows how these facts shift across lands, and how teams can reshape them to help more older adults take part.
pmc-11690790:
Annie Rhodes and Leland Waters describe a 2024 panel project that sets research and policy aims for long-term care with workers at the table. The quality of care for frail people tracks the quality of work for their carers, yet reform plans rarely join the two views. Staffing levels, for one, lift both care and safety, but a proposed staffing rule for nursing homes drew pushback from providers.

The project pairs with a large service workers' union in Washington State. Home care and nursing home workers with leader roles told why they took these jobs, why they stay, and how they push to make them better. Themes span the pandemic, staffing, advocacy, job safety, career ladders, and the deep rewards of the work. Panelists then probed how to co-design research and policy that lift both voices at once.
pmc-11691290:
Amanda Grenier argues that close-up case study methods can widen how aging research builds its knowledge in two thousand twenty-four. Older people labeled at risk are often read through trade checklists and fixed scores. Terms like frailty and mobility, now policy staples, come from those frames and can crowd out lived experience.

Field-style case studies, she proposes, watch how older people handle ties, routines, and needs over time in daily settings. They also show how proof gets made and used to grant or deny help. Such work can surface the gap between official labels and real lives. The essay takes a critical stance: gerontology's own findings are also discourse, not neutral fact, and method choice shapes what counts as truth.
pmc-11692290:
Seon Kim reviews research on home and community-based services for older adults in a paper from 2024. Most older people want to keep living at home rather than move into a care facility. As daily tasks get harder with age, these services bring help into the home and the local area. Kim searched major databases for studies published between 2005 and 2023.

From more than eleven thousand papers, twelve met the rules for the final review. The studies linked the services to better body health, mental health, and fewer hospital stays. The review also found gaps, since Black and Asian older adults had less access. Kim urges planners to fix those gaps.
pmc-11692590:
YoungBin Koh, Sunghyun Ko, and Yeonjung Lee published a systematic review in 2024 on how people in South Korea perceive the experience of informal caregiving for family members. Caregiving is known to harm health in many countries, but the Korean evidence had not been brought together. The state supports formal long-term care through national insurance, yet support for family caregivers is comparatively weak.

The reviewers searched five Korean databases and screened more than a thousand papers. Thirty-one met their criteria. Caregiving in Korea did show harms: worse physical and mental health and a lower chance of holding a job, with women affected most strongly. Benefits appeared as well, including warmer relationships with the person cared for. The authors call for measures that reduce the harms, with particular attention to women caregivers.
pmc-11692990:
Linda Göbl and co-authors published a 2024 study on why some older adults thrive with digital health tools and others stall. Online health services can help aging people manage multiple conditions, but only if they can use them. Two capacities matter: eHealth literacy, the skill of finding and judging health information online, and confidence in one's internet abilities. The team studied how the two relate.

Their data came from 327 internet-using German adults averaging about seventy-two years. Analysis tested whether plain digital literacy carries part of the effect, and whether confidence in specific tasks, like video-calling a doctor or searching health information, mediates the link. The question is practical: training programs must know which skill to teach first. If general digital fluency underpins health-specific skill, courses should start there. The study maps the ladder older users climb toward managing their health online.
pmc-11693290:
Sharon Ost-Mor, Nir Wittenberg, and Yossefa Birati explore AI use among older adults in Israel in a 2024 study. AI tools are now a daily presence, yet uptake by older people is uneven. The team surveyed two hundred and sixty adults aged sixty and over. Forms covered the five main traits of personality and feelings about time alone. Open-ended questions let people describe their own use in their own words.

Users were younger on average than non-users in the sample. Most users spent between half an hour and two hours a day with AI tools. Non-users felt older, in both body and mind, than users did. A positive outlook on life went with more trust in one's skill with AI. People praised new chances to learn, but also flagged tech troubles and doubts about answer quality. The authors offer the findings as a guide for raising uptake.
pmc-11693990:
Gabriel Leal and co-authors describe five women treated for dependence on a common sleep drug, in a case series from 2024. The drug is zolpidem, widely prescribed for insomnia. The women were treated at a service in Brazil built for women with substance use problems, one of the first of its kind in Latin America.

Records from a two-year span were reviewed. The women, aged twenty-five to forty-five, had raised their daily doses far above the prescribed level. Harms included memory loss, falls, seizures, and strain on social life. All had started the drug for insomnia and showed craving and rebound sleeplessness when they tried to stop. Past abuse and other mental health problems were common. The authors ask whether tighter rules on the drug are needed.
pmc-11698590:
Wei-Ling Lee and co-authors weighed the cost and benefit of a lung cancer drug mix in Taiwan in two thousand twenty-four. The mix pairs pembrolizumab with chemotherapy as first treatment for metastatic nonsquamous non-small cell lung cancer. They judged it from the view of Taiwan's public payer.

Their model ran ten years using survival data from a large trial. The mix gained zero point eight nine quality-adjusted life years at extra cost, giving a cost per gain below the set threshold. Gains were larger for patients whose tumors scored high on a marker called PD-L1. The authors call the mix cost-effective for this use in Taiwan.
pmc-11701690:
Perez-Riverol, Bandla, Kundu, and co-authors mark twenty years of the PRIDE database with a 2025 update. PRIDE stores data from proteomics work, where mass measurement identifies proteins in samples. It is described as the leading world store for such data and helped found the ProteomeXchange group.

The update sums up recent changes and growth in the archive. Depositing raw data in a shared store lets other teams check results and reuse them for new questions. For a fast-growing field, a stable home for its data protects the value of costly experiments.
pmc-11702490:
Deepak Kumar and four co-authors survey health workers on disability care in a 2024 study. People with disabilities often get poorer care than others. Gaps in staff knowledge and attitudes are part of the cause. The survey ran in a large hospital in eastern India.

An online questionnaire reached doctors, nurses, and support staff. Nurses formed the largest group among respondents. Men knew more about government support schemes in the results. Women showed a better grasp of care duties and backed free care more strongly. Doctors knew the disability certificate process best. Most nurses and support staff backed equal social chances for disabled people. The authors urge training that lifts both knowledge and attitudes.
pmc-11709490:
Jordan Kozuki and co-authors study prospective memory in a 2025 paper on aging and memory loss. The term means remembering to do a planned act later, such as taking medicine. It weakens in Alzheimer disease, and the team ask how well tests of it predict wider thinking skills.

Groups included healthy older adults, people with mild impairment, and people with Alzheimer disease. Ratings came from participants and informants, plus tasks done during a test battery. Simple and complex task versions were used. In the mild impairment group, informant ratings carried useful signal about thinking scores across several domains.
pmc-11709590:
Valentina Gumenyuk and co-authors ask whether patients with early memory loss can judge their own sleep in a 2025 study. Sleep trouble and thinking trouble feed each other in brain disease. Patients split into two kinds: those whose main loss is memory, and those whose loss lies elsewhere. Healthy peers of the same age form the comparison group.

Each person kept a sleep diary and also wore gear that measures sleep directly. The team checked how far the diary drifted from the gear in each group. If memory patients misjudge their sleep, clinics may lean too hard on their reports when planning care. The study speaks to a daily question in memory clinics: whose word counts for last night.
pmc-11709690:
Grace Selecky and co-authors build a lab model of progressive supranuclear palsy, a brain disease driven by faulty tau protein, in a 2025 paper. The disease strikes movement and balance and mainly harms nerve cells in the midbrain. Models that mimic the human brain closely have been missing. The team took skin cells from patients, turned them back into stem cells, and grew them into midbrain organoids, small balls of brain-like tissue.

The stem cells came from 22 patients, sampled in life or after death. Grown for four months in spinning flasks, the organoids showed the cell types and markers expected of midbrain tissue. The team also pulled out support cells called astrocytes and grew them on their own. They present the system as a reliable human model for probing how this disease begins.
pmc-11709890:
People with certain forms of frontotemporal dementia often react oddly to sounds, yet their hearing itself is rarely mapped. Jeremy Johnson and co-authors chart hearing skills in two of those syndromes in a 2025 study.

The team gave a specialist test battery to twelve patients with the behavioral form and seven with the right temporal form. Comparison groups held other dementia patients and healthy peers. Both target groups struggled to recognize everyday sounds and the emotion in sounds, and to tell where sounds came from. Those gaps held after standard hearing and thinking scores were weighed. The behavioral group also lagged on a two-ear listening task. The authors link the profile to patients' everyday sound troubles.
pmc-11710590:
Yi-Jun Ge and co-authors present a 2025 gene study of Alzheimer disease in Chinese and European groups. Most known risk loci came from late onset cases of European descent. The team ran a two stage search to find new loci and test if early and late forms share roots.

Their search covered thousands of Chinese cases and a far larger European set. They found a shared gene base for early and late onset disease. Past the known locus, three new loci stood out in Chinese samples, plus one ancestry linked variant. Two genes were marked as most likely to matter by gene role data. The authors stress the worth of diverse samples in gene research.
pmc-11710690:
Merci Best and co-authors present a 2025 study of tau clumps in the memory center of brains with a rare disease. The disease is progressive supranuclear palsy, the second most common tau disease. Past work held that its tau harm stays mostly below the outer brain, with little in the memory center.

The team picked donor brains where this disease was the main finding. They used glowing tags and protein tests to grade tangles in each part of the memory center. Results varied a lot from brain to brain. Five brains showed strong tangles in at least one part, most often in two zones. The authors say this harm may add to thinking loss.
pmc-11711390:
Ki Young Huh and Ildae Song map how Korean trial sites team up on clinical studies in this 2024 paper. Multi-center trials depend on which hospitals join forces, and the pattern may differ by trial phase and disease area. The authors borrowed a shopping-basket technique, association rule mining, to find the links.

They organized approval records from the national drug agency for 2012 to 2023, covering 209 sites and 11,107 trials. Phase one trials, the earliest human tests, were the most common and by far the most tightly linked. Their collaboration score ran near 5.4, triple that of later phases, and their network clustered around Seoul and its suburbs. Children's trials showed the strongest and most varied links of any field. The authors say the mining method exposes real teamwork structure that planners can use when assembling trial networks.
pmc-11711890:
Temitope Hannah Farombi and a large team of co-authors report on media work for dementia awareness in Africa in a 2025 paper. Dementia is rising fast on the continent, and many people still blame witchcraft, which adds shame and delays care. The African Dementia Consortium used media during World Alzheimer's Month to recruit for a genetics project and to teach the public.

The team reviewed the reach of social platforms, newspapers, radio, and television work. Media spread word of the study to many groups and helped counter myths. Stories and images framed dementia as a global health issue, not a curse. Teaching content also pushed early signs and prompt clinic visits. The authors credit both digital and traditional media with lifting recruitment and cutting stigma.
pmc-11711990:
Scott Dresden reviews how emergency departments are retooling care for patients with dementia, in a 2025 paper. People living with dementia use emergency departments twice as often as other elders and have more avoidable visits. They arrive sicker, cost more, return more, and die more after a visit. The loud, bright, fast department unsettles them, and they often cannot give their own history, so their distinct needs go unrecognized.

The review gathers tested changes: geriatric assessment, dedicated units, care-partner involvement, better pain checks, fall and delirium programs, hospital-at-home admission, and palliative care in the department. The assembled evidence gives emergency medicine a menu of proven adjustments for its fastest-growing vulnerable population.
pmc-11712290:
Omonigho Michael Bubu and co-authors study sleep and brain wiring in older Black and white adults in a 2025 report. All 170 people in the study had normal thinking and lived in the community. The team measured their sleep in a lab overnight and scanned the white matter tracts of the limbic system, a set of brain paths tied to memory and emotion.

Broken sleep and long times to fall asleep tracked weaker tract quality in Black participants across several paths. Breathing pauses in dream sleep also tracked weaker wiring in both groups. Some deep sleep features, such as sleep spindles, tracked stronger wiring in Black participants. The authors say race shaped many of the links, a point future sleep and brain studies should weigh.
pmc-11712390:
Joanne Ryan and co-authors study sex differences in dementia risk markers in a 2025 report with ten years of follow-up. The team drew on 19,114 healthy older adults in the United States and Australia. Blood markers of amyloid, tau, nerve damage, and brain inflammation were measured at the start in over thirteen thousand of them.

In all, 824 people developed dementia, at near equal rates in men and women. Age, family history, body weight, and slow walking raised risk in both sexes. All blood markers tracked risk, though one lost force once another was counted. Depression and diabetes mattered only in men, while weak grip mattered only in women. The authors argue prevention plans should be tuned by sex.
pmc-11712490:
Sanne CE Balvert and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on the burden felt by people who care for a relative with dementia at home. The team asked how plain facts about care link up with feelings. Those facts cover hours spent and how much help the person needs each day. The feelings cover stress, low mood, and a sense of skill.

The study used data from 170 caregivers and mapped the links between all the measures at once. Links turned out to be strong within each group of measures but weak between them. Feeling able and sharing good moments with the person tied most to mood. The work hints that help for caregivers should treat daily load and inner strain as two linked but distinct needs.
pmc-11712790:
Napolitano and co-authors design in 2025 a dimeric nanobody aimed at toxic amyloid beta oligomers in Alzheimer's disease. Small soluble oligomers, not mature fibrils, are the main neurotoxic agents in the disease. An earlier single domain antibody, DesAb-O, already binds these oligomers and blocks their harm in cells.

The new design links two DesAb-O domains with a flexible linker, to raise binding strength and avidity. After expression and purification, mass and structure checks confirmed the construct. Aggregation assays and binding assays then tested whether it blocks amyloid assembly and grips the oligomers. The dimeric form is offered as a stronger tool for detection and therapy research.
pmc-11712990:
Aaron Booth and co-authors report a 2025 mouse study that combines two risk factors for Alzheimer's disease: the APOE4 gene form and the tau protein, without amyloid in the picture. Past work on this pairing gave mixed results and rarely tested behaviour. The team also asked whether zinc in drinking water makes things worse.

Eight groups of mice, across four gene types and two water types, took behaviour tests at three and six months of age. Mice with tau, with or without the gene form, did worse on daily tasks and place memory than plain mice. Zinc showed no clear added effect in the early results reported here.
pmc-11713790:
Amit Kumar, Diksha Sharma, Pragati Silakari, and Amarjot Kaur Grewal test a gout drug against Alzheimer's-type dementia in mice in a 2025 paper. The drug, allopurinol, blocks an enzyme that makes uric acid. That same enzyme makes harmful oxygen waste that stresses the brain. A chemical that harms brain cells was used to model the disease in the mice.

Computer modeling first checked how the drug fits a memory-linked enzyme. Mice then got the drug for seven days and trained in a water maze. Memory was tested with maze trials and a step-down task. The work explores whether an old, cheap drug might gain a second use against dementia.
pmc-11714090:
Kamalini Sengupta and three co-authors test whether helper drugs can guard memory in mice kept on short sleep for weeks, in a 2025 conference paper. Poor sleep is tied to body illness, weak thinking, and higher risk of Alzheimer's disease. Lack of sleep strains the cell system that folds proteins, and long strain can harm memory.

Young adult mice had their sleep cut to eight hours a day, three days a week, for four weeks. Some got a helper drug that eases protein folding strain. Two weeks after the stint, all groups did alike on a place memory test. At five weeks, short sleep males without the drug did worse, while those on the drug did better. The authors say easing cell strain may shield memory from poor sleep.
pmc-11714890:
Giulia Solange Clas and eight co-authors present a fifty year old man with Down syndrome who shows no trace of Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 case report. Nearly all adults with the syndrome develop the disease's brain changes by forty, since the gene for its key protein sits on the extra chromosome. This man, part of an Argentine research initiative, had neither amyloid deposits on brain scans nor any thinking problems.

The team checked the obvious escape routes. He carries the usual three copies of the protein's gene, so no deletion spared him. A full exome scan found no known protective variant either. Stem cells grown from his blood, now being turned into neurons, offer a living model for deeper study. The authors frame him as an escapee whose biology may hide protective secrets.
pmc-11714990:
Reactive astrocytes, support cells that turn harmful, may drive part of Alzheimer's disease. Eric Siemers and a large team of co-authors report a randomized trial of pepinemab, an antibody that blocks a signal called SEMA4D. That signal switches astrocytes into their reactive state. The trial, named SIGNAL-AD, enrolled people with mild Alzheimer's dementia and tested the drug's safety and effect.

Earlier work showed the signal rises on sick nerve cells as the disease advances. Blocking it in a past trial in Huntington's disease was well tolerated and slowed a scan measure of decline. The report gives the design and results of this phase 1b/2 test in Alzheimer's disease. It shows whether the same approach is safe enough and active enough to take further in this illness.
pmc-11715090:
Woo Sik Kim and six co-authors mapped tiny fluid-filled gaps around brain vessels in a mixed dementia group. Wider gaps are read as a sign that the brain's wash-out system works poorly. Such gaps show in both Alzheimer's disease and vessel-based dementia. The team asked if the place of the gaps tells the two apart.

The Seoul cohort held ninety-nine adults with sharp thought and one hundred ninety with weak thought. Experts sorted the weak group by amyloid load and vessel harm from scans. A smart tool then gauged gap size by brain zone. In the amyloid groups, gaps grew most at the side and back of the brain. In the vessel-harm groups, gaps grew in all zones, most of all in a deep core zone. Place, not just size, may thus mark which ill is at work.
pmc-11715190:
Ilaria Pola and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on inflammation in Alzheimer's disease. Swelling and immune activity in the brain seem to feed both amyloid and tau build-up, yet blood signs of that brain state have been hard to pin down.

The team worked with a cohort of people across the Alzheimer's range who had three kinds of PET scans. One scan type marks immune activity in the brain. Blood from one hundred fifty-one of them was screened for seventy-two inflammation-linked proteins. Five proteins ran higher in people whose immune scans were positive. Those same proteins tracked amyloid and tau scan signals in several brain regions. The authors say blood tests may one day mirror the brain's immune state. That would ease tracking of the disease and of drugs that calm it.
pmc-11715290:
Ashley N Price and six co-authors tested whether specks in the retina can flag amyloid in the brain. The specks are thought to hold the same amyloid that builds up in Alzheimer's disease. If a plain eye scan could read brain amyloid, checks would be far cheaper. The team worked with older adults whose thought was still sharp.

Thirty-six adults aged fifty-five to eighty had eye scans and past brain scans. Twenty had amyloid in the brain and sixteen did not. Two trained raters counted the specks and gauged their size, and the two agreed well. Yet speck count and size did not split the two brain groups. Used in a stats model, the specks called the brain result right only about six times in ten. The eye specks, at least in this small group, do not stand in for a brain scan.
pmc-11715390:
Daniel J Levendowski and co-authors tested whether sleep marks can sort folk by the kind of brain disease they face. A head band worn at night reads sleep stages, muscle tone, and wave mixes. A smart tool turned those marks into odds for four states: Alzheimer's disease, Lewy body disease, an early sleep-act-out state, and health. The pilot scored how well the tool's calls matched clinic calls.

Trained on one set of records, the tool was then let loose on a fresh set. That set held folk with each disease, mild thought loss, and health. Calls matched the clinic or leaned the right way in most records. Health was read right in about eighty-six of a hundred cases. The disease groups scored in the same span, from about three in four to just under nine in ten. Sleep marks alone thus carry real clues.
pmc-11715490:
Elina Ziukelis and co-authors examine in a 2025 study whether getting close in age to a parent's dementia onset links to brain changes. Earlier work had used that age gap as a stage marker for late onset Alzheimer's disease. The team tested whether the gap predicts levels of two proteins in spinal fluid. Data came from a large European study of Alzheimer's prevention.

In 688 people, a smaller age gap linked to lower levels of one key protein, a sign of more buildup in the brain. The link was strongest in people with a known risk gene, and a second gene form seemed to protect them. The gap did not predict the second protein. Readers learn how family timing may help select people for early disease studies.
pmc-11715890:
Ella Rowsthorn and co-authors test a new MRI measure of the blood-brain barrier's water traffic as an early signal of Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 study. The barrier's plumbing falters early in the disease, possibly before memory does. The measure, called kw, rates how fast water crosses the barrier. Lower values have been tied to vascular risk, but links with age, brain vessel health, and Alzheimer's proteins were unclear.

The team scanned 108 dementia-free volunteers aged fifty-five to eighty. Alongside the water measure, they imaged swollen perivascular spaces and free water in tissue, and sampled spinal fluid for amyloid. Relating the measures shows whether barrier water traffic belongs in the early-warning panel. The authors frame the work as biomarker hunting: finding changes that arrive before symptoms makes prevention trials possible.
pmc-11715990:
Allison Gibson reports a pilot program that helps people who live alone while dealing with memory and thinking problems, in this 2025 paper. As many as a third of people with such problems live alone, and many miss medical care and social support. The program, called STAY Home, aimed to keep them safe at home and delay a move into care.

Twelve people took part in weekly home visits from social workers and student interns over twelve weeks. Before the program, fewer than half had seen a social service provider in the past year, and only a third had seen a health provider. Attendance at visits was high, at seventy-five percent, and reported quality of life rose. The small trial shows the model is workable and worth testing at larger scale.
pmc-11716090:
Lin Liu and co-authors study in 2025 changing brain network connections in Alzheimer's disease patients who show cognitive resilience. Resilience means keeping thinking skills despite disease changes. Prior work linked network separation to resilience, and dynamic measures now let that be tracked over short time windows.

They studied 164 patients, split into a high resilience group and a comparison group. A temporal variability metric measured how network links fluctuate. The resilient group showed lower separation within and between several brain networks. The dynamic features also aligned with clinical groups and thinking scores, the authors report.
pmc-11716190:
Juan Lopez-Alvarenga and co-authors test how type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure affect thinking in Mexican Americans, in a 2025 paper. Both conditions are known to strain memory and attention, yet this population has been studied less than others. Simple comparisons can mislead, since age and weight differ between groups. The team used a matching method that pairs people with similar profiles before comparing scores.

The data held 650 adults without dementia from a San Antonio family study of lower income households. Nine percent had diabetes, six percent had high blood pressure, and two percent had both. After matching, diabetes was tied to changes in face memory and a test of steady attention. High blood pressure was tied to weaker word-list learning and recognition. The authors call for screening shaped to each condition.
pmc-11716390:
Mohammad Taghvaei and co-authors report a 2025 study on blood flow in the brain across the Alzheimer's disease path. A scan method that tags blood water can map flow with no dye or dose of rays. Flow tends to drop in key areas in mild loss and in the full disease. Vessel disease, a common added cause of memory loss, also cuts flow.

The team used data from 258 people: 180 with no loss, 54 with mild loss, and 24 with the disease. Flow was read in grey and white brain tissue and in areas tied to the disease. Flow was lower in the disease group in most areas read. Plaque status and vessel risk traits each shaped the flow maps in their own ways.
pmc-11716890:
Wyllians Borelli and co-authors use a 2025 Brazilian cohort study to ask which social and health gaps best predict thinking scores in later life. In lower-income countries, unfair social conditions may weigh on brain health more than age or sex alone.

The team drew on more than nine thousand adults from a national aging study. They weighed changeable factors, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, income, schooling, and access to care, against fixed ones like age and region. Thinking was scored from orientation, word fluency, and recall tasks. Sorting which gaps matter most can point health programs in Brazil toward the fixes with the largest payoff.
pmc-11722090:
Han leads a large team in the ARCHIVE study of clonal hematopoiesis, HIV, and aging outcomes, in work from twenty twenty-four. Clonal hematopoiesis is the expansion of a mutated blood cell clone with age. Both it and HIV infection are linked with inflammation and aging related disease.

Their relationship with clinical geriatric syndromes, like frailty and falls, was not well defined. The cohort study measured both factors in people living with HIV. Knowing whether the blood clone adds geriatric risk on top of HIV can sharpen screening and care for an aging patient group that medicine once never expected.
pmc-11727490:
Alin Nicola and co-authors tracked quality of life before and after surgeons removed a lung lobe for benign disease, in a study published in 2024. Such surgery treats tuberculosis, widened airways, and harmless lung nodules. Gains in physical measures are well recorded, but how life feels afterward is less known. The team split 84 patients by cause and scored quality of life, mood, and stress before surgery and six months later.

All three groups gained in physical and mental scores. The tuberculosis group gained most in physical health and shed the most worry and low mood. The widened airway group gained most in social life. Stress fell across all groups. The authors say the surgery lifts more than breathing, because it lifts the mind as well. They urge teams to weigh quality of life in decisions about such surgery.
pmc-11727990:
Abeer Al Shahrani and co-authors published this survey study in 2024. It asks how ready medical students in Saudi Arabia are to use artificial intelligence in their future work. Schools there teach little about these tools, even as hospitals adopt them fast.

The team surveyed 572 students across the country with an online form and a standard readiness scale. Only about one in seven had any formal teaching on the subject, though a third had trained on their own time. The average readiness score sat in the middle range. Scores ran higher for women, for students in the central region, and for those with strong English and computer skills. The authors urge medical schools to build the topic into the main curriculum.
pmc-11728290:
Saku and nine co-authors grade heart valve fix risk for a two-flap valve in this twenty twenty-four study. Fix work on such a valve can leave the new gap too tight for blood flow. A tight gap shows as a high push grade on sound scans post-fix.

Inside, fix cases split into two-flap, three-flap, and full swap groups for the checks. Two-flap fixes showed the top push grades at one week and one year. Three-flap fixes showed the least push of all groups in the same checks. In the two-flap group, high and low push halves fared the same by mid-term. Leak-back and re-cut rates sat near tied in those halves at five years.
pmc-11728790:
Dumitriţa Rugină and co-authors packaged a birch bark extract into tiny fat-based carriers and tested it against cancer cells in the lab, in a study published in 2024. Compounds from birch bark are gaining interest as gentler cancer fighters than standard drugs. The extract holds several such compounds, including betulin and betulinic acid.

The team built two carrier types, classic fat bubbles and a newer structured form, and checked their contents, size, and shape with lab instruments. Both trapped the extract well and kept it stable. In dishes, the loaded carriers pushed melanoma and a second tumor cell line toward controlled death. The bubble form worked strongest, while harming cells less than a standard cancer drug. The authors credit the improved delivery for the gains.
pmc-11748890:
Mengxue Qin and five co-authors study whether elderly-friendly surroundings soften the heart risk from fine particle pollution in Wuhan. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The city is urbanizing fast, and older residents face both dirty air and uneven support infrastructure.

A case-crossover design compared pollution on the day each patient entered hospital with matched control days. Clustering grouped neighborhoods by their elderly-supportive features. Over one hundred and seventy thousand case days were included. Pollution's cumulative effect over days raised heart admissions. Whether that rise shrank where infrastructure was strong was the core question. Curve analysis checked for non-straight shapes. The work links city design for aging with air risk management.
pmc-11757890:
Magdalena Blaszkiewicz and co-authors present a needle-array device that listens to tiny nerves through the skin, in work the text dates to 2024, though the catalog lists 2025. Diabetes often damages small nerve fibers first, and early damage is hard to catch with current tests. Their device, called DEN, is a patch of fine conductive needles that picks up nerve signals in skin and the tissue below.

In mice fed a diet that harms nerves, the device tracked nerve activity over time and matched other accepted measures. The team then reshaped it on a flexible board that molds to a human leg. It recorded real nerve and muscle signals in both mice and people, with and without stimulation. The authors say such a tool could bring earlier, sharper diagnosis to clinics.
pmc-11769790:
Shilei Zhang and colleagues studied a plant compound against cancer-related fatigue in mice carrying colon tumors. The compound, acteoside, comes from a desert plant used in traditional medicine. Mice with growing tumors were treated with the compound, a chemotherapy drug, both, or neither over three weeks. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team measured fatigue-like behavior, tumor growth, and muscle structure under the microscope, then profiled small molecules in blood plasma to find what the treatment changes. Binding tests checked whether changed molecules interact with the compound directly.

Fatigue worsened as tumors grew, and the compound eased both tumor burden and the extra fatigue caused by chemotherapy. Plasma profiling flagged a panel of shifted molecules tied to amino acid and energy pathways. The authors present the metabolic map as a starting point for anti-fatigue drug design.
pmc-11772190:
Hongye Wang and co-authors map the antibody landscape against non-polio enteroviruses in this review, published in 2024. This large virus family spans enteroviruses, coxsackieviruses, echoviruses, and rhinoviruses. Its members cause illnesses from the common cold to brain infection and sudden paralysis. Two members have become serious public threats in recent years. One drives hand, foot, and mouth disease epidemics in Southeast Asia. Another sparked outbreaks of severe breathing illness in children world-wide.

Apart from one vaccine made in China, no proven prevention or treatment exists. Antibodies are central to the body's defense against these viruses. The review surveys which antibodies neutralize which family members. It then lays out future strategy for vaccines and antibody drugs. The work serves researchers racing a family that keeps producing outbreaks. Neutralizing antibodies are the main shield the body raises here.
pmc-11794490:
Sang and a large team map in twenty twenty-four the genes that make tumours immunologically hot or cold across many cancer types. Hot tumours are full of active immune cells and tend to respond better to immune drugs. Cold tumours shut immune cells out, and no agreed rule sorted the two kinds until now.

Using a large public cancer atlas, they sorted tumours by immune cell mix, killing activity, and survival. Three hub genes stood out as controllers of the tumour setting. One was confirmed in pancreatic cancer tissue and linked to worse outlook. Computer screening then flagged two existing drugs that might warm up cold pancreatic tumours. The work offers targets for turning resistant cancers toward treatment.
pmc-11798790:
Jing Sun, Zhenzhen Li, and Xiaming Zhu pool studies on a nutrition score and outlook in bladder cancer, in work from 2024. The score joins a blood protein level with a white cell count. Single studies on its worth for forecasting survival had clashed.

The team searched three data stores through April 2024 and kept twelve studies with 2,951 patients. A low score tied to worse overall survival and to worse time without the cancer returning. The survival link held in every subgroup they tried. The return link held in most subgroups. The authors say a cheap blood-based score can help flag patients who need closer watch and stronger support.
pmc-11863890:
Sridhar Mishra, Swati Kumari, and Nuzhat Husain reviewed liquid biopsy for gallbladder cancer in a 2024 paper. This cancer still causes much illness and death, and tumor checks most often use tissue cut out in surgery or by needle. Tissue gives just one view at one time and can miss parts of a mixed tumor.

A liquid biopsy instead looks for tumor traces in blood or other body fluids. The review sums up what is known so far and what may come next. Such tests can be repeated over time, which helps track the disease, pick care for one patient, and spot when a drug stops working. The authors weigh both the gains and the current limits.
pmc-11888690:
Panigrahi and five co-authors validate a fluorescent camera for dental plaque measurement, in work from twenty twenty-four. Plaque detection and quantification matter in both clinical dentistry and research. Established clinical indices depend on examiner judgment and have clear limits in busy practice today.

The double blind study was carried out on twenty children aged nine to fourteen. Two examiners measured plaque with the fluorescent camera device, called QScan Plus. Reliability between examiners and validity against standard indices were tested. A camera that quantifies plaque consistently could make hygiene trials and school screenings far more objective.
pmc-11948590:
Fan and a large team traced in twenty twenty-four how two signals talk back to each other in face and jaw bone. One signal, through a switch called PTH1R, helps bone renew. Its control in mouth bone, in health or in sore states, was not proved by gene tests.

When they cut that switch in a set of stem-like cells in mice, bone growth and bone loss both rose. A growth signal, IGF1, rose too when the switch was cut. Cutting both calmed the bone changes back down. A third path, Hedgehog, sat between them and drove the rise in the growth signal.
pmc-12259690:
Faiza Sharif, Ashfaq Ahmad, Syed Amir Gilani, and Dania Mahmood review three treatments for patellar tendinopathy, in a paper whose journal version is dated 2024. The condition is a painful knee tendon problem common in jumping athletes. The treatments are dry needling, holding a muscle tight without moving the joint, and lowering a load slowly under control. The review followed standard reporting rules and searched four databases for trials from 2010 to 2022.

Nine trials met the bar, and their quality ranged from fair to high. Dry needling and the slow-lowering exercise gave better long-term pain relief and knee function. The holding exercise helped more in the short term, above all during sport itself. The authors say these therapy-based options look promising for lasting care, but the small evidence base calls for stronger trials.
pmc-12400390:
Takahiko Nagamine wrote a scoping review in 2025 on the state of nutritional psychiatry, a field that studies how food and diet may shape mental health. The review set out to judge how strong the proof is so far, with a focus on trials where people were assigned by chance to a diet plan or a control plan.

The search found only seven such trials, and many of them dealt with depression and the gut microbiome. Sample sizes were often small, and diet studies are hard to run because many life factors can blur the results. Probiotics helped, but the effect was modest. Nagamine argues that future work needs better markers, plus other methods that can test cause and effect.
pmc-12490490:
Domagoj Lemac and co-authors report a rare and dangerous shoulder joint injury, in a 2024 case paper. A young man crashed a vehicle and dislocated the joint where the collarbone meets the breastbone, backward. The broken end of the collarbone sat close to the great arch vessel of the heart. A plain X-ray showed no bone injury at all, which makes the case a warning in itself.

A CT scan revealed the damage, and surgeons fixed the joint and fragment with a plate and screws. The hardware was removed after eight weeks when the plate broke. No complications followed, and five years on the man had full movement in the joint. The authors stress early scanning and sound surgery to avert life-threatening harm.
pmc-12664090: Sagun Ghimire and co-authors present a case report in 2025 about a patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome, a rare illness where the immune system attacks the nerves. The patient also had severe narrowing in three heart vessels and bleeding inside the skull, a mix very rarely reported. No known theory links the three conditions. The team weighs whether the extra problems were a complication of the syndrome, a side effect of its treatment, or pure chance. Despite the hard choices, the patient ended with a good outcome.
pmc-12695890:
Kevin Thomas and co-authors used machine learning to predict and tune how thin metal films handle light in a 2025 paper. Such films are core parts of sensors, light-based electronics, and solar cells. Their light behavior depends on the metal, the thickness, and how the film was made, in ways that are hard to untangle by hand.

The team trained combined models on more than a thousand measured samples across six metals and a wide band of wavelengths. The models predict how much light a film lets through, reflects, and absorbs at once. Tuning can then search for film recipes that hit a target mix. The framework could save many trial coatings in the lab for film designers.
pmc-12696290:
Barbara Pesut and co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, how Canada can build robust systems for a hard class of assisted dying cases. In Track 2 medical assistance in dying, natural death is not reasonably foreseeable, which makes the assessments more complex than in end-stage care. Systems built for the first track strain under the second. The team interviewed 55 care providers, program administrators, and key informants.

The work was described as complex, heavy, and risky, and in some areas poorly paid. Hub centers worked best when they ran as teams. A set intake process that backs assessors and sets clear expectations for applicants helped. Teaching and guidance for applicants and families mattered too, most when an applicant had no doctor of their own. Case discussions across fields before a decision were seen as essential. The authors say such systems exist in only some regions so far.
pmc-12697290:
Xu Dong and co-authors use machine learning to find a drug lead against sepsis damage to the heart. Sepsis can stun the heart muscle, and a protein called PTP1B helps drive that injury, making it a drug target. Their screening pipeline mixed two classic strategies, learning from known active molecules and docking candidates into the protein's shape, to search chemical libraries.

One compound, PI-2, emerged with moderate blocking power against PTP1B and good selectivity over its closest relative. In heart cells stressed by a bacterial toxin, PI-2 lowered corrosive oxygen species and restored the energy membranes of mitochondria, protecting the cells. The authors present both the pipeline and the compound as starting points: the method for other targets, and PI-2 for optimization into a treatment candidate.
pmc-12705690:
Saadia Masood, Khawar Ibrar, Zabihullah Movaheedi, and Hafsa Jabeen improve a control chart used to watch process means in two thousand twenty-five. Factories use such charts to spot drift in quality before defects pile up. Extra data on a related variable can sharpen the chart's eye.

Their chart builds on a double smoothing design and adds a regression step that uses the helper variable to gauge the mean. Bounds are set for both early and steady use. Long-run tests through simulation compare how fast each chart flags a shift. The new chart beats the standard one for small to mid-size shifts. A real factory case shows the method at work.
pmc-12706990:
Zhang and Liu studied in twenty twenty-five how a hard childhood can echo into social anxiety at university, and what softens or carries that echo. Adverse childhood experiences are known to raise later anxiety, but the chain of influences in between needed mapping.

The team surveyed nine hundred sixty-four students at Chinese universities with standard scales. A painful childhood predicted stronger social anxiety in adulthood. Two links carried much of the effect: weaker attachment to parents, and being bullied online, which fed on each other in a chain. Personal resilience blunted the whole chain. Family structure changed the pattern too: in two-parent homes, secure attachment guarded more strongly against online bullying. In single-parent homes, childhood hardship hit online bullying harder. The authors offer the model as a guide for campus prevention and counseling.
pmc-12707090:
Jose Cárdenas-Quesada and six co-authors wrote a 2025 opinion piece on why clinical research barely happens in Spanish primary care, and how to fix that. Family doctors see patients first and follow them for years, an ideal setting for studies, yet Spain's primary care research stays weak even as the country leads Europe in starting trials overall. The authors compare Spain with stronger European models in a narrative review spanning three decades.

Working models abroad share shared data systems, dedicated research support, and protected time for doctors. Spain's barriers are heavy workloads, thin training, uneven facilities, and slow approvals. Digital registries and remote monitoring open new room to grow. The authors propose four reforms, from linked registries to simpler ethics paths, to turn primary care into a research hub.
pmc-12708790:
Concrete at sea faces salt water, load stress, and slow decay through its pores, so the size and spread of those pores decide its working life. Zhaoyong Chen and co-authors test whether mixing concrete under vibration improves marine grades C30 and C50 compared with ordinary mixing. They compared water absorption, pore structure, and chloride drift in samples made both ways.

Vibration mixing cut average water absorption by about thirty percent in both grades, and the results varied far less from sample to sample. Average pore size shrank by roughly a third, and total pore volume dropped by about half. After ninety days in salt water under half load, chloride drifted through the vibrated samples about twenty percent more slowly. The authors conclude that vibration mixing tightens the pore network, densifies the concrete, and lengthens its durability at sea.
pmc-12711090:
Lassa fever, a bleeding illness native to West Africa, hits pregnant people and children hardest, yet no vaccine for it has ever been licensed. Ariel Bardach and co-authors run a living review of every candidate in a 2025 paper, set up to refresh as new results land. Their sweep gathered dozens of studies, most in animals, with only two human trials so far.

The two human trials tested vaccines built on harmless carrier viruses and enrolled fewer than one hundred adults in total. Shots stung at the site, but no serious harm tied to the vaccines appeared. Immune responses were strong, with most adults converting within a month. No trials at all cover pregnant people or children. The review's public dashboard tracks the field as it grows.
pmc-12711590:
Toutou and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on feeding waste wet dates to farmed fish. Date waste is cheap and plentiful where dates are grown. The team tested whether adding it to feed could help two species raised together in one pond: Nile tilapia and thin-lip gray mullet. Five feed mixes were tried, from none up to a fifth of the diet by weight.

The fish swam in concrete tanks for sixty days, with each mix run three times. Tilapia grew and used feed best on the ten percent mix. Mullet did best at fifteen percent. Blood readings told the same split story: tilapia on the ten percent mix showed the lowest fat, sugar, and enzyme levels. Mullet flesh on the fifteen percent mix gained a richer profile of healthy fats. At twenty percent, mullet readings worsened.
pmc-12712090:
Jiang Xiong and co-authors watched waves grow in a time crystal in a 2025 study. A photonic time crystal is a material whose traits pulse in time in a steady beat, rather than varying in space. Like its space kin, it opens gaps where waves of some momenta cannot run, and it can host special states at time seams.

Their test rig was a microwave line whose traits were switched in time. Inside the gap, waves grew stronger, and the power spectrum narrowed and shifted toward the gap. A seam in time let them probe the mid-gap state. The work brings time crystals from theory into bench proof.
pmc-12714090:
Zahra Aminparast, Zeinab Shakibaee Fard, and Amirmohammad Khodaei published a 2025 case report on a rare growth that is not cancer. The growth is a mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor. It is a lump of immune cells tied to mycobacteria, seen mostly in people with weak immune systems.

Their patient was an 18-year-old woman born with HIV. She had bad stomach pain, nausea, and swollen lymph nodes. Scans showed lobed masses, and a needle biopsy gave the diagnosis. The tissue held spindle-shaped immune cells and acid-fast bacteria. The authors also review nine cases reported since 2017. Rare lumps like this can be mistaken for cancer, so clear reports help doctors.
pmc-12718290:
Jonas Rast and four colleagues grade how well chatbots answer mouth health questions from head and neck cancer patients, in a twenty twenty-five study. Patients often ask such tools about sore mouths and treatment side effects. The team first drew forty common questions across twelve topics, then sent them to eight large language models.

Trained raters scored each answer for trust, quality, clarity, and whether readers could act on it. Reading ease and false content risk were also scored. Scores differed a lot between models, with two search-based tools on top and some chat models rated only fair. Most answers were easy to grasp. The authors say patients should treat such answers with care and check with their care team.
pmc-12719290:
Alexis Leonard and Julie Kanter published a 2025 comparison of the two gene therapies approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for sickle cell disease. This inherited blood disorder deforms red blood cells and causes severe pain crises. Curative options were historically limited to bone marrow transplant from a matched donor.

In December 2023 the FDA approved lovo-cel and exa-cel, both made from the patient's own edited blood stem cells. The authors compared the trials behind them: design, eligibility, manufacturing requirements, and reported efficacy and safety. Patients treated with lovo-cel had more severe disease at baseline, with a higher median rate of vaso-occlusive events, despite a stricter definition of those events. The comparison helps clinicians counsel patients choosing between the therapies.
pmc-12719890:
Wang and eight co-authors build a two-headed antibody that hunts a tumor marker with one arm and a T cell homing signal with the other. The goal is to strip HER2-positive tumors of the regulatory T cells that shield them. Blocking that shield body-wide has proven toxic in blood cancers.

Their designs hide the second arm to different degrees, so the drug prefers tumor tissue. The lead candidate, XL-11, killed tumor cells and shield T cells in dishes and shrank tumors in mice with human immune systems. It spared T cells elsewhere better than the older drug it improves on. Memory and drug-level studies rounded out the tests.
pmc-12721490:
Per Nilsen and co-authors interviewed radiology staff in a Swedish hospital about living with a new AI tool in a 2025 qualitative study. Artificial intelligence in radiology has raced ahead technically, yet studies of how it changes daily work for the people in the department are scarce. Adoption succeeds or fails at that desk level.

Staff described how the application reshaped reading routines, trust, and teamwork. Case studies like this one surface the frictions vendors never see: alert fatigue, unclear blame, and quiet workarounds. Hospital leaders planning AI rollouts elsewhere can borrow the lessons early, designing training and oversight around real workflow instead of brochure promises. The Swedish case adds European public-hospital evidence to the debate.
pmc-12727190:
Maria Ertl, Florian Beuer, and Axel Bumann compare four quick screening tests for jaw joint and muscle disorders, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Such disorders cause pain and clicking in the jaw, yet hidden cases can pass without symptoms. The team asked whether quick tests can catch those quiet cases in healthy people.

Two hundred people aged ten to fifty, with no medical history, took all four tests. A full standard exam served as the yardstick. Jaw findings did show up in this healthy group. Two of the tests agreed with each other in every case, but differed from the others on some diagnoses. None of the tests hit the target accuracy for every diagnosis. The results show which quick tests suit which jaw problem.
pmc-12727990:
Pearl John and C. Sudandiradoss map, in a 2025 computer study, how small genetic changes could disturb a signaling protein tied to the commonest form of lung cancer. The protein, NOTCH1, helps control cell fate, and its role in this cancer is double-edged. The team screened its variants with prediction tools, hunting the damaging ones, then simulated how those changes behave.
