Forty-three candidate variants were flagged, with thirteen predicted both harmful and damaging. Several sit in conserved, working regions of the protein. A long stretch of the protein is intrinsically disordered, floppy rather than folded, and carries chemical tags that mark the protein for destruction. The authors argue these variants, tags, and the floppy region talk to each other in ways that feed the cancer's spread program. The work is hypothesis-building for later lab tests.
pmc-12729090:
Hayley Trower and a team of co-authors describe building a checklist in two thousand twenty-five for children with intellectual disabilities. The tool helps parents, carers, and clinicians spot and track causes of behaviors that challenge. Families were partners in the work, not just subjects of it.

A development group of parents, clinicians, and researchers met monthly for eight months to revise a first draft. Two more focus groups added feedback on clarity and use. Family input reshaped items to match real life and simplified the guidance notes. Users saw the checklist as an aide for spotting patterns and structuring clinic talks. It was readied for a pilot study of feasibility and acceptability.
pmc-12729490:
Satheesan and co-authors pool proof on hear loss in young hosts as a mind risk. Unmet hear loss oft drags thought down in old hosts. Load on the mind and thin sense feed are the blamed paths. Its mark on young and mid hosts had gone un-pooled till now. A Lancet board named mid hear loss the top fix-able mind risk. Four banks gave works that set sound hosts next to loss hosts.

Hosts in the pool span age 18 to 65 in the fit works. Grade checks used a Briggs list for cross-cut works in the pool. Seven works stood in the word pool of the sweep. Their grade sat at mid to sound on the check list. Pooled gaps and spread marks came per thought field.
pmc-12730490:
Khushbu Kumari and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on growing the spice plant asafoetida in the lab, guided by machine learning. The plant is not native to India and its seeds sleep for a long time, so farms struggle to raise it at scale. Growing it from leaf pieces in dishes offers a way around both problems.

The team varied three growth chemicals and photographed the cultures to score new embryos and shoots. Seven learning methods, plus a deep model, were trained to predict which mixes work best. One chemical, thidiazuron, stood out as the key lever for both embryos and shoots. The models promise fewer wasted trials in plant labs.
pmc-12731890:
Valeria Korolenya, Maxim Filipenko, and Mariya Smetanina hunt for markers that tell two kinds of cell DNA apart in a 2025 study. Blood vessel samples mix DNA from the vessel lining and from white blood cells that stick to it. Chemical tags on DNA, called methylation, differ between cell types and could separate the sources.

Using data from gene chips, the team screened for spots where the tag level stays near full or near zero for one cell kind. They found forty-seven spots that separate lining cells from white blood cells in a stable way. They also compared tag patterns among subtypes of each group. The markers should help future studies of vessel lining damage, where telling the DNA sources apart matters.
pmc-12733090:
Liang Yue and co-authors review, in 2025, how hard training changes the heart's natural pacemaker in athletes. A slow resting heartbeat is a classic sign of fitness and is usually seen as harmless. Yet long, intense endurance training has been linked to pacemaker problems later, and the review asks where healthy change tips into disease.

Across seventeen studies, training reset the pacemaker's electrical currents in humans and some animals. In large animals, the slow beat came only from nerve signals, not from the pacemaker itself. Heavy loads, training type, and aging all shaped the risk. The authors frame the change as a reserve that can wear down.
pmc-12734890:
Chen and co-authors model how braiding angle affects the strength of 3D braided composites. These woven materials serve in parts that face strong push and pull forces. Their behavior depends on the angle at which fiber bundles cross inside the material.

The team joined lab tension and compression tests with finite element computer models. This pairing traced how damage starts at the small scale, spreads, and then weakens the whole part. Braiding angle shifted both stiffness and failure patterns. The results help engineers tune braid designs for parts that must stay strong under load.
pmc-12735490:
Gabriel Galeano-Garcia and co-authors test whether mixing fibers makes gut microbes produce more helpful acids than the parts alone in this 2025 study. These acids, brewed by fermenting fiber, support gut and immune health. The team reanalyzed fermentation data from 33 people across healthy and three disease groups.

The mixture beat most single fibers and produced about a third more total acids than simple addition predicts. Synergy appeared in every health group, sometimes topping 80 percent for an individual. People showing synergy carried more of two butyrate-making bacterial families, which network analysis flagged as hubs. The authors suggest designed fiber blends could make stronger prebiotic products.
pmc-12735890:
Gianpiero Greco and co-authors wrote this 2025 narrative review on lifestyle as a lever against cancer. Cancer still ranks among the top causes of illness and death worldwide, and much of its risk is shaped by daily choices. The team searched the literature from 2001 to 2025 across diet, movement, body weight, and exposures like tobacco and sunlight.

Avoiding tobacco and excess sun remains the bedrock of prevention. Plant-rich diets, regular activity, and healthy weight track with lower rates of breast, bowel, and liver cancers. Calorie restriction, ketogenic diets, and fasting-style plans show early promise for helping treatment work better. The review also covers rest, metabolic health, and add-on therapies, framing lifestyle care as part of treatment, not an extra.
pmc-12736190:
Hongyan Cheng and others studied soil nitrogen release across Chinese forests in two thousand twenty-five. Microbes free nitrogen from soil for plant use. Which microbial pathways drive that release was unclear. Forests ranged from temperate to tropical zones. The transect stretched thousands of kilometers north to south. Soil gene surveys paired with release rate readings.

Subtropical forests released nitrogen fastest. Their soil life carried more nitrogen-cycling genes too. Warm climate and soil type explained most of the gap. Two pathways explained more of the gaps than others. Denitrification genes did the most to explain the pattern. Nitrification genes followed closely behind. Forest managers gain a new lens on soil richness. Warming may shift these patterns further.
pmc-12737790:
Five authors present a software toolbox in two thousand twenty-five for fixing a blind spot in epidemic tracking. Case counts arrive late: days pass between falling ill and being reported. Those delays warp real-time forecasts, and delay patterns themselves shift during an outbreak.

Their toolbox, Nowcast-It, adjusts today's counts using survival analysis borrowed from actuarial science, allowing the delay pattern to change over time. It pairs an R code base with a point-and-click app, so users without coding skills can correct delays interactively. The authors present it as a tutorial, filling a gap where no flexible tool existed.
pmc-12738490:
Di Tang and six co-authors published a randomized trial in twenty twenty-five on whether real exercise sharpens video game performance. Esports is now an official sport in many countries, but its training science is thin. Short workouts were known to help briefly; a longer program's effect was the open question.

Eighty-three first-person shooter players finished the six-week study, half assigned to high-intensity interval training. The exercise group improved flicking, tracking, decision-making, reaction time, and shooting accuracy in game tests. Their aerobic fitness and sleep quality also rose, and fitness gains correlated moderately with faster reactions. The result gives competitive gaming a physical training pillar that coaches have mostly guessed at until now.
pmc-12738690:
Adel Bakhshipour and Shahriar Ramezanpour use special imaging to tell peanut plants apart from weeds in a 2025 study. Precise weed control needs fast, accurate spotting of weeds among crops. Their imaging captures many narrow bands of light, far more than a normal camera, and machine learning sorts the patterns.

They tested ways to clean the image data and to pick the most useful light bands from hundreds available. The best mix used a median filter, a selection method, and a classic classifier. It reached very high accuracy in training and strong accuracy on fresh test data, using only twelve chosen bands. The method separated peanuts from each of four weed species. The authors advise testing it under varied field conditions next.
pmc-12743790:
A rare gene fault can look like ordinary type 2 diabetes. Xiuchuan Hu and co-authors report a Han Chinese family carrying a broken HNF1β gene. Three members share the same nonsense mutation. All have kidney cysts, kidney damage, high uric acid, and low magnesium. Only the father showed high blood sugar, a malformed pancreas, and genital differences. His sons differ again: one has raised liver enzymes, the other a small left kidney.

The father needed dialysis for kidney failure. His sons improved on targeted drugs and diet. The authors urge genetic testing when diabetes travels with kidney cysts. A firm diagnosis spares patients needless biopsies and wrong labels.
pmc-12747090:
Leonardo Bocca and co-authors report the return of a rare spinal cyst found by CT myelography. The cyst grows inside the spinal cord from skin-like tissue. A man aged twenty-three had long follow-up for such a cyst after leg tremor and pain. His first surgery removed the mass without fixing the spine. Years later, spine curve and canal narrowing led to a second fix.

At age eight in his care path, worse weakness and bladder issues prompted fresh checks. CT with contrast in the spine canal showed an enlarged upper cord segment. A new full removal of the cyst followed that scan. The authors note the scan still serves when MRI cannot run, and cysts need long watch since they can return years later.
pmc-12748090:
Alix Brusseau and colleagues watched how male guppies use information from other males when danger may be near. Prey must balance feeding and mating against staying alive, and males may lose mating chances if they overreact to risk. The team worked with wild-caught male Trinidadian guppies. A focal male could inspect a group of alarmed males, and in some trials a female was also present as a competing draw. Chemical risk cues and visual cues were varied to see which source the males leaned on. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five.

Without a female present, males inspected the alarmed male group more, showing they do use social information. With a female present, they largely ignored the alarmed group and inspected her instead. The authors read the switch as a reproductive trade-off shaping how social risk information is used.
pmc-12748690:
Amin Rezazadeh, Alireza Najafpour, Ali Soleimanzadeh, and Amir Amniattalab test copper particles for castration. Their study from twenty twenty-five deals with male mice. Chemical castration is a non surgical path to sterility.

Adult male mice were split into seven groups. Doses of copper oxide particles went into the testes. A surgical group and control groups set the baseline. Fertility, sperm quality, and tissue state were checked. Testis weight, sperm marks, and testosterone fell with dose. Oxidative stress and DNA damage rose with dose. Death switch genes shifted in the same direction.
pmc-12749190:
Hirofumi Tazawa and co-authors test a nanoparticle drug against stomach cancer in mice in this 2025 study. The drug carries small RNA that silences a protein called TMPRSS4. That protein helps cancer cells spread and marks poor outlook in gastric cancer. Fat-based nanoparticles were built to ferry the RNA into tumors. Nude mice grew human gastric tumors under the skin. The team tracked where the particles went and whether tumors shrank.

Particles gathered in tumors far better than naked RNA did. Treated mice showed a real reduction in tumor growth. Silencing one surface protein is a targeted strike, unlike broad chemotherapy. The delivery vehicle is half the invention here. Such RNA drugs degrade fast without protection in the body. The study is preclinical, a step toward possible human trials.
pmc-12749890:
Yang Liu, writing alone in twenty twenty-five, built a neural network that reads emotion in instrumental music. Knowing what a piece feels like powers recommendation and media tagging. The proposed model stacks three components. A convolutional network extracts local emotional features from audio. A bidirectional recurrent unit then models how those features evolve over time, in both directions. An attention mechanism finally spotlights the most emotionally telling segments.

Low-level audio features and high-level semantic features are fused at several scales during extraction. Validation used three datasets, including two public collections and a large emotion-annotated music database. The design aims at accuracy plus generalization across collections. Liu's architecture treats musical emotion as something that builds and shifts across a track, not a single static label.
pmc-12750390:
Felix Mehrens and five co-workers tested a live way to gauge fumes from hot plastic as it is made new again. Gas compounds foul new plastic stock. They come from added agents, drift from pack wrap, and wear over time. Such foul stock blocks top uses like food packs and car trim. Old tests use chance samples. They can miss bad spots in mixed loads. The 2025 study used a mass test method called SIFT-MS right at a twin screw press.

Gas was gauged nonstop at the press vent dome while stock ran through. The team found and gauged scents such as limonene, plus test agents that match FDA rules. Gas levels tracked the foul load in the raw stock quite well. Nonstop checks at the line could catch dirty loads that spot checks would miss.
pmc-12753690:
Wei Pan and Fengwei Liu propose a risk identification model for power companies in a 2025 paper. Grids with lots of wind and solar power face new risks from variable output. Their model combines a convolutional neural network with a stacking ensemble method that blends several learners for a stronger final call.

The team built wind farm output scenarios on a standard thirty nine bus test grid. The model performed best at thirty percent renewable penetration, reaching about ninety eight percent accuracy with a low missed detection rate. It clearly beat a single neural network alone. The authors present the model as decision support for operators managing grids with diverse generation mixes.
pmc-12756390:
Jiecheng Zheng and co-authors surveyed patients with hand eczema in Guangdong, China, about what they know, feel, and do regarding their condition, in a study published in 2025. Hand eczema is common and can wear down daily life and work. Six hundred twelve patients at one hospital completed a purpose-built questionnaire.

Scores showed modest knowledge, middling attitudes, and uneven daily practices. Statistical modeling traced a chain: knowledge shaped attitude, and attitude shaped practice most strongly. Knowledge also reached practice indirectly through attitude. A positive attitude score was the clearest marker of proactive self-care. The authors conclude that teaching patients more, in ways that shift attitudes, could improve how the condition is managed day to day.
pmc-12764890:
France Caza, Fanny Fronton, Lina Ennia, Dominique Robert, and Yves St-Pierre published a 2025 study on diagnosing pathogens in wild fish from a single drop of blood. Climate change is promoting pathogens that threaten key fish populations, and monitoring programs must adapt. The test case was Atlantic herring, a commercially vital species.

The team combined standard PCR tests with transcriptomic analysis of blood stored on FTA cards. They measured the prevalence of erythrocytic necrosis virus and the Ichthyophonus parasite across 2023 and 2024. Thirty-three percent of samples tested positive for the virus and ten percent for the parasite. Virus-positive fish were found more often in estuarine and coastal areas. Blood-based molecular surveillance lets managers track fish health without killing the animals sampled.
pmc-12771190:
Li-Qin Lian and five colleagues published a 2025 systematic review on non-coding RNAs and febrile seizures in children. Febrile seizures are convulsions triggered by fever in children between six months and five years of age. They affect roughly 2 to 5 percent of children worldwide, more often boys and those with a family history.

Non-coding RNAs are RNA molecules that do not build proteins but instead regulate gene activity. The review covers three kinds: microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs. It examines how they may drive the brain inflammation and excitation imbalance behind febrile seizures. The authors also assess whether these molecules could serve as biomarkers for diagnosis or as targets for future treatments.
pmc-12776590:
Chun-Ting Yang and six co-authors compare two drug choices for delirium in older patients in this two thousand twenty-five study. Delirium is a sudden state of confusion that can follow a hospital stay. Doctors often give antipsychotic drugs, but these carry risks for older adults. Trazodone, a sleep and mood drug, has been floated as a safer pick. The authors set out to test that claim with real-world data.

They used US Medicare records and a large claims database, spanning roughly a decade. Their design mimics a clinical trial, a method called target trial emulation. They followed patients aged sixty-five and up with no psychiatric history. Each person had a new prescription for one drug or the other soon after leaving hospital. The study weighs harms side by side to guide safer prescribing.
pmc-12784490:
MacLellan and co-authors co-design postnatal health info with mothers who face care barriers. Death and illness after birth hit minoritized and poor mothers hardest in the UK. Leaflets on danger signs vary in quality and clarity. Language and access barriers can block mothers from acting in time. The BEAMS project worked with charities and two peer researchers.

Workshops drew 60 women with lived experience of access struggles. The group reviewed current NHS postnatal materials together. Arts-based and trauma-aware methods guided the sessions. They judged what worked and what failed in the materials. The goal was guidance staff can use to reach mothers now left unmet.
pmc-12785990:
Andreu, Obis, and del Olmo compare a salt-loving yeast grown in seawater and freshwater in this 2025 study. The yeast Schwanniomyces etchellsii runs chemical conversions better in seawater than in fresh water, for reasons unknown. Higher rates and fewer by-products make it attractive for green chemistry.

Protein and lipid profiles were measured at several growth stages in both media. Seawater cells raised stress proteins, including a glycerol-making enzyme, a glycerol transporter, and a sodium pump. They also boosted several membrane lipid builders and carried more simple glycerol fats. Freshwater cells instead favored general biosynthesis enzymes. The molecular portrait explains how the yeast thrives on salt instead of merely enduring it.
pmc-12787490:
Giulia Matteoli and co-authors published a 2025 study on gold nanoparticle clusters that fall apart only when they meet a prostate cancer marker. The marker, PSA, signals recurrence after prostate surgery, so catching it early and sensitively matters. The team's sensor is an aggregate: ultrasmall gold particles linked by short DNA-like strands fitted with aptamers, molecular traps shaped to grab PSA.

When PSA appears, the aptamers prefer it to their linking partners, and the cluster disassembles. That break-up changes the particles' light absorption and size, both easy to measure. The design was tuned with computer simulation as well as bench work, aiming at strong detection and eventual use inside the body. Switchable aggregates are a general trick: build a cluster whose links answer to one molecule, and presence becomes visible. The paper demonstrates the trick on a marker where early warning changes treatment.
pmc-12787790:
Jiawei Yu, Hongde Dai, Juan Li, Xin Li, and Xueying Liu improve camera-based navigation for moving scenes in a paper from 2025. Visual-inertial systems estimate motion from cameras plus motion sensors. Passing people and vehicles corrupt their feature points. The new algorithm rebuilds the feature extractor to fuse fine texture with deep meaning. A tracking module then spots moving objects in real time and deletes their points.

Only static background features reach the pose solver. On a standard driving data set, trajectory accuracy improved by about fifteen percent over the base system. Each frame processed in roughly twenty-four milliseconds. The authors target robots and vehicles in busy environments.
pmc-12789490:
Jayjit Kumar Dey and co-authors measure hidden tilts at an oxide interface and tie them to magnetism in a 2025 study. Perovskite oxides stack oxygen octahedra whose tilts steer electronic behavior. At a crafted junction of two such oxides, the team projected the oxygen angles directly, quantifying how substrate strain bends them.

A stretched substrate produced far stronger tilt than a squeezed one. X-ray probes then mapped how orbitals and magnetic coupling rearranged at the interface. Cobalt and manganese moments opposed each other across the seam. Computer theory matched the trend: stretch raised atomic moments, squeeze lowered them, with bond angles doing the steering. Single films of either oxide behaved differently from the pair. The authors present tilt measurement plus strain control as a knob for designing interface phenomena atom by atom.
pmc-12790990:
Keyan Zhu and six co-authors tested a probiotic strain against fatty liver disease in mice, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The strain, known as LG2055, was fed to mice raised on a high-fat diet that mimics the human condition. Fatty liver is tied to gut imbalance as well as to fat buildup in the liver itself.

Treated mice showed lower liver enzyme and blood fat levels, and less fat stored in the liver. Their gut lining proteins strengthened, harmful inflammation signals fell, and calming signals and antibodies rose. Gut microbe mix shifted as well, with some groups falling and others rising. The authors conclude the strain eases liver damage by calming gut inflammation and restoring balance.
pmc-12801490:
Haohai Huang and colleagues quantitatively assess sumac supplementation effects on cardiovascular risk factors through a meta-analysis of randomized trials. Their 2025 review addresses contradictory findings from individual clinical trials of this spice.

Searches across major databases ran to March twenty twenty-five for trials lasting at least two weeks in adults. Primary outcomes covered lipid profiles, blood pressure, blood sugar control, and body measurements. Secondary outcomes included inflammation and oxidative stress markers. Trial quality was rated with a standard Cochrane bias tool. Effects were pooled with a random-effects model as weighted mean differences. The synthesis aims to settle whether sumac meaningfully improves heart risk profiles.
pmc-12801590:
Bowen Li and co-authors ask why two major arteries suffer different diseases in this 2025 study. Plaque disease favors the neck's carotid artery. Aneurysms favor the belly's aorta instead. That split hints the vessels' wall cells differ by nature. Fat-like molecules called sphingolipids sway how those cells behave. The team mined public gene data from both vessels' smooth muscle cells.

They compared fat metabolism patterns between the two sites. Differences there may explain the disease split. A vessel's identity, written in its cells, shapes its risks. The study seeks mechanism, not just description. Public data reuse drives the whole analysis. Findings could point to vessel-specific prevention. The work is a data-driven vascular biology paper.
pmc-12802290:
Mohamed and co-authors count poor sleep in med school hosts in Mogadishu, Somalia. Sleep is a base body act key to thought, feel, and school work. Med hosts face poor sleep from hard class work and odd plans. Mind strain adds to that risk in the med host pool. World counts show high poor sleep counts in that pool at large. Proof from low-means school lands like Somalia stays thin though.

A cross poll ran in mid 2025 cross four schools in the town. Two and six dozen hosts, 272 in all, took the poll set. Poll bits span host traits, class facts, acts, and mind marks. Set tools span a sleep mark list and a mood list in the poll. The Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index heads the sleep list there. Aims span poor sleep counts, tied facts, and path checks.
pmc-12808490:
Juan Manuel Pérez-Pozuelo and six co-authors systematically review drug-free pain relief for children and the nurse's role in delivering it, in a two thousand twenty-six systematic review. Pediatric pain is rising and drives many hospital visits.

Following PRISMA guidelines, the review found the most useful method to be a vibrating cold device, the bee, paired with a distractor, with virtual reality the ideal distractor. The studied non-pharmacological techniques reduced pain across the scales used in each trial. Nurses proved essential at every step: detecting pain, choosing the method, and administering it. The authors position these techniques as standard adjuncts in pediatric care.
pmc-12811790:
Youseff Elrayes, Marton Miko, and Mohamed Hany Elrayes report a 2025 case of a lung lump that looked like cancer but proved to be dust disease. The man, aged 65, had his prostate gland removed for cancer in 2013, so a new lung mass raised fear of spread. Scans showed a mass near the lung root and hot spots in chest glands.

Repeated tissue tests through the airways and chest found no cancer. Surgery cut out part of the chest lining and lung and gave the true answer. The tissue held scar, black dust pigment, and silica crystals. Those signs point to a dust disease of coal and rock workers. No cancer cells showed on a broad stain test. The case warns that hot scan spots alone cannot prove cancer.
pmc-12812990:
Mannino and five co-authors map a swelling hub and its small RNA brakes in mouth cancer in this twenty twenty-six review. The hub is a cell guard knot that can trip death and free rage scents. In mouth tumors it most often acts as a growth aid, not a guard.

Inside, high hub counts go with spread to neck nodes, late stage, and short life in case sets. Muting the hub by gene or drug lifts cell death and shrinks tumors in tests. Small RNA bits form a brake layer that can hold the hub in check. One such bit cut tumor growth, move, and break-in in mouth cancer tests. The team weighs hub-plus-brake cures as a path for care.
pmc-12816190:
Jun Rao and co-authors published a study that the text dates to 2025; the catalog lists 2026. The study probes a plant root used in Chinese herbal medicine. The root is known to calm swelling and fight tumors, but most past work looked at just one class of its compounds.

The team used many lab methods at once to scan the root's chemistry. They found close to thirteen hundred compounds across eight processed forms of the root. One compound stood out for its rise during processing and its links to cancer paths. Tests in colon cancer cells showed it shifted many proteins. Two cell-surface enzymes bound it strongly in docking tests. The authors say the compound attacks cancer through many targets at once.
pmc-12817090:
Kristine Siseho, Roswitha Mahalie, and Tuwilika Endjala survey mental health among students at Namibia's public universities, in work from twenty twenty-five. Anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts are common in students worldwide. Local data for Namibia were scarce.

Five hundred seventy-eight students across six campuses filled standard questionnaires. About half reported moderate to severe anxiety. Nearly three quarters met depression criteria. About one in eleven reported an active suicide plan. Current mental illness linked strongly with both depression and suicidal thoughts. Family conflict also predicted depression. Age played a smaller role for suicidal thoughts. The authors urge awareness drives and campus level action to lower suicidality.
pmc-12819590:
Shiying Guo and nine co-authors published a multicenter study in twenty twenty-six asking whether gene sequencing of lung wash fluid actually improves outcomes for immunocompromised patients with opportunistic lung infections. Conventional tests often miss the culprit in these fragile patients. One hundred sixty-two patients across four centers were compared, with statistical matching to balance the groups.

Sequencing results changed antibiotic therapy in four of five tested patients. After matching forty-one pairs, the study weighed oxygenation improvement, clinical recovery, mortality, and shock rates between sequencing-guided and conventional care. Detection rates were higher with sequencing. The authors frame the test as a therapy-steering tool whose value shows in decisions changed, not just organisms named.
pmc-12820090:
Kimia Marvi and eight colleagues survey 2,311 Ukrainian households about the winter when attacks on energy infrastructure left homes cold, then use machine learning to find who got sick. Three quarters of respondents reported respiratory infections; about four percent suffered cold injuries, rising to ten percent among older adults.

Bigger households bred more respiratory infection, while areas under Russian control saw more cold injury. Age, household size, finances, and heating practices predicted infections; anxiety and region predicted injuries. The authors describe the first machine learning study of cold-related illness during infrastructure attacks in an active war zone, and argue for targeted cold protection of older adults in conflict settings.
pmc-12820490:
Ida Bergholdt Jul Christiansen and five co-authors study when family doctors in Denmark add video to after-hours phone triage. Their register-based study was published in twenty twenty-five. Video use varies a lot between doctors, and the team asked whether traits of the doctor explain the gap.

They used records of all after-hours contacts during twenty twenty-one. Video was used in about eleven in each hundred phone contacts. Doctors who worked more after-hours shifts used video more often. Younger doctors used it more than older ones. Rates also differed by region, with two regions well above the lowest one. The findings show video triage is still a minor share of care and depends on who is on duty. That may matter for equal access as video care grows.
pmc-12821890:
Minghui Du and co-authors build a model to predict poor recovery ninety days after stroke patients get vessel-opening treatment plus a clot drug, in a study from 2025. The treatment reopens blocked brain arteries at high rates. Yet some patients still recover poorly when small vessels fail to reperfuse or the artery closes again.

The added drug, tirofiban, is meant to guard against those risks, but who gains from it is unclear. The team studied nearly one hundred and eighty patients at one center. They built prediction models from clinical, scan, and procedure data, using both classic statistics and machine learning. Model quality was judged by accuracy scores and calibration checks. The goal is to flag patients likely to do poorly despite treatment.
pmc-12821990:
Hongjiu Yu, Jiaying Wu, and Lianghui Gao test three tissue markers as warning signs in liver cancer, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. All three markers run high in this cancer, but their value for outlook was unclear. The team read public data sets, stained tumor samples, and tracked patients after surgery.

Each marker sat higher in tumors than in nearby healthy tissue. High levels of each went with shorter time free of disease and shorter survival. Each marker also stood as a lone warning sign in the math checks. Marker levels tied to tumor count, size, and grade in set patterns.
pmc-12822090:
Yajie Li and co-authors link indoor smoke to slow early growth in young children, in a 2025 study from the Tibetan plateau. Many homes there burn solid fuel for cooking and heat. Past work hints that such smoke can harm brain and body growth, but town and country gaps were little studied.

The team checked more than one thousand children aged five and under. Cooking smoke went with delays in fine hand skills and in speech. Heating smoke hurt hand skills and problem solving. Both smokes together raised the risk far more, and the harm ran stronger in rural homes. The results argue for clean fuel as a child health step.
pmc-12824090:
Menghuang Zhao and Lulu Zhou build a prognosis score for womb cancer from the genes of its T cells, in a 2025 study. Endometrial carcinoma is a leading cancer of the female reproductive tract, and advanced cases do poorly. Immunotherapy helps some patients, and T cells are the immune system's main cancer fighters.

Mining single-cell data, the authors identified marker genes defining the tumor's T cells. They then trained an eight-gene signature on bulk data from five hundred forty-four patients. The score predicted five-year survival with good accuracy and tracked immune activity in the tumor. It also carried signals about likely responses to immunotherapy and chemotherapy, and about mutation patterns. A T-cell-based score could help clinicians sort patients toward the treatments likeliest to work.
pmc-12827590:
Xuechao Ji and co-authors ask whether the side of an ovarian tumor predicts survival in a 2025 paper. The catalog lists 2026, but the journal record in the text gives 2025. Malignant ovarian teratomas are rare, since about ninety-five percent of these tumors are benign. No earlier study had checked left side against right. The team reviewed fifty-one patients treated at one hospital across ten years, from 2012 to 2021.

Survival curves and adjusted risk models compared left-sided, right-sided, and bilateral cases. Right-sided tumors carried a strikingly lower risk of progression in the adjusted analysis. With so few patients, the signal needs outside confirmation, but laterality is free information every chart already holds.
pmc-12827790:
Longyi Zheng and colleagues published a 2026 study comparing inflammation scores after stroke. Inflammation strongly affects survival after stroke. Many combined blood scores exist. Nobody knew which generalize best. The team calculated twelve such indices. Two patient cohorts provided the test data.

One cohort came from a national American survey. The other came from the authors' stroke center. Several indices linked to later death. One ratio stayed significant in both cohorts. That ratio compares neutrophils with lymphocytes. Subgroup checks explored where it holds up. A robust, cheap score could guide follow-up care. Validation across settings is the study's core strength.
pmc-12830890:
Kejin Wang and co-authors study how disulfiram, a long-approved drug against alcoholism, switches on cell cleanup in bowel cancer. Their study appeared in 2025. The drug's copper product blocks the cell's protein shredder. That blockage alone can kill cancer cells, but its effect on autophagy, the backup cleanup path, was unclear. The team traced two routes by which the drug raises autophagy.

First, with the shredder blocked, cells compensate by raising autophagy. Second, the drug boosts a gene switch that turns on a key autophagy gene. Pairing disulfiram with chloroquine, which blocks autophagy, killed far more cancer in dishes and in mice. With both disposal paths shut, proteins pile up fatally. The authors propose the pairing for further cancer testing.
pmc-12831190:
Harold Rivera-Alvarado and co-authors report a case of white cord syndrome, a spinal cord injury that can strike during neck surgery. A seventy-two-year-old woman with asthma and type 2 diabetes had surgery to relieve pressure on her cord. During the operation, the signals monitoring cord function suddenly vanished.

The team responded with high-dose steroids to cut swelling and drugs to push her blood pressure up, hoping to keep the cord supplied. Even so, her movement worsened after surgery. In the recovery unit she regained some strength, but progress stalled, and she moved to a rehabilitation facility. The authors use the case to examine how blood sugar control around surgery, steroid use, and the syndrome interact. They present the report as a guide for surgical teams facing this crisis, where minutes and pressure management may decide how much function a patient keeps.
pmc-12835690:
Aikaterini Strouza, Andrew Lawrence, Lora Dimitrova, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It uses brain scans to study how people with dissociative identity disorder handle words tied to their own life story. Some words are noticed openly, and others slip past awareness.

People with this disorder shift between identity states, some of which avoid trauma memories. Fifty-six people took part in the study. The group held patients, actors simulating the disorder, healthy controls, and people with post-traumatic stress. Words drawn from each person's own history were shown openly or flashed too briefly to notice. Patients answered more slowly than simulators and controls. Brain data showed stronger activity in frontal and parietal areas for some contrasts. The study probes whether hidden processing of self-relevant words differs in this disorder.
pmc-12836890:
Ahmed Abdelsamad and eight co-authors studied how the COVID-19 pandemic changed gallbladder surgery at their hospital, in this 2025 analysis of 1,075 patients. The team compared patients who had the operation before the first German lockdown in March 2020 with those treated after it. They tracked delays, disease severity, surgical choices, and outcomes.

Patients waited far longer before coming in during the pandemic, and more arrived as emergencies with acutely inflamed gallbladders. Keyhole surgery stayed the main approach, but open operations tripled as cases grew harder. Complications rose only slightly and not beyond chance. Hospital routines held up well despite the strain. The authors read the shifts as a warning to plan surgical care for future crises.
pmc-12837490:
Di Geronimo, Moramarco, Romano, Mete, and Fontana review imaging inside eye surgery, in work from twenty twenty-five. Optical coherence tomography gives cross section views of tissue. Built into the surgical microscope, it works during the operation itself.

Cloudy corneas, swelling, or altered anatomy can hide the structures a surgeon must see. Real time imaging reveals those hidden structures and lets the surgeon watch tissue and instrument interact. Precision and safety rise in complex corneal and front segment cases. The review covers where the technology changes outcomes in operations once done partly blind.
pmc-12840190:
Zongqin Feng and colleagues mapped the sucrose transporter gene family in peanut in 2025. Sweetness is a valued peanut quality, but high-sugar varieties are rare. Transporter proteins move sucrose into developing seeds, so knowing the full gene family could point breeders toward sweeter lines.

Sixteen family genes were found across the peanut genome, clustered in places rather than spread evenly. All carried the expected transporter domain and membrane-spanning structure. Gene activity differed by tissue, with several genes most active in seed parts. Three genes ran higher in a high-sugar variety than in a standard one, and yeast tests confirmed they can move sucrose. Those genes become clear breeding targets.
pmc-12843990:
Hariri and co-authors survey in 2025 hardware accelerators for heart signal processing, from a system on chip view. Heart disease leads global death and illness, which drives demand for fast, accurate monitors. Their review covers ECG, PPG, and blood pressure systems built for real time use.

Following standard review guidance, they analyzed 59 papers from 2014 to 2024. Work splits into signal cleaning, feature extraction, and decision support by machine learning. Benchmarks span energy, speed, and clinical accuracy. Hybrid chip designs and edge AI accelerators look most promising for next generation monitors. Gaps named include ultra low power and robustness at clinical scale.
pmc-12845290:
Chiara Barisione and co-authors build a gold nanoparticle aimed at neuroblastoma, the most common solid tumor outside the brain in children. The tumor's surroundings carry extra amounts of a fibronectin form called FN-EDB, which healthy tissue lacks. The team attached an antibody L19, which binds that form, to gold particles so the particles would home to the tumor.

Staining confirmed the target in cell-based and patient-derived animal models of the disease. The antibody kept its tight binding after attachment, and the particles stayed stable over time, unlike bare ones. In living models, the targeted particles gathered in tumors, most strongly where the target was most abundant, and barely appeared in healthy organs. The authors present the particle as a diagnostic tool for now. They see it as a first step toward combined particles that could find the tumor and deliver standard therapy to it.
pmc-12847990:
Royer and co-authors ask what shapes the rhythms of activity across the human cortex. The brain is both a physical object and a dense network, and its rhythms span many time scales. Local traits and long-range links both play a part, but their shares were unclear. The team used recordings from electrodes placed inside the skull. They built a coordinate map of cortical dynamics from those signals.

Brain imaging showed distance between regions explains much of the pattern. In higher-order association areas, likeness in tissue makeup and wiring added more. The work sorts where simple geometry rules the rhythm. It also shows where network layout takes a larger role.
pmc-12849290:
Qiang Zhang and four co-authors pool past studies to list risk marks for low blood sugar in adults with type one diabetes. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. Low blood sugar is a grave and common risk for adults who must take insulin each day. The team searched nine bases for group and case studies on the risk.

Thirty-one studies with more than fifty thousand adults were pooled. Of many marks checked, nine held as firm risks. Past lows, lost sense of lows, and nerve harm raised risk most. Long ill span, smoke, high insulin dose, and many shots a day also raised risk. One kidney mark read as a slight shield. The list aims to guide early steps to cut lows.
pmc-12850990:
Six doctors led by Romy Megahed report the first case of whole-body radiation that shields the liver, given with a spiral scanning machine. The patient was a man of twenty-three whose childhood blood cancer had returned. He already had liver disease, and full-body radiation can harm the liver, so the team shaped the dose.

The whole body got the planned dose in eight sessions, while the liver's average dose stayed well under the safety cap. The authors say the scan-guided machine made this shaping possible. The case shows liver-sparing treatment is feasible for patients who need body-wide radiation but have a weak liver.
pmc-12853790:
Fatima Tu Zahra, Rehan Ahmed Khan, and Rahila Yasmin present a 2025 study of curriculum co-creation at a private dental college in Pakistan. Co-creation means students and faculty share decisions about what and how to teach. The aim is better learner-teacher relationships and real student empowerment. The study uses an interventional, lived-experience design. Interviews cover eleven participants: six dental students and five faculty who took part in the process. Thematic analysis organizes what they said.

Challenges, merits, and downsides of sharing curriculum power are weighed from both sides of the classroom. Medical educators get a ground-level account from a setting rarely heard in this literature. Co-creation can flop into tokenism; hearing where it strained is as useful as where it soared. Dental training is hierarchical by tradition, which makes shared design a genuine cultural test.
pmc-12855990:
Yuqi Tang and co-authors dissect how the leftover circulation of Typhoon Fitow shaped a bout of rain over Shanghai in 2013. The rain fell unevenly across the city. Using weather station data, satellite products, reanalysis fields, and the typhoon's track, the team linked the surface wind field to where the rain fell hardest and longest.

Three findings stand out. The city center slowed the eastward drift of the northerly wind from the typhoon's remains. The calm zone and bent winds round the center forced air to converge in the districts round it. Slow-moving storm cells then parked the rain in place. A diagnostic called Q-vector convergence held strong while rain lasted. It faded just before the rain stopped, and the rain died within two hours of its weakening. A city's skyline, bending the wind, decided which neighborhoods flooded.
pmc-12857090:
Mostafa, Sameh, and El-Khamisy compared denture bar stuffs in twenty twenty-five with a three-dim sim of a lower jaw set. The bar joins a part denture and must be stiff to guard teeth and gums. They set a metal bar as the base case and three plastic kinds at the same size.

All three plastics bent far more than the metal bar did. Two of them also passed more stress to the gum than metal. One plastic kind passed the least stress of all to the gum. Same-size plastic swaps raise stress and flex in the mouth, they find.
pmc-12864990:
Sitong Chen and co-authors present a 2025 data set of brain waves recorded while people read and hear Chinese text. Brain decoding needs large paired sets of brain and language data, and non-English sets are rare. ChineseEEG-2 adds two live modes to a past silent-reading set: reading aloud and passive listening, all on the same text. Four speakers were recorded for near eleven hours as they read aloud.

Their audio then played to eight listeners, whose brain waves were caught for near twice that span. The set ships brain waves, audio, aligned meaning codes from language models, and task labels. Close time locks across modes let teams train decoders that span speaking, hearing, and reading. The set backs brain-to-model alignment work in Chinese.
pmc-12875990:
Ghanashyam Patel, Saumin Shah, and Christopher D'Adamo published a randomised trial in two thousand twenty-five on a plant-based drink for liver health. Herbal extracts like turmeric, milk thistle, dandelion, and ginger each show liver promise, but swallowing many capsules discourages use. A combined liquid was tested in healthy adults.

One hundred thirty participants drank the formula or a placebo twice daily for one hundred eighty days. All four liver enzymes improved significantly more with the herbal drink. No adverse events were reported in either group. The authors say a purified multi-herb liquid can support liver markers safely over six months. They frame it as an adherence-friendly alternative to capsule stacks.
pmc-12964790:
Chaoyong Wei and six co-authors report a heart injury case tied to a new cancer drug in a 2025 paper. Drugs that block both PD-1 and CTLA-4 help advanced cancers but can inflame the heart muscle. Their patient, a 61-year-old woman with ovarian cancer, is the first formally reported case on a new two-in-one antibody of this class.

After her second cycle she developed weakness, breathlessness, and chest tightness, with blood tests and heart tracings pointing to myocarditis. Steroids and other immune-calming drugs stabilized her by day 24. Lasting heart weakness led doctors to implant a defibrillator and stop the cancer immunotherapy for good. The authors warn that clever drug design does not erase heart risk.
pmc-13133290:
Keiichi Torimoto and Yosuke Okada review how glucose sensor accuracy is managed in a paper from 2026. Continuous glucose monitors guide daily diabetes decisions and insulin pumps. As use spreads, accuracy itself becomes a safety issue. The mini-review sorts progress along three forces: better technology, shared regulatory frameworks, and public demands for transparency. Four dimensions of accuracy are defined, from lab agreement to trend fidelity.

American and European standards anchor the discussion. Study design pitfalls and the clinical risks of sloppy accuracy get attention. Future directions include multi-analyte and needle-free sensors plus AI tuning. The authors aim to align clinical and research perspectives on safe sensor use.
pmc-13135690:
Geraldine Lee and Alexandra Manta report a single patient case in a paper dated 2026. The patient, a seventy-three-year-old woman, developed weakness of the face over six months. Doctors first blamed a common nerve problem called Bell's palsy. Her past told a more serious story.

Forty years earlier she had surgery for a glomus jugulare tumour, a slow-growing growth near the base of the skull. The new weakness turned out to be a return of that tumour, not a simple palsy. Her old surgery had left her with voice and hearing problems, which made the early visits harder to read. The authors urge quick brain imaging when face weakness appears in patients with such a history.
pmc-13136690:
Milad Hassani and Seyed Hossein Hosseinimehr compare two exercise programs for athletes with lower crossed syndrome, a posture problem where weak and tight muscles tilt the pelvis and arch the lower back. Their trial came out in 2026. Thirty-six young male athletes were split into three groups.

One group did core stability exercises, one followed a national sports medicine academy's corrective program, and one served as control. Both programs ran three sessions a week for eight weeks. Both reduced the back arch and pelvic tilt and improved front and back trunk endurance equally. The academy program alone also strengthened the side trunk muscles on both sides. The authors recommend either program, with the academy version favored when side strength matters.
pmc-13139290:
Mattia Ornaghi published a math paper in twenty twenty-six. It settles a basic question about a class of algebraic objects called A-infinity categories. Can this class carry a model structure, the setup that lets math treat sameness up to deformation in a strict way? The maps allowed here are the strict ones, and the ground ring can be any commutative ring.

The answer is yes, and the structure is built from a small set of basic maps. Every object is fibrant. The cofibrant objects have well-behaved maps. As a payoff, the semi-free categories come out cofibrant, and their resolutions behave as hoped. Papers of this kind give a whole style of proof a firm base.
pmc-13141790:
Thao Nguyen and eleven co-authors present a 2026 imaging review on scimitar syndrome, a rare birth defect of the heart and lung, in children. In this condition the right lung's vein drains to the wrong vessel, the right lung and its artery are underdeveloped, and extra arteries feed the lung's lower lobe. The review shows how the syndrome and its variants appear on cardiac CT and magnetic resonance scans.

Treatment ranges from surgery to vessel-blocking procedures to watchful waiting. Operations reroute the vein or remove a lobe, and outcomes are generally good, yet complications can be heavy and the case for operating on symptom-free children is unclear. The authors argue that combined imaging is essential for diagnosis, blood-flow assessment, and follow-up. Decisions, they stress, should be tailored child by child. The paper serves clinicians who meet this rare anomaly.
pmc-13143090:
Li, Wang, Liu, Song, and Ma build in twenty twenty-six a framework to find what drives fire risk most in cable tunnels. These tunnels carry dense power cables through tight spaces, so fires there are grave threats. Risk scores alone do not show managers where to act first, so the team weighted risk factors and tested how much each one moves the total score.

A case study showed a few drivers dominate, not all factors equally. Fire door condition and joint defects led the list, joined by key management factors. Risk varied sharply by tunnel segment, and fixes paid off unevenly by place. The authors offer the method to target spending where it cuts risk most.
pmc-13150390:
Frenzar Tshiruruvhela and co-authors explore, in twenty twenty-five, why cervical cancer is found late in women living with HIV at a hospital in Limpopo, South Africa. Cervical cancer is more common in HIV-positive women and often advanced at diagnosis. The team ran a qualitative study: individual interviews with purposively sampled women who had HIV and cervical cancer. Interviews were recorded, transcribed, translated, and analyzed thematically. Four themes emerged.

First, women saw Pap smears as a diagnostic test for symptoms, not as screening. Second, fear and embarrassment delayed them. Third, many consulted traditional healers first. Fourth, system faults delayed diagnosis: missing equipment, weak follow-up, low suspicion, and staff unwilling to do the test. The authors call for patient education and health worker training.
pmc-13153590:
Mauro Sartore and four co-authors report an eye tumor case that cleared during cancer drug therapy, in a paper from 2026. A 63-year-old woman with von Hippel-Lindau disease had a stubborn blood vessel tumor beside the optic disc of her left eye. It had resisted injections, steroids, and surgery, and leakage kept returning, with new tumors forming.

In 2022 she started cabozantinib, a targeted drug, for kidney cancer. Within weeks the eye leakage shrank, and the tumor then resolved fully. Three years on, the eye stayed quiet with no new tumors and no eye treatments needed. The authors urge study of such systemic drugs for these tumors.
pmc-13170790:
Ma and Chen test in twenty twenty-six whether the fever load a child carries into hospital forecasts how a lung infection will unfold. The infection, caused by a germ called Mycoplasma, can turn stubborn or severe, and admission blood tests alone sort risk poorly. They built an index from the area above normal temperature across the two days before admission, in a cohort of several hundred children.

About a quarter of cases turned stubborn or severe. Each standard rise in the fever index raised the odds of that outcome clearly, even after adjusting for standard clinical factors. Adding the index sharpened prediction accuracy and decision value over the base model. Results held at other fever cut-offs. The authors urge outside validation.
pmc-13176890:
Mónica Rodrigues and co-authors follow children with asthma to see whether they gain more body fat by their teens in a 2026 paper. Asthma and obesity travel together in childhood, but the arrow's direction is murky. Body mass index alone can mislead, so the team also measured body fat share with a mild electric signal method. The data come from a Portuguese birth cohort.

Children with doctor-diagnosed asthma at age four were tracked to ages seven, ten, and thirteen. Those already heavy at four were set aside for each check. Risk math adjusted for family and social traits. Knowing whether asthma itself fattens children would change how pediatricians counsel families about activity and steroids.
pmc-13177690:
Theresa FitzGerald, Amit Garg, and Erika Basile describe a research ethics prompt project in Ontario, Canada, in a 2024 article. Linking trial data with large administrative databases lets researchers follow participants long-term at far lower cost than direct contact. Many researchers, though, do not know the option exists or what rules govern it.

In twenty seventeen, Western University's human research ethics office added a prompt to its online protocol form, asking whether researchers had considered linking with ICES, an Ontario health data institute. A yes answer brought linkage details and consent wording. Over five years, a small average share of protocols declared intent to link, and the office verified their regulatory care, smoothing ethical, privacy, and legal steps.
pmc-13178890:
Nima Kianfar and co-authors review citizen science in the fight against mosquito-borne disease. Their 2026 scoping review weighs public reporting against official surveillance. Agency systems are costly, patchy, and slow to spot local surges. Phone-armed citizens can widen the net cheaply.

Sixty-one studies passed the screen from over three thousand records. Most appeared after 2017, led by Europe and the Americas. The review maps recruitment, data types, and validation habits. It also catalogs effort bias fixes and ethical practices. Citizen data proved a workable complement to agency systems. Standard habits for checking and crediting reports remain the weak point.
pmc-13183290:
Muthulakshmi Kirubakaran and Jayalakshmi Mohan built a brain tumor imaging system in 2026. Outlining tumors on MRI scans guides diagnosis and treatment planning. The task is hard, and hand work is slow. Their system merges three ideas. A three-dimensional network traces tumor regions in the scans. An evolutionary search tunes the network's shape and settings automatically. A rival network then pushes the outlines toward realistic boundaries. They trained it on a public challenge dataset with multi-modal scans.

The system marked whole tumors, tumor cores, and bright tumor parts. Its overlap scores beat several leading methods on held-out scans. Cross-checks across data splits stayed consistent. The method costs more computing time than simpler rivals. The authors accept that trade for sharper boundaries. They present the blend of evolution and adversarial learning as the gain. Such tools could support faster, steadier scan reading in clinics.
pmc-13184790:
Gian Luca Di Tanna, Niklaus Meier, and Matthias Schwenkglenks offer a two thousand twenty-six methodological comment on pooling cost-effectiveness studies. A recent proposal pooled added costs and added benefits separately. The commenters support the goal but question its readiness as a general blueprint.

They argue the motivating examples fail stated combinability checks. Standard data harmonization steps were skipped, they say. Pooling costs and benefits apart also loses their within-study link, muddying the joint ratio. Their alternative runs structured checks and cleaning first, then models costs and benefits together. Health economists get a caution and a path forward.
pmc-13185390:
Kayleigh Maxwell, Steve Leung, and Gozde Ozakinci review how showing patients 3D models of their own bodies affects their minds, in a 2026 paper. Printed or imaged models can make a condition concrete during a consultation. The team searched five databases and kept eleven studies that measured psychological outcomes. Nine of them used the models before surgery.

Outcomes included anxiety, quality of life, distress, and conflict over decisions. Results ran both ways: models calmed many patients yet left some feeling fearful or powerless. The authors say the potential is real, especially before big decisions, but the right patients and settings remain unclear. How the clinician talks while showing the model matters too. More research is needed before routine use.
pmc-13185490:
Shweta Meshram, Oluwatoyosi F. Akintayo, and Madan K. Bhattacharyya review extra-large G proteins in plants in this 2026 survey. G proteins pass signals inside cells and steer growth and defense. The extra-large kind is found only in plants and is built unlike the standard kind. It has a long head part with tags that send it to the cell's core, and it lacks the self-off switch of the standard kind.

Three members of the family do most of the known work. Two of them help the plant sense germs and fire its defense. The proteins team with catcher proteins on the cell skin and with other G parts to form shifting groups. Their jobs take in root shape, leaf green body growth, and stress from heat, drought, and germs. The authors close by weighing how this lore could breed tougher crops.
pmc-13191690:
Chen and co-authors build a fast test for drug traces left in food and feed. The drugs are three forms of tetracycline, a drug class used in farm animals. Their test uses tiny gold clusters that glow blue under light.

The clusters form in one pot with proline and sodium alginate as stabilizers. This mix glows more brightly and lasts longer than proline alone. When the target drugs are present, the glow changes in a way that can be measured. The method aims at low cost checks of meat, milk, and feed.
pmc-13193390:

Blocking this route may suggest new anti-viral strategies.
pmc-13194490:

pmc-13196390:

Immune therapy for this blood cancer depends on finding markers that appear on cancer cells but not on healthy ones. Kinase drugs affect cell signals and protein turnover, which can change those markers.

Blocking three key kinases reshaped the set of markers on the cells, affecting about four thousand displayed fragments. By combining several large scale methods, the team traced three ways the display changes. About ninety fragments were specific to the cancer and became more visible after drug treatment. pmc-13196890:

The authors offer the catalogue as a base for wildlife virus research on the island.
pmc-13198490:
Ali Nail Yagci and colleagues compared patient views in a specialist pituitary clinic versus general hormone clinics in a 2026 study. Pituitary tumor centers aim to standardize team care for pituitary disorders. Their effect on quality of life and satisfaction was little known, so the team surveyed patients at two centers.

That group scored lower on several quality-of-life parts, such as physical role and body pain. Yet they held a more informed view of their illness and reported higher satisfaction on every scale. Team care seems to please even sicker patients.
pmc-13200990:
Ke Shi and co-authors test a football program guided by sports medicine in a school trial from 2026. The program adds feedback from a learning model that can explain its calls. The team asks if ten weeks of the program beats standard gym classes for fitness and injury risk in teens.

One hundred ninety-five junior high students took part, with an average age near fourteen years. Tests covered lung capacity, stamina, sprint speed, long jump, and mid-distance runs. The new program group improved more on key fitness tests. The model also flagged injury risk in a way teachers could check. Schools get a tested model for safer sport.
pmc-13201290:
Coral reefs depend on tiny algae living inside coral tissue, and a 2026 laboratory study by Loris Marcel tests whether those algae release electrons to their surroundings. The research article studies cultures of Symbiodinium microadriaticum, a dinoflagellate that forms partnerships with corals and other marine animals.

Using an electrochemical setup, Marcel and colleagues show that the alga does transfer electrons outward, carried by diffusible chemical species. The signal also reflects photosynthesis and respiration, and it changes with temperature, acidity, and light. Such measurements could give scientists a new way to study coral symbiosis and the stress responses behind bleaching.
pmc-13202090:
Hayley Susan Mountford and co-authors published a 2026 paper describing new reading and language measures in a large Scottish family health study. Reading skills matter for education, work, and well-being across life. Yet research on the genetics of reading has mostly covered children and young adults. The largest gene study so far stopped at age twenty-six. The authors argue adult skills stay stable enough to extend that work.

Participants also reported diagnoses and how often they read books as children and as adults. The paper describes these additions for about 1,595 participants. Analyses check how the scores relate to age and how steady they remain across adulthood. The resource aims to boost the power of gene discovery for literacy by including older adults.
pmc-13202390:
Johan Sundelöf, Bodil Holmberg, and Christina Melin-Johansson adapt a spiritual assessment tool for Swedish end-of-life care, in work from 2026. The tool, named HOPE, helps clinicians ask about sources of hope, faith, and meaning. Sweden's secular, mixed culture calls for wording that fits more than churchgoing patients.

Starting from a plain Swedish translation of the eighteen-item original, the team simplified text, sharpened focus, and added prompts on non-religious concerns. The draft came to sixteen items. Eighteen experts in specialist comfort care, spanning nurses, doctors, and social workers, judged its clarity and coverage. The study reports how the adapted tool was received and where experts saw gaps.
pmc-13203490:
Gyuree Kim and four co-authors review peroxiredoxins, guard proteins that steer redox balance in nerve cells. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. Free oxygen bits serve as cell signs, but excess harms nerve work and life. These guards were long seen as mere peroxide mops, yet fresh work shows wider jobs.

pmc-13205290:
A laser that acts like a neuron fires in bursts across two time scales at once, fast peaks riding on slow spikes. Julian Feiveson and co-authors study that photonic neuron when its own signal is fed back after one delay, or after two. They read the output with pattern tools that care about the order of ups and downs, not exact sizes.

Yet when the results were plotted in a symmetry-based space, every case fell on one shared curve. That collapse hints at a hidden rule governing the system across scales and feedback setups. The authors argue such pattern methods can expose order in delayed, nonlinear devices that standard tools miss.
pmc-13206290:
Learning anatomy through a live ultrasound probe is tested in a 2026 pilot study headed by Dylan Ledbetter at an osteopathic medical school. Pre-clinical students were split into staggered groups that received clinician-led point-of-care ultrasound workshops on the abdomen, shoulder, and heart at different times.

Quizzes after each round compared students who had the workshop with those still waiting for it. Only two individual questions differed clearly between groups, although total test scores rose from start to finish for participants. Students also reported feeling far more comfortable using ultrasound in clinical practice afterward, and the authors back earlier exposure while calling for bigger, longer studies.
pmc-13207890:
A kidney cancer's surface flag becomes the delivery address for gene silencing in a 2026 study by Yuyang Ye. The research article targets carbonic anhydrase IX, abundant on clear cell renal carcinoma, with liposomes carrying small RNA against the transcription factor ETS1.

Genomic analyses first showed ETS1 and MYC switched on together in tumor cells, and bench experiments proved ETS1 directly turns MYC on. The team engineered a peptide that homes to the surface flag and decorated drug-loaded liposomes with it for delivery. The particles silenced the ETS1 and MYC axis and slowed tumor growth in cell lines, patient organoids, and mouse grafts.
pmc-13209490:
Drones that charge wirelessly lose power when their receiver twists out of line, hitting dead angles where transfer dies. Jaewoo Jeong and Sangwook Park built a tiny coupler cell designed to dodge those dead spots. The cell carries a patterned surface and switches between two excitation states. Each state transmits strongly where the other fades: one fades at a quarter turn, the other at an eighth. Tests ran in full-wave simulation at a standard charging frequency.

Peak transfer topped zero point nine in both states. Switching states thus keeps power flowing across a full spin. The work stays at the single-cell level on purpose, since arrays must be built from proven cells. Scalable charging pads for drone fleets are the target.
pmc-13209690:
Lizzi Herrera and five colleagues built a mouse model of infection with the parasite Leishmania panamensis, a cause of skin disease in people. They placed the parasite in the ears of two mouse strains and watched what came next. One strain grew slow-healing sores packed with parasites. pmc-13210190:
A Japanese city has run gene-guided nutrition advice since 2006, and a 2026 evaluation by Yasuo Kagawa reports its long-term health and cost footprint. The Sakado Folate Project counseled residents on folate and lifestyle using variants in genes for folate processing, blood pressure, and metabolism, then tracked markers and city outcomes.

Sakado recorded lower stroke prevalence than its prefecture and lower per-person medical spending than the national average in 2021 comparisons. The authors present community nutrigenomics as a candidate model for aging societies.
pmc-13211590:
Carlos Fierro and colleagues reported a cytomegalovirus vaccine trial in 2026. No licensed vaccine exists against this virus. Infection can pass from mother to baby. Serious brain development harm can follow. An mRNA vaccine entered dose-finding testing. Healthy adults joined the randomised trial.

Binding antibodies stayed durable for years. Responses persisted through month forty-eight. Later data supported that durability further. Phase three work can build on this.
pmc-13212790:
Hadeer Khaled and colleagues test in 2026 whether resveratrol, a plant compound found in grapes, can shield rat hearts from a prostate cancer drug. Cabazitaxel can damage the heart through oxidative stress, so an early warning measure and a protectant would both help.

Twenty rats were split into control, standard-dose, high-dose, and high-dose plus resveratrol groups for four weeks. High-dose drug slowed heart rate, widened a major artery, raised oxidative markers, and injured heart muscle. Adding resveratrol eased many of those changes and preserved tissue structure. Some pressure measures stayed abnormal, though, and one heart wall remained thin, so protection looked partial rather than complete.
pmc-13214290:
Cuicui Liu and co-authors published this microbiology study in 2026 on Acinetobacter baumannii, a hospital germ that shrugs off many drugs. From a clinical strain, the team found a new switch protein, AbCro, kin to a virus protein of the same name. They built a strain with the switch deleted and one with it restored, then compared the germ's harm.

Without the switch, the germ formed far weaker biofilms, the slimy mats that shield bacteria. It also hurt wax moth larvae and mice less, and mouse lungs showed less damage. Gene reads showed the switch turns on a pair of genes that make trehalose, a stress-guard sugar. Lab tests showed the switch grips those genes' start zone directly. The authors name the switch a drug target for taming this germ.
pmc-13216290:
Arne Van de Vyver and co-authors present a 2026 cadaver study of a new navigation platform for knee replacement surgery. The system feeds the surgeon live information on bone cuts, implant position, joint motion, and ligament stretch during the operation.

Most motion measures after surgery closely matched the native knee, although internal rotation of the shin differed over part of the range. Strain in the inner ligament matched well, while the outer ligament's strain differed in deeper bending. The authors see the feedback as a practical aid to restoring natural knee behaviour.
pmc-13217290:
Yiwei Zhao and co-authors present a 2026 study of Triphala, the three-fruit Ayurvedic formula, as a treatment for gum disease, combining computer-based target prediction with bench and animal tests. Periodontitis destroys the tissues holding teeth, and a multi-target herbal agent is an attractive adjunct.

pmc-13217890:

Patients scoring high on the signature died sooner, with a hazard ratio of 1.50, and the score stayed predictive after allowing for stage and other clinical factors. The atlas also exposed Helicobacter-linked diversity in precancerous intestinal metaplasia, which the authors flag for follow-up.
pmc-13218090:

Costs will cover delivering the intervention, putting it into practice, and household spending. pmc-13218190:
Peter M. Izmirly and colleagues check the eyes of children exposed to hydroxychloroquine before birth, in a 2026 PATCH cohort study. A specialist blind to each child's exposure history read the scans. Cord blood confirmed exposure after birth. Every scan looked normal, with no thinning in the ganglion cell layer, photoreceptors, or pigment layer, and retinal thickness in both groups sat within healthy child norms. The authors conclude hydroxychloroquine leaves no sign of retinal toxicity in offspring by school age.
pmc-13218690:
Ke Ding and co-authors sort breast cancers, in a 2026 study, by the pattern of gene mutations in each tumor. Patients in the first group lived markedly longer, and their tumors held more immune cells and answered immune therapy better. The second group responded more to chemotherapy drugs instead. pmc-13222590:
Yue Wang and co-authors review nanozymes, nanomaterials that mimic enzymes, as tools for bone regeneration, in a 2026 article. pmc-13223090:

pmc-13223190:

Artesunate comes from artemisinin and shows cancer fight traits. It shifts marks tied to poor outlook in these cells. Breast, lung, and colon cell lines were all tested. pmc-13224690:

pmc-13226790:

pmc-13226890:

pmc-13229590:

pmc-13230290:

pmc-13230990:

pmc-13232290:

pmc-13232590:

pmc-13232790:

pmc-13233190:

pmc-13233890:

pmc-13233990:

pmc-13235490:

pmc-13236890:

pmc-13237190:

pmc-13237690:

pmc-13239090:

pmc-13239290:

pmc-13239590:

pmc-13239790:

pmc-13239890:

pmc-13240190:

pmc-13240390:

pmc-13240490:

pmc-13240890:

pmc-13242190:
Lutong Gan and co-authors report a 2026 hunt for gene markers that connect sleep deprivation to autophagy, the cell recycling system. Sleep loss harms health through routes that stay poorly mapped. The team merged several public gene datasets from sleep-deprived brain tissue.

pmc-13242590:

pmc-13242690:

pmc-13242890:

pmc-13242990:

pmc-13243090:

pmc-13243490:

pmc-13245190:

pmc-13247090:

pmc-13247290:

pmc-13247390:

pmc-13248390:

pmc-13249190:

pmc-13250190:

pmc-13250390:

pmc-13251090:

pmc-13252290:

pmc-13253090:

pmc-13255290:

pmc-13255490:

pmc-13255590:

pmc-13256390:

pmc-13256690:

pmc-13256790:

pmc-13257990:

pmc-13258690:

pmc-13258790:

pmc-13258890:

pmc-13259790:

pmc-13260390:

pmc-13260490:

pmc-13260690:

pmc-13261990:

pmc-13262890:
