Cone beam scans of single missing teeth were used to teach and test the system in five rounds. Scores for outlining teeth and jaw parts were high across test rounds, and sorting of hollow shapes proved highly accurate as well. Planned implant spots kept a clear gap from the nerve canal and left enough bone on both sides.
pmc-13320590:
Zeyu Wu and co-authors examine a plant compound in a 2026 mouse study of kidney injury caused by the cancer drug cisplatin. Cisplatin often harms the kidneys, which limits its use, and the full chain of that harm stays unclear. Sulforaphane, found in cruciferous vegetables, switches on a defence protein called NRF2 and has calming and protective effects.

Mice given a single cisplatin dose were treated with or without sulforaphane, and blood, tissue, and cell harm marks were compared. Tests covered kidney function in blood, cell death proteins, tissue stains, swelling signals, and harmful oxygen levels. The design lets readers judge whether NRF2 linked defence can blunt drug caused kidney harm.
pmc-13321490:
Konanov and colleagues chart how temperature changes DNA methylation in the plague bacterium. Their study from twenty twenty-six compares flea and host temperatures. Yersinia pestis cycles between fleas and mammals during its life. Temperature shifts help switch its behaviour between those hosts.

Eleven strains from different subspecies had their methylomes mapped. Only two methylation patterns appeared across all genomes. One pattern stayed nearly complete at both temperatures. The other faded at mammal body temperature versus flea temperature. Ancient lineage strains showed the fading most strongly. Plasmid copy numbers also shifted with temperature in the study. Epigenetic tuning may help the bacterium change hosts.
pmc-13322190:
YuChung Lin and co-authors borrow strength from large gene studies to sharpen risk scores for small patient groups in a 2026 study. Polygenic scores need huge data sets, which blurs fine clinical types, while small well defined cohorts alone are too weak. Their external score framework blends target cohort evidence with genetic correlation to a larger source study.

Simulations showed gains across a range of genetic links between source and target traits. Applied work refined an epilepsy score to separate juvenile myoclonic epilepsy from sister types and used a large ADHD study to predict impulsivity in that group. A cystic fibrosis cohort test predicted diabetes linked to the disease, with checks for platform artefacts.
pmc-13322390:
Jayant Raikhelkar and a large team train an AI model to spot weak heart pumping from ordinary chest scans in a 2026 study. Many people with early heart muscle weakness feel no symptoms, yet early treatment can slow decline. The model reads plain, non-contrast chest CT scans that were never meant for heart checks.

Training used 34,058 paired scans and ultrasound reports from two centres, with testing on 8110 pairs from a third centre. The model scored 0.786 on held out tests and 0.762 on outside checks for spotting an ejection fraction below 50 percent in the study. It beat expert radiologists on accuracy and speed and highlighted the image features behind its calls.
pmc-13322490:
Luciana Cássia de Jesus, Luciana Mendonça Alves, and Luciana Macedo de Resende validate an online hearing skills questionnaire for Brazilian adults in a 2026 study. The expanded EAPAC scale asks adults how well they handle central auditory processing in daily life. A total of 1274 people aged 18 to 59 answered it, with smaller groups getting full hearing and thinking tests.

Factor checks led to five questions being dropped for weak fit. Curves testing how well scores flag true processing disorder gave no clear signal, and sensitivity and specificity were judged fragile. Answers stayed stable when 63 people retook the scale later. The tool still helps surface daily hearing complaints and guide coping strategies, even if it cannot diagnose risk alone.
pmc-13322690:
Brian Yarahmadi and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether emergency brain scans help people with known epilepsy who arrive after a breakthrough seizure. Scanning is well supported for a first seizure, but guidance for repeat events in diagnosed patients is vague. Many emergency departments scan routinely anyway.

Records from 2019 to 2023 at their centre yielded 121 encounters where adults with epilepsy had an emergency non-contrast head scan. Falls were the commonest reason, followed by altered mental state. Three quarters of scans were normal, and the rest showed old stroke, surgical changes, small vessel disease or old trauma. No scan revealed new pathology compared with earlier imaging, and none changed acute management. The authors argue the yield is low and guidelines should curb unnecessary scans.
pmc-13322790:
Dongyan Zhang and co-authors build a light AI model to classify Alzheimer's disease from brain scans in a 2026 study. Standard networks read local detail well but miss long range links, while transformer models capture those links at heavy computing cost. Their HDFT-MViT model mixes both, using cheap early layers and dynamic filters plus a light transformer deeper in.

On two public ADNI scan sets, accuracy reached 98.85 percent for three class sorting and 98.07 percent for four class sorting, with only 3.46 million parameters in the model. Channel attention helped separate the classes. The balance of accuracy and small size suits clinics with modest computing power.
pmc-13322890:
Hongmei Wang and Xiaoou He study what teens like in art from other cultures, in a 2026 survey of 400 adolescents aged 14 to 18 years. Participants came from Chinese and Western backgrounds, judged art from both traditions, and answered measures of art exposure, openness and mental flexibility.

Teens tended to favour art from their own tradition, and cultural background strongly predicted those choices. Wider exposure to global art weakened that home bias and partly explained it, acting as a bridge in the authors' models. Teens high in openness or flexibility showed less cultural bias as well. The findings link family and school art contact with broader taste during a key stage of cultural learning.
pmc-13323090:
Huangtianzhi Zhu and his team report, in 2026, a trick for making organic molecules glow from their usually dark triplet states at room temperature in plain solution. Triplet states are prized for displays, photochemistry and medical uses, but spin rules forbid direct excitation and make their light emission very weak. Known organic phosphorescence usually needs crystals, deep cold or oxygen-free conditions.

Attaching light-absorbing molecules to the surface of nanocrystals doped with lanthanide metals changed the rules. Spin exchange between the metal ions and the attached molecules allowed direct excitation of the triplets. The resulting glow lasted nanoseconds, ignored oxygen and appeared in solution and films alike. Swapping the organic and metal partners shifted emission from visible into near-infrared light, suggesting broad use in devices and medical imaging.
pmc-13323490:
Şafak Yalçın Şahiner and colleagues ask Turkish university students how addiction should be fought, in a 2026 qualitative study. Their group held 119 undergraduates who answered an online form in their own words, analysed through descriptive thematic methods.

Students backed a wide mix of action, spanning structural steps and individual support. The most stressed themes were prohibitions, sanctions and monitoring on one side, and education and awareness work on the other. Knowledge of existing policy proved considerably weak, which the authors flag as a gap in current campaigns. They argue that prevention gains force when young people join the design of anti-addiction strategy rather than only receiving its messages.
pmc-13323590:
Christian Staehr and co-authors investigated why brain blood flow stays disturbed after a cardiac arrest caused by lack of oxygen. Their 2026 mouse study used transgenic animals whose pericytes, the cells that wrap capillaries, glowed under a fluorescent label, with cranial windows implanted three weeks ahead. After four minutes of asphyxial arrest and resuscitation, two-photon microscopy tracked brain microcirculation at 3 and 24 hours after circulation returned.

Capillary diameters shrank at 3 hours, red blood cell speed fell through the network, and capillary flow stalling increased, with longer artery-to-vein transit times. By 24 hours, diameters, speeds, transit times, and stalling had all returned to sham levels. The authors link the early vasospasm to pericyte contraction after resuscitation, pointing to a window in which protecting the microcirculation might limit secondary brain injury.
pmc-13324290:
Zi Han Gao, Xie He, and Hong Mei published a control engineering study in twenty twenty-six on keeping flapping-wing aircraft steady in disturbed air. Such craft are strongly nonlinear, with coupled channels and messy aerodynamics, so one fixed controller struggles. Their answer switches strategies as conditions change.

A disturbance measure sorts flight into low, medium, and high disturbance, and a nested controller switches its inner loop among three designs under a classical outer loop. Simulations in two software environments cross-checked the setup. At the standard flapping frequency, attitude error shrank to a small bound. Resistance to heavy disturbance improved by nearly half over plain PID control, with fast computation.
pmc-13324790:
Sunyoung Jang and Kyung Hyun Yoo review how the folding of the genome goes awry in cancer. Their 2026 paper explains that spatial architecture runs gene use, guards genome health, and sets each cell type's own gene reading. In tumors, this folding breaks down through altered control parts, faulty building proteins such as CTCF and cohesin, faulty chromatin looping, and rework of topologically associating domains.

Such breakage can switch on cancer-driving switches, forge inappropriate promoter-enhancer contacts, and reprogram DNA packing on a large scale to sustain malignant states. High-resolution tools including Hi-C, HiChIP, and single-cell 3D genomics have exposed widespread spatial reorganization across tumor types, revealing progression mechanisms invisible to linear mutation analysis alone. The review evaluates emerging therapies aimed at genome folding, from epigenetic modulators to switch breakage and phase-separation-based interventions.
pmc-13325490:
Xin Xu and colleagues link kidney lymphatic vessel growth to IgA nephropathy severity in a 2026 cohort study. The vessels may tie tissue injury to immune activity in this common kidney disease.

Biopsy samples from 127 untreated patients at Tongji Hospital in Wuhan were stained and scored for vessel density. Density ran higher than in controls and tracked with urine Gd-IgA1, complement parts, and IL-6 levels. Patients in the densest group carried more protein in urine and worse tissue scores. Over a median 93 months of follow-up, that group faced a hazard ratio of 3.67 for doubled creatinine and 19.81 for end-stage kidney disease.
pmc-13327890:
Sarah Johnston, Yu Jo Chua, and Alisha Azmir present a 2026 case series on a paradoxical gut blockage during cancer immunotherapy. About 15 percent of colorectal cancers carry mismatch repair deficiency, respond poorly to standard chemotherapy, and often shrink well on PD-1 blocking drugs such as pembrolizumab. At their center, several such patients developed bowel obstruction anyway.

Scans and course showed the blockage came from lasting narrowing at the original tumor site even while the cancer itself responded excellently. The series walks through the cases, including a 40-year-old woman with widespread disease, to sharpen recognition of this rare complication. Teams may still need surgery for the narrowed bowel despite a winning drug response.
pmc-13327990:
Huizhong Bai and co-authors present FreeMMIF, an interactive system for merging medical scans, in a 2026 article. Fusion joins functional and structural images to aid diagnosis, but older methods fix one aim and cannot adjust on the fly. Their framework pairs a vision-language model with a diffusion generator steered by text instructions.

During training, the language model picks the best outputs of older methods as stand-in targets, removing the need for reference images. A re-weighting branch then teaches the generator to balance source images against those targets, and at use time doctors type instructions to shift the blend between scan types. Tests showed fused images of diagnostic quality that matched stated clinical intent.
pmc-13328190:
Gulce Coskun Senturk, Asli Kaya, and Cagri Basbug build a scale for music exam self-belief in a 2026 study. High-stakes aptitude exams stress adolescent musicians, and what they expect of themselves beforehand may shape results. Drawing on social cognitive theory, the team developed the Music Aptitude Self-Efficacy Scale and tested it on 2,030 adolescents.

Factor work supported three parts: cognitive-auditory belief, psychomotor performance belief, and emotion regulation belief, and the scale held together reliably while matching other self-efficacy measures. In a live performance simulation judged by experts, higher pre-exam scores went with better technical playing under stress. Teachers and counselors could use the scale to spot students needing support before exam day.
pmc-13328490:
Liang Zhang and co-authors show a plant compound restoring cisplatin power in lung cancer in a 2026 study. Morusin, from mulberry plants, suppresses non-small cell lung cancer, and the team asked whether it also sensitizes tumors to cisplatin, called DDP in the study. Cell tests measured survival, drug synergy, and iron-driven death signs.

Morusin triggered ferroptosis and sharply raised cisplatin sensitivity, even in a resistant cell line, by binding the protein GDF15 and sending it for destruction. Restoring GDF15 erased those gains, while removing it made resistant cells drug-sensitive again, and tumor data linked high GDF15 to the cancer. A natural compound may thus reopen a standard drug's usefulness in stubborn lung tumors.
pmc-13329390:
Yan Li and co-authors review tiny membrane bubbles drawn from immune cells as a possible therapy for autoimmune disease in a 2026 article. Current drugs often act broadly, cause side effects, and fail to restore immune tolerance. Bubbles shed by red blood cells, platelets, neutrophils, dendritic cells, or macrophages keep surface marks from their parent cells.

Those marks can guide bubbles to swollen tissue and calm immune action. Bubbles can also carry drug cargo or added targeting tags. The review covers making and loading methods, then uses in illnesses such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, bowel disease, and type 1 diabetes. Hurdles include large-scale making, keeping membranes intact, and loading cargo well. Fixes for those hurdles will decide clinical use.
pmc-13330090:
Prince Imani-Musimwa and a large team report a maternal death in an Ebola unit in DR Congo in a 2026 case account. The patient was a pregnant teenager in her second pregnancy, admitted at 32 weeks with high virus load after vaccination and antibody treatment. Virus levels fell over the first days of care.

On day 3 she delivered a live preterm baby after efforts to halt labour failed. Heavy bleeding followed, with tears in the cervix and vagina and urine leaking through a fistula. Staff removed retained tissue and gave womb-tightening drugs, but lack of surgical gear in the unit blocked full repair. She died 14 hours after delivery from blood loss and clotting failure. The authors call the death preventable with better obstetric tools on site.
pmc-13330690:
Soudeh Ashrafipour and colleagues study whether puberty timing shapes brain network links in teens in a 2026 report. Timing was scored as a puberty age gap, the split between model-predicted puberty age and true age. Data came from the ABCD Study with about 3,500 young people, covering 12 large brain networks.

Earlier timing tied to altered resting links within and between networks in same-time checks, the authors report. Most patterns echoed normal age-related change, while some control network links looked specific to puberty. Sensorimotor, attention, and control networks featured most, in both sexes but wider in males. Later change over time showed weaker links. Timing beyond age matters for brain wiring, the authors argue.
pmc-13332390:
Marco F. Monteros and co-authors name a new orchid species from northwestern Ecuador in a 2026 taxonomy paper. Pleurothallis pembertonii grows in lower montane cloud forest inside the Dracula Reserve in Carchi Province, in the western Andean foothills, and is known from a single locality.

The species sits in a small series whose members look so alike that they are often confused, and its closest match is P. forceps-cancri. The new plant stands apart through wine-colored, oblong and slightly S-curved petals that taper to long points, plus an arrow-shaped three-lobed lip with a kidney-shaped glenion and two small spreading basal ridges. The authors note the area's many range-restricted species and the growing pressure from mining, which makes naming and mapping such plants urgent for protection.
pmc-13332690:
See Ming C Wong and colleagues report a 2026 case in which extreme anemia first appeared as a convulsive seizure. Anemia below two grams per decilitre is rarely seen, and its clinical picture stays unclear. The patient was a woman in her sixties in previously good health who felt generally unwell for two weeks and then suddenly had a convulsive seizure. Blood tests showed hemoglobin of 1.7 grams per decilitre, with acute kidney injury and raised liver enzymes and creatine kinase.

She was then diagnosed with myelodysplastic syndrome with erythroid hypoplasia, a marrow disorder with underproduction of red cell precursors. After supportive blood transfusion, her clinical and lab measures improved markedly. The case shows that extreme anemia can present with seizure and multi-organ dysfunction from tissue oxygen starvation. Clinicians facing unexplained seizure should check blood counts early, since transfusion can reverse a dangerous, treatable cause.
pmc-13332790:
Shalini Yadav and colleagues study 2026 SOX2 expression across cervical squamous lesions, from normal tissue to cancer. Cervical cancer remains a major health concern for women, notably where resources are scarce. SOX2 is a transcription factor involved in cell self-renewal and differentiation, and it has been linked to tumor growth and malignancy. The team asked how its staining pattern changes across the lesion spectrum and whether it tracks with clinical and pathology features.

The cross-sectional study at Gandhi Medical College in Bhopal, from May 2023 through October 2024, examined eighty cervical specimens: twenty normal, twenty precancerous intraepithelial neoplasia, and forty squamous cell cancers. SOX2 was measured by immunohistochemistry with a semi-quantitative score combining staining strength and percent of positive cells. Readers learn whether SOX2 rises with lesion severity and could serve as a marker of progression, a question with real weight for screening and triage.
pmc-13333590:
Xukun Liu and co-authors present a robot learning framework in 2026 for teaching two arms to work together from demonstrations. Bimanual imitation is unforgiving. The arms must stay in sync, avoid colliding, plan over long horizons, and ignore clutter. Diffusion-based policies tend to sacrifice either the long view or fine precision while latching onto background cues.

Their system, SCH-DIL, splits the diffusion process into temporal and spatial branches, so multi-scale action structure survives. It learns visual features forced to carry little information about confounding surroundings. It estimates observation uncertainty during denoising. And it adds a penalty that discourages distraction and keeps attention steady over time. On the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark the framework beat diffusion and imitation baselines, holding success rates in clean scenes and randomized, shifted ones. The authors note the gains come at little added cost, making the approach practical for real-world deployment.
pmc-13333890:
Mohamed Ibrahim, Zhang Xiao, and Jiajun Xu test how starting metal thickness changes the final switchable oxide film. Their study from twenty twenty-six oxidises vanadium layers into vanadium dioxide. That material flips properties at a set temperature, suiting smart windows. Oxidising thin vanadium is a cheap fabrication route.

Five thicknesses from very thin to thicker were deposited identically. All were annealed under the same gas conditions. Crystal and vibration analyses measured phase composition afterwards. Infrared testing found each film's switching temperature. Heating and cooling curves showed the hysteresis loop. Cross-section tools checked thickness and oxygen spread. One recipe does not fit all starting thicknesses equally.
pmc-13334090:
Thomas Williams and co-authors ran a 2026 follow-on analysis of the MS-STAT2 randomized trial, asking whether treating vascular risk changes the course of secondary progressive multiple sclerosis. Blood vessel risk factors track with worse disability in MS, but whether modifying them helps was unknown.

The trial randomized 964 patients to simvastatin at 80 mg or placebo for three years, with 246 of them also getting yearly MRI scans. Vascular risks and cholesterol profiles were taken at baseline. The parent trial found no benefit of simvastatin on its main medical outcomes. This analysis tests a narrower idea: whether assignment to simvastatin weakened the link between a harmful cholesterol profile and later disease worsening, against placebo.
pmc-13334790:
Wenjing Yu and co-authors looked at the type III-A CRISPR-Cas system of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in a 2026 article, arguing it does far more than fight invading DNA. The tuberculosis bacterium keeps this system fully built yet barely collects new spacers, a hint that its job has changed.

The machinery still interferes with targets, working through transcription-dependent recognition and cyclic oligoadenylate signals that switch on the Csm6 effector. Proteins of the system also shape antibiotic susceptibility, resistance to oxidative stress, and interactions with host immunity, and some may be released to sway the host directly. The review organizes the system's genomic layout and regulatory wiring, and weighs its roles in stress coping and infection, which could matter for future tuberculosis control.
pmc-13336090:
Yiyu Wang and colleagues study 2026 mixing RT-treated tumor vaccines with Mn-MOF nano-helpers to amplify RT induced anti-tumor immune effects. Vaccine effect is badly curbed by tumor surroundings that weaken immunity. Gene analysis showed B16F10 tumor cells given lab ray treatment closely match part of the RT-induced mutation map seen in skin tumor models.

Based on these findings, a body-mimicking cancer vaccine was developed through mixing RT-treated tumor cell membranes and Mn-based metal organic framework nano-helpers. This vaccine can deliver RT-induced membrane proteins directly to lymph nodes to boost the in situ vaccine immune response. Moreover, Mn-based nano-helpers boosted antigen showing power by nearly two-fold through switching on of the cGAS-STING pathway in branching cells. The vaccine further improved the lymph node immune surroundings.
pmc-13336390:
Anastasia Shihabi and co-authors reviewed the mechanics of the egg cell in a 2026 article arguing that physical properties belong in judging oocyte quality. A good oocyte must complete two lopsided divisions that keep the mother's reserves while halving the genome.

Those divisions run on actomyosin networks at the surface and in the cytoplasm, and the remodeling of these networks sets the cell's stiffness and flow. Mechanics in turn govern cytoplasm organization, spindle placement, chromosome segregation, and the final pinch into polar bodies. Errors climb with maternal age, and fertility preservation by freezing has sharpened the hunt for quality markers beyond looks. The review covers the pathways controlling oocyte mechanics, their failure in disease, and possible clinical uses.
pmc-13336990:
Luca Zangrando, Emanuele Buratti, and Francesca Paron review the double life of the protein TDP-43 in a 2026 article. TDP-43 normally manages RNA tasks from splicing to transport, and its clumps mark diseases such as ALS and much frontotemporal degeneration. Newer work shows its self-gathering is not always harmful.

Reversible assemblies and liquid droplets help TDP-43 do its normal jobs. Mutations, altered RNA binding, chemical tags, or cutting can tip that balance into permanent toxic aggregates, much like prion proteins. The review maps the structural switches in its prion-like domain and surveys strategies to clear aggregates or steer its phase behavior. Keeping the healthy side of the balance is the therapeutic goal.
pmc-13337390:
Jia-yun Wu leads a 2026 team teaching an AI model to spot thyroid autoimmunity risk from lip gland tissue. Patients with connective tissue disease often develop autoimmune thyroiditis, flagged by thyroid antibodies. Lip gland biopsies are already common in this group, so the team asked whether their slide images hide predictive patterns.

Slides from 121 patients were split by antibody status into positive and negative groups. A pre-trained EfficientNet-B5 network extracted image features, combined with multi-instance and ensemble learning. The integrated model reached an AUC of 0.829 across internal and external validation sets in the reported evaluation, and it highlighted the tissue features tied to high risk. Slide-based screening could flag patients for earlier thyroid checks.
pmc-13337890:
Matthew J. Slarve leads a 2026 broad review of antibody drugs aimed at bacterial infections. Rising antibiotic resistance has pushed the search for other ways to treat hard infections. Antibodies built to target single bacterial features offer one such path.

Findings are sorted by bacterial species and by molecular target. Both antibodies that helped and those that failed are covered, so design lessons stand out. Biofilms that shield bacteria receive attention as well. New molecular methods that speed antibody building and tuning are also reviewed, pointing to a growing era for antibacterial antibody therapy.
pmc-13338390:
Yan Zhuang and a large team build a clinical language model centered on medical records in a 2026 study. Their system, AI4Doctor, aims to mimic how doctors reason through complex cases. General chat tools give information but rarely copy that layered judgment.

Training mixed distilled knowledge from electronic records with insights from practicing doctors during fine-tuning. A staged curriculum helped merge the two sources in order. A reward system then pushed answers toward qualities valued in doctor expertise, such as sound diagnosis. The design tries to create a realistic practice setting inside the model, so its advice follows clinical logic more closely.
pmc-13338990:
Gabriele Riccio and colleagues tested ChatGPT-4o in 2026 on Parkinson disease quizzes and patient questions. The chatbot is increasingly used for medical learning and health advice, yet its reliability, quality, usefulness, and readability need checking against expert judgment. Twenty two professional quizzes went to both the chatbot and two neurologists, while answers to 20 patient questions were scored by three neurologists.

Agreement between neurologists and the chatbot was only fair. Readability scores and quality ratings reveal where chatbot answers help and where they mislead. The study gives patients, students, and clinicians a measured view of when to trust chatbot answers on Parkinson disease and when to seek expert care.
pmc-13339390:
Vinu Chandralayam Ayyappa Menon and colleagues described preclinical dose work in 2026 for ISB 2001, a trispecific antibody for relapsed multiple myeloma. The antibody binds CD38 and BCMA on tumour cells and links to CD3 on T cells, directing T cells to kill myeloma cells. It is now in a first in human trial, TRIgnite-1, yet its CD3 binding part does not react with monkey CD3.

Without a fully reactive animal species, standard pharmacokinetic and toxicology data could not guide the first human dose directly. The paper lays out the alternative modelling used to predict a safe starting dose. The approach matters for complex antibodies where animal models fall short of human biology.
pmc-13341090:
Julia Kaulfuss and co-authors report on feedback tools used at a surgical training workshop in Germany in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The workshop, held in two thousand twenty-four, trained urology residents in scope and resection skills by simulation. All fifteen trainees said they wanted feedback, yet most had only ever had loose, informal comments.

Two scoring tools were used side by side: a general rating scale and a scale built for urology scope skills. Scores on the two tools moved together, most strongly for the scope task. After the workshop, nearly all trainees rated planned feedback as helpful. Most also found both tools clear and useful for training.
pmc-13341190:
Jinyoung Kim and colleagues tracked tumour growth in 2026 during active surveillance of papillary thyroid microcarcinoma, small thyroid cancers often watched rather than removed. Patients who deferred surgery for over a year after diagnosis were enrolled and followed to 2023, with tumours at most 1 centimetre and BRAF testing available. Diagnosis years spanned 2014 to 2021. A total of 85 patients took part, median age 49, with 74 percent female.

BRAF mutation positivity was 51 percent, and 16 patients, 19 percent, showed rapid growth by tumour volume doubling time. The study tests whether BRAF status and other clinical factors predict progression during surveillance. Such predictors help doctors decide who can safely watch and who needs earlier surgery.
pmc-13341390:
Unnikrishnan Ambika Gopalakrishnan and colleagues weighed lab made semaglutide against brand Ozempic in 2026 in Indian patients with type 2 diabetes. The phase 3, randomised, open label, active controlled study ran across 35 centres in India. Adults aged 18 to 65 took part. Their HbA1c was at least 7 percent and at most about 10 percent despite metformin plus diet and exercise, and they were randomised one to one.

Volunteers got weekly shots under the skin for 24 weeks on an identical dose rise from a quarter milligram to 2 milligrams. Efficacy, safety, and immune response were weighed between lab made and brand semaglutide. A good non inferiority result would back a lower cost lab made swap for Indian diabetes care.
pmc-13341990:
Neutrophil genes forecast pancreatic cancer outcomes, in a 2026 modeling study by Zhengrong Ou's team. Drawing candidate tumor-linked neutrophil genes from cancer genome and gene banks, the team used penalized and Cox regression to build a prognostic signature, tested in a separate expression dataset.

Four genes made the model: AIM2, PSCA, IL18BP, and LIPE. Immune infiltration and drug sensitivity guesses added background context, and protein atlas plus single-cell resources checked where the genes act. Tissue staining and PCR on patient samples confirmed expression patterns in the lab. Pancreatic cancer badly needs prognostic tools, and immune-cell genes offer an underused angle.
pmc-13342190:
Delayed brain damage after carbon monoxide poisoning gets a risk chart, in a 2026 study by Wanqiu Zhu's team. The project reviewed 200 poisoning patients admitted between 2017 and 2024, of whom 140 developed delayed brain illness and 97 severely.

Severe cases skewed older, with longer blackouts, more hypertension and high homocysteine, higher D-dimer, and lower albumin than the others. Regression distilled separate predictors into a chart checked by accuracy, calibration, and decision curves. Because severe delayed damage disables long after the emergency fades, flagging risk during the first hospital stay could change follow-up depth.
pmc-13342490:
Jun Wu and co-authors present a 2026 chemistry paper on keeping two quarreling catalysts apart so both can work. Dynamic kinetic resolution makes chiral molecules by racemizing one mirror form while an enzyme converts it, but the two catalysts often poison each other. Their fix is a membrane that separates the steps in space while letting the chemistry flow.

Run as a two-stage process, the system no longer demands the strict speed matching that hobbles classic setups. Efficiency climbed sharply over the conventional route. The products are chiral phthalide esters with crowded, fully substituted centers that older methods struggle to reach. Tuning also became simpler, since each stage can be adjusted on its own. The authors offer the membrane trick as a general platform for mixed catalysis.
pmc-13343090:
Armando Del Prete and colleagues tested a novel nail in 2026 for hip fractures in older adults, a major cause of illness and death. Nail fixation is widely used for fractures outside the hip joint capsule, yet best implant choice for stable patterns stays debated. The Chimaera system from Orthofix uses a telescoping lag screw plus an optional anti twist part to boost compression and twist stability.

The look back, multicentre, post market study took in 44 patients, mean age about 74 with about two thirds female, treated with the long Chimaera nail in routine care. Clinical benefit and safety were assessed. The study tests whether the novel nail design lifts outcomes for stable hip fractures in elderly patients.
pmc-13345790:
Maryam Ali and Rebecca Brooks review treatment of returning low-grade serous ovarian cancer in 2026, a rare, slow-growing form that shrugs off chemotherapy. Unlike its high-grade cousin, this cancer often runs on the MAPK growth pathway through KRAS or BRAF changes and answers to hormones, and patients commonly live years with recurring disease.

Repeat surgery and hormone blockers such as letrozole serve many patients, while combined BRAF and MEK blocking suits the V600E mutation group. The authors center the RAMP 201 trial of MEK inhibition as the field's current test of pathway targeting. With median survival near 92 months, gentler, durable control matters more here than short bursts of harsh chemo.
pmc-13346090:
Aravindhan Manivannan and Anthoniraj Amalanathan present GeoGuard-PTI in 2026, a security framework that forecasts cyber attacks by place and time instead of waiting for them. Live intrusion signals, geofencing, and forensics feed a graph attention network plus a diffusion predictor that treats attack spread like an epidemic over a world map.

Forecast maps run from 15 minutes to a full day ahead. Tested on five public datasets with synthetic spread traces added, the system hit 96.4 percent accuracy at 15 minutes and 91.2 percent at two hours, with false alarms under 1.9 percent. Live trials cut successful intrusions by about a third and slashed blocking time, pre-arming defenses in under three milliseconds.
pmc-13346290:
Xiaoqi Liao and co-authors present a 2026 journal article hunting DNA methylation markers of early stomach cardia cancer. This aggressive cancer at the stomach's entrance is usually caught late. The team profiled methylation across 69 tissue samples spanning normal lining, two precancer stages, and cancer, then let two machine learning methods converge on candidates.

Two marks, in the EDNRB and SALL1 genes, separated diseased from normal tissue with high accuracy. Methylation errors grew stage by stage, flipping pattern between precancer and cancer. Staining confirmed the EDNRB protein fading as tissue worsened. The authors offer the pair as candidate early-warning markers.
pmc-13347390:
Elena Bray and colleagues synthesise a brominated tryptamine and profile its biology as a base for new analogues, in a study from 2026. The compound, 4-Br-DMT, was built as a late-stage hub so palladium coupling could attach varied carbon groups at the 4-position, speeding a library of ring-swapped tryptamines for receptor studies.

Direct tests compared the new compound with psilocin and plain DMT on serotonin targets and in mice, and the profile stayed serotonergic in the reported assays. Unlike its comparators, it showed no psychedelic-like effects in mice, yet its safety margin looked weaker than both reference drugs. The route, more than this single compound, is the main offer for analogue hunters.
pmc-13348290:
Lijin Gu and colleagues audited in 2026 the quality of dried blood spots used to screen Beijing newborns for inherited metabolic diseases between 2020 and 2024. A poor spot can delay diagnosis of a treatable disorder, so tracking why samples fail matters for every baby screened.

Reviewing 714,369 samples from all obstetric institutions in the city, the team found 1,735 unqualified spots, about 0.24 percent, and analysed failure rates by year, season, hospital type, and screening volume, with recall rates for repeat collection. Causes ranged from collection technique to handling and transport. The analysis yields targeted quality improvements, from staff training to volume-based support, to keep newborn screening reliable at city scale.
pmc-13349890:
Xiaoxue Ding and colleagues profiled blood chemicals in a 2026 study of two heart artery conditions. Thirty patients with chronic coronary syndrome, thirty with artery calcification, and thirty healthy people gave plasma samples for broad chemical testing.

Simple blood tests already differed between the groups. The calcification group had higher creatinine and fasting glucose. Both patient groups had higher urea nitrogen than controls. Deeper profiling found clear gaps between the two patient groups. Two fatty acids, oleic acid and arachidonic acid, helped set them apart. Markers like these could aid earlier detection of calcified disease, though the team treats the work as a first step.
pmc-13350590:
Jiankun Liao and co-authors pooled evidence in a 2026 meta-analysis on tumour deposits in stage III colorectal cancer. These separate cancer nodules near the bowel may worsen outlook independently of lymph node spread, with implications for staging and treatment.

Eighteen solid studies covering 236,867 patients were gathered from five databases through the end of 2025. Patients with both tumour deposits and positive nodes fared significantly worse on five-year overall and disease-free survival than comparison groups. If deposits carry their own risk, staging rules that treat them as an afterthought may undertreat patients who need stronger follow-up.
pmc-13350690:
A multi-team panel led by the Chinese Society for Tuberculosis issued in 2026 rules for stopping and handling mother-to-child transmission of tuberculosis, a threat to both mother and infant. Proof remains thin. Practical guidance across preconception, pregnancy, postpartum, and neonatal spans has been split.

Experts in tuberculosis, obstetrics, paediatrics, infectious disease, imaging, and disease control built standardised, proof-based advice through a structured method. The rules cover screening, treatment safety in pregnancy, breastfeeding, infant prophylaxis, and infection control. By unifying split advice, they give clinicians a single path to guard mothers and babies from a preventable transmission route.
pmc-13351690:
Syed N Barmaver and colleagues report 2026 lab findings on KIF21A, a motor protein linked to type 2 diabetes, in pancreatic islet cells. Beta cells release insulin at set spots near blood vessels, and the cell skeleton that guides release is still unclear. The team combined large and single-cell RNA data with protein databases and detailed imaging of mouse islets.

KIF21A was lower in human islets from donors with type 2 diabetes at both RNA and protein levels. Within islets, the protein was richest in delta cells, then alpha cells, then beta cells. Levels also varied widely from cell to cell within each type. The pattern hints at specialised roles that merit further study.
pmc-13351890:
Xucheng Zheng and colleagues tested in 2026 how dietary protein level and amylose to amylopectin ratio affect growth and breast muscle development in geese, using a two-by-two factorial design. Starch structure influences digestion and protein use, yet its interaction with protein level in goose diets was poorly understood.

Two hundred forty male Jiangnan White geese, 35 days old, were assigned to four groups for 21 days: normal or low protein combined with normal or high amylose ratio. Compared with normal protein, low protein diets increased average daily gain in some measures, while high amylose ratio promoted breast muscle protein deposition. The factorial design separates protein and starch effects, guiding goose feed formulation for growth and meat quality.
pmc-13352990:
Ruihua Ma leads a 2026 study of radiation work, blood lipids, and high blood pressure risk. Two designs were paired: a cross-sectional study of 2,548 radiation workers and a follow-up cohort of 484 workers, all examined in Shijiazhuang from October 2021 to March 2025. Models tested exposure links, lipid mediation, and prediction of new hypertension.

Longer radiation work years and industrial exposure raised hypertension risk after adjustment, with all P values below 0.05. HDL cholesterol protected, while total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL cholesterol raised risk. Lipid ratios such as fasting glucose over HDL also mattered. The authors argue lipid checks could flag at-risk radiation workers early.
pmc-13353890:
Changi Baek led a 2026 review of label-free ways to watch single cells change state over time. A cell's working state shapes drug response, disease course, and manufacturing quality, but repeated tagging damages cells through bleaching, harm, and probe interference. Measuring intrinsic body signals avoids those problems, shifting the burden to instrument firmness.

The review orders the field into imaging, vibrational light tests, and electric sensing ways, comparing what each reveals about cell structure, composition, and dielectric traits. It also weighs the useful limits of each method. Teams gain guidance for choosing a monitoring plan that can follow the same cells often without disturbing them.
pmc-13354090:
Weifeng Guo, Long Chen, Licheng Chen, and Wanxia Zhang review animal models of diabetes-related shoulder disorders in 2026. Diabetic shoulder disease has tangled mechanisms and no unified research model. Three mainstream models are compared: diabetes with frozen shoulder, diabetes with rotator cuff injury and repair, and natural tendon degeneration in type 2 diabetes.

Each model mimics parts of human disease but misses others, such as a true type 2 metabolic background or whole-joint change over time. An ideal model would copy type 2 metabolism, progressive multi-tissue damage across tendon, capsule, and bone, and pain plus function testing. The authors urge a shift from single-disease copies toward integrated simulation.
pmc-13354590:
Réka Tóth and co-authors tested an old drug, trifluoperazine, in mice with stroke in a 2026 study. The drug is used for mental illness and can change how brain support cells handle water. After blood flow was restored in the mice, the team gave the drug and checked brain harm, blood flow, and early recovery.

Treated mice had smaller areas of brain harm and got better sooner than untreated mice. The drug also eased cell swelling, calmed harmful brain waves, and lowered a key water channel in support cells. Since the drug is already in clinic use, the authors see it as a lead for stroke care trials.
pmc-13354990:
Christen Rachul and co-authors compared two ways medical learners report mistreatment in a 2026 study at one school. One way came through end-of-rotation forms that prompt every learner, and the other was a voluntary web form learners chose to use. The team coded reports filed from 2015 to 2021 for type, place, and people involved.

The prompt forms gave 90 reports and the web form gave 240, with much overlap in mistreatment types. Web reports more often named disrespect, bias, and unfair treatment, and covered a wider range of places. The authors say running both systems gives schools a fuller picture and gives learners more choice in how to speak up.
pmc-13355690:
Zhicheng Luo writes a 2026 letter to the editor about a study testing a child kidney disease risk tool in a Korean cohort. The study was the first check of the calculator, which predicts need for kidney replacement therapy, in an East Asian group of children. Luo praises its promise but questions whether routine clinic use is justified yet.

The letter notes mismatches between the study's abstract and its results tables on sample size and accuracy values, and unclear counts of excluded children. It also notes that accuracy tests flagged poor fit, so local recalibration may be needed first. Luo asks for clarified numbers and updated performance before wider use.
pmc-13357090:
Christoph Schultheiss and co-authors reply in a 2026 letter to commentary on the FOCUS trial, which tested a cancer vaccine plus an immune drug in recurring or spread head and neck cancer. The phase 2 trial randomized 75 patients to pembrolizumab alone or with the UV1 vaccine, which targets a protein most cancer cells need. The combined arm did not meet its main goal.

Six-month progression-free survival was lower with the vaccine, at 31 percent versus 42 percent, though the vaccine was safe and sparked target-specific T cells in most patients. The authors defend the chosen dose range, citing wider trial data, and discuss why blood immune responses may not control tumors.
pmc-13358490:
Nizhen Xu and co-authors present a 2026 study on papillary thyroid cancer, the most common cancer of hormone glands. Most cases grow slowly, but some turn aggressive, and genes plus immune cells shape that path. The team joined gene data from many sources to build a model that sorts patients by risk.

They mixed gene data from six public sets with genetic study data to find genes that truly drive risk, not just track it. They also mapped the immune cells inside tumors. The model aims to flag patients who need stronger care early, and to point at new drug targets for this cancer.
pmc-13358990:
Sarah Rodriguez-Louette examines how racist ideas spread through memes in a 2026 article. On the platform X, memes that borrow the look of science revive old claims that races differ by nature. The author studied 68 viral items and four cases in depth, using a model that splits memes into content, form, and stance.

The analysis shows quick visual contrasts doing the work of argument, helped by feeds that reward fast judgment. Old hierarchies reappear in neutral words about competence. The memes travel across racist, masculinist, and tech-elite circles, reaching mainly young men. The article shows how a joke format can quietly rebuild discredited ideas.
pmc-13361290:
Jinhu Peng and co-authors tested a plant extract against eczema-like skin disease in mice in a 2026 study. Atopic dermatitis is a long-lasting skin inflammation driven by a weak skin barrier and a confused immune response. The team used an extract of Bidens bipinnata fruit in alcohol. Mice with drug-triggered dermatitis got the extract painted on their skin daily at three dose levels.

The extract eased the visible symptoms, skin thickening, and redness scores. It also improved skin moisture and helped restore two barrier proteins that the disease had lowered. A standard steroid drug, used for comparison, did little for the moisture measures. These results suggest the plant extract both calms inflammation and repairs the skin barrier, a pairing worth more study for skin care.
pmc-13361890:
Guang Yang and co-authors engineer membrane-coated nanoparticles that calm two drivers of rheumatoid arthritis at once, in a research paper from 2026. In the inflamed joint lining, immune cells called macrophages both burst in a fiery death and run faulty metabolism. Blocking the death alone leaves the cells angry and harmful.

The particles pair a gene silencer against the bursting machinery with a compound that repairs cell metabolism. A macrophage membrane coat steers them to inflamed tissue, and a vitamin tag boosts uptake. Silencing curbs the fiery death while the compound reprograms the cells toward calm. The design attacks the disease's twin barriers together.
pmc-13362990:
Dennis Patrick Wilhelm and colleagues report a 2026 machining study on a MAX phase composite, a layered ceramic-metal material strengthened with titanium carbide. Its heat expansion can be tuned to match glass, which makes it a candidate for molds in precision glass molding, where hot glass is pressed into shape. The team ground the material at ultra-fine settings, varied the process inputs, and checked forces, surface finish, and the zone just under the surface.

Fine grinding produced sound surfaces overall, and the authors judge the method fit for making such molds. Close inspection did flag hidden damage below the surface, which could limit use in the most exacting optics. The work gives mold makers a base recipe plus a clear warning to check the subsurface.
pmc-13368890:
Duygu Erkal and three colleagues published an imaging study in two thousand twenty-six on how anaemia reshapes bone marrow. When blood haemoglobin falls, marrow works harder and its mix of fat and water shifts. MRI measures can capture that shift without a biopsy.

Ninety-three patients with abdominal scans and blood results were split into four groups by haemoglobin level. Three scan measures were compared: water movement, fat share, and a signal ratio. Fat share rose with haemoglobin, while water movement fell. Measures of red cell size spread tracked the scan values too. The most anaemic group had the lowest fat share and highest water movement. Reader agreement was excellent. The authors back MRI as a window on marrow adaptation.
pmc-13374190:
Serhat Atalar and co-authors sought fair rules to shorten germ drug care in a 2026 study. The ill in view is lung germ growth in patients on a breath machine in intensive care. Guides say seven to eight days of drugs, but long rounds stay common in real wards.

Charts held 147 ill rounds in 111 patients from 2015 to mid 2018. Short rounds ran seven to ten days, and long rounds ran past ten. The team hunted for day five signs that marked who could stop soon and safe. Clear stop rules could cut drug harms and cost, and slow drug-proof germs, with no loss to the sick.
pmc-13374290:
Tao and co-authors study how chemotherapy may help pancreatic cancer spread to the liver. More than a third of patients with this cancer develop liver spread after chemotherapy given before surgery. The team asked how treated tumors shape the liver before cancer cells arrive there.

Their focus is on tiny packages, called extracellular vesicles, shed by tumor cells aged by chemotherapy. These packages appear to reprogram fat-based molecule use in the liver. That change builds a niche that favors incoming cancer cells. The work points to steps that might block liver spread in future care.
pmc-13375390:
Yusuke Hara and co-authors tell of blood sac growths that mimicked a brain tumor in a 2026 case report. A woman aged 55 had a dull head pain, and scans showed three lumps near the top seam of the skull. They were read as one type of slow brain wrap tumor and just watched.

Six years on the lumps had grown a bit, and she chose to have them out. A dye test of brain vessels showed no feed vessels, a clue missed at first glance. Lab views of the cut tissue named them blood sac growths of the wrap, not the thought tumor. The team backs vessel tests in such reads.
pmc-13377790:
Song and colleagues improve confidence tuning for AI answering questions about surgical images, in 2026 medical AI research. In surgical question answering, an overconfident answer can mislead a clinical team. Their framework builds a scene graph, marking objects, tools, and tissues and their relations. It then splits uncertainty into object-level, relation-level, and scene-level parts instead of a global score, fusing them as it goes and tuning with a Dirichlet-based method that supports declining to answer.

On the SSG-QA surgical benchmark, the method reached overall accuracy of 63.58 percent, an expected error of 16.97 percent, and a risk-coverage score of 0.0861. It improved probability scores over baselines, with the largest accuracy gain on relation-type questions, at 0.92 percent above the comparison model. Ablation tests showed the uncertainty split contributed most to accuracy, while the Dirichlet step drove probability quality. Song argues graded, explainable doubt makes surgical AI safer.
pmc-13379390:
Pradeepta Kumar Sarangi and colleagues present a 2026 study on detecting Parkinson's disease from voice recordings using machine learning. Parkinson's affects movement and speech, and there is no single proven test for it. Voice measures offer a low-cost, non-invasive signal that a computer can assess.

Using a public data set of voice recordings, the team compared four methods, including boosted trees, random forest, and support vector machines. They built the work in stages: a baseline model, careful cross-checking, balancing the groups with synthetic examples, and reducing the number of measures. The comparison shows which approach classifies patients most accurately. Better early detection could help patients get care and support sooner.
pmc-13380290:
Yilong Liu and co-authors published a 2026 overview of clinical trials testing electrical stimulation of acupuncture points around the time of surgery. The method is non-invasive and uses no drugs, and it may ease pain and gut problems after operations. A global picture of the trial activity was missing.

The authors analysed 239 trials registered between 2012 and 2025 across three major registries in the United States, China, and Europe. Registrations rose notably, with a clear jump in 2024. Most trials involved adults and digestive surgery, and most measured pain or gut recovery. Children and bone surgery were rarely studied, and trial designs varied widely, leaving clear gaps for future work.
pmc-13380790:
Reuben Yap and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of premature ventricular complexes, extra heartbeats that start in the lower chambers of the heart. Such beats are common in the general population. Many are harmless, but frequent beats can cause symptoms, weaken the heart muscle, or, rarely, trigger dangerous rhythms.

The review explains how these beats present and which tests patients need. Checking for underlying structural heart disease is essential, because it shapes advice and treatment. Options range from watchful waiting and medicines to a catheter procedure that burns away the source of the extra beats. Treatment is guided mainly by symptoms and by any decline in heart function.
pmc-13380890:
Ali Tayhan and co-authors examine how regret about COVID-19 vaccination relates to distrust in the healthcare system and willingness to vaccinate in future. Their 2026 cross-sectional study interviews 402 people face to face, combining regret and distrust questionnaires with open-ended questions about the reasons for regret.

Most participants, 87.1 percent, reported no adverse effects from their COVID-19 vaccine, yet 56.2 percent regretted getting it, and 35.8 percent were undecided about accepting a future vaccine. Experiencing a side effect after vaccination significantly increased distrust in the healthcare system, and regret and distrust scores were weakly but significantly correlated. Open answers clustered into two themes: worry about long-term effects and a belief the vaccine was unnecessary. The authors warn that regret and distrust together will complicate control of future pandemics, and they call for communication strategies that rebuild trust.
pmc-13381090:
Ravisankar Vijayan and Latheef Vadakkepediyakkal present a 2026 lab comparison of three brands of stainless steel orthodontic archwire, the wires used to move teeth during braces treatment. Steel remains the preferred wire for pulling teeth back, but brands of the same size may not perform alike. The brands covered three price tiers, from a United States maker to an Indian maker.

Seven samples of each brand were examined under a microscope with elemental analysis, and pulled in a testing machine until they stretched and broke. Carbon content differed between brands, with the highest-priced brand highest. Strength and stiffness measures were compared across the groups, giving orthodontists hard data behind brand choice.
pmc-13382790:
Mason C. Wilkinson and co-authors build a rat Schwann cell line whose human PMP22 output can be dialed up or down in 2026 work. Extra or missing copies of the PMP22 gene cause the most common forms of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, a nerve disorder. Fine control of the protein level has been hard to achieve in lab cells.

Adding the drug doxycycline set the tagged protein level, with peak output at mid-range drug doses. At high levels, less protein reached the cell surface and more gathered in clumps inside the cell. The line gives researchers a clean tool to study how excess PMP22 may damage the insulation around nerves.
pmc-13385690:
Sheikh Rahaman and colleagues trace brain circuits that time daily torpor in mice. Their neuroscience study from twenty twenty-six studies the master body clock. Torpor drops body temperature and metabolism to survive hard conditions. The clock was suspected to schedule torpor, without a known circuit.

Inhibitory signals from the clock region proved key to timing. Activating one projection to the preoptic area suppressed torpor. That projection contacts two opposing cell types there. One type promotes torpor, the other restrains the first. Cutting clock output erased torpor timing altogether. A specific clock cell group carrying a hormone signal drives the circuit. The work maps a full timing pathway.
pmc-13386690:
Shishuang Zhou's team explored how culture shapes coping in Chinese children on chemo, in a 2026 interview study. Children on chemo face major mental stress, yet cultural and relational influences on coping in Chinese children's cancer care were little studied. The team interviewed 22 children aged 7 to 14 with blood cancers at a tertiary children's hospital, analyzing themes by Braun and Clarke's method.

Stress stemmed not only from physical discomfort and emotional distress, but from family burden worries, disrupted schooling, and lost everyday normality. Children coped mainly through emotion-focused tactics: holding emotions in, creative activities, and reframing illness more positively. The findings call for culturally sensitive mental-health care in children's cancer services.
pmc-13386990:
Febri Gunawan Sugiokto, Yuxin Liu, and Renfeng Li hunted in two thousand twenty-six for host proteins that keep Epstein-Barr virus asleep. The virus infects nearly everyone for life, hiding quietly and waking at times through two early genes. Using a guided DNA-pull-down method with mass measurement, they listed proteins sitting on one wake-up gene's switch.

One protein stood out and proved to hold the virus down. Removing it raised wake-up gene activity, drew in the gene-reading machinery, and pushed more cells into active virus production across several cancer cell models. Virologists gain a named guardian of viral sleep and a possible drug angle.
pmc-13389290:
Chong Li's team shows that gut germs steer a leaf beetle's choice of where to lay eggs, through a feedback loop with the plant itself. Female Plagiodera versicolora beetles feed on young leaves yet prefer mature leaves for eggs. Wiping out gut germs erased that choice, while moving germs brought it back.

The germ Pseudomonas putida drove the effect. Beetle feeding raised a plant hormone that helped the germs move from feeding sites onto new leaves, at some cost to the next generation's fitness. Knocking down the beetle gene TO1 erased the choice. Germ supplements brought back both the gene's activity and the egg-laying choice.
pmc-13391990:
Liyong Zhuo leads a 2026 deep learning study that grades a liver bile duct cancer from scans before surgery and explores outlook prediction. Intrahepatic mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma varies in grade, which affects prognosis, but grade usually requires tissue.

Scans taken before surgery from 333 patients at three centres trained the system. A test at a fresh centre checked it. The system blends two deep learning designs. Key facts from clinic notes, lab tests, and scans were merged with image traits and the scores. The merged model can be read by humans, not just run as a black box. Liver cancer doctors gain a grading aid that needs no tissue cut. It could shape plans for surgery and drug care at an early stage.
pmc-13392190:
Saleh Alwadei presents, in 2026, orthodontic treatment of an open bite in a teenager whose teeth also had abnormally short roots. An eighteen-year-old man had front and side open bite, chewing difficulty, and poor oral hygiene, and imaging showed short roots on the upper front teeth and premolars.

He also had a history of scleroderma, adding tissue considerations. Treatment used segmented mechanics and an extrusion archwire without surgery. After twenty-two months the bite closed fully. Molar and canine relationships were correct and facial appearance improved. There was no significant further root shortening. Orthodontists gain a cautious success case for moving short-rooted teeth, where force control is critical.
pmc-13392390:
Ashmita Saigal and a large team use, in 2026, AI digital pathology to profile mouse models of fatty liver disease and scarring in fine spatial detail. Sharper models are key to grasping this liver disease and to judging would-be drugs.

Past standard tissue work, the pipeline reads each liver zone on its own. It maps where key disease traits sit side by side in the organ's layout. Blood tests and gene profiles round out the profile of these diet-fed male mice. Liver drug developers gain a richer model benchmark, since a drug that lifts mean scores but misses the sick zones could be misjudged by a plain read.
pmc-13392790:
Yeongbin Lee's team cut iridium use in anion exchange membrane water splitting by fixing tiny iridium oxide nano bits straight onto nickel-based foams without binder. Lifting oxygen-release action while minimising precious metal is crucial for green hydrogen splitters.

Iridium oxide on nickel phosphide performed best, with a low extra voltage of 232 mV and stable operation over four hundred hours at modest current density. Strong edge charge transfer enriched electron density around iridium and shifted its d-band centre, tuning middle binding, and the glue-free plate sustained 3.1 amps per square cm at two volts in real-world testing.
pmc-13393290:
Lavender Otom and six colleagues describe a woman in her sixties whose six months of recurrent diarrhoea and intermittent rectal bleeding turned out to be intestinal tuberculosis. It is the commonest form of abdominal tuberculosis. Bleeding from the lower gut is an uncommon face of the disease, and early endoscopy found nothing decisive. Scans later showed disease scattered through small and large bowel, including the ileocaecal junction and the rectoanal area, with swollen abdominal glands.

Repeat colonoscopy biopsies settled the question, showing the cheese-like granulomas and acid-fast bacilli that mark tuberculosis. Testing then revealed previously unknown HIV infection with a very low immune cell count. Anti-tuberculosis drugs followed by HIV therapy brought marked improvement. The authors stress blending clinical, imaging, endoscopic, and tissue findings when bleeding could equally suggest inflammatory bowel disease.
pmc-13393790:
Guiping Zhao and seven colleagues reviewed duct stenting in fifty-one children with chronic pancreatitis at one centre from 2015 to 2024. They asked what predicts the chief complication and how long stents can safely stay. The complication, pancreatitis flaring after the endoscopy, struck in about eighteen percent of one hundred thirty-one successful procedures, always mildly and settling with conservative care.
