pmc-13416390:
Shifa Shamim and colleagues present a giant growth hormone secreting pituitary tumor that grew for years before diagnosis, in a 2026 image case. A woman aged twenty-seven arrived after a seizure, with headache and stopped periods following six years of enlarging hands, feet, and facial features. Hormone tests confirmed acromegaly, with growth hormone and its partner marker far above normal ranges.

Brain imaging showed a multilobulated adenoma measuring about ninety-five by seventy-three by seventy-nine millimeters. Thyroid and adrenal shortfalls were replaced with daily hormones before surgery through the skull. A temporary hormone deficiency followed the operation. Giant tumors form six to ten percent of pituitary tumors.
pmc-13416590:
Enrico Paci and a team of Italian researchers pilot urine testing for fungal toxin exposure among pig farm workers, in 2026. Mycotoxins from moldy feed can ride farm dust into workers' bodies, yet Italian human data are scarce. Urine from thirty-five swine workers and thirty unexposed controls was screened for four toxin markers plus five oxidative stress markers.

Aflatoxin M1 appeared most often among workers, detectable in about twenty-three percent and quantifiable in about eleven percent. Controls showed lower detection and no quantifiable results. Mixed low dose exposure is the picture that emerges. Pairing urine results with earlier farm air and feed monitoring strengthens exposure assessment.
pmc-13417890:
Lu Shen and colleagues measure hepatitis B vaccine response in low birth weight infants after the full three dose course, in a 2026 study. Small babies were feared to respond weakly. The study enrolled 511 infants vaccinated at birth, one month, and six months, with blood drawn weeks after the last dose. Catch up growth and mother and baby traits were examined.

Protection was near universal, with about 99 percent of infants above the antibody threshold and high average levels. Catch up growth did not predict antibody strength, nor did maternal infection status. Maternal thyroid disease linked to higher infant antibodies, a surprise finding the authors say needs prospective checking.
pmc-13417990:
Thuy Thi Thanh Nguyen and colleagues blend bacterial cellulose with a common polymer and silver zinc oxide particles to make an active food film, in a 2026 study. The film aims to fight bacteria, slow oxidation, and keep fruit fresh longer. Several particle loadings were compared for strength, vapour blocking, and protective effects.

A loading of 0.20 percent by weight performed best, with the strongest antibacterial and antioxidant action plus good strength and low permeability. Wrapped Vietnamese tangerines kept well for up to 15 days at room temperature with less weight loss. The biodegradable blend is proposed as a greener wrap for fresh produce.
pmc-13418790:
Yixin Chang and colleagues mapped in 2026 how a long noncoding RNA, Lnc00892, makes bladder cancer cells more sensitive to cisplatin chemotherapy. Drug sensitivity varies widely, and RNA markers could help pick patients likeliest to benefit, so the team traced the RNA's binding partners in treated cancer cells.

Lnc00892 binds BTAF1, loosening a transcription complex from the MDM2 gene, which lowers a chain through STAT5B to XIAP and pushes cells toward death. The paper nominates Lnc00892 as a clinic marker for cisplatin sensitivity and a lever for improving bladder cancer chemotherapy.
pmc-13420190:
Hammad surveys nurses who work in critical care units in Palestine. The study asks how their values, work setting, and job contentment link. It drew 263 nurses from fifteen hospitals in the West Bank. Nurses scored their values high. They scored their work setting and contentment at a mid level. The work setting was the strongest link to contentment.

High workload linked to lower contentment. So did plans to leave the job. Values linked to contentment through the work setting, not on their own. Hammad urges fair staffing, shared choices, and praise for good work. Those steps, the study says, help keep skilled nurses in post.
pmc-13420290:
Tuan Huynh and colleagues characterize carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii from a tertiary hospital in southern Vietnam, a germ the World Health Organization ranks as its top priority for new antibiotics. Carbapenems are last-line drugs, so resistance to them closes most treatment doors. The team re-examined 156 stored isolates with gene tests for the enzymes that break these drugs.

Resistance showed in 70.51 percent of isolates in the reported share, a heavy burden for one hospital. Two resistance genes traveled together most often, appearing in 23.64 percent of the resistant set by the count given. That pairing defeats more drugs than either gene alone. Gene maps like this one guide both bedside choices and hospital infection control in the region.
pmc-13421590:
Khalil M Abdelnaby and four colleagues propose, in a 2026 paper, an artificial intelligence framework that trims the energy use of wireless networks without surrendering performance. Traffic growth keeps raising network power bills, and in interference-heavy access schemes the choices about power and timing are tightly entangled.

Their framework first learns the interference geography with a graph neural network and the rhythm of traffic with a recurrent network. Those representations feed a multi-agent reinforcement learning controller that sets power and scheduling decisions as conditions change. In realistic simulated 5G conditions with heavy interference, the system saved up to fifteen percent of energy. The authors present adaptive, learning-based control as a route to greener networks.
pmc-13421790:
Hamilton and colleagues reflect on what happens when the public helps build a policy model, warts and all. The model in question estimates how income support policies would change population health. Their 2026 account draws in thirty two people who have lived with income insecurity and over sixty professional stakeholders. They work through three systems mapping workshops and five policy priority workshops. A poverty charity partner guides the work with trauma informed practice.

The dividends were real: a systems map, co drawn with contributors, steered the modeling strategy and shifted team choices. The disconnects were real too. Research teams split into silos struggled to turn stories into model inputs, workshop formats did not suit everyone, and paying and protecting contributors needed more thought. The authors' advice is plain: budget for involvement, build rooms where people can speak safely, and keep translators between the story side and the math side.
pmc-13423190:
Jia and colleagues present in 2026 DuSSM, a computer system that extracts drug-drug interactions from biomedical text, a backbone task for drug safety monitoring worldwide. The challenge is that local word cues can distort the long-range logic of a sentence.

The design splits the work into two parallel streams. A convolutional stream scans for local trigger patterns, while a state-space stream tracks the sentence's evolving meaning in a single efficient pass. Tested on four biomedical benchmarks, the system reached an F1 score in the low eighty percent range on the main drug interaction benchmark. An F1 score combines precision and recall, and the system scored notably well on precision for sentence pairs. Precision on cases with no interaction was especially high, which matters because false alerts tire the pharmacists who must review them.
pmc-13423490:
Kai Wang and seven colleagues hunt for the proteins that the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel touches in resistant breast cancer, using tailor-made chemical probes of the drug itself. Resistance blunts taxane treatment and drives recurrence, so knowing the drug's hidden partners could expose new targets.

Of four probes built, PTX-4, joined by a stable carbon bond, fished out binding proteins most efficiently from parent and resistant cells. The catch included AKT2, a growth-signalling protein never before tied to paclitaxel. Follow-up tests confirmed direct binding, and silencing or blocking AKT2 made resistant cells sensitive to the drug again. The team proposes AKT2 as both a driver of resistance and a target for restoring taxane power.
pmc-13424090:
Peter Pothmann and three colleagues refine a habitat model for Aedes vexans, a floodplain mosquito, showing that biased sampling data can hide what really drives the species. Records of the mosquito cluster in towns, so a first model barely credited flood hazard, even though the insect breeds in temporary flood water.

The team thinned clustered records and filtered out over-sampled environments, then compared models with and without the clean-up across several test sets. Bias correction improved accuracy more than adding the flood variable alone. The final model mapped suitability far more reliably, especially in flood-prone ground that earlier data had neglected. Their lesson reaches beyond mosquitoes: cleaning occurrence data can matter more than adding predictors.
pmc-13424190:
Shubham Vishnoi and three colleagues design, on the computer, a peptide drug meant to hit three hormone receptors at once for diabetes and obesity. Drugs like tirzepatide already pair two of these signals; adding the third receptor, GIPR, alongside GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, could tighten glucose control and weight loss in a single molecule.

The team mutated peptide sequences in software, then ran long molecular simulations to score how each design gripped the three receptors. Their candidates showed balanced, favourable binding across the trio, better than natural hormones and reference drugs in the models, with clean targeting. Weak spots where enzymes snip peptides were swapped out for stability. Lab testing is the stated next step.
pmc-13424590: Linmei Dong and five co-authors publish a correction only, fixing the record of their study on enzyme-assisted extraction of polyphyllins from Paris polyphylla rhizomes. Two sets of initials, “Y. J.” and “L. C.”, had been added to the author group by mistake as seventh and eighth authors; the notice restores the correct six-author list, running from Dong to Rui Sun. A keyword is also corrected, with its first letter now capitalised as “Pectinase-assisted extraction”. The publisher notes the original article has been updated to match.
pmc-13424790:
Fang and co-authors measure three decades of ear infection burden in American males, in this 2026 epidemiological study. They use Global Burden of Disease 2021 estimates for otitis media. That family covers middle-ear inflammation: acute infections, fluid buildup, and chronic discharging ears.

Case counts rose from roughly 4.10 million in 1990 to 4.57 million in 2021, and the age-standardized incidence rate climbed from 3,899 to 4,147 per 100,000 males across the period. Deaths fell overall, from about 32 to 21 a year in the modeled estimates, though trend analysis found mortality rising again during 2010 to 2019. Disability burden concentrated in boys aged five to nine, while deaths clustered in older adults. Tobacco use and secondhand smoke stood out as the leading attributable risks, making smoke exposure the authors' prime prevention target.
pmc-13425890:
Jiahui Fu and coworkers developed silk microneedles for sampling skin fluid in a 2026 bioengineering study modeled on plant xylem channels. Chronic inflammatory skin diseases need repeatable access to local molecules, yet biopsy is invasive and surface samples poorly reflect the skin environment. Their anisotropic porous needles use directional freezing, solvent-exchange crosslinking, and a salting-out step to form aligned channels with strong penetration.

One patch collected over 10 microliters of interstitial fluid within five minutes and recovered large molecules of at least 150 kilodaltons efficiently. Such sampling could support biomarker and protein profiling of skin disease with minimal harm. A patch that pulls this much fluid this fast could let staff track flares at home with far less pain and far less fuss for sick skin.
pmc-13426490:
Huijuan Lei and colleagues explored anxiety in early pregnancy after perinatal loss in a 2026 qualitative phenomenological study in Guangdong. Sixteen women pregnant again after losing a baby joined the study at a women and children's hospital in Guangdong. Interviews ran from December 2025 into April 2026 and followed a semi-structured guide. Transcripts were analyzed with Colaizzi's seven-step method using NVivo software.

Four themes emerged from the interviews. The earlier loss stays present in the new pregnancy, and vigilance under uncertainty intrudes on daily life. Women also hold a fragile balance through reassurance seeking and boundary control, while support expectations go unmet. Findings should inform individualized psychological support and continuity of care for this group.
pmc-13427090:
Sukhbir S. Singh and coauthors present a French-language 2026 case of deep endometriosis causing kidney shrinkage, bowel blockage, and sciatic nerve compression. Endometriosis affects about ten percent of women of reproductive age, as endometrial-like tissue grows outside the uterus and often causes disabling pelvic pain and infertility. Its deep form, the most severe, infiltrates underlying tissues, organs, muscle, and nerves and can irreversibly damage target organs.

Damage reaching kidney, intestine, and the sciatic nerve in one patient shows how far infiltrating disease can travel beyond the pelvis. Clinicians reading in French gain a stark reminder to image urinary, bowel, and nerve symptoms in known endometriosis.
pmc-13427790:
Hu and colleagues published a 2026 study on bile signals shaping immune cells in gut disease. Inflammatory bowel disease inflames the gut lining and resists full control. Helper T cells of a newer kind gather in the inflamed gut tissue. The team asked how a bile acid sensor on scout immune cells affects them.

Helper cell shares ran high in inflamed gut tissue samples from patients. Turning the bile sensor on in mice raised helper cell counts further. Scout cells lacking the sensor failed to mature and guide helper cells well. A partner signal path switched on instead, cutting a key helper signal. The work links bile chemistry to gut immune balance in new ways.
pmc-13430190:
Farahnazsadat Ahmadi, Fatemeh Nakhaei, and Mahboubeh Tajaldini study, in a 2026 Iranian cohort, whether injecting a woman's own platelet-rich plasma into the womb lifts IVF success after repeated failures. Recurrent implantation failure, where good embryos repeatedly fail to attach, has few proven fixes. The study covered 100 women aged 21 to 42 at a Gorgan infertility center in 2023. Fifty-one received the plasma injection two days before a frozen embryo transfer, while 49 had the standard transfer alone.

Clinical pregnancy occurred in about 27 percent of the treated group versus about 8 percent of controls. Implantation rates mirrored that gap. Miscarriage rates and pregnancy complications did not differ between groups, and no side effects from the injection were reported. Womb lining thickness did not explain the gain. The authors call the approach cheap and practical, while the design, a backward-looking cohort, caps the certainty.
pmc-13430890:
Grace Tannous and colleagues report a rare chest-wall synovial sarcoma in a fifteen-year-old boy. Synovial sarcoma forms 5 to 10 percent of soft-tissue sarcomas, mostly near large joints in teens and young adults, while chest-wall disease is extremely rare.

The boy came in with numbness and pain in the right arm plus worsening breathlessness. Examination found a firm, painless lump above the right collarbone with mild arm swelling, and a chest X-ray showed a right upper-lung shadow pushing chest contents left. Diagnosis needs tissue staining and gene tests, since look-alikes abound, and treatment centres on full removal plus added therapy by a team.
pmc-13431590:
Katharina Kopp reviewed in 2026 how response teams should pick genome reading plans for grave RNA virus outbreaks. The fresh Bundibugyo virus outbreak in Congo and Uganda serves as the test case. Full genome reads anchor outbreak work, yet their worth hinges on sample quality, lab safety, and the tools at hand as much as on the machine used.

The virus was known from two past outbreaks, yet old genome samples stayed sparse, and past tests leaned toward its Ebola kin. Kopp sorts reading routes by how much prior knowledge of the virus each one needs, from direct reads to copy-based and trap-based routes. For like outbreaks, the review backs a staged plan. Teams start broad and cast a wide net across fever causes. They win a first genome with tolerant tools, then scale a proven route across places and weeks.
pmc-13431790:
Wang and colleagues review intron retention, a quirk of gene reading in which the segments normally cut out of a gene's RNA copy stay in. Those leftover segments were once dismissed as junk, and retained copies were thought only to mute a gene's output. Their 2026 review gathers new work on retention in health and in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the fatal disease that paralyzes by killing motor neurons.

Retained copies behave differently by location: some stay in the nucleus and some reach the cell body, with distinct jobs in each place. They can steer where RNA protein complexes gather, drain the pool of working RNA binding proteins, and shift the droplet like clumping of cell material, all themes in ALS biology. Retention itself can act as a regulatory element beyond making protein. The authors flag retained introns as drug targets and expect machine learning to speed discovery.
pmc-13431990:
Luiz and colleagues traced in 2026 how food insecurity moved over a decade in Brazilian households, sorted by the sex and race of the household head. Food insecurity means lacking steady access to enough good food, and in Brazil it falls hardest on Black families. The team compared three large national surveys, covering hundreds of thousands of homes.

Between 2013 and 2018, food security fell for every group. By 2023 it had recovered, most sharply in homes headed by Black women. Yet the worst forms of insecurity stayed concentrated in homes headed by Black and brown Brazilians, with Black women heads facing the highest rates. Models showed relative risk shrinking for severe insecurity in that group while staying well above white-headed homes. The authors call for policies aimed at the roots of racial inequality.
pmc-13432290:
Emergency departments are hard places to care for people in mental health crisis, and nurses carry much of that load. Caitlin Kent, Catherine Stephen, and Elizabeth Halcomb interviewed ten nurses at one large hospital in Australia's Northern Territory about their experience of this work, and studied the interview records for shared themes.

Four themes stood out. Crowding, staff shortages, long waits, and unsuitable rooms limited calm, healing care and added to patient distress. The emotional weight of the work, plus stigma and a reactive staff culture, fed moral distress and burnout. Clear communication and teamwork helped, while thin training in mental health left nurses learning on the job. The nurses asked for clear protocols, focused training, and steady support, steps the authors say would help both patients and the workforce.
pmc-13434190:
Zariry and co-authors build in 2026 a framework to judge head motion tracking and correction inside MRI scanners, using live human scans. Motion spoils brain images, but mitigation tools lack rigorous tests. Their setup pairs guided head moves with a reference measure from the images themselves.

Six people had brain scans at a strong field strength while making small guided turns of the head. A camera based markerless system and a fat signal method were compared against the reference. Each method won on some moves and lost on others in accuracy and precision. Image quality scores for corrected scans are also reported.
pmc-13434690:
Mohammad Rezvani Ghalhari's team tracked parabens in 2026 across three wastewater plants, river water, and river mud in their study region. Parabens are preservative chemicals that can disturb hormones, and they reach people through water. Samples were concentrated and read by liquid chromatography, with recovery in an acceptable band, and the highest levels turned up in inflows to the hospital plant.

No plant removed parabens fully, but a three-stage anaerobic, anoxic, and aerobic process did best, cutting each of the four parabens by roughly seven to eight tenths. The authors urge that process as a first step and call for methods that can clear these pollutants outright. Water managers get a ranked, practical view of what current treatment can and cannot do.
pmc-13435490:
Aviya L Levy's team piloted narrative medicine in 2026 for children with juvenile muscle and joint diseases, groups with high anxiety and depression rates. Narrative medicine gathers patients to reflect on illness stories, and adult work links it to better reported outcomes, but pediatric rheumatology data were thin. Twenty-one patients aged six to twenty-one joined four groups by diagnosis and age for six sessions over three months.

Attendance was strong, with all reaching at least half the sessions and most reaching four or more, yet pre-post mood and illness-attitude scores did not shift significantly. A subgroup with higher baseline distress showed hints worth a closer look. Care teams get a feasibility win and a caution: story work engages young patients, but mood gains need larger, longer trials.
pmc-13435590:
Shiqing Wang's team reviewed cancer-associated fibroblasts in 2026, the dominant stromal cells that shape whether checkpoint immunotherapy works. Checkpoint drugs restore killer T cell activity, yet resistance is common, and tumor cells alone do not explain it. Fibroblasts build matrix barriers, release signals that recruit and steer immune cells, and are in turn reprogrammed by immune signals, forming feedback loops.

Those loops turn the tumor neighborhood into a self-adjusting system that governs growth and drug response. The review argues for reprogramming fibroblast-immune circuits rather than wiping fibroblasts out, to restore lasting immunity. Cancer teams get a synthesis that reframes resistance as an ecosystem problem, with new combination strategies as the payoff to test.
pmc-13435890:
Li Jiang and a large team link a simple insulin resistance score to hidden heart weakness in diabetes in 2026. Heart scans for 235 patients with type 2 diabetes measured shape, squeeze, energy yield, and blood flow. Patients split into thirds by the triglyceride glucose index.

The high score third showed more heart remodeling and weaker squeeze in all directions. Energy yield and resting flow also sagged in that group. The score held its link after matching for other risks. Energy yield and flow carried part of the score effect in path models. A cheap blood score may flag hearts that need scan follow up.
pmc-13435990:
Tharindu Wickramaarachchi and coauthors model the payoff of curbing teen pregnancy and child marriage in five Southeast Asian countries in 2026. Girls aged fifteen to nineteen were modeled by marriage, poverty, and school status. Survey and census figures drive the national level runs.

Base spending of 1.4 billion dollars over 2024 to 2030 still leaves 2.4 million unintended pregnancies and 2.1 million child marriages projected. Raising proven programs to ninety five percent cover costs five billion more. That scale up averts 1.3 million pregnancies and 1.1 million marriages. Sex education, cash aid, and life skills lead the program list.
pmc-13437390:
Yunshu Zhang and colleagues used scalp recordings to find shifting brain patterns in depressed teenagers, comparing those who lived through childhood trauma with those who did not. Their 2026 pilot study recorded resting brain waves in eighty-four adolescents: twenty-five depressed with trauma histories, twenty-seven without, and thirty-two healthy peers. Trauma and severity were scored with standard questionnaires, and the team tracked how brain networks link and unlink.

The trauma group fell ill earlier and scored more severely depressed than the other depressed group. Sorting the changing connections produced three recurring brain states. Features of those states tracked with trauma scores, which the authors read as a possible fingerprint of trauma-linked depression. They propose resting recordings, cheap and painless, might one day spot which depressed teenager carries a trauma history. That could guide trauma-focused care, though the small pilot needs larger tests.
pmc-13437490:
Jiahui Ding and Yanjuan Teng built learning models that estimate body makeup in people on long-term dialysis from a simple electrical test. Bioimpedance sends a weak current through the body and reads how tissues resist it. Muscle loss in dialysis patients predicts poor function, so tracking fat-free mass and body fat share matters. Their 2026 study trained several model types on routine test outputs and used an explanation tool to rank which inputs drove each estimate.

Grouped ensemble models beat single models across all four targets, with one method reaching near-perfect fit scores. Total body water and height dominated every prediction, followed by water inside and outside cells, minerals, and weight. Real value would come from a readable body profile flagging patients sliding toward muscle loss. They insist the models earn clinical use only after checks against measured function in larger, multi-center groups.
pmc-13437590:
Magdalena Zaniewska, writing alone in 2026, traces the two-way traffic between serotonin and alcohol use disorder. When its signaling runs low, vulnerability to heavy drinking rises, most sharply in the early-onset form marked by violence and antisocial behavior. Animal evidence runs parallel: mice bred without brain serotonin drink more, and alcohol-preferring rats show thin serotonin wiring.

Genes that build and carry serotonin, shaped by stress, help set each person's risk. That variety also explains why standard serotonin-raising antidepressants disappoint in most drinkers, helping mainly in milder, later-onset cases. Fresh interest centers on psychedelic therapies acting through a specific serotonin receptor in the prefrontal cortex. Zaniewska argues the disorder must be split into subtypes before serotonin drugs can be aimed well. Her review sets out the known links and calls for markers sorting patients by serotonin profile, so treatment can match biology rather than diagnosis alone.
pmc-13437690:
Shumin Lin and colleagues lay out a registered plan for a blinded acupuncture trial against constipation tied to Parkinson's disease. Constipation is among the most draining non-movement complaints in Parkinson's, and standard fixes often help little. Their 2026 protocol will enroll sixty-six patients, assigned by chance to real acupuncture or a sham version. Patients, assessors, and analysts will not know who got which.

Treatment runs four weeks, with four more weeks of follow-up. Weekly counts of bowel movements and stool form fill out the picture. Fluid samples will probe possible biology: short-chain fatty acids from gut microbes, an enzyme tied to gene control, and a marked form of the Parkinson's protein. The team grants sham needling can stir its own effects, so the gap between arms is the real test. Results should show whether needle treatment earns a place in gut care for Parkinson's.
pmc-13437790:
Domenico Vicari and a large team asked whether a simple maturity estimate explains power differences among young off-road cyclists. Teen athletes grow unevenly, so a stronger rider may simply be an earlier developer. Their 2026 study tested twenty-two young cyclists. Each rider's maturity offset, years from their fastest growth spurt, was estimated from body measures, then set against two lab tests: repeated six-second sprints and a rising ramp to exhaustion.

Maturity offset predicted top power in both tests with clear statistical support. The maturity measure failed to predict power relative to weight, the figure deciding climbing speed. The authors read this as maturity feeding raw output more than efficiency: bigger bodies push more watts without gaining an edge once weight is counted. They suggest coaches use the offset to read results fairly and track growth paths, rather than ranking teens on raw power and mistaking timing for talent.
pmc-13438190:
Fernández‐Lebrero and a large team test a blood marker in patients with a brain vessel disease in this 2026 study. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy deposits amyloid in brain blood vessels and often overlaps with Alzheimer's disease. The blood marker p-tau217 is a strong indicator of Alzheimer's, but whether it still works when vessel disease is present was unclear. The team studied 231 people, including 50 with the vessel disease and 154 with Alzheimer's.

Among the vessel-disease patients, 29 also met spinal fluid criteria for Alzheimer's. The blood marker separated those with and without the overlap very well. It scored a discrimination value of about 0.92 in this cohort's analysis, a strong result. The marker showed no relationship to scan measures of vessel disease severity, supporting that it reflects Alzheimer's pathology specifically. Two pre-set cut-off values both identified the overlap accurately.
pmc-13438390:
Kyle Siler replies to two critics of his study claiming a sharp post-2022 shift in words academics use, widely read as the fingerprint of large language models. In the 2026 reply, Siler grants each point, arguing they trim the edges of his claim without touching its center.

On scale, he clarifies that his statistic measures how far the word distribution moved, not a head count of AI-written papers. Read as a share, fifty-seven percent is a floor, and only under stated assumptions. On measurement, he concedes the word set was picked for its surge, so the chart alone proves nothing. Yet the words jumped when ChatGPT launched and partly fell back in 2025, timing editorial drift cannot explain. On his field and publisher breakdowns, he accepts the critics' math: those figures cannot be separately identified. The descriptive core, a rapid, patterned vocabulary change, survives intact.
pmc-13438690:
Yue Jiang led a very large team asking whether the hormone shot triggering egg release in fertility treatment leaves marks on children conceived that way. Assisted reproduction shapes chemical tags on offspring DNA, yet the trigger drug was unexamined. Their 2026 study followed a birth cohort of 365 families and 1,333 more children, then tested the chain in mice.

Higher trigger-day doses of human chorionic gonadotropin tracked with lower overall DNA methylation in the blood of assisted-reproduction children. In the larger group, higher doses also tracked with more suboptimal early development. Mice told the causal half: brief exposure dulled offspring learning behavior, cut new neuron growth in a memory region, and lowered a key methylation-guiding enzyme. Injecting that enzyme's message into exposed embryos restored neuron growth and behavior. The authors urge clinics to tune trigger doses for a child's long-term health, not only the cycle's success.
pmc-13439190:
Jingwen Yu and a large team hunt for rice genes that leave plants open to root-knot worms, publishing their findings in 2026. The worm Meloidogyne graminicola bores into rice roots and cuts yields across Asia, yet few resistant rice types are known. Genome-wide scans, multi-layer molecular data, and gene tests pointed to a factor named Rsf1, which codes a small cysteine-rich protein. A single letter change in the gene's switch region separated types by risk.

Plants with the risky letter made much more Rsf1 once worms attacked, while the safer letter kept levels low and plants held up better. A regulator called Myb44 was shown to drive Rsf1 output. Knocking the gene out in rice and in a model weed both raised resistance, pointing to a shared weakness that breeders could target.
pmc-13439690:
Ajay and colleagues built VIDEO in 2026, a web tool that layers several kinds of gene data. It shows how enhancers, the DNA switches near genes, may work in specific tissues of the fruit fly. Gene regulation studies juggle gene activity, open chromatin, and factor binding data. Few tools let researchers view them together against the binding motifs, the short DNA words a factor recognizes, in a tissue-specific gene set.

Starting from a custom gene list, VIDEO finds which switching factors are present in the tissue, locates their motifs in nearby enhancers. Overlays open chromatin maps and binding data for those factors. The team showcased it on a well-known system, the factor CrebA and the secretory pathway in the larval salivary gland, then used it to form hypotheses in the less-studied embryonic hindgut. The authors offer VIDEO as a hypothesis engine for developmental gene regulation.
pmc-13439890:
Arianna Calistri's team paired cancer-killing virus with light therapy in 2026 against glioblastoma, the most harsh adult brain tumor with near-certain return. A neuro-weakened herpes virus related to a cleared cancer-killing drug was built to carry a membrane-targeted photosensitizer, KillerRed. It was then tested in human and mouse tumor lines, patient-derived cells, and spheroids, including immune-cell transfer.

The virus infected and killed tumor cells across models, light activation boosted killing in patient spheroids especially at low virus doses, and a chemical light drug similarly enhanced virus killing. Immune-cell transfer moved virus to spheroids while keeping light responsiveness. Brain tumor teams get a dual-modality lead that may lower virus doses needed. Human safety trials remain distant.
pmc-13439990:
Li Wang and co-authors survey college students in China on drug clinical trials in a 2026 study. Trials test new drugs before they reach the market, and informed participants are vital to their success. Raising awareness among students could strengthen the national research landscape.

More than eight hundred students from three regions answered a questionnaire in early twenty twenty two. Just over half had sufficient awareness of trials. Awareness differed by age, gender, schooling, background, and financial and healthcare pressure. Surprisingly, awareness correlated negatively with willingness to take part. Regression analysis explored which factors predicted each outcome.
pmc-13441290:
Jaime Piquero-Casals and colleagues revisit a modern skin steroid, methylprednisolone aceponate, weighing its power against its gentleness in a 2026 review. Skin steroids remain the backbone of care for inflamed skin, yet strength often trades against thinning and whole-body effects. The reviewed drug is a fourth-generation, non-halogenated steroid built for local punch with limited body exposure. A literature search spanning 1990 to 2025 gathered pharmacology and clinical studies across eczema types.

Twin ester groups and a methyl tweak in its structure drive strong local action with low thinning potential. The drug activates inside skin, then breaks down quickly once absorbed, keeping body-wide exposure small. Trials showed fast itch relief and high clearance in atopic, contact, and seborrheic eczema, usually with once-daily use. Long-term thinning and hormone-axis suppression stayed rare in the record. The authors position it for both flare control and maintenance care.
pmc-13441890:
Ifen Ayu Malinda, Imam Budi Putra, and Ariyati Yosi test whether the hormone progesterone tracks with syringoma, a benign sweat-gland growth, in a 2026 Indonesian study. Syringomas appear as small skin-coloured bumps, often around the eyes, and can trouble patients' confidence. Hormone influence has long been suspected in their origin. The cross-sectional study enrolled thirty-five patients with syringoma and thirty-five without, each examined by eye and dermoscope and tested for blood progesterone.

Most patients were women in their late twenties to mid-thirties, and the localised form was commonest, with familial cases making up a quarter. High progesterone appeared in ten patients with syringoma against only two controls, a statistically significant association with odds several times higher. Receptor staining evidence points the same way in the authors' reading. They conclude that hormonal involvement in syringoma growth deserves weight in future work on causes and care.
pmc-13441990:
Naomi Wilson's team followed women in 2026 from childhood ADHD and deprivation into early adult multimorbidity, where two or more long-term conditions cluster. Female ADHD has been underrecognized and undertreated, and its adult health burden plus social patterning were understudied. A longitudinal cohort of women aged eighteen to thirty-two was analyzed for ADHD, childhood deprivation, multimorbidity risk, interaction effects, and disease clusters.

Childhood ADHD raised adult multimorbidity risk, deprivation added risk alone and synergistically, with about thirty-nine percent of burden attributable to their interaction, and the worst cluster carried psychiatric complexity. Health systems get a high-risk group for earlier, integrated care: girls with ADHD from disadvantaged backgrounds. Prevention should start in childhood, not adulthood.
pmc-13442690:
Leonardo Rigon and colleagues report a rare clue to where excess beta rhythm in Parkinson disease begins in a 2026 case paper. The rhythm, a fast brain wave, runs too strong in the loop that links the cortex to deep brain hubs. A patient with a deep brain stimulator grew brief swelling on one side of the brain, which let the team watch the rhythm through the device.

The excess rhythm on the swollen side fell silent while the swelling lasted. It came back once the cortex swelling cleared, even though deep hub swelling had healed sooner. The team reads the timing as proof that a sound cortex is required for the deep rhythm to run wild. That points drug and device work at the cortex link in the loop. One case cannot settle the debate, yet the timing here is hard to explain away.
pmc-13442790:
Kristina S. Boye's team developed a pediatric diabetes impact measure in 2026, the P-TIM, for children with type 2 diabetes facing new non-insulin treatments. Existing patient-reported measures missed items sensitive to newer therapies, yet children's lived impact was incompletely captured. Concept interviews with thirteen children and caregivers mapped impacts on eating, emotions, school, family, activities, and social life, plus treatment views on ease, glucose control, and weight.

A draft child-reported questionnaire was built from those concepts and refined through interviews with ten more children, yielding a measure tuned to pediatric type 2 diabetes. Trial teams get a content-valid starting measure for new drug studies. Psychometric validation in larger samples must confirm reliability and responsiveness.
pmc-13442890:
Zhenan Ruan and colleagues review how gut microbes shape asthma through the gut-lung axis in a 2026 paper. Asthma fills lungs with chronic swelling, and standard drugs fail some hard forms. Work from 2011 to 2025 spans group studies, animal tests, clinic records, and small trials.

Gut microbes tune airway swelling by coaching immune cell growth, by sending chemical signals, and by guarding the gut wall. Microbe marks differ between allergic and plain asthma, and between child and adult forms. Cures that target microbes span live cultures, feed goods, mixed packs, waste goods, and stool swaps. Early gains look bright, yet cause proof stays weak and trial plans vary wildly. The authors ask for tighter trials before gut care joins asthma care.
pmc-13443290:
Yun Wen and Pengfei Luo size up a cell enzyme, UBE2A, as a cancer mark across tumor types in a 2026 study. The enzyme tags proteins for fate calls inside cells, and its cancer role stayed blurry. Public sets from tumor banks and gene banks fed checks on levels, outlook, gene traits, and immune ties.

UBE2A ran high in many cancer types, and high marks tracked with worse survival odds. Its levels also tracked with immune cell mix and brake gene marks in tumors. Single-cell reads placed the enzyme thick in fast-growing T cells. Bench tests in breast cancer cells showed that silencing UBE2A curbed growth, spread, and invasion. The authors pitch UBE2A as a broad outlook mark with immune links worth drug study.
pmc-13444090:
Ling-Dong Shi and colleagues find jumbo DNA rings riding with methane-eating archaea in a 2026 study. Side DNA in archaea is the least grasped class of genetic goods, and rings past 200 kbp are rare. Their rings reach 535 kbp in Methanoperedens, microbes that burn methane without air.

One 409 kbp ring sits woven into some host chromosomes, the largest woven element known in archaea. Ring growth came from heavy DNA gains drawn from the hosts. Rings carry methane, nitrogen, and sulfur work genes, plus shield systems their hosts lack. Copy counts hold steady near 1.44 rings per host in their checks. The authors place the rings on a slide from plasmid-like to mini-chromosome-like.
pmc-13444490:
Hadi Koohi and colleagues report two cases where treating one giant liver hemangioma shrank its untreated kin in a 2026 paper. Hemangiomas are the most common benign liver growths, and giants past 5 cm can ache. Both patients had sore giant lumps treated by direct needle sclerotherapy with a bleomycin-lipiodol mix.

The treated giants shrank as hoped after the sessions. Far lumps in other liver zones, never touched by the needle, shrank in step, a surprise the team calls synchronous regression. That echo hints at body-wide or inflammatory paths set off by the local fix. The authors share the pair as a hypothesis, not a rule. Planned trials must test whether one hit can calm distant lumps for real.
pmc-13445190:
David Czell and Melina Anina Brandenberger test whether a single dose of caffeine raises the rate of small muscle twitches in healthy adults, in a 2026 ultrasound study. Such twitches, called fasciculations, are often harmless, yet they can also hint at nerve disease. Knowing what caffeine does to them could sharpen how doctors read muscle scans.

Fifty-four adults aged twenty to fifty had six muscles scanned before and again forty-five minutes after a caffeine dose set by body weight. Twitch rates rose in most muscles, with the largest gains in the calf and foot and the smallest in the thigh. Younger adults gained more in arm muscles, older adults more in leg muscles, so the authors advise asking about recent caffeine before muscle tests.
pmc-13445290:
Kai Wang and colleagues review a two-stage spine operation for adults whose worn spines curve sideways and tilt forward, in a 2026 records study. Side curves near the pelvis are hard to straighten, above all when the lowest curve is stiff. The staged plan first works from the side of the body, then adds screws from the back.

Charts covered fifty-one patients treated in sequence at one center. X-ray measures of side curve, trunk shift, and forward lean improved step by step after each stage, and the gains largely held at the last check. Back pain scores and daily function scores also improved. The authors read the pattern as stepwise straightening that lasts, within the limits of a single-center review.
pmc-13445490:
Annika Müller-Eigner and colleagues review the double-edged role of reactive oxygen species from mitochondria, the cell's power plants, in aging, in a 2026 paper. These reactive molecules were long cast as pure harm, waste from breathing that rusts the cell. Newer work shows they also carry signals, and effect depends on place, timing, and dose.

The review sorts output by its source inside the power plant, at three named sites of the breathing chain. From there it traces how local bursts touch each hallmark of aging, from worn gene caps to failed clean-up systems. The authors argue that blunt anti-oxidant plans miss this detail, and that future work must target the right site at the right moment.
pmc-13446190:
Ibironke W. Apata and colleagues compare infection control habits in United States dialysis centers between 2015 and 2021, in a 2026 survey study. Bloodstream infections in dialysis patients fell sharply over the late twenty-teens, after national pushes for safer catheter care. The team asked which habits spread in step with that fall.

In 2021 more than seven thousand centers, serving over half a million patients, filed the national survey. Use of strong skin antiseptic at catheter exit sites rose by about six points, and ointment or treated dressings rose by a like step. Alcohol care of catheter hubs jumped near ten points. Near half of centers had adopted germ-killing catheter caps, a new tool in that span. The authors urge wider uptake of the lagging habits.
pmc-13446290:
Kanta Kumaki and colleagues devise a way to measure the twist, or chirality, hidden in fine bone vessel networks, in a 2026 methods study. Bones look mirror-matched left to right, yet their tiny canals wander off true symmetry, and random noise can mask a real bias. Their bipixel rotation method turns flat images step by step and counts aligned pixel pairs at each angle.

The angle with the richest count marks a center, and the lopsided spread around it yields a bias score. Letter fonts and wallpaper patterns with known twist validated the math. Applied to pig thigh bone canals seen by nano-scale scans, the method picked out up-right against down-right leanings. The team offers it for mesh networks across the body.
pmc-13446490:
Marr and colleagues describe in 2026 an outreach model that brings crystallography, the science of crystal structure, into kindergarten classrooms, a subject usually left until graduate school. They examined crystals under microscopes and drew what they saw, then colored pages teaching that crystals are built from atoms. The fourth center read a new children's book the team created, a sugar crystal mystery story published in 2025 that links kitchen crystals to laboratory science. Instructors observed every child set up crystals safely and record observations, and most grasped the atom and X-ray ideas at an age-appropriate level.
pmc-13447190:
Tanmay Boob leads a 2026 study of day-long blood pressure checks before discharge after a heart failure flare in India. Risk tools at that handover point are scarce. Patterns across day and night, plus how much pressure swings, might flag who faces death or a return stay in the next three months.

Three hundred patients at a referral centre wore the monitor after stabilising, before going home. Just over half showed a normal night-time dip, while smaller shares showed flat, reversed or extreme patterns. Death within three months affected a small share, yet readmission touched more than four in ten. Reversed and extreme dipping, plus low daytime pressure, linked to higher death risk after adjustment, supporting discharge checks as a practical sorting tool.
pmc-13447290:
In Ha Kim and Jae Kwang Yun evaluate a move from many-port to single-port robot chest surgery in a 2026 weighted comparison. Lung cancer removal through one small entry promises less pain, yet surgeons need proof that a structured switch keeps patients safe. All operations in the series came from one surgeon, which sharpens the learning-curve question.

One hundred fifty-four patients treated between 2022 and 2025 were split between single-port and multiport robot approaches. Statistical weighting balanced the groups before comparison. Complete tumour removal was achieved in every case, with similar drainage time, hospital stay and complication rates across groups. Single-port operations ran shorter on average, and patients reported less pain in the first two days. The authors conclude the transition proved safe and workable within their pathway.
pmc-13448190:
S Anderson leads a large team setting out a study protocol for response-adapted radiotherapy in throat cancer in a 2026 paper. Cancers of the oropharynx, the middle throat, are rising, and poor-prognosis cases often fail standard radiation. Blanket dose increases for everyone have not improved survival, so the trial instead escalates dose only for tumours that respond poorly early on.

All participants start standard radiation, with diffusion MRI scans at the first and tenth sessions measuring water movement inside tumours. Slow improvement marks a tumour as a non-responder, earning a higher total dose to the visible tumour in later sessions. Responders stay on the standard course. The main goal is feasibility, meaning whether the scan-guided adapted workflow can be delivered without treatment gaps, before any large comparison trial.
pmc-13448290:
Maia and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract TLSB-33, a Johns Hopkins study of sacituzumab govitecan. This antibody-drug conjugate is approved for later-line metastatic breast cancer. The study asks how well it controls disease inside the central nervous system versus elsewhere.

Progression-free survival averaged about thirteen months for central nervous system disease and nearly sixteen for skull bone, against only five for visceral disease. pmc-13448690:
Balram Yelamasetti and colleagues test a 2026 welding study of post-weld friction stir processing on low-heat cold metal transfer joints in 6-millimeter AA6061 aluminum. Joints were checked by radiography and microscopy, with hardness, tensile, impact, and corrosion tests comparing as-welded joints against friction-stir-processed ones.

Processing refined the stir zone into fine equiaxed grains with clean interfaces, lifting tensile strength from 216 to 252 megapascals, yield from 198 to 215, elongation from 12.6 to 23.8 percent, and impact energy by 62 percent. pmc-13449890:
Diana Berzan and colleagues commented in 2026 on a single-center study of liver transplantation for widespread colorectal liver metastases. When cancer spreads only to the liver but fills both lobes, surgeons face a choice between two-stage liver removal and transplantation under the TRANSMET protocol. All patients had received chemotherapy before surgery.

Forty-two were planned for two-stage removal and sixteen for transplantation, with some in the first group never reaching the second stage as tumors progressed. The commentary weighs what transplantation changes for patients once deemed unresectable, and where its limits lie.
pmc-13449990:
Rametta and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a rare kidney cancer displays two targets used by modern antibody drugs. Collecting duct carcinoma is a rare, aggressive kidney cancer with few treatment options. It resembles bladder-lining cancer in origin, so the team checked tumour samples for two drug targets, Nectin-4 and Trop-2, used by antibody-drug conjugates proven in bladder cancer. Samples came from 59 patients in a multi-centre study and were stained in a central lab.

The authors say the frequent presence of both targets supports a biological kinship with bladder-lining cancer. They stress that staining alone does not prove the drugs will work in patients.
pmc-13451890:
Habeeb Abood and Farah Hasan AlHusseini review in 2026 six studies of a curvature measure on two families of near-complex shapes. pmc-13452290:
Nakamura and co-authors report a spinal fluid leak pinned to a tiny bone spur in the lower back. pmc-13452390:
M Aldiki Febriantono and three co-authors present a photo set of Manalagi apples grown in Indonesia, built so computer models can learn to spot fruit disease. The 2026 data paper covers fruit gathered in orchards from August 2024 to June 2026. Each fruit was photographed in natural light with phone and DSLR cameras.

The team logged 1,168 distinct fruits and about 5,100 raw photos before checks for image quality began. Each kept photo was cropped to one fruit, resized to a square of 1024 by 1024 pixels, and saved as a JPEG file. The final set holds 482 labeled images in four classes: healthy fruit, anthracnose, black pox, and powdery mildew. pmc-13453490:
Hao Ding and thirteen co-authors build barbed microneedle patches to treat melasma, the stubborn brown facial patches that resist creams. The exosomes mop up those oxygen species, while the drug breaks up the extra tiny blood vessels that feed the patches. pmc-13453990:
Yaqi Liu and others probed biofloc clumps made by Acidovorax soli Q11 in 2026, to find the genes that drive them in fish ponds. Biofloc farming lifts yields by turning ammonia and nitrite into germ clumps that filter-feeders eat, in place of plain nitrification. The team took clump germs from many pond set-ups and read strain Q11, from a sturgeon pond, by full gene scans and gene tests. Clump-making seemed steered by cellulose-making genes, with slime coats charted by light scans. The work points to gene levers for steadier biofloc ponds. Fish farmers gain a gene-level base for a green farm method.
pmc-13454290:
Han-Lin Li and five colleagues report a 2026 brain imaging study of children with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder who had never taken medication for it. The group included 62 children with the disorder, aged 6 to 15 years, and 46 healthy peers. Some stronger links tracked with lower hyperactivity scores, while others tracked with better test control. The authors say these patterns may help explain mixed past findings on brain wiring in the disorder.
pmc-13455090:
Hassani and co-authors review the search for protein biomarkers in breast cancer in this 2026 paper. So do overlap with other conditions, differences between platforms, and small mixed patient groups. The authors call for standardized workflows, targeted verification, and multi-center validation before panels can guide routine care.
pmc-13455190:
Chang Su and others built TestNet in 2026, a net-inference tool for microbes with false-find control for grouped and ungrouped samples. By giving calibrated significance for microbe links, it lets researchers tell true net edges from noise. Microbe researchers gain a strict net-inference tool.
pmc-13456990:
Fatma Shalabi and four colleagues present, in a 2026 case series, three patients whose brains were struck by fat embolism after broken long bones. Fat entering the blood after fractures can reach the brain, with effects from mild confusion to sudden coma and death. About one in ten patients with the brain form dies.

The three cases span that range. One patient lost consciousness with startling speed. Others showed milder or slower courses, with different scan pictures and different recoveries. Diagnosis leaned on the injury story and clinical signs, since magnetic resonance imaging is not always at hand when decisions must be made. The authors walk through the symptoms, imaging, and care choices in each case. Their point is recognition: after a major fracture, a fading mind should trigger suspicion of fat in the brain, not only bleeding or swelling.
pmc-13457190:
Yassir Adam Shuaib and Stéphane Coisne present a 2026 step-by-step protocol for a rapid tuberculosis test that tracks how treatment is working. pmc-13457390:
Yun Yu and colleagues build two scoring charts, called nomograms, to help doctors spot sepsis in newborns without waiting for blood culture results. The second adds two routine labs, white cell count and C-reactive protein. Accuracy, measured as area under the curve, reached 0.839 to 0.852 for the clinical model and 0.905 to 0.923 once labs joined. Calibration held up reasonably. pmc-13457490:
Ricardo E. Nunez-Rocha and a surgical education team measure how fast robotic operating skill fades once practice stops. Thirty residents returned after a break of at least a month; fifteen kept training, with at least three extra sessions past the proficiency bar.

The returning group, back after a median of 91 days, had slowed from 30.5 to 34.5 minutes and slipped from 30 to 28 on the OSATS skill scale. By six months, scores had fallen 17.6 percent and times had worsened 19.3 percent, with technical decay typically setting in near 84 days. Residents who kept practicing moved the other way, rising to 34 and cutting their time to 25.5 minutes. Higher starting scores oddly predicted steeper decline. The authors recommend refresher sessions around the three-month mark and practice beyond first proficiency.
pmc-13458190:
Dominic Augustine and colleagues present a diagnostic riddle in a 3-year-old girl with a fast-growing swelling over her left cheek. They were negative for S-100 and CK-19, pinning the diagnosis as embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, a rare childhood muscle cancer seldom appearing in the mouth. Chemotherapy followed, and PET-CT showed tumor shrinkage. pmc-13458390:
Lian and colleagues uncover how a tumor suppressor protein helps repair broken DNA in this 2026 study. The protein, menin, is best known because its loss causes inherited tumor syndromes. A reader protein then spots the mark and brings in CtIP, which trims DNA ends to start repair. A drug that restored the mark rescued repair in menin-deficient cells.
pmc-13458490:

The work supports apoptosis as the mechanism and bacterial components as candidates, pending tests on normal cells and animals.
pmc-13458790:
Felix Kwasi Nyande and colleagues explore self-care among pregnant women with gestational diabetes in Ghana in a 2026 interview study. Health services gain a case for targeted education and support that addresses distress, time and family help, not only diet sheets.
pmc-13459190:
Coffey, Simons, Taylor, and Kingston describe redesigning an evaluation of virtual reality in hand therapy in this 2026 service improvement report. Seven clinicians and twelve patients answered the new questionnaires, mixing open and closed questions. The findings showed virtual reality created a low-pressure, engaging setting that encouraged participation, something the original measures would have missed entirely. Participants also flagged practical conditions for success: enough physical space, reliable technology, attention to culture and language, and continued hands-on guidance from therapists alongside the headset.
pmc-13459290:

Self-esteem ran lower in older patients and in those receiving more stents, while education, income, and longer time since diagnosis each tied to higher scores. Where a patient lived also mattered. The authors recommend psychological support aimed at the most vulnerable groups during recovery.
pmc-13460190:

Thirty received surgical stabilization of the rib fractures and twenty-nine were managed without surgery.

Pneumonia, tracheostomy, and hospital death all occurred less often after surgery, with no deaths in the surgical group. Adjusted analysis confirmed the operation itself as the factor tied to faster liberation.
pmc-13461390:
Lin Gui and colleagues studied in 2026 newly diagnosed multiple myeloma patients whose disease arrived with high blood calcium, a marker of heavy tumor burden. pmc-13461990:

 Each rare variant was weighed using several lenses. They included how firmly the gene links to disease, how common the variant is in the population, computer predictions, classification rules, and protein shape modeling. The structured sorting ranked which variants most likely matter. The authors stress how varied the genetic picture is under one label. Their message: finding a variant is only the first step. Careful, layered interpretation decides what it means.
pmc-13462090:
Li-ping Yu and colleagues map how RNA methyl tagging drives a liver cancer route in a 2026 study. pmc-13462390:

pmc-13462990:

The integrated design catches changes that any single data layer would miss, from microbial shifts to bile acid routing. Findings feed breeding and feeding strategies for an industry where small per-hen gains multiply across billions of birds.
pmc-13488190:
Martin J. Batty and colleagues ask whether drugs can prevent chronic Chagas disease in a 2026 review. The parasite infection, spread by insects in the Americas, can damage the heart years after a silent start. Two old drugs kill the parasite early, yet their benefit once the disease turns chronic stays debated. The review weighs trials and cohort studies of treatment at different disease stages.

Treatment cleared the parasite from blood in many studies, while gains in heart outcomes were slower and less certain. Side effects often stopped courses early. Newer drug candidates aim for shorter, gentler treatment. The authors call for trials with heart outcomes, not blood tests alone, to settle who benefits from treatment.
pmc-13488290:
Shreyas Hulusemane Karunakara and colleagues study a silenced microRNA cluster in liver cancer in a 2026 laboratory and data analysis. The cluster, called C14MC, holds many tiny RNAs that normally restrain growth genes, and it was switched off in liver cancer cell lines and in a large public tumor cohort. Chemical marks called methylation, which attach to DNA and mute nearby genes, covered the cluster's start region in cancer cells.

Restoring two cluster members with synthetic copies shut down several cancer-driving genes and slowed cell movement and invasion in dish tests. Cluster levels and target gene patterns also tracked with patient survival in the cohort data. The authors propose the cluster and its targets for early detection, prognosis, and treatment design.
pmc-13488590:
Hailemichael Mulugeta and colleagues describe work injuries reaching emergency departments in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in a 2026 prospective study at three public hospitals. Over five months, 868 injured workers aged eighteen to sixty took part through interviews and chart review, drawn from more than five thousand injury patients seen. Severity followed World Health Organization surveillance guidance, and statistical models hunted for factors tied to severe injury.

Work cases made up about eighteen percent of injury visits. Manufacturing and construction dominated, young men were the typical patients, and hands and arms were hurt most often, mainly by cuts from sharp objects. About one fifth of injuries counted as severe. Low education, fall mechanisms, and no fixed work area linked with severity in the reported models.
pmc-13490490:
Giorgio Musto and Marco Percoco examine whether compact city shapes are linked to lower carbon emissions. In 2026, the study builds a global panel of more than eleven thousand urban centers from 1975 to 2020, joining harmonized city definitions with high-resolution data on residential and road transport emissions. Most prior work looks at density or city size, not geometric form.

Results held across alternative specifications, though the authors caution that these are associations, not proven causes. pmc-13490590:
Gulyás and team pooled outcome studies of blood markers in melanoma, the deadliest skin cancer, to judge which markers genuinely forecast death or spread. Clinics measure many candidates, but single studies disagree. Their 2026 meta-analysis followed registered protocol and reporting guidelines across three databases, combining hazard ratios, the standard measure of risk over time, for each marker on its own and in fuller models.

IL-6 carried the highest pooled hazard, at about three times the death risk for elevated levels in those checks. Lactate enzyme marker, tumor DNA in blood, and an inflammation ratio from blood counts predicted shorter progression-free time as well. The same core markers survived adjustment for other factors. Gulyás concludes a small panel, not the whole catalog, deserves routine forecast use.
pmc-13490890:
Halvaeezadeh and colleagues compared the enzyme arsenals of Aspergillus flavus fungi taken from human ear infections with species collected from the environment. Their 2026 study ran in Ahvaz, Iran. The fungus secretes enzymes that double as weapons for invading tissue, so clinical strains might be more armed. They produced hemolysin in nearly all cases against about seventy percent. The isolates showed catalase activity, which neutralizes the bursts immune cells use to kill fungi. The pattern supports the idea that enzyme output helps separate fungi from invasive ones.
pmc-13493990:
Jian, Wu, and Xiao improve a nature-inspired search method called the parrot optimisation algorithm, which imitates how green-cheeked conures flock, forage, and stay alert. Such methods hunt for the best solution to hard problems by trial and adjustment. The original parrot method, though, slows down and gets stuck on merely good answers in high-dimensional problems. On the standard CEC2017 and CEC2022 benchmark suites, STPO earned the best average rankings against twelve rival algorithms in most dimension settings. It sat near the top from ten dimensions up to one hundred. Statistical checks and component-removal experiments backed each added strategy's contribution. The team also ran five classic engineering design problems through the method successfully. They caution that no optimiser suits every problem shape.
pmc-13495090:
Mączka and colleagues presented a biographical-narrative toolkit for studying anxieties and coping strategies across countries, developed in research in Poland, Ukraine, and Hungary, in a 2026 methods article. Anxiety is hard to study because worries span health, family, and the environment and are entangled with language and local context. Their approach uses life-story interviews that place each anxiety within a person's life course.

Mączka situates environmental anxieties beside the other anxieties participants report. lets researchers see how climate or nature worries compete with everyday fears and reduces the bias of asking about one topic alone. The toolkit standardizes the hardest parts of qualitative work: building the codebook in stages, training coders uniformly, paired review of coding, and harmonizing codes across the three countries. The authors offer the framework as transferable to other topics needing context-sensitive, comparable qualitative evidence for policy and practice.
pmc-13495290:
Taebyeong Kang and four co-authors compare how men and women recover after minimally invasive bunion surgery, in a paper dated 2026. The operation combines two small-incision bone cuts to straighten the big toe. Sex-based outcome evidence for it was thin.

The study reviewed three hundred feet, half male and half female, matched so the groups started alike in age and deformity angles. Pain scales, foot function scores, patient questionnaires, and X-ray angles were tracked before surgery, at three months, and at one year. Complication rates entered the comparison too. Matched designs like this try to isolate sex itself from the many ways men's and women's feet differ before the operation. The results inform how surgeons counsel patients about the first year of recovery.
pmc-13499790:
Masazumi Katayama tests which muscle math best copies human three-joint arm reaching and its muscle picks, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Full arm models with up to twenty-six muscles and angle-bound leverage faced reaches in eight flat directions. Several cost rules competed.

A squared stress-change rule copied moves best, above all posture and wrist share. That rule favored big muscles and spared thin ones from overload. A tension rule leaned on leverage and sometimes loaded thin muscles hard. A cubed stress rule woke nearly all muscles but copied moves a bit worse. Team-like muscle patterns arose from body shape plus the cost rule. Readers get a balanced law for arm control.
pmc-13499890:
Hussain Ahmad Bhatti reports in 2026 a case of severe muscle disease linked to rosuvastatin, a cholesterol-lowering statin drug, first recognised in an outpatient clinic. Statin muscle complaints range from mild aches to rare immune-driven muscle destruction. His patient was a 62-year-old woman who had taken the drug daily for about four months. She arrived with four weeks of worsening fatigue, widespread muscle pain, weakness near the trunk, and trouble walking.

Blood tests showed a muscle enzyme level many times above normal, raised inflammation markers, and liver enzyme changes, while kidney function held. The drug was stopped at once, she was sent urgently to emergency care, and family reports described a four-day hospital stay whose records the author could not obtain. Enzyme levels available through day 54 peaked higher before easing downward, and the case warns that liver enzyme rises here may signal muscle injury, not liver disease.
pmc-13500090:
Kei U Wong and Harsh Sule describe in 2026 a training innovation that folds brief child emergency drills into the daily morning case conference of an emergency medicine residency. Residents get limited exposure to high-risk child emergencies, and standard simulation is squeezed by space, scheduling, and cost. From September 2021 to May 2025 their four-year programme ran 27 paediatric simulation sessions inside weekly morning reports. Sessions used basic mannequins, a portable setup, and scripted or web-based cases with evolving data, followed by guided debriefing.

Post-session surveys drew replies from most participants, mainly residents alongside students, attending physicians, and other staff. Respondents generally agreed the sessions improved their knowledge, comfort, and teamwork for child emergencies in the reported survey. Because the format reuses existing conference time and cheap equipment, the authors present it as a route to repeated practice that scales and sidesteps the usual barriers to such training.
pmc-13500390:
Yoshimichi Goda and colleagues report in 2026 a brain form of feline infectious peritonitis, a fatal viral disease of young cats, that appeared on scans as a single tumour-like mass. Their patient was an 11-month-old neutered male mixed-breed cat brought in with worsening loss of coordination. MRI revealed a well-defined, egg-shaped solitary mass on the fourth ventricle's left side, a fluid cavity deep in the brainstem region.

Staining of the surgically removed tissue identified the viral disease, settling a diagnosis that is notoriously hard to prove before death. The authors state this is the first report of the central nervous system form presenting as a solitary fourth-ventricle mass on MRI. They urge clinicians to include this disease among the possibilities when a young cat shows such a lesion, since its usual scan patterns look quite different from a discrete mass.
pmc-13501190:
Christopher Rentsch and co-authors profile a giant veterans health data resource in a 2026 paper. The resource draws on the electronic records of the United States veterans health system, the country's largest integrated care network. As of late 2025 it held records for over fourteen million veterans treated since 2000. Care from more than thirteen hundred sites feeds in, in structured codes, semi-structured reports, and free-text notes.

Drug records land nearly in real time, including biologics, vaccines, and devices. The long follow-up and diverse population suit studies of drug safety and effect in real practice. Profiles like this one tell outside researchers what the data can and cannot answer before they apply for access.
pmc-13501690:
Yasaman Sadat Nabipour leads a five-author team with a 2026 study of green-made quantum dots against drug-resistant wound infections. Using extract from Quercus brantii acorns, the team synthesized silver, copper, and zinc oxide quantum dots by a hydrothermal route, then verified their quantum behaviour with light spectroscopy. The dots were tested against multidrug-resistant clinical isolates of four problem bacteria, including MRSA and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and for safety on human skin cells.

Silver dots, averaging 7.2 nanometres, performed best: they killed bacteria at concentrations from 4.5 to 18.1 micrograms per millilitre and blocked up to 85 percent of biofilm growth at half that dose. Radical-trapping tests supported oxidative stress as the killing route, and the effective doses spared human keratinocytes and fibroblasts. In infected mouse wounds, a silver-dot hydrogel closed 95.3 percent of the wound by day 14 and cut bacterial load by more than four orders of magnitude.
pmc-13501790:
Mina Shojaee and co-authors offer a 2026 review and meta-analysis of lifestyle teaching for women with gestational diabetes. The programs gave food advice, tips on being active, and self-care skills such as checking blood sugar. The team tracked two results: quality of life and fasting blood glucose.

The authors searched several major databases for work up to late 2025 and kept to standard reporting rules. They took in randomized trials and quasi-experimental studies of women with this form of diabetes. Each program had to be planned, with set sessions, clear learning goals, and follow-up. Readers get one pooled view of whether teaching without drugs helps mothers handle the condition while pregnant.
pmc-13503790:
Siva Shanmukha Anjaneya Babu Padavala leads a team testing two waste powders as partial cement swaps in concrete, in a 2026 study. Cement making drives a large share of world carbon output. Silica fume and Alccofine are fine powders that can fill some of that role while raising strength.

Trials first set silica fume at three swap levels, then varied Alccofine on top of the best one. A blend with set shares of both raised crush strength by about a third over plain concrete. Bend and split strength rose by about a sixth. Water uptake and salt passage both fell by more than two fifths. Smart models predicted crush strength well. A life-cycle check found the best blend cut warming impact by about a tenth.
pmc-13503890:
Zhigao Zhang leads a team charting plant growth change in China's Taihang Mountains from 2000 to 2024, in a 2026 study. The range shields the North China Plain and holds key ecosystems. Knowing what drives greening or loss guides land care in the region.

Satellite greenness data rose steadily over the period, with gains across most of the range. High values sat in the south, and low values in the northwest. A persistence test hints that much of the area may slip back toward decline. Splitting the drivers, the team credits human action for about 86 percent of the change, far above climate. Pines gained most under human care, while farm and mixed plots lost the most.
pmc-13503990:
Humaid Sadiq and four colleagues recount a case of a massive lung artery clot that struck without the usual warning signs, in a 2026 report. The patient, a woman in her early forties, came in with dizziness, racing heart feelings, and deep tiredness rather than chest pain or breathlessness.

Scans confirmed a huge clot blocking flow from the heart to the lungs. Her heart stopped, and clot-busting drugs given during resuscitation brought her back. The same drugs then caused severe belly bleeding that needed emergency surgery. More clots formed in an arm artery and in the lungs' blood circuit during her stay. That pattern raised suspicion of a clotting disorder. She recovered after 33 days and went home on blood thinners.
pmc-13504290:
Catley and colleagues produced the first direct images of two DNA molecules recognizing and pairing with each other in the presence of doubly charged metal ions. Their 2026 biophysics study combines high-resolution atomic force microscopy with atomistic computer simulations. How matching DNA sequences find each other underpins recombination and genome packing, yet the structural basis of the pairing has never been seen.

Catley found strongly paired DNA duplexes often settle into groove-to-groove alignment. In that arrangement the helical groove of one molecule faces the other's, held by ionic bridges in which the metal ions link the minor grooves of both partners. Sequence-specific contacts added further stability, and their strength and specificity varied with which ion was used. The authors argue this ion-mediated groove alignment supplies the molecular mechanism behind a long-standing helical alignment model of homology recognition, with implications for chromosome condensation and genome organization.
pmc-13506190:
Ramesh Nadarajah leads a wide international team behind FIND-AF 2.0, a machine-learning model that reads routine health records to flag people likely to develop atrial fibrillation within six months. The model uses only age, sex, and ten common conditions, so it can run inside ordinary record systems. Training and checks drew on millions of records from the United Kingdom, Japan, Israel, Canada, and China.

Prediction quality ranged from good to excellent across all five countries, beating two established risk scores. In a prospective test, 1,923 volunteers wore a handheld heart recorder four times daily for three weeks. New atrial fibrillation appeared in about five percent of the high-risk group but well under one percent of the low-risk group, and nearly all detected cases started blood-thinning treatment. Registry data showed untreated high-risk patients faced a notable stroke rate, strengthening the case for risk-guided screening.
pmc-13506590:
Ethan Wainman, Tomer Guy, Nora Hernandez, Phyllis Faust, and Elan Louis published this study in 2026. It examines the cerebellum in essential tremor and related degenerative diseases. The focus is Purkinje cells, the cerebellum's main output neurons, and the basket cells that wrap around them.

The team measured three features in 332 postmortem brains. They counted how densely Purkinje cells line up, how many baskets sit empty after their Purkinje cell died, and how thickly basket fibers swell around survivors. Groups covered essential tremor, several ataxias, and healthy controls. Across all groups, fewer Purkinje cells meant more empty baskets, though the strength varied. Basket swelling tracked the other measures only in some diseases. The same linked pattern appeared in control brains, suggesting a general rule of cerebellar decay. The authors say these measures should be read together when judging cerebellar degeneration.
pmc-13507090:
Rachel Lau and colleagues present, in 2026 work, cellGeometry, a very fast tool that estimates cell mixes in bulk gene samples from single-cell references. Bulk samples blend signals from many cells, and older unmixing tools struggle as reference atlases grow to millions of cells. In tests built from datasets with over three million cells, the tool proved more accurate than leading rivals and steadier under noise. It also flags odd genes that may reveal disease shifts or missing cell types. Checks on real blood and tissue samples gave more realistic mixes. Speed plus accuracy suits large clinical studies.
pmc-13508190:
Zebedee Kerry leads a twelve-author team asking people in Papua New Guinea how they view new tools against malaria-carrying mosquitoes, in 2026 work. Villagers showed a strong grasp of malaria risk, seasons, and where mosquitoes breed. They mixed traditional steps with program tools already in use. Views on bringing back indoor spraying depended on past practice and local context, the team found. Health system readiness was also part of the picture. pmc-13508290:
Hafsa Kanwal and six co-authors run a trial testing whether pharmacist-led care improves outcomes for lung disease patients who also carry other illnesses, in 2026 work.
