The trial placed 120 patients into three groups at random: standard care, pharmacist counselling, or full pharmaceutical care guided by treatment rules. Care ran for 24 weeks. Scores tracked symptoms, breathlessness, lung function, flare-ups, and quality of life.

The full pharmaceutical care group improved most. Symptom scores dropped far below the standard care group, and breathlessness eased more as well. Lung function declined least in that group over the study span. Flare-ups that did occur were shorter, and disease progression scores were lower. Quality of life rose more with pharmacist-led care. The authors argue pharmacists should sit inside the care team for such patients, not at its edge.
pmc-13509190:
Eman Alkhammash, Fuad Ghaleb, Faisal Saeed, and Sultan Noman Qasem build a guard against fake data attacks on medical sensors. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. pmc-13509990:
Michele Gottardi and eleven co-authors review how the bone marrow setting shapes acute myeloid leukemia, in 2026 work. Leukemia stem cells live inside marrow niches that send survival signals, and the review argues the setting does more than host the disease. Trials aiming to break niche protection show early activity in some groups, yet firm randomized proof remains scarce.
pmc-13510590:
Anastassiya Ganina and seven co-authors review stem cell therapy for recovery after stroke, with a focus on cells taken from the jelly of the umbilical cord, in 2026 work. Cells from bone marrow and fat are used more often, yet those sources carry a more mature state that limits growth and repair power. Such care would join clot drugs, vessel procedures, therapy exercises, and digital tools over long recovery periods.
pmc-13510690:

Searching five major databases and regulator websites, they found deep learning now rebuilds and cleans scans while preserving the numbers doctors rely on. Uses span cancer, brain, and heart care, along with paired diagnosis-and-therapy approaches. Yet most studies were small, single-center, and retrospective, with little outside validation and thin coverage of Latin America. The authors call for multicenter testing, open standards, and a clear seat for radiopharmacists in oversight.
pmc-13512090:
Molly J. Taylor, Tait D. Shanafelt, and Lisa G. Drivers include grant pressure, publication demands, and thin control over time, while the fallout reaches staffing, discovery pace, and the wider care system. The authors urge institutions to build collegial ties on purpose, guard teaching time, renew a sense of meaning in the work, and back autonomy for lab leaders. They also call for research and intervention effort to stop lagging so far behind the clinician side, starting by asking scientists themselves what would help.
pmc-13513490:

Emotional arousal, mental overload, and shattered daily routines fed all three forms. Two kinds of bedtime thinking mattered most, one pressing and worried, the other comforting, and they pushed sleep in opposite directions. Sleep apps and guided meditation tools were widely available, yet most participants never took them up, citing doubt or plain inertia. The proposed model ties personal traits, pre-sleep habits, and stress response into one loop. The author urges public health programs to offer simple, trusted sleep help during large crises.
pmc-13517090:
Roberta Perego, Giada Giuliani, Eva Spada, and Daniela Proverbio count skin yeasts on healthy dogs in a 2026 survey. pmc-13518090:
Yang and colleagues hunt for gene clues to a childhood kidney illness that answers well to steroids. In the illness, filters in the kidney leak protein into urine. Past gene hunts were small, so much of the inherited risk stayed hidden.

The team scanned genomes of children in China, then pooled data across world groups. Two new risk spots stood out near genes tied to immune system jobs. One spot links to a gene that, when more active in immune cells, raised risk. The other links to a gene where more activity cut risk. A combined gene score also tied to illness starting at a younger age.
pmc-13518290:
Daniel Vered, Zoya Katzir, Idan Daniel Grosbard, Avner Thaler, and Inbal Maidan sort Parkinson's patients into brain-wave subtypes, in a research paper from 2026. Recordings from 116 patients and 30 healthy people were taken at rest and while walking. Features covered rhythm power, background signal shape, and signal complexity. Grouping methods settled on three sturdy clusters with distinct brain profiles. The clusters also differed in clinical, gait, and genetic traits. Such subtypes may guide tailored treatment trials.
pmc-13518790:
Sona Ayadi Hassan, Leila Rezaei Somee, Parinaz Ghadam, and Ahya Abdi Ali describe in 2026 a green way to make silver-copper nanozymes using extract from walnut green husks. Laboratory tests showed strong enzyme-like activity, killing of both major bacterial groups including resistant strains, action against Candida albicans fungus and mature biofilms, and free-radical scavenging. The paired metals outperformed single-metal versions, pointing toward medical and cleanup uses.
pmc-13518890:
Estelle Stoltmann and colleagues mapped which advanced digital skills the wind energy industry now needs from its workforce. Published in 2026, the study blended expert interviews, a survey, and job-posting analysis, reading the postings and interviews with automated language tools. The aim was to guide schools before they rewrite courses, using three sources to check one another rather than trusting any single one.

Scientific programming and numerical modeling stood out across all sources as core skills, while machine learning, connected devices, and cybersecurity mattered more in some roles and firms than in others. About 44 percent of engineering-related postings asked for advanced digital skills, and interview and survey voices pointed to a still wider set of emerging skills. The authors close with training formats and lifelong learning needs, setting up a fuller gap study that pairs industry demand with what courses now teach.
pmc-13520290:
Mine Esen Baris and three colleagues test in 2026 whether phenylephrine eye drops, the standard pupil dilator, quietly alter front-of-eye structures in healthy adults. Twenty volunteers received three doses of the 2.5 percent drop in the right eye, with the untreated left eye as control. Scleral thickness was imaged at three depths, and protein haze in the front chamber was measured by laser photometry 45 minutes later.

The white wall thickened significantly right at the scleral spur on both sides of the eye, while thinning occurred one millimeter behind the spur on the temple side. Chamber haze drifted upward without reaching significance. Baris and colleagues conclude the drops reshape the sclera locally yet leave inflammation essentially untouched.
pmc-13521290:
Poirier and Aparicio Chacón review the PHO1 protein family in this 2026 plant biology paper. Recent cryo-electron microscopy images, which freeze proteins to reveal their shape, show these proteins act as channels with two gates controlled by inositol polyphosphate signals. The parts that bind phosphate and work the gates are nearly unchanged across species, suggesting an ancient shared job. The review also covers puzzles. The proteins sit mostly on inner cell compartments rather than the surface. The plant version also shapes responses to the stress hormone abscisic acid in seeds and leaf pores.
pmc-13521390:
Samia Yaqoob and co-authors report a 2026 study of a new gel for wound care built from chia seed mucilage. That mucilage holds a sugar polymer that swells in water. The team linked it with a common acid monomer to form a stable gel. Lab tests checked that the gel's make-up was as planned. They also tested whether it harms blood or forms clots in a dish.

The gel proved gentle on blood in those tests. It showed strong action against harmful oxygen forms, a trait that can aid healing. It also slowed two kinds of bacteria, one from each major class. A feeding test in animals checked for acute harm from swallowing it. The authors present the gel as a candidate dressing material. More work in living wounds would be the next step.
pmc-13521890:
Keshab Raj Paudel and colleagues link in 2026 national drug exam scores with school scores for 290 medical students. The classes graduated from 2019 to 2023. Schools want to know if in-house teaching tracks board-style skill in drug knowledge. Entry scores were part of the check.

School drug scores tracked national scores strongly. Entry test scores tracked at a mid level. Grade averages tracked weakly but still clearly. Joint models kept school scores and entry scores as predictors. The model explained just over half of score spread. Overlap checks showed no bad redundancy. In-house exams mirror national hopes fairly well, the team concludes.
pmc-13522190:
Salahddine Chafiki and seven co-authors present a 2026 study of a plant oil blend as a biofungicide against green mold of citrus fruit. The mold, a Penicillium species, is among the costliest postharvest diseases of citrus. Control today leans on synthetic fungicides, with their residue and resistance worries.

The team tested oils from rosemary, a lavender species, and lemongrass, alone and mixed. In lab dishes, every treatment slowed the mold's growth clearly. The blend's joint effect is the paper's focus, since mixes can beat single oils and slow resistance. Greenhouse or fruit level trials would be the next step for this green alternative.
pmc-13522490:
Lei Wang and colleagues introduce a new laboratory method for making circular RNA in a 2026 study. Circular RNA forms a closed loop, which makes it more stable than straight RNA and appealing for future medicines. Existing enzyme-based methods use each helper enzyme at most once and leave cleaning difficult, limiting scale and options.

The new design separates the ribozyme, a catalytic RNA, from the material it acts on, so one ribozyme can be reused many times. The system produced both plain and chemically modified circular RNA, and fixing the ribozyme in place reduced impurities and improved yield. The authors argue the approach could support wider variety and larger-scale production of circular RNA treatments.
pmc-13522590:
Peishen Li and co-authors show how to reshape a confined light wave into a flat-topped profile in a 2026 photonics study. Waves trapped in a finite space normally form uneven standing patterns with peaks and dips. The team used spatial phase engineering, which acts like an artificial gauge field, to tune the trapped modes in a photonic crystal slab.

Adjusting the accumulated phase drove a flow in the mode spectrum and morphed ordinary oscillating profiles continuously into a uniform, nonzero flat-top state. Measurements of near and far fields during single-mode lasing confirmed the transition. Such uniform states could benefit quantum emitters, optical antennas, and lasers, where even coverage matters more than peaked intensity.
pmc-13523090:
Christina Feng and three colleagues write a guide to finding genes that affect several traits at once, using summary data from genome scans, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Such shared effects, called pleiotropy, are common in human disease. Finding them from summary data is hard: effects are small, tests are many, and effects can point in opposed ways across traits. Joint methods that read several traits together can help.

The guide reviews five widely used tools and shows each on breast and thyroid cancer data. It stresses care with mixed effects, trait links, and gene and pathway grouping. The authors aim to give researchers hands-on help in choosing and reading these methods.
pmc-13523490:
Helene Smith and colleagues present a 2026 qualitative study on contraception access for women in prison in New South Wales, Australia. Justice-involved women show high unmet need for contraception, shaped by violence, unstable housing, substance use, and poor mental health. Little Australian research had asked incarcerated women about their own experience of family planning services.

Seventeen women aged 19 to 45 from two correctional centers gave semi-structured interviews within a larger prisoner health study. Access problems stemmed less from mistrust of providers than from an unreliable system, with unanswered requests, long delays, and unsafe attempts to remove implants themselves. Time in custody also prompted reflection on readiness for motherhood. Limited method choices and side effects pushed some women toward sterilization, which some later regretted.
pmc-13524690:
Teresa K. Chen leads a large team in a 2026 prospective cohort study mapping metabolomic signs of inflammation in chronic kidney disease. Inflammation predicts kidney decline, cardiovascular events, and death, and the chemical environment of the blood may reveal why. The team linked hundreds of small molecules to a panel of inflammatory proteins.

The main cohort held 491 people from a kidney disease study in African American adults, with replication in two further cohorts. Among 718 metabolites tested, hundreds of cross-sectional links survived correction, mostly positive for two tumor necrosis factor receptors and mostly negative for uromodulin and epidermal growth factor. Distinct pathways appeared for distinct proteins, and 45 links predicted two-year change in inflammatory markers. Replication was strong for the receptor proteins and poor for one interleukin.
pmc-13525590:
Georgia Ramantani and colleagues surveyed how children reach epilepsy surgery worldwide and what workups they receive. Published in 2026, the International League Against Epilepsy task force study gathered group-level data from 61 surgery programs across 29 countries, covering 2,427 children and adolescents treated in 2023. Surgery is well established for childhood epilepsy, yet current global practice patterns were poorly mapped.

Mean age at surgery was about nine years after more than five years of epilepsy, despite some operations in infancy and before drug resistance. Repeat operations were common, with resection outpacing neuromodulation. Brain glucose scans and genetic testing each reached about half of patients, while advanced imaging and brain-wave mapping varied widely by region. The authors flag long waits and uneven access to modern workups as the key gaps.
pmc-13525890:
Kassandra M. Jade leads a large team in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on how life-context factors shape sinonasal outcome scores in chronic rhinosinusitis, a long-lasting sinus inflammation. Social conditions, demographics, and health behaviors were suspected influences, yet their effects on the standard 22-item symptom score were unclear.

Searches of four databases through December 2024 produced sixty-one eligible studies from over three thousand records. Women scored worse at baseline but improved similarly after surgery. Younger patients often started worse, and race and ethnicity data were limited with no clear differences. Medicaid and privately insured patients started worse than Medicare patients, while smokers scored worse than nonsmokers. Education, income, and environmental effects were inconsistent. Standardized collection of context data is urged.
pmc-13526690:
Huidong Guo and Xiao-Jun Huang review, in a 2026 paper, bone marrow transplantation as an immune reset rather than simple cell replacement. Transplantation has long been framed as a cure for blood cancers through swapping a diseased blood-forming system for a healthy donor one. The authors argue the process runs deeper, collapsing and rebuilding immunity itself.

After transplant, immunity does not return to its former state. Instead it settles at a new equilibrium shaped by conditioning injury, donor-recipient immune interactions, regrowth of supporting stroma, and ongoing treatments. The review gathers evidence on how tolerance is reinstalled and stability maintained under those forces. By treating transplantation as a human model of immune reprogramming, the authors extract principles that may guide therapies for autoimmunity, immune aging, and other immune diseases.
pmc-13526790:
Yahan Qin and colleagues identify, in a 2026 study, an enzyme called PARP10 as a driver of lung cancer spread to bone, a complication marked by resistance and severe illness. Sequencing of bone metastases across cancers found PARP10 consistently raised, and high levels in primary tumors tracked with poor survival. The team probed how it works.

Removing PARP10 damaged tumor DNA, raised oxidative stress, and switched on a second enzyme, BCAT2, under control of the MYC regulator, boosting breakdown of branched-chain amino acids. That shift fed tumor energy production yet starved the bone environment of those amino acids, suppressing the bone-eating cells that metastasis needs. A PARP10-blocking drug shrank bone metastatic burden in mice without visible toxicity, attacking tumor cells and their niche together.
pmc-13526890:
Saranya Matta and Sambhudutta Nanda present a 2026 antenna design for sub-6 GHz wireless services, combining a slotted bowtie radiator with dual polarization in a compact form. Access points and small cells need antennas with strong isolation between channels, clean radiation patterns, and good forward gain. Bowtie shapes are simple to build and suit polarization diversity.

The design arranges slot-cut bowtie elements at right angles on a common circuit board material, fed in a balanced configuration, then adds a metal reflector plate set behind them to sharpen performance. Measured operation centers near 2.52 and 4.42 gigahertz with usable bandwidths around 220 and 420 megahertz. Isolation stayed above thirty decibels, cross-polarization stayed low, and the reflector lifted gain from about two to over seven decibels on average.
pmc-13527490:
Geteneh Moges Assefa and colleagues made the policy case for vaccinating Ethiopians across the whole lifespan, not just in childhood. Published in 2026, the policy brief notes that Ethiopia's immunization system, though much improved for infants, leaves adolescents, pregnant women, adults, and older adults unevenly covered, with missed chances even near clinics. Life course immunization means vaccination at every age through integrated routine care.

Barriers span demand, supply, and system design: low awareness beyond childhood, low perceived risk, side-effect worries, gendered decision limits, weak adult service platforms, and poor age-split monitoring. The authors urge embedding lifespan vaccination into national policy and primary care, creating repeated contact points and stronger risk communication. Readers get a reform blueprint tying vaccination to equity and universal health coverage.
pmc-13527990:
Lin Liu and eight colleagues describe a 2026 biodegradable implant for internal radiation therapy. The device is a calcium-based reservoir labeled with radioactive iodine-131. It is built to break down inside tumors rather than stay in the body forever. Once there, it slowly releases hydrogen peroxide, oxygen, and calcium ions. Those releases stay minimal in normal tissue because breakdown speeds up in acid conditions.

The oxygen eases tumor hypoxia, a state that helps cancers resist treatment. Extra peroxide and oxygen boost radiation damage. Calcium overload disrupts cell power plants and triggers a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis. Oxygen also lowers PD-L1, a shield tumors use against immune attack. In the team's models the implant cleared both treated and distant tumors. The authors pitch it as internal radiotherapy and immune therapy in one.
pmc-13528090:
Yuhan Zhang, Jianquan Cheng, and Lian Duan review how health appears in city master plans across China in a 2026 study. The team read the Territorial Spatial Planning 2035 schemes of thirty-six major cities. A framework built from global writing and policy sorted the health content. Word networks and gap measures compared the cities.

All thirty-six plans mention healthy city goals. Eight themes appear, led by green open space and disaster readiness. Sports facilities, pollution control, and medical services follow. Equity gets the least attention in most plans. Higher-rank cities wrote broader and richer health sections. Lower-tier cities often stayed thin and generic. The authors place China at a middle stage of health planning. They recommend stronger laws, open plan texts, and tailored support for smaller cities.
pmc-13528690:
Spatial transcriptomics maps which genes are active at each tiny spot of a tissue slice, but the loudest signals often drown out rare cell types. Roxana Zahedi and co-authors present SemanticST, a graph learning framework built to hear the quiet patterns too. It is the first of its kind to train in small batches, so it can chew through the largest modern datasets.

Instead of one blended graph, the method fuses several graphs that each carry a different kind of meaning about the tissue. On a gold-standard brain dataset it beat rivals by up to twenty percent on the usual scores. In breast cancer data it flagged a rare region positive for three receptors at once. It also stitched together multiple samples more robustly than the established tools.
pmc-13529890:
Pecoraro and colleagues reviewed in 2026 treatments aimed at a protein called DLL3 in advanced prostate cancer. Some prostate cancers stop responding to hormone-blocking therapy and take on nerve-like features, a state called neuroendocrine prostate cancer. These cancers grow fast, spread widely, and respond poorly to standard chemotherapy. DLL3 sits on the surface of such tumour cells but is rare in healthy adult tissue, making it a target.

DLL3 was found in about three in four resistant neuroendocrine tumours but only about one in eight ordinary resistant tumours. Early trials suggest benefit mainly in tumours that carry DLL3, echoing success in a similar lung cancer. The authors stress that picking patients by DLL3 testing will decide whether these drugs help. They urge prostate-specific trial designs as the field moves forward.
pmc-13530290:
Kathleen White, Tesfa Alamneh, Josephine Walker, and Aaron Lim measure hepatitis B vaccine uptake in young Ethiopian children, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Chronic hepatitis B is common in Ethiopia and infant vaccine targets are missed. The team used a national health survey from twenty sixteen covering 3,855 children aged one to three years. They mapped coverage by region and tested which family traits linked to full vaccination.

About half the children had the complete course. Coverage varied widely by region. Older, better-schooled, and wealthier mothers had better-vaccinated children, as did families near health posts. Larger households lagged. The authors urge campaigns aimed at poorer mothers and big families.
pmc-13530590:
Tokish, Iturregui, and Lai present in 2026, as conference poster 245, animal experiments on improving rotator cuff repair with bioengineered patches and biologic materials. The repairs were tested biomechanically, genetically, and under the microscope at eight weeks after surgery.

Four augmentations were compared against traditional repair, alongside sham controls in the rat model used for this work. They were an electrospun synthetic patch mimicking the tendon-to-bone junction, a sheet of amnion membrane from the placenta, and a combination of the two. Breaking strength ran higher on average in every patch group than in traditional repair, and the yield loads showed the same ordering. The combination patch's tissue maturity score matched traditional repair. However, the electrospun products provoked an exaggerated immune reaction with giant cells and fibrotic growth, a warning the authors say warrants further investigation before clinical enthusiasm.
pmc-13531590:
Helen Leach and co-authors warn in a 2026 essay that general practice reforms in Britain must be tested against rural reality. Current policy prizes same-day appointments and digital access. Rural patients, older and spread over wide areas, face distance, thin staffing, and transport limits that city-focused plans overlook.

Access in the countryside also means continuity with a clinician who knows local life, a bond tied to better outcomes and fewer hospital stays. Speed-first reforms risk trading that relationship away. The authors propose routine rural-proofing, a systematic check of every policy for geographic fairness before rollout.
pmc-13531790:
Seok Joo Chae and colleagues build in 2026 a screening model that flags South Korean firefighters at risk of post-traumatic stress. Stigma keeps reported rates low in this workforce, so indirect signals matter. Records covered 52,428 firefighters, of whom 2,305 had probable disorder on a standard checklist.

Seven features carried the model: poor concentration, appetite change, guilt feelings, sleep trouble, work pressure, poor adaptability, and doubts about seeking help for others. The gradient-boosting model classified risk with strong accuracy, and a fresh year of data confirmed the performance. A short flagged list could steer early support toward hidden cases.
pmc-13534690:
Nureeda Che-alee, Ninadia Jitprasitporn, and Lakkhana Kanhayuwa Wingfield study in 2026 pigments from a fungus living inside healthy plant leaves for textile dyeing. Natural dyes face low yields and seasonal limits, while synthetic dyes raise health and pollution concerns. The strain made a vivid red pigment in liquid culture.

Chemical analysis named oosporein as the main pigment compound. The colour held up well under heat and light, shifted with acidity, and showed low harm to human skin cells in tests. Cotton took the dye strongly with alum, and the pigment blocked one common skin bacterium.
pmc-13536690:
Johan Diaz and colleagues present a 2026 case report of synovial sarcoma, a rare and aggressive soft tissue cancer that can grow slowly and look harmless at first. The patient was a 43-year-old man with leg pain and chest pain who had a large, tender calf mass. Earlier visits had treated the mass as benign. New scans and lung biopsies changed that view and pointed to cancer that had already spread.

Imaging showed a large lobulated mass inside the calf muscle with calcium deposits, plus many lung nodules suggesting spread. Lung tissue showed markers consistent with the monophasic form of the disease, though a confirmatory gene test was not obtained. Combination chemotherapy was planned, yet the patient declined further care and died about six months later from lung complications. The authors urge prompt workup of slow-growing soft tissue lumps.
pmc-13537190:
Lei Fan and six co-authors report, in a 2026 study, a way to turn carbon dioxide into useful acids using a common metal. The acids they target, arylacetic acids, form the base of common pain drugs and other fine chemicals. Past routes to them relied on precious metals, had limited substrate scope, or needed large amounts of additives.

Their route uses titanium(III), an earth-abundant metal, to catalyze the reductive carboxylation of benzyl chlorides with carbon dioxide. It works on primary, secondary, and tertiary forms, and also on related bromides and allylic chlorides. No magnesium salt additives are needed, and the reaction tolerates oxygen. Mechanistic tests point to a radical-carbanion relay: a radical forms first, gains charge, and then captures the carbon dioxide. The team demonstrated the route at gram scale and made several pain drugs in one step.
pmc-13537590:
Do-Eun Lee and co-authors lay out a trial protocol for virtual reality therapy in post-traumatic stress in a 2026 paper. Emotion-to-Emotion Therapy, drawn from traditional Korean medicine, calms over-strong feelings by pairing them with opposing ones. Its meditation part is hard to deliver the same way twice. A headset version promises steady, absorbing delivery.

Seventy-two adults with the disorder will be assigned by chance to headset therapy, standard therapy, or a waiting list. Both therapy groups get sixteen sessions over eight weeks. A standard symptom checklist at week eight is the main yardstick, with safety and cost tracked too. Protocol papers like this one lock the design in public before results arrive.
pmc-13538290:
Daniel Zarhin and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-six on Parkinson's patients who also carry Alzheimer's disease markers. Some Parkinson's patients decline faster in mind and movement, and hidden Alzheimer's pathology may be one cause. Knowing who carries it matters for prognosis and for sorting patients into trials.

The team used data from a large international cohort of newly diagnosed patients. Among four hundred forty-nine patients positive for the Parkinson's seed test, about nine percent met spinal fluid criteria for Alzheimer's markers. At baseline the groups looked alike. Over five years the double-marker group lost more ground in thinking, and by eight years in movement as well. A low score on a standard cognitive test helped flag the group.
pmc-13538390:
A team led by Marina Sanaki-Matsumiya grew beef-like tissue from cow embryo stem cells, with muscle, nerve, and blood vessel cells forming together. Lab-grown beef often needs each cell type made apart and then assembled. Embryo stem cells can renew and turn into many types, unlike adult stem cells. The team steered them step by step toward early body tissue.

Within fifteen days, muscle fibers with working bands appeared. They pulsed with calcium in response to signals from nerve cells grown alongside. Vessel cells formed even networks inside the tissue. The soup was free of animal serum. The authors call it a milestone toward self-building steaks with vessels and nerves built in.
pmc-13538490:
Ayush Mahanta and colleagues propose a quantum-inspired hybrid optimizer for clustering and routing in wireless sensor networks in a 2026 study. Battery limits dominate sensor network life, while separate handling of grouping and routing wastes energy. The framework fuses swarm search with genetic search and scores options on leftover energy, crowding, distance, and stability. Simulations ran one thousand rounds on hundred-node layouts against five rival protocols.

The hybrid outlasted every rival, with first-node-death gains ranging widely over classic protocols and a clear edge over the strongest hybrid rival. Total energy use fell, high-delivery operation lengthened, and delays dropped, with tight repeatability across thirty runs. The authors present the method as ready support for industrial sensing, environment watching, and smart city systems.
pmc-13538590:
Can Rong and colleagues built a worldwide dataset of city commuting flows. Published in 2026, the dataset covers 2,358 cities across 179 countries and six continents. Commuting flows trace daily moves from homes to workplaces, the main form of within-city travel, yet counting heads is slow and costly.

The team fed fine-grained people data, space photos, and place lists into a deep model that builds flows between city zones by role. Checks showed the built flow patterns closely matched real-world counts. The set supports work on greener travel, zone planning, and city toughness against shocks. Readers get an unmatched span of city movement data for green city research.
pmc-13538690:
Rukiye Sumeyye Bakici and colleagues compare outer ear shape among young adults from ten countries in a 2026 morphology study. Photographs of 1,351 ears from 676 student volunteers aged 16 to 30 years at a Turkish university were scored for shape, folds, lobes, and small landmarks. Participants hailed from countries across Africa, the Middle East, and Central Asia.

Overall ear shape differed sharply by country, with round forms leading in one nation, triangular in two others, and oval in three more. Helix form also varied significantly across groups. The authors present the dataset as a standardized reference for forensic identification, anthropology, and ear reconstruction planning, noting ears vary by population much like other facial traits.
pmc-13539190:
Haopeng Yang and a large team of co-authors published this study in 2026. It describes a public bank of patient-derived tumor models for large B-cell lymphoma, an aggressive blood cancer with many subtypes. The models, called xenografts, grow human tumors in mice so new drugs can be tested before human trials.

The bank, named X-LYMPH, opens with forty-eight models that span the cancer's known gene and expression groups. Twenty-three came from patients whose disease returned after CAR T-cell therapy, the hardest cases in the field. Those models replay real escape routes, such as tumors losing the target the therapy hunts. Each model carries full molecular notes. The authors offer the bank as shared ground for labs hunting cures and studying resistance.
pmc-13540290:
Tao Yu, Guangzhi Shi, Zi Ye, and five colleagues lay out, published in 2026, a trial design on tube feeding after severe stroke. It tests whether feeding on a schedule beats feeding around the clock. Constant feeding is standard in intensive care, but it ignores the day-night rhythm of normal eating. The TENET trial will enroll patients with severe stroke across several centers. Patients are assigned by chance to daytime-only feeding windows of eight to twelve hours, or to nonstop feeding. Feeding runs until it is no longer needed, capped at twenty-eight days.

The main yardstick is poor function at ninety days on a standard stroke scale. Secondary measures cover awareness, strength, daily living skills, and time in intensive care. The authors say the trial will give the first solid evidence on timed feeding for this group, where belief currently runs ahead of proof.
pmc-13541390:
Magnus Høgevold and co-authors compare two ways to pin a hip fracture, in work published in 2026. The breaks sat at the neck of the thigh bone and had not shifted. One group got plain pins, while the other got pins locked through a small plate. Lab work hinted the plate would hold twist better.

Twenty-five patients joined the trial at two hospitals, and seventeen finished a full year of checks. Precise X-ray tracking showed the plate group twisted far less by week fifty-two. Shift along the bone and daily function scores did not differ. Five patients needed new surgery. The authors say the gain in hold may not change daily outcomes.
pmc-13542090:
Zhen Wen and colleagues propose a tuning method in a 2026 study. The setting is electric vehicle energy systems. Each system pairs a battery with a supercapacitor. The supercapacitor handles power bursts. That spares the battery and slows its ageing. The gain hinges on how control settings split the work.

Their method is called Decision-Flux Optimization. It searches settings by simulation. It accepts only changes that keep every trace inside safe limits. The limits cover charge, voltage, and power. On a standard driving cycle, battery stress came out lowest. Eight rival strategies scored worse. Modelling projected about 3,720 cycles before the battery faded to eighty percent.
pmc-13542390:
Mazloum and co-authors show how a single alarm signal drives pancreas inflammation toward scarring. Pancreatitis is a dangerous inflammation of the pancreas, in both sudden and chronic forms. Dying pancreas cells release interleukin-1 alpha as an alarm. That signal wakes local fibroblasts into an inflammatory state. The fibroblasts then send out chemokines that pull immune cells in. Signals named include CXCL5, CCL2, and IL-6.

Without the alarm, acute disease ran milder and chemokine output fell. The signal also primes fibroblasts to lay down scar tissue. Receptors tied to fibrosis rose under its effect. The chain links first injury to lasting damage.
pmc-13542590:
Ilaria Mancini and colleagues published a 2026 genetic study of early-onset coronary artery disease in Iranians, a population largely missing from research dominated by European and East Asian samples. The case-control study enrolled 697 patients whose artery disease was confirmed by angiography at young ages, alongside 911 matched controls. Twenty-four gene variants were tested: twelve already linked to coronary disease elsewhere, and twelve candidates from genes governing blood clotting.

Only some known variants replicated in this population, and several effects appeared only within particular ethnic groups, underlining how ancestry shapes genetic risk. A six-variant risk score separated people clearly, with each extra risk allele raising odds by about a fifth. Genetic burden also multiplied the danger from metabolic conditions far beyond simple addition. The authors argue that risk tools built on other populations cannot simply be imported into Iranian care.
pmc-13543390:
In 2026, Yang Liu and colleagues published a study of a new Trichoderma asperellum strain, called M2. It fights root rot in Angelica sinensis, a medicinal plant grown mainly in China's Gansu province. Root rot is a destructive soil disease cutting yield and quality. The fungus was tested against the Fusarium pathogen in dishes and on seedlings, and its broth was checked for destroying neosolaniol, a toxin the pathogen leaves behind.

Under the microscope, M2 hyphae wrapped around and parasitised the pathogen, whose threads collapsed and shrivelled. Applied before the pathogen, it blocked growth by up to about fifty-eight percent. Treated seedlings grew taller and heavier, with root length up about sixty-seven percent, and their defence enzymes rose sharply. The broth degraded about eighty-seven percent of the toxin in eleven days. One microbe thus offers disease control, growth promotion, and toxin cleanup together.
pmc-13543590:
Vivian Salama and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of artificial intelligence for predicting and imaging heart damage caused by radiotherapy. Radiation to the chest can injure the heart years later, and AI promises earlier warnings. Searching four databases to October 2025, the reviewers included sixty-five human studies and graded prediction work and imaging work with separate quality frameworks, pooling performance figures where that was defensible.

Thirty-one studies built risk predictors and thirty-four worked on cardiac imaging; deep learning dominated both. Predictive models reached a median accuracy measure of 0.82, and imaging models traced large heart structures well, though coronary arteries stayed hard to segment. The weaknesses were glaring: only a tenth of prediction studies checked calibration, a fifth validated externally, and most studies in both camps carried high risk of bias. Promise is real, the authors conclude, but clinical readiness is not.
pmc-13543890:
Xiang Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 study of how a gut bacterium, Bacteroides acidifaciens, protects the liver from immune-driven injury by reshaping bile acids. Mice were fed the bacterium and then challenged with concanavalin A, a standard trigger of liver hepatitis. Bile acid profiles in the liver shifted, and one acid, glycocholic acid, was pursued through cell experiments using receptor blockers and gene deletion to find its route of action.

The bacterium raised hepatic glycocholic acid, which lowered the death receptor CD95 on liver cells at both the gene and surface-protein levels. Blocking or deleting its receptor, TGR5, abolished that protection, and a transcription factor called FOSL1 carried the signal onward. Mice given the acid in drinking water for thirty-five days resisted the hepatitis with less cell death. A gut microbe's bile-acid messenger, the authors show, can disarm a liver death pathway.
pmc-13544190:
Paolo Reho and seven colleagues published this 2026 study searching for early-pregnancy epigenetic marks linked to small for gestational age births among Black women in the United States. About a tenth of American infants are born small for their stage, with doubled risk in babies of Black mothers, and the biology behind the gap is poorly understood. Using the nuMoM2b cohort from eight centres, the team scanned DNA methylation, chemical tags on DNA, in blood taken at 6 to 13 weeks of pregnancy.

The analysis covered 931 non-Hispanic Black women, 133 who delivered small babies and 798 whose babies were grown. Fourteen methylation sites differed, mapping to genes involved in placental development, blood vessel remodelling and fetal growth control. Enrichment analysis highlighted pathways for embryonic and placental function. The authors propose that methylation patterns in early pregnancy could become a biomarker for SGA risk, and a window into how the disparity arises.
pmc-13544290:
Aman Mamodia, Suman Singhal, Narayan Solanki, Harsh Mahajan, and Arun Agarwal report a rare pairing of two transfusion complications in one patient. A sixty-five-year-old man with colon cancer, on chemotherapy after surgery, got a red cell transfusion. Within three hours he struggled to breathe, and scans showed fluid in both lungs: a known lung injury from transfusion. He then grew agitated, with headache, vision changes, and odd eye movements.

Brain scans showed swelling at the back of both sides of the brain, a reversible syndrome also tied to transfusion. Both problems cleared with care, and monthly checks found no lasting harm. The paper walks through look-alike causes the team ruled out and urges alertness to such overlaps.
pmc-13544790:
Alaa Eid Alfarhan and colleagues published a 2026 case report of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a throat cancer behind the nose, already spread to bone in an eight-year-old girl. The disease is exceptionally rare under age ten, and metastatic presentation rarer still. She arrived after eight months of a growing neck mass with fever, weight loss, night sweats, bone pain, and exhaustion. The mass measured ten by eight centimetres, with enlarged nodes on both sides of the neck.

Scans showed the primary tumour with extensive nodal disease and bone metastases confirmed on bone scan, and biopsy proved non-keratinising nasopharyngeal carcinoma. She received three cycles of cisplatin and fluorouracil, then chemotherapy delivered alongside radiotherapy, and the combined approach brought the disease under control despite its advanced stage. A persistent neck lump with systemic symptoms in a child, the authors stress, should trigger consideration of this cancer.
pmc-13545090:
Jingjing Deng, Yinjie Ye, Ming Zhang, and Lunjie Lu report how a machine that scrubs carbon dioxide from the blood bought time to fix a blocked airway, in a 2026 case report. The patient suffered a flare of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term lung condition, together with a severe narrowing of the central airway. Carbon dioxide built up in the blood, and the failing breathing had to be steadied before any airway repair was safe.

The team ran the patient's blood through an external device that removes carbon dioxide, a gentler cousin of full heart-lung bypass. With breathing stabilized, doctors could place a stent through a bronchoscope to hold the narrowed airway open. The strategy worked, and the authors present the pairing as a useful bridge: control the gas problem first, then fix the airway for good.
pmc-13545290:
Choumad and coauthors report kneecap groove faults in a young girl seen on MRI. A 9-year-old girl had front knee pain and gait trouble. She had no trauma and no prior kneecap dislocation. Adult scan cutoffs may mislead in growing children.

MRI showed a shallow groove at just one millimeter deep. The groove angle was wide at 164 degrees. Her kneecap shape and height ratio were also off. Those last two signs were read with care in a child. The team joined many measures for one sound verdict. Age-aware reads can dodge false calls in children.
pmc-13546590:
Jiyang Li and colleagues used a national cancer registry in 2026 to study mucinous adenocarcinoma of the colon and rectum. They asked whether this mucus-producing subtype carries a worse outlook than the conventional form after curative surgery. Their cohort held 69,335 patients with stage I to III disease treated between 2010 and 2022. At first glance the mucinous group survived less well, yet the detailed breakdown changed the picture.

The disadvantage held only in stage III disease, and only among patients who received chemotherapy, suggesting these tumors benefit less from standard drug treatment. Stage I and II patients showed no independent difference. In rectal cancer at stage III, patients given chemotherapy both before and after surgery lost the disadvantage entirely, which points to treatment planning rather than biology alone.
pmc-13547190:
Hang Ruan and co-authors reviewed in 2026 the double-edged role of GRP78, a helper protein that manages stressed cells, in viral pneumonia caused by influenza, RSV, and coronaviruses. Where the protein sits in the cell changes what it does. On the cell surface it helps viruses attach and enter, while inside the cell's protein factory it supports viral copying and can worsen lung inflammation.

The same protein also protects lung tissue by limiting cell death and calming overload in that factory. Drug strategies under study include small molecules that block it, larger biological drugs, indirect regulators, and natural products. The authors map these approaches and their early evidence, aiming to guide precise treatments that blunt the viral help without losing the protection.
pmc-13547290:
Sivasundaram Karnan and a large team screened 1,374 compounds in 2026 looking for something that slows cancers driven by mutant KRAS, a growth switch long considered hard to drug. The standout was nintedanib, a drug known for blocking vessel growth receptors. It killed KRAS-mutant cells more selectively than its peers and shrank such tumors in mice.

Inside the cells, the drug quieted the VEGFR2 receptor and the growth signals running beneath it. Removing that receptor exposed a chain in which KRAS activity itself depends partly on the receptor's signals, and mutant KRAS in turn raises receptor levels, forming a self-feeding loop. Pancreatic tumor samples showed the receptor abundant in most cases. The authors propose it as a fresh target for these cancers.
pmc-13547690:
Xi Wang, William Laskin, and Hao Wu reported an unusual sarcoma case in two thousand twenty-six. A man in his thirties had a mass near his adrenal gland. Biopsy showed small round cells forming rosette patterns. Two cancers can look alike under the microscope here. Strong marker staining favored Ewing sarcoma. A gene rearrangement test confirmed that diagnosis.

After chemotherapy, surgery removed the tumor. Most of it now resembled a different nerve tumor type. A minor part kept the original sarcoma look. Such treatment-driven maturation is rare in adult Ewing cases. Pathologists must not let the changed look mislead them. Original markers settle the true identity.
pmc-13547790:
Xiaohui Li and fourteen co-authors propose a leaner design for materials that carry oxygen ions, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Such solids power fuel cells, sensors, and gas separation, but most rest on heavy atoms in stiff frames. That makes them heavy and slow, and hard to improve.

Their idea builds everything from the smallest working unit: a boron atom ringed by three oxygens. A test material made of these lone units carried oxygen ions well at high heat and stayed strong and stable. Missing oxygens were held in paired units rather than lone broken ones. Ions moved by constant exchange between the two unit forms. The authors offer the recipe as a general route to light electrolytes.
pmc-13548090:
Zoë Pipa and Newton Howard review the link between Crohn's disease and depression in a 2026 paper. Depression is common in Crohn's, a long-term gut inflammation, and it tracks with worse flares, more hospital stays, and poorer quality of life. The authors look beyond the burden of illness to the gut-brain axis, the two-way network joining gut and brain.

pmc-13548490:

pmc-13548590:

pmc-13551690:

pmc-13551790:

pmc-13552890:

pmc-13553590:
Zhang and colleagues publish a cleaned-up record of how the built environment changed across the Global South. pmc-13554090:

pmc-13554790:

pmc-13554890:
Sapna Kumari leads a ten-author team unravelling clotting chaos after heart bypass surgery in a sixty-eight-year-old man in a 2026 case report. pmc-13554990:
Hot race days slow marathon runners, and a warming climate will bring more of them, so knowing who suffers most in heat is practical knowledge. pmc-13555990:

pmc-13556090:

pmc-13558290:

pmc-13558790:

pmc-13558990:

pmc-13559690:

pmc-13560290:

pmc-13560490:

pmc-13561090:

pmc-13562690:

pmc-13563790:

pmc-13563890:

pmc-13564890:

pmc-13565390:

pmc-13565490:

pmc-13566290:

pmc-13569090:

pmc-13569690:

pmc-13570590:

pmc-13570790:

pmc-13572390:

pmc-13573490:

pmc-13573590:

pmc-13574590:

pmc-13575090:

pmc-13576790:

pmc-13578290:

pmc-13578690:

pmc-13579490:

Patients with treatment-resistant depression, post-traumatic stress, anxiety disorders, or obsessive-compulsive disorder each received two ketamine doses and an active control in a blinded crossover design. The disorders differ on the surface but share an internalizing core, so the team analyzed them side by side.

Both doses, half and one milligram per kilogram injected into muscle, beat the control on each disorder's own rating scale. Effects peaked a day after dosing and shrank by one week. The higher dose did no better than the lower, and no disorder responded more than another. A narrow, upside-down-U dose curve is their proposal.
pmc-13579890:
Qiuhui Jiang and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on a blood index that flags high-risk early-stage lymphoma of natural killer and T cells. This cancer behaves very differently between patients, and early-stage cases lack sharp prognostic tools. The team built an index, CTI, from three routine labs: an inflammation marker, blood fat, and blood sugar.

They reanalyzed 166 early-stage patients from a multicenter trial. High CTI values meant clearly worse survival, rising in a straight dose pattern. High-CTI patients also showed more fever-type symptoms and higher stress markers. Animal work and lymphocyte checks probed the biology. A final model combined the index with body mass and a blood protein, and sorted risk well in internal tests.
pmc-13579990:
Patrick Weldon and colleagues chart who survives thyroid cancer at an urban safety net hospital, in a 2026 study. Registry records covered 336 patients diagnosed from 2000 to 2023, most of them women and most under fifty five. The well differentiated form of this cancer usually carries a good outlook, which makes survival gaps stand out.

Five year survival ran worse for patients over fifty five, for White patients, and for those on Medicaid. Death risk also ran higher for men. The White patient result cuts against national patterns, a surprise the authors flag plainly. Coverage type split the group into rough thirds across Medicaid, private, and public plans. The team calls for a closer look at what drives the local gap, so fixes can target the right group.
pmc-13580590:
Hammad Syed and co-authors build, in twenty twenty-six, a reference atlas of the zebrafish eye as it grows. Zebrafish are widely used to model human eye disease. Their retina has a high-acuity zone, a patch built for sharp vision, much like the human fovea. No stage-by-stage atlas of normal growth existed. The team used enhanced micro-CT scans, tiny three-dimensional X-rays, to map the eye at five larval stages, from three to eighteen days after fertilization.

They tracked the light-sensing layer, the lens, and the whole eye. That layer thickened in the zone's expected region by day five. Growth came in four phases, mixing fast layer growth with matched growth. The eye's shape shifted from nose-heavy to temple-and-below heavy over time.
pmc-13581590:
Asor and co-authors watch one virus-like shell build up, part by part, in real time. Cell build-up by self-join is a base rule of live form. Virus shells are the stock case for that rule in labs. Yet the paths and pace of shell growth had stayed out of view. The team pairs mass light checks with a trap for lone bits. That pair tracks each shell as it forms, at part scale.

Weak, flip-back links steer the build, the team finds. Those links let the shell test and pick a few closed mid forms. Shifts in pace, set by shell shape, pace the whole build. Each step then locks in as a one-way pass in time. Gaps in time split the first closed forms from the last.
pmc-13581990:
Sakrapee Paisalnan, Yashar Moshfeghi, and Frank Pollick scan the brain while people hunt for information, to find where gains in knowledge register. When we are unsure, we seek facts until we have enough. The team used Shannon's information theory to score, tile by tile, how much an image gave away. Nineteen volunteers in the scanner viewed image tiles one by one and signaled when a caption matched the picture.

Two brain patterns tracked information gain in different ways. One set of regions, in the right parietal and left intraparietal areas, rose in step with the gain, as if tallying the evidence in hand. A second set, spanning both sides of the parietal lobe with frontal and visual areas, peaked at middling gains. That second pattern fits a system that weighs what has been gathered against what the task expects.
pmc-13582790:
Bin Ke and colleagues present a 2026 study of a long RNA strand called LINC00323 in non-small cell lung cancer, the most common form of lung cancer. The strand is found at high levels in tumors, and patients with more of it tend to do worse. The group asked how it helps tumors grow and form new blood vessels, a process tumors need to feed themselves.

Tests on tumor tissue and on lung cancer cells showed that raising LINC00323 sped up cell growth and vessel growth, while lowering it slowed both. The strand works by holding on to a protein named CDC5L and keeping it stable, which switches on two growth pathways. Tiny parcels sent out by cancer cells also carried the strand to vessel-lining cells.
pmc-13583190:
Ayşegül Özdoğan Bircan and colleagues measured central sensitisation, a state where nerves overreact and pain signals run loud, in Behçet's disease. Behçet's is a relapsing vessel inflammation with wide-ranging symptoms, and whether this state tracks with mood, sleep, and disease scores was unclear. Their one-time study compared 99 patients with 67 healthy controls using a sensitisation checklist with a cutoff score of 40.

This state appeared in 39.4 percent of patients versus 3.0 percent of controls. Those with it carried higher anxiety, depression, pain, disease scores, limits, and sleep trouble, and lower quality-of-life scores. Only depression flagged this state on its own in checked models. The authors link the state closely to mood factors rather than disease scores alone, while noting the design cannot prove cause.
pmc-13583490:
Jonathan Bricker and co-authors lay out a trial of a culturally adapted quitting app for Native smokers, in a 2026 protocol paper. American Indian and Alaska Native adults quit commercial cigarettes at about half the rate of other groups. Distance, underfunded clinics, and few culturally fitting programs all shrink access to proven help. The trial tests IndigeQuit, a phone app adapted with and for these communities, in a randomized design.

A phone-based program can reach people far from any clinic, if it speaks to their lives. The protocol details recruitment, adaptation, and the outcomes that will judge success. If the app works, the same adaptation playbook could carry other health programs into communities that standard services keep missing.
pmc-13583690:
For a heart attack with no ST rise, guidelines say start the second antiplatelet drug after angiography, not before. The trials behind them had fast angiography, unlike British practice. One UK centre then stopped routine pre-treatment. It compared one thousand two hundred nineteen patients before the switch with one thousand two hundred eighty-seven after it. The median wait for angiography was three point six days.

After the switch, in-hospital STEMI rose from zero point four percent to one point seven percent. The adjusted odds ratio was four point four zero. Bleeding that called for action fell from zero point nine percent to zero point two percent. The harm of skipping pre-treatment grew with longer waits. The authors argue the guideline's balance of risk and gain shifts where waits for inpatient angiography run long, as they do across the UK.
pmc-13584290:
Minxuan Hu and colleagues uncover a self-feeding loop that fuels asthma in this 2026 study. Asthma involves long-term airway inflammation, and the cells lining the airways help drive it. The team focused on lactylation, a chemical mark placed on histone proteins when cells burn sugar quickly and release lactate, a waste product of that burning.

Samples from patients and cell studies showed both sugar burning and the mark, called H3K18la, running high in asthma airways. The mark sat on the control region of a gene named CSF1R and switched it on harder, which set off a signaling loop that kept inflammation going. Blocking sugar burning or the mark-making step calmed the response, while adding lactate made it worse. The authors name this loop a fresh drug target.
pmc-13584590:
Haarmann and co-authors review institutional conflicts of interest in health research on humans. Personal conflicts draw much attention, but conflicts held by institutions have been studied far less. A hospital or university that funds, hosts, and profits from research may face split loyalties.

The scoping review followed JBI guidance for mapping a wide literature. It focused on conflicts that arise when a research group is affiliated with a healthcare provider. The team charted how such conflicts are defined, disclosed, and managed. The map shows where clear rules exist and where practice still relies on goodwill.
pmc-13584790:
Kuan Wu and five co-authors improve prediction of carbon monoxide buildup in mined-out coal areas, an early warning of spontaneous combustion, in a two thousand twenty-six mining safety paper. Existing forecast models were inaccurate, slow, and poor at generalizing.

Their hybrid couples a random forest with cuckoo search optimization, replacing hand-tuned parameters with adaptive global search. Trained on monitoring data from one working face of the Tiejishan Coal Mine, the model cut error measures by roughly twelve and twenty-four percent against a plain random forest. Training ran about seventy-five percent faster as well. Predictions landed within about seven percent of on-site readings, supporting practical early warning.
pmc-13585890:
Eric Luiz Domingos and colleagues build a fast test for a fungal skin disease in cats in this 2026 study. The disease, sporotrichosis, spreads to people and is common in Brazil, while standard lab checks are slow and costly. The team read blood plasma with an infrared light method that leaves a chemical fingerprint, then trained computer models to sort infected from healthy cats.

Seventy-five cats took part, sorted by fungal culture as the trusted standard. Several models sorted the training cats almost perfectly, and the toughest checks, leaving one cat out at a time or testing a fresh set, still scored well. The telling parts of the fingerprint sat in zones tied to sugars and fats, which mirror the body's response to infection. The authors see a quick, low-harm test that fits a One Health view of animal and human care.
pmc-13587190:
Jiwon Jung writes on forecasting the future of children born with malformed kidneys or urinary tracts in this 2026 piece. Such defects, grouped under the name CAKUT, are the top cause of long-term kidney disease in children in rich countries. Pregnancy scans can spot them from about the middle of pregnancy, yet a scan picture alone predicts a child's kidney future poorly.

Jung discusses a study of 55 infants followed from before birth through their first year, and sets it against larger cohorts. Kidney tissue defects, where the filtering units form badly, carried far higher rates of chronic disease than defects in the drainage plumbing alone. Early warning signs across studies included small kidneys, extra defects, early birth, and low birth weight. The message is that risk sorting must blend the scan with what follows after birth.
pmc-13589090:
Chrissy Liu and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a gene-guided drug pair for a rare womb cancer. Uterine carcinosarcoma is harsh, and a common gene flaw in it, ARID1A, may open a weak point. Two drugs that strain DNA repair could hit that weak point as a pair. A woman of 54 with stage IIIB disease carried the flaw. Her cancer spread to one lung spot soon after first-line care.

She took the pair in three-week cycles off label. After four cycles, scans showed a full response. She stays in remission, with clean blood marks and no tumor DNA found. Blood platelet counts fell hard at times but recovered. One case can not prove a therapy, yet it earns the pair a formal trial.
pmc-13589190:
Yanni Zheng and seven co-authors compare the roles of Schwann cells in injury and cancer in this two thousand twenty-six review. Schwann cells wrap and support peripheral nerves. After a physical injury, they change form and drive regrowth, a rare power in the nervous system. Tumors, though, can hijack the same helpful cells. Cancer cells recruit them to invade along nerves, a route called perineural invasion.

The review sets the two roles side by side. It also notes cases where Schwann cells seem to hold tumors back instead. Context decides which face they show. Understanding that switch could yield treatments for both nerve repair and cancer spread. The paper serves neuroscientists and oncologists alike.
pmc-13589990:
Yiqi Feng and co-authors study in 2026 whether mild cooling during surgery eases acute pain afterward. Unintended cooling is common under anesthesia, but its link to pain was unclear. They followed 229 adults having laparoscopic abdominal surgery with continuous temperature monitoring during the operation.

About a third of patients reported moderate to severe pain within a day. Patients cooled for at least thirty percent of surgery had far lower odds of such pain. Mouse experiments probed a mechanism: cooling slowed breakdown of a common pain drug by the liver. The team presents cooling as a possible lever on early pain.
pmc-13590390:
Lujun Shao and four co-authors test a simple food-health score against the standard liver score for short-term death risk in very ill liver patients. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The food score, called PNI, adds two blood values: albumin and a white cell count. Both values shift with body-wide swelling as well as with food, so the score may not add much.

Three groups of patients, in North America, in many sites, and in China, were checked. The food score sorted deaths just past chance and no better than albumin alone. The liver score did far better in each group. The authors say food risk should be gauged with tools made for that job.
pmc-13592390:
Wioleta Kitowska leads an evaluation of Koronavilkku, Finland's COVID-19 exposure notification app, against a set of performance marks. The study mixed system records with a survey of more than 4,000 people from April 2022. At its peak the app reached about half of active smartphone users. Men, people over 34, and those living alone used it less, while parents and the highly educated used it more.

Over half of users who got a code from health staff entered it, keeping alerts flowing. Yet about seven in ten positive users said no code ever reached them, a bottleneck the team flags hard. Users followed pandemic guidance more than nonusers. Kitowska and the team urge automated code delivery and steady public engagement in future outbreaks.
pmc-13592490:
Florent J M Boyer-Aymé leads a 2026 study of brief slow wave bursts on brain recordings as a signpost of hidden seizure networks. Scalp EEG often looks normal between seizures, which stalls diagnosis. The team tracked these bursts in a rat model of temporal lobe epilepsy and in patients under long term monitoring, some with electrodes inside the brain. Bursts clustered in temporal frontal networks and rose around seizures.

In rats the bursts marched in step with deep temporal discharges and answered to drugs that raise or lower seizure risk. In patients, scalp bursts mirrored spike and wave activity in the hippocampus. A look back over 137 seizures in 18 patients confirmed the rise before and during events. The team offers the marker for spotting silent deep foci.
pmc-13592790:
Kamenski-Rathmanner and colleagues report a 2026 study of pulmonary hypertension, high pressure in the lung arteries, in people with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, a lung disease triggered by inhaled allergens. The team studied two groups: patients with severe lung scarring awaiting transplant, and patients with mild disease at a rehabilitation program, who were screened on purpose. Ultrasound and catheter pressure checks tested for it.

In the severe group, ultrasound pressures ran high, and half of those measured crossed the line for likely pulmonary hypertension. In the mild group, screening confirmed the condition in only about one in twenty patients, and every confirmed case had another plausible cause. In advanced disease the pressure deserves close attention; in mild disease, a positive screen should prompt a search for other causes.
pmc-13594590:
Fejes, Szucs, and Poor test whether scanning sprays harm forensic DNA work, in work from twenty twenty-six. Three dimensional scans help record crime scenes and objects. Shiny or clear surfaces scan poorly, so sprays add a matte layer that later vanishes.

The team faked crime samples with blood drops and touch deposits on glass slides. After spray treatment, DNA was extracted and typed with a standard forensic kit. Blood samples gave all markers cleanly, with no block from the sprays. Touch samples varied a lot, as low amount DNA does, but no clear spray effect appeared. The result reassures scene teams.
pmc-13594990:
Ladislav Jedlicka, Matus Kudela, and Tatiana Kudelova list blackflies of Europe. Their work from twenty twenty-six sorts which species are real. It pulls from both first hand and second hand sources.

All named forms from Europe were put in one raw pool. Forms with no proper name were then cut from the core set. Most core forms are judged valid and well shown in Europe. A small set stays in doubt and needs more checks. Two old names were brought back as valid species. The list gives a firm base for fly work.
pmc-13595490:
Xu Qiang and co-authors publish a gap-free apricot genome and track how fruit ripening is switched on. Past apricot assemblies had holes that blocked study of fruit quality genes. Their build spans the full genome end to end at 248.3 million bases. It holds 22,786 protein-coding genes across eight chromosomes.

Gene and chemical reads across five growth stages fell into five joint modules. A map of DNA methyl marks showed wide reshaping as fruit grew. One mark class rose in gene promoters and tied to two genes that build red pigments. A regulator gene that may drive the pathway was also found and tested. Tests showed it switches one pigment gene on directly. The work lays a base for breeding better fruit.
pmc-13596790:
Pia Pennekamp and colleagues used eye tracking to test a theory of how eyewitnesses decide in police lineups. Diagnostic feature detection theory holds that witnesses compare faces. They lean on features only one person has, since shared features cannot distinguish anyone. The team checked whether gaze behavior actually follows that logic.

One hundred participants memorized twelve faces, then viewed lineups in which one feature, the nose, eyes, or mouth, had been digitally copied onto every member, making it useless for telling them apart. Eye movements showed no extra attention to the genuinely distinguishing features, and viewing patterns did not differ between lineup types or between accurate and mistaken witnesses. The authors conclude that whatever witnesses do with shared features, they do not appear to do it through overt visual attention, which trims one proposed mechanism of the theory.
pmc-13597090:
Serap Öner and Eylül Tutar surveyed 253 midwifery students about how they perceive accreditation, the outside quality stamp on their degree program, and what shapes their view. Students filled in forms on their knowledge of quality checks and accreditation, and a scale for how favorably they view it.

Views sat at the middle. Two factors did the real work. Students who knew more about accreditation viewed it more positively. Those willing to take part in the process viewed it more positively still. Together the pair explained about seventeen percent of the differences between students. Year of study and joining research events made no difference. The authors conclude that goodwill toward accreditation grows from understanding and involvement rather than seniority. They urge weaving structured teaching on quality systems into the course plan. That would build a lasting quality culture.
pmc-13598890:
Luiz Alexandre Silva de Paula Soares and colleagues polled vape use in doctors, trainees, and med students at a big hospital in Amazonas, Brazil. Just 36 people took the half-set poll, mostly young women med students aged twenty-one to thirty. Know-how on vapes and their harms hit 91.7 percent.

Yet sixteen people said they vaped for fun. The gap from know-how to deeds, most of all in soon-to-be health staff, calls for school-led lessons and stop plans aimed at this group. The small group bars broad claims, but the trend fits wide worry on vape use in young adults up north in Brazil.
pmc-13599090:
Qi Wu and co-authors sequenced the complete chloroplast genomes of twenty-three Gastrochilus orchids, a genus prized in gardens and traditional medicine, to chart how these compact genomes evolve. Their 2026 comparative study describes each genome's structure, gene content, and repeat landscape in detail.

Every genome kept the classic four-part layout and the same 120 genes. Yet a set of ndh genes kept decaying. They turned into pseudogenes or vanished across species. The authors link the pattern to life in dim forest understory. There, those photosynthesis helpers matter less. Ten highly variable regions and eight genes stood out as candidate identification markers, and two genes carried marks of positive selection. Family trees built from the full genomes split the genus into four well-supported branches. The authors call the framework the most complete yet for Gastrochilus, while noting the adaptive story needs experimental proof.
pmc-13599690:
Cory Shulman, Danielle Bitton, and Zili Nir study 110 autistic children in 2026. They ask how daily living skills and sensory responses relate to behavior problems, and whether those links differ for girls and boys. Parents and caregivers rated each child's adaptive functioning, meaning everyday skills like communication and self-care, plus sensory processing and emotional or behavioral difficulties. The children averaged about 86 months old: 50 boys and 60 girls.

Girls showed more behavior problems, both inward kinds like anxiety and outward kinds like acting out. Boys showed larger sensory processing differences. The patterns of association split by gender: among girls, stronger adaptive skills tied to fewer behavior problems, while among boys, sensory differences tied to behavior problems instead. Formal moderation tests confirmed gender changed the adaptive-skills link. Support plans, the authors argue, should weigh these different pathways for girls and boys.
pmc-13600190:
Tommaso Rondini and colleagues published a 2026 study of bitter taste, genes, and eating habits in two hundred Italian adults. People differ in how strongly they taste a bitter test chemical, partly because of variation in a taste-receptor gene. Whether that difference shapes everyday food choices has been unclear, so the team tested it directly.

Participants gave saliva samples for gene testing, rated the bitter chemical on a labeled scale, and answered questions about food preferences, Mediterranean diet habits, and exercise. Linking the three measures in the same people lets the researchers see whether being a strong bitter taster really changes what lands on the plate.
pmc-13601890:
Wilson Lim and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-six, how ways of handling emotion shape responses to sad or upsetting videos. Two tactics are compared. Self-distancing means viewing your feelings from a step back, like an observer. Self-immersion means plunging into the feelings as if reliving them. Forty-five people watched negative and neutral videos in short blocks. They were cued to just watch, distance, or immerse. The team recorded their rated feelings, the emotion words they chose, and body signals such as heart and breathing rates.

Distancing softened felt emotion, and immersion heightened it, as predicted. Distancing cut fear words in free labels. It had less effect on words for disgust, sadness, and anger.
pmc-13602290:
Annalise Miner and colleagues asked whether soccer heading plus head injury together raise Parkinson's risk in former players. Past work studied repeated head impacts and traumatic brain injury separately, with mixed results, yet combined lifetime trauma may predict better. Their cross-sectional study drew on 1,231 Fox Insight participants averaging 66 years old, 278 of them soccer players, comparing Parkinson's reports by soccer play and injury history.

Soccer players with brain injury involving loss of consciousness faced about 2.6 times the odds of Parkinson's versus non-contact athletes without injury, and a hazard ratio of 1.47 for earlier diagnosis. No such combined effect appeared for milder injury histories. Miner and colleagues conclude cumulative head trauma raises Parkinson's risk and lowers onset age.
pmc-13603590:
Ed Siegwart, Ajay Mistry, and John George report in 2026 on new uses for an approved asthma drug called zafirlukast. Drug resistance is rising, and few new antibiotics are in development, so reusing known safe drugs is one way forward. The team tested the drug against a range of bacteria, including resistant staph strains.

The drug killed some bacteria on its own and made several existing antibiotics work better when paired with it. Staph strains forced to resist the drug became sensitive again to a class of antibiotics they had once resisted. Gene checks pointed to a bacterial enzyme as the likely target, one that no approved drug yet blocks. Further chemistry work would still be needed before clinical use.
pmc-13604090:
Alaeddin Koska, in a solo review from twenty twenty-six, asked how smart industry tools help copy nature at scale. The topic is biomimetic design: forms drawn from living models. The worth of such design rests on a plain test. Can the living trick be turned into a thing that can be made, checked, scaled, and traced in use? Koska read the field from a production manager's view.

The base held fifty full texts picked with care from a big index. Each was coded for its living model, design rule, tech, material, and make path. Gains and proof levels were read too. Readers in design learn which Industry 4.0 tools carry a nature trick from lab to line.
pmc-13604790:
Alessandro Giacomoni and five co-authors ask how to treat liver spots that vanish. Their paper from twenty twenty-six deals with bowel cancer spread to the liver. Strong drug care can make a spot fade from scans.

A faded spot may still hold live cancer, or may not. Cutting out each old site can waste good liver tissue. The team weighs marking, watch plans, and treating the old site. They propose heat care first for a few small high risk spots. Choice should turn on the chance a spot is lost later.
pmc-13605090:
Ruijia Jin and colleagues count lung injuries after total body irradiation for bone marrow transplant in the modern era, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Radiation conditioning saves high-risk blood cancer patients but can scar lungs. The feared non-infectious form, idiopathic pneumonia syndrome, struck twenty patients, eighteen percent of the cohort, split before and after the hundred-day mark.

Rates matched older published cohorts despite modern care. No clinical or radiation factor predicted who developed the syndrome. Two survival findings stood out: early lung infection cut overall survival, in adjusted landmark analysis too. Paradoxically, acute graft-versus-host disease was independently tied to better survival, perhaps marking a graft active against the cancer. The authors close on the infection warning: lungs that infect early after transplant doom disproportionately.
pmc-13607290:
Ekaterina Finkina and five co-authors review the fungi the World Health Organization ranks as critical priority threats. Their twenty twenty-six review covers four species, among them Candida albicans, Candida auris, Aspergillus fumigatus, and Cryptococcus neoformans. These fungi kill many patients with invasive infections, and drug-resistant strains are spreading.

Only four drug classes form the standard arsenal, and resistance to them is rising while new approvals lag. The review explains the molecular routes to resistance for old and new drugs. It surveys counter-moves: drug pairs, repurposed drugs, targeted delivery, antibiofilm tactics, and immune therapy. A long section weighs antifungal peptides from plants, animals, and microbes as a fresh source.
pmc-13607890:
Murat Firat and four co-authors predict visual field results with deep learning in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Glaucoma slowly steals side vision, and care depends on mapping what a patient still sees. The standard map is a long, tiring test. The team asked whether eye scans could predict its results. They used four kinds of OCT scan images plus patient and disc measures. Nearly nine hundred eyes from five hundred ninety-one patients took part.

They tested three designs: one eye alone, both eyes fused, and a design where the fellow eye refines the answer. The question was whether the second eye's data truly helps. Such prediction could shorten testing and flag change sooner. Eye specialists who manage glaucoma are the audience.
pmc-13608090:
Yuhei Komaki and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six physics study of a vibration feature in volcanic glass. All glasses show a puzzling extra vibration, called the boson peak, at terahertz frequencies. Obsidian, a natural volcanic glass, was measured with time-of-flight spectroscopy.

Its boson peak sat slightly lower in frequency than that of pure silica glass. Metal ions in obsidian likely loosen the silica network, shifting the peak. Its coupling between light and vibration was far stronger than silica's. Charge fluctuation values resembled those of sodium-bearing glass. The results link glass chemistry to this universal vibration.
pmc-13608290:
Luyi Xu leads a nine-author team studying how fear of progression moves through couples after a stroke. Self-care after stroke is often poor, and spouses carry much of it, so the team treated recovery as a two-person system. Between August 2024 and March 2025, 384 patient-spouse pairs completed questionnaires on fear of progression, daily self-care, and the spouse's contribution. A moderated network analysis mapped how each dimension pushed on the others, and whether the patient's sex changed the wiring.
