Fear dimensions within each partner, and self-care dimensions across the pair, pulled positively together. Fear and self-care pulled negatively on each other in both directions. Sex mattered: male patients' fear related negatively to their wives' fear, while female patients' fear rose with their husbands'. Wives' fear damaged their caregiving contribution more than husbands' fear did. The authors translate this into tailored advice for each couple type.
pmc-13609090:
El Ahmadi and coauthors review a dry-land herb prized in folk medicine. The herb holds strong plant compounds with wide effects. Its oils vary by plant part, place, and season. Past work on the herb is spread across many small studies.

The review joins facts on oil makeup and pull-out methods. It also sums up lab tests of germ, pain, and mood effects. Harms and safe dose get full weight in the review. New uses in drugs, food, and farm goods are mapped. The team calls for shared test rules to make results match across labs.
pmc-13609290:
Siyuan Wang, Panpan Huang, and Ping Lu published a fungal study in two thousand twenty-six on how grey mould edits its genes while infecting plants. Botrytis cinerea attacks many crops. Alternative splicing lets one gene make several message versions, which may help the fungus adapt to each host.

The team compared splicing during infection of tomato and strawberry. They found over one thousand seven hundred splicing events across more than one thousand genes. Shared events clustered in gene-control and signalling roles. Host-specific events had their own role patterns and swung more strongly over time. The introns involved were longer than usual but kept standard splice marks. The fungus runs both a shared and a host-tuned programme.
pmc-13610190:
Guang Hu and co-authors present a 2026 review of how radiation reshapes carbon based materials. Radiation was long seen as a source of damage to these materials. Fresh proof shows that doses set with care can instead tune flaws, surfaces, and pores to gain useful traits.

The review covers four material families: graphene forms, carbon nanotubes, carbon fibers, and porous carbons. Each family reacts in its own way, from new gaps and surface groups in graphene to cross links between tubes. Fibers gain better grip in mixed materials, and porous carbons change how they soak up matter. The authors build a frame that links starting shape and dose to the final use. They also name open tasks, such as exact dose choice.
pmc-13610390:
Muidh Alheshibri studies how laser pulses reshape zinc oxide nanorods in water, in a research paper from 2026. Zinc oxide is a widely studied semiconductor with useful traits. Laser treatment in liquid can change particle shape after making, but links between laser settings and shape change are hard to pin down.

Rods made by a water-heat method were treated for thirty or ninety minutes. Images show rods partly reshaped at the shorter time. At the longer time, they became near-round, well-spread particles. The core crystal form stayed the same, with no new phases. Grain size grew with treatment. The work gives a clean, additive-free route to tune particle shape.
pmc-13610590:
Sasithorn Khawprapa, Nuttaset Manimmanakorn, Yohei Otaka, and Jittima Saengsuwan test, in a 2026 trial, whether magnetic pulses to the arm can ease stiffness after stroke. Many stroke patients are left with a tight, overactive arm. The method, repetitive peripheral magnetic stimulation, is painless and works from outside the body. The team ran a double-blind trial against a sham treatment.

Thirty-two patients with strong elbow stiffness took part, half in each group, on top of standard rehabilitation. The real treatment cut stiffness more than sham by the end of the course, on a standard clinical scale. Two weeks later the edge was gone. Muscle stiffness measured by ultrasound, arm function, and daily-living scores showed no clear group differences. The authors call the benefit real but brief.
pmc-13611790:
Maria Rogalidou, Konstantina Dimakou, Kalliopi Stefanaki, Amalia Patereli, and Alexandra Papadopoulou report a baby whose severe diarrhea from birth traced to a rare gut disorder, in a 2026 case report. The girl, admitted at 53 days old, passed ten to twenty watery stools a day and fell below the third weight percentile. Feeding changes and a full stop of gut feeding did not help. A gut biopsy showed the tufted surface cells that name congenital tufting enteropathy.

Genetic testing found two altered copies of the EPCAM gene, one from each parent. Fed through a vein, she battled line infections, gallstones, and pancreas inflammation that needed surgery. She later tolerated small feeds but stayed dependent on vein feeding, growing normally with support. The authors stress pairing biopsy with gene tests in such infants.
pmc-13612090:
Alvaro Pérez-Collar, Carlos Velasco, Javier Bezos, and Jose Luis Izquierdo-Garcia offer a two thousand twenty-six review of magnetic resonance metabolomics in veterinary medicine. The technique reads small-molecule patterns in body samples. Animal medicine has adopted it fast over the last decade.

The review covers cancer, infection, breathing, gut, kidney, hormone, and muscle disease. Across areas, the method repeatedly finds disease-linked chemical shifts. Those patterns reveal how diseases work and suggest test markers. Barriers include natural variation between animals and uneven standards. The authors chart what clinics need before routine use becomes practical.
pmc-13612390:
Jason Smucny and colleagues compared resting brain scans of people with early psychosis against healthy controls from a large brain project. They measured how strong the slow natural fluctuations are in each brain area, a signal tied to local activity.

The study covered 109 people with early psychosis and 55 healthy controls, all scanned while resting. Fluctuation strength ran clearly lower in the movement and touch cortex of the psychosis group. Weaker signal there matched poorer hand dexterity and weaker thinking scores in the same patients. That quiet area also linked more strongly than usual to the cerebellum, the anterior cingulate, and the insula, Smucny reports.
pmc-13614190:
Svyatoslav Kondrat and co-authors review low-dimensional ionotronics, a field where ions and electrons control each other in devices, in work published in 2026. The field covers energy storage, sensing, water cleaning, and computing that mimics the brain. Its roots reach back over a century, though the name is new.

The review focuses on electrodes built from thin materials such as graphene, carbon tubes, and layered compounds. In such thin systems, the layer where electrode meets fluid behaves in unusual ways. Ions may be squeezed into a few layers, which changes how they move and store charge. The authors explain the physics that sets performance in these systems. They aim to give readers a clear, broad view of a fast-growing field.
pmc-13614290:
Grisell Díaz Leines and six co-authors published a software protocol paper in twenty twenty-six on PDBe PISA, a service that analyzes how proteins in a structure touch and assemble. Interfaces decide much of what proteins do and offer drug targets. PISA has long been the standard analysis tool, and the European Protein Data Bank now exposes it through a new programming interface.

The updated software expands the interface data for each assembly and lets users query selected assemblies efficiently instead of whole files. The team serves the results as JSON with each weekly data bank release. Their protocols walk users through the interface step by step. The paper is a practical guide for structural biologists mining interaction data at scale.
pmc-13614990:
Emma McCarthy leads a team reviewing in 2026 how diet and supplements affect iron status in active women of reproductive age. Iron shortage affects an estimated 15 to 35 percent of female athletes, draining energy and performance. Searching five databases through March 2026, the team gathered intervention trials that tested food-based plans or supplements and measured at least one iron marker in the blood.

Pooling the trials showed that iron pills in the form of ferrous sulfate raised blood iron stores in a clear way. The review also weighed other diet routes and tracked effects on performance and inflammation marks. For coaches and clinicians, the combined results sort which eating strategies genuinely move iron levels and which rest on habit, helping active women treat a common and fixable problem.
pmc-13615690:
Gillian Clifford and four co-authors published a study in 2026 on the feeding machinery of a tiny ocean hunter. Diplonemids are single-celled swimmers that swarm through the seas, yet how they eat was largely a black box. Their feeding tube sits beside the pocket where their two tails emerge, braced by protein rods.

Using a swelling microscopy method that enlarges samples for viewing, the team placed seventeen proteins at parts of the feeding and tail apparatus. Some matched proteins known from a parasitic relative, while others marked parts unique to this group. Two familiar checkpoint proteins turned up on the bracing rods, a surprise worth follow-up. The map lays groundwork for explaining how these plankton catch their food.
pmc-13616090:
Ouso and Pollastri build in 2026 SCL2205, a benchmark dataset for predicting where inside a cell a protein ends up, a task called subcellular localization. They argue that flashy scores in this field partly rest on data leaking between training and testing sets.

Built from the UniProt protein knowledgebase with careful preprocessing, manual label mapping, and strict separation of similar sequences, the dataset targets trustworthy evaluation. On independent test sets, models trained on SCL2205 beat state-of-the-art baselines by up to about eleven percentage points on a precision-recall measure. The largest gains came beside modern protein language models. The team also measured the hidden problem directly: standard similarity-based expansion of training data leaked at a rate of roughly five percent. The dataset is openly licensed.
pmc-13616290:
Shujuan Cao, Chunping Ren, Jing Qin, Xiujuan Wang, and Xiaoming He show how the choice of linker in an organic battery cathode can unlock a second electron per unit and lift performance. Their cathodes build on phenothiazine, a molecule that gives up electrons at a high voltage, prized for lithium-organic batteries. Single-electron use caps the stored charge, and the small molecules tend to dissolve into the battery fluid, shortening life.

Chaining the units into three polyamide polymers fixed the dissolving problem and turned the linker into a design lever for light, charge, and ion flow. The benzene-bridged version balanced those traits best and ran two reversible electron steps. Smarter links, the study shows, can matter as much as the active molecule itself in organic battery design.
pmc-13616590:
Kryštof Prášil and colleagues test how often the automatic control of the heart and blood vessels fails in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, an inherited nerve disorder best known for weak hands and feet. They studied 36 patients with the CMT1A gene duplication, 24 with the CMTX1 mutation, and 62 matched controls. Tests covered reflex heart responses to breathing and standing, blood pressure on standing, and heart rate patterns over ten minutes lying and standing.

Autonomic failure of the heart appeared in 30.6 percent of the first group and 33.3 percent of the second, against 10.0 percent of controls. Only the duplication group had definite cases, at 11.1 percent, though the gap between disease types was not firm. Linking failure rates with neuropathy severity scores helps clinics decide which patients need heart monitoring alongside nerve care.
pmc-13617090:
Yian Wang and colleagues report a lung cancer patient whose blood marker for infection rose sharply weeks before scans showed the cancer had returned. The marker, procalcitonin, is normally used to spot bacterial infection, but it can also climb in lung cancer without any infection. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team describes a patient with advanced large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung who had responded partly to combined treatment. During remission the marker sat at a raised but steady personal baseline, far above the normal range.

The marker then jumped many-fold while scans still showed no clear regrowth, and it climbed higher still when recurrence was finally confirmed on imaging more than a month later. No infection was found at any point. The authors suggest tracking the marker over time may add an early warning for recurrence in this cancer type.
pmc-13618390:
Mugheesa Rab and five colleagues report an eighteen-year-old man whose new diabetes and pancreatitis traced to being born with most of his pancreas missing. He arrived with eight weeks of stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, excessive thirst and urination, and four kilograms of weight loss. Blood tests showed high glucose with ketones and mild acidosis, fitting mild diabetic ketoacidosis, alongside enzyme levels showing pancreatic inflammation.

CT imaging showed the neck, body, and tail of the pancreas were absent while the head was enlarged. A later duct study confirmed complete dorsal pancreatic agenesis, the failure of one early bud to develop. Insulin production ran extremely low three months on, while the usual autoimmune diabetes markers were negative, pointing to the malformed pancreas as the cause, though antibody-negative type 1 diabetes cannot be excluded. The authors advise suspecting this anomaly in young patients with unexplained pancreatitis plus insulin-poor diabetes.
pmc-13618690:
Shuangshuang Zhang and two colleagues sort nurses by their health resources and compare compassion fatigue, the emotional exhaustion of caring work, across the groups. Drawing on the salutogenic model, which asks what keeps people well, they profiled five hundred sixteen nurses by sense of coherence, perceived organizational support, and mindfulness. Latent profile analysis found natural groupings rather than imposing cutoffs.

Two profiles emerged. Just under half the nurses fell into a low-resource profile, below average on all three resources, while the rest formed a high-resource group above average on each. Compassion fatigue was twice as high in the low-resource group, roughly sixty-three against thirty-one on the scale used. Within the low-resource group, working more than four night shifts a month added to fatigue, while no job or demographic factor mattered inside the high-resource group. The authors suggest tailoring support to these profiles.
pmc-13618890:
Lei Zhu and twelve colleagues expose how circoviruses, the smallest known mammalian viruses and costly livestock pathogens, steal the host's DNA copying machinery. Their own replication protein cannot build DNA, so the team screened host polymerases and found the workhorse is POLD1, the catalytic core of DNA polymerase delta. Infection even boosts the cell's production of this enzyme.

The viral protein grabs PCNA, the sliding clamp that organizes replication, through a short motif at its tip that matches a motif on the clamp. Thereby it drags POLD1 into viral replication centers indirectly. A screened small molecule, R428, blocks this handshake for the pig virus PCV2. In cells it stopped complex formation, and in mice and piglets it suppressed viral replication and eased tissue damage. The authors propose the mechanism as a general antiviral target for circovirus diseases that vaccines cannot fully prevent.
pmc-13619290:
Lan Wang and colleagues quiz adults in Nanchong, China, on the eye disease most have barely heard of, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Age-related macular degeneration blinds older adults, yet its risk factors pile up from midlife. Four hundred twenty-four people aged thirty and up, recruited at a hospital eye clinic, took a knowledge, attitude, and practice survey. Eleven percent already had the disease.

Knowledge was thin: an average of about five points on a twenty-two-point scale. Attitudes were moderately positive, but practices lagged, the classic know-feel-do staircase with the top step missing. Statistically, knowledge fed attitude, and both fed practice, attitude partly carrying knowledge's effect. The authors argue awareness campaigns are not enough; education must hand people concrete risk-reduction habits and eye-care routines to climb that last step.
pmc-13619390:
Zhang and six colleagues trace how health beliefs reach life quality in stomach cancer through food habits in twenty twenty-six. Two hundred seventy-four patients filled validated surveys on beliefs, eating behavior, body nourishment, and life quality. A chain model tested the paths between them. Beliefs linked to life quality both directly and through the food chain.

Eating behavior alone carried about a quarter of the total link. Nourishment alone carried a smaller share. The full chain, beliefs to habits to nourishment to quality, added a further slice. Direct belief effects still held about half the total. The authors back belief based programs for future trials.
pmc-13619690:
Akira Kawai and co-authors review a century of Japanese work on bone and soft tissue sarcomas, written for the centennial of the national orthopaedic association. These rare and varied cancers are hard to diagnose and treat. In Japan, orthopaedic surgeons have long acted as both lead surgeons and overall cancer doctors for such patients.

The review spans five areas. Japanese teams set quantitative rules for surgical margins, pioneered a total spine removal technique, and reused a patient's own treated bone as graft. Research milestones include caffeine-boosted chemotherapy, peptide vaccines, virus-based therapies, and carbon-ion radiation. A national tumor registry has run for six decades, backed by several collaborative study groups. A newer frame, called onco-orthopaedics, widens care to the movement problems of all cancer patients. The authors present the surgeon-led network as a durable model for rare cancer care.
pmc-13619890:
Acupuncture at the ST36 point is used for many conditions, but its body-wide effects are hard to track. Seung-Nam Kim reanalyzed two published microarray data sets from male mice in which a bacterial toxin drove brain inflammation, with and without ST36 acupuncture. Using an empirical Bayes method with false discovery control, he looked for circulating exosomal microRNAs whose levels after acupuncture looked like the healthy control pattern rather than the inflamed one.

Eight candidates emerged: five that the toxin raised and acupuncture brought back toward normal, and three that the toxin lowered and acupuncture restored. None matched the original study's fold-change picks. The predicted target genes, 1,596 of them, clustered in MAPK, PI3K-Akt, and Wnt pathways and in nerve and synapse processes. Kim presents the eight microRNAs as exploratory markers for later study of acupuncture's peripheral effects in neuroinflammation.
pmc-13620190:
Kim and colleagues used machine learning in 2026 to sort blood pressure patterns during dialysis sessions and link them to body makeup in long-term dialysis patients. Pressure often swings during treatment. The team recorded pressure every thirty minutes across 928 sessions from 179 patients and let a clustering algorithm find natural groups, alongside body composition scans.

Three patterns emerged: a steep fall, a mild fall, and a rise during treatment, covering roughly a sixth, just under half, and a bit over a third of sessions. Body weight index did not differ between groups, but muscle measures rose steadily from the falling groups to the rising group, while body fat fell. The rising group carried the most extra water between cells. The links held after adjustment, suggesting pressure patterns could guide fluid targets.
pmc-13620290:
Nana Wang, Manrong Li, and Guozhen Zhang ran a randomized trial on waking patients from coma after severe traumatic brain injury. Eighty-six patients received one of three four-week treatments: magnetic stimulation of the scalp, electrical stimulation of a wrist nerve, or both together. The team tracked awakening rates, brainwave grades, blood flow in the head, consciousness scores, and safety.

The combined group woke at a far higher rate than either single-treatment group, with about nine in ten patients awakening. Consciousness scores climbed most in the combined group, brainwave patterns normalized most often there, and blood flow measures improved most strongly. Thinking scores among patients awake enough to test also favored the combination, though the authors flag that comparison as biased by who could take the test. No seizures occurred, and side effects were least common in the combined group.
pmc-13621390:
Thomas T Livecchi, Mark C Pierce, and Steven L Jacques released an open-source Python tool that predicts how light spreads through layered tissue, a calculation at the heart of optical diagnosis. Shining light on skin and reading the glow back can reveal blood, pigment, and water levels, but only if a model translates the signal. Gold-standard simulations crawl, while simple formulas pretend tissue has one uniform layer.

Their implementation solves the diffusion approximation for any number of layers with a fast banded-matrix method. Four hundred randomized comparisons against heavy simulations, covering one to eight layers, showed the fast model's spectra hugging the reference closely. Calculation time dropped by more than five orders of magnitude, to a tiny fraction of a second per spectrum, and error did not grow with extra layers. The authors offer the code freely for real-time tissue profiling work.
pmc-13621890:
Ahmad Wadi and three co-authors feed a tropical forage grass with composted cattle manure over two years and track what grows, in this 2026 study. The grass, a dwarf late type of Napier grass, feeds livestock across the tropics but needs steady nutrients, and the trial soil was poor. Four manure rates, from none up to a high dose, were compared in blocked field plots.

Manure lifted dry matter yield in a straight line with dose. At the top rate, first year yield rose about tenfold over the unfertilized control, and protein content climbed while tough fiber fractions fell. Digestibility of stems improved in the second year as well. The authors recommend the highest rate as a sustainable way to get more and better forage from marginal land.
pmc-13623090:
Ghada Elhadari and four co-authors review what helps or blocks the setup of triage systems in hospitals across low- and middle-income countries. Triage means sorting arriving patients by urgency so the sickest are treated first. Good emergency care could prevent many deaths in these countries, yet triage often fails to take hold.

The team searched eight databases and kept fifty-seven studies that named barriers or supports. Each factor was mapped onto a standard framework for putting new practices into place. Reports clustered most around how programmes are run day to day, the traits of the people involved, and the inner life of each facility, such as staffing, space, and leadership. Features of the triage tools themselves also mattered. The authors offer the map as a planning guide for emergency care leaders who want triage to last, not just launch.
pmc-13623390:
Beatriz Caroline Leão Lima leads a time-series study of violence by neglect or abandonment against older women in Brazil from 2009 to 2022. Neglect here means failing to give needed care, and it is among the most common yet least reported forms of elder abuse. Data came from the national notifiable diseases reporting system.

The study counted 34,860 reported cases in women aged sixty or more. The Southeast region recorded the most cases, while the Northeast showed the fastest proportional growth, rising by roughly a third each year on the trend measure used. Eight in ten episodes happened at home, and in about two thirds the offender was a family member, the very person expected to give care. Two in five victims reported repeated violence. The authors describe a rising, uneven pattern and urge stronger protection and reporting routes for older women.
pmc-13624090:
Ephraim Senkyire leads a team that sets out a review on COVID vaccine doubt. Their protocol from twenty twenty-six deals with lactating people. Such folks face extra body, mind, and social strain after birth.

Despite the worth of COVID shots, uptake in this group stayed low. The review will search four major data sets for past work. Search terms cover breastfeeding, COVID vaccine, and hesitancy in many forms. The goals are to learn views on uptake in this group. It will also map what helps or blocks their choice. Those lessons can guide future vaccine campaigns.
pmc-13624490:
Ismat Jabeen and four co-authors survey satisfaction with video-based palliative care at a Karachi hospital. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Remote care can reach patients with serious illness where specialists are few, but its quality in this field is little tested.

One hundred thirty patients and caregivers who used the virtual clinic answered a structured survey. About ninety-four percent praised access, and ninety-two percent praised care quality and doctor interaction. Most found visits convenient and cost-effective, and ninety-one percent wanted to keep them. Privacy worries stood out: forty-six percent feared a breach. Patients averaged sixty-three years old, with follow-up visits common. The authors judge remote palliative care welcome, with privacy as the fixable flaw.
pmc-13624590:
Yang Yang and colleagues charted the burden of chronic kidney disease in children and teens across South-East Asia and the Western Pacific, from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-one. They used a world disease database for people under twenty. Rates of new cases, deaths, and lost healthy years were compared by age, sex, and country wealth.

Total burden fell in both regions over the three decades. The youngest children had the most new cases, while older teens carried the most deaths and lost years. Boys fared worse than girls. Richer countries improved fastest, but some Pacific island nations kept a high burden, tied to distance and thin care access.
pmc-13624690:
Jana Radosavljevic, Deniz Bengi, and Benicio Frey review what is known about bipolar disorder in perimenopause, in a 2026 paper. Perimenopause, the years around the final period, can worsen mood in some people. Its link with bipolar disorder has been little studied, so the team searched recent literature for fresh studies. Fourteen studies from many countries met their rules.

Evidence converges that perimenopause is a window of higher risk for first onset of the disorder. In people who already live with it, depression and anxiety rose most consistently during this stage. Results for high mood episodes were mixed across studies. Hardly any evidence guides talk therapy, drug choices, or hormone treatment here. The authors urge standard staging of menopause in future work and closer clinical attention in the meantime.
pmc-13625890:
Patricia Marin-Maicas and Angela Soler-Sanchis adapt, in a 2026 study, a knowledge test about basic life support for ordinary citizens. When a heart stops outside hospital, bystanders who start resuscitation and use a defibrillator save lives, yet public training is patchy and few good tests exist to measure what citizens know.

The authors reworked an existing scale for lay adults, had experts judge every item through a Delphi process, then piloted the test. Expert agreement ran above ninety percent on all items, and every question was judged essential. Early statistics support the adapted scale, giving trainers a checked tool for spotting knowledge gaps in the public.
pmc-13626190:
Ritika Kamlesh Patel and colleagues work with family doctors in Alberta to build a care pathway for gut infections that keep coming back. Clostridioides difficile causes the most common hospital-linked infectious diarrhea, and its recurrences are hard to manage, partly because stool transplant therapy, though guideline-backed, is unfamiliar to many primary care doctors. The team of specialists first drafted a pathway, then refined it with its future users.

Family doctors joined two rounds of long video interviews, thinking aloud while they worked through staged cases with the draft in hand. Their struggles with test reading, drug choice, and referral timing surfaced as barriers and helpers, which fed straight back into the design. Building the tool with its users, the authors argue, is how a pathway earns trust and real use.
pmc-13626790:
Duc-Tin Nguyen and co-authors published a study in 2026 on preparing a powder rich in phycocyanin, the blue pigment of Spirulina algae, for use as a colorant in set-type yoghurt. The researchers sought an environmentally friendly way to extract and dry the pigment while preserving its strength.

They extracted the algae by repeated freezing and thawing in salt water. Salt water outperformed plain water on both yield and purity, and twelve cycles worked best. The extract was dried with a refractance window system at three temperatures. The lowest temperature retained the most pigment and the most intense blue color. Higher temperatures degraded the main pigment more than its pigments, although all powders dissolved and flowed. Added to yoghurt, the powders gave a blue-green coloration. The powder dried at the lowest temperature produced the strongest color, but also the most whey separation in the yoghurt.
pmc-13628190:
Akin, Özgen, and Cesur follow up girls with early periods in this 2026 single-centre retrospective study, asking what early menarche costs in height, gynecological health, and mental health. The cohort comprised 58 patients whose first periods arrived between 9.5 and 10.75 years of age, unusually early, with adult outcomes gathered from records and questionnaires.

Final adult height averaged 157.71 centimeters against a predicted target of 159.27 centimeters from parental heights, a significant shortfall at p equals 0.029 in the analysis, concentrated in girls who also had chronic illness, especially asthma. Half the group reported painful periods, about 15 percent were diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome, and 22.4 percent had psychological problems, with 15.5 percent receiving treatment for them. The authors conclude early menarche travels with more PCOS and psychiatric difficulty than peers typically report.
pmc-13628290:
Sara Cignola and two colleagues translated the Anticipated Turnover Scale, a twelve-item questionnaire measuring nurses' intention to leave their jobs, into Italian and checked whether the adapted version still measures soundly. Their test group was 168 nurses at a public university hospital in northeastern Italy.

Expert review and statistical checks supported the scale's content, and the full version held together reliably, though its content validity score was modest. A trimmed ten-item version performed better on both content coverage and internal consistency, settling into two underlying factors. Even so, the authors judge the Italian scale promising rather than finished, calling for confirmatory testing, stability checks over time, and a cut-off score before managers use it to plan retention work.
pmc-13629190:
Yaqi Li and four co-authors ask why the germ of tuberculosis can live through months of drug care that should kill it. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-six, gives a work frame in place of a loose label.

The old label, persister, names germs that hold on. But its use has spread to blur unlike causes: slow kill, stress-tuned germ states, safe nooks in the host, weak drug reach, and the power to wake back up. Each is a unlike drug task. The team's frame tracks four links: the germ's state, its nook, the drug's reach, and its fate. One drug, whose clean-out work shows all four at play, serves as the worked case.
pmc-13629790:
Miranda Hendry and two colleagues tracked how overweight and obesity spread among South Asian women of childbearing age. Their analysis pooled survey data for over one and a half million women. The women were aged fifteen to forty-nine. They lived in Bangladesh, India, Nepal, the Maldives, and Pakistan. The years ran from 2000 to 2022.

Rates climbed clearly everywhere except the Maldives. The condition clustered among urban and wealthier women. In many places it also clustered among less schooled women. National rates spanned from single digits to well over a third. Some of the fastest growth appeared among the poorest women in Bangladesh. The authors describe a marked shift in disease patterns. It carries direct weight for pregnancy health and chronic disease policy in the region.
pmc-13631290:
Wang and a large team built in twenty twenty-six a fuel cell coat that traps a film part to keep it from fouling the core. Fuel cells that swap protons need a thin film spread even for low costly metal loads. In plain cores the film clumps on the base and its acid parts foul the metal.

A lone-atom layer on the core pulls those acid parts by charge and spreads the film in an even way. The cell then gave far more peak power than a trade core. Loss af-ter long square-wave runs was a third of the trade core's loss. Film cover of the metal fell by more than half.
pmc-13632790:
Joseph Burns and Justin Zachariah report a child whose gene test suggested a rare fat-handling disorder that blood tests then failed to confirm, in work from 2026. The disorder floods the blood with plant sterols and can bring skin lumps, early artery disease, and high cholesterol readings. A faulty gene pair is the usual cause.

The child came to a heart clinic for children with one clear faulty gene copy and one variant of unknown meaning. Fasting blood fats were normal, and plant sterols had not built up. The case argues for phenotype-led care: treat what the body shows, not just what a gene panel says. The pair also back wide lipid screening for children.
pmc-13633490:
A hospital's antibiogram, the chart of which drugs still kill which germs, guides antibiotic choice but is often misread. Claudio Pérez-Oliva, Andrés Giglio, and Marcio Borges-Sa offer a seven-step reading frame called PRECISE. Each letter names an action, from judging the pathogen and its resistance pattern to checking drug levels and setting an endpoint. The frame targets doctors without infectious disease training. Three patient stories show it in use, including one where steps pull against each other.

Guideline-based first choices cut deaths by about a third, and narrowing drugs by culture cuts them further. No earlier frame walks a clinician through one report to a plan, the authors argue. Their mnemonic fills that bedside gap.
pmc-13633690:
Rui Zeng and five colleagues ran a randomized trial on the timing of a nerve block for older hip fracture patients. Confusion after surgery, called delirium, is a feared outcome in this group. The block numbs the front hip region through a space near a deep muscle. Seventy-nine patients aged sixty-five and over, all set for hip replacement after fracture, received the block either the day before surgery or one hour before.

Seventy-six patients finished as planned. Delirium appeared in a small share of both groups, slightly fewer with earlier timing, yet the gap was well within chance. Early pain scores looked better with the earlier block, but that edge faded once the many comparisons were properly corrected. One inflammation marker hinted at a calmer stress response, a lead the authors flag as exploratory. They call for larger trials before timing becomes standard practice.
pmc-13633890:
Linisa Williams and co-authors link looping negative thoughts to how the brain handles conflict in a 2026 study. Repetitive negative thinking, worry and rumination in one trait, cuts across anxiety and depression and goes with weaker cognitive control. What it does at the level of single decisions was not understood. The team puts thinking style, brain waves, and a math model of choice in one frame.

Thirty-seven people played a flanker task, answering a central cue while flankers agreed or clashed, as scalp electrodes recorded their brain signals. A standard conflict wave grew more negative in high scorers on the thinking trait. A hierarchical drift model showed their evidence gathering swung more between easy and clashing trials. Plain behavior, though, showed no gap. The mind's extra effort is invisible without the instruments.
pmc-13634090:
Junya Yokoyama and colleagues report a man whose minor leg injuries exposed a genetic vessel disease that can kill. Arterial lesions on both sides after minor trauma are rare and suggest vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, in which faulty collagen makes arteries fragile. A forty-year-old man developed pseudoaneurysms of both anterior tibial arteries after being kicked.

The right limb, with compartment syndrome, was treated by artery tying, aneurysm incision, and removal of the hematoma. The left was treated by coil embolization, a hybrid open and in-vessel approach the authors judge safe in this syndrome. Standard sequencing of the COL3A1 collagen gene was negative. But copy-number analysis by multiplex probe amplification showed a whole-exon deletion on one copy, and settled the case. Two lessons follow: hybrid technique limits treatment trauma, and copy-number testing is a must when suspicion stays.
pmc-13637590:
Yuetian Jia and colleagues chart brain-like optical computing in a 2026 review, a step beyond matrix optics toward machines that sense, decide, and act with light itself. Edge and embodied systems, from robots to autonomous vehicles, must react in microseconds to milliseconds on milliwatt budgets. They process sensor data locally to avoid delay, privacy risk, and network dependence. Electronic designs struggle here because moving data between memory and processors burns time and energy.

The review organizes the field into optical neural networks for perception, spiking optical networks for event-driven decisions, state-based networks for learning and memory, and optical memristors for plastic, in-memory storage. Each type maps loosely to a brain region. Reported designs hint at picosecond to nanosecond responses, gigabit to terabit bandwidth, and femtojoule operations. Readers get a roadmap from edge intelligence to embodied intelligence, with notes on noise, training, stability, and integration to solve.
pmc-13645590:
Zhanying Lin and six colleagues pool trial evidence on acupuncture for swallowing problems after radiation treatment for nasopharyngeal cancer, a cancer behind the nose. Radiation for this cancer often leaves patients struggling to swallow safely. The team searched eight databases through March 2026 for randomized trials. Twelve trials with 863 patients met their rules.

Patients who received acupuncture scored better on a standard water swallowing test than control groups. More of them reached a favorable swallowing status, and imaging-based swallowing scores also improved. Quality of life and nutrition measures moved in the same direction. Safety was poorly reported, so firm claims about harm are not possible. The authors describe acupuncture as a possible add-on therapy, while noting the trials were small and their methods uneven.
pmc-13645690:
Junmei Zhang and four colleagues describe seven breast cancer patients whose cancer spread to the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, a complication with a very poor outlook. All seven received an antibody-drug treatment called trastuzumab deruxtecan together with whole-brain radiation. Four also received a blood-vessel drug and chemotherapy placed into the spinal fluid. The paper pairs the case series with a review of the wider literature.

In the four patients who got the fuller combination, brain and nerve symptoms eased fast, and survival ran longer than older reports suggest for this condition. No severe or fatal side effects appeared in the group. The authors are careful to frame this as early experience from very few patients. Still, the cases give other cancer teams a concrete regimen to consider where no standard treatment exists.
pmc-13645890:
Dongha Lee and nine colleagues describe, in a 2026 case report, how a drainage shunt rescued a fifty-five-year-old woman from stubborn fluid buildup after pancreatic cancer surgery. Her cancer had first been judged inoperable, then shrank enough for surgery that removed part of the pancreas and nearby vessels. Six months later, milky lymph fluid began filling her abdomen, a problem called chylous ascites. Diet measures, drainage procedures, and repeated needle removal all failed.

After checks ruled out infection and leftover cancer cells in the fluid, surgeons placed a Denver shunt to move the fluid back into a neck vein. The buildup cleared quickly, her weight and blood protein recovered, and she left hospital safely. The shunt came out twenty-nine months later over a vein clot, yet the fluid never returned. Five years after the cancer surgery she remained alive with no recurrence, a notable salvage success.
pmc-13645990:
Voskamp and co-authors track sugar coatings on antibodies through pregnancy, in this 2026 paper. These coatings tune how the immune system behaves, and early pregnancy requires the mother's system to tolerate the growing baby. Past work showed the coatings shift toward calmer forms late in pregnancy.

The Rotterdam cohort gave blood samples from two hundred two women at five points from week nine to week thirty-two. Lab analysis measured coating traits for two antibody types. Calm-linked traits rose already in the first trimester and kept rising for one type. The authors also link early patterns to body weight, first pregnancies, and how conception happened.
pmc-13647090:
Laura Schellhas and nine colleagues search for chemical marks on DNA that track with young children's inward-turning symptoms, such as anxiety and withdrawal, in a 2026 study. Three European birth cohorts supplied blood DNA data at birth and at age six, plus mother-reported behavior at ages three and six. The analysis was run within a large pregnancy and childhood epigenetics consortium. Sample sizes ran above one thousand per analysis.

No single DNA site linked reliably with symptoms at either age. Looking at whole regions instead, the team found a handful of stretches in newborn blood tied to symptoms at three and at six, and two more in blood taken at age six. Some nearby genes had prior links to depression, including one already tied to teenage depression. The authors say bigger samples and sharper symptom measures are needed to judge whether these marks truly matter.
pmc-13647990:
Li Hong and seven colleagues report a national cross-sectional study of complementary feeding and growth among children aged zero to thirty-six months in China. Their work asks whether eating a wider range of solid foods alongside milk relates to length, weight, and weight for height in very young children.

The sample held 26,266 children from thirty-three provinces, with parents answering questionnaires posted through a maternal and child health association. Greater food diversity was linked with better linear growth in every age group, while diversity was linked with lower weight for height after six months. Iron-rich foods such as liver were rarely used, and many parents favoured supplements over varied meals, so the authors call for clearer feeding guidance.
pmc-13649290:
Tillis and co-authors study dropout in this 2026 mixed-methods study of a telehealth trial. The trial coached parents to deliver behavioral therapy to toddlers with tuberous sclerosis complex. That genetic disorder causes seizures and developmental delay. Fifty-nine children aged 12 to 39 months joined the randomized waitlist trial. The team modeled which parents did fewer sessions. They also interviewed them about why.

The models found no dominant factor. Two exploratory signals emerged, though. Children with more severe seizures did sessions at a rate ratio of 0.95 per severity step in the model. Parents who joined during the COVID era came in at 0.77 against other periods in the regression. Distance from the hospital and socioeconomic risk, classic dropout drivers, showed no link under telehealth. Interviews filled the gaps. Medical crises, competing demands, and doubts about fit or benefit drove quitting more than logistics.
pmc-13649490:
Erxinxian Bei and four colleagues asked if leg vein clots after stroke raise the risk of later seizures. Both problems strike stroke patients, and they share roots in weak limbs, swelling, and thick blood. The team reused data from more than 21,000 patients at many centres, tracked for one year after an artery-block stroke.

At first pass, patients with a leg clot had near double the odds of seizures. Once stroke severity and the brain areas hit were taken into account, the link all but vanished. Adding clot status to a risk model did not sharpen its calls at all. The authors read a leg clot as a sign of a harder stroke case, not a cause of seizures in its own right.
pmc-13649990:
Feng Yang and six colleagues show how stress inside a dangerous yeast can breed resistance to the drugs used against it. The yeast, Candida auris, spreads in hospitals and already resists many treatments. When the team exposed it to a chemical that stresses the cell's protein-folding compartment, the survivors that grew back had gained resistance to a common antifungal.

Gene activity readings showed the stressed parent cells turning up wall-building, transport, and cleanup genes while turning down protein production and energy use. Resistant survivors leaned on a pump that pushes drug out of the cell, and one isolate also raised a drug-target gene. A smaller set of survivors tolerated a second drug by thickening the cell wall with extra chitin, a wall material, through a separate route involving two well-known stress proteins.
pmc-13650490:
David Haynes and nine colleagues build a public dataset estimating, neighborhood by neighborhood, how many Americans qualify for lung cancer screening. Screening with low-dose scans saves lives, yet fewer than a fifth of eligible people get it, partly because eligibility hinges on a detailed smoking history that records and surveys usually lack.

A tool called the Smoking History Generator was woven into national surveys. It reconstructs how much and how long older adults smoked, letting the team count those who cross the twenty pack-year threshold at census tract level. The dataset can be grouped by county or state and filtered by age, sex, race and ethnicity, and current or former smoking. Health programs can use it to aim outreach where eligible people actually live, rather than guessing from clinic records alone.
pmc-13651490:
Brianna Murray and four colleagues track atrial fibrillation and blood-thinning treatment in British patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a pairing where an irregular heartbeat raises stroke risk against fragile lungs. Their primary care cohort ran from 2010 to 2022 through a national research database.

Over four hundred forty thousand patients contributed more than two million person-years, and close to thirty-eight thousand developed atrial fibrillation. Its incidence rose by roughly thirty percent across the period, running higher in men, white patients, the over-eighties, and severe lung disease. Only about two thirds of new cases started an anticoagulant within a year, although prescribing nearly tripled over the study years. The oldest and youngest age bands, non-white patients, and severe COPD cases lagged furthest behind. The authors call the gaps a target for stroke prevention research in this high-risk group.
pmc-13652290:
Albert Cahyopoetro and six co-authors test two blood markers in two thousand twenty-six as predictors of response to chemotherapy in colorectal cancer. The patients, treated in Makassar, had advanced disease and got a drug pair called CAPEOX before surgery. The markers were MTHFR and CEA, both measured in serum before treatment.

The prospective study followed thirty-six patients with stage three or four disease. Tumor shrinkage was judged from scans using standard criteria. Both markers correlated strongly with how much tumors shrank. A combined model predicted shrinkage well, and a chart built from it sorted patients with high accuracy. The authors propose the pair as a simple, low-cost tool for planning care where resources are limited.
pmc-13652590:
Pooja Gupta led a 2026 case series on giant cell glioblastoma, a rare and aggressive brain tumor subtype whose molecular signature remains poorly defined. Giant cell tumors show abnormal large cells, many multinucleated giant cells, necrosis, new vessel growth, and brisk cell division, and they rank as grade 4 tumors with poor prognosis. The team reviewed a decade of cases at one institute, from 2014 to 2023, among 256 glioblastoma cases.

Eleven cases, or 4.3 percent, were giant cell glioblastoma, with a mean age near twenty-nine and a male-to-female ratio of 1.75 to 1. All tumors sat above the tentorium, most often in the frontoparietal lobe, and all stained positive for the glial marker GFAP, with TP53 mutation in ten cases and high proliferation. The authors stress the tumor's hybrid character, sharing features of both IDH wild-type and IDH-mutant grade 4 tumors, and note its better outlook despite the grim grade.
pmc-13657390:
Mari Jawad and a large team of colleagues validate a combined tissue score for predicting colon cancer survival, checking whether it behaves differently on the right and left sides of the colon. The Tumor Microenvironment Score merges immune reaction grade, stroma percentage, and tumor budding into four groups. Two retrospective cohorts totaling over fifteen hundred patients were scored from standard stained slides.

Higher scores meant worse five-year disease-specific survival on both sides. In adjusted analysis the highest score roughly tripled risk in the first cohort. Validation showed a stronger effect in right-sided tumors. The score also stratified better than an earlier two-component version. The authors propose it as an integrative prognostic marker, especially for right-sided disease.
pmc-13672290:
Jonatan Kendler and co-authors show that removing two driver genes together blocks a T cell lymphoma in mice, in this 2026 study. The drivers, CDK6 and STAT5B, each fuel cancers, but their teamwork was unclear. In a mouse model driven by the ALK fusion, deleting both genes at once fully prevented tumors. Single-cell gene reads traced the cancer's origin to immature thymus cells at a set stage.

The double loss broke the tumor's growth path and shifted cell development. The two drivers share targets that govern cell division and death at the starting stage. In human lymphoma cells, the double deletion killed cells in a context-dependent way, hinting at a drug opening. A gene signature from the pair also marked high-risk patients.
pmc-13675990:
Heba A Ramadan and co-authors use a soil fungus to make silver nanoparticles for treating drug-resistant wound infections. Their 2026 paper targets MRSA, a staph germ that resists standard drugs. The fungus grows on decaying matter, and using it to make particles is a greener route than chemical methods.

The particles were checked with light, imaging, and X-ray tools, and came out very small and fairly stable. In lab tests, low doses stopped and killed MRSA taken from patients. Microscope views showed damage to germ walls and a sharp drop in living germs. In infected mouse wounds, treatment raised healing from a low share to near full and cut germ counts. The work joins green making with a pressing drug resistance problem.
pmc-13676690:
Alamoudi and nine co-authors test when to dose a slow sugar drug in fast-ing type one patients in this twenty twenty-six trial. Fasts at Ramadan run from dawn to dusk, which can drop blood sugar low. Guide lines urge an early dose of the slow drug, but proof was thin.

Inside, one hundred eighty-five fasters were split by lot to early or bed-time dose groups. Both groups broke fasts at near the same rate, most for low sugar scares. Low sugar hits came most in the morn hours in both groups alike. Grave lows and acid blood cases were few and near matched by group. Time in the safe sugar band sat near the same in both groups too.
pmc-13676790:
Matthias Becher, Willi Sauerbrei, and Heiko Becher study a common flaw in health data called heaping, in a paper from 2026. Heaping means values pile up on round numbers, such as ages ending in zero or five. It can come from loose recall or from hiding exact values on purpose.

The team asked how much heaping in a measured factor weakens a study's power to find true effects. They ran computer simulations with varied levels of heaping and also showed the effect in a real data set. Mild heaping cost little power and may be acceptable. Heaping into broad groups, though, cost a great deal of power. The authors advise against broad grouping when data are masked or reported.
pmc-13677390:
Ali Hassan Nawaz and co-authors pool gene data to find shared heat-stress answers across chicken tissues in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Heat waves hurt poultry health and yields, but single studies are small and clash with each other. A joint read across tissues could find the steady signals.

Eleven public data sets gave two hundred twelve samples from liver, breast muscle, and heart of heat-stressed broilers. Expression changes, network modules, and consensus filters were combined to certify hub genes. Each tissue showed its own division of labor: the liver rewired fuel pathways, muscle hit a cell-cycle brake and protein care, and the heart tuned calcium and adrenaline signaling. The atlas guides breeding and feed fixes for a warming world.
pmc-13678090:
Kiera Vassallo and a large team of co-authors present a 2026 study hunting new drug targets for a lung cancer type that resists immune therapy. Tumors with a mutation in the STK11 gene respond poorly to checkpoint drugs, the standard of care. Fresh targets are needed for these patients.

The team ran gene cutting screens in living mice and in cell dishes, hunting genes whose loss makes tumors sensitive again to immune attack. One gene stood out: MGAT1, which builds sugar chains on proteins. Removing it reversed resistance in mouse tumors with the mutation. Bench tests backed the hit, marking a new target class.
pmc-13678290:
Xiaolan Chen and co-authors build a prediction model for fungal infections in patients with chronic lung disease, in this 2026 study. People with COPD face a raised risk of fungal infection, yet clinics lack tools to spot high-risk cases early. The team reviewed records of 498 patients admitted to a Shanghai hospital between 2021 and 2023. Seventy-eight had fungal infections.

Six factors went into the final model, including blood oxygen level, a mold allergy marker, and white cell counts. The model sorted patients with fair accuracy, and repeat internal checks plus calibration tests held up well. The authors offer the tool for early flagging of high-risk patients, while noting it rests on one hospital's records.
pmc-13679190:
Anindita Sen and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six paper device that detects small molecules using aptamers wired to CRISPR machinery. CRISPR tests spot genetic material exquisitely but struggle with ordinary chemicals. Drying the whole reaction into paper removes laboratory plumbing.

One channel senses the energy molecule ATP through a signal-off design. A second, signal-on channel detects cocaine, a first for its aptamer paired with CRISPR. Both readouts ran side by side on one chip fed by passive flow. Detection limits stayed sensitive in solution and on paper. Cheap, equipment-free multiplex testing moves closer for clinics and fieldwork.
pmc-13680590:
Sarah Glick and a large consortium describe Switzerland's first national workshop for families facing inherited cancer risk, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Such family workshops are rare, though they can help patients and relatives alike. The day-long event served families with inherited breast and ovarian cancer risk or Lynch syndrome.

Over a hundred adults gathered in Bern, drawn from all three main language regions. Most carried a genetic risk themselves. Expert talks covered care and research, and small-group sessions surfaced unmet health, emotional, and learning needs. Satisfaction ran very high, and the group exchanges were prized most of all. A talk on immunotherapy drew the strongest ratings. The authors offer the event as proof such workshops work.
pmc-13684390:
Naofumi Suematsu, Alberto Vazquez, and Takashi Kozai present a 2026 study on what months of brain stimulation do to the cortex. Tiny electrodes planted in the visual cortex can send signals for future prosthetic devices. For such devices to last, doctors must know whether repeated stimulation slowly changes the tissue it touches.

The team implanted electrodes in awake mice and imaged their brains over 12 weeks. They delivered six stimulation rates and also showed light flashes to the other eye. Calcium signals and blood flow signals were tracked week by week. At 25 hertz, calcium responses grew larger and longer over time. High rates and visual input showed fading depression effects instead. Cell bodies and their fine branches followed distinct paths.
pmc-13688190:
Sasaki, Uchita, and Shimamura described a case in twenty twenty-six where expert guidance reached an endoscopy suite in real time over a high-speed mobile network. Remote coaching could spread scarce specialist skill, but live use across borders has stayed rare.

The patient was an eighty-year-old man whose severe acid reflux persisted after stomach surgery and resisted medicine. A remote expert watched sharp, low-delay video, spoke with the local team, and could pause the picture and draw on it to direct each step. The procedure, which reshapes tissue at the stomach entrance to block reflux, finished without any problems. The man went home on the fourth day. Two weeks later his symptom scores had fallen sharply, and a follow-up scope showed the reflux damage healed. The authors present the case as proof the approach works.
pmc-13688390:
Marko Dardi and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six laboratory model of fat formation using stem cells from children's fat tissue. Childhood obesity may stamp lasting molecular changes, called obesogenic memory, onto fat progenitors. Whether those changes are already built into children's cells was unknown.

Stem cells came from normal-weight, overweight, and obese children. Grown in dishes, they were coaxed into fat cells over two weeks. Fat accumulation, gene activity, and metabolic behaviour were compared across groups. The model lets researchers test whether obesity rewires progenitors themselves, shaping prevention thinking for paediatric care.
pmc-3047790:
Coutinho and Chapman review the anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing effects of glucocorticoids. These steroid drugs were discovered in the 1940s and quickly recognised for calming inflammation. Since then they have ranked among the most widely used and effective treatments for inflammatory and autoimmune disease.

Their clinical power, though, is compromised by side effects with long use. The authors gather recent developments and mechanistic insight into how the drugs act on immune cells. Better understanding of those pathways points toward safer steroids that keep the benefit while shedding harm.  Dose and duration limits in clinics reflect exactly this balance of effects.
pmc-3882890:
Proctor, Powell, and McMillen offer advice for naming and reporting rollout strategies. Such strategies are the how-to part of changing healthcare practice, and they carry central importance in this field. Yet researchers and others involved could not fully use study findings about them.

The problem is vague reporting: strategies are named without saying who acts, on what, and how often. The authors propose a reporting framework covering those elements. Precise detail lets others copy what worked and lets reviewers compare strategies across studies honestly.  Checklists in the paper name the information each rollout report should always contain.
pmc-4103590:
Bolger, Lohse, and Usadel introduced Trimmomatic in 2014, a tool that cleans raw sequencing reads. Before analysis, reads from Illumina machines often need trimming to remove adapter pieces and low-quality ends. Many tools existed, but the authors found none that met all their needs at once.

Trimmomatic was built to be flexible, fast, and correct with paired-end data, where two reads come from the same DNA piece. It chains trimming steps in the order the user chooses. Clean input reads improve every later step, from genome assembly to variant calling. The tool became a standard first pass in sequencing pipelines worldwide.
pmc-4167990:
Geeleher, Cox, and Huang presented pRRophetic in 2014, an R package that predicts how tumors will respond to chemotherapy. The team had earlier shown that response could be predicted in several separate clinical trials. Their method was trained on gene and drug response data from hundreds of cancer cell lines.

For each cell line, the method uses gene expression data paired with measured drug sensitivity. It then applies those models to a patient's tumor gene profile to forecast response. Such forecasts could help doctors choose the drug most likely to work for a given patient. The package made the method open for other cancer groups to test.
pmc-5624990:
Shaffer and Ginsberg gave an overview in 2017 of heart rate variability metrics and norms. Healthy living systems vary in complex patterns, the kind that chaos mathematics describes. Heart rate variability, or HRV, is the pattern of gaps between one heartbeat and the next, called interbeat intervals.

A healthy heart is not a metronome; its timing varies in rich patterns that reflect nervous system control. The overview explains the main HRV metrics, in time, frequency, and nonlinear forms, and gives normative values for each. Norms let clinicians and researchers judge whether a recording is unusual. HRV is used in cardiology, stress research, and biofeedback, so shared references matter.
pmc-5753190:
Simon Harding and many coauthors reported the 2018 update of the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology. The guide collects expert-checked facts about drug targets and the chemicals that act on them. It has grown from a database first built in the early two thousands.

The update adds new targets and drugs and launches a companion guide on immune pharmacology. Each entry links targets to ligands with data drawn from key papers. Drug hunters use the guide to check what is known before planning experiments. Because experts curate it by hand, users treat it as a reliable first source.
pmc-6292890:
Pramod Darvin, Salman Toor, Varun Sasidharan Nair, and coauthors reviewed immune checkpoint inhibitors in 2018. Tumors survive partly by switching on brakes that quiet immune attack. Antibodies that block those brakes produced a breakthrough in cancer care.

The review covers recent trial progress across cancer types and the uneven pattern of response. Only some patients gain lasting benefit, so markers that predict response are badly needed. The authors survey candidate markers, including tumor mutation load and immune cell patterns. Their survey helps readers see both the real gains and the open search for better selection.
pmc-6872490:
The One Thousand Plant Transcriptomes Initiative published this green plant study in 2019. Green plants number near half a million species and shape land and water ecosystems. Their family tree still had many unresolved branches.

The team sequenced the active genes of more than a thousand species chosen across the whole group. Comparing those data rebuilt relationships among algae, mosses, ferns, and flowering plants. Several long-debated splits gained strong support. The shared data set gives plant science a backbone tree for studying how traits like flowers and wood evolved. All sequence data were released openly for reuse by the wider plant science community.
pmc-6889290:
Mark Pittenger, Dennis Discher, Bruno Péault, and coauthors gave a perspective on mesenchymal stem cells in 2019. These cells, also called mesenchymal stromal cells, can form bone, cartilage, and fat. They are found in marrow and many other tissues.

The authors trace the field from early marrow studies to today's clinical trials. They stress that the cells' healing power may come more from signals they release than from rebuilding tissue directly. Naming confusion and uneven trial quality get frank treatment. The piece helps readers judge bold stem cell claims against the evidence.
pmc-7005290:
Reed Sutton, David Pincock, Daniel Baumgart, and coauthors gave an overview of clinical decision support systems in 2020. These computer systems help clinicians with complex choices at the point of care. They have evolved fast since their first use decades ago.

Modern systems are woven into electronic records and can warn, suggest, and order on the spot. Benefits include fewer errors and more uniform care. Risks include alert fatigue and blind trust in bad advice. The authors offer strategies for design and rollout that keep clinicians in charge, which decides whether such systems help or hinder.
pmc-7144090:
Richard Challis, Edward Richards, Sujai Kumar, and coauthors presented BlobToolKit for genome assembly checks in 2020. Assembling a genome from mixed DNA is confounded by contaminants. Foreign DNA can sneak in during sampling or lab processing.

BlobToolKit plots each assembled piece by its composition and likely species of origin. Contaminant pieces stand out as separate blobs that users can inspect and remove. Interactive views suit the huge assemblies of biodiversity projects. The toolkit became part of the quality routine for the Darwin Tree of Life and similar efforts. Case studies show the plots catching contamination that standard summary statistics had missed entirely.
pmc-7164390:
Jianzhong Shi, Zhiyuan Wen, Gongxun Zhong, and coauthors tested animal susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 in 2020. The pandemic virus likely came from bats, but its route into humans was unknown. Knowing which animals it infects helps science and farming alike.

The team exposed ferrets, cats, dogs, pigs, chickens, and ducks to the virus under lab conditions. Ferrets and cats caught and spread it readily, while dogs were poor hosts and farm birds resisted it. The results picked ferrets and cats as models for vaccine tests. They also warned that pets and farmed animals needed watching.
pmc-8280690:
Hannah Davis and co-authors, several of them patients themselves, characterized long COVID in 2021 by studying an international group of people still ill months after infection. Many patients with COVID-19 go on to suffer prolonged symptoms, yet few systematic studies had examined them, especially people never admitted to hospital. The team surveyed patients about the full course of their illness over about seven months.

They catalog which symptoms appear, how they ebb and return, and how deeply they cut into work and daily life. Memory problems, exhaustion after effort, and relapses triggered by exertion feature strongly in their account. The study gave early, detailed shape to a condition patients had been reporting long before medicine had a name or a plan for it.
podcast-powerfuljre-33Fc_mLqY90:
Jesse Michels returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2545, filed here under the PowerfulJRE channel. Michels hosts American Alchemy, where he interviews scientists and witnesses at the edge of accepted knowledge. His repeat visits show how central that fringe beat is to Rogan's show.

Michels digs into his latest cases, from UFO reports to inventors he says history ignored. He argues that curiosity, not credentials, should drive hard questions. Rogan compares his stories with years of similar guests and claims. The curious get another long-form trip along science's edge with a practiced guide.
podcast-tuckercarlson-sO-sy5ut490:
Car builder Casey Putsch tells Tucker Carlson why he believes the EPA wants to destroy his custom-made car. Putsch built a one-off vehicle by hand, then ran into federal rules on emissions and safety. The fight became his gearhead grievance against the regulatory state.

Putsch explains the rules he says make small builders' work nearly impossible. He argues the agencies crush craft and choice in the name of standards big makers helped write. Carlson frames it as the builder versus the bureaucrats, the state versus speed. Car lovers and libertarians get a craftsman's case in full.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-the-christ:
Readers of Punch, the London comic weekly, got a special Christmas number for 1890, opened by a picture of Mr. Punch among the planets. In the opening tale, Father Time sits in his observatory tower on a clear, starry night as the old year nears its close.

Mr. Punch enters with his dog Tobias and finds Time at work on his reminiscences, a vast work running to thousands of volumes. Their talk mixes greeting, teasing, and talk of publishers. Holiday readers get a fanciful frame tale in the paper's usual playful voice, made for the season.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-99-:
Punch for August 16, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Modern Types," number seventeen in a series drawn by the magazine's own type writer, on the Spurious Sportsman. The essay picks apart a familiar figure of clubs and country houses in late Victorian Britain.

Such a man longs to seem a great hunter, fisher, and shot, though his real trips were few and bare of success. He reads widely, listens to other men's tales, and slowly turns their feats into his own, building a bright suit of false sporting deeds. The piece grants him one excuse: few men tell of their longest shot without adding a foot or two.

Volume 99 of Punch for August 2, 1890 opens with a Highland cartoon. A beaten husband still defies his wife from under the bed. A verse address to a battalion of Guards bound for Bermuda follows. The poem scolds soldiers who had shamed their name in a row.

Quoting Juvenal on who guards the guards, the verses grant that harsh officers may have driven the men too far, yet insist that British redcoats must not copy street mobs. Discipline, called a parent who must not spare the rod, closes the appeal. A piece called "Robert's American Acquaintance" follows.

Punch dated August 23, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Novelty Up to Date," a short Scots play printed in full to test a charge of copying. The new Adelphi play The English Rose had been called unoriginal, so the magazine answers with a drama of its own, Telmah, in three short acts.

Telmah is Hamlet in Scots dress, set at the Horse Guards Parade, Elsinore, near Edinburgh. MacClaudius and MacGertrude greet the moody prince, the colours are trooped, and the ghost of Telmah's father walks on cue. The joke rests on how well readers know the source play, line by line.

Punch for August 30, 1890, volume 99, leads with a set of mock letters under the heading "Why Not Live Out of London?" a subject lately raised in the Daily Telegraph. Each writer answers the question in a way that serves his own comfort first.

One husband, signing himself One in a Thousand, urges that his wife and family move to the country. He, the bread-winner, would keep a club and a room in town. He would visit now and then. A cheesemonger named Charles Cheddar replies that he lives out of London and makes a good living out of it too. A third writer wishes everyone he dislikes would leave town.

Volume 99 of Punch for August 9, 1890 opens with "First Aid to Tommy Atkins," a letter from a former Yeomanry man who visited the Military Exhibition in London. Lame and leaning on a young friend, he asks to be taken to the battle pictures and lands instead in the open arena.

There, detachments of citizen soldiers run through ambulance drill with stretchers and simple kits, ten groups in all. The sight moves even his scoffing friend. Wishing the scene had cannon fire and bursting shells, the writer supplies them in fancy and begins a mock battle account, with a sergeant dressing the ranks and calling on Jenkins.

Punch dated December 13, 1890, volume 99, leads with number nine of Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, "The Curse of Cognac," credited to a parody author called Water Decant. His note to the editor praises the tale as a cure for too much Christmas cheer, fit to read aloud in small groups.

Chapter one finds George Ginsling alone in his rooms at Christ's College, Cambridge, after his friends have gone. Stung by a question about refusing a seat in the Trial Eights, he paces the room. He sips his seventh tumbler of neat brandy. The nightly habit, he claims, steadies him for his Greek verse.

For December 20, 1890, Punch in volume 99 offers a Voces Populi piece, "The Riding-Class," set in a bare, gas-lit riding school on a raw afternoon. Mothers and friends watch from an alcove while grown pupils wait on the tan for their horses.

Mrs. Bilbow-Kay explains that her son Robert rode well as a boy but needs lessons again, on doctor's orders for exercise. The riding master then pairs each man with a mount: the lively Shar for Bilbow-Kay, Lady Loo for Mr. Tongs, Kangaroo for Mr. Joggles, the Artful Dodger for Mr. Bumpas, and a bucking starter called Frar Diavolo for Mr. Sniggers.

Punch for December 27, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Our Booking-Office," the magazine's chatty column of book notes for the Christmas season. The Baron, its reviewer in chief, moves from French duelling terms to ghost tales and Cambridge letters in a few pages.

He praises the tale of the phrase Le Coup de Jarnac in Macmillan's Magazine. He notes two seasonable ghost stories in The Argosy under Charles Wood. He also enjoys Harry Fludyer at Cambridge. Those letters were first printed in The Granta and issued by Chatto and Windus. One novel, The Missing Member, he calls muddle-headed, and French picture books go up to the nursery.

Volume 99 of Punch for December 6, 1890 leads with "Modern Types," number twenty-two, on the Manly Maiden, drawn by the magazine's own type writer. The essay takes aim at a young woman who tries to win the title of good fellow by copying men's rough ways.

She swears, slaps backs, and scorns peril, hoping for the praise men give bluff, strong men. The piece argues that men in fact prize softness and calm in women, and that her act costs her the courtesy she might have claimed. Born to rich town parents, she meets country life at about fourteen, and the sketch follows from there.

Punch dated July 12, 1890, volume 99, opens with a Voces Populi sketch, "At the Military Exhibition," set in an avenue facing the arena. An unreasonable old lady arrives breathless with her grandson and her niece Maria, sure that a balloon is about to go up from that very spot.

No balloon can be seen, since leaves block the view, yet the crowd is proof enough for her. Maria slips away and returns with word of a fine open view elsewhere. The old lady, who had sworn she would not move to fare worse, at once agrees to go, saying it is all the same to her.

For July 19, 1890, Punch in volume 99 leads with "Our Booking-Office," where the Baron reviews Oscar Wilde's Dorian Gray, printed whole in one number of Lippincott's Magazine. A cartoon pairs Wilde's hero with the fat boy from Pickwick, each startling a respectable lady.

The Baron calls the romance weird and sensational, fit to be read in one late sitting by those who love dark tales, and in small doses by day for the rest. He sums up its plot of a portrait that bears the marks of sin while its sitter stays young. He faults the ending. He quotes Wilde's claim that the book is poisonous yet perfect.

Punch for July 26, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Modern Types," number sixteen, on the Hurlingham Girl, a portrait of a young woman of the smart London set. Her spirits, the essay says, run higher than her aims, which have drifted off almost out of sight.

She has been taught to scorn school learning: history, geography, classics, maths, and tongues all bore her. In their place she knows the season's fixtures by heart, from Sandown and Ascot to Hurlingham and Ranelagh. Rich parents help but are not required; what counts is a place in the world that thinks itself good, and a mother long used to being thwarted.

Volume 99 of Punch for July 5, 1890 opens with "Week by Week," a column of comic notes on Parliament, weather, and plain speech. The House of Commons had been restless for three weeks, and the column hunts for wild causes.

One politician hints at cave-men living in barrows under the House. The weather report dissolves into mock sums involving an earl's hat, a costermonger's buttons, and street cries in the Old Kent Road. A vestryman who voted down a pay rise is told by a road sweeper that his head would fetch twopence, a breach, the column notes, in that trade's usual fine manners.

Punch dated November 1, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Modern Types," number twenty-one, on the Average Undergraduate. The essay answers older men who claim that the young have lost all courtesy, modesty, and respect since their own golden youth.

Every age, it argues, finds its young men selfish and slangy, and the charge is at best half true. Follies exist, yet the mass of students at Oxford and Cambridge match their fathers in manliness and modesty. London shows youth at its worst, the piece warns, so the fair test is the average undergraduate at either university, not the loud few in town.

For November 15, 1890, Punch in volume 99 offers number six of Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, "Thrums on the Auld String," credited to the parody name J. Muir Kirrie. A note explains that the tale came with a glossary of Scots words that the magazine has no room to print.

Chapter one gathers its cast on a pig-sty at T'nowhead's farm, the old sow listening within and grunting now and then. The narrator, a dominie, drifts into memories of childhood on the brae. He recalls thick bread and thin butter. He tells how the balance shifts with age. All this comes before any plot has had time to start.

Punch for November 22, 1890, volume 99, opens with a cartoon of the actor-manager Bancroft, retired from the stage, tempted by General Booth's relief scheme after offering a thousand pounds to it. Short comic pieces follow, each built on a newspaper item.

One piece praises a kind storm off Beachy Head that broke men's ribs yet kindly landed them at Dover Hospital. Another marvels at a schoolmaster's advertisement: a teacher aged three, with ten years of practice, offers maths, science, French, drawing, piano, organ, and singing for twenty pounds a year, without a house.

Volume 99 of Punch for November 29, 1890 leads with number eight of Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, "Jonnie," credited to Dick Dody and written in French. The tale mashes two famous Dickens figures into one small hero, Jonnie Dombey, brought to Paris by a pretty Madame Copperfield.
